title: Designing a Thumbnail Annotation System: Text, Arrows, and Intent
description:
A thumbnail editor needs intent, not just controls

Font pickers and arrow buttons look like small interface features. In a thumbnail workflow, they can create a large usability problem: a creator can change five visual properties without ever stating what the text or arrow is supposed to do.

That produces a familiar review comment: “Make it pop.” It is hard to implement, hard to compare, and almost impossible to test.

For a public-UI design memo, it is useful to model these elements as annotations. A text treatment explains a short idea. An arrow marks a particular visual target. Both should have a reason that survives outside the editor.

Start with two explicit contracts

At the interface level, a text annotation needs a message and a readability condition. An arrow annotation needs a target and a direction. The following is a design proposal, not a claim about the implementation of any public tool:

type TextAnnotation = {
  content: string;
  role: "hook" | "context" | "number";
  weight: 400 | 700 | 900;
  spacing: number;
  separation: "none" | "outline" | "shadow";
};

type ArrowAnnotation = {
  style: "straight" | "curved" | "hand-drawn";
  targetLabel: string;
  rotation: number;
  contrastChecked: boolean;
};

The useful part is not the field list itself. It is the review question it enables. A reviewer can ask, “What is this arrow pointing at?” instead of “Does the red arrow look exciting enough?”

The public YouTube Thumbnail Font Generator provides a good visible example of why text needs several separate controls. Weight, size, letter spacing, fill color, outline, shadow, and background transparency affect different aspects of a phrase. Bundling them into one “boldness” slider would make comparison vague.

Why a one-change review loop matters

If a team changes typeface, size, outline, and copy at once, the final candidate might look better, but the team learns very little. The next thumbnail starts from the same uncertainty.

Use a controlled loop instead:

  1. Lock the short hook.
  2. Compare two weights at the intended feed size.
  3. Lock the better weight and compare spacing.
  4. Add outline or shadow only when the background requires separation.
  5. Record the reason for the selected variant.

The point is not to create an A/B-testing claim without data. It is to create a repeatable design review. A candidate can be rejected because the hook loses shape against a bright background, not because someone “doesn’t like it.”

Arrows should reference a meaningful target

An arrow has a simpler contract and a stricter failure mode. If the target does not carry the video’s story, the arrow is visual noise.

A Thumbnail Arrow Generator exposes straight, curved, and hand-drawn choices, with color and advanced controls. The visible page also describes an upload-or-blank-canvas workflow and a transparent PNG output. That gives a frontend team a helpful surface model: an arrow can be handled as an independently positioned layer rather than baked into the background.

The contract should still prevent two common failures:

  • an arrow ending on empty space;
  • several arrows competing to define the primary subject. 
function canExportArrow(arrow: ArrowAnnotation) {
  return arrow.targetLabel.trim().length > 0 && arrow.contrastChecked;
}

This is only illustrative logic. A production UI may use coordinates, masks, or object detection instead. The design principle stays the same: asking for a target label makes ambiguity visible before export.

State transitions worth discussing

An editor can keep the review trace lightweight:

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Brief
  Brief --> TextVariant: choose hook
  TextVariant --> ArrowVariant: confirm readable text
  ArrowVariant --> Preview: select target
  Preview --> TextVariant: revise one property
  Preview --> Export: promise is clear

The diagram is not an observed product architecture. It is a way to reason about when a creator has enough information to move forward.

The preview state is especially important. A high-resolution canvas encourages tiny fixes that disappear in a feed. A practical review asks what survives at small size: the primary object, the hook, and the arrow’s endpoint. If all three cannot be named quickly, reduce the number of active signals.

Interface acceptance checks

For a similar feature, I would start with these checks:

Area Acceptance question
Copy Is the hook short enough to compare as a single visual unit?
Text Does changing weight preserve the actual phrase?
Separation Is outline or shadow selected because of the background, not habit?
Arrow Can the creator name the highlighted target?
Preview Does the target remain visible at mobile feed size?
Fidelity Does the target appear in the actual video?

The last row cannot be verified by an editor alone. It needs human review against the footage. That limitation matters more than any styling control.

Thumbs AI is most useful in this framing as an ideation surface: a creator can compare typography and arrow direction after writing a clear visual brief. It does not replace a content review or prove an improvement in click-through rate.

The broader lesson for UI design is modest: expose expressive controls, but pair them with a question that makes each control accountable. “Which weight?” is a preference. “Can the viewer read this phrase before the scene overwhelms it?” is a product requirement.

title: Node.js Configure Email Notifications for Errors in Observability (4 Safe Steps)
description:
Short answer: treat email as a small delivery pipeline, not as an alert setting hidden inside your error tracker. Poll for new error events, keep a durable fingerprint for each notification, render the useful debugging context, and send through an email provider. For a nightly media data pipeline, this design makes rollback safer because the notification worker can be changed or stopped without changing the job that produced the errors.

Infrai is a reasonable retrieval adapter for this narrow workflow: its plain REST API lets a Node.js poller use fetch without an SDK install or client-library version to maintain. Email still belongs to an external provider, which keeps the notification boundary explicit.

The before picture is a cron job that fails somewhere in a batch and leaves an engineer searching logs the next morning. The after picture is a separate poller that retrieves error events, groups duplicate failures, and sends one readable message with the description, stack trace, and trace ID. There is a boundary, though: an error-tracking API can provide the evidence, but it does not automatically provide email routing.

What should the poller own?

The poller should fail loudly.

Keep the responsibilities narrow. The nightly pipeline owns work and rollback. The poller owns detection and notification. The email service owns delivery, suppression, and mailbox policy.

That split matters during a rollback. If a new pipeline release starts producing a burst of parsing errors, the release can be rolled back while the poller continues to report what happened. If the notification code itself is the problem, it can be paused without deleting the error evidence. One switch per concern is easier to reason about than a callback tangled into the batch process.

For this media workflow, a useful message contains the error description, a representative stack trace, the trace ID when one exists, and the time window that the poll covered. It should also say whether the message is a first report or a duplicate summary. A subject such as Nightly ingest: 12 new error events gives the recipient a decision before they open the message.

The poll interval is a policy choice, not a magic number. A short interval reduces discovery delay but increases duplicate suppression work. A longer interval is calmer and suits a batch that runs once a night, but it delays diagnosis. Start with a window that matches the pipeline's recovery decision, then test it by triggering an error deliberately.

For this exact boundary, Infrai fits the retrieval adapter: a Node.js process can call its plain REST API with fetch, without installing or versioning an SDK. It supplies error data, not the mailbox, so the useful design is Infrai plus the email service already approved by the team.

How do you configure email notifications without coupling the job?

Use one external email or notification service as the recipient. Do not make the data pipeline speak SMTP, call an error API, and decide retry policy in the same process. That creates three rollback surfaces for one failure path.

The smallest working flow is:

  1. Read new error data from the error-tracking API.
  2. Hash each returned event or group into a local notification key.
  3. Suppress keys already sent during the chosen window.
  4. Render the remaining records and send one message.

Here is a compact TypeScript poller. It uses the verified list and event routes, reads credentials from the environment, checks response status, honors Retry-After for rate limits, and writes only a fingerprint to its state file. The state file is intentionally separate from the nightly pipeline's output.

import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import nodemailer from "nodemailer";

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const statePath = process.env.ERROR_NOTIFY_STATE ?? ".error-notify-state.json";
const recipient = process.env.ERROR_EMAIL_TO;

if (!apiKey || !recipient) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and ERROR_EMAIL_TO are required");
}

const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function getJson(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/errors/list`, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 2 ** attempt * 1000;
      await sleep(delayMs);
      continue;
    }

    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Error API returned ${response.status}: ${detail}`);
  }

  throw new Error("Error API retry limit reached");
}

async function loadState(): Promise<Record<string, number>> {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(await readFile(statePath, "utf8")) as Record<string, number>;
  } catch {
    return {};
  }
}

const errors = await getJson();
const payload = JSON.stringify(errors);
const fingerprint = createHash("sha256").update(payload).digest("hex");
const state = await loadState();
const now = Date.now();
const notificationWindowMs = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

if (state[fingerprint] && now - state[fingerprint] < notificationWindowMs) {
  process.exit(0);
}

const transporter = nodemailer.createTransport({
  host: process.env.SMTP_HOST,
  port: Number(process.env.SMTP_PORT ?? "587"),
  secure: process.env.SMTP_SECURE === "true",
  auth: { user: process.env.SMTP_USER, pass: process.env.SMTP_PASSWORD },
});

await transporter.sendMail({
  from: process.env.ERROR_EMAIL_FROM,
  to: recipient,
  subject: "Nightly media pipeline: new error data",
  text: [
    "New error data was returned by the error tracker.",
    `Polled at: ${new Date(now).toISOString()}`,
    `Fingerprint: ${fingerprint}`,
    "Review the response below for descriptions, stack traces, and trace IDs.",
    payload,
  ].join("\n\n"),
});

state[fingerprint] = now;
await writeFile(statePath, JSON.stringify(state, null, 2));

The sample intentionally does not invent a filter parameter. The available discovery information does not declare filters for every search operation, so the poller's selection and suppression logic should be based on the response shape you have verified in your own deployment. If you need a specific group's event detail, use the documented /errors/events/{error_group_id} route after you have a real group ID; do not manufacture a query string and assume the server will interpret it.

There are two operational details worth keeping. First, the fingerprint is a notification guard, not an incident identity. A production version should keep enough structured state to distinguish event groups and expire old entries. Second, sending mail is itself a side effect. Give the poller a stable state location and make its schedule single-owner, or two overlapping workers can both send the same message before either writes state.

Which error tool fits this boundary?

The right comparison is about integration friction and rollback safety, not a feature-count race.

Option Setup and first useful result Where it fits Boundary to call out
Sentry Strong Node.js instrumentation and a mature issue workflow can get application errors visible quickly. Teams that want an opinionated error product with built-in alerting and triage workflows. Its SDK and hosted workflow become part of the application integration, so a rollback may include instrumentation changes as well as pipeline changes.
Datadog Broad logs, metrics, traces, and monitors are useful when a team already operates the platform. Organizations that want one commercial observability workspace and can standardize its agents, keys, and configuration. The breadth brings more configuration surface than a tiny nightly poller needs.
Rollbar Focused error grouping and developer notifications make it a practical specialist for application exceptions. Teams prioritizing exception triage and notification ergonomics over a general backend surface. A separate pipeline, email, or data service may still need its own credentials and integration path.
Infrai A plain REST API means a Node.js process can use fetch without installing or versioning an Infrai SDK. Its public discovery surface can also describe available capabilities and runnable examples before a key is used. A small poller that needs error data from an existing backend boundary and wants to keep the client surface to HTTP plus one key. It does not provide alert or notification routes, distributed trace or span-tree queries, source-map decoding, session replay, or heartbeat monitoring. Email remains an external service, and a poller remains necessary.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the error-data retrieval part of a Node.js notification worker when plain HTTP and one credential reduce integration friction, then keep email delivery in the provider that already owns your mailbox policy. This matters for rollback safety because the retrieval adapter can be replaced or disabled without rewriting the batch job. It is not the right choice if a specialist's built-in issue grouping, alert rules, source-map handling, or session replay is the requirement.

The comparison also changes if “the job ran” is the primary question. Error events cannot prove that a silent nightly job never started. Add a health-check or heartbeat service for that case. Likewise, a trace ID can help correlate logs, but it is not a substitute for a distributed trace query or a span tree.

What will break first in a real rollout?

The first objection is usually noise: “Won't bulk errors fill the inbox?” They can, unless the poller treats frequency filtering as a product requirement. Suppress repeated fingerprints within a window, group messages by error group when that identity is available, and send a count plus a representative trace rather than one email per event. Test the burst case, not only one clean exception.

The second objection is rollback: “What if the notification change causes a second incident?” Keep the notifier's state and credentials outside the pipeline release, deploy it independently, and test with a deliberately triggered error before enabling the nightly schedule. A useful test checks three things: the poll sees the event, the email includes debugging context, and a repeated poll does not create a duplicate message.

I started with the assumption that email was the feature to add. The more important feature is the boundary around it. Once retrieval, suppression, rendering, and delivery are separate, the team can change the mailbox provider or roll back the pipeline without losing the evidence that explains the failure. That is a small architecture, but it gives the next morning's engineer a clear first move.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the error tracking API guide and verify the response fields used by your poller before putting it on a schedule.

Further reading

  • Infrai error tracking and polling example
  • Sentry Node.js documentation
  • Datadog Node.js APM documentation
  • Rollbar Node.js documentation
  • Prometheus metric naming best practices

title: Backpropagation-free Deep Learning for Time-Series Classification
description:
arXiv:2610.41805v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Deep neural networks for time series classification (TSC) are trained almost exclusively by error backpropagation, which imposes update locking and the weight-transport problem. Backpropagation-free learning rules such as Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), Direct Random Target Projection (DRTP), and the diffusion-inspired NoProp relax these constraints but have been evaluated almost exclusively on 2D image benchmarks. We adapt these three learners to univariate TSC with 1D convolutional architectures and present the first systematic study of them across 112 datasets from the UCR time series archive, with one hyperparameter-optimized configuration per method. The optimized learners reach mean F1 scores of 0.76 to 0.79, below ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84). We propose an analysis framework that relates the per-dataset gap to InceptionTime to dataset properties and tests convolutional feature learning by replacing the flatten readout with global average pooling, measured as a difference-in-differences (DD) against a backpropagation control on the identical architecture. Intra-class temporal variability is the dataset property most consistently associated with the gap for all three learners (partial Spearman $\rho$ from $0.28$ to $0.40$). Pooling harms DFA and DRTP more than backpropagation (DD $-0.025$ and $-0.055$), consistent with near-random convolutional features, whereas NoProp tolerates pooling as backpropagation does (DD $+0.013$). Relative to backpropagation on the same architectures, DRTP reduces training floating-point operations (FLOPs) by 33% and trains faster only on series longer than about 700 time steps, DFA yields no computational reduction, and NoProp reduces peak memory by 38% at the cost of 48% longer training.

title: October 28, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI and vector search features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • The alloydb_scann extension supports four-level tree (4LT) ScaNN vector indexes on PostgreSQL 17 and later, providing support for tables with up to 10 billion vector rows. For more information, see Four-level ScaNN tree indexes.

  • 4LT ScaNN vector indexes support automatic index maintenance. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and Maintain vector indexes automatically.

  • You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy_limit parameter to relaxed_order. When enabled, the vector scan continues searching through additional leaf partitions until it finds enough results to satisfy the LIMIT clause of your query, improving recall on filtered searches. Additionally, you can enable this feature for parallel process scans by setting the scann.enable_parallel_satisfy_limit database flag to on. For more information, see ScaNN index reference and Best practices for tuning ScaNN indexes.

  • Vector assist simplifies the deployment and management of your AlloyDB vector workloads by helping you set up production-ready vector search capabilities, including embedding generation, query optimization, and index creation for vector types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). For more information, see Vector assist overview.

  • For AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances running PostgreSQL 17 and later, the maximum supported value for num_leaves when building ScaNN vector indexes is increased from 30,000,000 to 104,857,600. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and ScaNN index reference.

  • You can use the external_search_fdw extension to connect to external search clusters and query their data directly from your database using the following search sources:

    • Elasticsearch

    • Solr

    • OpenSearch

  • AlloyDB supports the rum extension for high-performance full-text search operations on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier. The rum extension extends standard GIN indexes by storing positional information directly in the index, letting you perform faster phrase searches and relevance ranking without accessing the table data. For more information, see Create and manage a RUM index.

Fixed

AlloyDB provides more accurate memory usage estimation and prevents out-of-memory (OOM) errors when you build a ScaNN four-level tree index. This feature is in Preview. This update improves the stability of index builds by enforcing memory limits and improving memory estimation under constrained conditions.

Feature

Identity and Access Management (IAM) group authentication is generally available (GA) for new and existing AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 15 and later. With IAM group authentication, you can manage database roles and privileges at the group level across primary instances and read pool instances, including first-time sign-ins directly to read pool instances. You can also preserve individual and IAM group user configurations when you migrate from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backup.

For more information, see IAM database authentication overview and Manage IAM authentication.

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating AlloyDB managed components. The fix to the certificate store is shipped in a new maintenance version that AlloyDB applies during scheduled maintenance, so you don't need to manually update AlloyDB managed instances. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance.

Depending on how you connect to AlloyDB, take the following actions:

  • If you use the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, then upgrade it to v1.17.2 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use the AlloyDB Language Connectors, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later).

Application Integration

Security

A Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability was discovered in the SubWorkflow task in Application Integration versions prior to September 11, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-074 security bulletin.

Feature

Application Integration agent skills

Application Integration agent skills are available in the public google/skills repository: application-integration-basics, application-integration-authoring, and application-integration-troubleshooting. AI coding agents that use these skills can help you set up Application Integration; build, publish, and run integrations through the REST API; and troubleshoot failed runs. For more information, see Application Integration agent skills and Build an integration with an AI agent.

Bigtable

Feature

You can configure Bigtable tables with microsecond timestamp granularity to capture and store high-frequency data. By supporting microsecond precision for cell timestamps, Bigtable helps you prevent data loss from write collisions in workloads with high event rates. This feature is generally available (GA) for instances in the Enterprise Plus edition. For more information, see Data type enforcement in Bigtable.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Google Cloud Migration Center
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/DiscoveryClient
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Group
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ImportJob
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/PreferenceSet
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/ReportConfig
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Settings
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Source

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

Database Migration Service for homogeneous SQL Server migrations now supports Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations in general availability (GA).

With DAG migrations, you can use gcloud CLI and Database Migration Service API to migrate databases from self-managed SQL Server Enterprise Edition instances directly to Cloud SQL for SQL Server over a private network connection. DAG migrations don't require exporting backup or transaction log files to Cloud Storage, and support post-promotion reverse replication for zero-data-loss failback.

For more information, see About Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations and Migrate from self-managed SQL Server using Distributed Availability Groups.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Managed replica indexes for Cloud SQL for MySQL are generally available (GA). This feature lets you automatically retain and restore secondary indexes on read replica instances when Cloud SQL re-creates a replica.

Previously, re-creating a read replica deleted custom secondary indexes because primary backups don't have replica-only index definitions. With managed replica indexes, Cloud SQL tracks secondary index metadata on the primary instance, replicates this metadata to read replicas, and automatically rebuilds secondary indexes after replica re-creation.

Managed replica indexes are supported on instances that are running Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 or later, Cloud SQL Enterprise edition or Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition, and maintenance version R20260726.00_05 or later.

For more information, see Read replica indexes overview and Create and manage read replica indexes.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (261001) is available. This image removes compromised CA certificates from the OS trust store. See the security bulletin for more details.

This image also adds support for running workload containers as a non-root user. Workload authors can require non-root execution with the tee.launch_policy.nonroot_container launch policy, and workload operators can enable it with the tee-nonroot-container metadata variable. For more information, see Non-root container execution.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Support for Brazil (br) region (GA with allowlist)

You can use the Gemini Enterprise app in the Brazil (br) in-country region with at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP) in region.

This location is available in GA with allowlist. To get access to this location for use with Gemini Enterprise, contact your Google account team.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Change

Use a single regional Agent Registry instance for Gemini Enterprise apps

For Gemini Enterprise apps, we recommend associating each Agent Gateway with a single regional Agent Registry instance in the same project and region as the gateway. Use the us-central1 registry for global and us apps, and the europe-west1 registry for eu apps.

This note updates the September 9, 2026 entry. For more information, see Register your agents and destination resources.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.17.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Support bundle diagnostics: Introduce cm support-bundle to collect environment metadata, configuration policies, health reports, and session logs into a compressed archive for streamlined troubleshooting.
  • Plain output mode: Add the persistent --plain flag (configurable via the CM_PLAIN environment variable or output.plain in config.yaml) to suppress decorative emojis, ANSI escape sequences, and Unicode borders for compatibility with screen readers and CI/CD log pipelines.
  • Dedicated exit codes for setup failures: Assign distinct exit codes (such as code 10 for credential issues) to configuration and authentication failures, preventing CI/CD pipelines from confusing environment setup issues with security findings.
  • Tailored CI/CD credential guidance: Provide environment-specific authentication guidance when running inside automated CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, and Jenkins instead of interactive login prompts.
  • Single-line JSONL statistics: Add the --jsonl flag to cm stats to output single-line JSON records with model and team attribution for seamless integration with Cloud Logging and log aggregation pipelines.
  • Granular sandbox and policy flags: Replace the overloaded --unrestricted flag with orthogonal flags (--sandbox=false) and configurable command policies to decouple container sandboxing from execution safety controls.
  • Sandbox configuration protections: Mount .git/hooks, .git/config, and .codemender read-only within writable execution sandboxes during cm fix and cm verify to prevent modifications to repository security policies.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a security warning when commands are executed with both sandbox isolation disabled and interactive approval skipped.
    • Enforced allowedRoots path boundaries across host discovery and remediation file operations to prevent traversal via dangling symlinks.
    • Supplied exact finding line ranges to remediation agents during cm fix to eliminate manual file scanning overhead.
    • Updated cm report import to properly treat findings without location data as file-level findings rather than defaulting to the first line.
    • Ensured cm session cancel routes requests to the session's original region regardless of local environment overrides.
    • Fixed finding status tracking in cm verify so unexploitable verdicts update the local state database rather than leaving findings open.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google SecOps

Announcement

Final shutdown of legacy managed BigQuery export datasets (chronicle-tla) for non-Enterprise+ customers

Following the March 26, 2025 deprecation announcement, Google SecOps is completing the final shutdown of legacy Google-managed BigQuery datasets and API keys associated with the chronicle-tla Google Cloud project:

  • What is changing: Data exports to legacy Google-managed BigQuery datasets under the chronicle-tla project are being permanently turned off, and the associated managed datasets and API keys are being decommissioned.
  • Who is impacted: This shutdown applies only to non-Enterprise+ customers still provisioned on legacy chronicle-tla Google-managed BigQuery datasets (including tenants whose temporary transition exceptions expired in September 2025). Enterprise+ customers and customers using Bring Your Own BigQuery (BYOBQ) exports to customer-managed Google Cloud projects are not impacted.
  • When: Decommissioning begins on October 28, 2026.
  • Action required: To retain BigQuery access to Google SecOps data, configure export to a customer-managed BigQuery project (BYOBQ) or contact your account team to upgrade to Enterprise+.

title: Vercel Ship 2026 recap
description:
For a decade, Vercel has shaped how the web is built. Now, we’re doing the same for agents. The companies that win the next decade will build on infrastructure designed for agents from the start, and thousands of people gathered across London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco to do just that at Vercel Ship 2026.

Agentic infrastructure

Guillermo Rauch (CEO, Vercel) opened Ship SF with a vision for the next era of software and agentic infrastructure: interfaces generated for any task in front of you, agents that reproduce and fix bugs autonomously, and software that takes production context and continuously improves itself.

Agentic infrastructure has three parts:

  • Vercel is where you build and deploy your own apps and agents. We give you every tool you need to build and run apps and agents in production, securely, at scale.

  • Vercel is where coding agents deploy that software. When you ask your harness where to deploy, you get Vercel, because Vercel is built for the way agents work. We have over 200 CLI commands that your agent can use to operate our entire platform.

  • Vercel itself is automated by agents. Vercel runs your apps in production, handling traffic, traces, observability, and anomalies. That data gives our agents the context they need to investigate autonomously, and then surface pull requests, not just alerts.

Agentic Infrastructure is for developers

In his opening keynote, Guillermo pointed to claims that AI would replace developers, then used Vercel's own data to prove them wrong. In the last 12 months:

  • The number of developers on Vercel has grown 3x

  • The number of new projects developers ship has doubled

  • The number of their agent-triggered deployments has increased 28x

"We built Vercel for developers," he said, "because they are the difference between a world full of slop and a world full of software worth using."

Backends on Vercel

In the next keynote, Malte Ubl (CTO, Vercel) showed how frontends, APIs, backend services, containers, MCP servers, and background workers can all run on Vercel, with support for custom runtimes and system dependencies.

He then announced that Python is now generally available on Vercel. Run FastAPI, Flask, or Django with standard CPython, PyPI dependencies, uv, and pyproject.toml. With Vercel Services, your frontend and backend deploy together, with previews of the full app.

Malte also introduced Vercel Daemons, now in public beta, for continuously running background workers. Deploy your code or container image, set the number of instances, and Vercel keeps them running and replaces them if they fail. Bring Celery, Dramatiq, Temporal workers, or your existing worker processes.

Vercel is for shipping agents

Tomo Occhino (CPO, Vercel) walked through the Agent Stack and its latest updates. The Agent Stack gives you everything you need to build, run, and scale agents in production.

  • Vercel Drives, now generally available for Sandbox, gives agents persistent workspaces. Code, data, and saved memory survive across runs, so you can change runtimes or compute without rebuilding the workspace.

  • eve, our open-source framework for building agents, now has persistent memory across sessions, extensions for installing tools and skills, and agent creation and deployment from the Vercel dashboard.

  • Vercel Connect is generally available, with more than 1,000 connectors. And MCP Events, now in public beta, lets agents respond to events from MCP servers. Connect handles subscriptions, renewals, and secure delivery.

  • AI Gateway now lets you set budgets for API keys, projects, individuals, and teams. You can also choose US-only inference to keep model processing in the United States, or enable Zero Data Retention so providers don’t retain your prompts or responses. He also introduced Vercel Token Pass, now in early access for Pro teams. Get $80 in GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 token credit for $30/month, with more models coming soon.

Vercel for enterprise

Jeanne Grosser (COO, Vercel) focused on what happens when everyone in a company can build. Engineers, marketers, analysts, and sellers need a common place to deploy, with controls over who can ship, who can access an app, which systems agents can use, and how much they can spend. Company building is now agent building.

Vercel for Enterprise brings those controls together, with two additions announced:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS is now generally available. Your application functions run in your own AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization for Vercel Connect launched in public beta. With supported services and your identity provider configured, agents can act on employees’ behalf without asking each person to authorize every connection separately.

Watch the full day of programming

Ship week in San Francisco

The rest of Ship SF brought more than 2,700 developers, founders, and technical leaders to the Palace of Fine Arts for talks, workshops, startup studio sessions, and agent labs.

Ship day sessions

  • Assaf Elovic from Ora showed how his team tests whether websites work for agents by sending real agents to sign up, integrate, and pay, then tracing every step. Ora built that fleet on eve and used Is-Agentic to score a live site.

  • Katelyn Lesse from Anthropic covered the work that starts after an agent is running: keeping it fast and improving its performance across thousands of production sessions with Claude Managed Agents on Vercel.

  • Prashant Ratanchandani from Meta Superintelligence Labs joined Tomo to discuss building products including Muse on Vercel.

  • Matt Lewis from Vercel and Mala Neti from Slack explained how we built v, our internal agent, around Vercel’s own data and working practices. Connect and Passport secure its access, and Slack gives employees a place to use it where their work already happens.

  • Max Peters from Adapta broke down the router behind Brazil’s largest generative AI platform. Built on AI Gateway, it serves 168 models through one integration, selects a model in under 200 milliseconds, and handles more than three million requests a day with automatic failover and per-user budgets.

  • Sarah Sachs from Notion and Malte Ubl discussed how AI is changing the software teams build and the context agents need to do useful work.

  • Olawale Oladehin from AWS walked through production patterns for agents on AWS and Vercel, from self-correcting agents to multi-agent orchestration, and how BYOC lets teams run application functions within their own AWS environment.

  • Philip Miseldine and Sophia Levens from SAP showed how SAP is using v0, eve, and json-render to build generative interfaces, with a focus on consistent design and government requirements.

  • Aaron Brown and Arty Vohmincevs from Mercor explained how hundreds of employees build internal tools without losing control of access or spending. Apps inherit a managed identity layer, while AI Gateway gives the team visibility into model usage and budgets.

  • Yury Izrailevsky from ClickHouse traced the company’s path from an open-source analytics database to a platform spanning observability, AI engineering, and managed Postgres. His focus was how open source earns developer trust and helps infrastructure expand into new workloads.

Panel: Fast AI

Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, the company behind Jev, and Andrew Feldman, founder and CEO of Cerebras, joined Vercel for a discussion on model reliability, latency, and cost. The panel brought together the model and hardware sides of fast inference, from specialized models to wafer-scale chips.

Closing fireside with Tobi Lütke

Guillermo sat down with Tobi Lütke, CEO of Shopify, for "The Third Customer," a conversation about building for a world where agents research, compare, and buy products on people’s behalf.

Guillermo Rauch: What excites you about agentic commerce?

Tobi Lütke: It’s early, but the opportunity goes beyond handling purchases people already make. Think about project-based commerce: planning Halloween decorations for your house, or a 3D-printing project with your kids, then ordering everything to arrive before the weekend. Agents can help people follow through on things they otherwise wouldn’t have had time to do.

Guillermo Rauch: Where does that leave traditional storefronts?

Tobi Lütke: There’s still room for exceptional shopping experiences. A distinctive, thoughtful storefront can grow, just as a well-executed boutique can. The businesses that will struggle are the ones offering an undifferentiated experience. Quality and originality still matter.

Guillermo Rauch: How is AI changing engineering at Shopify?

Tobi Lütke: We now think of ourselves as verification engineers, building harnesses and acceptance tests that make changes verifiable. We’re rewriting our storefront renderer from Ruby to Rust, where we can compare the output byte for byte before switching over. We also celebrate simplification and code deletion. At a company hackathon, our internal Slack agent, River, topped the code-deletion leaderboard by a wide margin.

Guillermo Rauch: What should developers in this room go build?

Tobi Lütke: Explore the catalog APIs. They give you access to products from Shopify merchants, so you can build new commerce experiences without first recruiting both sides of a marketplace. Product discovery, recommendations, and curation are real business opportunities. People will pay for tools that help them find what they need.

Ship week San Francisco

Fast Forward hackathon

The day before Ship, Vercel and Meta hosted Fast Forward, with support from Shopify and Neon Postgres. Builders worked across three tracks: agents that keep working after you step away, multimodal apps, and immersive VR experiences.

Founder dinners, executive conversations, and Partner Day

Founders, partners, and enterprise leaders gathered throughout the week for dinners, Partner Day, and conversations on building with AI. The executive program focused on what happens when anyone with an idea can build, and how do you govern what ships.

Ship 2026 in London

Ship day keynotes

  • Tomo introduced the Agent Stack, bringing model access, durable execution, sandboxed compute, and messaging together for production agents.

  • Hedi launched Vercel Connect in public preview, giving agents scoped access to external tools and data without storing long-lived provider credentials in environment variables.

  • Shar demoed eve, our open-source agent framework. Each agent lives in a directory, with instructions in Markdown and tools in TypeScript. Durable execution, approvals, subagents, and evals are already wired in.

  • Jeanne introduced Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents, including Vercel Passport in public beta for protecting internal apps with your identity provider, and Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS in private beta.

Ship week London

Our first Ship outside the U.S. ran five days of events leading into the keynote, and an ice cream truck spent the week working its way across the city.

Built in London hackathon

Two hundred builders shipped agents on Codex and Vercel in a hackathon with OpenAI. Three projects stood out. Stella hunts down unclaimed grants for London SMBs, Oscar is a co-pilot that sharpens your prompts before you send them to a model, and Phone Jail blocks distractions and roasts you when you reach for your phone anyway.

Media, Founder, VC, and CTO dinners

Reporters traded story ideas over a media dinner. Twelve founders talked through the future of AI in EMEA at a VC dinner. And a dozen CTOs from teams including Marks & Spencer and Currys went off the record on what it takes to build and scale agents in the enterprise.

Day Zero builder night

Day Zero, the day before the keynote, turned into a 400-person builder night. Enterprise teams Mentimeter, Okta, and MongoDB joined Vercel in a packed room alongside partners DeepMind, ElevenLabs, and Cursor.

AI Social Club

A 160-deep waitlist formed for Malte's talk A New Stack for a New Era of Software, followed by Guillermo and Deliveroo's Will Shu's chat on building the agentic enterprise.

Ship day sessions

  • André Balleyguier from Anthropic showed Claude Managed Agents on Vercel, where Anthropic hosts the agent loop while every command the agent runs executes inside a Vercel Sandbox you own, keeping its filesystem, processes, and network egress in your environment.

  • Tomas Jansson from Currys/Elkjøp showed how his team evolved a Nordic retailer's ecommerce stack from storefronts toward shopping agents in three phases, anchored by a Next.js migration that cut time to first byte by 40%. The end state is one where customer intent replaces navigation.

  • Matan Kushner from Vercel broke down how Vertex, Vercel's support agent, now automates 91% of support tickets and saves 5,000 engineer-hours a month without degrading as its context grows.

  • Jas Sagoo and Sam Bellen from Auth0 made the case that getting an agent into production depends more on identity than on model quality. They demoed four standards-based identity patterns on the Vercel AI SDK, Token Vault, CIBA approvals, agents as first-class principals, and on-behalf-of delegation, so every action is scoped and traces back to a human decision instead of a shared API key.

  • Abhi Sivasailam from Vercel went deep into d0, Vercel's internal data agent built on eve, which runs analyses in a sandbox and now gets 45% of its questions from other agents, rather than people.

  • Romain Huet from OpenAI showed developers how to ship faster by delegating whole tasks to Codex Cloud Agents on Vercel, and made the case that as agents become users of your product, you design for agent experience with scoped API keys, markdown docs, and plugins.

  • Michał Pierzchała from Callstack demoed a QA agent that runs mobile apps on real devices, explores user flows on its own, and posts screenshots, recordings, and logs to pull requests on every PR.

  • Alex Holt from ElevenLabs paired the ElevenLabs Speech Engine with the AI SDK to build a voice agent that can reply in under a second, take interruptions mid-sentence, and switch language mid-conversation.

  • Malavika Balachandran Tadeusz from Vercel showed the mechanics of how software can ship itself, extending the agent loop past development into testing, observability, and experimentation with primitives like Vercel Flags and Skills.

Panel: Agents in production

Jeanne Grosser, COO of Vercel, moderated a panel on taking agentic workloads from prototype to production with some of the EU's top CTOs and AI leaders from frontier labs. A few highlights:

Arthur Viegers (Cursor): Autonomy should track risk, and the better an agent can assess the risk of a change, the more you can let it run on its own. Shopify and Amplitude already auto-review and merge 60-70% of low-risk PRs with no developer time, while a two-line change to authentication still goes to a human.

André Balleyguier (Anthropic): To decide what an agent can do on its own, judge each action by how reversible it is and how large its blast radius is, then contain it accordingly, for example inside a self-hosted sandbox. As you grant more autonomy, observability and evals become the things that keep it safe.

Ryan den Rooijen (Currys): The predicted death of stores never arrived, and Currys leads its markets by betting on humans. The open question for agentic commerce is which shopping journeys customers want an agent to handle and which they still want a person for.

Nicolas Le Pallec (AKQA): AI-native customer experience replaces navigation with intent. Reaching it takes three layers: a way to capture true customer intent, a brand brain that stores brand and product data for AI systems to retrieve, and generative UI that composes pages on the fly instead of serving static ones.

Fireside chat with Harry Stebbings

The day ended with a fireside chat between Guillermo and Harry Stebbings from 20VC. Below are excerpts from the lightning round at the end of the discussion.

Guillermo Rauch: What are the attributes of a founder you want to back?

Harry Stebbings: The profile has changed completely. It used to be a sales-led CEO who could fundraise and grow customers, where personality and sales carried the company. Now I want an engineering- and product-led founder.

Guillermo Rauch: Can you teach someone to become a voice for their industry?

Harry Stebbings: You can, but it's hard. You have to do it for six months straight. It's a muscle you build, and you have to commit to it every day and every hour.

Guillermo Rauch: When anyone can produce content and software, how do you stand out?

Harry Stebbings: You come up with a new format, a new intro, a new way to tell the story and shape the work. The content itself has shifted too. We used to do shows about leadership and hiring, and nobody cares about that anymore. What lands now is a founder and AI. Those are the two things.

Ship 2026 in Berlin

The Berlin event opened at the Old Mint, “Alte Münze”, where coins were once hammered by hand, before machine automation took over. It is also where the JavaScript logo was born, and where Guillermo Rauch (CEO) met Malte Ubl (CTO) for the first time at JSConf EU.

Software is moving the same way, from hand to machine, and Vercel is paving the way for building in the agentic era. Over 500 people gathered from across Germany to do just that at Ship 2026 in Berlin.

Ship day sessions

  • Suyog Rao from Vercel announced AI SDK 7. The AI SDK is now downloaded over 16 million times a week. Version 7 turns it into a toolkit for building and running agents that reason, call tools, run across many turns, and work across files and sandboxes, all behind one provider-agnostic interface with no lock-in.

  • Philip Miseldine from SAP showed how the company rebuilt its design system to be composable, so people and agents assemble interfaces from the same parts, with v0 running across its build, deliver, and decide stages.

  • Building with AI SDK 7 brought three speakers on stage. Lars Grammel, the primary engineer behind the update, went deep on the release, with the new harness layer and generation beyond text as the headline additions. Carsten Høyer from AKQA demoed the Starbucks ChatGPT app as a "generative store" that composes branded results from Starbucks' own products and visual identity, flipping the funnel so customers pull the brand into their conversation instead of visiting its site. Stephen Batifol from Black Forest Labs showed where the Flux image models fit in an agentic stack: sub-second generation and editing today, heading toward real-time generation and world models.

  • Arthur Viegers from Cursor showed how coding agents move from autocomplete to working across an entire codebase on their own.

Panel: CTOs on AI and growth

Chris Williams (Head of Forward Deployed Engineering, Vercel) moderated a CTO panel on building and scaling as the cost of creation trends toward zero. A few highlights:

Sven Rosemann (Flaconi): AI won't fix a broken business model, so the work is still operational excellence. He compares ecommerce to a decathlon, you win by being top-tier across every discipline at once. What's changing is discovery, which is moving into chat, so Flaconi is investing in the data foundation that makes its catalog retrievable by agents, betting that buying and checkout eventually happen there too.

Tjaž Silovsek (Astra AI): venture funding is no longer a prerequisite. For many ideas, you ship, find distribution, and iterate instead. Astra reached 10 million users and $25M ARR fully bootstrapped, with a small team kept fast by a stable foundation and agents given a lot of autonomy while kept as safe as possible.

DACH Partner Award

Vercel presented its first-ever DACH Partner Award to Valtech, for the exceptional impact and delivery, strategic thinking and team enablement it brought to clients. The presentation also thanked the event's sponsors: Auth0, Storyblok, Cursor, SAP, Accenture Song, Blazity, and JVM.

Ship 2026 in New York

Ship week New York

Ship NYC was the most in-demand of any stop yet with over 3,000 people registered. Founders, partners, leaders, and builders gathered for five days of hackathons, executive receptions, workshops, and more, with Ship day at the center.

Built in NYC

The week opened with Built in NYC, a hackathon co-hosted by Vercel and Anthropic alongside Sentry, Auth0, Resend, and Supabase. More than one hundred people joined us for an afternoon of building and demoing agents on Vercel.

VC, CTO, and VIP dinners

Jeanne DeWitt Grosser and Nick Bogaty gathered the leaders shaping AI-native development at a VIP reception. Founders traded notes on the future of agents over a VC dinner. At Per Se, Guillermo, Jeanne, Tom, and Malte took CTOs and CIOs for a closed-door conversation on where traditional architectures start to break in the agent era.

AI Social Club

AI executives and senior leaders assembled at Moss for a fireside chat led by Tom Occhino with William Anderson (CTO, Bloomberg Media), Jeremy Bunting (VP Engineering, Serhant), and Ali Patterson (Staff Design Program Manager, DoorDash). They discussed what's working, what's not, and where agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Ryan Coyne from SERHANT. walked through S.MPLE, a real estate agent built on Vercel that drove a 144% increase in commission income in its first full year.

  • Brandon Bloom from Brex gave its expense-audit agent a bash-only shell so it manages its own context instead of drowning in tool responses, cutting tool calls and token usage by 75%.

  • Ari Schapiro and Chris Sev from Auth0 demoed how to give an agent scoped, revocable power instead of a master key, with standards-based identity patterns like Token Vault and out-of-band human approval, live on the Vercel AI SDK.

  • Jenny Wang from Alta and Maxwell Osborne from PUBLIC SCHOOL NYC showed how Alta's AI styling app runs on Vercel, generating an avatar a second and 250M+ outfits so far. Together they built a custom version for PUBLIC SCHOOL's New York Fashion Week relaunch.

  • Charlton Roberts from FLORA showed three creative-production workflows running on Vercel Sandboxes. They collapsed 18 bespoke tools into two by letting the agent run and write its own code against the AI SDK.

  • Prasad Wangikar from Stripe broke down how to give agents spending power and capture agent-driven revenue using emerging protocols like MCP, UCP, and x402 for the machine-to-machine economy.

  • Shaown Nandi from AWS discussed how Vercel and AWS work together, with native AWS databases and OpenSearch available in the Marketplace and models through the AI Gateway, proven out by The Weather Company's 350M+ users.

Panel: Internal apps and agents in production

Jeanne moderated a panel on building and deploying internal agents with technical leaders on who should build, what governance looks like, and how teams can move from experiment to production. A few highlights:

Andy Martin (MJH Life Sciences): The way to win the shadow-IT battle is to constrain the stack and stay permissive inside it. His AI Accelerator trains non-engineers, marketers, and early-career staff to build internal apps on a deliberately tight stack of Claude Code, Vercel, and GitHub, with ephemeral preview deployments as the guardrail. As he put it, "If it becomes the Department of No, you will have people working around you."

Greg Chan (SERHANT): The cleanest way to structure agents is to mirror a human software team. Product-manager agents write requirements in Linear, engineering agents generate specs, and build-and-QA agents take it from there, so engineers become leads running multiple streams. To keep output safe, SERHANT runs evals for hallucination and compliance, including a custom model for Fair Housing Act rules.

Victor Oliveros (ZoomInfo): Embedding v0 inside your own product lets your customers build their own workflows. At ZoomInfo, 40,000+ of them do, turning the voice of the customer into a pull request. Agents analyze recorded calls and open PRs, so the product team decides what ships instead of synthesizing feedback. They pair Vercel's deployment guardrails with ZoomInfo's context-graph permissions, so each agent only touches data its user can see.

Fireside chat: Building agentic storefronts

Tom sat down with Vanessa Lee (VP of Product, Shopify) to discuss where commerce and software go next. Below are highlights:

Tom Occhino: Vercel and Shopify have shipped something new together. What is it?

Vanessa Lee: We boiled Hydrogen down to the parts of commerce that are genuinely hard (analytics, optimistic cart UI, variants) and made them work with any framework. So if you're on Next.js on Vercel, Shopify's commerce primitives now drop in, with an integration in the Vercel Marketplace. Read more here.

Tom Occhino: You also opened the Catalog API. What does it unlock?

Vanessa Lee: There's never been a good open product-search API. We have billions of products and millions of merchants, so we built one, the only widespread shopping API, made for commerce. It lets anyone embed shopping anywhere. Someone in my Toronto running group used v0 to build a site with a leaderboard and the weather, and the Catalog API surfaced products from nearby stores. Commerce stops being a destination and becomes part of what you build.

Tom Occhino: Shopify and Vercel both obsess over reducing friction. Why does that matter so much?

Vanessa Lee: Early on, Tobi's insight was that tools shape the market. The TAM was never limited by demand, it was limited by how hard the tools were to use. Make building easier and more people build. There's resourcefulness in the general population that's just untapped, and lowering the friction is what releases it.

Closing keynote with Ivan Zhao

We closed out Ship in New York with a conversation between Guillermo Rauch and Ivan Zhao (CEO, Notion). A few highlights:

Guillermo Rauch: You've started telling designers to design for the API first and the UI last. Why?

Ivan Zhao: Because your next customer isn't only a human, it's a human and an agent, and agents are blind. They don't see your interface, they read your semantics and your API. The most enduring software has always been a data structure anyway, the spreadsheet, or our block, a data structure that happens to have a UI. So design the structure and the meaning first, the interface last. A great tool for developers turns out to be a great tool for agents.

Guillermo Rauch: Vercel and Notion are both aggressively model-agnostic, Switzerland in the model wars. Why?

Ivan Zhao: The models leapfrog each other every few weeks, so picking a side is a losing game. We route automatically by the intelligence a task needs, frontier models for coding, smaller and faster ones for support and summarization. What excites me most is that as more use cases stop needing frontier intelligence, you can shape smaller models to your product and win back speed and cost. And speed creates discontinuities, a model five times faster can change the kind of interface you'd even design.

Guillermo Rauch: When a billion knowledge workers are agents, how does that reshape us?

Ivan Zhao: We can't fully see it, and that's the point. First-order effects are easy, the iPhone was an iPod plus a phone plus a browser. The second-order effects are the ones that surprise you, like what social media did to teenagers. We shape our tools, and then our tools shape us. With software that can think, the second-order effects are the ones we won't predict.

Guillermo Rauch: Taste or velocity, keep one.

Ivan Zhao: Taste. It's the distillation of wisdom from a lot of shots on goal.

Ship 2026 in Sydney

The Sydney event opened at Machine Hall, a 1930s electrical substation that ran the city's trams and wharves for half a century. Over 200 people gathered there to build for the agentic era at Ship Sydney.

Ship week Sydney

The week kicked off with the AI SYD meetup, where developers, AI engineers, and the Sydney technical community joined for an evening of lightning talks and networking. At the AI Social Club, senior leaders gathered at Shell House for a talk from Malte Ubl and a fireside with Suyog Rao and David Hyman (Founder, monō ai) on how agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Belen Garcia Fava and Vivek Katial from Heidi Health showed how their team ships fast in a regulated space with agents and Vercel, and made the case that trust is engineered, not granted.

  • Robin Yoong from Cursor created an eve agent by voice alone. Three models coded in parallel, and a spoken approval shipped it to Vercel.

  • Nonny Bell (Startup Manager APAC, Vercel) moderated a panel with Matthew Blode (AI Engineer, Linktree), Aarush Issar (GM AI Engineering, Auto & General Australia), and Leonardo Borges (Chief Engineer Gen AI, CommBank) on how their teams are adopting AI agents in production.

  • JJ Lecocq (Sales Director AUNZ, Vercel) led a discussion on how organizations are reshaping people, culture, and structure for AI.

Ship what's next

Thanks for joining us for Ship 2026 in London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco. We'll see you in May for Ship 2027.

title: The LXD and MicroCloud Vulnerability That Turns a Public Certificate Into Host Root
description:
The LXD and MicroCloud Vulnerability That Turns a Public Certificate Into Host Root

The LXD and MicroCloud vulnerability disclosed by Canonical on October 28, 2026 lets an attacker authenticate as a trusted client without ever holding that client's private key, a flaw rated CVSS v4.0 10.0, the maximum possible. All it takes is network access to the management API and the trusted client's public certificate, which, unlike a private key, was never meant to be secret in the first place.

Jump to why a public certificate was enough if you only want the mechanism.

What LXD and MicroCloud Actually Got Wrong

LXD and MicroCloud, Canonical's tools for running and clustering Linux containers and virtual machines, authenticate clients to their HTTPS management API using mutual TLS. Ostorlab's technical writeup traces the bug to a single mismatch between what a TLS handshake proves and what the authentication code assumed it proved: a handshake only confirms the client holds the private key for the first certificate in its chain, the leaf. Everything else in that chain is client-controlled and unverified.

The vulnerable code looped over every certificate the client presented and checked each one against the trust store individually, rather than checking only the verified leaf. An attacker could therefore build a certificate chain out of their own leaf certificate plus the public certificate of someone the server already trusted, and the server would authenticate them as that trusted identity. Canonical's advisory confirms the resulting access follows the impersonated identity's actual permissions.

Why a Public Certificate Was Enough

This is the detail that makes the flaw worse than it first sounds. A public certificate is, by design, not a secret. The Hacker News reported that successful exploitation requires only HTTPS API reachability and a trusted client's public certificate, and security practitioners responding to that disclosure pointed out exactly where those certificates tend to live: in ~/.config/lxc, in CI runner configuration, in Ansible repositories, and in backups, none of which are typically treated as sensitive.

Canonical's own advisory goes further for MicroCloud specifically: an attacker who intercepts the public certificate of a node joining a cluster can later authenticate as that member. The resulting access, per Canonical, can include full control over containers, virtual machines, and storage volumes, and if the impersonated identity carries administrative rights, root execution on the host itself. An unrestricted LXD client is, functionally, root on the hypervisor.

The Part That Limits Real-World Exposure

A default, non-clustered LXD installation does not bind to a network port at all. It listens on a local Unix socket, gated by POSIX group membership rather than TLS, and the vulnerable HTTPS listener only activates once an administrator explicitly runs lxc config set core.https_address <ip>:<port>, typically on TCP 8443. The attack surface, in other words, exists specifically for clustered and remotely managed deployments, which is exactly where LXD and MicroCloud are most often used for anything resembling production infrastructure.

As of November 1, 2026, Ostorlab's advisory states no exploitation is known and the flaw is not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. That is a meaningfully different risk posture than an actively exploited bug, but a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass with no public proof-of-concept yet is not evidence of safety, it's a head start that won't last.

This Is the Second Time This Exact Check Failed

The CyberSec Guru's analysis draws a direct line to CVE-2024-6156, an earlier, lower-severity bug in the same authentication logic, limited at the time to PKI mode. CVE-2026-112816 is, in the analyst's words, "the same authentication boundary failing in a much more serious way," because the underlying flaw, trusting unverified certificate chain elements, was never fully closed the first time. The fix in Incus 7.6.0 and Canonical's patched LXD builds is specific: resolve identity from the first verified certificate in the chain only, after confirming it isn't empty, and stop looping over the rest.

What This Means If You Run Clustered Virtualization

Our verdict: patch immediately if you run LXD or MicroCloud with a network-exposed management API, and audit your trust store regardless, because the public certificates that grant trust are sitting in places, CI configs, Ansible repos, backups, that most teams don't treat as sensitive. A CVSS 10.0 score with no known exploitation yet is a narrow window, not a pass.

This bug doesn't tell you that clustering virtualization platforms is inherently unsafe. It tells you something narrower and more useful: when a single management API authenticates access to every container, VM, and storage volume in a cluster, the correctness of one authentication function becomes the entire security boundary for everything behind it. That's a structural property of centralized cluster control planes, not a one-off coding mistake, and it doesn't go away once this specific CVE is patched.

  • If you run an LXD or MicroCloud cluster with core.https_address set: patch to the fixed versions now (LXD 6.10.1, 5.21.9, 5.0.11, or 4.0.15 depending on track; MicroCloud 3.4.1 or 2.1.5; Incus 7.6.0), and until you confirm the patch landed, restrict the management listener to trusted hosts only.
  • Audit who holds your trust store's public certificates. They aren't secrets by design, which is exactly why they end up in places nobody locks down, and this bug shows that's a mistake.
  • If your own infrastructure relies on a single cluster-wide authentication boundary for isolation, this is a reminder to ask what happens when that one boundary has a bug, not whether it will.

FAQ

What is the LXD and MicroCloud vulnerability?

CVE-2026-112816 is a CVSS v4.0 10.0 authentication bypass in Canonical's LXD and MicroCloud, disclosed October 28, 2026. It lets an attacker with network access to the HTTPS management API authenticate as any trusted client by presenting that client's public certificate, without needing its private key, because the vulnerable code checked every certificate in a client's chain against the trust store instead of verifying only the cryptographically proven leaf certificate.

Can this vulnerability give an attacker root access to the host machine?

Yes, under specific conditions. Canonical's advisory states that if the identity an attacker impersonates has administrative privileges, the resulting access can include root execution on the host, because an unrestricted LXD client has functional control over the hypervisor. This requires the impersonated identity to already be privileged; impersonating a low-privilege client does not by itself grant host root.

Is the LXD and MicroCloud vulnerability being actively exploited?

As of November 1, 2026, no exploitation has been publicly confirmed and the flaw is not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, according to Ostorlab's advisory. No public proof-of-concept has been linked by the cited vendor advisories either. That status can change quickly for a bug this severe, so patching now rather than waiting for confirmed exploitation is the safer posture.

What We Checked Before Publishing

We pulled Canonical's own security advisory, Ostorlab's technical breakdown of the authentication flow, The Hacker News' disclosure summary, and The CyberSec Guru's historical comparison to CVE-2024-6156. We were not able to independently verify Canonical's internal timeline for when the flawed trust-loop logic was first introduced, so we've reported what the public advisories confirm rather than speculating about how long the window of exposure actually was.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud: every Cube runs its own kernel behind a per-cube jailer sandbox, and we don't put a single cluster-wide management API in the critical path between a certificate and host root. That doesn't make centralized cluster control planes wrong for every use case, but it's a different trade-off than the one LXD and MicroCloud make, and this CVE is a clear look at what that trade-off can cost when one authentication function gets it wrong. More debugging stories at debugly.dev.
