It is available in English, French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Some features may not be available in all regions or languages.
  • Siri AI is currently unavailable in the EU in iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS. Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward.

title: Storing email bodies without building a data swamp
description:
Email is the largest unstructured dataset most products own, and the default approach — dump the whole raw message into a database column — becomes a problem at around a hundred thousand messages.

Split the record

Store the metadata in the database: message id, thread id, participants, subject, timestamps, direction, and a pointer to the body. Store the raw message and the rendered parts in object storage keyed by message id. Listing an inbox then reads small rows, and opening one message reads one object.

Skew the schema

Bodies are large, variable, and rarely queried. Metadata is small, uniform, and queried constantly. Putting them in the same table means every index carries the weight of the part you never search.

Retention has to be per mailbox

Support conversations and agent inboxes have different legal expectations. If retention is a global setting, someone will eventually ask you to delete one conversation and you will have to write a migration instead of a delete.

The detail that makes search work

Index the extracted text, not the HTML. Indexing raw HTML puts tag names in your search results and multiplies the index size for no benefit. Extract once at ingest, store the extracted text next to the metadata, and search that.

Volanea keeps message metadata queryable and bodies addressable, so inbox listing stays fast as a mailbox grows.

title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
description:
Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments.

We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox. Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off.

Persisting state with a drive

Create a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI:

Or from the Sandbox SDK:

In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it.

The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive.

Sharing state across sandboxes

Agents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. If one agent builds a dataset on a drive, other agents can mount read-only copies to analyze the data or generate reports without rebuilding the dataset. They use the shared files as input and save their results separately.

Agents can also fork a drive to explore different approaches independently. Each fork starts with the drive’s contents and provides its own writable workspace. Agents can try different transformations of the dataset in parallel without changing the original or affecting one another. Forks don’t merge back into the original drive.

Forking is generally available.

Get started

Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on all plans.

Drives default to 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, with up to 16 TiB available. See the documentation for configuration, snapshots, and limits, or the changelog for what changed at GA.

title: Reproducing, disclosing, and fixing the libheif vulnerability with Hacktron and the maintainers
description:
In August 2026, Hacktron reported what looked like a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Next.js image optimization. Their investigation found that the vulnerable code was not in Next.js itself, but upstream in libheif, an AVIF image decoder used by Next.js, ImageMagick, WordPress, sharp, and much of the web.

Shortly after Hacktron notified us, we worked with them to reproduce the RCE against a current Next.js build and disclose it to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. We then deployed a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and started working with the maintainers on a fix.

The dependency chain

Next.js image optimization lets applications resize and optimize images through the <Image> component (next/image). For AVIF images, the image-processing dependency chain is as follows:

  • <Image> invokes /_next/image,

  • /_next/image calls sharp

  • sharp calls libvips

  • libvips uses libheif to decode the image

That meant the vulnerable code was not in Next.js, but it was still reachable through Next.js image optimization. A malicious AVIF image sent to the image optimization endpoint would invoke libheif through sharp and libvips.

As such, one obvious mitigation was to disable AVIF optimization in Next.js. Malicious AVIF images would then stop at the image optimization endpoint instead of being passed through sharp and libvips to libheif. The exploit would not propagate upstream.

However, only mitigating Next.js, without an upstream fix, posed a disclosure problem.

Disclosing the vulnerability and coordinating the upstream fix

After we worked with Hacktron to successfully reproduce the issue, we rolled out a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and reached out to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif to disclose the vulnerability and begin working on a fix.

Here is the timeline:

  • August 11-12: Hacktron reported the issue to Vercel; Hacktron and Vercel reproduced the RCE with a working proof of concept.

  • August 13: Vercel applied a platform mitigation through its Image Optimization Service.

  • August 19: The Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and began coordination across sharp, libvips, and libheif.

  • August 24: Next.js informed its security partners.

  • August 25: Next.js published a security release that disabled AVIF optimization.

The Vercel security team contacted the maintainers of sharp and libvips by email, and opened coordination with libheif through a GitHub Security Advisory. Hacktron had also submitted vulnerability and exploit details to libheif. On August 19, the Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and aligned on the path forward across sharp, libvips, and libheif. The libheif maintainer continued remediation through Hacktron’s GitHub Security Advisory.

On August 24, Next.js informed its security partners of the libheif vulnerability and its impact on Next.js (partner notifications are a routine part of Next.js’ security release process).

On August 25, six days after the August 19 meeting, the libheif maintainer released v1.23.2, which remediated the RCE.

Vercel and Next.js mitigations

Securing Vercel and its customers was straightforward: all Next.js image optimization requests on Vercel go through a central Image Optimization Service. Therefore, we disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in that central service. Any incoming AVIF images were not passed to libheif for decoding and RCE was not possible on Vercel.

Protecting self-hosted applications required a Next.js release. On August 25, Next.js published a security release that had originally been planned to address a separate issue. After coordinating an upstream fix, we bundled the AVIF mitigation into that release and shipped it a day earlier than planned. The release disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in Next.js; given that the patched libheif release was still propagating downstream, this was the most timely option. We also published a security advisory to communicate the issue’s severity.

Our commitment to making the web more secure

The volume of OSS vulnerabilities discovered continues to increase, and the numbers are overwhelming:

  • In 2026, the CVE program has published more than 35,000 CVEs.

  • Private vulnerability reports on GitHub grew from 500 per week in January to 3,000 per week in May.

  • GitHub also reported 1,560 reviewed advisories in May 2026, the highest monthly volume in the advisory database’s history.

As LLMs accelerate vulnerability research, we expect to see more upstream vulnerabilities like the libheif RCE surface across the OSS ecosystem. There have been a higher number of Next.js security releases in recent months, and we expect that trend to continue as we mitigate new vulnerabilities that both we and the research community uncover.

We are committed to proactively finding vulnerabilities before attackers, responsibly disclosing everything we find, and collaborating with researchers and maintainers on fixes.

Credit

Thanks to Hacktron for responsibly disclosing the AVIF vulnerability, working with us to reproduce the issue, and coordinating with the upstream maintainers through remediation.

We also want to thank the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. Their work on the upstream fix made coordinated remediation possible across the image processing dependency chain.

We work with a talented set of researchers to secure Next.js and other open source frameworks through Vercel's Open Source Bug Bounty. Anyone interested in contributing to the security of eligible frameworks is encouraged to participate there.

References

  • Next.js August 2026 security release

  • Upstream libheif advisory

  • Vercel security release changelog

  • Just a rumor of a bug is enough to find a security exploit

title: Webhooks or polling for inbound mail, and when to use both
description:
Webhooks feel modern and polling feels dated, but the right answer depends on what happens when a delivery is missed — and every webhook system misses deliveries eventually.

Webhooks give latency, not guarantees

A webhook is an HTTP request to your endpoint, retried a few times with backoff. If your service is down for longer than the retry window, or returns 500 consistently, the event is dropped unless the sender keeps a replayable log. Latency is excellent, guarantees are not.

Polling gives completeness, not speed

Polling an endpoint for messages since a cursor is boring and reliable: you control the pace, you can replay, and an outage costs you delay instead of data. The cost is a constant trickle of requests and a latency floor equal to the poll interval.

The combination that works

Webhook for latency, poll as reconciliation. On each webhook, enqueue the message id; run a periodic poll that asks for anything newer than the last processed id and fills the gaps. The poll makes the system correct, the webhook makes it fast.

One detail that makes reconciliation cheap

Make the cursor the message id, not a timestamp. Timestamps collide at second granularity and drift between clocks, so a poll built on them either re-fetches or skips messages. A monotonic id gives you exact resume semantics.

Volanea delivers inbound mail by webhook and also exposes a cursor-based read endpoint, so reconciliation is a loop instead of a guess.

title: How I compute a "typical price" for 22,000 LEGO offers (and why shop discounts are mostly theatre)
description:
Every price comparison site eventually has to answer one question, and it is not "where is it cheapest". It is: is this actually cheap?

Retailers answer it for you, loudly, with a red badge: -50%. The badge means that the current price is half of the regular price the shop declares. That number is a field in a feed. Nobody audits it.

I run https://klockers.pl/, a LEGO price comparison for the Polish market: 18 shops, 5,600 active sets, roughly 22,000 offers, all built on Symfony 8 and MariaDB. This post is about the part that took the most iterations - turning a firehose of affiliate offers into a price history I can reason about. The code is real, trimmed for readability.

The dataset

At the time of writing: 22,842 offers, 5,595 sets with at least two shops, 18 shops, daily snapshots since October. LEGO is a friendly domain for this because two numbers are public for every set: the retail price and the piece count. Price per piece is the metric collectors actually argue about, and it is the one thing a shop cannot fake without changing the product.

Step 1: do not store offers per day

The obvious schema - one price_history row per offer per day costs about 8M rows a year at today's volume, and grows linearly with every shop you add. Most of those rows are useless: nobody asks what shop #7 charged for set #412 three weeks ago.

What people ask is "what was the cheapest I could get this set for, and when". So I store one row per set per day:

CREATE TABLE price_history (
  id           INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  set_id       INT NOT NULL,
  recorded_on  DATE NOT NULL,
  price        DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  offers_count INT NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE KEY uniq_set_day (set_id, recorded_on)
);

That is ~2M rows a year, and every point in it is a daily minimum - the only number that matters for a deal. The cost is that per-shop history is gone. I decided I would rather have a dense, cheap, meaningful series than a sparse, expensive, archival one.

Step 2: make the snapshot idempotent

The snapshot runs after every feed import and again at 23:45, in case the evening import failed. Running it twice must not create a second row for the day, otherwise every median downstream quietly skews.


final class PriceHistoryRecorder
{
    public function __construct(private readonly Connection $db) {}

    public function capture(?\DateTimeImmutable $day = null): int
    {
        $date = ($day ?? new \DateTimeImmutable('today'))->format('Y-m-d');

        $this->db->executeStatement(
            'INSERT INTO price_history (set_id, recorded_on, price, offers_count)
             SELECT id, ?, min_price, offers_count FROM lego_set
             WHERE offers_count > 0 AND min_price IS NOT NULL
             ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
               price = VALUES(price), offers_count = VALUES(offers_count)',
            [$date]
        );

        return $this->eligibleSets();
    }
}

Two details that matter more than they look:

WHERE offers_count > 0 - a set with no live offer must not pollute the series with a zero or a gap. A gap is meaningful; a zero is a bug.
The upsert is the whole point. Cron overlap, manual re-runs, a deploy in the middle of the window - none of it can corrupt the day.
Step 3: median, not average
Median of the daily minimums over the last 30 days is my "typical price". The average is the wrong statistic here, and the reason is boring: one feed error is enough. A shop that publishes 14.99 zł instead of 149.99 zł for a day moves the mean by several złoty and the median by nothing.

The naive implementation is a SELECT per set. With 5,600 sets that is 5,600 queries every night. Instead: one query, group in PHP, bulk upsert, one join.


$rows = $this->db->fetchAllAssociative(
    'SELECT set_id, price FROM price_history
     WHERE recorded_on >= CURDATE() - INTERVAL '.($days - 1).' DAY
     ORDER BY set_id ASC, recorded_on ASC'
);

$bySet = [];
foreach ($rows as $row) {
    $bySet[(int) $row['set_id']][] = (float) $row['price'];
}

$updates = [];
foreach ($bySet as $setId => $prices) {
    sort($prices);
    $count  = \count($prices);
    $middle = intdiv($count, 2);
    $median = 0 === $count % 2
        ? ($prices[$middle - 1] + $prices[$middle]) / 2
        : $prices[$middle];

    $updates[] = [$setId, number_format($median, 2, '.', '')];
}

foreach (array_chunk($updates, 500) as $chunk) {
    $values = [];
    $params = [];
    foreach ($chunk as [$setId, $median]) {
        $values[] = '(?,?)';
        array_push($params, $setId, $median);
    }

    $this->db->executeStatement(
        'INSERT INTO _price_stats (set_id, typical_price) VALUES '.implode(',', $values).'
         ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE typical_price = VALUES(typical_price)',
        $params
    );
}

Then a single UPDATE ... JOIN pushes the values onto the catalog table, and the temp table is dropped. The whole refresh for 5,600 sets runs in a couple of seconds.

Note what is not here: no window function, no PERCENTILE_CONT (MariaDB does not have one), no ORM. The statistics are the one place where I want SQL and arrays, not entities.

Step 4: the guards that actually save the data

Matching is where a price comparison dies. The feed gives you a title, an optional manufacturer number, sometimes an EAN, and a price. Everything else is inference.

Three guards earn their keep:

  1. Set number extraction. Prefer the explicit field, then the pattern. Empik puts the number at the end of the title, some shops put polybag numbers (3 digits) in the middle: 

$explicit = trim($fields['attr_201105'] ?? $fields['Numer produktu'] ?? '');
if ('' !== $explicit && ctype_digit($explicit)) {
    return ltrim($explicit, '0');
}

if (preg_match('/\b(\d{4,6})\b/', $name, $match)) {
    return ltrim($match[1], '0');
}

return preg_match('/(?<!\d)(\d{3})(?!\d)/', $name, $match) ? ltrim($match[1], '0') : null;

Careful: the base number is not the identity. 985 base numbers in the LEGO catalog have variants - 30066-1 through 30066-5 are five different sets. Keying on the base number produced 2,513 duplicate records in my first import.

  1. Reject non-sets. A title is a no-go if it smells like a knockoff, an incomplete set, a used one, or a box-less one: 
return (bool) preg_match(
    '/kompatybiln|lepin|podr[oó]b|niekomplet|without box|no box|bez pude[lł]ka|u[zż]ywan|uszkodz/u',
    mb_strtolower($title)
);
  1. The 4% rule. The average LEGO piece costs around 0.45 zł. If an offer works out to less than 0.04 zł per piece, it is not a bargain - it is a feed bug or a single part listed as a set: 
if ($pieces > 100 && $offer->price < $pieces * 0.04) {
    ++$skipped;
    continue;
}

The $pieces > 100 guard matters: for a 40-piece polybag, weird ratios are normal.

Every import prints what happened - seen, matched, saved, skipped, per shop - and a --dry-run flag runs the same code without writing. When a shop changes its feed format, the skip count jumps and you see it the same evening, not three weeks later in a graph.

What the numbers say
Once the pipeline behaved, the data became interesting:

Median price of a 2026 set: 151.99 zł, up from 221.52 zł average in 2025 - but that average is not comparable, the mix of sets changed.
Price per piece by year: 0.53 zł (2024) → 0.55 zł (2025) → 0.45 zł (2026).
Average discount against the shop-declared regular price: 25.3%.
That last number is the one to be suspicious about. 25% average discount across 2,054 sets does not mean the market is 25% off. It means shops are consistent about declaring a regular price that makes a discount look good.

Which is the whole argument for computing your own baseline: the shop's "regular" is an input, not a fact. The 30-day median is a fact, at least as long as your history is long enough to have one - and mine is only a few months old, which I say out loud on the site.

Five things I would do again

  1. Snapshot the minimum, not the offer. Cheaper, and it answers the actual question.
  2. Make every write idempotent. ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE has saved me from cron overlap, re-deploys and my own mistakes more times than any test.
  3. Dry-run first, always. Same code path, no writes, full statistics.
  4. Median for prices, mean for nothing. One bad feed row should not move the number.
  5. A set with one shop is not a comparison. I only publish a set once at least two shops stock it. Fewer pages, more honest ones.

Disclosure: I run https://klockers.pl, a LEGO price comparison for Poland. The site earns affiliate commission from some of the shops it links to. The method described here is documented publicly at https://klockers.pl/jak-liczymy-ceny, and the aggregate numbers come from the 2026 price report. No data in this post comes from a source I was paid to mention.

title: Know What Your Agent's Tools Can Do to You: Scanning MCP Servers Before You Install Them
description:
In an April 2026 audit, 27 detections from MCP security scanners boiled down to 6 genuine concerns. The scanners weren't missing attacks — they were crying wolf, which in a CI pipeline is the same failure wearing a different coat.

So I built a scanner whose first feature is its own error profile: every rule publishes a measured precision from a labelled corpus of planted positives and near-miss traps. This is how it works, what it catches — tool poisoning, rug pulls, dangerous sinks, hardcoded secrets — and where its numbers say it still gets things wrong.

One command before you install

Sentinel Scan is a security and conformance scanner for MCP servers and SKILL.md agent skills. One command scans a server or skill for tool poisoning, rug pulls, dangerous code sinks, and hardcoded secrets — and reports each rule's measured precision rather than just asserting it.

pip install sentinel-scan
sentinel-scan demo

The demo scans the bundled 12-tool corpus in about a second: 6 benign tools — two of them near-miss traps — and 6 with planted findings, producing 7 findings. The two traps produce no findings: a tool that "ignores previous cached results" and a security tool that quotes an injection as an example. That restraint is the product.

Pure Python, no API keys, no GPU, no network. Python ≥ 3.10.

What it catches

  • Tool poisoning: hidden instructions in tool descriptions — markup directives, "note to the AI" framing, ignore-instruction phrasing — plus descriptions that direct credentials, files, or conversation contents out, and covert actions a tool takes "without telling the user."
  • Rug pulls: a tool's description changing after you pinned it. Sentinel Scan stores a SHA-256 pin of the normalized description and flags quiet changes (whitespace-only edits ignored).
  • Dangerous sinks: command execution (shell=True, os.system, string commands — fixed argv with shell=False does not fire), dynamic code (eval/exec — ast.literal_eval does not fire), and sensitive-file access (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, /etc/passwd, key files, full environment dumps — a comment merely mentioning a path does not fire).
  • Hardcoded secrets: AWS key ids, GitHub tokens, OpenAI-style keys, private-key blocks, assigned credential literals (${VAR} references do not fire).
  • Skill rules: hidden instructions in a SKILL.md body, capabilities the body uses but the frontmatter does not declare, and filesystem servers scoped to /, ~, or a home directory instead of a project directory.

Measured, not asserted

Each rule is deliberately narrow: it fires on a specific, explainable signal shape. The rates are measured with scripts/measure.py over the labelled corpus in fixtures/corpus/ — 32 cases of planted positives and benign near-miss negatives for every rule. Across all rules: 18 true positives, 0 false positives, 0 false negatives.

Those are corpus rates, not a promise about the open internet. Re-run the measurement yourself:

python3 scripts/measure.py

Using it

Scan an MCP config, a tools manifest, server sources, or skill folders:

sentinel-scan scan ~/.config/...

Exit codes are CI-shaped: the scan exits 1 when any finding is at or above --fail-on (default high). Outputs are terminal text, JSON, and SARIF, which renders in the GitHub Security tab. There is also a GitHub Action (ranadhir19/sentinel-scan@v0.1.0) that runs the scan, writes SARIF, and uploads it to the Security tab.

What it does not do: no dynamic execution of scanned servers, no LLM judgement calls, no network calls. It is static analysis. There is also a local web demo in demo/ (React front end, FastAPI backend) if you want to paste a description, a SKILL.md body, or source and watch it scan.

Repo: https://github.com/ranadhir19/sentinel-scan

description:
What does Java Based Interview at Hugues Systique Corporation look like?

Recently I had gone through the interview process for the role of Associate Engineer at Hughes Systique Corporation.

It involved a lot more than just DSA questions.

There were aptitude questions, Java questions, AI/ML questions, project related questions, and managerial questions.

In this blog, I wanted to walk through my experience of the interview and the questions I faced and also the questions my friends faced.

This will help you know what to expect in your interview. 👇

ROUND 1 - ONLINE ASSESSMENT (OA)

OA had 4 sections:

1) Aptitude - 20 Questions

Basic aptitude questions on:

Time and Work

Percentages, Ratios

Time Speed Distance

2) Programming Concepts - 20 Questions

Java and C++ Concept based questions.

Have a good understanding of Programming fundamentals.

3) Programming - 2 Questions

We had to answer one of the two questions.

Snack problem based on DP.

Arrays and Strings

This section tests your problem solving skills and your ability to find out the right approach.

4) AI/ML Questions - 40 Questions

40 questions based on AI/ML.

Having a good understanding of AI/ML fundamental helps.

ROUND 2 - TECHNICAL INTERVIEW

First round of interview focused on basic DSA, problem solving, core CS subjects and aptitude.

DSA & Problem Solving:

Reverse String

Maximum Sum Subarray using sliding window

XOR based questions

Two pointer based questions

Second largest element in array

Palindrome check

Find duplicates in array

Time and Space Complexity analysis.

They focussed on the approach you take to solve the problem.

Core CS Questions:

Difference between Thread and Process?

What is multi-threading in Java?

Difference between stack and heap?

What are 4 pillars of OOPS?

Difference between Array and LinkedList?

Aptitude:

Basic aptitude questions were asked. Especially Time and Work.

ROUND 3 - TECHNICAL + MANAGERIAL

This round focused on Core Java questions, project understanding, architecture and behavioural questions.

One thing I realised was:

Your Resume is your blueprint for your interview.

Core Java & OOPs:

What is exception handling in Java?

Difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?

How to create custom exceptions?

Difference between throw and throws?

What is finally block?

What if an exception occurs in finally block?

Explain 4 pillars of OOPS with examples.

Method Overloading vs Overriding.

Abstract class vs Interface.

== vs equals().

Java Collection Framework.

ArrayList vs LinkedList.

What is HashMap? How does it work internally?

How are Hash Collisions resolved in hashMap?

What if 2 keys have same hashcode?

Why is HashMap not thread safe?

HashMap vs Hashtable.

MVC Architecture:

What is MVC architecture?

What is the role of Model, View and Controller?

How are requests handled in MVC?

Difference between MVC and Layered Architecture.

Project Related Questions:

This was one of the most important sections.

I was asked to explain my full internship project. Including:

Design the architecture of your project.

Explain complete flow of application.

What was your role in the project? What did you contribute?

Why did you use SQL?

Why did you choose a specific database?

How did you handle exceptions/errors?

How did you develop the APIs?

What were some issues you faced?

How would you improve the architecture of your project?

What happens when a request is made to your backend API?

The interviewer dove pretty deep into my project.

If you mention a project on your resume, make sure you know how it works internally.

Managerial & Behavioural Questions:

What are your strengths and weaknesses?

Where do you see yourself in 10 years?

Why should we hire you?

Why did you choose Java as your main programming language?

How do you deal with conflicts in a team?

Tell me about a challenging situation during your internship.

How do you deal with pressure and tight deadlines.

What would you do if you disagree with your manager?

Are you okay with learning new technologies?

WHAT TO PREPARE:

If you are preparing for an interview like this here is what I would prepare.

DSA - Sliding Window, Two Pointers, XOR, Arrays, Strings, Basic DP.

Core Java - OOPs, Exception Handling, Collections, HashMap, Multi-threading.

Core CS - OS, Processes, Threads, Memory Management.

AI/ML - Brush up on fundamentals. If it is part of your OA then definitely revise.

Projects - Know your architecture, APIs, database choices, how you implemented.

Behavioural Questions - Answer truthfully.

The main thing I learnt was:

You don’t need to know everything. But you should know the fundamentals. Be able to describe your approach and know your projects inside out.

Remember these can vary depending on the candidate. This was my experience and my friends experience.

LET ME KNOW YOUR EXPERIENCE TOO! 👇

Have you done an interview like this for HSC or any Java based company?

What questions did they ask? What would you advise future candidates to prepare?

Let’s help each other out! 🚀

HughesSystique #HSC #InterviewExperience #AssociateEngineer #Java #DSA #CoreJava #AI #MachineLearning #PlacementPreparation #TechnicalInterview

title: Ship /v2 of a Go API Without Forking the Service: Two HTTP Adapters, One Use Case
description:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Product wants /v2/orders/{id} to return customer instead of customer_name, and money as an integer instead of a float. Someone copies handlers/orders.go to handlers/v2/orders.go. Then the service it calls needs a different return shape, so OrderService gets copied to OrderServiceV2. Three months later a soft-delete bug gets fixed in v2 and nobody remembers v1 has the same bug. Your two versions now disagree about which orders exist.

A better copy won't save you. A version is a wire contract, and wire contracts belong at the edge. Stripe described this approach back in 2017: their API is written against the current version, and version change modules transform responses backward for older clients, which "keep older API versions abstracted out of core code paths." You don't need Stripe's machinery to get the same property in a Go service. Ports and adapters gives it to you for free.

In hexagonal terms, v1 and v2 are two driving adapters. Each owns its request and response types and the mapping to and from the domain. Both call the same use case through the same port, and the whole thing runs on the standard library.

The layout: one core, two doors

Here is the whole tree. order is the core. Everything under adapter is replaceable. The module needs nothing beyond the standard library:

module example.com/orders

go 1.22

orders/
├── go.mod
├── cmd/api/
│   ├── main.go
│   └── main_test.go
└── internal/
    ├── order/          # domain + ports + use case
    │   └── order.go
    └── adapter/
        ├── httpv1/     # driving adapter, old contract
        ├── httpv2/     # driving adapter, new contract
        └── memrepo/    # driven adapter, in-memory store

The domain holds money the way money should be held: an integer count of minor units plus a currency code. That float in v1's JSON was a wire decision, so it lives in the v1 adapter and nowhere else.

package order

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
)

var ErrNotFound = errors.New("order not found")

type Order struct {
    ID         string
    Customer   string
    TotalMinor int64 // 1999 = 19.99 in a 2-decimal currency
    Currency   string
    Deleted    bool
}

// Repository is the driven port.
type Repository interface {
    ByID(ctx context.Context, id string) (Order, error)
}

// Getter is the driving port. Both HTTP versions call it.
type Getter interface {
    Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (Order, error)
}

type Service struct{ repo Repository }

func NewService(r Repository) *Service {
    return &Service{repo: r}
}

func (s *Service) Get(
    ctx context.Context, id string,
) (Order, error) {
    o, err := s.repo.ByID(ctx, id)
    if err != nil {
        return Order{}, err
    }
    // The soft-delete fix lives here, once, for every version.
    if o.Deleted {
        return Order{}, ErrNotFound
    }
    return o, nil
}

Notice what this file does not know: JSON, HTTP, URL paths, version numbers. When v3 shows up, this file does not change.


Two driving adapters, one use case: the version lives at the door, not in the room.

The v1 adapter keeps the old contract, warts included

v1 promised clients customer_name and a float total. The adapter keeps that promise. It also does the division that v1 always did, which assumes two decimal places. For a zero-decimal currency like JPY, where Stripe's API takes 10 to mean 10 JPY, that division was already wrong. That is one of the reasons v2 exists, and it is a good reason not to "fix" v1 quietly: clients have coded around its behavior.

package httpv1

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "net/http"

    "example.com/orders/internal/order"
)

type orderResponse struct {
    ID           string  `json:"id"`
    CustomerName string  `json:"customer_name"`
    Total        float64 `json:"total"`
    Currency     string  `json:"currency"`
}

func toResponse(o order.Order) orderResponse {
    return orderResponse{
        ID:           o.ID,
        CustomerName: o.Customer,
        Total:        float64(o.TotalMinor) / 100,
        Currency:     o.Currency,
    }
}

type Handler struct {
    uc     order.Getter
    policy Policy
}

func New(uc order.Getter, p Policy) *Handler {
    return &Handler{uc: uc, policy: p}
}

func (h *Handler) Register(mux *http.ServeMux) {
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /v1/orders/{id}",
        deprecated(h.getOrder, h.policy))
}

func (h *Handler) getOrder(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    o, err := h.uc.Get(r.Context(), r.PathValue("id"))
    if errors.Is(err, order.ErrNotFound) {
        http.Error(w, "order not found", http.StatusNotFound)
        return
    }
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "internal error", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(toResponse(o))
}

v1 also has to tell clients it is going away. Two headers do the work. RFC 9745, published in March 2025 on the Standards Track, defines Deprecation as a structured-field date: an @ followed by Unix seconds, like Deprecation: @1688169599. It also defines a deprecation link relation that points at your migration docs. RFC 8594 defines Sunset, the moment the endpoint is expected to stop responding, as a plain HTTP-date. RFC 9745 adds one rule tying them together: the Sunset timestamp "MUST NOT be earlier than" the Deprecation timestamp.

All of that is wire behavior, so it goes in the v1 package:

package httpv1

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Policy struct {
    Deprecated time.Time
    Sunset     time.Time
    DocsURL    string
}

func deprecated(next http.HandlerFunc, p Policy) http.HandlerFunc {
    dep := fmt.Sprintf("@%d", p.Deprecated.Unix())
    sun := p.Sunset.UTC().Format(http.TimeFormat)
    link := "<" + p.DocsURL + `>; rel="deprecation"`
    return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        h := w.Header()
        h.Set("Deprecation", dep)
        h.Set("Sunset", sun)
        h.Add("Link", link)
        next(w, r)
    }
}

The headers are set before next runs, so they are already in the header map when http.Error writes a 404 or 500. Clients that hit a missing order still learn the endpoint is going away. The .UTC() call matters: the http.TimeFormat docs say the time "must be in UTC for Format to generate the correct format."

The v2 adapter renames a field and fixes the money

v2 is a sibling package with its own DTO and its own mapping. It calls the same order.Getter.

package httpv2

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "net/http"

    "example.com/orders/internal/order"
)

type money struct {
    AmountMinor int64  `json:"amount_minor"`
    Currency    string `json:"currency"`
}

type orderResponse struct {
    ID       string `json:"id"`
    Customer string `json:"customer"`
    Total    money  `json:"total"`
}

func toResponse(o order.Order) orderResponse {
    return orderResponse{
        ID:       o.ID,
        Customer: o.Customer,
        Total: money{
            AmountMinor: o.TotalMinor,
            Currency:    o.Currency,
        },
    }
}

type Handler struct{ uc order.Getter }

func New(uc order.Getter) *Handler { return &Handler{uc: uc} }

func (h *Handler) Register(mux *http.ServeMux) {
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /v2/orders/{id}", h.getOrder)
}

func (h *Handler) getOrder(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    o, err := h.uc.Get(r.Context(), r.PathValue("id"))
    if errors.Is(err, order.ErrNotFound) {
        http.Error(w, "order not found", http.StatusNotFound)
        return
    }
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "internal error", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(toResponse(o))
}

Yes, the error branches look the same as v1's. Leave them duplicated. Error shape is part of the contract, and the day v2 moves to a JSON error body you want to change one file without a shared helper dragging v1 along. The duplication that hurts is duplicated business rules, and there is none here: the soft-delete check exists exactly once, in order.Service.

Mounting both on one ServeMux

Since Go 1.22, net/http.ServeMux patterns accept a method and wildcards, so GET /v1/orders/{id} is a complete route and r.PathValue("id") returns the segment. The routing announcement also notes that a GET pattern matches HEAD, and that when two patterns overlap the most specific one wins. Keep the go line in go.mod at 1.22 or later: the new matching is controlled by the httpmuxgo121 setting, and GODEBUG defaults follow the Go version in your go.mod.

The in-memory store is the driven adapter. It doubles as the test fake.

package memrepo

import (
    "context"

    "example.com/orders/internal/order"
)

type Repo map[string]order.Order

func (r Repo) ByID(
    _ context.Context, id string,
) (order.Order, error) {
    o, ok := r[id]
    if !ok {
        return order.Order{}, order.ErrNotFound
    }
    return o, nil
}

Wiring happens in one function, so the test can call the exact same code main runs:

package main

import (
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "time"

    "example.com/orders/internal/adapter/httpv1"
    "example.com/orders/internal/adapter/httpv2"
    "example.com/orders/internal/adapter/memrepo"
    "example.com/orders/internal/order"
)

var v1Policy = httpv1.Policy{
    Deprecated: time.Date(2026, 11, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC),
    Sunset:     time.Date(2027, 5, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC),
    DocsURL:    "https://api.example.com/docs/v2-migration",
}

func newMux(uc order.Getter) *http.ServeMux {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    httpv1.New(uc, v1Policy).Register(mux)
    httpv2.New(uc).Register(mux)
    return mux
}

func main() {
    repo := memrepo.Repo{
        "ord_1": {ID: "ord_1", Customer: "Acme GmbH",
            TotalMinor: 1999, Currency: "EUR"},
    }
    uc := order.NewService(repo)
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", newMux(uc)))
}

Count the places that know there are two versions: two Register calls and two packages. The service, the repository port and the domain type are shared, and none of them carry a version number.


Same order, two shapes on the wire. The mapping is the only thing that forks.

One table test, both versions, one fake repository

This is where the design pays rent. One fake repo, one mux, and a table that sends the same orders through both doors. The deleted-order row is the regression test for the bug from the opening: fix it once in the use case, and both versions return 404.

package main

import (
    "net/http/httptest"
    "strings"
    "testing"

    "example.com/orders/internal/adapter/memrepo"
    "example.com/orders/internal/order"
)

const v1Body = `{"id":"ord_1","customer_name":"Acme GmbH",` +
    `"total":19.99,"currency":"EUR"}`

const v2Body = `{"id":"ord_1","customer":"Acme GmbH",` +
    `"total":{"amount_minor":1999,"currency":"EUR"}}`

func TestOrdersBothVersions(t *testing.T) {
    repo := memrepo.Repo{
        "ord_1": {ID: "ord_1", Customer: "Acme GmbH",
            TotalMinor: 1999, Currency: "EUR"},
        "ord_2": {ID: "ord_2", Customer: "Gone Ltd",
            TotalMinor: 500, Currency: "EUR", Deleted: true},
    }
    mux := newMux(order.NewService(repo))

    tests := []struct {
        name, path, body string
        code             int
        deprecated       bool
    }{
        {"v1 found", "/v1/orders/ord_1", v1Body, 200, true},
        {"v2 found", "/v2/orders/ord_1", v2Body, 200, false},
        {"v1 missing", "/v1/orders/nope", "", 404, true},
        {"v2 missing", "/v2/orders/nope", "", 404, false},
        {"v1 deleted", "/v1/orders/ord_2", "", 404, true},
        {"v2 deleted", "/v2/orders/ord_2", "", 404, false},
    }

    for _, tc := range tests {
        t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
            req := httptest.NewRequest("GET", tc.path, nil)
            rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
            mux.ServeHTTP(rec, req)

            if rec.Code != tc.code {
                t.Fatalf("code = %d, want %d", rec.Code, tc.code)
            }
            got := strings.TrimSpace(rec.Body.String())
            if tc.body != "" && got != tc.body {
                t.Errorf("body = %s\nwant  %s", got, tc.body)
            }
            dep := rec.Header().Get("Deprecation") != ""
            if dep != tc.deprecated {
                t.Errorf("Deprecation set = %v, want %v",
                    dep, tc.deprecated)
            }
        })
    }
}

Three things in that table are worth a second look. The body constants are the contract, written down: if someone reorders fields in a DTO or renames a JSON tag, a row fails. The Deprecation column proves the header is scoped to v1, including on its 404s. And the two deleted rows go through one rule in one place, which is the whole argument of this post in two lines of test data.

strings.TrimSpace is there because json.Encoder.Encode writes a trailing newline. The test goes through mux.ServeHTTP instead of calling the handlers directly, because r.PathValue is filled in by the mux during routing, and because you want the test to fail if a route pattern breaks.

Where this stops working

This pattern covers read-shape changes: renames, nesting, unit changes, header policy. It does not cover everything, and it is better to know the edges before you rely on it.

Behavior changes are the hard case. If v2 must validate an order differently, or charge a card at a different step, that is not a mapping. Put the choice in the use case as an explicit option the adapter passes in, with a name that says what it does rather than which version wants it. Stripe hits the same wall: their post describes flagging changes with side effects, turning their response transformation into a no-op, and handling them with checks elsewhere in the code.

Request bodies follow the same rule as responses. A POST /v2/orders adapter decodes its own DTO into a domain command. When v2 accepts amount_minor and v1 accepts a float, each adapter converts to TotalMinor before calling the core, and the v1 adapter is the one place that rounds.

On sunset day you remove internal/adapter/httpv1, delete one Register line, and drop the v1 rows from the table. If the domain had grown a V1Total field or an if version == 1 branch, you would be hunting through the core instead.

If this was useful

The move in this post (a version is an adapter, the use case is the product) is the same move Hexagonal Architecture in Go makes for databases, queues and third-party APIs. The book walks through the layout, the port boundaries and the persistence side, which is where most Go services start leaking SQL types into the core. If your /v2 folder is already a copy of /v1, it shows you how to pull the shared part back into the middle.

title: Claude Message Threads Are Fast Until Your Agent Waits 5 Minutes
description:
Someone on r/ClaudeAI summed the whole launch up in five words: "5 minutes ttl is such BS."

That was one of the top comments under Anthropic's message threads announcement, posted hours after it went live.

The feature itself is clean. You send the conversation once. Every turn after that sends only the new message plus a previous_message_id.

Anthropic says median time to first token drops about 35% on requests between 500k and 1M tokens.

And the API throws your thread away 5 minutes after the last request.

I read that comment and thought, yeah, that is the story. Not the latency win. The timer.

Because the numbers are real. This shipped on by default for most Claude Code users, so it is already running under thousands of them right now.

Payloads in long sessions drop from around 800 KB to under 2 KB. That is not marketing math.

But the expiry window is where the excitement hits the pavement. And almost nobody writing about this led with it.

Here's what i mean.

What it actually saves

The headline everyone repeats is the 35% faster first token. The number almost nobody repeats is that your bill does not move.

Straight from the docs:

Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same.

So message threads are a latency feature. Not a cost feature. If you want a cheaper bill, you still need prompt caching with breakpoints placed by hand.

That is fine. But the framing matters.

Half the posts i read treated this as a way to cut long context spend. It isn't. It just stops you from uploading 800 KB of JSON every few seconds.

The 5 minute problem

Here's a question people always ask. What happens if my tool call takes longer than the thread lives?

You replay the whole thing. Full conversation, new create request, new thread id.

One developer in that Reddit thread ran this on a 600k context loop and saw about 30% better TTFT, close to Anthropic's claim.

But their tool calls sometimes stalled 3 to 4 minutes waiting on slow endpoints. Add a human approval click and the window is gone.

Another developer called the idle TTL the edge case to watch. Their words, more or less.

A multi repo test suite or a database migration will blow through 5 minutes and you silently pay the full re upload again.

One commenter pointed out the 5 minute window lines up with the default prompt cache TTL. Slow tool calls were already paying for a cold read. Nothing changed there.

That is a fair defense.

But a fair defense is not a feature.

How it compares

Claude threads OpenAI Responses
Resume by previous_message_id previous_response_id
Stored for 5 min idle 30 days default
Written to disk No Yes
Works with ZDR Unclear Forced off

Two commenters asked the obvious thing. Isn't this just OpenAI's Responses API a year later?

Partly. The shape is the same. The retention is not.

OpenAI keeps response objects 30 days by default and lets you turn storage off. Anthropic keeps your thread encrypted in memory, writes nothing to disk, and deletes it 5 minutes after the last request.

That is a real difference in how the two companies think about holding your data. Make of it what you will.

And if your team requires zero data retention, one commenter said this whole feature means very little to you.

The fingerprint trap

Most tutorials tell you to add the thread param and go. Then you hit thread_fingerprint_mismatch and lose an afternoon.

Threads split fields into three buckets:

  • Create only: system and tools. Send either on a continue request, even as null, and you get a 400.
  • Fixed: model, tool_choice, thinking, output_config, your beta header set, top level cache_control. These must match every turn.
  • Free: max_tokens, stream, metadata, service_tier.

Want to change the system prompt mid conversation? Start a new thread. There is no edit.

A thread is append only, and each response id can be continued exactly once.

I like this constraint. It is honest about what a thread is. But it will surprise anyone who treats it like a chat object they can mutate.

Keep your own copy

The first time i read "your application stays the source of truth," i skimmed past it. Then i thought about what it means at 3am.

It means no response, create or continue, tells you whether the API stored that turn.

You find out on the next request, when you get a 404 with thread_not_found. And the error does not say why.

Expired. Not stored. Written by a fallback model.

Different workspace. Different service account.

So you keep every message yourself and you build the replay path on day one. Not later.

The SDK helper handles it, but only while the helper object is alive. It holds the conversation in memory and saves it nowhere else.

Restart your process and that history is gone.

Now the part that has nothing to do with any of this.

I spent two hours in Anthropic's docs one evening trying to work out why my cache breakpoints kept failing. Read the whole page. Took notes.

Felt smart. Then found a single line in a table saying a threaded request can carry at most 4 breakpoints. The top level one counts as one of them.

Four. That was it. That was the bug.

I have done this maybe a dozen times now. The answer is always in a table I scrolled past.

My coworker keeps a folder of screenshots of docs he almost missed. He calls it his graveyard. It is 300 images deep and every one of them saved him a day.

There is something humbling about paying for speed with a footnote.

The real talk

Most people don't need this.

If your agent runs 5 turns and then stops, the thread never expires and never saves you anything worth measuring.

If you are under 100k tokens of context, the upload was not your bottleneck. Your model choice was.

And if a human has to approve steps, the 5 minute window is working against you. You will replay constantly and feel like the feature is broken.

It isn't. It was built for tight machine loops, not for people thinking.

The honest read is that this is infrastructure for coding agents and computer use loops. Screenshots stay on the server instead of getting re uploaded every turn.

That is the real win, and it is a good one.

For everyone else, plain prompt caching still does the job.

The ending

I keep coming back to that Reddit commenter who said they would not be surprised if the cache actually lives longer than 5 minutes and Anthropic just doesn't hand it to you.

I don't think that's true. But i understand the instinct.

When a feature saves you time and costs you nothing, you start asking where the catch is. Here the catch is written in the docs in plain text, and it is a clock.

Five minutes is enough for a machine. It is not enough for a person who stepped away to get coffee.

Maybe that is the point. Maybe the API is telling us who it was built for.

title: Spring Boot @Transactional: 7 Interview Traps That Catch Experienced Developers
description:
Most backend developers have put @Transactional on a service method and moved on. It usually works, which is exactly why interviewers like it. A few follow-up questions show quickly whether you know what the annotation does or just where to put it.

Here are seven of those follow-ups, with answers written the way I'd say them out loud. Everything assumes Spring Boot 3.x (Spring Framework 6.x), Jakarta Persistence, Hibernate 6 and Java 17-21.

1. "Why didn't my @Transactional method start a transaction?"

The usual cause is self-invocation.

Spoken answer: "Spring applies @Transactional through a proxy. Callers get the proxy, the proxy opens the transaction, then delegates to the real object. If a method inside the same class calls another annotated method with this., that call never goes through the proxy, so the annotation is ignored."

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }

    public void placeOrders(List<Order> orders) {
        for (Order order : orders) {
            saveOrder(order); // same as this.saveOrder(order): no proxy, no transaction
        }
    }

    @Transactional
    public void saveOrder(Order order) {
        orderRepository.save(order);
    }
}

Fixes, in the order I'd suggest them: move saveOrder into a separate bean and inject it, use TransactionTemplate for programmatic control, or switch to AspectJ weaving if you really need it. Self-injecting the bean with @Lazy also works, but it's a workaround most reviewers won't love.

2. "Can I put @Transactional on a private or final method?"

Spoken answer: "With the default proxy mode, no for private, and no for final. Spring Boot uses class-based (CGLIB) proxies by default, which work by subclassing your bean and overriding methods. A private method can't be overridden, and neither can a final one, so no transaction is applied."

Two details make this answer stand out:

  • Since Spring Framework 6.0, protected and package-private methods can be transactional with class-based proxies. Before that, only public methods counted. With interface-based JDK proxies, the method still has to be public and declared on the interface.
  • A final method on a proxied bean is a nasty bug. The call runs on the proxy instance itself, whose injected fields are usually null, so you can get a NullPointerException instead of a missing transaction.

3. "My method threw an exception. Why did the data still commit?"

Spoken answer: "By default Spring rolls back only on RuntimeException and Error. A checked exception, like IOException or your own PaymentFailedException extends Exception, does not trigger rollback. The transaction commits whatever was written before the exception."

Fixes:

  • @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) on the method or class.
  • Since Spring Framework 6.2 you can change the default globally with @EnableTransactionManagement(rollbackOn = RollbackOn.ALL_EXCEPTIONS).

A related follow-up: if you catch the exception inside the method and don't rethrow it, Spring never sees it, so it commits. And if an inner REQUIRED method throws a runtime exception that the outer method catches, the shared transaction is already marked rollback-only. The outer commit then fails with UnexpectedRollbackException. That surprises people the first time they see it.

4. "REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW: when would you use each?"

Spoken answer: "REQUIRED is the default. If a transaction already exists, the method joins it; if not, it starts one. Everything commits or rolls back together. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the current transaction and starts an independent one, which commits or rolls back on its own."

A real use case: recording a failed payment attempt. You want the audit row saved even when the payment transaction rolls back.

@Service
public class PaymentAuditService {

    private final PaymentAuditRepository auditRepository;

    public PaymentAuditService(PaymentAuditRepository auditRepository) {
        this.auditRepository = auditRepository;
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void recordFailure(Long orderId, String reason) {
        auditRepository.save(new PaymentAudit(orderId, reason));
    }
}

PaymentService.charge() runs in its own REQUIRED transaction, calls paymentAuditService.recordFailure(...) (a different bean, so the proxy applies), then throws. The charge rolls back, and the audit row stays.

The catch worth mentioning: REQUIRES_NEW needs a second database connection while the first one is suspended. Under load, heavy use of it can exhaust a small connection pool.

5. "What does readOnly = true actually do?"

Spoken answer: "It's a hint, and with Hibernate it has real effects. Spring sets the Hibernate session to manual flush mode and marks it read-only, so Hibernate skips dirty checking and doesn't keep snapshots of loaded entities. That saves memory and CPU on big reads. By default Spring also passes the read-only flag to the JDBC connection, and some drivers and databases use it for optimisations, or a routing data source can send those calls to a read replica."

What it doesn't do: it isn't a security guarantee. Whether a write fails depends on the driver and the database, so don't rely on it to block writes. Use it on query methods so you get the performance benefit, and keep writes in methods without it.

6. "Two users update the same row at once. What happens?"

This is the lost update problem. Both transactions read balance 1,000, one adds 200, the other subtracts 100, and whichever commits last wins. One change disappears.

Spoken answer: "@Transactional uses Isolation.DEFAULT, which means the database's default: READ COMMITTED on PostgreSQL and Oracle, REPEATABLE READ on MySQL InnoDB. READ COMMITTED does not stop a read-modify-write lost update. You can raise isolation, but in a JPA application the common fix is optimistic locking with a version column."

@Entity
public class Account {

    @Id
    private Long id;

    private BigDecimal balance;

    @Version
    private Long version;

    public void deposit(BigDecimal amount) {
        this.balance = this.balance.add(amount);
    }
}

Hibernate adds WHERE version = ? to the update. If another transaction changed the row first, zero rows are updated and Spring throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. You then retry or return a conflict to the client. When conflicts are frequent, like a hot counter, pessimistic locking with @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) on a repository query can be the better choice.

7. "Why do I get LazyInitializationException, and why doesn't it happen in my controller?"

Spoken answer: "A lazy association is loaded only when you touch it, and that needs an open Hibernate session. If you access order.getItems() after the transaction and session are closed, for example in a mapper or a scheduled job, you get LazyInitializationException."

It often doesn't show up in controllers because Spring Boot enables Open Session in View by default (spring.jpa.open-in-view=true). The session stays open for the whole web request, so lazy loading works in the controller and during JSON serialisation. Boot logs a warning about it at startup for a reason: it hides N+1 queries and holds a connection for the whole request.

Better fixes: fetch what you need inside the service with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection, and set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false so problems show up in tests instead of production.

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "items")
    Optional<Order> findWithItemsById(Long id);
}

Quick revision checklist

  • Self-invocation skips the proxy. Call through another bean or use TransactionTemplate.
  • Private and final methods aren't proxied. Protected and package-private work on class-based proxies since Spring 6.0.
  • Default rollback is unchecked exceptions and errors only. Use rollbackFor, or rollbackOn = ALL_EXCEPTIONS on Spring 6.2+.
  • A caught inner exception can still mark the transaction rollback-only and give you UnexpectedRollbackException.
  • REQUIRES_NEW is for work that must survive the outer rollback, like audit logs. It costs an extra connection.
  • readOnly = true turns off Hibernate dirty checking and flushing. It's not a write lock.
  • Default isolation comes from the database. Use @Version against lost updates.
  • Fetch lazy data inside the transaction and consider turning off open-in-view.

Which of these has bitten you in a real project? I'd like to hear about it in the comments.

If you're preparing for Java backend interviews, my Java & Spring Boot Interview Prep Guide has 240 questions like these (Core Java, Spring Boot 3, JPA, microservices, system design). Get it here: https://topmate.io/anantghadi/2384289 (India, ₹299) or https://payhip.com/b/pNo2T (international, $7). There's also a free 8-page sample on my Topmate: https://topmate.io/anantghadi

title: Designing Real-Time Party Games for 15+ People: Lessons from Wobbly Bottle
description:
Why Most Party Games Fail at Social Gatherings

Most digital party games look great in the app store, but when you actually try to bring them out at a real party or pre-drinks, they crash and burn for three reasons:

  1. Onboarding Friction: Asking 10 people to register accounts, download 500MB updates, or remember passwords instantly kills the mood.
  2. The "Single Screen Squeeze": Nobody wants to crane their neck trying to read a 6-inch phone screen across a crowded coffee table.
  3. Aggressive Paywalls: Hitting players with a $9.99/week subscription on turn 3 creates immediate resentment.

When we designed Wobbly Bottle, our mission was to eliminate all three friction points.

Rule 1: Zero-Friction Room Codes (The Jackbox Model on Native Mobile)

Instead of complex matchmaking, we implemented a 6-digit PIN system:

  • The host taps "Host Room" and holds up the screen with a PIN and QR code.
  • Guests tap "Join Room", type 6 digits, and boom—they are in the lobby with their own chosen avatar and color.
  • No logins, no emails, no friction.

Rule 2: Synchronized Bottle Physics Across All Devices

A party game lives on shared anticipation. When the bottle spins, everyone needs to watch it slow down together.

Using synchronized physics:

  • When the host swipes to spin, the rotational velocity and wobble frequency are computed and broadcasted.
  • The bottle visibly bends, wobbles, and tilts dynamically on every connected phone at the exact same millisecond.
  • When it lands, the questioner and answerer glow in neon lasers on everyone's screen.

Rule 3: Tailoring Dares to the Environment

Not every party is the same. We built three dedicated operational modes:

  • Table Mode: For classic pass-and-play when only one phone is available.
  • House Party Mode: Physical challenges, group voting, and drinking penalties.
  • Remote Party Mode: Designed specifically for Discord and FaceTime calls with screenshot dares, webcam photo proofs, and voice confessions.

Try it Free on iOS & Android

Wobbly Bottle is live on both major platforms:

  • 🍏 iOS App Store
  • 🤖 Google Play Store
  • 🌐 Official Web Landing

Check it out for your next game night or house party and let us know what you think!

title: 1,000 users, 1 API call: the fan-out pattern that saved my rate limit
description:
If every visitor's browser polls your API, your usage grows with your audience. Mine doesn't: whether one person or a thousand open the app, the upstream API gets a single call.

The app is this live airspace visualizer, a 3D globe that shows live air traffic, with new aircraft positions every 15 seconds. If you wonder how the aircraft keep flying smoothly between updates, I explained it in this other article.

The data comes from a third-party API with a rate limit per account, not per user. If each browser called it directly, a hundred open tabs would mean a hundred calls every 15 seconds, and I'd hit the limit long before the app got any traffic. Besides, the API key can't live in the frontend.

One poller, many clients

The solution is a small proxy between the browsers and the API. It has a single poller that asks the API for new data every 15 seconds and sends the result to every connected browser over Server-Sent Events (SSE). The number of users only changes how many connections the proxy keeps open, not how many requests reach the API.

Each browser opens a connection to /api/states. The proxy sets the SSE headers, keeps the response open and hands it to the poller. When the browser closes the connection, the poller forgets about it.

  app.get('/api/states', (req, res) => {
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/event-stream')
    res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'no-cache')
    res.flushHeaders()

    const client_id = poller.register(res)
    // The browser closed the tab or lost the connection
    req.on('close', () => poller.unregister(client_id))
  })

On every tick, the poller makes one request and writes the result to every connection it has. An SSE message is just text, so writing to an open response is enough. If the request fails, the clients get an error event instead and the poller tries again on the next tick. There's also a lock so two requests don't overlap when the API is slow, and a timeout so one that never answers can't hold that lock forever.

  private broadcast(event: string, data: unknown) {
    // An SSE message: event name, data and a blank line
    for (const res of this.clients.values()) {
      res.write(`event: ${event}\ndata: ${JSON.stringify(data)}\n\n`)
    }
  }

  private async dispatcher() {
    // The previous request is still running: skip this tick
    if (this.is_fetching) return
    this.is_fetching = true
    try {
      // One request, no matter how many clients there are
      const data = await this.get_data_with_timeout()
      this.latest_data = data
      this.latest_data_at = Date.now()
      this.broadcast('success', data)
    } catch (error) {
      this.broadcast('error', { message: this.error_message(error) })
    } finally {
      this.is_fetching = false
    }
  }

The poller only runs while someone is watching. The first client to connect starts it. Since the latest result is cached, anyone who connects later gets it straight away instead of waiting up to 15 seconds for the next tick. If the cache is more than a minute old, it's thrown away rather than served stale.

  register(res: express.Response) {
    const client_id = randomUUID()
    this.clients.set(client_id, res)

    // Older than a minute (or nothing yet): discard it
    const age = Date.now() - (this.latest_data_at ?? 0)
    if (age > MAX_DATA_AGE_MS) this.latest_data = null
    // The new client doesn't wait for the next tick
    if (this.latest_data !== null) this.write_sse(res, 'success', this.latest_data)

    // First client: start polling
    if (this.interval_id === null) {
      void this.dispatcher()
      this.interval_id = setInterval(() => void this.dispatcher(), this.time_ms)
    }
    return client_id
  }

When the last client disconnects, the interval is cleared and the proxy stops calling the API until someone comes back.

  unregister(client_id: string) {
    this.clients.delete(client_id)
    // Last one out turns off the lights
    if (this.clients.size === 0 && this.interval_id !== null) {
      clearInterval(this.interval_id)
      this.interval_id = null
    }
  }

Why SSE and not WebSockets

WebSockets would work too, but they solve a problem I don't have. Here the data only goes one way, from the server to the browser, and that's exactly what SSE is for. It works over plain HTTP, so it goes through proxies and load balancers without extra setup, and the browser reconnects on its own if the connection drops. On the client it's just a few lines:

  const event_source = new EventSource(api_url('states'))
  event_source.addEventListener('success', (event) => {
    layer.update_aircrafts(JSON.parse(event.data))
  })

With WebSockets I'd have to handle the protocol upgrade, the reconnection and a message format myself, for a channel where the browser never sends anything.

Disconnecting when no one is watching

There's one case left. If someone opens the app and leaves it in a background tab, the SSE connection stays open. If they're the only user, the poller keeps calling the API every 15 seconds for nobody.

To avoid it, the frontend listens to the visibilitychange event. When the tab is hidden it starts a one-minute timer, and when the timer runs out the stream is paused. If the user comes back before that, the timer is cancelled and nothing happens.

  const INACTIVE_DISCONNECT_MS = 60_000

  const handle_visibility_change = () => {

const handle_visibility_change = () => {
  clearTimeout(timeout)
  if (document.hidden) {
    // Hidden tab: pause the stream after a minute
    timeout = setTimeout(() => set_stream_paused(true), INACTIVE_DISCONNECT_MS)
  } else {
    set_stream_paused(false)
  }
}
document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', handle_visibility_change)


typescript

Pausing the stream closes the EventSource. To the proxy that's just another client leaving, so if it was the last one, polling stops. When the user comes back, a new connection opens and gets the cached data if it's still fresh, or starts the poller again if it isn't. I also add a "Paused" prefix to the page title, so the tab bar shows why the data isn't moving.

useEffect(() => {
  if (stream_paused) return
  const event_source = new EventSource(api_url('states'))
  // ...
  // Closing it unregisters this client in the proxy
  return () => event_source.close()
}, [stream_paused])

Conclusion

This pattern works for any project that needs regular updates from an API you don't control: prices, weather, scores, the status of a deploy. If the data is the same for everyone, there's no reason for each user to ask for it. One poller, a cache and a list of open connections are enough, and the cost stays the same with one user or a thousand.

It has its limits: it only works when everyone sees the same data, and the connections live in the memory of one process, so if you run several instances, each one has its own poller. For a project like this one, it's a good trade-off.

You can see it live at airspace.juanesroig.com. The code is on GitHub: the frontend in airspace-visualization and the proxy in opensky-proxy.

title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
description:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

Update @ai-sdk/harness-fx to the latest version to use the new adapter. Learn more in the fx harness documentation.
