title: Wilson's Laws of Branching
description:
A language almost exactly like yours, except it doesn’t like keeping secrets

Every conditional contains at least two outcomes. Writing down only one does not eliminate the other. It merely delegates its interpretation to the next person.

Usually that person is you, six months later, during an incident.

Wilson’s Law of Branching:

Every branch has an alternative. An alternative that is not expressed becomes a secret, and every secret eventually acquires a maintainer.

This is not a mathematical law. Mathematical laws have proofs. This one has deployment history.

The original Wilson Else proposed making certain missing alternatives visible, particularly inside nested conditionals. But requiring an else everywhere would confuse acknowledgment with punctuation. Prohibiting else everywhere would confuse flat code with complete reasoning.

Perhaps the problem is not whether we wrote else. Perhaps the problem is whether we told the truth about the decision. The original Wilson Else classified the original problems as "lies" versus "truths" but this essay attempts to soften the message as "secrets" vs. "truths". Secret is still a pejorative word but it is less pejorative than lies.

To investigate, we will invent a language almost indistinguishable from a normal programming language. Its distinguishing feature is that it gets uncomfortable when you appear to know something you have not told it.

1. First, declare what kind of decision this is

Ordinary languages let one keyword perform several jobs.

An if might mean:

  • Do this only when appropriate.
  • Reject this input and stop.
  • Choose between two outcomes.
  • Start a priority-ordered sequence of alternatives.
  • Conceal a question nobody answered.

Our language distinguishes three forms:

Construct Meaning
if Perform a conditional action, or terminate through a guard. No else.
realisedIf Make a binary decision with two nonempty executable branches.
wilsonIf Perform an action or explicitly acknowledge that nothing happens.

This does not make the program correct. It makes certain kinds of evasiveness syntactically inconvenient.

realisedIf (condition) {
  positiveAction()
}
// SYNTAX ERROR: unrealised-else
// Provide an alternative, or declare a conditional action.

The author has announced a binary decision and delivered half of it.

We could automatically insert:

else {
  // TODO: nothing
}

But that would manufacture evidence that a decision had been acknowledged when, in fact, a tool had inserted some braces.

We have promoted an omission into a compliance artifact.

Instead, the author must choose: supply the alternative, use an ordinary conditional action where permitted, or explicitly declare inaction.

2. Nothing is an outcome, not an explanation

Sometimes the correct alternative really is to do nothing.

That should be expressible without pretending that an empty block is an implementation.

realisedIf (condition) {
  positiveAction()
} else {
  // do nothing
}
// SYNTAX ERROR: empty-realised-else
// Use wilsonIf to declare intentional inaction.

The valid form is:

wilsonIf (condition) {
  positiveAction()
} else nothing

The false path is now acknowledged.

It is not justified. It is not proven safe. But it is no longer indistinguishable from a missing piece.

There is an unfortunate naming complication: once we explicitly acknowledge an “unrealized else,” it is no longer unrealized.

The terminology has developed the condition it was intended to diagnose.

Ordinary if remains useful for simple conditional actions:

if (cacheEntryExpired) {
  removeCacheEntry()
}

A permissive project allows that. A stricter project can require wilsonIf for nonterminating conditional actions, perhaps only in nested or consequential code.

That preserves the original article’s useful restraint: apply pressure where the missing alternative matters, not everywhere a keyword can be counted.

And the compiler’s knowledge remains limited:

realisedIf (condition) {
  positiveAction()
} else {
  accomplishAbsolutelyNothing()
}

There is an executable statement. The structural requirement is satisfied.

Whether it accomplishes anything is a separate investigation. The compiler verifies the paperwork, not the wisdom.

3. Guards do not need an escort

A guard clause states a condition under which execution cannot proceed.

if (!authorized) {
  throw Unauthorized()
}

performOperation()

The unauthorized path terminates. The authorized path continues.

Adding an else would not discover a missing outcome. It would merely place the main operation inside another block.

if (!authorized) {
  throw Unauthorized()
} else {
  performOperation()
}
// SYNTAX ERROR: realised-else
// Ordinary if forbids else.
// Prefer the terminating guard.

The else has been dismissed because its services are no longer required.

This is the strongest case for an anti-else policy: not that alternatives are bad, but that a terminating branch already makes the separation visible.

Our strict acknowledgment policy therefore exempts terminating guards.

There is no requirement to conduct a small ceremony after every return.

4. Three alternatives are not a binary decision

Now consider:

realisedIf (state == READY) {
  deploy()
} else if (state == PENDING) {
  wait()
} else {
  reject()
}
// SYNTAX ERROR: strict-binary-decision
// Use switch for alternatives over one discriminator.

We declared a binary decision and then installed a third outcome.

An else if is an alternative with terms and conditions. We actually submit that we should ban else if completely:

if (condition) {
  doSomething()
} else if (someOtherCondition) {
// SYNTAX ERROR: no-else-if
// Use separate blocks

Because else if is identical to:

if (condition) {
  doSomething()
}
if (otherCondition) {
  doSomethingElse()
}

For alternatives over one state value, a switch exposes the structure more clearly:

switch (state) {
  case READY:
    deploy()

  case PENDING:
    wait()

  default:
    rejectUnsupportedState(state)
}

Our language does not fall through by default. Selecting one arm executes that arm.

However, not every chain is secretly a switch:

if (temperature > limit) {
  shutDown()
} else if (batteryLow && disconnected) {
  conservePower()
}

Those are arbitrary predicates, potentially overlapping, with an ordering that matters.

Demanding a conventional switch would change the costume without necessarily improving the decision. Our language therefore also offers an ordered predicate case, whose first matching arm wins.

The important distinction is between dispatch over a value and priority among conditions.

A rule that cannot distinguish them has discovered a preference, not a principle.

5. Default is not another word for safe

Requiring a default sounds responsible.

Every possibility gets handled. Nobody falls through a crack.

Unfortunately, “handled” can mean this:

switch (state) {
  case READY:
    deploy()

  default:
    wait()
}

Pending, failed, deleted, corrupt, and any state introduced after the author leaves the company will all wait.

The default has excellent coverage and questionable judgment.

Our rule is therefore:

A switch must be exhaustive over its declared domain, or explicitly handle unmatched input.

For a closed set of states, the compiler can require every variant. Adding a new variant then produces an error at decisions that need reconsideration.

For external values, explicit rejection or fallback may be necessary. A type declaration is not a border checkpoint; unexpected runtime values can still arrive through poorly defended boundaries.

The compiler should know whether the author is claiming:

  • These are all the possible states.
  • Other states are valid and share this behavior.
  • Other states are invalid and must be rejected.

Those are different claims.

A default that quietly accepts everything may be the largest secret in the program.

6. Fallthrough must introduce itself

Fallthrough lets a case execute not because it matched, but because it lives downstairs.

There are legitimate uses. Our language permits them, but requires an explicit declaration:

switch (mode) {
  case FULL:
    runExtendedChecks()
    fallthrough

  case BASIC:
    runBasicChecks()
}

Without fallthrough, each arm stops at its boundary.

Grouped labels are different:

case PENDING, QUEUED:
  wait()

Two labels share one body. No body spills into another.

The benefit of explicit fallthrough is not that it prevents every mistake. It makes physical case ordering an acknowledged dependency.

Implicit fallthrough makes that dependency a surprise.

Actual fallthrough into or out of default is prohibited in this language. Default already has a difficult job: explaining what happens when selection finds no match. It should not also serve as a corridor for matched cases.

Shared follow-up work belongs after the switch if it is unconditional, or in an explicitly called helper if it is not.

Default is not the communal kitchen.

7. Logging is not a branching problem

There is one conditional our language rejects for a different reason:

if (debug) {
  emitLogs()
}
// SYNTAX ERROR: conditional-logging
// Use log.level(...) instead.

The answer is not:

wilsonIf (debug) {
  emitLogs()
} else nothing

We have clarified the wrong decision.

Logging policy belongs to the logging system:

log.level(DEBUG, "Placement candidate evaluated", candidate)

Here, log.level(...) is our fictional logging API: it submits an event at a specified severity. Configuration determines whether that event is emitted.

The application reports what happened. The logger decides which reports are currently wanted.

Otherwise, logging policy becomes distributed across dozens of booleans and branches. During an incident, we discover that the evidence we need was conditional on a flag whose location was also a secret.

Expensive diagnostic construction may still need a lazy logging API or an enabled-level check. That is a resource decision, not a reason to scatter ordinary log filtering throughout the application.

8. What the language knows—and what it does not

Wilson’s Law does not require every alternative to contain work.

It requires the program to distinguish:

  • Conditional action.
  • Terminating guard.
  • Binary choice.
  • Intentional inaction.
  • Multiway dispatch.
  • Ordered predicates.
  • Unexpected input.
  • Deliberate fallthrough.

A normal language can already express these. Our fictional language makes some of the distinctions compulsory.

A linter could approximate much of this without inventing new keywords: reject redundant else, check exhaustive switches, require explicit fallthrough, flag selected empty branches, and keep ordinary logging policy out of application conditionals.

But neither a compiler nor a linter can establish that every declared decision is a good one.

We can remove every else from a codebase. The conditions will continue to be false.

We can add every missing else. The alternatives may remain unconsidered.

The objective is not more branches or fewer branches.

It is fewer secrets.

The alternative exists whether we write it down or not. The paperwork is optional; the consequences are not.

Appendix

title: When the Past Shapes Action: Understanding Embodied Memory
description:
arXiv:2610.41688v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the capabilities of embodied AI, enabling increasingly general navigation, manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. However, effective interaction with dynamic environments requires more than only strong perception and reasoning: agents must act with partial knowledge and retain, retrieve, and update information from past observations, actions, and experiences. This survey examines embodied memory as a mechanism for preserving decision-relevant information beyond the current observation. We organize existing approaches along two complementary dimensions: six fundamental memory requirements, spanning world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning; and eight architectural categories, including recurrent states, fast weights, visual and symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems. We analyze their capabilities and limitations, and examine how existing benchmarks evaluate memory-dependent behavior, distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task performance. Finally, we identify open challenges in selecting relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs in changing environments, and consolidating knowledge across episodes. Our analysis provides a framework for understanding memory as an essential component of reliable, adaptive, and lifelong-horizon embodied intelligence.

title: My Learning Notes: HTML & CSS
description:
What I Learned in Class: HTML & CSS Basics
In class,we discussed the main three used in front-end development:HTML CSS and JavaScript.we then looked a diagram which was easier to understand.

HTML (The Skeleton): Provides the content and acts as a structural backbone of a webpage. It holds headings, paragraphs, images.
CSS (The Look): Gives styling to the webpage. It controls the colors, fonts, layout.
JavaScript (The Brain): It makes the page to do actions by giving life it makes the whole interactive.

HTML & CSS in real applications:
HTML: Every single website on the internet uses HTML—whether it's Google, YouTube, or online news sites—to structure text, images, and links.

CSS: Without CSS, every website on the web would just look like black&white text where CSS turns normal text into creative layouts.

  1. What is a Markup Language, and why is HTML one?
    HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. A markup language is a system for "marking up" text with tags so that a web browser knows how to structure and display it.
    HTML is classified as a markup language because it doesn't solve math problems, execute functions, or handle logic. It simply defines where both machine and human can understand.

  2. What is the difference between HTML and other programming languages?
    Unlike programming languages like Python, Java, HTML does not have logic. It doesn't use variables, if/else conditions, or loops. Programming languages process data and perform actions, while HTML just structures and organizes content.

  3. What is the latest version of HTML in use today?
    The latest version of HTML is HTML5. It introduced modern features like native video/audio playback, new semantic tags (header, footer, article), and better mobile support. Today, HTML5 is the living standard maintained across all modern web browsers.

  4. Are there replacements for HTML? Why or why not?
    I also searched about alternatives to HTML. Things like JSX (used in React), Pug, or Markdown are often used by developers to write templates faster.

However, these are not true replacements for HTML! Tools like JSX or Markdown are just converted back into standard HTML before the browser reads them. The web browser only understands pure HTML, which is why HTML remains irreplaceable for web structure.

To write my code, I use Visual Studio Code (VS Code), which is an IDE (Integrated Development Environment).
Created a project folder and opened it in VS Code
Created an index.html file.
Installed the Live Server extension. whenever I save my code the browser updates instantly without me needing to refresh

The 3 Ways to Use CSS

  1. Inline CSS
    You write the styling directly inside the HTML tag using the style attribute.
    but typing over and over makes code hard to read.

  2. Internal CSS
    You write your CSS inside a style block in the head section
    easier than inline CSS but it only works for that single page.

  3. External CSS
    You create a completely separate file like style.css and link it to your HTML page inside the head tag.
    This is best among the three as it can control many pages with one CSS file which makes it easier and faster.
    I'm excited to keep learning.

title: Cloud vs On-Premises Infrastructure
description:
Modern businesses require reliable IT infrastructure to manage applications, store information, and provide support for staff. But what will you choose, cloud infrastructure or on-premises infrastructure?

Cloud infrastructure provides flexibility and scalability plus you are able to take advantage of managed technology. On the other hand, on-premises provides you with full control over hardware, predictable scalability, and you are managing the technology.

It really depends on your workload, needs, security requirements, and cost.

What is Cloud Infrastructure?

Cloud infrastructure enables you to utilise computing resources such as servers, storage, databases, and networking from third party cloud providers.

Rather than buying your own hardware, you can lease what you need. Some popular options are Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud.

Advantages of Cloud Infrastructure

  • Scalability – Easily increase or decrease resources to meet demand.
  • Lower up front cost – You will not have to buy expensive hardware.
  • Remote access – Employees will have access to applications.
  • Faster – New environments and applications can be deployed quickly.
  • Managed – You can take advantage of managed databases, monitoring, backups, etc.

Cloud infrastructure can be useful for businesses with changing workloads, expanding digital platforms, and remote teams.

What is On-premises IT Infrastructure?

  • On-premises infrastructure is where you will purchase, install, and manage computing resources.
  • You will be managing your own servers, storage, networking hardware, security, and updates.

Advantages of On-premises Infrastructure

  • More control – You are managing your own hardware.
  • Management – You have full control over where your information is stored.
  • Predictable costs – Once you have bought your hardware, there will be less costs depending on how much you use each month.
  • Low latency – Systems on the same network will have low latency.
  • Customisable – You can set the infrastructure to suit your needs. This option may be suitable if you have steady workloads, specialised hardware, strict data handling, or have invested in infrastructure.

What Workloads Benefit Most from Cloud Infrastructure?

There are some workloads that will greatly benefit from using cloud infrastructure.

Websites/E-commerce

Websites and e-commerce sites can suffer from unpredictable traffic. Cloud infrastructure means you can easily scale resources when running promotions, seasonal sales, or high traffic periods.

Development

Development teams often require temporary environments to develop, test, and deploy software. With cloud infrastructure these can easily be created and removed.

Data Analysis

If you have large amounts of data to analyse, you can utilise cloud based analysis tools. This means you are not having to invest in extra computing hardware. You can also reduce unnecessary data transfer by keeping your analysis tools close to your data.

Backup

Cloud storage can assist with backup and disaster recovery. This means you can keep copies of your important business information in different locations.

Unpredictable resource demand

If you have applications that require unpredictable resources, cloud infrastructure can help you scale your resources. This will save you having to buy hardware for occasional peak times.

What Workloads Benefit Most from On-premises Infrastructure?

Despite the move towards cloud infrastructure, on-premises infrastructure can still be useful.

Predictable resource demand

If you have systems that are always running with predictable resource demand, you may want to invest in dedicated hardware. This will save you having to pay for unused cloud infrastructure flexibility.

Strict data handling

Some businesses will have strict data handling requirements due to contractual, regulatory, or internal policies. Depending on your requirements, you may want to utilise dedicated on-premises infrastructure.

Low latency

If you have manufacturing systems, industrial machinery, or applications that are talking to local hardware you may require very fast local network responses. On-premises or edge computing can help with this.

Legacy applications

Some legacy applications will require specific hardware, or operating systems. This may mean that you will have to heavily redevelop them to use them in the cloud.

Specialised hardware

If you have specialised computing hardware or bespoke infrastructure then on-premises infrastructure may be more suitable.

Why Hybrid Infrastructure is Becoming Important

  • Sometimes you may not want to choose just one option.

  • Hybrid infrastructure enables you to use a mix of both cloud and on-premises infrastructure to ensure your workloads are in the best environment.

For example:

  • Main business applications can be hosted on cloud infrastructure.
  • Sensitive databases can be kept on a secure on-premises infrastructure.
  • Development can be completed on temporary cloud resources.
  • Backups can be done via cloud storage.

This gives you flexibility, whilst still keeping control over your workloads.

Hybrid infrastructure will need to be properly integrated. You will need to have centralised identity, monitoring, network access, and backup.

Things to Consider

Before choosing your infrastructure, you should consider:

Total Cost

Infrastructure costs can be more than just servers or monthly costs. You will need to consider electricity, cooling, maintenance, licences, staff, storage, network usage, and data transfer costs.

Security

You need to know what security requirements you will have. What access control, encryption, and regulatory requirements you have.

Scalability

If you expect to grow quickly or have unpredictable workloads then cloud infrastructure can help you scale. If you have predictable workloads then on-premises can be more cost effective.

Current Infrastructure

You should consider your current hardware, application requirements, and migration needs.

Technical Skills

Cloud infrastructure requires you to have knowledge of cloud architecture, identity, networking, and optimising costs. On-premises will require you to have hardware, networking, and virtualisation skills.

Common Mistakes

When choosing between cloud and on-premises infrastructure, you should not make your decision purely based on industry trends.

Common mistakes include:

  • Moving everything to the cloud.
  • Not considering data transfer/storage costs.
  • Underestimating hardware maintenance and replacement costs.
  • Ignoring licence requirements.
  • Assuming cloud infrastructure will be more secure.
  • Keeping identities and monitoring separate.

By analysing your workloads you can avoid unnecessary costs of migrating.

Final Thoughts

Both cloud and on-premises infrastructure play an important role in modern IT. Cloud infrastructure provides scalability, flexibility, and faster deployment. On-premises infrastructure provides you with full control over your hardware, predictable scalability, and the ability to customise.

Many organisations choose hybrid infrastructure.

The best option is to analyse each of your workloads, understand your technical requirements, calculate the total cost, and choose the infrastructure that will provide the most value in the long term.

Want to know which infrastructure will be best for your business?

Check out this detailed guide:
Cloud vs On-Premises IT Infrastructure: Which Is Right for Each Workload?

See how your workloads, scalability, security, costs, and hybrid infrastructure can impact your infrastructure choice.

title: Your PDF export is becoming a second frontend
description:
The ticket says "Add PDF export."

Four words. Very calm words.

You build an invoice. Three line items. One page. The logo is where logos traditionally live.

Then someone adds a longer company name, 87 line items, and a payment note.

The total lands on page three. The footer starts a solo career.

The file still downloads successfully. Apparently, everything is fine.

A successful render and a usable document are two different acceptance criteria.

I'm building Bitavu, a visual template editor with a JSON-to-PDF API. This is the design problem behind it: how do you let a document evolve without making every layout adjustment another application change?

The useful answer starts with how you test and release the template.

The first PDF is the easy one

A demo invoice is an extremely cooperative customer.

It has a short name. Its address fits. Its three descriptions are roughly the same length. It would never order enough things to inconvenience your page margins.

Real documents have less interest in your demo.

A request like "make the description column wider" can change row heights. Those heights affect page breaks. A page break can separate a total from the lines that explain it.

That is how a small layout change earns a surprisingly large review.

Treating the template as something you can test and release gives you a way to handle that review deliberately.

Give the layout its own home

There are two different jobs inside an invoice.

Your application knows what happened: who bought what, which amounts apply, and when payment is due.

The template decides how to present it: columns, spacing, branding, repeated headings, and where content continues onto another page.

A useful boundary looks like this:

Application data + tested template revision → PDF

That boundary can live entirely in your own codebase. You do not need a separate service to adopt it.

What matters is being able to change the layout while keeping its expected input clear.

In Bitavu Studio, that separation is expressed through visual document blocks, JSON bindings, and saved template revisions. A repeating table can take its rows from an items array; the backend supplies the data.

The visual editor gives layout work a place to happen. You still need to review the result.

Give your invoice some deeply inconvenient data

Before changing the design, save a small set of synthetic fixtures.

Start with a tidy invoice so you can spot obvious mistakes. Then make the data less polite.

Fixture What to check
One item, then enough items to span several pages Table continuation, repeated headings, and footer placement
The last row count that fits, then one more row The exact transition onto the next page
A long company name and multi-line address Wrapping and the space left above the table
One very long item description Row splitting and whether its quantity and amount remain easy to associate
Missing optional notes or address lines Intended fallbacks and unwanted blank space
Names with accents and symbols used by your customers Font coverage, shaping, and alignment

The "one more row" case deserves special attention.

If 18 rows fit and 19 spill over, keep both fixtures. Those numbers belong to that particular template, font, and data; they are not a universal page capacity.

Also try the same row count with longer descriptions. Counting rows alone will not tell you how tall a table becomes.

The goal is to find the point where the layout changes behavior, then keep a test on either side of it.

Your least cooperative fake customer is doing valuable work here.

Make the backend request boring

Once the template has a clear input shape, the integration should be straightforward.

Here is a synthetic Bitavu invoice request. Save it as request.json:

{
  "templateId": "invoice",
  "revision": 3,
  "data": {
    "invoice": {
      "number": "INV-2027-014",
      "date": "2027-01-12",
      "due": "2027-02-11"
    },
    "client": {
      "name": "Bitavu Studio",
      "address": "74372 Washington Ave\nColumbus, 7206"
    },
    "items": [
      {"description": "Brand strategy workshop", "quantity": 1, "unitPrice": 650},
      {"description": "Design system", "quantity": 3, "unitPrice": 280},
      {"description": "Project support", "quantity": 2, "unitPrice": 95}
    ],
    "notes": "Thank you for working with us."
  }
}

invoice and revision 3 identify the example. Use a saved template ID and revision from your own workspace, with data that matches its bindings.

With your scoped API key in BITAVU_API_KEY, this Bash example creates a key for one render operation and sends the request:

# Create once for this operation. Reuse it for this operation's retries.
BITAVU_RENDER_KEY="$(node -e 'console.log(require("node:crypto").randomUUID())')"

curl --fail-with-body --retry 2 --retry-delay 2 \
  https://api.bitavu.com/v1/render \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BITAVU_API_KEY" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $BITAVU_RENDER_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data @request.json \
  --output invoice.pdf

The successful response is the PDF itself.

Keep the API key on your server. For a new operation, generate a new idempotency key. For a retry of the same operation, preserve the key, request body, and template revision.

If you retry later, do not rerun the key-generation line and accidentally turn the retry into a new operation.

A saved design should not surprise production

Suppose production requests revision 3.

You adjust the column widths and save a new revision. Production should keep using 3 while you review the change.

A practical release sequence is:

  1. Render the saved fixtures against the candidate revision.
  2. Check the resulting pages, especially the page-boundary cases.
  3. Approve the layout and confirm that the application's data still matches.
  4. Update the revision requested by production.

A revision pin controls which template you request. It is not a promise that every byte of every PDF will be identical: renderer changes, fonts, and referenced assets also matter.

For the same reason, a PDF binary diff is a poor substitute for checking the document. Metadata can change without changing the page; a misplaced total can matter enormously even though the file opens.

If a field changes from client.name to customer.legalName, treat that as an integration change too. Moving the layout into an editor does not make the data contract disappear.

When a visual editor earns its place

For one fixed document that rarely changes, a small rendering function in your application may be all you need.

The balance shifts when layouts keep changing, several templates share branding, or someone needs to adjust the document without editing application code.

That is the workflow I'm building Bitavu for: a visual place to maintain the template, with a versioned API for the application that uses it.

You still choose the data contract. You still test the awkward cases. You get a clearer place to make and review the layout changes.

The paper monster gets a new job.

What is the most uncooperative thing you have ever had to fit on an invoice?

title: How Featured's users make 100K media pitches per month on Vercel
description:
Featured on Vercel

  • 3 engineers supporting 3 brands and 100,000+ users on Vercel

  • Migrated 374 Sanity sites from AWS Elastic Beanstalk to Vercel

  • AI SDK and AI Gateway power Featured's chat bot across 17 models

  • Workflow SDK replaced custom long-running job infrastructure

Featured is a co-pilot for public relations (PR) that subject matter experts and PR teams use to find media opportunities. Tell Featured's agents what you know, and it surfaces opportunities across journalist requests, podcasts, awards, and GEO, with no PR background required.

Founder Brett Farmiloe knows from experience how hard and time consuming getting press is. He spent 10 years running Markitors, a digital marketing agency with 500 small business clients. Every client, from an eyelash extension supplier to an equipment financing company, had real expertise to share, but no way to get it in front of journalists. PR, as Farmiloe puts it, "has always been about who has access to what." He founded Featured to change the question from who has access to who has knowledge.

Featured connects one of their users with a journalist or publisher every 6 seconds. Their agents deliver more than 100,000 media pitches per month, and have sent over 100 million Help A Reporter Out (HARO) emails in the past year.

Behind it all is an engineering team of just three people. With a team that lean, there's no time to manage servers or piece together custom integrations. Every hour spent on infrastructure is an hour taken away from building features what will help their customers land more media placements.

The cost of managing infrastructure by hand

Before Vercel, Featured’s infrastructure work pulled the team away from product development. Hosting lived on AWS Elastic Beanstalk, AI features depended on custom provider integrations, and long-running, multi-step jobs ran on separate orchestration infrastructure. Each layer worked, but each one added operational overhead for a three-person team supporting multiple brands.

One platform for compute, AI primitives, and model access

The migration to Vercel started with a forcing function: Featured needed to launch 374 Sanity sites at once, and every Elastic Beanstalk deploy had to be manually spun up, migrated, and then torn down.

When you multiply that process by almost four hundred, the math doesn't work, even when you divide it across a team of three. Vercel collapsed each site launch into to a single-click deploy.

Once the sites were live, the team evaluated Vercel for background jobs and AI tooling, eventually migrating their entire app and the agents that run in it.

Compute without the clusters

Deploys that once meant standing up a new EB instance, migrating the URL, and terminating the old one became a single click. On Vercel, all 374 sites shipped from one platform, and rollouts across all three brands now happen centrally, instead of one cluster at a time. "In hindsight, doing each one of those by hand was kind of crazy," Farmiloe admits.

AI SDK and AI Gateway: one abstraction for every model

AI SDK and AI Gateway handle all of Featured's model traffic through a single abstraction, so their team doesn't have to manage custom rate-limit or API integrations from multiple providers.

Featured routes across 17 models at any given time. Calling a model is one standardized function with a schema, and swapping providers is a configuration change instead of a rewrite. When a new model ships, the team can test it against Featured's use cases right away.

Workflow SDK for long-running backend jobs

After migrating their AI stack, Featured moved long-running jobs from a separate orchestration system onto Workflow SDK. These are the processes that can't live in a request cycle: monitoring the media around the clock, qualifying opportunities, and combining all of those signals to deliver more than 100,000 pitches a month.

Chat became the product

As users kept choosing conversation over navigation, the team made chat Featured's primary interface, and they deliver it through eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework.

eve's useEveAgent hook made the new interface easy to implement. Instead of wiring up an agent by hand, the team got durable sessions, streaming, tool calls, and approval prompts out of the box, with model calls routed through AI Gateway so they can pick the right model per task without managing provider keys.

What would have been a months-long rebuild was a week-long replace and refactor. Now, instead of a dashboard with dozens of buttons, users ask Featured questions, and the team adapts the product to their needs, not the other way around.

What's next

Featured is building toward being the AI layer for public relations, the same way dedicated agent platforms have emerged for legal and finance. The goal is to make it faster and easier for anyone with expertise to share their knowledge and get featured in the media.

The team's advice to other founders building in the agentic era:

  • Know that your data is your moat. For us, access to good information is what lets Featured connect people with the sources that want to publish them.

  • Lean on tested abstractions like Vercel instead of reinventing security and infrastructure by hand.

About Featured: Featured is a co-pilot for public relations that helps people find media opportunities, submit pitches, and get featured in the press. Featured also owns and operates Help A Reporter Out (HARO) and Connectively, journalist request platforms connecting sources with publishers.

title: ORION: An Outcome-Driven LLM Advisor for RL-Based Multi-Domain 6G Slice Placement
description:
arXiv:2610.41563v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. Experiments on a parametrized family of multi-domain topologies show that no fixed planning strategy dominates across all regimes: the performance ranking reverses between topology classes, and feasible placements exist for most rejected requests but remain undiscovered. These findings identify the plan layer as the decisive performance lever. We introduce ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and generate abstract placement plans. A cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, while per-domain agents place the functions. ORION main contribution lies at the plan layer: an outcome-driven episodic memory that records, for each completed attempt, the network-condition profile, the proposed plan, and its verified feasibility outcome. The memory feeds verified successes and labelled failures back to the planner, thereby closing the adaptation loop using deployment feasibility rather than a scalar reward assigned to the planner's own proposals. To isolate the effect of the plan quality, we evaluate the planner on held-out topology families while keeping the downstream selection and execution mechanisms fixed. Under this controlled setting, the proposed memory improves admission by $4.6$--$11.5$ percentage points over the same planner without memory, while importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.

title: Per-Tenant Buckets or Shared Prefixes: Signed Upload and Download for Private User Files
description:
Use one private bucket per tenant, keep every object private, and issue short-lived signed URLs for the upload and for every later download. Then keep the deletion deadline in your database rather than in a bucket rule, because the storage layer is the wrong place to park a promise you will one day have to prove you kept.

That is the whole architecture.

The system I have in mind is a healthtech SaaS: forty clinics on one platform, each pushing signed intake and consent PDFs straight from a browser, each document carrying an explicit deletion deadline — years for the clinical record, thirty days after an erasure request under GDPR Article 17, and immediately when a clinic offboards. App users never touch the bucket. They get a URL that works for one object, for a few minutes, and then expires.

The retention clock nobody owns

Capacity planning first, because it decides most of what follows. Forty clinics, roughly 120 signed documents a day each, averaging 900 KB, is about 4.3 GB a day and 130 GB a month, and that pile only grows, since almost none of it is eligible for deletion in the year it arrives. Uploads are cheap: one PUT per document, one grant issued. Downloads are the interesting side, because every document gets pulled a handful of times by clinicians and billing staff, and each pull is a signed URL your API has to mint plus egress your provider will invoice.

The failure mode isn't the upload path. It's the clock.

A consent PDF lands with a deadline attached, and in most systems that deadline ends up living in exactly one place — a lifecycle rule somebody configured in a console eighteen months ago, or a spreadsheet, or nobody's head. Then a patient files an erasure request, you have thirty days, and the question on the table isn't whether the object is gone but whether you can show which objects were deleted, when, and by what. That is an audit question, and buckets keep almost no audit state. Rows do.

So write the service level objective down before you write any code: zero objects alive past their deletion date, measured daily by a job that reports a count. An auditor cares about that number. You should care about it for a duller reason, which is that a count of zero every morning is the only evidence your retention worker is still running at all.

Which vendor holds the bytes matters less here than how long it takes to wire the second and third capability around them — the queue that drains the deletion backlog, the scheduler that wakes the worker. That is the argument for Infrai in this particular workflow, since the API is self-describing and each capability publishes its own request schema, response schema and runnable examples, so adding the signed-upload step is a matter of reading one endpoint description instead of adopting another SDK. If you are a small platform team that wants storage, scheduling and queueing behind one key and one bill, Infrai is worth trying for exactly this slice of the system.

Should each tenant get its own bucket for private file upload and signed download?

Bucket per tenant, if the tenant count lets you. The isolation is the kind you can explain to a security reviewer without drawing a diagram: a credential scoped to one bucket cannot read another clinic's documents, per-bucket usage reporting hands you a real per-tenant number for the invoice, and offboarding a clinic becomes a delete on one bucket instead of a paginated walk over a prefix you hope you filtered correctly.

The catch is that buckets are a bounded resource. Every S3-compatible provider caps how many an account may hold, some of them behind a quota request, so bucket-per-tenant is comfortable in the tens and hundreds and stops being comfortable somewhere in the thousands. If you run self-serve signup, where a tenant is created by a form submission at three in the morning and half of them never upload anything, a shared bucket with a strictly server-derived key prefix is the honest choice, and the isolation moves into your authorization layer where at least you can unit-test it.

Either way the database is your index. Storage list operations filter by prefix and nothing else, so ownership, MIME type, logical state and the deletion deadline belong in rows; the bucket holds bytes and only bytes. The beginner version of this design puts the tenant id in the object key and calls that isolation. It isn't. It's a naming convention that survives exactly until one handler forgets to check who is asking.

The API call that hands out an upload grant

The flow is four steps. Your API authorizes the request against tenant and role, inserts a row in state pending with the deadline already computed, asks the storage layer for a presigned PUT with a short expiry, and returns that URL alone to the browser. The browser uploads the bytes directly. A confirm endpoint then flips the row to stored once the object is really there.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const presignPath = "/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"

type uploadGrant struct {
    URL       string            `json:"url"`
    Method    string            `json:"method"`
    ExpiresAt string            `json:"expires_at"`
    Headers   map[string]string `json:"headers"`
    MaxBytes  *int64            `json:"max_bytes"`
}

// presignPut asks for a short-lived upload URL for one tenant's object.
// The bucket stays private; the browser only ever sees the returned URL,
// and it must never see the Bearer token used here.
func presignPut(bucket, key, idempotencyKey string, ttl time.Duration) (uploadGrant, error) {
    payload, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "op":              "put",
        "expires_seconds": int(ttl.Seconds()),
    })
    if err != nil {
        return uploadGrant{}, err
    }
    path := strings.NewReplacer("{bucket}", bucket, "{key}", url.PathEscape(key)).Replace(presignPath)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.infrai.cc"+path, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return uploadGrant{}, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return uploadGrant{}, err
        }
        raw, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(backoff(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
            return uploadGrant{}, fmt.Errorf("presign %s: status %d body %s", key, res.StatusCode, raw)
        }

        var envelope struct {
            Data uploadGrant `json:"data"`
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &envelope); err != nil {
            return uploadGrant{}, err
        }
        return envelope.Data, nil
    }
    return uploadGrant{}, fmt.Errorf("presign %s: rate limited on every attempt", key)
}

func backoff(retryAfter string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if secs, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && secs > 0 {
        return time.Duration(secs) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func main() {
    key := "clinic-8842/2026/consent/patient-4471-intake.pdf"
    grant, err := presignPut("tenant-clinic-8842", key, "grant:"+key, 10*time.Minute)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Println("could not issue upload grant:", err)
        return
    }
    fmt.Println(grant.Method, "until", grant.ExpiresAt)
}

Two things in there carry weight. The idempotency key means a retry after a network wobble returns the same grant instead of minting a second one, which matters because the platform treats Idempotency-Key as a convention on cost-incurring writes, derives a deterministic key when you omit it, and deduplicates over a 24-hour window by default. The other is what is absent: no Authorization header goes anywhere near the presigned URL. That header belongs to your server, and the browser holding a copy of it is the single most expensive mistake available in this design.

Ten minutes is my default expiry for uploads. Downloads I would cut shorter, maybe two, because a download link is the one that ends up pasted into a support ticket.

Buy versus build, against the actual bill

The effective cost of this workload is not a per-GB line. It's four lines: bytes at rest that grow every month and never shrink, egress on every staff download, one API call per grant issued, and the engineering time to build a retention worker plus the on-call attention to keep it honest. That last line is the one that gets left out of the spreadsheet, and it's usually the largest.

Option How you integrate Ops load Fits when Main limit
Amazon S3 SDK per language, IAM policy per tenant High — IAM, lifecycle and keys are yours You need Object Lock, replication, or you are already deep in AWS The IAM model is a project of its own
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible SDK Medium Download-heavy workloads where egress dominates Thinner surrounding ecosystem than S3
Backblaze B2 S3-compatible SDK Medium Long cold retention of finished documents Fewer regions for pinning EU data
MinIO, self-hosted S3-compatible SDK on your hardware Highest — durability is your problem Bytes are contractually forbidden to leave your racks You are now on call for storage
Supabase Storage Client SDK with Postgres-backed rules Low Small apps already living on Supabase Couples the file layer to one platform
Infrai Plain REST over one key, no SDK to install Low Signed upload and download wired next to a queue and a scheduler No object versioning or write-once lock

Two rows in that table are disqualifying depending on your regulator. If legal needs write-once retention that an administrator cannot delete early, you want S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, and no amount of application discipline substitutes for it — Infrai's storage layer lacks object versioning and an immutability lock, so that requirement sends you to AWS and you should let it. The same goes for automatic multi-region copies: if the design says an EU replica must be maintained by the platform rather than by you, this layer does not do that, and you either stitch replication yourself or buy from someone who ships it. Stick with a specialist when the compliance control is the product.

Verifying the deadline, and the failure you cannot roll back

The daily verifier is nine lines of SQL wrapped in a job: count rows where delete_after < now() and state is not deleted. Alert on anything above zero. Then sample a dozen keys that should already be gone and confirm the object store agrees with your database, because the day those two disagree is the day you find out your worker has been marking rows without ever calling the delete.

Deletion itself should be two-phase — mark, wait out a short grace window, then delete — and the reason is a real constraint rather than caution for its own sake. There is no object versioning here to undo a wrong delete, and no conditional write to arbitrate two workers racing on the same key, so the arbitration has to live in your own code as a row lock or a single consumer per tenant. A lifecycle rule is a good backstop for whatever the worker misses, though its granularity is a day at minimum, so it can never express "delete within the hour" and should not be sold to compliance as if it could.

One operational footnote that costs an afternoon if you skip it: switch paid billing on before your first production write, since trial credit does not cover durable storage.

Rolling back the isolation decision is easier than it looks, and worth planning for while the tenant count is small. Server-side copy lets you re-lay-out objects from per-tenant buckets into a shared prefix layout, or the other way, with keys stable and the database untouched. I am not sure there is a clean answer for the reverse case, where you have already deleted on a deadline and someone asks for the document back — that direction has no rollback at all, which is the strongest argument I know for the grace window.

If that boundary fits your system, the signed-upload walkthrough is a reasonable next step for checking the request shape against your own key derivation before you commit.

Further reading

  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • GDPR Article 17, right to erasure — https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/
  • Sharing an object with a presigned URL, Amazon S3 — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html
  • Locking objects with S3 Object Lock — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

title: What migrating a Vuetify 2 dashboard to Vue 3 actually took
description:
Vue 2 reached end of life on 31 December 2023. Vuetify 2 followed on 25 January 2025. If your admin panel still runs on them, it gets no security fixes, and every SOC 2 or ISO 27001 review asks why.

To show what the move involves, I migrated a well-known open-source app in public: Creative Tim's Vuetify Material Dashboard (MIT, 1.3k GitHub stars). The full branch is here: https://github.com/SayedEsmail/vuetify-material-dashboard. Every commit handles one concern and lists the breaking changes it fixed, so the commit log reads as the migration plan. I wrote the plan, did the work with an AI coding assistant, and reviewed every change myself at the end.

The starting point

  • Vue 2.6, Vuetify 2.2, Vuex 3, Vue Router 3, Vue CLI 4 on webpack 4.
  • 33 single-file components and 5,620 lines of JavaScript and Vue.
  • 553 lines of custom SASS written against Vuetify 2's internal class names.

The target was Vue 3.5, Vuetify 3, Pinia, Vue Router 4 and Vite.

Step 0: delete before you migrate

Seven of the 33 components could not be reached. Five views had no route, and two components were only used by those views. A form-validation library was registered globally and never used. The test suite still asserted the Vue CLI scaffold text, so it could never pass.

Deleting that first removed a third of the code before any migration work started. It is the cheapest saving in every migration, and an audit finds it in an afternoon.

Why Vuetify 2 projects can't migrate "gradually"

The usual Vue 2 path is the @vue/compat build: run on Vue 3 in compatibility mode, then fix warnings one by one. That path is closed when the app uses Vuetify 2, because Vuetify 2 cannot run on Vue 3 at all. The UI layer has to move in one step.

So the order matters:

  1. Tooling first: Vue CLI to Vite, then the new dependency set.
  2. App bootstrap: createApp, createVuetify, the i18n adapter.
  3. State and routing: Vuex to Pinia, Router 3 to 4. These are mechanical.
  4. Vue-2-only plugins: the chart wrapper had no Vue 3 version, so it became a 56-line local component on Chartist 1.x.
  5. Vuetify, from the outside in: layout shell, then the shared component library, then the views.
  6. The custom CSS layer last.

Where the real work is

Component APIs changed a lot, but those changes are well documented: v-list-item-content is gone, activator slots give props instead of on and attrs, v-tabs-items became v-window. I hit 43 distinct breaking changes and logged each one. That list is now the checklist I run in every audit.

The expensive surprises were elsewhere:

  • Custom CSS on framework internals. 470 lines targeted classes like .theme--light, .v-size--default and .v-card__text. Not one of them exists in Vuetify 3. Nothing errors. The styles silently stop applying.
  • Behaviour that changed without an error. In Vuetify 3, a navigation item linked to / stays highlighted on every page unless you mark it exact. Alerts now clip anything positioned outside them. The build stays green and the UI is subtly wrong.
  • Bugs that were already there. The theme colour picker never reached dark mode because it read a property that was never defined. Turning the sidebar image back on stored the value true instead of an image URL. Neither was caused by the migration, but a migration is when someone finally reads every line.

The result

  • Vue 3.5, Vuetify 3.13, Pinia, Vue Router 4, Vite 8, ESLint 10.
  • 26 components, 3,644 lines of JavaScript and Vue, and 350 lines of SASS in one file.
  • The same 8 routes and the same behaviour, minus the two bugs above.
  • A test suite that runs: every route renders in the full layout with zero Vue warnings.

What I'd tell a team planning this

  1. Run an inventory first. Dead code, undeclared dependencies and tests that can't pass are common, and they change the scope.
  2. Budget for CSS and visual QA, not only for component syntax.
  3. If you use Vuetify 2, plan the UI layer as one cut-over, behind a feature branch, with route-level smoke tests in place before you start.
  4. Decide the target versions up front. Vuetify 4 is out now. Going to Vuetify 3 first is still the shorter step from Vuetify 2, and 3 to 4 is a much smaller change.

If your product still runs on Vue 2, Nuxt 2 or Vuetify 2, I do a fixed-price migration readiness audit: a written report with the dead code, the breaking changes that apply to your codebase, the risks, and a fixed quote for the migration.

Sayed Esmail · https://github.com/SayedEsmail · https://linkedin.com/in/sayed-esmail-khattab

title: Building Production Features with the Claude API in Java
description:
Why Claude Belongs in Your Java Architecture

Most Java teams first meet large language models through a demo: a chat window, a clever prompt, a convincing answer. Turning that demo into a production feature is a different job. The model call becomes one more remote dependency with latency, rate limits, timeouts, and failure modes. Its output is probabilistic, so it needs validation before anything downstream trusts it. And it handles data that often belongs to customers, so security and auditability matter from the first request.

Claude, the family of models from Anthropic, fits well into this kind of backend. It is available through the Claude API, it supports tool use so the model can call your own functions, and it can process long documents and structured inputs. This article shows how to integrate it into a Java service in a way that you can test, observe, and operate. We will cover the request model, a minimal client, structured output with validation, tool use, error handling, and the operational concerns that determine whether the feature survives contact with real traffic.

The Messages API in Brief

The Claude API exposes a Messages endpoint. You send a model name, a token limit, an optional system prompt, and a list of messages alternating between the user and the assistant. The response contains content blocks, usually text, and metadata such as token usage and a stop reason.

Three headers matter. The x-api-key header carries your secret key, the anthropic-version header pins the API version so behavior does not change under you, and content-type declares a JSON body. Keep the key in a secrets manager or environment variable, never in source code. Use a dedicated key per service so you can rotate it without affecting other systems.

Model choice is an engineering decision. Smaller, faster models suit classification, extraction, and routing. Larger models suit multi-step reasoning and nuanced writing. Pick the smallest model that meets your quality bar, measure it, and revisit the choice as your requirements change.

A Minimal Java Client

Java 21 ships with a capable HttpClient, which is enough for a first integration without adding a dependency. The example below sends a single message and returns the text of the first content block. It uses a plain JSON string for clarity; in a real service you would use Jackson to build and parse the payload.

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.Duration;

public class ClaudeClient {

    private static final String ENDPOINT = "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages";
    private static final String API_VERSION = "2023-06-01";

    private final HttpClient http = HttpClient.newBuilder()
            .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
            .build();
    private final String apiKey;
    private final String model;

    public ClaudeClient(String apiKey, String model) {
        this.apiKey = apiKey;
        this.model = model;
    }

    public String ask(String systemPrompt, String userMessage) throws Exception {
        String body = """
                {
                  "model": "%s",
                  "max_tokens": 1024,
                  "system": %s,
                  "messages": [
                    {"role": "user", "content": %s}
                  ]
                }
                """.formatted(model, jsonString(systemPrompt), jsonString(userMessage));

        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                .uri(URI.create(ENDPOINT))
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(60))
                .header("x-api-key", apiKey)
                .header("anthropic-version", API_VERSION)
                .header("content-type", "application/json")
                .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body))
                .build();

        HttpResponse<String> response = http.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Claude API error " + response.statusCode() + ": " + response.body());
        }
        return extractFirstText(response.body());
    }

    private static String jsonString(String value) {
        return "\"" + value.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("\"", "\\\"").replace("\n", "\\n") + "\"";
    }

    private static String extractFirstText(String json) {
        // Illustrative only: use a JSON library such as Jackson in production.
        int start = json.indexOf("\"text\":\"") + 8;
        int end = json.indexOf("\"", start);
        return json.substring(start, end);
    }
}

Two points deserve attention. First, the timeout is set on the request, not only on the connection, because a model call can legitimately take tens of seconds and a missing timeout can exhaust your thread pool. Second, the status check is explicit. A non-200 response should become a typed error in your domain, not a string that leaks into a user interface.

Getting Structured Output

Free text is hard to use in code. For most backend features you want a predictable shape: a category, a list of fields, a score. The reliable approach is to ask for JSON, describe the exact schema in the system prompt, and validate the result before using it.

public record TicketTriage(String category, String priority, String summary) {}

Ask the model to respond only with a JSON object matching this structure, then parse it with Jackson into the record. Validation is not optional. Check that the category belongs to your allowed set, that the priority is one of your known values, and that the summary is within your length limit. If validation fails, retry once with the validation error included in the prompt, and then fall back to a human queue. Treat the model as an untrusted input source, the same way you would treat a partner API.

Tool Use: Letting Claude Call Your Code

Tool use lets the model request an action from your application. You declare tools with a name, a description, and a JSON Schema for their inputs. When the model decides a tool is needed, it returns a tool_use block. Your code runs the function, then sends a tool_result block back in the next message. The loop continues until the model returns a final text answer.

This pattern is powerful for banking, support, and operations workflows, where the model should look up an account balance or a ticket status rather than guess. Keep the tools narrow, read-only where possible, and authorize every call against the end user's identity, not the service's. A model should never be able to do something the requesting user could not do directly.

Set a maximum number of tool-call iterations, such as five, so a confused model cannot loop indefinitely and multiply your costs.

Operational Concerns

Calling a model is cheap for a demo and expensive at scale, so design for cost from the start. Measure token usage per request and log it with the feature name, so you can see which parts of the product drive spend. Prompt caching lets you reuse a long, stable system prompt or document across requests at a lower cost, which is valuable for support assistants that repeat the same policy text.

Rate limits and transient errors are normal. Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter for 429 and 5xx responses, and respect any retry guidance in the response headers. Put a circuit breaker around the client so that a degraded provider does not drag your whole service down. Degrade gracefully: if the assistant is unavailable, show the standard workflow instead of an error page.

Observability is part of the feature. Track latency percentiles, error rates by status code, token usage, tool-call counts, and validation failures. A rising validation failure rate often signals a prompt regression or a change in input data before users notice.

Security and Data Handling

Before sending any data to a model, decide what it may contain. Customer identifiers, account numbers, and personal data should be removed or pseudonymized unless there is a clear need and an approved basis to include them. Review your provider terms and your organization's policies for data retention and processing. In regulated industries such as banking, involve your security and compliance teams early, not after the prototype works.

Protect against prompt injection. Text from documents, emails, or web pages can contain instructions that try to override your system prompt. Keep untrusted content clearly delimited, never let model output decide authorization, and validate every tool call against the current user's permissions.

Testing the Integration

Test the parts you control. Unit-test the prompt builder, the response parser, and the validation rules with fixed inputs. Keep a small set of representative examples and expected categories, and run them as a regression suite whenever you change the prompt or the model version. Model outputs are not deterministic, so assert on properties, such as valid JSON, allowed categories, and presence of required fields, rather than exact wording.

For the client, use a fake HTTP server in integration tests to simulate timeouts, 429 responses, and malformed bodies. Your retry and fallback logic should be exercised without calling the real API on every build.

Best Practices Checklist

  • Keep API keys in a secrets manager and use one key per service.
  • Pin the API version and choose the smallest model that meets your quality bar.
  • Set explicit timeouts and treat the model as an external dependency.
  • Require structured output and validate it before use.
  • Keep tools narrow, authorized against the end user, and capped per request.
  • Redact sensitive data before it leaves your boundary.
  • Defend against prompt injection in untrusted content.
  • Measure cost, latency, and validation failures per feature.
  • Test with fixtures and a fake server, not only with live calls.

Conclusion

Claude gives Java teams a capable model behind a straightforward HTTP API. The hard part is not the first request; it is everything that surrounds it: validation, timeouts, tool authorization, cost control, and testing. Treat the model like any other critical dependency and design the boundary carefully, and it becomes a dependable part of your architecture rather than a fragile experiment.

Key Takeaways

  • The Claude Messages API is a plain HTTP integration that Java handles well with the standard library or Jackson.
  • Structured output plus validation turns free text into something your code can trust.
  • Tool use lets the model act through your authorized functions, never around them.
  • Production readiness depends on timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, observability, and data protection.

title: How Does Website Speed Affect Search Engine Crawling and User Experience?
description:
Website speed plays an important role in both search engine optimization (SEO) and user experience. When a website loads quickly, visitors can access information easily, navigate between pages smoothly, and interact with the website without unnecessary delays. On the other hand, slow-loading websites can frustrate visitors, increase bounce rates, and make it harder for search engines to efficiently process website content.

In today's competitive digital environment, website speed is not just a technical requirement; it is an important part of building a successful online presence.

  1. Website Speed and Search Engine Crawling

Search engines use automated bots, such as Googlebot, to discover and crawl website pages. Website performance can influence how efficiently these bots access and process content.

A slow server response, frequent timeouts, or technical errors may make crawling less efficient. Improving server performance and reducing unnecessary loading delays can help search engines access website content more reliably.

  1. Faster Websites Improve User Experience Visitors expect websites to load quickly, especially when browsing through mobile devices. If a page takes too long to display, users may leave before finding the information they need.

A fast website provides:

  • Smooth navigation.
  • Faster access to important information.
  • Better mobile browsing.
  • Improved interaction with website elements.
  • A more comfortable overall experience.
  1. Website Speed and Google Rankings

Google considers page experience signals when evaluating search results. Core Web Vitals are important performance measurements that help website owners understand the experience visitors receive.

The three main Core Web Vitals are:

  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): Measures how quickly the main content becomes visible.
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP): Measures how quickly a page responds to user interactions.
  • Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): Measures unexpected movement of page elements during loading.

Improving these metrics can contribute to a better page experience, although good Core Web Vitals scores do not guarantee higher rankings.

  1. Slow Websites Can Increase Visitor Drop-Off

When users encounter slow-loading pages, they may lose interest and move to another website. This can reduce engagement and potential conversions.

For example, imagine a customer searching for a local digital marketing agency. If one website loads within a few seconds while another takes much longer, the customer may prefer exploring the faster website.

  1. Mobile Website Speed Is Equally Important

A large number of users access websites through smartphones. Websites should therefore be optimized for different screen sizes, network conditions, and mobile devices.

Responsive design, optimized images, lightweight scripts, and
efficient hosting can help improve mobile performance.

  1. How Can Businesses Improve Website Speed?

Businesses can follow several practical steps:

  1. Compress and optimize website images.
  2. Use reliable web hosting.
  3. Enable browser caching.
  4. Minimize unnecessary CSS and JavaScript.
  5. Use a Content Delivery Network (CDN).
  6. Remove unnecessary plugins and scripts.
  7. Optimize website code and database performance.
  8. Regularly monitor Core Web Vitals using Google PageSpeed Insights.
  9. Website Speed and Business Growth

Website speed can influence how customers interact with a business online. A fast and responsive website makes it easier for visitors to explore services, read information, submit enquiries, and complete purchases.

For small businesses, improving website performance can support better customer experiences and help create a more professional online presence.

Conclusion

Website speed affects more than just loading time. It influences how efficiently search engines access website pages and how comfortably visitors interact with online content. Businesses should focus on technical performance, mobile optimization, and Core Web Vitals to create websites that are both search-engine-friendly and user-friendly.

title: When an AI SDK Installation Guide Doesn't Match Its Code Example
description:
Installing an SDK and following its integration guide should lead developers toward a compatible implementation.

But what happens when the installation instructions and the code example appear to target different generations of the SDK?

Consider a common integration scenario: building a streaming AI chat interface using a provider's API and a React SDK.

A developer follows the provider's guide:

  1. Installs the recommended SDK packages.
  2. Creates a React chat interface.
  3. Imports the chat hook using the documented import path.
  4. Implements message handling using the example provided.

The difficulty appears when the package installation and the example are compared against the current SDK API.

In newer versions of the Vercel AI SDK, React hooks are imported from "@ai-sdk/react", rather than the older "ai/react" export.

The newer API also introduces a transport-based architecture and changes how chat input and message content are handled.

This distinction matters.

A developer following an older example alongside an unversioned installation command may need to reconcile the SDK versions or adapt the implementation.

That introduces additional work that isn't necessarily obvious from the initial integration instructions.

The implementation responsibility

The provider makes its API available and supplies an integration example.

However, the developer still needs to establish:

  • Which SDK generation the example targets.
  • Whether the installed packages support the demonstrated imports.
  • Whether the chat hook uses the expected API.
  • Whether message rendering follows the installed SDK's message structure.

These responsibilities don't disappear simply because an integration example is provided.

The broader lesson

An integration guide is not just a collection of working-looking code snippets.

Its installation instructions, dependencies, imports and implementation examples need to describe a compatible implementation path.

When they don't clearly align, developers inherit the responsibility of reconciling those differences.

That is an important part of understanding the actual developer experience of a product.
