title: Accurate and Auditable ECG Classification via Visibility Graph Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.41795v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Physicians read electrocardiograms (ECGs) from waveform shape and timing, yet accurate deep-learning classifiers rarely show which waveform regions drive their predictions. We introduce LYNX-ECG, a graph neural network that represents each heartbeat as a sparse visibility graph of timestamped turning points. On CODE-Test, LYNX-ECG reaches a macro F1 score of 0.889, outperforming five baselines including the ECGFounder foundation model, while its graphs need about 14% of the storage of graphs built from every sample. Because each node maps to a specific ECG time, we can delete clinically defined waveform regions and alter beat timing to audit predictions. For conduction disorders, the clinically expected region was the strongest evidence in more than 90% of correct predictions. Bradycardia and tachycardia calls follow heart rate with conduction intervals held fixed, and atrial fibrillation calls vanish when beat-to-beat variation is removed. Sparse visibility graphs thus pair accurate ECG classification with clinically grounded, testable explanations.

title: I Built an SDK Because I Was Desperate
description:
This is not a story about a great idea I had in the shower. It's a story about
being hungry, tired, and slightly greedy, and deciding that the fastest path out
of that was to build something for a bank.

I'm writing it down because most "how I built X" posts skip the embarrassing
part. They start with "I noticed a gap in the market" and end with "and then it
was a huge success." That's not what happened here. What happened is: I was
desperate, I built an SDK, it mostly broke, I fixed it, and then I wrote about
it because that's how I process things.

Here's the honest version.

The foolish idea

I'd been looking at ALATPay's developer documentation for a different reason —
I wanted to integrate their payment gateway into something I was building. The
docs were fine. The JavaScript SDK was fine. But there was no Java SDK.

My first thought was the wrong one, and I want to be specific about why it was
wrong.

I thought: "If I build the Java SDK, maybe they'll pay me."

Not "maybe they'll hire me." Not "maybe it'll be a good portfolio piece." I
genuinely thought a bank would notice a random developer's unrequested
open-source project and decide to compensate them for it. That is not how banks
work. I knew that at the time, in the abstract. I chose not to know it in the
specific, because I was hungry and tired and looking for something to be true
that wasn't.

The SDK took five days to build. The compensation has, so far, been zero
naira. The portfolio piece has, so far, been worth more than I expected.

If you're reading this because you're thinking about building something for a
company hoping they'll pay you for it: don't do that. Build it because you
need it, or because it's a portfolio piece, or because you want to learn the
API. But don't build it for the money. The money is not coming.

What "everything broke" actually means

I want to describe this carefully because "everything broke" is what I told
a friend at the time, and it's accurate but not useful.

What actually happened is: everything broke at a specific moment, and then
one thing at a time after that.

The first version didn't work at all. The authentication was wrong. ALATPay
uses three headers — Authorization, Business-Id, and
Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key — and I was sending two of them. The third one
(Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key) is an Azure API Management convention that I
hadn't encountered before. I sent it under the wrong name, or not at all,
depending on the hour of the night.

I got 401s for a full day. Every 401 response told me the same thing — "invalid
subscription key" — and every time I read it, I thought "that can't be right, I
put the key in." I read it as a bug in their system, not a bug in my code. It
was a bug in my code.

The second version authenticated correctly but couldn't parse the response. The
list of transactions in ALATPay's response has more fields than I'd modelled.
My Jackson classes were missing feeAmount and settlementId and a dozen other
things. Jackson doesn't crash when it sees unknown fields by default — it
ignores them — but it does crash when it sees a field it thinks it knows, with
a type that doesn't match. Which was happening, because I'd guessed at the
types.

The third version worked. Then the tests failed.

This is the part that took longest, and it's the part I want to talk about
because it's not in any tutorial.

The test problem nobody warns you about

When you're building an SDK, you can't test it against the real API. Not
comfortably. Every test call costs you a real request against a real merchant
account, and if you're testing in production you're going to trip rate limits
and log a lot of nonsense in someone's audit trail.

So you use a fake server. In Java, that's usually MockWebServer — it spins up
a local HTTP server that you can tell to respond with whatever you want.

The problem I hit is that MockWebServer is a different server from ALATPay.
It doesn't authenticate, it doesn't rate-limit, it doesn't have a schema. You
tell it what to respond, and it responds. That's the whole point. But it means
that a test that passes against MockWebServer can still fail against ALATPay,
because the test is verifying my assumptions about ALATPay, not ALATPay.

The first test I wrote checked that my SDK could fetch a list of transactions.
It passed. Then I ran the same code against the real API and got a 404. My test
had been testing whether Jackson could parse a JSON string I'd written, not
whether my SDK could talk to a real server. Which is a real thing to test, but
it's not the thing I thought I was testing.

The fix was to be honest about what the tests verify. The README now says:
"All tests use MockWebServer — no real API credentials required to run them."
Which is true. It's not the same as "the SDK works against ALATPay" and I
learned not to imply that it was.

The five days between "shipped" and "actually shipped"

The commit history tells this part better than I can.

My initial commit was on October 11th. Then, five days later, on October 16th,
the last commit message is: "URL-encode user input in query and path
segments."

That's the whole story of the intermediate five days. I shipped. I told myself
it was done. Then I kept finding things.

The URL-encoding thing is a good example because it's the kind of bug that
doesn't show up in testing. If you pass a transaction ID with a space in it —
or a slash, or an ampersand — the URL is malformed and the server returns
nonsense. My tests used IDs that were safe. Real transaction IDs are not always
safe. Five days later I noticed and fixed it.

There's a version of this story where I say "I shipped the SDK in one weekend,
here's the link." That version is true in the sense that the repo existed after
the weekend. It's not true in the sense that the SDK was finished, because the
SDK wasn't finished. It was started, and it kept being started for five more
days.

I think the "shipped in a weekend" framing is a lie that hurts the people who
read it. It makes them feel bad about the fact that their project is still
breaking after a week. Their project is supposed to be still breaking after a
week. Yours was too.

What the SDK actually doesn't do

The README is honest about this, and I want to be honest about it here too:

Bank transfer is stubbed. The endpoint for generating virtual accounts
isn't in the public API documentation, so my BankTransferService throws
UnsupportedOperationException and tells you to check the docs. It's a
placeholder. It doesn't work.

USSD and static wallets are "planned." Planned means not built. I have
notes on what they'd look like. I haven't written them.

The SDK isn't on Maven Central. You can't add it as a dependency yet. You
have to clone it and build it locally. That's a real friction point, and I
haven't paid the cost of getting a publishing account set up.

You need your own credentials. The SDK doesn't come with test keys, and it
doesn't have a demo mode. To run it against anything, you need a merchant
account with ALATPay, three credentials from their dashboard, and the patience
to get them. Without those, the SDK is a very well-documented way to throw
AlatPayAuthException.

That last point is the one that limits the SDK most in practice, and it's the
one I'd change first if I were doing it again. A version of this with a
sandbox credential flow — or with a mock mode that returns fixture data without
touching the network — would be more useful than the version I shipped.

I didn't build that because I didn't know how to. That's the honest reason.
Not "I chose not to because of scope." I didn't know how.

What it was actually worth

The SDK has, at this point, been read by fewer than a hundred people. It has,
as far as I know, zero users. Nobody has opened a pull request. Nobody has sent
me an issue.

By the metrics that matter to a venture capitalist, it's a failure.

By the metrics that matter to me, it's not, because of three things that
happened after I built it:

I learned what an SDK actually is. Not "a wrapper around an API" in the
abstract, but the specific mechanics: a client object, a config object, typed
exceptions, a shared HTTP layer, tests that mock the server. I can read any
other SDK now and understand what it's doing, because I built one.

I learned how banks think about security. The three-header scheme on
ALATPay isn't decorative. It's a specific model of what can go wrong and who's
responsible for what. Building a client for it meant I had to understand it,
and understanding it taught me more about payments infrastructure than reading
a blog post would have.

I got a piece of code I can point at. When I talk to people about what I
do now — when I say I build SDKs — I have a URL. That URL is a thing I made,
and it exists, and it has tests, and it has a license, and somebody can clone
it and run it. That's worth more than the compensation I was imagining when I
started.

The compensation did not arrive. The thing I actually got was better.

If you're going to build one anyway

Build it for yourself, or for the portfolio, or because you want to learn the
API. Not because you're hoping a company will notice.

Here are the four things I'd tell anyone building their first SDK:

1. Get the auth headers right on day one. Before you build anything else,
build a single request that authenticates correctly. If the API has three
headers, test all three before you write the client. The 401 loop I spent a
day in is the most avoidable part of this entire story.

2. Model the response types conservatively. Use @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) on every response class. Don't guess at field types. Test against a real response before you decide a field is a long instead of a String.

3. Be honest about what your tests test. MockWebServer is for verifying your own logic, not the remote server. Say that in the README.

4. Ship it before it's done, and then keep shipping it. The five-day gap between my first commit and my last is the realistic version. Nobody builds a working SDK in a weekend. If you tell yourself you have to, you'll never start.

The link

The SDK is at
github.com/Agenda-X-PR/alatpay-java-sdk.
It's MIT licensed. It works for transaction listing, single transaction
lookup, and settlements. It doesn't work for bank transfers yet, because ALATPay
hasn't published the endpoint, and I'm not going to pretend I can guess at it.

If you're a Java developer integrating ALATPay, use it. If it saves you the
401 loop I spent a day in, it's done its job.

If you're a developer thinking about building something for a company hoping

title: A100 vs H100: is the H100 worth it for LLM training?
description:
The H100 is worth it when it finishes your training job at least as many times faster as it costs more per hour. On Nodus the NVIDIA H100 SXM is listed at $2.60/hr and the A100 80GB at $1.09/hr, so the H100 must run 2.39 times faster to be the cheaper way to finish. Large BF16 or FP8 training usually gets there; small, memory-bound or poorly fed jobs often do not.

That ratio is the whole decision, and it changes with each provider's price list. Under the line, the A100 gives you the cheaper finished job. Over it, the H100 gives you a cheaper job that also finishes sooner.

How much faster is an H100 than an A100 on paper?

Between 1.50 and 3.17 times, depending on which part of the chip your job leans on. Every number here comes from NVIDIA's own spec tables for the A100 80GB SXM and the H100 SXM.

A100 80GB SXM H100 SXM H100 ÷ A100
BF16 Tensor Core, dense 312 TFLOPS 989.5 TFLOPS 3.17x
FP8 Tensor Core, dense Not supported 1,979 TFLOPS New on H100
Memory 80 GB HBM2e 80 GB Same capacity
Memory bandwidth 2,039 GB/s 3,350 GB/s 1.64x
NVLink per GPU 600 GB/s 900 GB/s 1.50x
Max power 400 W Up to 700 W 1.75x

NVIDIA lists H100 Tensor Core figures with sparsity (1,979 BF16 and 3,958 FP8 TFLOPS). Dense training gets half of those, which is what the table shows.

These ratios bracket what a real job sees. A job limited by matrix math, like a large model at a big batch size, moves toward the 3.17x compute ratio. A job limited by moving bytes, like a small model, a short sequence or heavy optimizer traffic, moves toward the 1.64x bandwidth ratio. Neither number is a benchmark, and a slow data loader holds both GPUs to the same speed.


The Nodus price ratio sits between the bandwidth ratio and the compute ratio, so your workload decides the winner.

When does the H100 cost less per finished job?

When your measured speedup beats the hourly price ratio. The rule is one division: H100 price per hour divided by A100 price per hour. If the H100 finishes the job faster than that multiple, it is the cheaper choice.

The ratio depends on where you run. We divided each provider's own listed rates for the 80 GB A100 and the H100 SXM:

Where A100 80GB per hour H100 SXM per hour Speedup the H100 needs
Nodus $1.09 $2.60 2.39x
RunPod (Pods, A100 SXM) $1.79 $3.99 2.23x
Modal ($0.000694 and $0.001097 per second) $2.50 $3.95 1.58x

Sources: Nodus pricing, RunPod pricing, Modal pricing. Prices checked November 2, 2026.


A cheap A100 rate raises the bar the H100 has to clear.

On Modal the H100 wins almost by default, because its premium over the A100 is small. On Nodus the A100 is cheap enough that the H100 has to earn its place with a compute-bound job.

What does that look like for a real fine-tune?

Take a fine-tune that needs 20 hours on one A100 80GB. On Nodus that is 20 x $1.09 = $21.80. The same job on one H100 at the three speedups that matter:

H100 speedup H100 hours H100 cost on Nodus
1.64x (bandwidth-bound) 12.20 h $31.71
2.39x (breakeven) 8.38 h $21.80
3.17x (compute-bound, at the spec ceiling) 6.31 h $16.40


A memory-bound job costs 45% more on the H100; a compute-bound one costs 25% less.

The spread is large. Picking the wrong GPU for this job costs between $5.40 and $9.91, before you count the hours you wait. On Modal the same job runs $49.97 on the A100 and $48.16 on an H100 at only 1.64x, which is why the answer flips between providers.

How do you measure your own speedup in 30 minutes?

Run a short probe of your real training script on each GPU and compare steady-state throughput. Keep the model, batch size, sequence length and data identical. Skip the first few dozen steps, because compilation and warm-up distort them.

Add a timer to your loop that prints tokens or samples per second every 50 steps. Then launch the probe twice with a hard spending cap, using the nodus run flags from the Nodus Jobs guide:

nodus run --name probe-a100 --gpu A100-80GB --image nodus/pytorch --max-cost 1.00 --timeout 20m -- python train.py --max-steps 300
nodus run --name probe-h100 --gpu H100 --image nodus/pytorch --max-cost 1.00 --timeout 20m -- python train.py --max-steps 300

At listed rates, 15 minutes costs $0.27 on the A100 and $0.65 on the H100. Divide the H100's tokens per second by the A100's. Compare that number with the breakeven for where you will run the full job.

If you want FP8, test it as a third probe. FP8 only exists on the H100, and NVIDIA credits its Transformer Engine with up to 4x faster training than the prior generation on GPT-3 175B. That is NVIDIA's projection for a very large model, so check that your loss curve holds before you count on it.

Where is the A100 the better choice?

The A100 wins whenever your job cannot keep an H100's Tensor Cores busy. These are the common cases:

  • Small models and LoRA fine-tunes on 7B to 13B models, where batches are small and memory traffic dominates.
  • Data pipelines that cannot feed the GPU faster. If an A100 already waits on the loader, an H100 waits longer.
  • Code pinned to FP16 or TF32 kernels that predate Hopper, or libraries without FP8 support.
  • Long runs without a deadline, where a lower cost matters more than finishing sooner.
  • Power or rack limits on your own hardware: 400 W per A100 against up to 700 W per H100.

Memory is a tie. Both have 80 GB, so a model that does not fit on an A100 80GB will not fit on an H100 SXM either. For more memory per GPU you need an H200 or a B200, and our VRAM guide for 70B models shows the math.

When is the H100 clearly worth it?

Pay for the H100 when time matters or the job is compute-bound. Pretraining and continued pretraining, full fine-tunes of 30B and larger models, long sequences and FP8 recipes all push toward the compute ratio.

Multi-GPU jobs lean the same way. NVLink is 1.5x faster on the H100, so gradient and tensor-parallel traffic between 8 GPUs costs less time. For why the H100 holds its price in the first place, see why the H100 is so expensive.

A deadline can also justify an H100 below the breakeven. At 1.64x, our 20-hour job finishes 7.8 hours sooner for $9.91 more.

How do you let Nodus pick between A100 and H100?

List both types in the Job and set a cost cap. The Nodus GPU guide says the scheduler picks among the accepted types by expected cost to finish.

apiVersion: nodus.dev/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: finetune
spec:
  image: nodus/pytorch
  command: [torchrun, train.py]
  resources:
    gpu: {type: [A100-80GB, H100], count: 8}
  timeout: 24h
  maxCostUSD: "250.00"

If your probe already settled the question, pin one type instead, for example --gpu H100:8. Run nodus apply -f job.yaml --dry-run=server -o estimate first to see the offering, the expected cost and the startup time without spending anything. For an 8-GPU launch with torchrun, our multi-GPU PyTorch guide walks through the setup.

FAQ

Is the A100 better than the H100?

Not on any performance spec; it only draws less power. The A100 is the better value when your job runs less than about 2.4 times faster on the H100 at Nodus list prices.

Is the A100 40GB worth considering for LLM training?

Only for small models or LoRA on 7B-class models with short sequences. Its 40 GB fills quickly once you add optimizer states and activations, so most LLM training plans should start from the 80 GB version.

Can I train in FP8 on an A100?

No. The A100 has no FP8 Tensor Cores, so FP8 recipes fall back to BF16 or fail. The H100 adds FP8 through its Transformer Engine.

Do H100 PCIe-based cards match the H100 SXM?

No. NVIDIA lists the PCIe-based H100 NVL at 1,671 BF16 TFLOPS with sparsity against 1,979 for the SXM, and 600 GB/s NVLink against 900 GB/s. On Nodus, H100 accepts any variant, while H100-SXM or H100! pins the SXM version.

Does a cheaper A100 rate still pay off if the run gets interrupted?

Only if the run resumes from a checkpoint. A restart from zero repeats the work and erases the saving. Nodus restores the latest checkpoint on new capacity, which our checkpointing guide covers.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: Enforce Data Sovereignty With MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies
description:
Editor’s note: This post is the fourth in a five-part series exploring how MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies help you strengthen database security and enforce consistent guardrails across your organization. Read the first post on IP access list management, the second on defense in depth strategies, and the third on blocking the wildcard IP address.

Maintaining control in a multi-cloud world

As organizations scale their database infrastructure, maintaining consistent security and compliance policies becomes increasingly complex. Development teams need agility, but security teams need control. One misconfigured cluster deployed in the wrong region or on an unapproved cloud hyperscaler can lead to:

  • Compliance violations with data residency requirements.

  • Security gaps from shadow IT deployments.

  • Cost overruns from unplanned multi-cloud sprawl.

  • Audit failures when infrastructure does not match documented policies.

Introducing MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies

MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies are organization-level controls that enable you to define and enforce infrastructure governance rules using policy as code. These policies act as intelligent guardrails, automatically constraining configuration options available to developers while maintaining the flexibility teams need to build and deploy.

Today, we’re diving deep into two of the most powerful policies for multi-cloud governance: Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler and Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler Region.

Policy #1: Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler

What it does

The Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler policy gives you fine-grained control over which cloud platforms—AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure—can be used for MongoDB Atlas cluster deployments within your organization.

Why it matters

Compliance and data sovereignty: Many industries have strict requirements about where data can be processed. If your compliance framework mandates AWS-only infrastructure, this policy ensures no clusters are accidentally deployed on Google Cloud Platform or Azure.

Cost optimization: Committed to an AWS Enterprise Discount Program? This policy prevents cost leakage to other hyperscalers and helps you maximize your cloud spend commitments.

Operational consistency: Standardizing on one or two cloud hyperscalers simplifies your operational model, reduces training overhead, and streamlines your disaster recovery procedures.

Security posture: Each cloud hyperscaler has unique security features and configurations. By restricting to approved hyperscalers, you ensure your security teams have deep expertise in the platforms you actually use.

Real-world examples

MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies are defined using the open-source Cedar policy language. Here are some examples of resource policies creating guardrails around which cloud providers can be used for MongoDB Atlas cluster deployments. 

Example 1: Block a specific hyperscaler

Prevent any clusters from being deployed on Google Cloud:

Example 2: Allow only one hyperscaler

Your organization has standardized on Google Cloud. Ensure all clusters must be deployed there:

Example 3: Enforce Project-specific restrictions

Lock down a sensitive MongoDB Atlas Project so that only AWS can be used for cluster deployment:

Policy #2: Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler Region

What it does

The Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler Region policy enables you to control the specific geographic regions where MongoDB Atlas clusters can be deployed, down to the individual region level (e.g., aws:us-east-1, azure:westeurope).

Why it matters

Data residency compliance: GDPR, California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), and other regulations often mandate that data must remain within specific geographic boundaries. This policy streamlines compliance, making it automatic rather than manual.

Latency optimization: Restrict deployments to regions closest to your users for optimal performance. No more clusters accidentally deployed on the wrong continent.

Cost management: Some cloud regions are significantly more expensive than others. Control costs by preventing deployments to high-cost regions.

Disaster recovery planning: Define approved regions for production workloads and separate regions for disaster recovery, ensuring proper geographic distribution for business continuity.

Security compliance: Certain regions may not meet your security certification requirements. This policy ensures only approved, audited regions are used.

Real-world examples

Example 1: Block a specific region

Your compliance team has determined that aws:us-east-1 has unacceptable data residency risks for your use case, so clusters must not be deployed there:

Example 2: Block multiple regions

Prevent deployments across three regions that don’t meet your requirements:

Example 3: Allow approved regions

Take a zero-trust approach—only permit deployments in preapproved regions:

Exploring a real-world use case: Financial services compliance

A global financial services company needed to ensure all customer data remained within GDPR-compliant regions while maintaining its commitment to AWS as its primary cloud hyperscaler. Its challenge required addressing multiple dimensions simultaneously: preventing deployments to unapproved hyperscalers, restricting geographic regions for data residency, and blocking insecure network configurations.

It implemented a layered approach that combined hyperscaler and region policies with network security controls:

This single policy restricts all Google Cloud Platform deployments while also blocking specific AWS regions that didn’t meet its data residency requirements. The company complemented this with an IP access list policy preventing wildcard access to address network security.

The result? Zero compliance violations were reported in their subsequent audit. Consequently, developers maintained full self-service capabilities within established guardrails, and security teams gained confidence in infrastructure governance. The policies transformed compliance from a documentation exercise into an automated enforcement mechanism, rendering violations technically impossible.

Understanding the key benefits of using resource policies

1. Automated compliance

Stop relying on documentation, training, and manual reviews. Resource policies are enforced automatically at the Organization level.

2. Proactive, not reactive

Resource policies prevent noncompliant configurations before they are created, rather than detecting problems after deployment.

3. Developer velocity

Teams can self-service their infrastructure needs within approved guardrails without waiting for security reviews.

4. Audit trail

MongoDB Atlas generates activity feed events when policies are created, updated, or deleted, providing complete auditability.

5. Noncompliant resource visibility

Use the API endpoint /orgs/{ORG-ID}/nonCompliantResources to identify any existing resources that do not meet your policy requirements.

6. No service disruption

Existing noncompliant clusters continue running. Policies only restrict modifications or the creation of new resources that would keep them out of compliance.

Take the next step

Infrastructure governance doesn’t have to mean slowing down development. With MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies, you can enforce security and compliance requirements automatically while empowering your teams to move fast.

You can implement resource policies through the MongoDB Atlas UI with its visual policy editor, the Atlas Administration API for programmatic policy management, Terraform for infrastructure-as-code integration, or AWS CloudFormation for native AWS deployment. The policies are defined using Cedar, an open-source policy language designed for clarity and expressiveness. If you can read JSON, you can read Cedar policies.

Try resource policies today

  1. Log into MongoDB Atlas with Organization Owner privileges.

  2. Navigate to Organization Settings > Resource Policies.

  3. Create your first policy using one of the examples above.

  4. Monitor noncompliant resources and plan remediation.

  5. Iterate and refine based on your organization’s needs.

Resource policies are included with all MongoDB Atlas deployments at no additional cost. There’s no reason not to start protecting your infrastructure today.

title: How a one-line scale-up can exhaust your database connections
description:
By the Proofline team. Originally published on the Proofline blog.

Raising a service's task count is a correct change in the diff. Whether production can absorb it depends on numbers that live in the environment, outside the repository.

What the reviewer sees: a service scaling from four tasks to twelve

The pull request changes one line. The API service on Amazon ECS goes from four tasks to twelve, because traffic grew and latency followed it.

resource "aws_ecs_service" "api" {
  name          = "api"
  desired_count = 12 # was 4
}

terraform plan shows one attribute changing in place. Nothing in the repository is wrong, and a careful reviewer approves it. The change is still dangerous, and the reason is not in the diff.

More tasks can exceed the database's connection limit

Each task opens a database connection pool when it starts. Most pools have a fixed ceiling: HikariCP defaults to 10 connections, node-postgres to 10, and SQLAlchemy to 5 plus an overflow of 10. Teams raise these under load, and 20 per task is common.

The database limits the total number of simultaneous connections. PostgreSQL sets this limit with max_connections, which on Amazon RDS is configured through the instance's parameter group. Some connections are reserved for superusers. Suppose the limit is 200 and three connections are reserved:

Connections
Four tasks at 20 each 80
Twelve tasks at 20 each 240
Available to the application 197

The steady state does not fit. The rollout is worse. ECS replaces tasks with a rolling deployment, and its default lets the service run up to twice its desired count while old and new tasks overlap. The migration job, the queue workers and the admin console draw on the same limit.

How it fails

New tasks start, open their pools, and PostgreSQL answers with FATAL: sorry, too many clients already. The tasks fail their health checks, so ECS stops them and starts replacements, which fail the same way. The deployment stalls. Depending on how connections are retried, tasks that were healthy before the change can lose their connections too.

The incident review will find the cause quickly.

Why code reviews can miss this problem

The three numbers that decide the outcome sit in three places:

  • the task count, in the Terraform diff;
  • the pool size, in the application's configuration, often in a different repository;
  • the connection limit, in a live parameter group that may have drifted from any file that describes it.

A person reviewing the pull request sees the first. A code reviewer that reads the repository may find the second. Neither can see the third, which is a setting of the environment the change deploys into.

What a review needs to catch it

Catching this class of failure takes two pinned inputs: the exact commit under review, and a recorded snapshot of the target environment that includes the database's limit and the other clients that share it. With both, the failure is arithmetic. Without the snapshot, the honest answer is that the review is incomplete, not that the change looks fine.

This is the review Proofline posts on the pull request for this change, with illustrative values:

 resource "aws_ecs_service" "api" {
   name = "api"
-  desired_count = 4
+  desired_count = 12
 }

Database connections run out before all tasks become healthy

Each task opens 20 connections before passing its health check. With 12 tasks, the service needs 240 connections. The production database allows 197.

Code: infra/ecs/api.tf:19 sets 12 tasks. The application opens its 20-connection pool before reporting healthy.

Environment: The pinned snapshot of orders-prod records max_connections = 200 and 3 reserved connections.

The extra tasks can fail their health checks and stall the deployment. Reduce the task count or pool size, or add a connection pooler.

Illustrative review in an example repository.

The finding names the trigger, the mechanism and the evidence behind each number, so the author can check it instead of trusting it.

Ways to fix it

  • Shrink the pool. Twelve tasks at 15 connections fit under 197, if nothing else connects.
  • Add a connection pooler. Amazon RDS Proxy or PgBouncer multiplexes many client connections onto fewer database connections.
  • Raise the limit deliberately. A higher max_connections costs memory on the database instance, so size it with the instance class.
  • Bound the rollout. A lower maximum percent on the ECS deployment keeps old and new tasks from doubling the count during a deploy.

title: Building German B2B lead lists from Gelbe Seiten with Python
description:
I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify with a free trial credit.

If you sell to small and mid-sized businesses in Germany, Gelbe Seiten is still the most complete public list of who exists where: electricians, tax advisors, dentists, lawyers, agencies, restaurants, sorted by category (Branche) and city. A category page shows 50 businesses; the rest load 10 at a time behind a "Mehr Anzeigen" button, and most emails only appear on each business's own page.

I'm an 18-year-old engineering student, and I built Gelbe Seiten Scraper to turn "Steuerberater in München" into one clean JSON row per business, over plain HTTP. This post covers how it works, calling it from Python and Node, what a row looks like, and a small project: ranking a city's businesses for outreach.

How it works

The category page (/branchen/<category>/<city>) server-renders the first 50 listing cards plus the total count and the parameters of its own "load more" form. The actor reads the cards (name, phone, website, address, district, rating), then posts the same load-more request the page sends to get the rest, 10 per request, in parallel. With business pages switched on, it opens each /gsbiz/<id> page and reads the schema.org LocalBusiness JSON-LD (coordinates, opening hours, services, payment methods, last update) plus the contact block (email, fax, social links).

Free-text searches (/suche/...) are excluded by gelbeseiten.de's robots.txt, so the actor never follows a redirect there. If you type Hotels and that is not a category, it tries hotel; if nothing matches, the search is listed in the run summary and costs nothing. Filters (must have email / website / phone, minimum rating) run before anything is charged. It connects directly and only retries blocked requests through a proxy.

Calling it from Python 

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")

run = client.actor("rel8ble/gelbe-seiten-scraper").call(run_input={
    "categories": ["Steuerberater", "Zahnarzt"],
    "locations": ["München", "Hamburg"],
    "maxResultsPerSearch": 100,
    "requireEmail": True,
})

for b in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(b["name"][:40], "|", b["phone"], "|", b["email"], "|", b["postalCode"], b["city"])

The same from Node:

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: '<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>' });
const run = await client.actor('rel8ble/gelbe-seiten-scraper').call({
    startUrls: ['https://www.gelbeseiten.de/branchen/elektriker/berlin'],
    maxResultsPerSearch: 0, // every listing
    scrapeDetails: false, // list data only: ~50 businesses per request
});
const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
console.log(items.length, 'electricians in Berlin');

What a row looks like

From a real run, trimmed:

{
    "name": "hansezahn I HAMBURG, Dr. Janke und Partner, Zahnärzte",
    "category": "Zahnärzte",
    "categories": ["Zahnärzte", "Schwerpunkt Endodontie", "Implantologie"],
    "phone": "040 6 53 99 82",
    "phoneE164": "+49406539982",
    "fax": "040 6 54 76 54",
    "email": "info@hansezahn-hh.de",
    "website": "http://www.hansezahn-hh.de",
    "address": "Rodigallee 250, 22043 Hamburg",
    "latitude": 53.57074,
    "longitude": 10.125491,
    "rating": 4.7,
    "reviewCount": 3,
    "openingHours": ["Monday 08:00-19:00", "Tuesday 07:30-19:00", "Wednesday 07:30-18:30"],
    "businessTypes": ["Dentist"],
    "premiumListing": true,
    "searchCategory": "Zahnarzt",
    "searchLocation": "Hamburg",
    "position": 9,
    "totalInSearch": 803
}

In a 120-business test (tax advisors and dentists in two cities), 93% of rows had an email, 90% a website and every row a phone number and coordinates.

Project: ranking a city's businesses for outreach

Say you sell websites or online booking to local businesses. The best prospects have a phone and email but a weak online presence: no website, few reviews, no opening hours online.

rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

def score(b):
    s = 0
    s += 3 if not b["website"] else 0          # no website: the obvious pitch
    s += 2 if b["reviewCount"] < 3 else 0       # barely any reviews
    s += 1 if not b["openingHours"] else 0      # hours not published
    s += 1 if not b["premiumListing"] else 0    # not paying for visibility yet
    return s

leads = sorted((b for b in rows if b["email"] or b["phone"]), key=score, reverse=True)
print(f"{'business':40} {'score':>5} {'district':18} contact")
for b in leads[:15]:
    print(f"{b['name'][:40]:40} {score(b):5} {(b['district'] or b['city'])[:18]:18} {b['email'] or b['phone']}")

Because every row carries searchCategory, searchLocation and coordinates, the same dataset also answers "how many dentists per district" or feeds a map for territory planning.

Pricing and limits

$0.35 per 1,000 businesses as of 3 Nov 2026, no start fee, same price with or without business pages. Filtered businesses, duplicates, unknown categories and failed requests are never charged. Categories must be Gelbe Seiten's German names (zahnarzt, not dentist), Germany only, up to 5,000 businesses per category and city (split big cities by district). Business contact data of sole traders can be personal data under the GDPR, and German law limits unsolicited ads by email and phone, so check your outreach rules.

Store page: https://apify.com/rel8ble/gelbe-seiten-scraper

Need a custom scraper or a ready dataset? Hire me on Fiverr: https://www.fiverr.com/rel8ble

This article was drafted with AI and published by me.

title: Savor: A Food Delivery Template for Restaurants and Local Fleets
description:
Delivery platforms take a big cut of every order, often between 15% and 30%. For a restaurant running on thin margins, that cut can be the whole profit. That's why so many restaurants, small chains and local delivery startups want their own ordering app, and why most of them give up when they see what it takes: a customer app, a kitchen screen, a courier app, an operations console, payments, maps and a server that ties it together.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Savor is all of that in one Java project. It's the third of this week's templates, after Skirmish and Parley, and it's a sibling of Wayline, the ride-hailing app from last week. Pick the food-delivery template in the Initializr, set your name and package, and you have a working delivery service. The source is under MIT-0, so the business you build on it is yours.

Restaurants near you.
Checkout.
Live tracking.

One app, four roles

Savor is a single app. The account's role decides the first screen: a customer sees restaurants, a merchant sees the order queue, a courier sees the delivery screen and an administrator sees the operations console. One build to publish, one code base to maintain.

Role What they can do
Customer Browse restaurants that deliver to their address, build a cart, pay by card or cash, tip, track the courier on a map and get refunds
Restaurant Accept or reject orders, mark them ready and see the queue update live
Courier Apply with documents, go online, accept offers, navigate to the pickup and the customer, and track earnings
Administrator Watch the dashboard and trends, review courier applications and manage accounts

The kitchen's queue.
A courier's offer.
The operations dashboard.

The hard parts are already handled

The screens are the visible part of a delivery service. The business rules underneath are where projects usually stall. Savor has them in place.

Money moves at the right time. The card is authorized for the total when the order is placed and captured when the food is delivered. A rejected or canceled order releases the hold, so customers are never charged for food they didn't get. From Payments.java:

/// Holds an order's total on the customer's card as the order is placed,
/// with no transaction open. Nothing is taken until the order arrives
/// ([#settle]); an order that never does lets the hold go ([#release]).
public String authorize(String orderId, String username, String methodId, long amountCents,
        String currency) throws IOException {
    if (CASH.equals(methodId)) {
        return CASH;
    }

With Stripe, cards are added on Stripe's own page, so card numbers never touch your app or your server. Other providers plug in through the PaymentProvider interface.

Orders and deliveries can't get confused. An order and its delivery are separate state machines that share an id. Every transition is a conditional update that names the states it can come from, so when a kitchen and a customer act at the same moment, only one of them wins.

Maps without an API key bill. Tracking uses OpenFreeMap vector tiles, OSRM routing and Photon place search. Updates arrive over a WebSocket as they happen, so the customer watches the courier move.

Everything Wayline learned, Savor reuses. Accounts, sign-in with phone verification, SMS and push providers, the live channel, the map, billing, the operations console, the database and hosting all come from Wayline. A delivery is, almost literally, a Wayline ride with a stop at the restaurant.

Make it yours

The guide covers the common ways to reshape Savor:

  • A single restaurant or a small chain. Turn off merchant sign-up and run Savor as your own branded ordering app. This is the case where avoiding platform commissions pays off fastest.
  • Pickup and scheduled orders, for when you don't want couriers at all, or not yet.
  • Your own couriers instead of a gig fleet.
  • Beyond food: groceries, pharmacy, flowers, laundry, anything that moves from a shop to a door. Point an AI agent at the project and describe the business. The model, the roles and the flow are already there.

The colors and corner radius are CSS variables in theme.css, the text is in five languages, and the SMS provider is a setting (savor.sms.provider takes Twilio, Vonage or MessageBird).

Try it

The development profile simulates kitchens and couriers, so you can place an order and watch it move through the whole flow with nothing installed. Use card 4242 4242 4242 4242 to pay, or 4000 0000 0000 0002 to see a decline. The Savor page has the overview, and the user's guide and implementor's guide go deeper.

Tomorrow the series moves from apps to the framework features they pushed into Codename One, starting with More of the Java API, and an Experiment With Unity Games.

title: Shared Modular Recurrence in Contextual MDPs for Universal Morphology Control
description:
arXiv:2506.08630v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A universal controller for any robot morphology would greatly improve computational and data efficiency. Steps have been made towards such multi-robot control by utilizing contextual information about the properties of individual robots and exploiting their modular structure in the architecture of deep reinforcement learning agents. When the robots have highly dissimilar morphologies, however, this becomes a challenging problem, especially when the agent must generalize to new, unseen robots. In this paper, we consider the fact that contextual features are often only partially available, but that they can be recovered through modular interactions. This can allow for better multi-robot control and generalization to contexts that are not seen during training. To this extent, we implement a transformer-based architecture with shared modular recurrence and evaluate its (generalization) performance on a large set of MuJoCo robots. The results show a substantial improvement in zero-shot generalization performance on robots with unseen dynamics, kinematics, and topologies, in four different environments.

title: How and why you need to speed up tests
description:
Many people write that the “bottleneck” in agent‑based development is the people who review the code. I believe this is more of a marketing statement than an engineering one. A person can perform code reviews quite quickly. Certainly faster than the code goes through the CI/CD pipeline and is deployed to the staging environment. As automation increases, the human code review process boils down to:

  • running one’s eyes over non‑obvious places in the code whose verification has not yet been automated,

  • check how the automation of deterministic development rule checks worked.

It takes me no more than 5-15 minutes per pull request. I see the “bottleneck” in a completely different place.

Now agents are writing code very quickly. This speeds up development.

They also write tests quickly and in large numbers. Tests are good — they fix contracts, ensure compliance with development rules, and confirm that the code does what we need it to do. We make agents test the code, and they do it easily and quickly. We rejoice: the amount of code is growing, the system is becoming larger, and it doesn’t lose its reliability.

It would seem that nothing can go wrong. But it can and definitely will go wrong.

There are too many tests. Over the course of a couple of years of my project’s existence, the software engineers have written about 3,000 tests. Half of them were written by me over the course of a year. I did a lot of refactoring (I put the application in order), updated library versions with broken backward compatibility, and needed a lot of tests as a guarantee that I hadn’t broken the application’s functionality.

Then spring 2026 came, and the agents got to work. The number of tests increased from 3,000 to 7,200 between March and November. Complex integration tests became almost free for us, and we ended up with a very large number of them.

The tests started consuming too many resources. The test bench encountered: OOMError, memory exhaustion in the database, exhaustion of lock and database connection limits. And the more tests we had, the slower they ran. If in spring a full test run took 10–15 minutes, in autumn it slowed down to 45 minutes.

The faster the agents wrote code and tests, the slower they started writing code — due to the need to run tests 3–5 times per task, the task completion time increased from 30–60 minutes in spring to 1–4 hours in autumn. In a year, there will be many times more tests, and it’s already clear that task completion will slow down significantly.

We had to think about how to reduce the time spent on tests without losing the point of having tests. After all, the simplest way not to waste time on tests is not to run them. But then what’s the point of them?

You can try the following ways to speed up the tests:

  1. Prohibit the agent from testing obvious things. I call such tests pointless. These include tests:

  • of the fact that migration scripts have been applied,

  • of the fact that a new value has been added to an enum,

  • of the fact that the list of dependencies in the project has been changed,

  • etc.

  1. Prohibit the agent from writing duplicate tests.

Duplicate tests do the same thing. But the first test checks the createdAt field, while the second checks the createdBy field of the same structure (object, table). Such checks should be combined into a single test. If you look for it, you can easily find a test audit skill that you can add to your agent as a separate skill and, as a rule, for writing tests and performing code reviews.

  1. Raise the context of your application only once for all tests. There are many articles about this, for different frameworks — it won’t be difficult to figure it out.

  2. Use the database on the host for tests, not in the test containers.

We save: on Docker memory (relevant for Macs), on the time it takes to start the test containers, and on the time spent recreating the database schema from scratch for each test.

We lose: the certainty that the project will be able to start on a clean database at any time. It’s also inconvenient if the database schema differs in different git branches — when switching between branches, you’ll need to prepare the database for tests manually or write complex automation for this.

  1. Deploy the database schema only once for all tests.

  2. In tests, clean the database not via [delete from ...], but by rolling back the transaction. The transaction starts before the test, and after the test, it’s rolled back. This takes 3–4 milliseconds (almost for free). But it doesn’t work for all test frameworks. The code under test may perform its transactions on a different database connection. In this case, the transaction started by the test won’t roll back the changes made to the database by the code under test. Also, this doesn’t work well with parallel test execution and mutual lock tests.

  3. Disable triggers before clearing the tables in the test database. For me, this reduced the time required to run all tests by 15 minutes.

  4. When writing code, run only those tests that check the code affected by the task.

Running 10–20 integration tests instead of 7,200 takes the agent 3–5 minutes.

  1. In the pipeline, tests can be sped up by playing around with the CPU core power‑saving mode.

Good luck, and remember: the faster the tests run, the faster the development progresses.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use.

Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases.

Our goals for Python on Vercel

Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications. We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions:

  • Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async/await, and context managers.

  • A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together.

  • Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on.

The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run.

Deploying Python applications on Vercel

We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv, and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN.

For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them.

For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies.

Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure

A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language:

These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application.

Start building with Python on Vercel

Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services.

To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code.

The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN.

Here’s how the main parts connect:

  • Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files.

  • Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel.

  • Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading.

  • Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow.

The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application.

Investing in the Python community

Last December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work.

At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026.

We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next.

We also published PEP 827, which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking.

What’s next for Python on Vercel

We’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work.

Resources

title: Plugins without the plugin jungle: a whole blog with comments in one sandboxed script
description:
I built ForgeCMS because I was tired of WordPress plugins. Every site I ran needed a dozen of them, each with its own updates, its own security holes and, more and more often, its own subscription. When my hosting provider simply removed my WordPress sites, I decided my next CMS would have no plugin jungle at all.

But a CMS without any way to extend it is a dead end too. Somebody always needs a guestbook, a poll, a price calculator. So the question was: how do you get plugins without getting the jungle back?

This week the answer went live.

A plugin is two files in your Git repo

ForgeCMS sites are Markdown and small SML files in a Git repo. A plugin is just two more files next to the pages:

plugins/guestbook/plugin.sml   what the plugin is and which permissions it wants
plugins/guestbook/plugin.sms   the script

The script is written in SMS, a small Kotlin-like language from our Forge project. It has one job: build a piece of the page.

fun render(props, ctx) {
    var out = "Heading { level: 2 text: " + sml.quote("Guestbook") + " }\n"
    for (e in store.list("entries")) {
        out = out + "Text { value: " + sml.quote(e["name"] + ": " + e["message"]) + " }\n"
    }
    return out
}

You put it on a page with one line, Plugin { name: "guestbook" }, push, and reload. No build, no deploy, no restart. ForgeCMS notices the changed script and loads it again.

The sandbox is the point

A WordPress plugin is PHP with all the rights of your server. An SMS plugin only has the functions ForgeCMS hands to it:

  • the language itself (strings, lists, maps, dates),
  • store.*: its own small records on the server, as plain files (no database),
  • content.*: read the text files of the content repo, never the server config,
  • mail.admins(...): a mail to the plugin's admins, nobody else.

No file system, no network, no programs. Each call gets a budget of one million steps, 250 ms and 32 MB; an endless loop is stopped after about 10 ms of work.

And the important bit: the plugin can only ask for permissions. The content repo is not trusted, so only app.sml on the server grants them:

Plugins {
    Plugin { name: "blog"  allow: "content store mail"  path: "/blog"  admins: "me@example.org" }
}

A compromised repo or a pull request cannot turn on a new plugin, give one mail rights or make somebody an admin.

What comes back from the script is SML, not HTML, and ForgeCMS cleans it: only layout elements, safe links, Markdown without raw HTML. A visitor who types "} HTML { ... } into a form just sees that text.

The test: a whole blog

A guestbook proves little. So I asked: could the blog itself be a plugin?

It can. The blog plugin is about 600 lines of SMS and does:

  • a list of posts with paging, and "the latest three" for a start page
  • a page per post: Markdown from the repo, preview image for link sharing, older/newer links
  • an Atom feed
  • drafts and scheduled posts
  • comments: moderated by default. The admin gets a mail with a link, logs in with their email address, and approves or deletes right under the post
  • German, English and Spanish

It reads the same blog.sml format as the built-in blog module, so my travel diary would run on it unchanged. On those 23 real posts a page takes about 2 ms.

Writing it was also the real test of the plugin API. It needed things the guestbook never did: its own addresses below /blog, a feed that is not HTML, a page title and preview image per post, an admin login, mail. All of that is now in the API, documented in one text: the plugin spec.

Try it: crowdware.info/blog-plugin-demo. Leave a comment; I get the mail and approve it.

The AI writes the plugin

This is the part I care most about. You don't need to know SMS. Give the AI the spec (forgecms --plugin-spec prints it) and say what you want:

"A plugin for my yoga site: a list of this week's classes with a sign-up form, at most 12 people per class, mail me when someone signs up."

The AI writes the two files, you push them, reload the page, done. Want it different? Tell the AI, push again.

Free software, made to be changed

Both plugins, the guestbook and the blog, are GPLv3 in the ForgeCMS repo. Copy one into plugins/ of your site and make it yours. Built something others could use? Send a pull request on Codeberg.

  • Demos: guestbook · blog with comments
  • Code: examples/plugins
  • Spec: SPEC.md
  • ForgeCMS for developers: crowdware.info/forgecms/developers

What plugin would you write first?

title: Backtest vs live: why execution friction kills good-looking strategies
description:
Your strategy’s logic was never the problem. Latency, slippage, and costs are the gap between a beautiful backtest and a losing live account — and the gap is measurable.

Assume your edge is real. Assume it survives out-of-sample testing, beats its baselines, and holds up across market regimes. It can still lose money live. The reason is not mysterious, and it is not your logic. It is execution friction — the gap between the price your backtest books and the price the market actually gives you.

Latency becomes slippage becomes losses

A backtest books the decision price as the fill price. Live markets deliver neither instant fills nor requested prices. Latency is the delay between signal and fill; slippage is the worse price you get because the market moved during that delay. They are one chain, not two problems: cut the delay, and most of the slippage goes with it.

The damage is invisible per trade and only shows up in aggregate — which is why it surprises people. Take a system backtesting at a small average profit per trade. Add routine retail slippage per round trip and the edge shrinks by more than half. Push slippage higher in a volatile session and expectancy turns negative. Across a year of trades, ordinary slippage alone can erase a year’s expected profit. The strategy did not break. The market charged it rent the backtest forgot to include.

The full friction list

  • Slippage and latency, worst during news and high volatility — exactly when backtests stay silent.
  • Brokerage, taxes, and exchange charges, per trade, every trade.
  • Spread and market impact, which grow with size and thin liquidity.
  • Partial fills and missed trades, which quietly change the strategy you thought you were running.
  • Outages and disconnections, which turn an automated strategy into an unmonitored bet while positions are live.

How to close the gap before risking capital

  • Model friction explicitly. Re-run the backtest with realistic slippage and full costs. If the edge survives, it is an edge worth discussing. If it does not, you have learned something cheaply.
  • Measure expectancy net of everything. Gross profit per trade is a vanity metric. Net expectancy per trade, after all friction, is the number that decides whether to trade.
  • Forward-test on paper first. Live data flow exposes latency, fill inconsistency, and data quirks that no historical simulation contains. Backtesting tells you if a strategy could have worked; forward testing tells you if it actually functions.
  • Watch the backtest-live divergence. A strategy whose live results shrink steadily against its backtest, with no explanation beyond “market conditions,” is usually confessing over-optimisation after the fact.

The sequence that works

Backtest to screen. Validate to filter — recompute, baselines, walk-forward folds, leakage, trial-count correction. Forward-test to confirm function. Then, and only then, trade small. Each stage exists to kill a different kind of false confidence, and skipping one means paying for its lesson with capital instead of time.

The validation stage is where BuildIT Index sits, and where the seven checks apply. It does not test execution, pick models, or promise a future return. It answers a narrower question that has to be answered first: does the record in the file support the number on the page?

If the answer is no, the live account was never the place to find out.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past backtest results do not predict future returns.

Originally published at startbuildit.online

GLM-5.3 is 50% off on AI Gateway through Tuesday, September 8, in partnership with DigitalOcean.

How to use the model during the offer period

  • Using the promo name (zai/glm-5.3-promo-50) gets the discounted rate. It routes only to DigitalOcean, with no fallback to another provider, and it stops serving when the offer ends.

  • Using the standard name (i.e., zai/glm-5.3) with provider options to sort DigitalOcean as the preferred provider keeps working after September 8 and routes across every provider that serves the model, at their usual rates.

Because the promo name goes away when the offer ends, treat it as something you switch on for the window rather than hardcode. To keep the standard name in your code instead, pin the provider with order: ['digitalocean'] under providerOptions.gateway, which prefers DigitalOcean and falls back to the others if it cannot serve the request.

GLM-5.3 takes text input, with a 1M token context window and a maximum output of 128K tokens. Discounted requests appear in your spend dashboard and carry a trace like any other request.

Try GLM-5.3 in the model playground.

To use it in a coding agent, see the coding agents guide, then run vercel ai-gateway coding-agents setup to connect agents like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Pi, and more and select zai/glm-5.3-promo-50 inside the agent.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.
