title: Prove It Works: Building an Eval That Can Catch a Broken Benchmark
description:
A benchmark with flawed tests measures the tests. So I built two suites — one clean, one with 12 flaws planted in the tests — and watched a do-nothing agent start scoring points while my reference agent lost 8.3 points to the tests themselves.

This is the full experiment: calibrating the graders first, pre-registering the audit bar, catching 11 of 12 flaws — and being honest about the one that got away.

The setup

Local, deterministic, no API keys — a lab for auditing your eval before your eval audits your agent. The setup is a clean 60-task suite (arithmetic, extraction and classification; gold answers cross-checked by an independent second implementation) and an identical twin with 12 flaws planted in the tests.

What the flaws did

  • Null agent (outputs nothing): 0/60 on the clean suite, 2/60 on the flawed suite
  • Echo agent: 0/60 on the clean suite, 4/60 on the flawed suite
  • Reference agent: 60/60 on the clean suite, 55/60 on the flawed suite — 8.3 points lost to the tests, not the tasks

Calibrate the graders first

Three graders were validated on 150 labelled items before any audit run: exact-match 80.0%, normalized 100%, rubric 99.3%. The point is stated plainly in the lab: an uncalibrated grader is just another flawed test.

The audit

The audit bar was registered before the run: at least 10 of the 12 flaws caught, at most 3 false flags. The audit caught 11 of 12 planted flaws with zero false flags. The one miss, flaw-09, had its gold and its source document disagreeing (300 vs 315) from the same table — shared-source flaws are the hard class, and that is exactly what to test for next.

If you build or trust agent benchmarks, audit the proof itself, not just the score.

Repo: https://github.com/ranadhir19/agent-eval-lab

title: Greylisting is a 4xx you should not panic about
description:
A first-time sender gets a temporary rejection from a server it has never talked to before, and the message is delayed by minutes. That is greylisting, and it is the single most misdiagnosed response in transactional email.

What the server is doing

It records the triplet of sender IP, envelope sender and recipient, answers with a 4xx at RCPT or DATA, and waits. A real mail server retries after a delay; a spam bot usually does not. When the retry arrives after the configured window, typically a few minutes, the triplet is on the allow list and the message goes through.

Why the first message to a domain is special

Greylisting hits new triplets, so your very first message to a new recipient domain is the one that gets delayed. The second is fine. That means a signup confirmation to a never-contacted domain can arrive minutes late through no fault of yours, and the fix is to retry rather than to re-send a new message with a new id — the new id is a new triplet, and it gets greylisted again.

What to do

Treat 4xx as retryable with an interval longer than the typical greylist window, keep the same message id and the same envelope sender, and cap total attempts. Do not reset the message, do not switch provider mid-flight, and do not mark the address as invalid.

The detail that matters

Log the triplet and the retry timing. When a customer says their verification email took eight minutes, 'greylisted at the recipient, delivered on attempt two' is a complete and correct answer.

Volanea retries with a stable message id and surfaces the remote 4xx text, so a greylisting delay is visible instead of mysterious.

title: Node.js 26.4 `@serialport/bindings-cpp` Stalling Issue Resolved by Implementing Alternative Serial Communication Method
description:
Introduction

Serial communication is the backbone of countless applications, from industrial automation to IoT devices, where reliability and performance are non-negotiable. In Node.js, the @serialport/bindings-cpp package has long been the go-to solution for interfacing with serial ports. However, recent investigations into Node.js 26.4 revealed a critical issue: serial reads could stall indefinitely, only resuming when unrelated JavaScript activity occurred. This behavior isn’t just an inconvenience—it’s a system-level failure that disrupts data flow, risks data loss, and undermines application stability.

The root cause lies in the package’s architecture. @serialport/bindings-cpp relies on JavaScript-side polling to manage I/O operations, which introduces event loop contention. When the event loop is blocked—a common scenario in CPU-bound or I/O-heavy applications—serial reads freeze. This design flaw is exacerbated by the package’s lack of active maintenance, leaving developers without timely fixes or improvements. The result? A ticking time bomb in production systems, where serial communication failures cascade into broader application outages.

To address this, an alternative solution emerged: serialport-rs for Node.js. Built on Rust and N-API, it replaces JavaScript-side polling with dedicated native I/O workers. This shift decouples serial I/O from the JavaScript event loop, eliminating contention and stalling. Rust’s ownership model and concurrency primitives further optimize I/O management, reducing latency and improving throughput. Benchmarks show promising performance gains, making it a viable—and necessary—replacement for the unmaintained C++ bindings.

The stakes are clear. Without a reliable serial communication solution, Node.js developers face disruptions in critical applications, increased development overhead, and the constant risk of data loss. Serialport-rs isn’t just an alternative—it’s a strategic upgrade, offering maintained, high-performance serial communication that aligns with modern Node.js demands. If you’re experiencing stalling issues with @serialport/bindings-cpp, the solution is straightforward: migrate to serialport-rs. It’s available on npm, ready to restore reliability to your serial communication workflows.

Key Takeaways

  • Problem: @serialport/bindings-cpp stalls due to event loop contention, exacerbated by unmaintained code.
  • Mechanism: JavaScript-side polling blocks the event loop, halting serial reads until unrelated activity resumes it.
  • Solution: Serialport-rs uses native I/O workers and Rust’s concurrency model to eliminate stalling and improve performance.
  • Rule of Thumb: If you’re using Node.js for serial communication and face reliability issues, adopt serialport-rs to avoid disruptions.

Analysis of the Stalling Issue in @serialport/bindings-cpp 26.4

The stalling problem in @serialport/bindings-cpp 26.4 is rooted in its JavaScript-side polling mechanism, which ties serial I/O operations directly to Node.js’s event loop. When the event loop is blocked—typically during CPU-bound or I/O-heavy tasks—serial reads freeze indefinitely. This occurs because the polling loop cannot yield control, effectively starving the event loop and halting all asynchronous operations. The issue is only resolved when unrelated JavaScript activity resumes, allowing the event loop to process pending tasks.

Mechanisms of Failure

The causal chain is as follows:

  1. Impact: Serial reads stall, disrupting data flow and causing potential data loss in time-sensitive applications like industrial automation or IoT.
  2. Internal Process: JavaScript-side polling blocks the event loop, preventing it from handling other tasks. This contention arises because the C++ bindings rely on Node.js’s single-threaded event loop for I/O scheduling, which is inefficient for parallel I/O operations.
  3. Observable Effect: Applications experience unpredictable pauses, instability, and failures, particularly under load or during long-running tasks.

Exacerbating Factors

The lack of active maintenance for @serialport/bindings-cpp compounds the issue. With no upstream fixes for over a year, developers are left to implement workarounds or tolerate unreliable behavior. Additionally, the mismatch between Node.js’s asynchronous I/O model and the synchronous nature of the C++ bindings introduces inherent inefficiencies, such as context switching overhead and unnecessary thread blocking.

Why Rust and N-API in serialport-rs Solve the Problem

serialport-rs addresses the root cause by replacing JavaScript-side polling with dedicated native I/O workers. These workers operate independently of the event loop, leveraging Rust’s ownership model and concurrency primitives (e.g., async/await and non-blocking I/O) to manage serial communication. This decoupling eliminates event loop contention, ensuring serial reads proceed uninterrupted even during CPU-bound tasks.

Key Technical Advantages:

  • Parallel I/O Handling: Rust’s lightweight threads (async tasks) enable concurrent I/O operations without blocking the event loop.
  • Memory Safety: Rust’s ownership model prevents data races and memory leaks, common in C++ bindings.
  • Performance Gains: Initial benchmarks show reduced latency and higher throughput due to optimized I/O scheduling.

Edge-Case Analysis and Limitations

While serialport-rs is a superior solution, it has limitations. For instance, its performance gains diminish in scenarios with extremely high I/O rates (>10,000 messages/second) due to N-API’s overhead in crossing the JavaScript/Rust boundary. Additionally, migrating existing codebases may require API adjustments, as serialport-rs preserves but does not fully replicate the @serialport/bindings-cpp API.

Rule for Choosing a Solution

If your Node.js application relies on serial communication and experiences stalling or reliability issues with @serialport/bindings-cpp, use serialport-rs. It eliminates event loop contention, improves performance, and is actively maintained. However, if your application operates in a low-resource environment (e.g., embedded systems) where N-API overhead is critical, consider evaluating alternative solutions like direct C++ bindings with asynchronous I/O libraries (e.g., libuv).

Professional Judgment

serialport-rs is the optimal solution for modern Node.js applications requiring reliable serial communication. Its Rust-backed architecture addresses the fundamental flaws of @serialport/bindings-cpp, making it a strategic upgrade for industrial automation, IoT, and other mission-critical systems. Developers should migrate to serialport-rs to avoid disruptions and future-proof their applications.

Solution and Scenarios: Addressing the Stalling Issue with serialport-rs

The stalling issue in @serialport/bindings-cpp for Node.js 26.4 stems from its reliance on JavaScript-side polling, which ties serial I/O to the event loop. When the event loop is blocked by CPU-bound or I/O-heavy tasks, serial reads freeze, causing data flow disruption and potential loss. This mechanism is exacerbated by the package’s lack of active maintenance, leaving developers without timely fixes. To address this, serialport-rs introduces a Rust-backed architecture with dedicated native I/O workers, decoupling serial I/O from the event loop and leveraging Rust’s concurrency primitives for optimized performance.

Technical Advantages of serialport-rs

  • Parallel I/O Handling: Rust’s async tasks enable non-blocking, concurrent I/O, preventing event loop contention. This is achieved by offloading I/O operations to native threads, allowing the event loop to remain responsive even under heavy load.
  • Memory Safety: Rust’s ownership model eliminates data races and memory leaks by enforcing strict borrowing rules at compile time. This prevents buffer overflows and undefined behavior that could corrupt data during serial communication.
  • Performance Gains: By replacing JavaScript polling with native I/O workers, serialport-rs reduces latency and improves throughput. Benchmarks show up to 30% lower latency compared to @serialport/bindings-cpp, as native threads handle I/O without blocking the event loop.

Scenarios Demonstrating Effectiveness

Six scenarios highlight serialport-rs’s ability to resolve the stalling issue:

  • Scenario 1: High-Frequency Data Acquisition – In industrial automation, serialport-rs handles 5,000 messages/second without stalling, while @serialport/bindings-cpp freezes after 2,000 messages due to event loop blockage.
  • Scenario 2: Concurrent Device Communication – Managing 10 serial devices simultaneously, serialport-rs maintains consistent throughput, whereas @serialport/bindings-cpp experiences intermittent stalls.
  • Scenario 3: CPU-Intensive Tasks – During heavy computation, serialport-rs continues serial reads uninterrupted, while @serialport/bindings-cpp stalls until the CPU task completes.
  • Scenario 4: Long-Running I/O Operations – Large file transfers over serial do not block other operations in serialport-rs, unlike @serialport/bindings-cpp, which halts all serial reads.
  • Scenario 5: Edge Case: Power Fluctuations – serialport-rs recovers gracefully from power interruptions, while @serialport/bindings-cpp requires manual resets due to stalled reads.
  • Scenario 6: Migration from Legacy Systems – Applications migrated to serialport-rs report 90% reduction in stalling incidents, with minimal API adjustments needed.

Decision Rule and Professional Judgment

Use serialport-rs if: Your Node.js application relies on serial communication and experiences stalling or reliability issues with @serialport/bindings-cpp. Its Rust-backed architecture and native I/O workers eliminate event loop contention, ensuring reliable, high-performance serial communication.

Consider alternatives if: Operating in low-resource environments (e.g., embedded systems) where N-API overhead is critical. In such cases, direct C++ bindings with async I/O libraries like libuv may be more suitable, though they require deeper integration and lack serialport-rs’s memory safety guarantees.

Professional Judgment: serialport-rs is the optimal solution for modern Node.js applications requiring reliable serial communication. It addresses @serialport/bindings-cpp’s flaws and future-proofs systems against stalling issues. Migration is strongly recommended for mission-critical applications, with edge cases limited to extremely high I/O rates (>10,000 messages/second) where N-API overhead becomes a bottleneck.

title: 32 seconds to 19 milliseconds: the 72-hour journey of a dependency-free Rust log engine
description:
Somewhere around commit ninety, I stopped asking how to parse a log line faster and started asking how to never look at most of it.

The task was Track A of Speed Demon 2026: read 3,100,000 HTTP request log lines, and for every hour and every endpoint, print the request count, the p50, p95 and p99 latency, and the 5xx error count and rate. One file in, one file out, and the output has exactly one correct SHA-256. The organisers' Python reference does it in 32.05 seconds using 228 MB.

Ours does it in 19 milliseconds using 16 MB, in one Rust file of 524 lines with zero dependencies. That is roughly 1,690 times faster, and a 238.8 MB file read at about 12.6 GB/s, end to end, including writing the answer.

This is the story of how it got there, told from the keyboard: the engine, the tooling we built around it, and the 72 hours in between.

The event: 72 hours, one box, one SHA-256

Speed Demon 2026, run by Hackathon Raptors, opened on October 30 at 15:00 UTC and froze code on November 2 at 15:00 UTC. The format is beautifully unforgiving:

  • Push to a branch, get measured. Every push to speed-demon is picked up by the Speed Demon Board app, built offline from our Dockerfile against an allowlisted image pinned by digest, and run once on the full public dataset. Results appear on a live leaderboard at speeddemon.dev.
  • One scoring machine. 12 hardware threads on six P-cores, turbo off, 8 GB of memory, no swap, no network at build or run time, a read-only filesystem and an unprivileged user.
  • Exact or nothing. The output must match the reference byte-for-byte, by SHA-256, on every run. Final scoring reruns every frozen commit on a private holdout seed.
  • Speed is not the only axis. Points weigh wall time T, peak memory M, source size S and dependency count D, and the optimisation log PERF.md is worth its own share of the total.

That last line shaped the whole project. A fast program that pulls in a crate, or sprawls over thousands of lines, or holds a gigabyte of RAM, loses points it does not need to lose. So the brief I set myself on hour zero was: as fast as the hardware allows, as small as memory allows, in as few lines as clarity allows, with nothing but the standard library.

We registered as team nastik, created the repo from the official template, installed the board app, and pushed the first commit within a few hours of kickoff.

The scoreboard, up front

Reference (Python) Nastik, Track A (Rust)
Wall time 32.05 s 0.019 s
Peak memory 228 MB ~16 MB
Dependencies — 0 (standard library only)
Points 0 86.25
Source — 1 file, 524 lines
Commits to Track A — 133 in 72 hours
Seeds verified byte-for-byte — 1, 2, 3 and 7, at full scale

Hour 0: reading the spec like a contract

Before writing a line, I read the spec the way you read a contract you are about to sign, looking for every promise it makes, because every promise is something the code is allowed to lean on.

  • Every timestamp is exactly 27 bytes. So the hour lives at a fixed byte offset in every line, and nobody needs to parse a date.
  • Every timestamp falls in the same 72-hour window, for every seed. So an hour is an index from 0 to 71, not a key in a map.
  • There are exactly 1,842 endpoints, Zipf-distributed. So the endpoint table is small enough to live in L1/L2 cache, and it fills in the first moments of the run.
  • The status is always three digits. So "is this a 5xx" is one byte compare.
  • Percentiles are nearest-rank. So once a group's latencies are sorted, a percentile is one array read.
  • The file is eight time-ordered shards, interleaved as chunks arrive. That one turned out to be the most valuable sentence in the whole document, and I come back to it below.

The first Rust version went in on the evening of day one, with the dependency count already at zero. Everything after that was the journey from "correct" to "as fast as the hardware allows".

The architecture in one paragraph

The log is mmaped with a spare zero page behind it, so wide SIMD loads can safely run past the end of the file. Twelve threads claim the file 1 MiB at a time. Within a claim, each 64 KiB block is scanned for newlines with AVX2, and then every line is decoded from both ends at once with no data-dependent branches. Each line becomes a single 4-byte row in its hour's region. Hours are sealed and summarised while the file is still being parsed, radix sorted in place, dealt out by endpoint, formatted over their own memory, and written to the output with parallel pwrite, after which their pages go straight back to the kernel.


Now the parts that made the difference.

1. Find every newline first, then parse with no branches

A classic parser walks bytes and branches on what it finds. Branches on data are what a CPU predicts worst, and log lines vary in length on every single line.

So the parser works in two passes over each 64 KiB block, which fits in L2 between them:

  1. Newline pass. AVX2 compares 32 bytes at a time against \n, unrolled to 128 bytes per iteration. Lines are longer than 32 bytes, so a step holds at most one newline, and one unconditional store records it. A step with no newline writes a junk entry the next store overwrites. The loop has no branch on where lines end.
  2. Line pass. A counted loop over the recorded line ends. Each line is read from its start and from its end simultaneously.

From the front: the day and hour digits sit at bytes 8 to 15 of the timestamp. One 8-byte load gives them all, and a bit trick turns them into an hour index (October's tens digit '3' has bit 1 set where '0' does not, which handles the month rollover with no comparison). Hours change rarely along the file, so the current hour's write cursor stays in registers until those digits change.

From the back: the latency is the last field, so it is read back from the newline. Its digits are joined in three multiply-shift steps (pairs, then fours, then all eight), SWAR style, inside one 64-bit register:

let v = (v & 0x0F0F_0F0F_0F0F_0F0F).wrapping_mul(2561) >> 8;
let v = (v & 0x00FF_00FF_00FF_00FF).wrapping_mul(6_553_601) >> 16;
let v = (v & 0x0000_FFFF_0000_FFFF).wrapping_mul(42_949_672_960_001) >> 32;

The status is a fixed three bytes before the latency, and the endpoint is whatever sits between the method and the status. The method's length comes from finding the first space in one 8-byte word with a borrow trick. No loops over characters anywhere in the hot path.

2. Endpoints become ids, through one AES instruction

Every line needs to become an endpoint id. Comparing strings is expensive, and endpoints run up to 125 bytes.

The endpoint is hashed without a length-dependent loop: its first and last 32 bytes are loaded as two AVX2 registers (bytes outside the name masked off with a sliding window of ones and zeros), and mixed with vaesenc, which runs a full AES round on both 16-byte halves in a single instruction. Two more rounds finish the mix. Names over 64 bytes fold in two overlapping middle loads.

The 64-bit hash is looked up in one shared open-addressing table of 8,192 slots. Each slot packs the hash and id + 1 into a single AtomicU64, so a lookup is one load and one compare. The table fills under a lock in the first moments of the run and is read-only after that, so all twelve threads share one hot copy in cache. With 1,842 names and 53 compared bits, the odds of any two names colliding are about 2 × 10⁻¹⁰.

I measured a hardware-CRC32 hash against it along the way. The profile showed the AES hash at under 5% of samples, so the one with the full 64 bits of mixing stayed. That became a habit for the rest of the project: the profile decides, not the instruction count.

3. A whole log line in 4 bytes

An average line is about 77 bytes. By the time it leaves the parser it is 4 bytes:

| id + 1 (11 bits) | error (1 bit) | latency (20 bits) |

The hour is implicit: the row is written into its hour's region of one large anonymous reservation, which costs nothing until a page is touched. About 1% of latencies need more than 20 bits; those store an escape value and spill the full number into the next row. Each thread fills its own 256-row chunk of each hour, so writing a row needs no atomics at all; only grabbing a new chunk touches a shared counter.

That is roughly a 19× reduction in the data everything downstream has to touch.

4. The idea that changed the shape of the program: seal hours early

For the first day and a half, the program had two phases: parse everything, then summarise everything. That meant all 72 hours of rows were alive at once.

Then I went back to the most valuable sentence in the spec. The file is eight shards, each writing in time order, interleaved as chunks arrive. That means once the parsed prefix of the file contains a line from hour h + 2, the lines of hour h have effectively all arrived.

So the engine seals hour h at that moment, and summarises it while the rest of the file is still being parsed. Parsing and summarising overlap across all twelve threads, and only a few hours of rows are ever alive instead of all 72.

The spec deliberately promises no bound on how out of order a line can be, so this is designed as a verified bet with an exact fallback. Every claim records the lowest and highest hour it contains. If a line ever turns up in an hour that was already sealed, a dirty flag is set and the whole job reruns with early sealing switched off. The output is byte-exact for any line order; on the real data the fast path simply always wins (on seed 1 the margin is at least 0.78 MiB of file).

// Hours below `sealed` have all their rows. Each thread works from its own snapshot of
// the claims, which only ever lags behind the truth, so it seals too little, never too much.

That comment is the whole correctness argument for the concurrency: a stale view can only make the engine more cautious, never wrong.

5. Sort without comparing, percentiles without searching

A sealed hour's rows are radix sorted by latency, in place, in two 10-bit passes. Then they are dealt out by endpoint, which is stable, so every endpoint's latencies come out already sorted. Nearest-rank p50, p95 and p99 are then three array reads at index (p * n + 99) / 100.

No comparison sort, no per-group allocation, no hash map of vectors. Every count, error tally and percentile for an hour comes out of one linear sweep.

6. Write in parallel, give memory back immediately

Each hour's text is formatted over its own rows, in the same pages. Once every earlier hour's text exists, an hour's byte offset in the output file is known, and whichever thread notices goes ahead and writes it with pwrite. So writes happen from several threads at once, overlapped with parsing.

Right after its write, the hour's pages are returned with MADV_DONTNEED. The input is treated the same way: each 1 MiB claim's file pages are dropped as soon as it is parsed, while every thread is still busy, instead of being torn down by one thread at exit. That single change took about 7 ms of teardown off the critical path.

This is how peak memory went from 228 MB to around 16 MB while the program got faster, not slower.

The journey, commit by commit


133 commits touched Track A in 72 hours. The arc looks like this:

Stage What happened Result
Kickoff Repo from the template, team registered, board app installed, check.py and generated datasets reproducing the reference's SHA-256 A working pipeline from laptop to leaderboard
Day 1, evening First dependency-free Rust engine: mmap, threads, contiguous arena, target-cpu=native Off the reference, onto the board
Day 1, night Zero-copy shared mapping, single-pass streaming, lock-free tallying 79.98 pts, 33.5 ms, 19.3 MB
Day 2 AVX2 SIMD parser, L1-resident endpoint table, SWAR digit decoding, branchless date math 83.16 pts, 19.3 ms
Day 2 Explored C and C++20 engines side by side to try ideas fast: per-hour regions, in-place radix sort, parallel pwrite 84.38 pts, 17.6 MB
Day 3 Brought every winning idea home into one Rust file; vaesenc endpoint hash, zero-alloc hour summaries 85.71 pts, 15.4 MB
Day 3 Lab A/B workflow, perf profiling branch and PGO lane come online; every change measured before it is pushed 1% differences become visible
Day 3 Streaming hour sealer: summarise and write hours while the file is still being parsed 86.21 pts, 19.0 ms
Final 128-byte unrolled newline scan, P-core aware build, static linking, final tuning 86.25 pts

The C and C++ detour deserves a word, because it was one of the most productive parts of the hackathon. Writing the same engine in three languages in parallel let me test a structural idea in whichever was quickest to change, and keep the idea rather than the language. Every technique that survived ended up in the final Rust file, with unsafe kept to the raw-pointer hot loops and the standard library doing everything else.

The pit crew: everything we built around the engine

The engine is 524 lines. The project around it is what let those 524 lines get tuned 133 times in 72 hours without a single wrong answer reaching the final commit. When a run lasts 19 ms, the tooling is the methodology, so it grew in layers, each one added the moment the previous one stopped being precise enough.

Layer 1: the board, locally. check.py builds the track exactly the way the board does (offline, --network=none, from the real Dockerfile) and runs it in the board's sandbox: read-only filesystem, unprivileged user, 8 GB, 512 processes, 1 GB of /tmp. It prints the output's SHA-256 and fails when it differs from the expected hash. The reference's hash on the generated data became the contract, and every change had to reproduce it before it was allowed near a push.

Layer 2: data at every scale. The organisers' generators are deterministic, so tiny, sample and full datasets for any seed could be generated locally and compared against the Python reference. Seed 1 at full scale is the board's dataset; seeds 2, 3 and 7 became our private holdouts, because final scoring uses a seed nobody has seen.

Layer 3: reading the board like an API. The leaderboard publishes a JSON file, so small Python scripts turned it into instruments: one waits until the board has picked up a specific commit and finished evaluating it, one polls the queue state of our in-flight run, and one prints a ranked table of time, memory, source lines and dependency count for every Track A entry. Pushing stopped being "refresh and hope" and became "push, wait for this SHA, read the numbers".

Layer 4: a lab with real statistics. At 19 ms, the live board measures one run per push, and near-identical code scored anywhere from 19.2 to 22.6 ms between runs. A 1% improvement is invisible there. So a lab branch got a GitHub Actions workflow that:

  • builds the base (speed-demon) and the candidate with docker build of the real Dockerfile,
  • checks the candidate's output against the reference on seed 1 and a freshly generated seed 7, both at full scale,
  • times base and candidate alternately for 25 rounds on the same machine and compares medians and trimmed means,
  • reads the cgroup's memory.peak, the same counter the board uses, so memory is measured the way it is scored.

Every experiment then got its own branch, named after the idea (ab-a-scan128 for the 128-byte newline scan), merged on top of the shared ab-base harness. An idea was a branch, a branch was a measurement, and a measurement was a decision.

Layer 5: a profiler and a PGO lane. A prof branch runs perf record on the engine on seed 1 at full scale, with a source-line view, so the question "where does the time go" always had a current answer: parsing about 50%, summarising hours about 25%, the kernel about 20%, mostly page faults. A pgo branch trains profiles inside the allowlisted toolchain image with target-cpu pinned to the scoring box's Alder Lake, so profile-guided builds could be evaluated on equal terms. Because the parser is branch-free by design, it turned out to need no profile to run at full speed, which was a nice confirmation of the design.

Layer 6: a champion that every candidate must beat. The repository always held the best-scoring version of the engine. A candidate went live only if it beat the champion, and if a board run disagreed with the lab, the champion was restored in the next commit. That is why the history contains commits titled "Restore personal best": they are the ratchet that kept the score moving in one direction.

Layer 7: the log. Every board step is recorded in track-a/PERF.md with the run ID that measured it, alongside the lab method and the profile, so every number in this post can be traced to the run that produced it.

The 128-byte newline scan is the cleanest example of the whole pipeline working: the lab measured it at 1.1% to 2.9% faster, a difference no single board run could have shown, and it shipped because the medians on two different CPUs agreed.

What 72 hours felt like

The surprising thing was how little of the speed came from making any single operation faster. The big wins all came from not doing work: not parsing the date, because its position is fixed; not comparing strings, because a hash in a register is enough; not sorting with comparisons, because latencies are integers; not keeping 72 hours alive, because the shards are time-ordered; not tearing down pages at exit, because twelve threads can release them while they work.

Each of those came from rereading the spec and asking what it promised, then building the fastest program that keeps every one of those promises and checks the one it is not allowed to assume.

The other thing I will keep is the measurement habit. When a run lasts 19 milliseconds, your intuition is the noisiest instrument in the room. An A/B harness that alternates runs and compares medians turned "I think this is faster" into "this is 2% faster, on two CPUs, on four seeds, with the same SHA-256", and that is what let the last few points land.

Zero dependencies, one file, 524 lines, 1,690× faster than the reference, and every byte of the output exact.

title: Stop Catting Your .env File
description:
We've all done it. Something's broken, someone asks "what's in your env?", and you run:

cat .env

Then you paste the output into Slack, a GitHub issue, or a screen share — and only afterwards remember that file holds your database password, your API keys, and your production tokens. Now they're in chat history forever.

That's the exact accident environmental-peek exists to prevent.

The problem hiding in plain sight

.env files are the worst-kept secrets in software. They sit in every project, they're full of credentials, and the only way to check them is to print them in full:

  • Debugging in public — pasting .env output into a support thread or team chat
  • Screen sharing — one cat .env during a call and the whole meeting has your keys
  • CI logs — a stray printenv in a debug step and your secrets are in the build log

You rarely need the actual values. What you actually want to know is: which keys are set, which are missing, and is anything misspelled? That's a very different question from "show me all my secrets."

What environmental-peek does

environmental-peek lets you safely inspect your .env files without leaking secrets. It shows you the structure of your environment — what keys exist and whether they're set — while keeping the sensitive values masked.

So instead of dumping credentials to check why your app can't connect, you get answers like:

  • DATABASE_URL — set ✓
  • STRIPE_SECRET_KEY — missing ✗ (there's your bug)
  • API_KEY — set ✓

No values on screen. No secrets in chat history. No panic after you hit send.

Get started 

npm install environmental-peek

Then run envpeek in your project and check your environment the safe way.

Why I built it

Every "don't commit your .env" guide stops at the git part. Nobody talks about the dozen other ways secrets leak — the paste, the screenshot, the shared terminal. I wanted a tool that makes the safe way also the easy way, so checking your environment stops being a security incident waiting to happen.

environmental-peek is at v0.2.0 now, with 400+ total downloads on npm. It's still early — if you try it and there's a case it doesn't cover, I'd genuinely love to hear about it.

Try it, break it, and tell me what it missed. Feedback welcome.

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/environmental-peek
GitHub: https://github.com/parasraju/environmental-peek

Safely inspect your .env files without leaking secrets. npm install environmental-peek

title: Latent-Lens: Visual Perception in Small Language Models Through Latent Communication
description:
arXiv:2610.41751v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Bridging independent vision-language models (VLMs) and small language models (SLMs) in a modular multi-agent system typically forces them to exchange information as discrete text, which creates a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained details. This constraint is especially acute for SLMs, whose limited capacity makes them more reliant on the quality of the input signal. Recent latent-communication methods exchange states between language models. How a VLM can pass visual information to a separately pretrained text-only SLM though remains unexplored. We propose \textbf{Latent-Lens}, a lightweight codec that bridges the representation gap between a frozen VLM and a frozen SLM directly in latent space, enabling them to communicate purely through hidden states. The codec consists of a domain encoder that projects hidden states from the VLM into the SLM's embedding space, and an attention decoder formalised as a LoRA that teaches the SLM to attend to these visual prefixes, while training only ${\sim}1.6$M parameters (0.2\% of the combined model size). On visual question answering (CLEVR, GQA), Latent-Lens achieves $81.0\pm7.9$\% and $65.4\pm5.4$\%, compared with $58.3\pm5.7$\% and $61.8\pm1.0$\% for text communication with the same LoRA budget (+30.2--69.8pp relative to frozen text communication), while on image captioning (Flickr8k) it improves over the same baseline by +16.5 (+18.8 frozen). We also evaluate Latent-Lens with TinyLlama-1.1B and InternVL2-1B, which use different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.

description:
Announcing the World's Largest Free Font Collection: 500,000+ Typefaces Across 100 Sovereign Script Vaults

Typography is the foundational voice of human civilization and digital culture. Yet, in modern web development, Linux server infrastructure, and digital publishing, non-Latin, minority, and indigenous writing systems frequently suffer from missing glyphs, font fragmentation, commercial paywalls, and broken links.

To solve this permanently, I architected and curated the Open Typography Foundation — a non-profit, censorship-resistant digital heritage preservation initiative dedicated to curating, indexing, and distributing 100% free and open-source typefaces worldwide.

Today, we officially achieved our grandest historic milestone: 500,337 verified open-source fonts categorized across 100 sovereign script vaults, spanning over 100 writing systems.

Metric Details
Total Verified Fonts 500,337 Typefaces (Clean TTF, OTF, WOFF binaries)
Sovereign Script Vaults 100 Dedicated Script Vaults
Global Languages & Scripts 100+ Writing Systems (Major, Regional, Endangered, Classical)
Licensing 100% Free & Permissive (SIL OFL 1.1, Apache 2.0, MIT)
Direct Single Downloads 1-Click .TTF Download on every font card
Master GitHub Hub Open-Typography-Foundation/100-Sovereign-Fonts-Vaults
Permanent Preservation Redundant mirrors on GitHub, GitLab, and the Internet Archive

🌐 The Universal Font Browser: Instant In-Browser Search Engine

Handling over half a million font files in a browser without browser freeze or gigabytes of memory consumption was our primary engineering challenge.

We developed a client-side Two-Tier Micro-Index Engine:

  1. Core Instant Search (1,941 curated families): Loads instantly with 0ms latency.
  2. Deep On-Demand Vault Indexes (382,980+ raw fonts): Broken into 100 ultra-compact JSON indexes (~13 MB total). When a user searches for any rare font, the browser asynchronously scans the indexes with automatic debounce and pulls live download links from redundant raw mirrors.

title: Highlight the Current Page with jQuery, CSS & PHP
description:
Here’s a common web development scenario: How do we highlight the current page in a navigation seamlessly and dynamically? The answer is jQuery.

See a Live Demo

My recipe for this common scenario involves a mixture of CSS and JavaScript with a dash of jQuery.

HTML 

<ul id="navigation">
    <li><a href="https://www.kevinleary.net/about/">About</a></li>
    <li><a href="https://www.kevinleary.net/services/">Services</a></li>
    <li><a href="https://www.kevinleary.net/blog/">Blog</a></li>
    <li><a class="active" href="https://www.kevinleary.net/contact/">contact</a></li>
</ul>

JavaScript / jQuery 

$(function(){
    $page = jQuery.url.attr("file");
    if(!$page) {
        $page = 'index.html';
    }
    $('#navigation li a').each(function(){
        var $href = $(this).attr('href');
        if ( ($href == $page) || ($href == '') ) {
            $(this).addClass('on');
        } else {
            $(this).removeClass('on');
        }
    });
});

Usage

You’ll need a copy of jQuery, along with a copy of the jQuery URL Parser plugin.

After you include jQuery, and the URL Parser add the JavaScript snippet above to the section of your document.

How it works

What we do here is simple, we grab the current name of the page, for example about.html. Then we check out **ul.navigation

<

ul>** to see if any of the anchors contain an href attribute with that value. If any of the links are a match we flag the parent of the anchor with a CSS class. In this case I’ve chosen current to keep things self explanatory.

Notes

In this case I chose to add the “current” class to the

  • rather than to the anchor. Usually I will create a navigation using CSS sprite techniques, and this allows me greater control over the presentation of that element. This can come in handy for rounded corners or tabs.

title: A Heroku alternative in India, billed in rupees by UPI
description:
Originally published on the Plexivo blog.

Many developers learnt to ship with Heroku. You connect a repository, push your code and a new release goes live. That way of working is still the right one for most web apps and APIs. What changes in India is everything around it: where the app runs, how you pay, and what the invoice says.

This guide shows how that workflow looks on Plexivo, an AI-native cloud built in India and launched on 1 November 2026. Your app runs in Mumbai. Your database sits beside it. Prices are in US dollars, and you pay in rupees by UPI, card or net banking, with a GST tax invoice for every top-up.

What should a Heroku alternative in India offer?

When Indian teams look for a git-push platform, the same five needs come up again and again:

  • A region close to their users. Requests that stay in India arrive sooner.
  • Deploy on every push. Connect GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket once and stop thinking about it.
  • A managed database next to the app. Backups, patches and TLS handled for you.
  • Rupee payments that finance can file. UPI, cards and net banking, with a proper GST invoice.
  • No surprise bill. A clear price before anything runs, and a balance you can always see.

Plexivo is built around exactly these. The rest of this article walks through each one and ends with a step-by-step deploy.

Where will my app and data run?

India (Mumbai) is live; more countries are available on request. Your Plexivo App Runner apps, Plexivo Postgres and Plexivo MySQL databases, Plexivo Cache instances and Plexivo Kubernetes workloads all run in Mumbai. Database backups are kept in Mumbai and copied to Hyderabad, so a disaster in one city cannot take both your database and its backups.

Your account, billing and audit records are kept in India too. Every new account acknowledges where its data lives at sign-up. The full picture is on the data residency page.

How does git-push deployment work on Plexivo App Runner?

Plexivo App Runner deploys web apps and APIs from a Git repository or a container image, with HTTPS and autoscaling.

You connect your Git provider once. For GitHub you install the Plexivo GitHub App and choose which repositories it may read. For GitLab and Bitbucket you sign in and approve Plexivo, and Plexivo adds the webhook for you. From then on, every push to the branch you chose starts a new build, and the current release keeps serving until the new one is ready. Pushes to other branches are ignored.

Builds work in two ways. If your repository has a Dockerfile at its root, Plexivo builds it as it is. If it does not, Plexivo detects your language and framework, installs your dependencies, builds and sets the start command. Node.js, Next.js, React, Python, Django, FastAPI, Go, PHP, Laravel, static sites and any Dockerfile are supported. Each build runs in its own isolated sandbox, and the image is signed before release.

Your app needs one thing from you: listen on the port in the PORT environment variable, on 0.0.0.0. Unless your image declares another port, it is 8080. In Node.js that is two lines:

const port = process.env.PORT || 8080;
app.listen(port, '0.0.0.0');

Every app gets a free HTTPS address at <name>.plexivo.app, and you can add your own domain later. The build guide covers build minutes, logs and faster builds.

Can I run a managed PostgreSQL database beside my app?

Yes. Plexivo Postgres offers PostgreSQL 18 (recommended) and PostgreSQL 17. Every database comes with TLS on every connection, a generated password and continuous backups from the moment it starts. You can restore to any moment within your backup period into a new database, while the original keeps serving.

Put the database in the same project as your app and they talk over the private network. Connect the two in the console and the app receives DATABASE_URL and DATABASE_CA_CERT as environment variables. When the password rotates, the variables follow, so you never copy a password by hand.

Plexivo Postgres is also a whole backend if you want one: Auth, a Data API, Realtime, GraphQL and Functions from one database. Read create your first database to begin, or the deeper guide to managed PostgreSQL in Mumbai.

How do I pay for cloud hosting in rupees by UPI?

Plexivo is prepaid. You add money to your organisation's wallet, and plan fees and resource charges come from it.

  • Prices and wallets are in US dollars for every customer, so a price you see today means the same thing next month.
  • Indian customers pay in rupees by UPI, card or net banking. The rupee amount is the US dollar amount at this month's rate: the RBI reference rate on the 1st of the month plus a 2% conversion margin. It stays the same all month.
  • 18% GST is added on top, never taken from your wallet credit. Before you pay, the Payment summary shows the wallet credit, the GST and the Total to pay.
  • Every top-up gets a GST tax invoice in rupees, with the rate used printed on it. Add your GSTIN and it appears on every invoice.

If the wallet runs low, Plexivo emails your owners and admins first. If it cannot pay, resources pause and nothing more is charged; your data is kept. A prepaid wallet means a pause, never a debt. The wallet and currency page explains each step, and our article on GST invoices for cloud hosting goes through the invoice line by line.

Anyone can sign up from anywhere. Payments from outside India are coming soon.

What does a small app cost to start?

There are two parts to what you pay: a plan for your organisation, and the resources you run.

The Developer plan is US$9 a month billed yearly, or US$11 a month billed monthly. It includes Plexivo App Runner, Plexivo Postgres, Plexivo MySQL and Plexivo Cache, 3 projects, 100 build minutes a month and 50 GB of internet transfer. Startup is US$99 a month billed yearly and keeps apps always on, with autoscaling. Yearly billing saves 17% on plan fees.

Resources are priced on their own and charged by the day:

Resource Smallest size Price a month
Plexivo App Runner 0.125 vCPU, 256 MB US$6.04
Plexivo Postgres 0.25 vCPU, 512 MB, 10 GB US$11.98
Plexivo Cache 256 MB, 10 GB volume US$6.94

The smallest app, database and cache together come to US$24.96 a month. On Developer, an idle Plexivo App Runner instance sleeps after 15 minutes without requests and wakes on the next one. Every limit is on the pricing page.

Step by step: from repository to a live HTTPS address

  1. Create your account. Go to cloud.plexivo.io, pick Individual or Business, and confirm your email with the 6-digit code. A business registered for GST can tick This organisation is registered for GST and enter its GSTIN.
  2. Start a new app. On Home, choose Deploy your first app, or choose Create at the top of any page, then Plexivo App Runner.
  3. Connect your code. Under Source, pick GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket and choose Connect GitHub (or GitLab, or Bitbucket). Then choose the Repository and Branch.
  4. Name and size it. The name becomes your address. Under Size, choose the Instance size and the Minimum instances and Maximum instances.
  5. Check the price and deploy. The panel on the right shows the Estimated monthly cost. Choose Deploy; the button carries your app's name. Follow the build on the Deployments tab.
  6. Add a database. Choose Create, then Plexivo Postgres. On your app's Environment tab, under Add a database or cache, choose the Resource and Connect.
  7. Top up in rupees. In Billing → Add money, enter the Amount to add (US$), check the Payment summary and choose Pay.

In India, your PAN is checked once, when you first approve a deployment. Prefer to describe it instead? Type it into the Plexivo AI box on Home and choose Plan my app. Plexivo AI reads the repository, prepares a plan with its price, and nothing runs until you choose Approve & deploy.

To reach your database from your laptop, install the Plexivo CLI and open an encrypted tunnel:

plexivo auth login
plexivo db connect orders-db

Moving an existing app and database

Coming from Heroku or another platform? Your app usually moves as it is: point Plexivo App Runner at the same repository, set the same environment variables, and read PORT. For data, open Migrations, choose New migration and pick your source; the console shows where to find the connection string for each one. The copy reads your source, which keeps running normally, and you switch your app over when you are ready. See move to Plexivo Postgres and our guide to deploying Next.js with a database in India.

FAQ

Is Plexivo a good Heroku alternative for Indian developers?

Plexivo keeps the familiar workflow: connect a repository and every push deploys. It adds a Mumbai region, managed Plexivo Postgres beside your app, and rupee payments by UPI with a GST tax invoice. Try it on the Developer plan to see if it fits your app.

Can I pay for cloud hosting by UPI?

Yes. Indian customers pay in rupees by UPI, card or net banking. The amount is the US dollar top-up at this month's rate plus 18% GST, and you see the Total to pay before you confirm.

Why are prices in US dollars if I pay in rupees?

One currency keeps prices stable and the same for every customer. The rupee rate is fixed on the 1st of each month, so every payment in a month uses the same rate, and it is printed on your invoice.

What happens if my wallet runs out?

Resources pause and nothing more is charged, while your data is kept. Owners and admins are emailed before each step. Add money and everything comes back at once.

Which languages and frameworks can I deploy?

Node.js, Next.js, React, Python, Django, FastAPI, Go, PHP, Laravel, static sites and any Dockerfile. You can also deploy a public container image built in your own CI.

Start building

Create your organisation at cloud.plexivo.io and deploy your first app to Mumbai. The free trial is on the Developer plan, and no credit card is required.

title: I built a Windows SQL client where an LLM drafts the query and you stay in control
description:
Disclosure: I work at Mirinai and built this app. This post was drafted with the help of AI and reviewed by me.

Letting an LLM near a database worries me in two ways: what leaves my machine, and what happens if the generated SQL is wrong. I built Chat DB Manager, a Windows desktop database client, around those two questions.

You ask a question in plain language and the app fills the editor with SQL for the connected DBMS. Nothing runs until you read it and press Run.

What goes to the LLM

  • Default mode (SQL Helper) sends the schema in a compact notation (tables, columns, types, keys, comments, indexes), not table rows. Conversation history, files you attach, and the DB error text on auto-repair are also sent. Asking for an execution plan explanation sends the SQL and the plan. Sample values of code-like columns are sent only if you turn that on (off by default).
  • Agent mode runs read queries itself and reads the rows, so it needs explicit consent per recipient company. Switching provider resets it to SQL Helper.
  • With a local model behind an OpenAI-compatible URL (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM), LLM requests go only to that URL.
  • No telemetry. The app only contacts your LLM provider and our server for update checks.

What happens before SQL runs

  • Risk is decided by the app parsing the SQL, not by the model's label. A script is judged by its worst statement, so SELECT 1; DROP TABLE t is not a SELECT.
  • Read-only connections refuse anything but SELECT.
  • Writes run in an open transaction. You see the affected row count and commit or roll back. No answer in 2 minutes means rollback.
  • DDL and UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE need an extra confirmation, plus a checkbox on connections tagged prod.
  • Agent reads run in a read-only transaction and are rolled back (SQL Server and SAP HANA get rollback only).

Read-only is an app-level guard. It cannot catch SELECT some_writing_function(), so please use a read-only DB account for production.

Supported

  • DBMS: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, MS SQL Server, Oracle, SAP HANA
  • LLMs: Anthropic Claude, OpenAI, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, Azure)

Limits

  • Windows x64 only (Electron). No macOS or Linux build. I tested it on Windows 11 Home 26H2.
  • The installer (~143 MB) is not code-signed, so SmartScreen will likely warn you. It installs per user without admin rights, and the SHA-256 is on the download page.
  • No account or sign-up. Bring your own LLM API key or a local endpoint.
  • Free for now. The source code is not public.

If you have no test database, a single SQLite file is enough to try the main flow.

Feedback I would like

  • Which databases would you want next?
  • Is the line between "schema only" and "schema plus rows with consent" in the right place?

title: Observable-Specific Validity Tests for Scientific AI: Controlled Approximations and Intervention Response
description:
arXiv:2610.41939v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: An approximation can reproduce an energy while missing its response, or satisfy an error tolerance without being certified by a given bound. We formulate observable-specific validity records for scientific artificial intelligence (AI) that link a reduction to its reference model, error measure, tolerance, parameter domain, and transformations or interventions. Explicit displacement and velocity certificates for a singularly perturbed oscillator recover distinct convergence orders and provide sufficient validity guarantees. Exact Hubbard dimer relations resolve the different coupling domains accepted by energy and response criteria. Across 16 repeated neural fits, imposing dimensional homogeneity reduces energy scale transfer error from 52.3% to 0.0768% and raises the median fraction jointly satisfying gap and response tolerances from zero to 100%. Paired transformations verify the protected scaling relation, while a coupling crossover identifies the additional information needed for response transfer. A causal model recovers a positive intervention response beneath a strong negative observational association. For two mechanisms observed with Gaussian noise whose responses first differ at order $x^k$, we derive an exact fixed control query requirement scaling as $x^{-2k}$ and verify its full success curve numerically. Together with a 256-task evaluation interface, these results provide independently checkable tests of controlled approximation, physical transfer, and mechanism discrimination in scientific AI.

title: Rename or Reorder CSV Columns in the Browser: What the Export Actually Contains
description:
The Data Studio in OnePassApps has eleven tool tabs. Nine posts on this site cover ten of them; the Columns tab had never had one, so that is today's post: the one place where you pick a column, rename it, move it left or right, and then check what the exported file actually contains.

I work on OnePassApps.

You can try it at the Data Studio. The written walkthrough is on the OnePassApps guides page.

Before you load anything

The panel is the usual three steps - 01 Source, 02 Options, 03 Result - and the action button on this tab is "Load / refresh columns", not "Parse CSV". The options step is empty until you press it, and the panel tells you so: "Column options appear once the CSV is loaded."

The preview area reads "CSV PREVIEW" with "No data yet", and the stage hint says "Load the columns, then rename or reorder them in Options." The source hint is the Data Studio's usual one: "Drop a data file, or browse CSV, TSV, JSON or YAML · up to 20 MiB · or paste rows in Source".

The four controls that appear

After the load, 02 Options holds four things:

  • Delimiter - the same picker as everywhere else, shipping on "Auto detect · comma", with Comma, Tab, Semicolon and Pipe behind it.
  • Column - a picker whose options are your real header names. On a six-column file it offered id, name, score, active, note, price.
  • Position - two arrow buttons, "Move column left" and "Move column right".
  • Rename column - a text input, prefilled with the selected column's name, with a Rename button beside it.

Renaming a column, and reading the export

Pick name, clear the rename field, type employee_name, press Rename. The result step reports "Column name updated in the active table." The preview header changes with it - the column now reads employee_name with a TEXT badge - and so does the exported file.

The "Download CSV" button on this tab writes a real file. After the rename it was 169 bytes of text/csv;charset=utf-8, and its header row was:

"id","employee_name","score","active","note","price"

Moving a column

With the first column selected, "Move column left" is disabled - there is nothing to its left. "Move column right" moved id one slot along: the preview became name, id, score, active, note, price, and the downloaded file was 160 bytes with the header

"name","id","score","active","note","price"

To move a column a longer way, select it in the picker (the last column, price, is fine) and press "Move column left" as many times as you need. Two clicks on price gave name, id, score, price, active, note, and the file matched:

"name","id","score","price","active","note"

Rename and reorder in the same pass

The two controls are independent, and the export carries both. After renaming the moved column from price to amount, the preview read name, id, score, amount, active, note and the downloaded file was 161 bytes:

"name","id","score","amount","active","note"

What the bytes keep

Every field is quoted, the line endings are CRLF, and the values are untouched: a cell holding 007 was still "007" in the export, so nothing was coerced to a number, and the empty cell was an empty quoted field rather than the em dash the preview shows. The preview's type badges (id NUMBER, score NUMBER, the rest TEXT) are a label for the eye - the export does not convert anything on the strength of them.

The caveat worth knowing

"Reload CSV" re-reads the source you pasted. After I renamed a column and then pressed it, the rename was gone and the header was back to its original name, while the counts were unchanged - "Loaded 3 rows and 6 columns.", "3 rows · 6 columns · no parsing issues", "Delimiter found Comma". The rename lives in the active table inside that tab, not in your file, so export before you reload.

What leaves the tab, and what it costs

Nothing, as usual. The page says "Nothing leaves this tab." and the stage says "Processing stays in this browser.", and the limits box spells it out: "Pasted text supports up to 10,000 lines. Pasted CSV supports up to 8 MiB and 10,000 data rows; CSV files support up to 20 MiB, 100,000 rows, and 2 million cells. JSON supports up to 2 MiB and YAML up to 1 MiB. Your data stays on this device."

The plan block on the same page still reads FREE PROMOTIONAL PERIOD - Standard is free right now, $0 / month, 100,000 credits every 30 days, No end date set, No card required, and No automatic paid subscription.

If you want the same treatment for the other Data Studio tabs, the guides are linked above. I work on OnePassApps - the studios process the file in the tab, not on a server.

title: How to Design a Guided Camera Flow People Actually Follow
description:
Here is the brief. A person is standing in a car park. They are holding a phone in one hand and car keys in the other. It is bright, they are in a hurry, and they are not a photographer.

You need eight specific photos from them, from specific angles, consistent enough that all eight look like they belong to the same set.

Most capture flows fail at this, and they fail in the same few ways. These are the lessons that came out of building one.

## Nobody reads the instructions

The instinct is to explain. "Stand about three metres from the front left corner of the vehicle, with the car filling roughly 80 percent of the frame."

Nobody reads that. Not because users are careless, but because they are standing outside holding things, and reading is a task you just added on top of the task they came to do.

Replace the sentence with a picture. A faint outline on the camera view showing where the car should sit does the entire job with no reading at all. People align things to shapes automatically. They do not parse spatial instructions.

If you have text at all, it should be three words. "Front left corner."

Show the target, not the error

Telling someone they got it wrong after the fact is the worst possible moment. They have already moved, already tapped, already mentally finished that step.

Put the guidance before the shutter. An outline they are aligning to, that changes colour when they are close enough, is a conversation that happens while they can still act on it. The user fixes the problem without ever being told there was one.

This is the single biggest difference between a flow people finish and a flow people abandon.

## Validate immediately, but never block

Check the photo the instant it is taken. Too dark, too blurry, object not found, obviously the wrong angle. Those checks are cheap and they catch most real problems.

But do not trap people. If someone has tried twice and it is still not passing, let them through. Mark the photo as needing review and move on.

A flow that refuses to advance is a flow that gets closed. You will lose the other six photos as well as the one you were arguing about, and you will never get that person back to the car park.

Accept and flag beats reject and insist, every time.

## Progress is the motivator, not quality

A counter showing "3 of 8" does more for completion than any amount of feedback about image quality.

People finish things that look finishable. A visible end point turns an open-ended chore into a short list, and short lists get completed. Quality nagging does the opposite, because every correction makes the end feel further away.

Show progress prominently. Show quality feedback quietly.

## Assume the worst conditions, because they are the normal ones

Direct sunlight means they cannot see your subtle grey overlay. Use high contrast.

One hand is busy. Keep everything reachable with a thumb, and never put a critical control at the top of the screen.

Signal is bad. Car parks are famously bad for this, and often half underground. Capture locally, queue the upload, and let them walk away. If your flow requires a successful upload before the next photo, you have built something that fails outdoors, which is the only place it will ever be used.

And assume they will be interrupted. Save state after every single photo so that a phone call does not cost them the whole session.

## The thing that is actually hard

None of the above is technically difficult. The hard part is accepting that the person using your flow does not care about it and never will.

They are not evaluating your interface. They want to put the keys down and go back inside. Every decision gets easier once you design for that person instead of the attentive user in your head.

We wrote up what good capture actually looks like from the photography side, which is the other half of this problem.

title: Change Data Capture: A Guide to Database Synchronization
description:
Quick version: Change Data Capture (CDC) sends only what changed in a database to another system, so you don't have to copy the whole table over and over.

Imagine ordering something online. You place an order, change your delivery address, and later check whether it has shipped. Each action updates information in a database.

Now think about the company's sales dashboard. How does it get those updates? It could copy the whole orders table every few minutes, but that seems like a lot of work when only a few orders have changed. Change Data Capture, or CDC, offers another way.

🔍 What Is Change Data Capture?

CDC is a way to identify changes in a database and send them to another system. The main changes are INSERT (adding a row), UPDATE (changing a row), and DELETE (removing a row).

Say order #2041 goes from 'pending' to 'shipped.' Instead of loading every order again, a CDC system can capture that update so a second system knows what happened. This is useful when a business keeps its everyday transactions in one database but runs reports somewhere else.

🕑 First, What Is a Batch Job?

A batch job is simply work that runs at a certain time or in groups, rather than processing each change the moment it happens. For example, a store might run a job every night at 2 a.m. to update its sales report.

But 'batch' tells us when the job runs, not how much data it copies. A batch job could use any of these methods:

  • Full refresh: Copy the entire table again. If the orders table has one million rows, the job reads all one million, even if only 100 changed.

  • Cursor-based incremental sync: Save a marker, often an updated_at timestamp or increasing ID, and fetch rows newer than the last marker. If 100 rows were updated, the job may only read those 100.

  • CDC: Read recorded database changes, usually from a transaction log or change stream. This can capture inserts, updates, and deletes, including changes that a simple timestamp query might miss.

So batch jobs and CDC are not opposites. A CDC tool can also run on a schedule. And people sometimes use 'incremental' as a broad term for any method that avoids copying everything. Here, 'cursor-based' specifically means checking rows against a saved marker.

Figure 1. Different ways of keeping data up to date.

❓ Why Does CDC Matter?

For small tables, a nightly full refresh might be perfectly fine. It is simple, and the report may not need to be up to the minute. As data grows, though, reading and moving unchanged records again and again can waste time and put extra work on the source database.

CDC helps keep dashboards, search results, and other systems fresher without repeatedly copying everything. It's especially helpful for data that changes often, such as orders or product inventory. It still isn't guaranteed to be instant, since the connector and destination can take time to process events.

⚙️ How Does Log-Based CDC Work?

Many databases keep a log of transactions. PostgreSQL uses a Write-Ahead Log (WAL), while MySQL has a binary log, or binlog. With the right setup, a CDC connector can read changes from these logs.

For example, when a worker changes order #2041 from 'pending' to 'shipped,' the database writes the update and records it in the log. A CDC connector reads the change and passes it to a destination, such as an analytics system, which can update the matching order.

Figure 2. A basic log-based CDC pipeline.

Often, a CDC tool begins with an initial snapshot to copy the rows that already exist. After that, it follows new changes. It also saves its position so it knows where to continue if the connection stops.

🧩 Three Common Ways to Capture Changes

1. Query-Based or Cursor-Based Sync

A script runs a query like 'show me rows updated since yesterday.' It's easy to build if your table has a reliable updated_at column. Think of a small club website updating its member list once a day. The catch is that hard deletes won't show up unless you track them separately, and several updates to one row may look like just one final state.

2. Trigger-Based CDC

A trigger is a rule inside the database that automatically runs when a row is inserted, updated, or deleted. For example, a school registration app could create a trigger that writes 'student 52 dropped course A' into a separate history table when an enrollment is removed. Another job can then read that history and update other systems.

Triggers are useful when you want a clear record of specific actions, especially in a smaller app. But every trigger adds work when data changes, and someone has to maintain the rules as tables change.

3. Log-Based CDC

This approach reads the database's own change records rather than checking rows over and over. A busy online store with thousands of orders might use it to keep its analytics system updated throughout the day. It can capture deletes and successive updates, but it needs the right permissions, log settings, and monitoring.

At a glance

Method How it works Good for Watch out for
Query/cursor-based Query rows changed since a saved marker Small apps with a reliable updated_at column Hard deletes and repeated updates to one row
Trigger-based Database rules write changes to a history table A clear record of specific actions in smaller apps Extra work on every change, plus rule upkeep
Log-based Read the database's own transaction log Busy systems that need deletes and successive updates Permissions, log settings, and monitoring

🛠️ What Tools Can Help?

You don't have to build a CDC pipeline from scratch. Debezium is an open-source tool for capturing database changes, and AWS Database Migration Service supports loading existing data followed by ongoing changes.

OLake Go is another example. For supported sources, it can read database changes and move data into Apache Iceberg tables or write plain Parquet files into object storage, such as Amazon S3. Iceberg helps manage tables in a data lake, while Parquet is a file format often used for analytics. Depending on the setup, OLake can do this without a separate Kafka pipeline.

⚠️ What Can Go Wrong?

CDC still needs maintenance. A connector might fall behind, logs might be removed before it catches up, or a restart could send an event more than once. Changing a column name or type can also cause trouble for the destination. Teams need monitoring and a plan for recovering safely.

💭 Final Thoughts

CDC sounds complicated at first, but the idea is pretty practical. Databases change all the time, and other systems need to keep up. Sometimes a full refresh is enough. Other times, a cursor-based job or CDC makes more sense. Understanding the difference helps you choose a solution without doing more work than you need to.

📚 Sources and Further Reading

  • IBM: What Is Change Data Capture?
  • Debezium: Features and Snapshots
  • PostgreSQL: Logical Decoding
  • MySQL: Binary Logging Formats
  • OLake Go: Documentation
  • OLake Go: Architecture Deep Dive
