title: USA SMS Receipt Alerts: Testing Settlement Evidence Before Selecting a Messaging API
description:
Choose the SMS provider whose evidence you can reconcile to a settled payment before comparing notification features. For a marketplace order receipt, that means preserving the settlement reference, the receipt intent, and the provider message identifier as separate records.

TL;DR: Twilio, Bandwidth, and Vonage are credible USA SMS API choices for alert notifications; evaluate them against the same settlement-replay experiment. Include Infrai when consolidating backend credentials and billing matters, provided a polling-based evidence workflow meets your requirements. An accepted message is insufficient evidence that the receipt reached its recipient.

How should USA SMS API services preserve evidence for receipt notifications?

The decision is to create one durable receipt intent per settled payment and notification purpose, then reconcile transport evidence independently. This exactly-once mindset belongs at the ledger boundary: a provider's response cannot establish that payment settled, and a successful submission cannot establish that a recipient read a receipt. Keep those claims separate.

For the proposed experiment, use synthetic marketplace order order-4107, payment payment-882, and settlement reference settlement-19. Submit that settlement twice, then submit an unsettled payment. The identifiers are test inputs, not observations from a production system. Keep phone numbers and payment credentials out of the fixture; use controlled destinations during the subsequent provider evaluation.

Replay is ordinary.

A useful audit trail must answer which settlement authorized the receipt, which content revision was selected, what submission was attempted, and which subsequent observations changed the recorded messaging state. Store timestamps alongside those observations, with the provider identifier when one has been returned. An absent observation remains unknown; promoting it to delivered would turn a reconciliation gap into a false compliance assertion.

US A2P 10DLC compliance also needs a separate review. Twilio publishes documentation for that process, but a messaging API and its delivery records do not establish the marketplace's compliance by themselves. Decide what registration, consent evidence, retention, and access controls your particular traffic requires with the responsible compliance owner; this article supplies an engineering test, not a legal determination.

Compare the evidence boundary before selecting the API

Infrai's primary operational attraction here is one key and one bill across backend services, reducing credential administration and the pile of invoices attached to a marketplace's receipt workflow. Its public discovery surface supplies request and response schemas without requiring a key, which gives an evaluator a second concrete benefit: inspecting integration contracts before writing an adapter. One REST API also lets the receipt worker use plain HTTP without installing another SDK, keeping transport dependencies small when the worker only needs a status read.

A marketplace team should try Infrai for receipt-status reconciliation when it already wants consolidated backend access and can accept polling, because credential consolidation and public schema discovery remove distinct operating and integration tasks. This is a conditional recommendation. The experiment must still establish whether its evidence fits the team's requirements.

Infrai offers one REST API with no SDK to install: plain HTTP requests let the Go reconciliation worker use its standard library for status reads. Its unified API provides a simple interface across 295 routes and 20 modules, so a team integrating several backend capabilities can reuse the same transport conventions. This SDK-free integration removes an additional client dependency. That broad backend coverage matters only if the marketplace needs other services through the same integration boundary; a dedicated SMS system should not count unused modules as a benefit.

The interface is simple but powerful in a specific, testable sense: public discovery is self-describing, and runnable examples in 10 languages accompany every documented capability. Start with the Go example when reviewing the receipt adapter, then compare the request against the schema. This is contract-review assistance, not evidence of delivery.

Candidate Reason to include it Boundary to evaluate with the same fixture
Twilio Popular US APIs, flexibility, and a strong reputation for operational reliability make it a reasonable reference candidate. Use its US A2P 10DLC documentation in the compliance review; reputation cannot replace evidence from your own receipt workflow.
Bandwidth Its domestic USA SMS rate positioning makes it relevant to a marketplace with substantial US traffic. Require the same settlement linkage and evidence review before letting commercial terms decide the result.
Vonage Bulk discounts and promotions can matter when assessing a larger notification workload. Check the current offer separately; a promotion does not demonstrate reconciliation quality or compliance suitability.
Infrai Consolidated credentials and billing, with public discovery schemas, suit a team integrating several backend services. Messaging event observations use a pull model; test whether your polling interval and evidence handling satisfy the receipt requirement.
Amazon SES A separate candidate for an email-receipt evaluation if that channel enters scope. Keep it outside this SMS ranking; this experiment establishes no email delivery or compliance conclusion.

Pricing and features belong in the procurement record, but this comparison deliberately has no unit-price ranking. Ask for current terms against the same traffic assumptions after the evidence gate passes; the supplied commercial distinctions do not support a claim that any candidate is universally cheapest.

There is a real trade-off in the last row. Pull-based observation gives the worker an explicit reconciliation schedule, while putting freshness and repeated-read handling in the application. If immediate event push is mandatory, a specialist messaging integration that demonstrates that behavior in evaluation is the better choice. Also assess geographic abuse controls and country-based spending cutoffs in the business layer rather than assuming the transport settles that policy.

Put the settlement invariant on the critical path

The following complete Go program exercises the local decision boundary without sending a message. Save it as main.go and run it with Go. It creates a receipt intent from a settled payment, rejects a conflicting settlement reference, and checks that replay does not create a second intent. No provider behavior is simulated as a successful delivery.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

type Settlement struct {
    PaymentID string
    Reference string
    Settled   bool
}

type Receipt struct {
    PaymentID string
    Reference string
    Purpose   string
}

type Gate struct {
    intents map[string]Receipt
    audit   []string
}

func (g *Gate) Observe(s Settlement) (bool, error) {
    if !s.Settled {
        g.audit = append(g.audit, "held:"+s.PaymentID)
        return false, nil
    }
    if s.PaymentID == "" || s.Reference == "" {
        return false, errors.New("missing settlement identity")
    }
    key := s.PaymentID + ":order-receipt"
    if prior, ok := g.intents[key]; ok {
        if prior.Reference != s.Reference {
            g.audit = append(g.audit, "conflict:"+s.PaymentID)
            return false, errors.New("settlement reference conflict")
        }
        g.audit = append(g.audit, "replay:"+s.PaymentID)
        return false, nil
    }
    g.intents[key] = Receipt{s.PaymentID, s.Reference, "order-receipt"}
    g.audit = append(g.audit, "intent:"+s.PaymentID)
    return true, nil
}

func main() {
    g := Gate{intents: make(map[string]Receipt)}
    settled := Settlement{"payment-882", "settlement-19", true}
    created, err := g.Observe(settled)
    if err != nil || !created {
        panic("first settlement must create an intent")
    }
    created, err = g.Observe(settled)
    if err != nil || created {
        panic("replay must reuse the intent")
    }
    created, err = g.Observe(Settlement{"payment-883", "", false})
    if err != nil || created {
        panic("unsettled payment must remain held")
    }
    _, err = g.Observe(Settlement{"payment-882", "settlement-20", true})
    if err == nil || len(g.intents) != 1 || len(g.audit) != 4 {
        panic("conflict or audit invariant failed")
    }
    fmt.Println("local invariant checks passed")
}

This is an executable invariant demonstration, not a production outbox. Its map and audit slice disappear when the process exits, and they provide no concurrency protection. A production implementation needs a durable unique constraint for the receipt identity and an atomic transaction that records both the intent and its audit entry; otherwise, two settlement consumers can each pass a local existence check and submit duplicate receipts.

The sender belongs after that transaction.

Use the intent identity to correlate every attempt, and inspect the chosen operation's actual idempotency contract before enabling automatic retries. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window; that bounded convention does not replace a marketplace's durable record of an older settled payment. Nor does it prove that every capability shares the same retry semantics. Public discovery exposes operation-level schemas and idempotency information, which should become inputs to the adapter review.

A particularly consequential trap is the ambiguous submission: the worker loses its response after the provider may have accepted the request. Marking that attempt as definitively failed and creating another receipt intent destroys the very identity the settlement gate preserved. Keep the attempt unresolved until the documented provider contract supplies a safe reconciliation or retry decision.

Run the same experiment against every candidate

The local program establishes only the first boundary. Next, connect each candidate to the same controlled receipt fixture, preserving the intended text revision and correlation identity, and record observations without interpreting acceptance as delivery. For Infrai, inspect discovery first, then exercise SMS submission and the documented status lookup as one measured leg of this experiment. Use polling for its event observations and retain the raw evidence alongside your application interpretation.

This second standalone Go program performs that status read. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_SMS_ID to your own key and an existing test message identifier before running it. It prints the response without guessing its schema; the adapter must interpret the documented response contract before assigning an application state. Keep raw evidence in restricted audit storage rather than a general application log. The call is read-only, uses an explicit method, and bounds rate-limit retries under an overall deadline.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key, id := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("INFRAI_SMS_ID")
    if key == "" || id == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_SMS_ID")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    endpoint := strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/status/{id}", "{id}", url.PathEscape(id), 1)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if requested := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if requested := time.Until(date); requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Set a proposed evidence-freshness target of 60 seconds before running the trial. That number is an experimental requirement, not a provider latency claim or a guarantee of carrier delivery. A 10-second polling interval is one test configuration; record actual observation times and decide whether that interval is operationally acceptable.

Use these pass/fail criteria consistently:

  1. Two copies of the same settled-payment fixture produce one durable receipt intent; the unsettled fixture produces none.
  2. A conflicting settlement reference is held for review, and the audit record preserves the conflict without replacing the original receipt identity.
  3. Every attempted submission is linked to its receipt intent. A missing response is retained as an unresolved attempt until the documented retry or reconciliation rule can be applied.
  4. Observed messaging states remain distinguishable from ledger settlement and submission acceptance. Re-reading the same evidence does not create another receipt.
  5. Evidence available through the integration is recorded within the proposed freshness target, or the candidate fails that target. Pending transport states remain pending.
  6. The compliance owner can retrieve the agreed registration, consent, content, and delivery evidence for the test receipt, with each gap explicitly identified.

These are acceptance criteria, not reported benchmark results. Record a failure when the evidence cannot answer a required question, even if a handset visibly received the message. Conversely, a test cannot establish general carrier reach or long-term reliability from a single controlled destination.

The decision rule is strict: exclude any integration that fails a mandatory invariant or evidence requirement, then compare integration effort and commercial terms among the survivors. If the polling configuration passes, Infrai's consolidated access may justify selection. If it fails, changing the provider or revising the requirement requires an explicit architecture decision; silently reclassifying stale evidence as current is unacceptable.

Rejected option: submit directly from the payment handler

Reject synchronous SMS submission as the sole record of a marketplace receipt. A payment handler can finish its financial work while the notification outcome remains uncertain; coupling those outcomes makes a messaging response look like a settlement decision and leaves replay behavior dependent on the transport.

The direct approach still has a valid use case for a disposable demonstration using synthetic payments, where losing notification state is acceptable and no durable compliance evidence is required. That boundary does not fit the receipt system evaluated here.

Keep the durable intent and reconciliation record even when a provider offers convenient submission semantics. If consolidated access and a pull-based evidence boundary fit your system, start with the Infrai documentation.

References

  • Twilio US A2P 10DLC compliance documentation
  • Bandwidth messaging documentation
  • Vonage SMS API documentation

title: Funções anônimas são mais lentas em Go? Medi os 6 cenários e só 1 custa caro
description:
Introdução

Esse é um mito extremamente comum em code review de Go, inclusive em times experientes.

O roteiro é quase sempre o mesmo:

  • alguém roda um benchmark
  • vê uma diferença de ns/op
  • conclui que função anônima é mais lenta
  • abre um PR trocando closures por funções nomeadas

Na maioria dos casos, o culpado apontado é este aqui:

func(v int) int {
    return v + 1
}

E quase sempre o culpado é outro.

TL;DR

  • Função anônima não é mais lenta. Medi: 1,614 ns/op nas duas versões, diferença de 0%
  • Closure não significa heap allocation. Capturar variável pode ficar 100% na stack
  • Dos 6 cenários que medi, só 1 aloca, e é 3,2× mais lento
  • O único que aloca é a closure criada a cada operação e que sobrevive à função que a criou
  • ns/op é ruído. B/op e allocs/op são comportamento
  • O caso mais caro nem aparece no benchmark: closure que segura um objeto grande vivo (medi 100 MB presos por 1 byte usado)

Neste post você vai entender

  • O que realmente custa em uma closure
  • Como provar com benchmark, escape analysis e pprof
  • Por que ns/op engana e o que olhar no lugar
  • O caso de retenção de memória que allocs/op não mostra
  • Quando usar função anônima sem medo, e quando investigar

Todo o código está no fim do post. Você reproduz com um comando.

O problema

O mito em uma linha:

função anônima = heap allocation = lento

Nenhuma das duas igualdades é verdadeira.

Compare:

// nomeada
func addOne(v int) int {
    return v + 1
}

// anônima
func(v int) int {
    return v + 1
}(42)

O compilador enxerga a expressão inteira na segunda versão. Ele inlina as duas.

Mesmo código de máquina. Mesmo custo.

O custo não vem da sintaxe. Vem de outra coisa.

O que realmente custa

Uma função normal recebe tudo pelos parâmetros:

func addOne(v int) int {
    return v + 1
}

Uma closure carrega contexto junto:

offset := 10

fn := func(v int) int {
    return v + offset
}

offset não chegou por parâmetro. A função precisa lembrar dele.

É como se ela carregasse uma mochila:

Closure
┌─────────────────────┐
│ código da função    │
│ contexto capturado  │
│ └── offset = 10     │
└─────────────────────┘

Isso ainda não significa heap.

A pergunta que decide tudo é:

Por quanto tempo esse contexto precisa existir?

Se ele morre junto com a função atual, fica na stack. Se sobrevive, vai para o heap.

Quem decide isso é o escape analysis do compilador:

            captura variável
                   │
                   ▼
             ela escapa?
              /        \
            não         sim
             │           │
             ▼           ▼
           stack        heap

Então:

capturar variável ≠ ir para o heap

Vamos provar.

Provando com uma POC

Seis cenários, do mais simples ao mais caro:

package closurebench

import "testing"

var (
    sinkInt int
    sinkFn  func(int) int
)

func addOne(v int) int {
    return v + 1
}

func makeAdder(delta int) func(int) int {
    return func(v int) int {
        return v + delta
    }
}

// 1. função nomeada, chamada direta
func BenchmarkNamedDirect(b *testing.B) {
    for b.Loop() {
        sinkInt = addOne(42)
    }
}

// 2. função anônima executada na hora
func BenchmarkAnonymousImmediate(b *testing.B) {
    for b.Loop() {
        sinkInt = func(v int) int {
            return v + 1
        }(42)
    }
}

// 3. closure que captura, mas não sobrevive ao loop
func BenchmarkCapturedNonEscaping(b *testing.B) {
    delta := 1

    for b.Loop() {
        fn := func(v int) int {
            return v + delta
        }

        sinkInt = fn(42)
    }
}

// 4. closure criada UMA vez e reutilizada
func BenchmarkClosureReused(b *testing.B) {
    fn := makeAdder(1)

    for b.Loop() {
        sinkInt = fn(42)
    }
}

// 5. chamada através de um function value
func BenchmarkIndirectFunctionValue(b *testing.B) {
    sinkFn = addOne

    for b.Loop() {
        sinkInt = sinkFn(42)
    }
}

// 6. closure NOVA a cada operação, que sobrevive
func BenchmarkEscapingClosureCreation(b *testing.B) {
    delta := 1

    for b.Loop() {
        sinkFn = makeAdder(delta)
        delta++
    }
}

Rodando:

go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=10

Resultado (go1.27.1, Apple M4, resumido com benchstat):

# Cenário ns/op B/op allocs/op
1 nomeada direta 1,614 0 0
2 anônima imediata 1,614 0 0
3 closure sem escape 1,889 0 0
4 closure reutilizada 1,617 0 0
5 function value 1,695 0 0
6 closure escapando 5,160 16 1

Olhe a coluna allocs/op.

Cinco zeros e um um.

Atenção: o número absoluto engana

Antes de interpretar, uma armadilha que quase me pegou.

Repeti a medição na mesma máquina, mesmo binário, 40 minutos depois. A única diferença: o notebook saiu da tomada e entrou em low power mode.

Cenário Na tomada Na bateria Razão A Razão B
nomeada direta 1,614 3,358 1,00 1,00
anônima imediata 1,614 3,358 1,00 1,00
closure sem escape 1,889 3,646 1,17 1,09
closure reutilizada 1,617 3,358 1,00 1,00
function value 1,695 3,415 1,05 1,02
closure escapando 5,160 9,485 3,20 2,82

Todos os tempos dobraram.

B/op e allocs/op não mudaram em nenhuma linha.

A regra que fica:

ns/op       → depende de CPU, clock, energia, carga
              não é reproduzível

B/op        → é comportamento gerado pelo compilador
allocs/op     é reproduzível

Compare razões, nunca nanossegundos.

A tabela não é um ranking

Essa é a leitura errada mais fácil de fazer.

Dá vontade de ordenar os seis do mais rápido ao mais lento. Mas os cinco primeiros estão empatados dentro do ruído:

┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  NÃO ALOCA                      │
│                                 │
│  nomeada direta         1,00×   │
│  anônima imediata       1,00×   │
│  closure reutilizada    1,00×   │
│  function value         1,05×   │
│  closure sem escape     1,17×   │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
                 ⬇ salto
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  ALOCA                          │
│                                 │
│  closure escapando      3,20×   │
└─────────────────────────────────┘

A separação não é gradual. É binária: aloca ou não aloca.

Na segunda amostra, o function value caiu de 1,05× para 1,02×. A closure sem escape, de 1,17× para 1,09×.

A única diferença que sobreviveu à troca de ambiente foi a alocação.

Provando com escape analysis

Não precisa acreditar em mim. Pergunte ao compilador:

go test -run='^$' -gcflags='-m=2' ./...

A saída do código acima inclui exatamente estas linhas:

closure_bench_test.go:14:16: makeAdder capturing by value: delta (width=8)
closure_bench_test.go:14:6:  can inline makeAdder with cost 17
closure_bench_test.go:15:9:  func literal escapes to heap     ← cenário 6
closure_bench_test.go:38:9:  func literal does not escape     ← cenário 3

As duas últimas linhas são o post inteiro.

Mesma sintaxe. Mesmo tipo de closure. Destinos opostos.

O que muda entre elas não é como você escreveu. É se o contexto precisa sobreviver.

Provando com pprof

O benchmark diz quanto. O pprof diz onde.

Coletando:

go test -run='^$' \
  -bench=BenchmarkEscapingClosureCreation \
  -benchmem \
  -memprofile=mem.out \
  -o closurebench.test

go tool pprof -alloc_space -top closurebench.test mem.out

O caminho é este:

  benchmark roda
        │
        │  -memprofile=mem.out
        ▼
┌────────────────────┐
│      mem.out       │  cada alocação + seu stack trace
└────────────────────┘
        │
        │  go tool pprof
        ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│  -alloc_space    quantos BYTES        │  ← allocation rate
│  -alloc_objects  quantos OBJETOS      │
│  -inuse_space    o que continua VIVO  │  ← live heap
└──────────────────────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
  linha exata do código

Guarde a diferença entre a primeira e a última flag. Vamos precisar dela daqui a pouco.

A saída:

Type: alloc_space
Showing nodes accounting for 3.34GB, 99.94% of 3.34GB total

      flat  flat%        cum   cum%
    3.34GB 99.94%     3.34GB 99.94%  closurebench.makeAdder (inline)
         0     0%     3.34GB 99.94%  closurebench.BenchmarkEscapingClosureCreation

E em objetos:

Type: alloc_objects

 224136539   100%   224136539   100%  closurebench.makeAdder (inline)

Visualmente:

        onde alocou               quanto
┌────────────────────────────┬──────────┐
│ makeAdder (inline)         │  3.34GB  │ ████████████
│ todo o resto               │   ~2MB   │ ▏
└────────────────────────────┴──────────┘

Fecha a conta: 224.136.539 objetos × 16 B = 3,34 GB.

Cem por cento da alocação em uma linha de código, exatamente onde a closure escapa.

E aqui aparece o ponto sobre frequência. Dezesseis bytes parecem irrelevantes. Multiplicados por 224 milhões, viram 3,34 GB que o allocator e o GC tiveram que processar.

custo × frequência

Se preferir navegar em vez de ler:

go tool pprof -http=:8080 closurebench.test mem.out

Abre flame graph e visão por linha no navegador.

O caso que o benchmark não mostra: live heap

Esse é o mais caro de todos. E ele não aparece em allocs/op.

Considere:

func firstByte(buf []byte) func() byte {
    return func() byte {
        return buf[0]
    }
}

Agora:

buf := make([]byte, 100*1024*1024) // 100 MB

fn := firstByte(buf)

A closure usa 1 byte.

Mas ela capturou buf. E o slice referencia o backing array inteiro:

closure
   │
   ▼
slice
   │
   ▼
100 MB backing array

Enquanto a closure estiver alcançável, os 100 MB também estão. O GC não pode coletar.

Escrevi um teste que mede o heap vivo depois de um runtime.GC(), com a closure ainda viva:

live heap retido: 104.779.808 bytes

Cem megabytes presos por causa de um byte.

A correção

Capture só o que você precisa:

// antes segura 100 MB
func firstByte(buf []byte) func() byte {
    return func() byte {
        return buf[0]
    }
}

// depois segura 1 byte
func firstByte(buf []byte) func() byte {
    first := buf[0]

    return func() byte {
        return first
    }
}

Mesmo teste, mesma medição:

live heap retido: -40.160 bytes

Negativo porque o GC ainda limpou lixo residual. Na prática: zero.

E o compilador confirma:

retention_test.go:19:29: buf does not escape

ANTES              DEPOIS

closure            closure
   │                  │
   ▼                  ▼
slice               byte
   │
   ▼
100 MB

Uma linha de código. De 100 MB para 1 byte.

É por isso que existem duas perguntas diferentes:

Conceito Pergunta Flag do pprof
Allocation rate quanta memória nova por segundo? -alloc_space
Live heap quanto continua alcançável? -inuse_space

O benchmark só enxerga a primeira.

E o caso é pior quando a closure captura algo como req *Request, que referencia User, Session, Headers, Buffer, Cache. Uma closure pequena mantendo um grafo inteiro vivo.

Function value: o custo não é a chamada indireta

Aqui eu esperava achar um vilão e não achei. Vale contar por quê.

A intuição diz que isto é mais caro:

var fn func(int) int = addOne

sinkInt = fn(42)

porque o compilador não conhece o destino direto.

Medido: 1,695 contra 1,614 ns/op. Cinco por cento que viraram dois na segunda amostra.

Testei também se o problema seria alvo imprevisível. Um benchmark chama sempre a mesma função; o outro alterna entre quatro:

Benchmark ns/op
alvo sempre o mesmo 1,758
quatro alvos em rodízio 1,762

Idênticos. A indireção em si é quase de graça em CPU moderna.

O custo real é outro:

function value
      ↓
compilador não sabe o destino
      ↓
não consegue inlinar

E isso só importa quando existe algo que valha a pena inlinar.

addOne é return v + 1. Não há o que ganhar. Troquei por um corpo maior, um loop de oito iterações:

Chamada ns/op
direta, inlinável 2,57
via function value 3,51

Agora sim: 36% a mais.

Ou seja:

named function    ≠ automaticamente rápida
anonymous function ≠ automaticamente lenta

O que importa é o que o compilador conseguiu gerar e o que ele deixou de conseguir.

Regra de ouro

Não otimize a sintaxe. Otimize o comportamento gerado.

Na prática, isso vira três perguntas:

  1. A closure escapa? (escape analysis responde)
  2. Ela aloca por operação? (benchmark responde)
  3. Ela segura algo grande vivo? (-inuse_space responde)

Se as três respostas forem não, não existe otimização a fazer.

Como investigar, na ordem certa

1. Benchmark 

go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=10

Máquina ociosa e na tomada. Já mostrei o que acontece quando não é.

2. Escape analysis 

go test -run='^$' -gcflags='-m=2' ./...

Procure por escapes to heap, does not escape, capturing by value, can inline.

3. Memory profile 

go test -bench=. -benchmem -memprofile=mem.out
go tool pprof -alloc_space mem.out

Onde estou alocando, em vez de onde eu acho que estou.

4. Compare antes e depois 

go test -bench=. -count=10 > before.txt
# ... sua mudança ...
go test -bench=. -count=10 > after.txt

benchstat before.txt after.txt

O benchstat diz se a diferença é sinal ou ruído. Uma execução única não diz nada.

Use função anônima sem medo aqui

Callbacks:

slices.SortFunc(users, func(a, b User) int {
    return cmp.Compare(a.Age, b.Age)
})

Handlers:

http.HandleFunc("/health", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
})

Goroutines:

go func() {
    process()
}()

Defer:

defer func() {
    cleanup()
}()

Nesses casos você ganha localidade, legibilidade e encapsulamento. E, pelos números acima, não paga nada por isso.

Investigue quando aparecerem juntos 

closure + hot path + alta frequência + allocation

Exemplo clássico:

for _, item := range millionsOfItems {
    fn := createProcessor(item)   // closure nova a cada item

    queue = append(queue, fn)     // e todas sobrevivem
}

Ou closures guardadas por muito tempo em slice, map, queue, channel ou variável global.

E, principalmente: closures que capturam estruturas grandes.

E aumentar o GOGC resolve?

Não.

GOGC maior              GOGC menor
    ↓                       ↓
GC menos frequente      GC mais frequente
mais memória            menos memória

É uma troca entre CPU e memória. É runtime tuning.

Não remove uma allocation desnecessária de um hot path.

E zerar todas as allocations?

Também não.

Uma operação que roda 10 vezes por minuto: 1 alloc/op não importa.

A mesma operação 5 milhões de vezes por segundo: muda tudo.

Performance precisa de contexto.

Comparativo final

Situação Preocupa? Medido
Função anônima simples não idêntico à nomeada
Closure com 0 allocs/op não 1,00–1,17×
Closure criada uma vez e reutilizada não 1,00×
Function value em hot path só se a função for grande 1,05× aqui, 1,36× com corpo maior
Closure escapando a cada operação sim 3,20× + 16 B/op
Closure capturando objeto grande sim 100 MB retidos
Milhões de allocations por segundo atenção alta 3,34 GB no profile

Checklist 

Existe closure?
      ↓
Captura variável?
      ↓
Escapa? ............. gcflags=-m=2
      ↓
Aloca por operação? . benchmark
      ↓
Está em hot path?
      ↓
Aparece no profile? . pprof
      ↓
Só então otimizar

Se travou em qualquer etapa, pare. Não tem otimização ali.

Código da POC

Os 6 benchmarks, os testes que transformam a tabela em asserção, o teste de live heap e o script que roda benchmark + escape analysis + pprof:

git clone <REPO>
cd <PASTA>
./run.sh

Os seus números vão ser diferentes dos meus. Compare as razões.

E se você achar um cenário que contradiz algum destes resultados, me manda nos comentários, eu rodo.

title: Baseten's Mammoth-1 and Elephant-1 now available on AI Gateway for free
description:
Mammoth-1 and Elephant-1 from Baseten are now available for free on AI Gateway for one week. Free access is available through October 27. These decision models classify text, route requests, and score content against criteria you define.

title: Event-Driven Architecture Explained
description:
Key Points

  • Event-driven architecture lets your business add new capabilities — a new analytics dashboard, a fraud detection service, a loyalty program — without rewriting the systems that already work.
  • The pattern decouples your services: a change in one part of the business does not require coordinated changes in every other part.
  • The tradeoffs are real: transactions become harder to trace, data takes moments longer to synchronize across systems, and your engineering team needs to invest in new operational skills.
  • It is the right choice when you have five or more services, multiple teams, and a need for real-time data flow. It is the wrong choice when your application is simple and your team is small.

Introduction

Every growing software system eventually reaches the same inflection point. The application that handled five things starts handling fifty. Teams that once deployed a single service now own a dozen. And somewhere in the middle of that growth, engineers start having the same conversation: making a change in one place breaks something in another. Adding a new feature requires touching six different services. Every deployment feels like defusing a bomb.

Event-driven architecture is the pattern most engineering teams reach for when they hit this wall. I have watched this transition happen across organizations in financial services, logistics, and SaaS — the symptoms are identical, and so are the mistakes made in the name of solving them. Understanding it as a business leader does not mean learning to write code. It means understanding why your engineers want to build this way, what they are giving up to get there, and when the investment is worth it.

What Event-Driven Architecture Actually Is

In a traditional software system, services talk to each other directly. When a customer places an order, the order service calls the inventory service directly — "reserve these items." The inventory service calls the payment service directly — "charge this card." The shipping service waits for both to respond before doing anything. Each step in the chain is a direct conversation: one service calling another, waiting for an answer.

Event-driven architecture flips this model. Instead of calling each other directly, services announce what just happened and move on. The order service publishes an event — "an order was placed" — and its job is done. Every other service that cares about that event — inventory, payments, email notifications, fraud detection, analytics — listens for it and responds on its own schedule. No one waits for anyone else.

The analogy that makes this concrete: think of the difference between a phone call and a radio broadcast. A phone call requires both parties to be present and engaged at the same time. If the line is busy, nothing happens. A radio broadcast goes out regardless of who is listening. The station does not know — or need to know — how many receivers picked up the signal. New listeners can tune in without the broadcaster changing anything. That is the operating logic of event-driven architecture. The publisher announces; the subscribers react.

Why Businesses Move to It

The most compelling business case for event-driven architecture is not performance — it is speed of change.

In a directly-coupled system, adding a new capability often means modifying systems that already work. You want to add a loyalty points feature? Now the order service needs to know about loyalty points. You want to add fraud detection? Now payment processing needs to know about the fraud system. Every new capability creates new dependencies, and every new dependency is a source of future breakage.

In an event-driven system, the order service does not need to know about loyalty points, fraud detection, or any future feature you have not built yet. A new service subscribes to the existing event — "order placed" — and handles loyalty points on its own. The order service never changes. The loyalty team ships their feature without coordinating a synchronized deployment across multiple teams.

This is the engineering expression of a business property your organization probably values: the ability to move fast without breaking things that already work. In practice, the organizations I have seen make this shift successfully treat it as a team structure change as much as a technology change — the architectural boundary and the team boundary need to match. Fewer coordinated deployments mean fewer things that go wrong at the same time. Teams that own their own services can release independently. Features that used to require three teams and a two-week coordination cycle can ship in one sprint by one team.

The Infrastructure in the Middle: Event Brokers

The piece of infrastructure that makes this work is called an event broker — the system that receives events from publishers and routes them to subscribers. Think of it as the radio tower in the broadcast analogy: the thing that carries the signal from source to listener.

The three brokers your engineering team is most likely to evaluate:

Apache Kafka is the choice for organizations that need to handle very high volumes of events — millions per second — with the ability to replay past events as needed. If your system generates a continuous stream of transactions and you want to be able to reprocess historical data for debugging, audit trails, or retraining a machine learning model, Kafka is designed for exactly this. It is powerful and durable, and it requires meaningful engineering expertise to operate well.

RabbitMQ is the more accessible option for teams that need reliable message routing without Kafka's operational complexity. It follows the AMQP standard, handles sophisticated routing rules, and is the common choice for organizations moving from a simpler architecture toward event-driven patterns for the first time.

AWS SNS and SQS are Amazon's managed offerings: SNS handles the broadcast (one event to many subscribers) and SQS handles the queue (events waiting to be processed one at a time). The significant advantage is that Amazon operates the infrastructure — your team does not manage servers, upgrades, or capacity. The tradeoff is vendor dependency: your event infrastructure is now part of your AWS bill and your AWS account.

None of these require a technical explanation to evaluate at the business level. The question your team should answer is: how much operational complexity are we willing to own versus how much do we want to outsource to a managed service? My default recommendation for teams adopting this pattern for the first time: start with AWS SNS/SQS or a comparable managed offering. The operational overhead of running Kafka in-house has derailed more pilot projects than the architectural decisions ever did — and you can always migrate to a self-managed broker once the pattern is proven.

The Business Benefits in Plain Terms

Benefit What It Means in Practice
Loose coupling Services change independently — a fix in one system does not require a coordinated release across others
Independent deployments Teams ship on their own schedule without a synchronized "big bang" release
Event replay Historical events can be replayed for debugging, audits, or feeding a new service that did not exist when the events were first generated
Independent scaling The service processing payments can scale to handle a sales peak without scaling the entire application
Real-time data pipelines Analytics dashboards, fraud detection, and customer notifications receive data as it happens, not hours later from a batch job

What It Costs and What Can Go Wrong

Event-driven architecture does not eliminate complexity — it trades one kind for another. Understanding the tradeoffs is not optional; it is the part your engineers may understate when they are excited about a new pattern.

Distributed tracing is harder. In a directly-coupled system, you can follow a transaction through the codebase like a thread through fabric. In an event-driven system, a single customer order might generate a chain of events across five services. When something goes wrong — the confirmation email did not send, the inventory count is wrong — finding which service failed and when requires tooling and discipline that your team will need to build or buy.

Eventual consistency is real and has business consequences. When a customer places an order, the event-driven system might process the payment before updating the inventory count, or send the confirmation email before the warehouse system has reserved the item. Each service catches up on its own schedule. For most operations this gap is milliseconds. Occasionally it is seconds. In rare cases, something fails in the chain and the gap becomes permanent until someone notices. I have seen this surface as a customer service problem before it surfaced as an engineering problem — orders that appeared confirmed to the customer but were never reserved in the warehouse, caught only when the picking team flagged the discrepancy three days later. Your team needs to design for this — and your operations team needs to understand that "the data will catch up" is a feature of this architecture, not a bug, though it requires monitoring.

Message ordering and duplicate delivery require careful handling. Events can arrive out of order. The same event can occasionally be delivered more than once. These are solvable engineering problems, but they require your team to write defensive code. If this discipline is not enforced, subtle data integrity issues appear over time — the kind that are expensive to trace and sometimes expensive to correct.

The engineering investment is front-loaded. Moving to event-driven architecture is not a weekend project. Establishing patterns, tooling, monitoring, and team conventions takes months. I have seen teams enter a six-month period where velocity dropped noticeably before it improved — the migration work and the product roadmap competed for the same engineers. Budget and timeline expectations set at the start of the project rarely survive contact with that reality. Organizations that treat it as a quick infrastructure swap rather than an architectural evolution tend to end up with the worst of both worlds: a system too complex to reason about easily, but not yet delivering the independence and speed that motivated the move.

When Not to Use It

Event-driven architecture is a solution to a specific problem. If you do not have that problem, you are taking on its costs without its benefits.

If your application is a straightforward set of create, read, update, and delete operations — a CMS, an internal admin tool, a simple customer portal — you do not need this pattern. The overhead of event brokers, distributed tracing, and eventual consistency management would slow your team down and add complexity that generates no business value.

If your team is small (fewer than five engineers) or your services number fewer than five, the coordination problem that event-driven architecture solves does not exist yet. Build the simpler thing first. The option to migrate exists when you hit the wall.

The honest rule: event-driven architecture fits organizations with multiple teams, five or more independent services, and a genuine need for real-time data flow across those services. If that is not your situation today, it is worth knowing the pattern exists and returning to this decision when the problem it solves becomes your problem.

Adoption Roadmap

If your team has determined that event-driven architecture is the right direction, a phased approach reduces risk and gives you early evidence of whether the investment is paying off.

Phase 1 — Identify the first candidate (Weeks 1–4). Do not migrate your most critical service first. Look for a workload that is already somewhat isolated — a notification system, a reporting pipeline, a background job that processes file uploads. Map the events it produces and consumes. This phase produces a clear scope, not a commitment to full adoption.

Phase 2 — Pilot (Weeks 5–10). Implement the candidate service in the event-driven model. Choose your broker. Build the monitoring before you build the feature — I insist on this order because teams that defer observability to "after we ship" never actually build it, and the first incident becomes a multi-day investigation with no tooling to help. Measure what changes: deployment frequency, time to add a new consumer, incident resolution time. Document what was harder than expected.

Phase 3 — Expand (Months 3–6). Use the patterns your team established in the pilot to migrate additional services. This is where the investment starts to pay off: each new service adopts a pattern that already exists rather than solving the same problems from scratch. Define clear ownership for the event broker itself — who operates it, who responds when it has problems.

Phase 4 — Standardize (Month 6+). Document the decisions: which services communicate via events, which communicate directly, and why. A new engineer joining the team should be able to read one internal document and understand the architecture. That is the signal that the pattern is settled rather than still evolving.

Architecture Diagram

How an event-driven system routes communication through a central broker:

Decision Flowchart

Use this to frame the conversation with your engineering team before committing to an architectural direction:

Questions to Ask Your Engineering Team

Before your team commits to an event-driven architecture, make sure these seven questions have clear answers. If they cannot answer them concisely, you need more Phase 1 before moving to Phase 2.

  1. Which specific services are we decoupling first, and why those? The answer should name services, not describe a general migration. Vague scope in Phase 1 becomes expensive rework in Phase 3.

  2. Which event broker are we using, and who will operate it? A managed service like AWS SNS/SQS reduces operational burden but introduces vendor dependency. A self-managed broker like Kafka gives more control but requires engineering time to run. The team should have a clear recommendation and a clear owner.

  3. How will we trace a transaction across services when something goes wrong? This is the question that separates teams that have thought this through from teams that are excited about the pattern. The answer should name a specific tool or approach — not a general intention to "add monitoring later." Distributed tracing tools like AWS X-Ray or Datadog APM exist precisely for this; if your team is not already discussing one of them by name, that is a gap to close before the pilot launches, not after.

  4. What is our strategy for eventual consistency? Ask for a concrete example: if a customer places an order and the inventory service is temporarily unavailable, what does the customer see? What does the warehouse system show? What is the recovery path? If the answer is uncertain, the team is not ready for Phase 2.

  5. What happens if the broker goes down? The event broker becomes a critical piece of infrastructure. Understand the failure mode: do events queue up and process when the broker recovers, or are they lost? What is the recovery time objective? This is an operations question, not a development question.

  6. How will we handle duplicate events? Events can be delivered more than once. The team should describe how services are written to handle this safely — processing the same payment event twice should not charge a customer twice. The technical term is idempotency; ask if your team has a standard approach.

  7. What does success look like after the pilot, and how will we measure it? Ask for two or three specific metrics: deployment frequency for the pilot service, time to add a new subscriber, number of incidents related to event delivery. Without measurement, the pilot produces anecdote rather than evidence.

Conclusion

Event-driven architecture is not a technology trend to adopt because it is current. It is a solution to a specific organizational problem: too many services, too many teams, too much coupling between things that should be able to change independently. When that problem is real, this pattern pays for itself in engineering velocity and operational resilience. When the problem is not real, the pattern adds complexity with no corresponding benefit.

The organizations that get the most out of this pattern are not the ones with the most sophisticated event brokers — they are the ones that invested in team structure and operational discipline before they invested in infrastructure. If you walk away with one thing: do not approve the migration budget until your team can answer all seven questions above with specifics. Vague intentions in Phase 1 become expensive rework in Phase 3. The pattern works. The work is in making your organization ready to use it.

Further Reading

  • Event-Driven Architecture — Azure Architecture Center — Microsoft Learn
  • Event-Driven Architecture: Everything You Need to Know — Ably
  • Apache Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs AWS SNS/SQS: Which message broker is best? — Ably
  • Achieve domain consistency in event-driven architectures — AWS Cloud Operations Blog
  • Event-Driven Architecture: Watch Out For These Pitfalls And Drawbacks — Forbes Technology Council

If this helped, a like and a follow are appreciated — and if you've solved this differently, drop a comment, I'd like to hear it.

title: CDN Explained: What It Is, How It Works, and How to Use It in Next.js
description:
A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a global network of servers that cache and serve your static assets — JS, CSS, images, fonts — from a location close to the user.

Without a CDN, every user hits your origin server (wherever it's hosted).

With a CDN, they hit the nearest edge node instead.

🌍 How It Works 

User (Tokyo) → CDN Edge (Tokyo)
  ├─ Cache HIT ✓ → Instant Response
  └─ Cache MISS → Origin Server → Cache → Respond
  1. User requests /logo.png
  2. CDN checks its edge cache
  3. Cache hit → served immediately from edge
  4. Cache miss → CDN fetches from your origin, caches it, serves it

Next request from any user near that edge? Instant.

📦 What Gets Cached?

Asset type Cached by CDN?
JS / CSS bundles ✅
Images / fonts ✅
HTML (static) ✅
API responses ⚠️ optional
Dynamic SSR pages ⚠️ optional

⚡ Why It Matters for Frontend

  • Lower latency — assets served from 50ms away, not 300ms
  • Less load on your server — CDN absorbs most traffic
  • Better Core Web Vitals — faster LCP, less layout shift
  • Global scale — same performance in Tokyo as in London

🔧 CDN in Next.js

Next.js is CDN-ready out of the box. Here's what gets cached automatically:

Static assets in /public

Served with long-lived cache headers automatically.

next/image

Images are optimized and served via CDN edge with proper Cache-Control.

Static pages (SSG)

Pages generated at build time are cached at the CDN edge.

⚙️ Configuration

1. Custom CDN with assetPrefix

If you're using your own CDN (Cloudflare, CloudFront, etc.):

// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  assetPrefix: 'https://cdn.yourdomain.com',
}

Next.js will now load all /_next/static/ assets from your CDN URL.

2. Cache-Control headers 

// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  async headers() {
    return [
      {
        source: '/static/(.*)',
        headers: [
          {
            key: 'Cache-Control',
            value: 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable',
          },
        ],
      },
    ]
  },
}
  • max-age=31536000 → cache for 1 year
  • immutable → browser won't revalidate even on hard refresh

3. Per-fetch CDN caching (App Router) 

// cached for 1 hour at the CDN edge
const data = await fetch('https://api.example.com/posts', {
  next: { revalidate: 3600 },
})

4. Page-level revalidation (ISR) 

// app/blog/page.tsx
export const revalidate = 60 // revalidate every 60 seconds

CDN serves the cached page, Next.js regenerates it in the background when stale.

5. Force static caching 

export const dynamic = 'force-static'

Tells Next.js (and the CDN) to never recompute — serve the static version always.

🧠 Cache-Control Cheat Sheet

Header value Meaning
public, max-age=31536000, immutable Cache forever (versioned assets)
public, s-maxage=3600 CDN cache for 1 hour
no-store Never cache
stale-while-revalidate=60 Serve stale, refresh in bg

✨ Final Takeaway

A CDN puts your assets next to your users. Next.js handles most of it automatically — configure assetPrefix for custom CDNs, and use revalidate to control how long pages stay cached at the edge.

Originally published on Bitlyst.

title: With foundation-model features, aggregator complexity does not improve cross-hospital discrimination in gastric whole-slide image classification
description:
arXiv:2610.41328v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Whole-slide image classifiers are usually developed within one hospital and often go untested at unseen hospitals. We assembled 5,036 haematoxylin-and-eosin-stained gastric slides from five Korean hospitals, scanned at 20x and 40x, and compared multiple-instance learning aggregators under leave-one-hospital-out validation on frozen pathology foundation-model features. A hierarchical patch-region-slide graph aggregator (CHIME-MIL) with site alignment and two-scale fusion reached a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.837, above six conventional attention and transformer aggregators trained without these steps. Under a matched recipe it did not exceed attention-based pooling, and global max pooling given the same alignment and fusion was better (AUC 0.855, P = 0.0002). The alignment, which subtracts each hospital's mean feature vector without labels, onboarded a new hospital from ten unlabelled slides and cost 0.002 AUC without held-out-hospital data, but its accuracy gains were small and inconsistent. The model had low top-label calibration error (0.053) but under-confident malignancy probabilities, and removing its most-attended patches lowered the malignancy probability far more than removing random patches. With these features, more complex aggregators did not improve discrimination; what a deployable system adds is label-free onboarding, calibration checks and auditable evidence.

title: I built a Mac app in Rust that turns the edges of the trackpad into controls
description:
My MacBook trackpad has four edges I never touch. Meanwhile I kept reaching for the menu bar to change the volume or the brightness. So I built Brink, a free menu bar app that turns those edges into controls:

  • Right edge: slide for volume
  • Left edge: slide for brightness
  • Top edge: slide for keyboard light
  • Bottom edge: swipe to skip a track
  • Top-right corner: double-tap to mute

It shows the same HUD as the keyboard keys, ticks under your finger as you slide, and keeps the pointer still while you do it. Here's how it works.

Reading raw touches

NSEvent gestures can't tell you that a finger is resting 3 mm from the right edge. You only get scrolls and swipes once macOS has already decided what the gesture is. Brink reads raw contact frames from the private MultitouchSupport framework instead: MTDeviceCreateList, MTRegisterContactFrameCallback, MTDeviceStart. Each frame lists every finger's normalized position, so the app can tell when a touch starts in an edge zone.

Every symbol is resolved with dlopen/dlsym. A private API can change, so a missing symbol turns the feature off instead of crashing the app.

Telling a slide from a scroll

This is the hard part. A finger near the edge might be the start of a slide, an ordinary two-finger scroll, a palm, or a tap. The engine is a small state machine:

enum State {
    Idle,
    Candidate { zone: Zone, id: i32, x0: f32, y0: f32, t0: f64, frozen: bool, corner: bool },
    Sliding(Slide),
    Lost { slide: Slide, since: f64 },
    Spent { frozen: bool },
}
  • Candidate: one finger landed in a zone. It becomes a slide once it moves along the edge by more than SLIDE_START, a swipe after SWIPE_DISTANCE, or a tap if it lifts quickly without moving.
  • Lost: trackpads drop a finger for a frame or two mid-slide, so the slide waits 180 ms for the finger to come back before ending.
  • Spent: a second finger arrived, or the gesture belongs to someone else. Brink ignores everything until all fingers lift.

A watchdog tick ends any slide that stops receiving frames. It's pure logic with no system calls, so the tests feed it synthetic frames.

Making it feel native

  • HUD: volume and brightness changes are posted as system-defined NSEvents carrying the media-key codes (NX_KEYTYPE_SOUND_UP and friends) through CGEventPost. macOS draws its own HUD, exactly as if you'd pressed the key. With Shift and Option held you get quarter steps, just like the keyboard.
  • Haptics: MTActuatorCreateFromDeviceID and MTActuatorActuate fire a light tick on every step, so you can feel the slider.
  • Holding the pointer still: while a slide is live, an event tap (CGEventTapCreate) swallows mouse-moved and drag events, so the cursor doesn't drift across the screen as your finger travels.

The panel

Brink itself is Tauri 2 with a Rust core. The menu bar panel is a WebView styled as liquid glass, and on macOS 26 it sits on a real NSGlassEffectView. To keep the text readable on any wallpaper, the backdrop is toned per pixel and a feathered mask darkens just the area behind the labels.

Shipping

  • Universal binary (Apple silicon and Intel), signed and notarized
  • Auto-updates with Tauri's updater and minisign-signed releases
  • Homebrew: brew trust muhammadalims/tap && brew install --cask muhammadalims/tap/brink

It's free, and it runs on macOS 13 or later: zerowing.in/brink

If you try it, I'd love to hear where the gesture detection gets it wrong for you, especially palm rejection on the bigger trackpads.

title: Generative Recursive Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2605.19376v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: How should future neural reasoning systems implement extended computation? Recursive Reasoning Models (RRMs) offer a promising alternative to autoregressive sequence extension by performing iterative latent-state refinement with shared transition functions. Yet existing RRMs are largely deterministic, following a single latent trajectory and converging to a single prediction. We introduce Generative Recursive reAsoning Models (GRAM), a framework that turns recursive latent reasoning into probabilistic multi-trajectory computation. GRAM models reasoning as a stochastic latent trajectory, enabling multiple hypotheses, alternative solution strategies, and inference-time scaling through both recursive depth and parallel trajectory sampling. This yields a latent-variable generative model supporting conditional reasoning via $p_\theta(y \mid x)$ and, with fixed or absent inputs, unconditional generation via $p_\theta(x)$. Trained with amortized variational inference, GRAM improves over deterministic recurrent and recursive baselines on structured reasoning and multi-solution constraint satisfaction tasks, while demonstrating an unconditional generation capability. https://ahn-ml.github.io/gram-website

title: MVVM, Micro‑Frontends, and Domain‑Driven Frontend — A Practical Guide
description:
This post gives you crisp mental models and copy‑pasteable patterns for three frequently‑confused topics:

  • MVVM (Model–View–ViewModel)
  • Micro‑Frontends (MFE)
  • Domain‑Driven Design applied to the frontend (DDF/DDD)

TL;DR: Use MVVM to structure components, DDD to structure the system/domain, and micro‑frontends only when org/scale complexity requires independent deploys.

Quick Compare (When to use what)

Concern MVVM DDD (frontend) Micro‑Frontends
Primary goal Decouple UI from state/logic Align codebase with business domains & boundaries Scale teams with independent deploys
Granularity Component/feature level App/system architecture App/organization level
Key benefits Testable UI logic, clearer components Low coupling, shared language, safer changes Team autonomy, parallel delivery
Typical cost Extra layer (ViewModel) Upfront modeling + boundaries Runtime integration, perf, shared deps
Use if… Components mix view & logic Features cross‑contaminate domains Many teams, large app, diff release cycles

MVVM in React (practical)

Model = domain data (entities/value objects).

View = React UI.

ViewModel = state + behaviors the View needs (pure, testable, no DOM).

// /features/todos/viewmodel/useTodosVM.ts
import { useState, useMemo, useEffect } from 'react'
import { fetchTodos, toggleTodo } from '../services/todoApi'

export function useTodosVM() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState([])
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false)
  const [error, setError] = useState(null)

  async function load() {
    setLoading(true); setError(null)
    try {
      const data = await fetchTodos()
      setItems(data)
    } catch (e) {
      setError('Failed to load')
    } finally {
      setLoading(false)
    }
  }

  async function toggle(id) {
    setItems(xs => xs.map(x => x.id === id ? { ...x, done: !x.done } : x))
    try { await toggleTodo(id) } catch {}
  }

  const stats = useMemo(() => ({
    total: items.length,
    done: items.filter(x => x.done).length,
  }), [items])

  return { items, loading, error, load, toggle, stats }
}

// /features/todos/components/TodoList.tsx (View)
import { useEffect } from 'react'
import { useTodosVM } from '../viewmodel/useTodosVM'

export function TodoList() {
  const vm = useTodosVM()
  useEffect(() => { vm.load() }, [])
  if (vm.loading) return <p>Loading…</p>
  if (vm.error) return <p role="alert">{vm.error}</p>

  return (
    <div>
      <p>{vm.stats.done}/{vm.stats.total} done</p>
      <ul>
        {vm.items.map(t => (
          <li key={t.id}>
            <label>
              <input type="checkbox" checked={t.done} onChange={() => vm.toggle(t.id)} />
              {t.title}
            </label>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </div>
  )
}

Why MVVM here works

  • ViewModel exposes only what the View needs → easier to mock/test.
  • UI stays dumb; side‑effects and decisions live in the ViewModel.

Tip: A custom hook is a great ViewModel. For shared state, use a store (Zustand/Jotai) and export selectors as VM surface.

Domain‑Driven Frontend (DDD for UI teams)

Goal: mirror business domains and bounded contexts so features don’t leak across layers.

Core ideas

  • Ubiquitous Language: same terms in code and meetings (e.g., Campaign, Offer).
  • Bounded Contexts: define clear borders; inside, a term has one meaning.
  • Entities & Value Objects: explicit types (e.g., PhoneNumber, Money).
  • Application services: orchestrate use‑cases; domain services: pure domain logic.

Foldering (Feature‑Sliced/Domain‑First)

src/
  app/                # app shell, routing, providers
  shared/             # cross‑cutting (ui, lib, api, styles, tokens)
  entities/           # reusable domain entities (User, Campaign, Money)
  features/           # user‑visible capabilities (CreateCampaign, SendSMS)
  pages/              # Next.js routes (compose features)
  widgets/            # page sections composed from features/entities

Example: Value Object

// /entities/money/money.ts
export class Money {
  constructor(readonly amount: number, readonly currency: 'EUR'|'USD'|'IRR') {
    if (!Number.isFinite(amount)) throw new Error('Invalid amount')
  }
  add(x: Money) { if (x.currency !== this.currency) throw new Error('Currency mismatch'); return new Money(this.amount + x.amount, this.currency) }
  format() { return new Intl.NumberFormat(undefined, { style:'currency', currency: this.currency }).format(this.amount) }
}

Application Service (use‑case)

// /features/create-campaign/application/createCampaign.ts
import { Money } from '@/entities/money/money'
import { CampaignRepo } from '../infrastructure/CampaignRepo'

export async function createCampaign(input: { title: string; budget: number; currency: 'EUR' }) {
  const budget = new Money(input.budget, 'EUR')
  // business rules…
  return CampaignRepo.create({ title: input.title, budget })
}

Outcome: Separation between domain and delivery (React/UI); safer refactors, clearer ownership.

Micro‑Frontends (MFE)

Split a large UI into independently built & deployed parts. Useful for many teams, different release cycles, or poly‑stacks.

Integration styles

  1. Build‑time: compose artifacts during CI (simpler, less dynamic).
  2. Runtime via Module Federation: load remote bundles at runtime (webpack MF) — most common.
  3. iframes/Web Components: hard isolation; tradeoffs in UX/sharing.

What to share

  • Design system (tokens, components) pinned to a version.
  • Contracts: types/protocols between MFEs (e.g., events, URL contracts).
  • Auth & routing: centralized shell or clearly defined hand‑offs.

Minimal Module Federation sketch

// host/next.config.mjs (webpack override)
module.exports = {
  webpack: (config) => {
    const ModuleFederationPlugin = require('webpack').container.ModuleFederationPlugin
    config.plugins.push(new ModuleFederationPlugin({
      name: 'host',
      remotes: { billing: 'billing@https://cdn.example.com/billing/remoteEntry.js' },
      shared: { react: { singleton: true, requiredVersion: false }, 'react-dom': { singleton: true } },
    }))
    return config
  }
}

Routing + Ownership

  • Each MFE owns its routes (/billing/**), telemetry, error boundaries.
  • Shell owns the top‑level layout, auth/session, cross‑app nav.

Pitfalls & mitigations

  • Duplicate deps → enforce shared versions; analyze bundle.
  • Design drift → versioned DS + visual regression tests.
  • Cross‑MFE state → avoid if possible; communicate via URL/events.

Use MFEs when organizational complexity dominates. If one team, one repo, don’t start here.

Putting it together

  • Use DDD to split the product into domains/bounded contexts.
  • Within each domain/feature, structure UI with MVVM (custom hooks as ViewModels).
  • If the org demands independent deploys per domain → consider MFEs and expose each domain UI as a remote module.
  • Keep contracts explicit (types, events, URL schemas).

Diagram (text)

[ App Shell ]
   ├── [ Domain A MFE ] -- MVVM inside
   ├── [ Domain B MFE ] -- MVVM inside
   └── [ Shared DS/Auth/Telemetry ]

Decision Guide

  1. Single team, growing app? → Start with DDD foldering + MVVM.
  2. Multiple teams, conflicting releases? → Add MFE for those domains.
  3. Migration: carve out a bounded context → expose via Module Federation → route traffic gradually.

Testing & Observability

  • Domain tests for entities/services (pure).
  • ViewModel tests for behavior without DOM.
  • Contract tests between MFEs.
  • E2E across shell + MFEs (Playwright).
  • Telemetry per MFE: errors, web vitals, perf budgets.

Starter Folder Blueprint (Next.js App Router) 

src/
  app/
    layout.tsx
    (routes)...
  shared/
    ui/ (design system)
    lib/ (utils)
    api/ (clients)
  entities/
  features/
  widgets/

Cheatsheet

  • MVVM: put UI logic in a ViewModel (custom hook/store). Keep views dumb.
  • DDD: align code with business domains and bounded contexts.
  • MFE: only when org scaling needs independent deploys; share DS & contracts.
  • Prefer URL/event‑based integration over shared global state.

title: A Hybrid SMT-NRA Solver: Integrating 2D Cell-Jump-Based Local Search, MCSAT and OpenCAD
description:
arXiv:2507.00557v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In this paper, we propose a hybrid framework for Satisfiability Modulo the Theory of Nonlinear Real Arithmetic (SMT-NRA for short). First, we introduce a two-dimensional cell-jump move, called \emph{2D-cell-jump}, generalizing the key operation, cell-jump, of the local search method for SMT-NRA. In contrast to the existing cell-jump, which updates assignments exclusively along a given line, the 2D-cell-jump enables search over an arbitrarily selected plane. Then, we propose an extended local search framework, named \emph{2D-LS} (following the existing local search framework, LS, for SMT-NRA). Finally, we present a hybrid framework for SMT-NRA integrating 2D-LS, MCSAT and OpenCAD, to improve search efficiency through information exchange. The experimental results demonstrate improvements in local search performance, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

title: Kotlin Null Safety Explained Simply: ?, ?., ?:, !! and Platform Types
description:
In short: In Kotlin, a type says if a value can be null. String can never be null. String? can. You must handle the null case before you use a String?. So most null crashes become build errors instead.

Every Android developer has seen this line in a crash report: java.lang.NullPointerException. The app tried to use something that was not there, like an order with no delivery note.

This post covers how Kotlin's null safety works, the tools you use every day, and where a crash can still get through.

What is null, and why does it crash apps?

null means "no value". Think of a contact in your phone with no phone number saved. Asking it for a number is fine. Calling that number is the problem.

In Java, any object can be null, and the compiler does not warn you. You find out at runtime, when the app crashes with a NullPointerException (NPE). Tony Hoare, who added null references to a language in 1965, later called it his "billion-dollar mistake".

The usual Java fix is if (x != null) everywhere. That works only until someone forgets.

How does Kotlin stop null crashes?

Kotlin puts the answer into the type itself. Every type comes in two versions:

  • String is non-nullable. It always holds a real string.
  • String? is nullable. It holds a string or null.

Non-nullable is the default. If you try var restaurant: String = null, the build fails with "Null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'String'."

The rule for String? is just as strict. If deliveryNote is a String?, then deliveryNote.length does not compile:

Only safe (?.) or non-null asserted (!!.) calls are allowed
on a nullable receiver of type 'String?'.

So you decide what happens when the value is missing. You decide it while writing the code, not at 2 AM from a crash report.

You already see this on Android. In onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?), the ? tells you the bundle is null on the first launch.

How do you use a value that might be null?

There are four everyday tools.

1. Check it with if After if (order != null), the compiler treats order as non-null inside that block. This is called a smart cast: the compiler changes the type for you because it saw the check.

2. Safe call ?. order?.total means "give me the total if order is not null, otherwise give me null". You can chain it: order?.rider?.phone. If any part is null, the whole result is null and nothing crashes.

3. Elvis operator ?: It gives a default when the left side is null: order?.deliveryNote ?: "No note". It can also leave the function early: val order = findOrder(orderId) ?: return.

4. let with ?. order?.let { show(it) } runs the block only when order is not null. Inside the block, it is non-null.

Why is !! risky?

!! is the not-null assertion operator. It tells the compiler: "Trust me, this is not null." If you are wrong, you get the same NPE that Kotlin was trying to prevent.

When the compiler shows a red line, adding !! is the fastest way to make it go away. That is true whether you, a teammate or an AI tool writes the fix. Here is what that looks like:

// Almost right: compiles, but crashes when the order is not found
fun orderTitle(orderId: String): String {
    val order = findOrder(orderId)          // can be null
    return "Order total: " + order!!.total  // crashes if null
}

// Right: the "not found" case has an answer
fun orderTitle(orderId: String): String {
    val order = findOrder(orderId) ?: return "Order not found"
    // From here, order can't be null, so no ?. or !! is needed
    return "Order total: " + order.total
}

The first version hides a decision. Nobody said what should happen when the order is missing. The second version answers that question with ?:, and after that line the compiler knows order is not null.

In code review, treat every !! as a question: "Why can't this be null here?" If there is a good reason, show it in code. For example: requireNotNull(order) { "Order must be loaded first" }.

Where can a NullPointerException still happen in Kotlin?

The Kotlin docs list a few causes. In everyday Android work, two matter most: !! and Java code.

Java does not say if a value can be null. So when Kotlin calls a Java method, the result has a platform type. The IDE shows it as String!, which means "String or String?, you decide".

Say an old Java class has public String getCouponCode(String orderId), and it returns null when there is no coupon. In Kotlin:

  • val code: String = cart.getCouponCode(orderId) compiles. At runtime it crashes on that line with "getCouponCode(...) must not be null".
  • val code: String? = cart.getCouponCode(orderId) compiles, and now the compiler makes you handle null.

So treat values from Java as nullable unless you know better. "Knowing better" means the Java code has nullability annotations like @Nullable and @NonNull. Kotlin reads them and gives you a real String or String? instead of String!. If you own the Java code, Android's Kotlin interop guide says to annotate every public parameter, return value and field.

Which null tool should you use?

You write What it means Use it when
String? This value can be null The value can really be missing
if (x != null) Check, then use it as non-null You need several steps with the value
x?.total Total, or null if x is null Null is fine for the result too
x ?: default Use a default when null You have a good fallback, or want to return early
x?.let { } Run the block only when not null One action that needs the value
x as? Type Cast, or null if it fails You are not sure of the type
x!! Crash if null Almost never; prefer a check or requireNotNull

Frequently asked questions

Why does the smart cast not work on my var property?
Because the property could change between the check and the use. The compiler tells you the smart cast is impossible. Copy it into a local val first, then check that.

Is !! always wrong?
No, but it should be rare. In tests it can be fine, because a crash there just fails the test. In app code, requireNotNull or checkNotNull with a message gives the same stop with a clearer reason.

What is the difference between as and as??
as throws a ClassCastException if the value is not that type. as? returns null instead, so you handle it with ?. or ?: like any other nullable value.

What should you remember?

Kotlin does not remove null. It makes you say, in the type, where null is allowed. Then the compiler checks every place you use it.

In everyday Kotlin code, watch two doors: !! and Java. Keep both small and easy to see.

If you want to test yourself, try the null safety interview questions. This post is the first topic in Stage 1 of my Android roadmap.

Where do most !! operators come from in your codebase: old Java code, framework callbacks, or habit?

This post first appeared on imayankkumar.com, where you'll find new posts first.
