title: A Software Factory Is a Trust Problem More Than a Speed Problem
description:
Everyone building with agents is chasing the same number: how fast can we go from idea to merged pull request. That number is the easy one now. An agent can produce a complete, tested, plausible feature in eleven minutes.

The hard number is the other one. How long until you know it is right?

That is what a software factory actually has to solve. Not producing output, which is cheap, but trusting it, which is not. And trust does not come from a better prompt. It comes from tooling that tells you, quickly and without interpretation, what changed and whether it still works.

So this is not a list of tools. It is what I look for in any tool before it goes anywhere near a factory.

1. It tells you what changed

A factory where you cannot see what happened is a factory you will stop trusting the first time something breaks.

That starts with observability in the product: traces, metrics and logs from day one, ideally on an open standard like OpenTelemetry so the data is not trapped in one vendor. When an agent ships a change, production should be able to tell you what it did before a user does. I put this first because it is the one most teams postpone, and postponing it means every agent change goes out blind.

It continues with observability of the factory itself. Every step an agent took should leave something a human can read at human pace: a ticket comment, a run report, a spec, a video of the tests running. If the only evidence of a change is the diff, you are reviewing the agent's opinion of what it built, not what it built.

2. It is deterministic and fast

Agents do not need long markdown files listing every rule of your architecture. They need checks that fail.

A rule written in prose is a suggestion. A rule enforced by a linter is a fact. I have written about this before in Prose does not beat determinism, and it holds for the whole factory:

  • CI from the first commit. Not when the project "gets serious". The first agent pull request is the first one that needs it.
  • Linters and type checks for the rules you would otherwise write in a CONVENTIONS.md.
  • Commit conventions enforced by a hook, so agent commits read the same as human ones and changelogs write themselves.
  • Static analysis that always runs: secret scanning like gitleaks, code analysis like SonarCloud or whatever fits your stack. These are boring, and boring is the point. They do not depend on the agent remembering anything.

Markdown still has a job. It records intent: what was agreed and why. Checks record rules. Mixing the two is how you end up with a 900 line instructions file that the agent reads, half follows, and nobody can verify.

3. It is simple enough to change

The easier the architecture is for a human to read, the easier it is for an agent to work in. And the easier it is to work in, the easier it is to throw away.

That last part matters more every month. The tools and models you use today will not be the ones you use in a year. A factory that cannot drop a piece and replace it is a factory that will slowly calcify around its first decisions.

Two things keep it changeable:

  • No speculative architecture. Build for the requirements you know. An agent asked to "make it extensible" will happily generate a framework for a problem you never had.
  • No lock-in you cannot price. Hosted is fine. The question is how much it costs to leave. If your framework decides where you deploy, or your test runner only works inside one platform, you have handed a decision that should be yours to someone whose business model depends on it.

4. It proves its own quality

This is my strongest filter, and the one that rules out popular tools most often.

If a tool cannot show me how it checks itself, I do not use it. That goes double for anything that is itself an AI component: a skill, a plugin, an MCP server, an agent prompt. Before adopting one I look at three things:

  1. Its CI. Does it run anything on every change, or does a new version just appear?
  2. How it is distributed. Versioned, with a changelog, or a file you copy and hope?
  3. Its evals. Is there evidence the skill does something useful, measured over more than one run, or is the evidence "I tried it and it worked"?

The third is the one almost nobody has yet. I wrote about why it matters in "I tried it and it worked" is not a test.

A note on popularity, because it is the objection I hear most. Popularity is no longer a proxy for ease of use, because agents read the docs for you. A small, well-tested tool with clear docs is as easy for an agent to adopt as the market leader. Popularity still matters for maintenance: you want the thing to exist in three years. It is a tiebreaker, not the deciding vote.

5. Testing you can review at human pace

Testing is where trust is either earned or faked, and agents make faking it very easy. When the same agent writes the code and the test, a green tick is the same model's opinion expressed twice.

What I look for in frontend testing specifically:

  • Every scenario mocked and deterministic, so the suite can run on every iteration of an agent loop without flaking.
  • Contract testing against the backend, so the mocks the tests rely on cannot drift away from the real API.
  • Something a human can watch. A short video of each test running, attached to the pull request, tells a reviewer in thirty seconds what the diff takes five minutes to suggest.

This is the set I ended up building into TWD for my own work, which is why I am biased. But the criteria matter more than the tool: whatever you use for any framework, ask whether it gives you all three.

6. The chain has no shortcuts

None of the above survives a team that routes around it.

A factory is a chain. A request becomes a ticket, the ticket becomes a spec, the spec a plan, the plan a change, the change gets verified against the ticket and handed over. Break one link (a requirement agreed in a chat, a fix pushed without an issue, a hero developer who "just does it") and you lose the thing the whole factory exists to produce: a record you can trust.

I call this chain of custody, borrowing the forensic term, and it deserves its own post.

It also means the factory is not an engineering project. Product, design and stakeholders work inside the same chain or the chain does not exist. That is the hardest part of all of this, and it gets its own post too.

The one question

Strip all of this down and every tool gets the same question:

Can it tell me, quickly and deterministically, what changed and whether it still works?

If yes, it belongs in the factory, popular or not. If no, it does not, popular or not. And when the answer changes, throw it away. A factory you are afraid to rebuild is not a factory, it is legacy that happens to be automated.

title: Open-weight models take 56% of token volume, Astra doubles Fable 5.1 spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — September 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from June, July, and August.

September 2026 summary

The September index reports on AI Gateway data collected through August 2026.

  • Open-weight models ran the majority of gateway tokens for the first time, up from 7% in December to 56% in August.

  • The average token costs less than half what it did five months ago. Price per token fell 23.2% in August, the third straight monthly drop, and the median team paid 7.6% less.

  • Fable 5, Anthropic's most capable model, lost two-thirds of its share of gateway spend in one month. Opus 5, at half the price, tripled its share. Anthropic kept 64% of all spend.

  • Gemini 3 Flash has lost 95% of its share of gateway tokens since May, and more than three-quarters of the volume it lost went to models from other labs.

Latest Index updates

The monthly report covers data through August. We add notable developments here between editions.

  • September 17: OpenAI launched Astra on September 3, and it took a third of OpenAI's spend within two days and twice Fable 5.1's share of gateway spend. Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend in its first twelve days while Fable 5.1, launched two days earlier at the same price, took 3.7%.

  • September 18: Jev is now the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history. Within its first 24 hours, it was being used by nearly 13% of paid teams, 2x as many as the GPT-5.6 family and over 6x as many as Fable 5.1.

Open-weight models take a majority of token volume for the first time

In August, open-weight models ran 56% of all tokens on AI Gateway, marking the first month they took the majority of volume.

In December 2025, they processed fewer than one in ten tokens, and only eight months later, they ran more token volume than all closed-weight models combined.

Though the frontier kept the majority of spend, open-weight dollar share is accelerating. As open-weight models become more capable, customers are moving more production workloads over to them.

Growth in open-weight model adoption helped push the average price per token across the gateway down 23.2% in August, its third consecutive monthly drop and the steepest since April. Among teams running more than ten million tokens in both months, the median team paid 7.6% less per token, more than double July's 2.9% decline.

Teams can now get more inference from the same budget and reserve frontier models only for the tasks that justify the premium.

Frontier plateaus as Fable spend goes to Opus 5

Production workloads that justify a frontier model don't always need the most expensive one. They need one that’s good enough.

Fable is the most capable model Anthropic sells. Opus is the tier below it and costs roughly half of Fable’s price per token. When the US export control on Fable 5 was lifted and its access restored on July 1, its gateway spend share surged to 13.2%. At the end of that same month, Opus 5 came online.

In August, Fable 5’s share of gateway spend fell to 4.9%, and Opus 5's share rose to 22.5%. Nine in ten of the teams that ran Fable cut their usage, and more of them moved their workloads to Opus 5 than any other model. Fable’s extra capability wasn’t worth double the price.

Teams left Fable, Anthropic's most expensive and capable model, but the lab retained the lion’s share of gateway spend because those workloads stepped down to Opus 5, not a different lab.

Anthropic has taken at least 61 cents of every dollar spent through AI Gateway every month since December, and 64 cents in August. Its models have held the top two spots by spend every month since December, even as the models in those spots changed.

Customer loyalty follows the model profile, not the lab

Lab loyalty doesn’t follow brand, it follows model profile, and consistency wins.

When a new model preserves what users valued in its predecessor, the lab retains its customers. When it doesn’t, those customers fill the need through other providers.

When Claude Opus 5 launched, it gained almost twice what Fable lost, because it handled the same workloads at half the price. And within five days of Z.ai launching GLM-5.3-Flash, it was running three times GLM-5.2's daily volume.

Google struggled to retain customers with its new models. Because the new offerings didn’t provide a relative advantage on capability or price, a majority of Gemini 3 Flash’s workloads moved to OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek.

About half of the volume that left Gemini 3 Flash went to cheaper models, led by GPT-5.6 Luna, which costs less than half as much per token. Most of the other half went to higher-priced models, led by Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, which cost roughly nine and three times as much as Gemini 3 Flash, respectively.

The flight to better-fit models meant that over the same period, Google’s share of gateway token volume fell from 30% to 5%, with Gemini 3 Flash accounting for 22 of the 25 percentage points lost.

Special report: Astra took a third of OpenAI spend within 48 hours and outpaced Fable 5.1 two to one at launch

GPT-6 Astra launched on the AI Gateway on September 3 at the same price as Fable 5.1 and two and a half times the price of GPT-5.6 Sol. Two days later, it accounted for one in every three dollars spent on OpenAI models through the gateway. Its share of spend has held, hovering between 28% and 39% since.

Within OpenAI’s model lineup, Astra and Sol processed 27% of OpenAI’s tokens but accounted for 71% of its spending from September 4 through 16. Luna and Nano processed more than twice as many tokens for about one-ninth as much spending.

Anthropic launched Fable 5.1 on September 1, two days before Astra. Over each model's first twelve days on the gateway, Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend, more than twice Fable 5.1's share of 3.7%, and was used by twice as many teams.

OpenAI’s cheaper models carry its volume, while Astra’s early lead over Fable shows it can also attract teams at the highest price point. Together, they let OpenAI compete with other frontier labs for both scale and premium spend.

Stay tuned for more in next month's report.

Also in August’s data

  • Google's Nano Banana took the lead in image spend for the first time, at 50% to GPT Image's 44%, even as GPT Image took back the lead in images generated, 46% to 39%.

  • Google's Veo rose to second in video spend, at 20%, up from 15% in July. Seedance remained in first on both videos generated and video spend.

  • The share of videos generated by xAI’s Grok Imagine has more than halved since June, from 42% to 31% to 19%.

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through August 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input, and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated using labs’ published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Statements about where volume moved compare changes among the same teams. They do not trace individual tokens between models.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, which is broader than the definition used in earlier reports.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: Least-privilege Azure RBAC for read-only architecture review
description:
TL;DR: Least-privilege Azure RBAC for a read-only architecture scanner is the Reader action */read plus two actions: Microsoft.Resources/deployments/exportTemplate/action and Microsoft.Network/networkWatchers/topology/action. Put them in a custom role with no data actions, assign it to a dedicated service principal at resource-group scope, and don't use Contributor for normal sync.

By Prateek Singh, founder of Ganak AI Labs. Updated 6 October 2026.

The fastest way to stall a security review is a setup guide that starts with az ad sp create-for-rbac --role Contributor.

The tool only wants to look at your Azure environment. So why should it be able to change it?

Usually it shouldn't. Most architecture tools need to read Azure Resource Manager metadata, plus one or two specific actions. Contributor shows up in quick-start guides because it's one line and always works.

Here's a least-privilege setup for read-only architecture review: what each permission is for, how to scope it and how to fix gaps without widening the role. The example is Cloudeval's Cloud sync, but the pattern fits any read-only scanner.

Disclosure: I'm the founder of Cloudeval.

Key terms used below

  • Azure RBAC: Azure role-based access control. A role definition lists allowed actions (control plane) and data actions (data plane). A role assignment grants it to a principal at a scope.
  • Service principal: the identity an application uses to sign in to Microsoft Entra ID and call Azure.
  • Cloud sync: Cloudeval's live Azure path. It reads deployed resources, exports templates for analysis and stores a project snapshot.

Why do scanners ask for Contributor in the first place?

Because it's convenient. Contributor can manage everything except access, so nothing fails during setup.

That convenience is the problem. A credential that can delete resources is a far bigger risk to store in a third-party service than one that can only read.

Microsoft's Azure RBAC best practices say it plainly: grant the least privilege needed, and "avoid assigning broader roles at broader scopes even if it initially seems more convenient."

Cloudeval Cloud sync doesn't need Contributor for normal sync. The full list is on the Azure Sync Permissions for Cloudeval page.

What permissions does a read-only architecture review need?

Permission What it allows Why Cloud sync uses it
*/read Read control plane information for all Azure resources (the only action in the built-in Reader role) Read subscription, resource group, resource, provider, deployment and topology metadata in scope
Microsoft.Resources/deployments/exportTemplate/action Export the template for a deployment Build report inputs from live resources
Microsoft.Network/networkWatchers/topology/action Get a network-level view of resources and their relationships in a resource group Add Network Watcher topology to the live architecture graph
Data actions None Not needed. No blob contents, no Key Vault secret values

That's Reader plus two actions. Nothing else goes in the role.

How do I set up least-privilege Azure RBAC for Cloud sync?

  1. Create a dedicated service principal with no role assigned.
  2. Define a custom role with */read and the two actions, and no data actions.
  3. Assign it at resource-group scope, plus NetworkWatcherRG if you want topology.
  4. Connect Cloudeval with those credentials and confirm what it can see.
  5. Fix gaps by adding the specific missing action, not a broader role.

Step 1: Create a dedicated service principal

Use one principal per tool, so you can rotate or revoke it without touching anything else.

Current Azure CLI versions don't assign a role in az ad sp create-for-rbac unless you pass --role. So the principal starts with no access:

SUB_ID="$(az account show --query id -o tsv)"
RG="<target-resource-group>"
SP_NAME="cloudeval-live-sync"

SP_JSON="$(az ad sp create-for-rbac --name "$SP_NAME" -o json)"
APP_ID="$(echo "$SP_JSON" | jq -r .appId)"
CLIENT_SECRET="$(echo "$SP_JSON" | jq -r .password)"
TENANT_ID="$(echo "$SP_JSON" | jq -r .tenant)"

Treat CLIENT_SECRET like any production secret. Keep it out of shared terminals and CI logs, store it in your secret manager and note its expiry date.

An expired secret is one of the most common reasons a connection test fails later.

Step 2: Define the custom role 

{
  "Name": "CloudEval Live Sync Reader",
  "IsCustom": true,
  "Description": "Read Azure resources and export deployment templates for Cloudeval Cloud sync.",
  "Actions": [
    "*/read",
    "Microsoft.Resources/deployments/exportTemplate/action",
    "Microsoft.Network/networkWatchers/topology/action"
  ],
  "NotActions": [],
  "DataActions": [],
  "NotDataActions": [],
  "AssignableScopes": ["/subscriptions/<subscription-id>"]
}

az role definition create --role-definition cloudeval-live-sync-reader.json

AssignableScopes controls where the role can be assigned, not where it is assigned. To change assignable scopes on an existing definition, run az role definition update with the same JSON.

Step 3: Assign it at resource-group scope

Resource-group scope is the right default:

az role assignment create \
  --assignee "$APP_ID" \
  --role "CloudEval Live Sync Reader" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/$SUB_ID/resourceGroups/$RG"

Repeat it for each resource group you want reviewed, and pick the same groups in the Cloudeval connection form.

Network Watcher usually lives in its own group, NetworkWatcherRG by default. If you want topology and Network Watcher sits outside your target group, assign the role there too.

Skip that and Cloud sync still reads resources and exports templates, but network relationships may be sparse.

Use subscription scope only when the tool should sync every resource group it can reach. It's a deliberate widening, so write down why.

Step 4: Connect Cloudeval and confirm what it sees

In Cloudeval, open Connections, then Add connection, and choose Azure and Cloud sync. Enter the client ID, client secret, tenant ID, subscription ID and target resource groups.

Cloudeval validates the credentials when it creates the connection. Then create a project from that connection and start the sync.


Link an existing Azure connection when you create a project.

The CLI does the same in one command. It reads the AZURE_* environment variables when you leave out the flags:

cloudeval projects create \
  --cloud-sync \
  --azure-tenant-id "$TENANT_ID" \
  --azure-client-id "$APP_ID" \
  --azure-client-secret "$CLIENT_SECRET" \
  --azure-subscription-id "$SUB_ID" \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name "Cloud sync $RG" \
  --format json \
  --output ./cloudeval-project.json

Here's the two-minute product demo, including connecting live Azure:

Start with one representative resource group. With a huge multi-subscription scope, it's hard to tell whether a gap comes from permissions or from the scope.

Step 5: Fix gaps without widening the role

When something looks incomplete, the fix is almost always one action or one assignment, not Contributor:

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Connection authenticates, but no resource groups appear Assignment hasn't propagated, or it's on another subscription or group Wait a few minutes, check the scope, test again
Resource group is visible, but reports fail to build Role is missing deployments/exportTemplate/action Update the role definition and re-run sync
Graph works, but network relationships are sparse Missing networkWatchers/topology/action, or no assignment on NetworkWatcherRG Add the action, assign on the Network Watcher group
Sync includes too many resource groups Role assigned at subscription scope, or no target groups selected in Cloudeval Assign at resource-group scope and select target groups


Check warnings and assumptions here after a sync that looks incomplete.

Re-run the sync only after you've confirmed the scope. Otherwise you just get a fresher copy of the wrong project.

Is the built-in Reader role enough?

Almost, and that's the point. Reader is exactly */read, with no other actions and no data actions.

For Cloud sync it's missing the two actions above. Without exportTemplate, report inputs can be incomplete. Without topology, the network graph is thinner.

Two caveats:

  • */read is a wildcard. Microsoft recommends listing actions explicitly in custom roles, because a wildcard also picks up future actions. Here it covers reads only and mirrors Reader, so your main lever is scope. Assign per resource group, and review the role if you need a stricter list.
  • Control plane only. With no data actions, the principal can't read blob contents or Key Vault secret values. If a report seems to expect them, don't add data actions to "fix" it. Cloud sync works from management-plane metadata.

Frequently asked questions

Does Cloudeval Cloud sync need the Contributor role?

No. Normal Cloud sync needs */read, Microsoft.Resources/deployments/exportTemplate/action and, for topology, Microsoft.Network/networkWatchers/topology/action. Keep Contributor for disposable smoke tests in a throwaway resource group.

Is the Azure Reader role enough for a read-only architecture scanner?

Not quite, for Cloudeval. Reader grants only */read. Cloud sync also uses the deployment export action to build report inputs and the Network Watcher topology action to map network relationships.

Can Cloudeval read Key Vault secrets or storage blob contents?

No. The recommended role has no data actions, and Cloud sync uses management-plane metadata only. Don't add data actions unless a separate workflow explicitly needs them.

Should I assign the role at subscription or resource-group scope?

Use resource-group scope by default. Choose subscription scope only when the tool should discover and sync every accessible resource group in that subscription.

Why are network relationships missing after a sync?

Usually the role lacks Microsoft.Network/networkWatchers/topology/action, or it isn't assigned on the resource group that holds Network Watcher, often NetworkWatcherRG. Add the action or the assignment and sync again.

Takeaway

A read-only scanner should have a read-only role. For Cloudeval, that's Reader's */read plus two named actions and no data actions, assigned per resource group to its own service principal.

The full reference, with the complete script, is Azure Sync Permissions for Cloudeval.

Related on cloudeval.ai

  • How do I understand an Azure environment I inherited?
  • How do I check whether my cloud inventory is complete?
  • Azure architecture assessment before changes ship

Try it

Create the custom role on one non-production resource group, then connect it. Open the Cloudeval app and follow Connect an Azure environment.

About the author

Prateek Singh is the founder of Ganak AI Labs and builds Cloudeval AI.

title: SparseGDN: Chunk Sparse in Linear Attention
description:
arXiv:2610.41420v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.

title: When AI glasses could be a worthy headphones replacement
description:
착용 시간이 전부다 — 웨어러블 논쟁에서 시각 훈련 소프트웨어를 설계한 이유

AI 글래스가 이어폰을 대체할 수 있을까 — 엔가젯의 이 질문은 사실 웨어러블 전체에 던져진 질문입니다. 답은 "무엇에 쓰느냐에 달렸다". 그리고 그 답 뒤에는 더 냉정한 기준이 숨어 있습니다. 기기가 아무리 뛰어나도, 매일 오래 착용하지 않으면 아무 일도 일어나지 않는다는 것.

이 기준은 시각 훈련 영역에서 훨씬 잔인하게 작동합니다. 약시(lazy eye, amblyopia)를 가진 사람에게 훈련을 포기하게 만드는 건 대개 의지 부족이 아닙니다. 접착식 패치의 불편함, 적청 안경의 어지러움, 그리고 무엇보다 지루함입니다. 재미없는 훈련은 3주를 넘기지 못합니다. 개발자 관점에서 보면 이것은 기능 문제가 아니라 리텐션 문제입니다. 아무리 정교한 알고리즘도 사용자가 매일 헤드셋을 쓰지 않으면 실행되지 않습니다.

그래서 Seven Sports는 순서를 바꿔 접근했습니다. 훈련을 위해 콘텐츠를 찾는 대신, 이미 매일 보고 있는 콘텐츠를 훈련의 장으로 만들었습니다. Amblyotube는 Meta Quest(Quest 2, 3, Pro, 3S)에서 YouTube 스타일 영상을 보면서 눈마다 다른 시각 경험을 제공하는 시각 협응·주의력 훈련 소프트웨어입니다.

왜 VR인가 — 두 개의 독립 디스플레이

핵심은 하드웨어 구조에 있습니다. VR 헤드셋은 눈마다 독립된 아이피스(eyepiece)를 가지고 있고, 소프트웨어는 각 눈에 서로 다른 피드를 동시에 보낼 수 있습니다. Amblyotube는 이 구조를 그대로 활용해 양안 훈련(dichoptic vision training)을 구현합니다. 왼쪽 눈과 오른쪽 눈에 완전히 다른 렌더링 결과를 전달할 수 있다는 점이, 기존의 패치나 아나글리프(적청) 안경으로는 불가능했던 설계 공간을 열어 줍니다.

이 지점이 사실 시스템 설계에서 가장 흥미로운 부분입니다. 전통적인 시각 훈련 도구는 '하나의 화면'을 전제로 만들어졌습니다. 패치는 물리적으로 한쪽 눈을 가리고, 적청 안경은 색 필터로 두 눈을 분리합니다. 둘 다 하드웨어에 종속된 트릭입니다. 반면 VR은 렌더 파이프라인 단계에서 좌안과 우안에 서로 다른 프레임을 밀어 넣을 수 있습니다. 훈련 파라미터가 콘텐츠 위에 얹히는 소프트웨어 계층으로 올라오는 순간, 실험실에서나 가능했던 프로토콜이 거실로 내려옵니다.

작동 방식은 계층적으로 단순합니다.

첫째, 우세안 화면에는 조절 가능한 디지털 블러(Dominant Eye Shader)를 겁니다. 블러, 대비, 밝기, 감마, 불투명도(opacity)를 개별적으로 조정할 수 있고, 100% 불투명도에서는 사실상 완전한 디지털 패칭이 됩니다. 하지만 주 목표는 대개 '부분 투명'입니다. 두 눈이 동시에 시각 정보를 처리하도록 만드는 것이기 때문입니다.

둘째, 약시안 화면에는 AI Sharpener(MFBF 모드)가 동작합니다. 이 엔진은 영상 안의 사람 형상(얼굴과 몸)을 식별해, 약시안 쪽 뷰에만 선택적으로 샤프닝을 적용합니다. 여기에 시각적 악센트(Visual Accents)가 더해집니다. 사람 위에 부드러운 형광 황록색 하이라이트를 입히거나, 인체 실루엣을 따라 굵은 적색 외곽선을 그리는 식입니다. 펄스(Pulse) 컨트롤로 이 효과를 일정한 Hz와 깊이로 밝아졌다 어두워지는 '호흡' 리듬으로 만들 수도 있습니다. 목적은 명확합니다. 무시당하던 눈의 시각 피질이 대상에 다시 주의를 기울이도록 만드는 것.

여기서 한 가지 흥미로운 엔지니어링 트레이드오프가 있습니다. 왜 프레임 전체를 샤프닝하지 않고 '사람'만 골라 강조할까요? 계산 비용도 이유지만, 더 큰 이유는 주의(attention)의 방향입니다. 화면 전체를 자극하면 시각 시스템은 어디를 봐야 할지 모릅니다. 반면 사회적 대상 — 얼굴과 몸 — 은 인간 시각이 진화적으로 가장 먼저 반응하도록 설계된 신호입니다. 약시안이 무시하던 바로 그 신호를 인위적으로 증폭시키는 것이 핵심입니다. 영상 전체가 아니라 관심의 대상에 개입하는 것. 이것이 소프트웨어가 하드웨어 위에서 할 수 있는 가장 정직한 일입니다.

셋째, 선택적 Wedge Occlusion이 있습니다. 양쪽 시야 일부에 검은 쐐기 모양을 덮어, 각 눈이 장면의 서로 다른 부분만 보게 강제합니다. 이는 두 눈의 상이 충돌하는 양안 경쟁(binocular rivalry)을 줄이는 고전적 기법을 소프트웨어로 옮긴 것입니다.

넷째, 양안 융합 훈련입니다. 약시안에는 자연 배경(피부톤, 녹색, 파란색)과 확실히 구분되는 고채도 마젠타 핑크 원형 단서를, 우세안에는 은은한 중립 회색 점을 띄웁니다. 사용자가 시선을 따라가면 뇌는 두 신호를 하나로 합치려 시도하고, 이 과정에서 양안 융합과 입체 깊이 지각이 연습됩니다.

캘리브레이션이 곧 정확도다

엔지니어링에서 흔히 놓치는 부분이 초기 설정입니다. Amblyotube는 실행 시 어느 눈이 영향을 받았는지(좌/우)를 먼저 고르게 합니다. 이 선택이 틀리면 필터가 반대쪽 눈, 즉 우세안을 훈련시키게 됩니다. 정확도가 곧 결과를 좌우합니다. 센서 캘리브레이션이 틀어진 로봇이 정확한 동작을 못 하듯, 기준이 뒤집힌 훈련은 아무리 오래 해도 방향이 반대입니다.

난이도는 두 가지 경로로 정해집니다. 하나는 조건 프리셋(Mild / Moderate / Severe) — 각각 시력표 마지막 2줄, 3~5줄, 5줄 이상을 읽지 못하는 정도를 기준으로 우세안 셰이더와 약시안 샤프너의 기본 레벨을 자동으로 맞춥니다. 다른 하나는 내장 LogMAR 시력 확인 도구입니다. 가상 3미터 거리에서 표준 Landolt C 시표를 사용해 눈별로 최대 30회 시행, 임상 스테어케이스 알고리즘으로 logMAR 값을 산출하고, 감지된 경도에 맞춰 훈련 프로필을 자동 갱신할 수 있습니다. 사용자가 감으로 난이도를 정하지 않아도 되는 구조입니다.

리텐션을 위한 인터페이스 결정

세션은 30~40분, 최대 1시간을 권장합니다. 13세 이상 대상. 컨트롤 패널은 VR 안에서 크기 조절과 이동이 가능한 플로팅 패널이고, Meta Quest 컨트롤러와 핸드 트래킹을 모두 지원합니다. YouTube 검색창이 내장되어 있고, 네트워크 없이 재생 가능한 아동용 카탈로그(만화 등)도 미리 담겨 있습니다. Room View는 AR 패스스루 모드로, 가상 룸 대신 실제 방 위에 영상을 띄워 훈련할 수 있게 합니다. 재생, 일시정지, 탐색, 볼륨, 음소거, 언어 선택, 그리고 기본값 복원(Reset All) 버튼도 포함됩니다.

인터페이스 결정 하나하나가 리텐션을 향합니다. 플로팅 패널을 굳이 VR 공간 안에 띄운 이유는, 훈련 중 시선을 헤드셋 밖으로 빼지 않게 하기 위함입니다. 컨트롤러와 핸드 트래킹을 둘 다 지원하는 이유도 마찬가지입니다. 입력 방식에서 막히면 그 순간 세션이 끊기기 때문입니다. 오프라인 카탈로그는 네트워크가 불안정한 환경에서도 훈련이 멈추지 않게 하는 안전장치입니다. 화려한 기능이 아니라, 매일 켜지게 만드는 마찰 제거입니다.

한계를 명확히 두는 설계

중요한 전제가 있습니다. Amblyotube는 진단·치료·완치 수단이 아니라, 양안 협응과 깊이 지각을 돕는 보조적 시각 훈련 도구입니다. 전문 의료 지침을 대체하지 않습니다. 소프트웨어가 할 수 있는 일은 꾸준히 실행될 기회를 만드는 것, 그리고 그 기회를 매일의 콘텐츠 위에 얹는 것입니다. 이 경계를 분명히 긋는 것도 설계의 일부입니다. 과장된 약속은 리텐션을 만들지 못하고, 정직한 범위만이 오래 갑니다.

검사실이 아니라 거실에서, 패치가 아니라 좋아하는 영상 위에서 훈련이 일어나게 하는 것 — 웨어러블의 성패가 결국 착용 시간에서 갈린다면, 시각 훈련도 같은 규칙을 따를 수밖에 없습니다.

Meta Quest에서 Amblyotube를 만나보세요: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: CCSP vs. CISM: Which Cybersecurity Certification Is Right for You?
description:
Introduction
The cybersecurity industry offers several professional certifications that help IT professionals develop specialized skills and advance their careers. Two notable credentials are the Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP), offered by ISC2, and the Certified Information Security Manager (CISM), offered by ISACA.

Although both certifications are respected in the cybersecurity industry, they serve different professional goals. CCSP focuses on securing cloud environments, while CISM emphasizes information security governance, risk management, and program leadership.

Understanding the differences between CCSP vs. CISM can help you choose the certification that aligns with your experience, interests, and long-term career objectives.

What Is CCSP Certification?
The Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP) certification validates knowledge of cloud security architecture, design, operations, and compliance. It is intended for professionals who want to demonstrate expertise in protecting cloud-based applications, infrastructure, and information.

The CCSP curriculum covers six domains:

Cloud Concepts, Architecture, and Design

Cloud Data Security

Cloud Platform and Infrastructure Security

Cloud Application Security

Cloud Security Operations

Legal, Risk, and Compliance

These domains help professionals understand cloud security risks, data protection, access management, infrastructure controls, and regulatory requirements.

CCSP can be particularly relevant for cloud security engineers, security architects, cloud consultants, and experienced cybersecurity professionals responsible for securing cloud services.

What Is CISM Certification?
The Certified Information Security Manager (CISM) certification is designed for professionals who manage, develop, oversee, or assess an organization's information security program.

Unlike CCSP, which concentrates on cloud security, CISM emphasizes the strategic and managerial responsibilities associated with enterprise security.

Its four domains are:

Information Security Governance

Information Security Risk Management

Information Security Program

Incident Management

CISM helps professionals develop the knowledge needed to align security initiatives with business objectives, manage information security risks, establish security programs, and oversee incident response.

It is especially relevant for information security managers, risk managers, security consultants, and professionals pursuing senior leadership roles.

CCSP vs. CISM: Key Differences
The primary difference between CCSP and CISM is their focus. CCSP develops specialized cloud security knowledge, whereas CISM develops information security management and governance expertise.

Comparison CCSP CISM
Certifying organization ISC2 ISACA
Primary focus Cloud security Information security management
Main emphasis Cloud architecture, data, infrastructure, and operations Governance, risk, security programs, and incident management
Number of domains Six Four
Ideal audience Cloud security professionals and architects Security managers and aspiring security leaders
Career direction Cloud security engineering and architecture Security management and governance
Both certifications are vendor-neutral and require ongoing professional development to maintain the credential. However, their different subject areas make them suitable for different career paths.

CCSP vs. CISM: Which Certification Is More Technical?
CCSP generally has a stronger technical focus on cloud security. Candidates study cloud architectures, data protection, infrastructure security, application security, and operational controls. The certification is particularly useful for professionals who design, implement, or evaluate cloud security solutions.

CISM focuses more heavily on organizational leadership and security management. Candidates learn how to establish governance structures, assess risks, develop security programs, and oversee incident management.

Neither certification is universally better. The right option depends on whether your responsibilities center on technical cloud security or managing an organization's broader information security program.

Eligibility and Examination Preparation
Both certifications are intended for professionals with relevant experience, although their eligibility requirements differ.

CCSP generally requires five years of cumulative paid work experience in information technology, including three years in information security and one year in a CCSP domain. Certain approved credentials and qualifications can affect the experience requirement. A qualifying CISSP credential can satisfy the CCSP experience requirement under ISC2 rules.

CISM generally requires five years of professional information security experience, including at least three years of information security management experience across at least three CISM domains. Applicable waivers and current certification policies should be checked with ISACA.

Before registering for either examination, review the official certification requirements and current exam outline. A structured study schedule, reliable preparation materials, practice questions, and real-world scenarios can help you prepare effectively.

Career Opportunities After CCSP and CISM
CCSP can support career development in cloud-focused security roles, including:

Cloud Security Architect

Cloud Security Engineer

Cloud Security Consultant

Cloud Security Specialist

CISM can support progression toward management and governance positions, including:

Information Security Manager

Information Security Risk Manager

Security Program Manager

Information Security Director

Experienced professionals may also pursue chief information security officer (CISO) positions, depending on their leadership experience and broader qualifications.

Certification alone does not guarantee a particular job or salary. Employers also consider practical experience, communication skills, technical expertise, and organizational responsibilities.

Can You Earn Both CCSP and CISM?
Yes. Some professionals may benefit from earning both certifications, particularly those responsible for managing cloud security programs.

For example, a security manager overseeing an organization's cloud transformation may need CCSP knowledge to understand cloud-specific controls and CISM knowledge to manage security governance, risk, and organizational priorities.

Holding both credentials can demonstrate a combination of technical specialization and management expertise. However, professionals should consider their immediate career goals, experience, and available study time before pursuing multiple certifications.

Prepare for CCSP Certification with CCS Learning Academy
If your career goals involve cloud security architecture, cloud infrastructure protection, or cloud compliance, CCSP training may be a suitable next step.

CCS Learning Academy offers a Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP) Certification Prep Course designed to help IT and cybersecurity professionals study the certification domains and prepare for the examination.

The course provides structured training covering cloud concepts, data security, infrastructure security, application security, operations, and legal, risk, and compliance topics.

Explore the CCSP Certification Prep Course at CCS Learning Academy to review the curriculum and available enrollment options.

Conclusion
The choice between CCSP and CISM depends on your professional objectives. CCSP is a strong option for professionals who want to specialize in cloud security, while CISM is better aligned with information security governance, risk management, and leadership.

Both certifications can strengthen your professional profile when supported by relevant experience and continuous learning. Evaluate your current responsibilities and future career plans to determine which credential offers the most relevant knowledge for your next step in cybersecurity.

title: Controllable User Simulation
description:
arXiv:2605.11519v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Using offline datasets to evaluate conversational agents often fails to cover rare scenarios or to support testing new policies. This has motivated the use of controllable user simulators for targeted, counterfactual evaluation, typically implemented by prompting or fine-tuning large language models. In this work, we formalize controllable simulation as a causal inference problem. By bridging natural language evaluation with off-policy evaluation methodology, we show that the standard practice of training simulators via supervised fine-tuning on post-hoc trajectory labels yields a structurally biased model. Specifically, these labels are inextricably coupled to the data-generating behavior policy, injecting a look-ahead bias that breaks causal consistency. Furthermore, we prove that under policy shift this failure causes the variance of evaluation metrics to explode geometrically, a phenomenon we term controllability collapse. To restore causal consistency, we establish theoretical conditions for accurate simulation and propose practical training mitigations: a priori controls, step-wise dynamic controls, and direct policy-conditioned learning. Empirical evaluation confirms that while standard global controls distort conversational distributions and collapse behavioral diversity, our causally grounded simulators eliminate look-ahead bias, preserve natural variance, and exhibit robust zero-shot generalization to unseen agent behaviors.

title: Amazon RDS for Oracle Expands M8i and R8i Availability Across More AWS Regions
description:
Enterprise applications depend on reliable databases. Whether you're running ERP platforms, financial systems, customer applications, or reporting workloads, database infrastructure plays a major role in application performance.

AWS has announced expanded regional availability for M8i and R8i instances on Amazon RDS for Oracle.

This gives organizations more opportunities to run Oracle databases on newer-generation AWS infrastructure across additional geographic locations.

In this article, we'll explore:

  • What's new in Amazon RDS for Oracle.
  • The differences between M8i and R8i.
  • Why the regional expansion matters.
  • Oracle licensing considerations.
  • How to check instance availability using AWS CLI.
  • A practical enterprise database modernization scenario.

1. What's New?

According to the AWS announcement dated November 3, 2026, M8i and R8i support has expanded into additional AWS Regions.

AWS Region M8i R8i
Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Yes Yes
Canada West (Calgary) Yes Yes
Europe (Milan) — Yes
Europe (Stockholm) — Yes
Europe (Zurich) — Yes
Israel (Tel Aviv) — Yes

Both instance families are available in New Zealand and Calgary. The additional European and Israeli Regions receive R8i availability.

These instance families use custom Intel Xeon 6 processors.

AWS reports the following improvements compared with previous-generation Intel-based instances:

  • Up to 15% better price-performance.
  • Up to 2.5x more memory bandwidth.

These are AWS-reported figures. Actual performance improvements depend on workload characteristics and database configuration.

Official announcement: https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/rds-oracle-m8i-r8i-instances-new-regions/

2. Understanding M8i and R8i

Both instance families provide newer-generation compute infrastructure, but they target different workload requirements.

M8i: General-purpose instances

M8i instances provide a balanced combination of compute, memory, and networking resources.

Potential use cases:

  • Enterprise applications.
  • ERP and CRM platforms.
  • Transaction-processing workloads.
  • General-purpose Oracle databases.
  • Applications with balanced CPU and memory requirements.

M8i is worth evaluating when your database needs balanced infrastructure resources.

R8i: Memory-optimized instances

R8i instances are designed for workloads that benefit from higher memory capacity.

Potential use cases:

  • Large Oracle databases.
  • Memory-intensive queries.
  • Complex reporting workloads.
  • Applications with large working sets.
  • Databases that benefit from keeping frequently accessed data in memory.

For memory-intensive workloads, R8i provides another option to evaluate.

M8i vs. R8i

Feature M8i R8i
Instance category General purpose Memory optimized
Main focus Balanced resources Memory-intensive workloads
Suitable workloads Mixed enterprise workloads Large, memory-heavy databases
Selection criteria CPU and memory balance Memory requirements and workload behavior

The best choice depends on actual workload measurements, not simply the instance generation.

3. Why Does Regional Availability Matter?

Regional availability is an important consideration when designing enterprise cloud infrastructure.

Lower application latency opportunities

Organizations can evaluate database deployments closer to their application infrastructure and customers.

This can help reduce network latency when the database and application are deployed in suitable locations.

However, actual latency depends on network architecture, application placement, and connectivity.

More infrastructure flexibility

Database administrators can evaluate newer instance families in additional AWS Regions.

This is useful for organizations with regional workloads, data residency requirements, or geographically distributed applications.

Performance optimization

The reported memory bandwidth improvements may benefit workloads that frequently access memory.

Database teams can benchmark representative queries to determine whether a newer instance family improves performance.

Database modernization

Organizations running Oracle on Amazon RDS can investigate newer instance classes without necessarily migrating to another database engine.

This makes instance-family evaluation a potential part of an existing infrastructure optimization strategy.

4. Oracle Licensing Considerations

Licensing is particularly important when deploying Oracle databases.

The November 3 regional expansion announcement specifies availability under the Bring Your Own License (BYOL) model for:

  • Oracle Database Enterprise Edition (EE).
  • Oracle Database Standard Edition 2 (SE2).

The announced instance-size ranges include:

Oracle Edition Instance sizes
Enterprise Edition (BYOL) Large through 48xlarge, plus metal-48xl and metal-96xl
Standard Edition 2 (BYOL) Large through 4xlarge, plus metal-48xl and metal-96xl

AWS also separately announced M8i and R8i support for Oracle SE2 License Included in May 2026.

Do not assume that all licensing options have identical regional availability. Verify the exact Region, engine version, instance class, and licensing model before deployment.

Useful resources:

  • https://aws.amazon.com/rds/oracle/pricing/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/CHAP_Oracle.html

5. Hands-On: Check Instance Availability Using AWS CLI

Let's see how a cloud engineer can investigate available Oracle instance configurations.

Prerequisites

You need:

  • AWS CLI installed.
  • An AWS account.
  • Appropriate IAM permissions.
  • A supported Oracle engine version.
  • The target AWS Region.

Step 1: Configure AWS CLI 

aws configure

Enter your AWS credentials and default configuration when prompted.

Step 2: Check M8i availability

Let's investigate an M8i instance in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region.

aws rds describe-orderable-db-instance-options \
  --engine oracle-ee \
  --db-instance-class db.m8i.large \
  --region ap-southeast-6

Step 3: Check R8i availability

Now check an R8i instance in Europe (Milan).

aws rds describe-orderable-db-instance-options \
  --engine oracle-ee \
  --db-instance-class db.r8i.large \
  --region eu-south-1

Step 4: Display important configuration details

You can use the AWS CLI query option to make the output easier to understand.

aws rds describe-orderable-db-instance-options \
  --engine oracle-ee \
  --db-instance-class db.r8i.large \
  --region eu-south-1 \
  --query 'OrderableDBInstanceOptions[*].{
    Class:DBInstanceClass,
    EngineVersion:EngineVersion,
    LicenseModel:LicenseModel,
    StorageTypes:StorageType
  }' \
  --output table

This helps you investigate:

  • Available instance classes.
  • Supported Oracle engine versions.
  • Licensing models.
  • Storage types.

Important: These commands are examples. For a production deployment, validate the exact engine version, Oracle edition, licensing model, and instance size. You can also specify an engine version using --engine-version when checking a particular configuration.

An empty response does not necessarily mean the entire instance family is unavailable. The specific combination you requested may not be supported.

6. Practical Enterprise Scenario

Imagine an organization running an Oracle-based ERP application on Amazon RDS.

Its database supports:

  • Financial transactions.
  • Inventory management.
  • Customer records.
  • Business reporting.
  • Operational dashboards.

As the organization grows, reporting queries become slower and database resource utilization increases.

How can the database team evaluate M8i and R8i?

Step 1: Analyze database performance

Use Amazon CloudWatch and Oracle performance diagnostics to review:

  • CPU utilization.
  • Database load.
  • Memory pressure.
  • Query execution time.
  • Read/write latency.

Step 2: Identify the bottleneck

Determine whether the workload is primarily CPU-intensive, memory-intensive, or affected by another resource constraint.

Step 3: Evaluate instance families

Compare M8i for balanced workloads and R8i for memory-intensive workloads.

Step 4: Benchmark the application

Create a representative test environment and compare query performance and application response times.

Step 5: Plan production changes

Review backups, maintenance windows, Multi-AZ configuration, application connectivity, and rollback procedures.

The objective is to select infrastructure that delivers measurable performance and business benefits.

7. What Should You Check Before Upgrading?

Before modifying an existing Oracle database instance, consider these points:

  1. Regional availability: Confirm that the required instance class is supported.
  2. Oracle licensing: Validate your licensing entitlements.
  3. Engine compatibility: Check the supported Oracle edition and engine version.
  4. Performance testing: Benchmark representative workloads.
  5. Cost analysis: Compare On-Demand and Reserved Instance pricing.
  6. High availability: Review your Single-AZ or Multi-AZ configuration.
  7. Maintenance planning: Understand possible interruptions during modification.
  8. Monitoring: Track CPU, database connections, IOPS, latency, and database load after the change.

A newer instance family does not automatically guarantee better performance for every application. Always test before making production changes.

8. Final Thoughts

The expansion of M8i and R8i availability is useful news for organizations running Oracle databases on Amazon RDS.

It provides additional infrastructure options across Asia Pacific, Canada, Europe, and Israel.

M8i offers a general-purpose configuration, while R8i is designed for memory-intensive workloads. AWS reports up to 15% better price-performance and 2.5x more memory bandwidth compared with previous-generation Intel-based instances.

For cloud architects and database administrators, the next step is to evaluate these instance families against actual workload requirements, licensing constraints, regional availability, and cost.

My key takeaway: Choosing the right database infrastructure is not just about selecting the newest instance. It's about matching compute, memory, availability, and cost to your application's real requirements.

Let's Discuss

If you're running Oracle databases on AWS, which factor matters most when selecting a database instance?

  • CPU performance
  • Memory capacity and bandwidth
  • Regional availability
  • Cost optimization

Share your thoughts and experiences in the comments!

Official References

  1. AWS What's New – Amazon RDS for Oracle M8i and R8i regional expansion
  2. Amazon RDS for Oracle Documentation
  3. Amazon RDS for Oracle Instance Types
  4. Amazon RDS for Oracle Pricing

If you found this article useful, follow me for more practical AWS, cloud architecture, database engineering, and hands-on technical tutorials.

title: Wix has no wholesale mode: ten wholesale apps compared, and where mine falls short
description:
Wix Stores has one price per product. If a bakery, a candle maker or a wine shop wants trade customers to pay less than the public, there is no wholesale switch to flip. Wix's own workaround is a members-only store page with duplicated products at wholesale prices, and its article (Creating restricted store pages) also names one app, SparkLayer.

Full disclosure: I make one of the apps below, Wholesale Prices & B2B Groups. I describe it last, with its limits. Everything else comes from each app's Wix App Market page, read on 3 November 2026. Where a page didn't say something, I say "not stated" and don't guess.

What the free workaround costs you

The members-only page works for a small catalog: duplicate each product at its wholesale price, put the copies in a "Wholesale" category on a page set to site members, and approve new members manually. The cost is upkeep. Every price change, photo and description has to be made twice, and the page itself doesn't enforce a minimum order. If you have thirty products and two trade customers, that may be fine. At three hundred products it isn't.

The questions that sort the apps

A search for "wholesale" in the App Market returns dozens of results, but most are dropshipping, catalog or quote tools. Ten of them are close fits for giving approved buyers their own prices on a Wix Stores shop. Before you read the list, decide:

  1. How does a buyer become a trade customer? An application form you approve, a label or group you fill yourself, or a group you fill by email.
  2. Do you need case packs and minimum order quantities, or only a percentage off?
  3. Do you need quotes and a buyer portal, or just a price in the cart?
  4. How many trade buyers will you have? The free plans cap this differently.

What the listings say

App Reviews Price (as listed) Free plan Notes
SparkLayer B2B & Wholesale 5 (3.4) $49 to $299 a month by B2B order volume Not stated Price lists, B2B payments, sales agents, API on the top plan, 14-day trial
B2B Wholesale Forms 4 (5.0) From $7.50 a month Not stated Order, inquiry and account-application forms
B2B Wholesale Pricing 1 (5.0) $15.99 and $23.99 a month Not stated Applications and discounts; MOQs and case packs on the higher plan
ElevenTrade Wholesale & B2B 1 (5.0) Free; $19.99 a month 1 pricing group, unlimited customers Volume breaks and trade applications on the paid plan
Wholesale & B2B by Optexia none Free; paid plan shown as "$7 - 90" 1 rule, up to 10 customers Quantity tiers, minimum order, auto-approve on the paid plan
Wholesale Prices none Free; $7.99 a month Up to 5 approved buyers Application form, approve or decline
Wholesale Pro: B2B Pricing none $7.99 a month Not stated Application form, store, category or product discounts, minimums; 14-day trial
TradePortal: B2B Wholesale none Free; $12 and $25 a month Yes, limits not stated Tiered pricing, MOQ, case packs, quotes
B2B Wholesale Discounts none "$4 - 49" a month Not stated Customer groups, discounts saved as Wix automatic discounts
B2B Login To See Price none "$4 - 49" a month Not stated Hides prices and Add to Cart from guests only

Most of these are new, with zero or one review. That isn't a reason to skip them, but test each on your own store with a real trade login before you hand it to a customer.

How I'd pick

  • A few trade accounts, want to try for free: one of the free plans above.
  • Buyers should apply and be approved from your site: the apps that list an application form.
  • Case packs, MOQs and quotes: TradePortal and B2B Wholesale Pricing list them; neither page explains how prices show in checkout, so test an order.
  • A real B2B operation with a sales team: SparkLayer, priced for that.
  • Only hide prices until login: B2B Login To See Price.

Where mine fits, and where it doesn't

Full disclosure, I built Wholesale Prices & B2B Groups. You mark trade customers with a contact label such as "Wholesale". When they are logged in as site members, they get the group price in the cart and at checkout. A group has pricing lines: a percentage off the whole store, a collection or chosen products, or a fixed price per product, with an optional minimum order subtotal.

What it doesn't do:

  • No application form. You add the contact label yourself.
  • One discount per product. Wix applies one automatic discount per product, so a trade customer gets the best price on that product, not a stack. A coupon code they type comes off on top.
  • No quantity tiers, case packs or quotes.
  • Collections are capped at 500 products per group, and the price line on the product page works on sites built in the Wix Editor, not in product grids.
  • Free is one group with one store-wide percentage. Pro is $9.99 a month, or $7.99 billed yearly, with a 14-day trial.

If you need applications, packs or quotes, one of the apps above fits better.

The full side-by-side guide, with a checklist and FAQ: Wix wholesale and B2B apps compared.

title: Node2Shell: one Brotli decoder bug, three runtimes to patch (Node.js, Bun, Python)
description:
Brotli is the compression format your browser has probably used to load this page. It's fast, efficient and everywhere. It's also why one bug in one C decoder means patching Node.js, Bun, .NET, Python packages and even PHP's Windows builds this month.

The bug is CVE-2026-111497, nicknamed Node2Shell (also HTTP2Shell). Since 27 October it has been on CISA's list of vulnerabilities known to be exploited.

What happened

On 21 October 2026, Node.js shipped security releases fixing ten vulnerabilities. The headline one was an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder that Node.js bundles. Google, which maintains Brotli, released fixed versions of the library the same day. BleepingComputer reports the bug was found by researchers at OpenAI.

Severity depends on who you ask. Node.js rates it High, Google's CVE record gives 9.2 (CVSS 4.0), and NVD published 9.8 (CVSS 3.1) on 28 October.

Then it moved quickly:

  • 22–26 Oct: proofs of concept appear. Imperva's red team got code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image on Linux arm64, after multiple attempts. Other public PoCs only crashed the process or worked against deliberately weakened builds.
  • 26–27 Oct: honeypot operators log exploitation attempts. In at least one firm's tests the attack chain crashed the target rather than giving a shell.
  • 27 Oct: CISA adds CVE-2026-111497 to its KEV catalog, with a 10 November deadline for federal agencies. CISA didn't publish details of the attacks.

Why Brotli shows up everywhere

Brotli isn't just in Node. The same decoder code is used across ecosystems, so one bug became many advisories:

Platform Fixed in
Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1 (20.x and older, plus 23.x and 25.x, are end of life with no fix)
Bun 1.4.4
Brotli (C library) 1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1
Python brotli / brotlicffi 1.2.1 / 1.2.1.0
.NET 8.0.33, 9.0.22, 10.0.14
PHP (Windows builds) rebuilt as 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1, 8.2.35-1 with Brotli 1.2.1

Node.js bundles its own copy of Brotli. Upgrading the system library doesn't fix Node, so you have to upgrade the runtime itself. The same applies to Bun.

When are you actually exposed?

The flaw is only reachable when your process decompresses untrusted Brotli data. According to Imperva's and Rescana's analyses, that includes:

  • Express 5.0.0–5.3.0 and body-parser 2.0.0–2.3.0, when the json() or raw() parsers accept request bodies with Content-Encoding: br and decompress them automatically. That's the remote, unauthenticated path.
  • Node's built-in fetch() reading Brotli-compressed responses. If your server fetches URLs from users (webhooks, link previews, scrapers), a malicious server can send the payload back to you.
  • Python HTTP clients (requests, urllib3, aiohttp, httpx), which decode Brotli whenever a Brotli package is installed. No Python-specific code execution had been shown publicly at the time of writing, but the vulnerable decoder code is the same.
  • PHP's cURL extension, when automatic response decompression is enabled. It's off by default, but some client libraries turn it on, according to PHP's advisory.

Imperva notes that a bare Node.js HTTP server doesn't decode incoming Brotli bodies by itself. Exposure comes from the middleware and client code you run on top.

attacker → POST /api  (Content-Encoding: br, crafted body)
              └─ express.json() / body-parser decompresses automatically
                    └─ bundled Brotli decoder → out-of-bounds write
                          └─ crash (DoS) — or, in some builds, code execution

your server → fetch("https://attacker.example/...")
              └─ response is Content-Encoding: br → same decoder path

This is a simplified view of the reachable paths, not an exploit description.

What to do 

# Check the runtime that actually serves traffic, not just your laptop
node -v          # need 22.23.4+, 24.22.1+ or 26.12.1+
bun --version    # need 1.4.4+
pip show brotli brotlicffi 2>/dev/null | grep -E "Name|Version"

# Find Express / body-parser versions in your app
npm ls express body-parser
  1. Upgrade Node.js everywhere it runs: servers, Docker base images, CI runners, serverless runtimes and Electron-style apps that bundle Node.
  2. Leave end-of-life lines. If you're on Node 20, this fix doesn't exist for you. Node 26 became LTS on 28 October.
  3. Patch the other copies: Bun, Python's brotli and brotlicffi, .NET, and system Brotli libraries.
  4. If you can't upgrade today, stop decompressing untrusted Brotli. body-parser's inflate: false rejects encoded request bodies, and you can strip or reject Content-Encoding: br at your reverse proxy. A WAF rule is a stopgap and won't protect fetch() responses.
  5. Review logs for services that accepted compressed bodies before you patched, and look for unexplained worker crashes from around 21 October onwards.

What this teaches us

Your runtime is a dependency tree too. npm audit won't flag a bug in the C code compiled into node. Track runtime versions with the same discipline as packages, including the versions baked into images.

"Automatic" features grow your attack surface. Transparent decompression is convenient and almost nobody remembers it's switched on. Every parser that runs on untrusted input before your code sees it is part of your exposure.

One library, many advisories. Brotli, zlib, libwebp and others are copied or bundled into dozens of runtimes. When one breaks, you'll see a wave of advisories with different version numbers for the same bug.

What might happen next (analysis)

This is analysis, not reporting.

KEV listing usually means more scanning, so expect exploitation attempts against unpatched Express 5 APIs to rise over the coming weeks, especially against older Node lines that will never be fixed. Reliable code execution currently seems to depend on the platform and build, but crashing unpatched servers is already easy, and that alone makes it worth fixing. Expect more downstream advisories as vendors who bundle Brotli in appliances and desktop apps catch up.

Conclusion

Node2Shell isn't a JavaScript bug, a Python bug or a PHP bug. It's a shared C bug that every runtime inherited. If you remember one thing, make it this: upgrade the runtime, not just the packages, and know which of your services decompress data from strangers.

Your turn: do you know which Node.js version is running in your production containers right now, without checking?

References

  • Rescana, "CVE-2026-111497 (Node2Shell): Node.js Brotli RCE" (23 Oct 2026, updated 29 Oct): https://www.rescana.com/post/nodejs-cve-2026-111497-node2shell-brotli-rce-october-2026
  • BleepingComputer, "CISA warns of hackers now exploiting critical Node2Shell flaw": https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-hackers-now-exploiting-critical-node2shell-flaw
  • Sysdig, "Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497): detecting the Node.js Brotli RCE": https://www.sysdig.com/blog/node2shell-cve-2026-111497-detecting-the-node-js-brotli-rce
  • SOCRadar, "Node2Shell Brotli flaw hits Python packages": https://socradar.io/blog/node2shell-brotli-flaw-hits-python-packages/
  • PHP, "Updated PHP Windows builds for Brotli security fix" (26 Oct 2026): https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php
  • Sophos, "Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) in active exploitation": https://www.sophos.com/blog/node2shell-cve-2026-111497-in-active-exploitation

Part of The Wire, a daily brief on the tech and security news that matters to developers. Details are as reported up to 31 October 2026.

title: Building and composing with boxr: what works, and what is still slow
description:
I built boxr to stay rootless by default, with no always on daemon, and still feel familiar if you already use Docker or Podman commands. This article focuses on two everyday jobs: building an image from a Dockerfile, and running a small app with a Compose file. Both are where a new engine either earns trust or loses it.

What to try first: build a simple Dockerfile with boxr, then run it as your own user, with no sudo on the default path. Next, take a small Compose file with two services, bring it up, check the logs, and stop it. If you already run containers rootless, try the same files you use today and note where the behaviour differs.

What the project reports so far: the project test reports list the Compose suites as passing, and a cold Dockerfile build at about 332 milliseconds in the project Linux benchmarks. Those are project reported results, not a fresh independent rerun, and the next step is to rerun them at one pinned release, with repeats and variance, on a stated machine.

What is still slow, stated plainly: in those same project benchmarks, boxr was slower than Podman on cached builds, on single container startup, and on volume input and output. A merged startup latency improvement landed on main today, with a version bump to v0.1.71, but that change does not by itself close the gap, and it still needs a fresh benchmark at a pinned release before any new speed claim is made.

What to report back: which Dockerfile step behaved differently, which Compose feature worked or failed first, and what felt slow or unfamiliar. That feedback decides what gets fixed next, more than any headline result does.

title: React memo vs useMemo vs useCallback — When to Use Which
description:
React memo vs useMemo vs useCallback

All three are about skipping unnecessary work. But they work differently.

🧠 The Core Idea

React re-renders a component whenever its parent re-renders — even if nothing changed. Memoization lets you say:

"Only redo this if the inputs actually changed."

1️⃣ React.memo — Skip re-rendering a component

Wraps a component. Skips re-render if props didn't change.

const Button = React.memo(({ onClick, label }: { onClick: () => void; label: string }) => {
  console.log("Button rendered");
  return <button onClick={onClick}>{label}</button>;
});

Without memo: Button re-renders every time the parent does.

With memo: Button skips re-render if onClick and label are the same.

2️⃣ useMemo — Cache a computed value

Memoizes the result of an expensive calculation.

const total = useMemo(() => {
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0);
}, [items]);
  • Runs only when items changes.
  • Returns the cached value on other renders.

❌ Without useMemo: recalculates on every render.

✅ With useMemo: recalculates only when items changes.

3️⃣ useCallback — Cache a function

Memoizes a function reference so it stays stable across renders.

const handleClick = useCallback(() => {
  console.log("clicked", id);
}, [id]);

Without useCallback, a new function is created every render — which breaks React.memo on child components.

🔗 How They Work Together

React.memo compares props with ===. Functions and objects always fail === unless their reference is stable.

// ❌ Button re-renders every time — new function each render
<Button onClick={() => doSomething(id)} label="Click" />

// ✅ Button skips re-render — stable reference
const handleClick = useCallback(() => doSomething(id), [id]);
<Button onClick={handleClick} label="Click" />

Parent re-renders → Props compared (===)
  ├─ Same reference → memo skips re-render
  └─ New reference → memo re-renders child

⚠️ When NOT to Use Them

Memoization has a cost — it takes memory and adds complexity. Don't use it by default.

Situation Use memoization?
Cheap calculation ❌ Not worth it
Component renders rarely ❌ Skip it
Heavy computation (sort, filter on large arrays) ✅ Yes
Passing callbacks to memoized children ✅ Yes
Passing objects/arrays as props to memoized children ✅ Yes

🧪 Quick Example: All Three Together 

const ProductList = React.memo(({ items, onSelect }: Props) => {
  // useMemo: only recalculate when items change
  const total = useMemo(
    () => items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0),
    [items]
  );

  return (
    <div>
      <p>Total: ${total}</p>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <ProductCard key={item.id} item={item} onSelect={onSelect} />
      ))}
    </div>
  );
});

function App() {
  const [cart, setCart] = useState([]);

  // useCallback: stable reference so ProductList doesn't re-render
  const handleSelect = useCallback(
    (item) => setCart((prev) => [...prev, item]),
    []
  );

  return <ProductList items={products} onSelect={handleSelect} />;
}

✅ Summary

API Wraps Skips
React.memo Component Re-render when props unchanged
useMemo Computed value Recalculation when deps unchanged
useCallback Function Recreation when deps unchanged

✨ Final Takeaway

React.memo stops a component from re-rendering. useMemo stops a value from recalculating. useCallback stops a function from being recreated. Use them together — memo needs useCallback to actually work.

Originally published on Bitlyst.

title: You Have Been Offered Shares Instead of a Pay Rise
description:
Your review went well. Your manager says so, the feedback says so, and then comes the part you were waiting for. There is not much budget for salary increases this year, but they would like to give you a grant of shares instead. A lot of them, they add, and they could be worth far more than a raise one day. You smile and say thank you, and then on the way home you realise you have no idea whether that was a good offer.

It might be. It is worth understanding before you decide how you feel about it.

Start with what you are actually being given. Shares, options and restricted units are different things. With options, you usually have to pay a set price to buy the shares later, sometimes a large sum, and sometimes with a tax bill attached. Ask which kind it is, and ask for the documents rather than a summary.

Then ask how they vest. Most grants are released over several years, often with nothing at all until the first anniversary. If you leave after eighteen months, how much is really yours? And what happens to unvested shares if the company is sold?

Ask what the number means. Ten thousand shares tells you nothing on its own. What percentage of the company is that, and how many shares exist in total? Will more be issued when the company raises money, making yours a smaller slice?

Most important of all, ask how you would ever turn them into money. In a private company there may be no way to sell until a sale or a listing that may never come. Plenty of people have held shares for years that ended up worth nothing.

So value the offer at a discount, perhaps a steep one. A pay rise pays your rent this month and lifts every future raise built on top of it. Shares are a bet. A bet can be worth taking, but it should not quietly replace your salary year after year.

It is perfectly reasonable to ask for some of both. You can say, I appreciate the shares, and I would still like to talk about base pay. Is there anything possible there?

Whatever you decide, decide it with the numbers in front of you, not the story.

– Asael Shinder
