title: Redis Memory Full and Keys Evicted: A Java Backend Checklist of 4 Spots
description:
Wednesday afternoon, cache hit rate dropped from 98% to 62%, and database QPS quintupled. Ops checked around and said: Redis memory is maxed out, some keys were evicted, it's normal behavior. But the keys that got evicted happened to be login sessions, and users were collectively kicked offline. Memory full means eviction—sounds perfectly reasonable. The problem is which keys get evicted and why those. This article walks through Redis memory eviction from policy configuration down to kernel behavior, and throws in a set of monitoring code you can run directly.

I. What Exactly Is This Problem

Conclusion: Redis deleting keys after memory is maxed out is not a bug—it's the maxmemory-policy setting doing its job by the rules. Pick the wrong rule, and it won't delete what you wanted deleted.

Redis is an in-memory database—all data lives in memory. Give it a limit, and it won't eat memory indefinitely. That limit is called maxmemory. Whether writes can still go through once you hit the limit, and who gets deleted when they can't, all depends on maxmemory-policy.

Many teams, to "keep things simple" at launch, just copy a chunk of config:

maxmemory 8gb
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

allkeys-lru means: when memory runs short, pick the least recently accessed key from all keys and delete it. Note the word "all." Sessions, product cache, rate-limit counters, distributed locks, feature flags—all treated the same. As long as it's the least recently accessed, it gets killed first.

Config-type data suffers the most. Take a feature flag stored in Redis: once written, nobody reads it again. An hour later memory gets tight, and it's the first to go. Then the business logic reads a null value, falls through to the default branch, and the feature quietly turns off—with no error whatsoever.

Redis supports 8 eviction policies in total. The difference comes down to two things: which pool to pick from and by what rule to pick.

PolicyCandidate ScopeSelection RulenoevictionNo evictionWrites return an errorallkeys-lruAll keysLeast recently accessedallkeys-lfuAll keysLowest access frequencyallkeys-randomAll keysRandomvolatile-lruKeys with TTL setLeast recently accessedvolatile-lfuKeys with TTL setLowest access frequencyvolatile-randomKeys with TTL setRandomvolatile-ttlKeys with TTL setShortest remaining TTL

The difference between allkeys-* and volatile-* is fatal. The former deletes your permanent config right along with everything else; the latter only touches data you explicitly marked as "expirable."

There's one more easily overlooked point: the default policy is noeviction. Instances that never configured maxmemory-policy won't delete anything when memory fills up—all write commands return OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'. Reads work fine; writes all fail. Some people treat this as "Redis is stuck," when in reality it's explicitly rejecting you.

To determine whether an instance has ever evicted anything, one metric is enough:

redis-cli info stats | grep evicted_keys

This number is the cumulative count of keys evicted since process start—it only goes up. It's a cumulative value, not a current value. It resets to zero on restart, so don't use it for business analytics. What you actually need to watch is its rate of growth—tens of thousands in half an hour means memory is under sustained pressure, not an occasional blip.

II. What's Really Happening Under the Hood

Conclusion: Redis's memory limit is "effective memory," not "physical memory"; eviction is a check performed before each command execution; LRU is sampled estimation, not exact ordering.

Where Memory Actually Goes

There are a few key fields in INFO memory, and many people only look at the first one:

  • used_memory: data memory as counted by Redis itself, including the data and the overhead of structures managing that data
  • used_memory_rss: actual process usage as seen by the OS, including memory fragmentation
  • used_memory_dataset: pure data portion, minus management overhead
  • mem_fragmentation_ratio: used_memory_rss / used_memory

A concrete example. You store 1 million string keys, each key averaging 20 bytes and each value averaging 80 bytes—the data itself is roughly 100MB. But Redis attaches a dictEntry and a redisObject to every key, plus jemalloc's fixed-size-bin allocation leaves holes. Actual used_memory often lands around 150MB—50% inflation is normal.

So for the question "My data is only 100MB, why is 8G of memory full?"—the answer usually lies in four areas: management overhead, big keys, replication buffers, and client output buffers—not the data itself.

Also watch the fragmentation ratio:

  • mem_fragmentation_ratio between 1.0 and 1.5: normal
  • Greater than 1.8: severe fragmentation, consider enabling activedefrag
  • Less than 1: some memory has been swapped out, and performance will fall off a cliff

Eviction Happens Before Command Execution

Redis processes commands single-threaded (referring to the main command execution thread). For every command that might increase memory—SET, LPUSH, HSET—before execution it checks once: has current used_memory exceeded maxmemory?

Once it exceeds the limit, it enters the eviction process, deleting keys in a loop until it drops below the limit or can't delete any more. This loop has a cap; it won't delete indefinitely, avoiding a single command getting stuck for too long.

The key point is here: this check is triggered per command, not by a background scheduled job. That is, if there are no writes for a while, memory can exceed the limit without being cleaned up. Conversely, a large batch-write script may repeatedly trigger eviction during execution.

LRU is sampling, not sorting

Textbook LRU maintains a full access linked list, which is costly in both memory and CPU. Redis doesn't do that.

It records a 24-bit timestamp for each key (the lru field, reusing space in redisObject). When evicting, it randomly samples maxmemory-samples keys, 5 by default, and deletes the least recently accessed among those 5.

Sampling 5 is obviously not accurate. But Redis compensates in two ways:

  1. Maintain a 16-element candidate pool (pool), compare each sample against the pool, and keep the "older" ones
  2. Eviction is continuous; if one pass isn't accurate, a few more rounds will make it accurate

Set maxmemory-samples to 10 and accuracy approaches true LRU, at the cost of a bit more CPU per eviction. In production, choose between 5 and 10; don't set it too high.

LFU is a different mechanism. It gives each key an 8-bit counter; each access increments it probabilistically, while decaying keys that haven't been accessed for a long time (lfu-decay-time, default 1 minute). The 8-bit max is 255, and it uses logarithmic growth, so the first few accesses increase quickly and later ones increase slowly.

LFU suits scenarios where "hot spots are stable," such as homepage recommendation slots. LRU suits scenarios where "hot spots drift," such as breaking news. Choosing the wrong one won't crash anything, but hit rate will be noticeably worse.

The nastiest case with volatile policies

Suppose you set the policy to volatile-lru, and in your business code a batch of keys is missing an expiration time.

When memory is full, Redis looks for "keys with a TTL" to evict. If it finds them, it evicts normally. What if it can't find any?

The answer is: it treats that as nothing to evict, and write commands directly return an OOM error.

This is exactly the root cause of many cases where "volatile-lru is set but writes still fail." The policy isn't wrong; the data doesn't meet the policy's precondition. The volatile-* family has a hard precondition: every key that should be eligible for eviction must have a TTL.

Deleting a big key can block the main thread

Evicting a key isn't just removing it from the dictionary; it also has to free the memory it occupies. If the key is a Hash with 5 million elements, freeing it can take tens of milliseconds.

Redis 4.0 and later provides asynchronous freeing:

lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes

Once enabled, eviction only performs a logical delete, and the actual memory freeing is handed off to a background thread. The cost is that memory reclamation is delayed, and used_memory will briefly be higher than the actual value.

Large keys should be split up in the first place. A single value over 10KB is a warning sign, and over 1MB is basically a design problem. Use MEMORY USAGE key to see the actual usage of a single key, and redis-cli --bigkeys to scan the entire database.

Eviction under primary-replica architecture

Only the primary node makes eviction decisions. After the primary deletes a key, it generates a DEL command and syncs it to the replicas.

Replicas do not evict on their own. So if a replica's maxmemory is set the same as the primary's, the replica's memory may exceed the limit. This is also why replicas are usually recommended to be configured with maxmemory-policy noeviction, so they are only responsible for copying the primary's delete actions and do not make decisions themselves.

What should maxmemory be set to

Do not set it to 100% of physical memory.

There are several areas that must be left room for:

  • Replication buffer (repl-backlog, 1MB by default, but it can spike during a full sync)
  • AOF rewrite buffer
  • Client output buffer (Redis 7 and later has maxmemory-clients to limit it separately)

Rule of thumb: set maxmemory to 60%–75% of physical memory. If the machine runs only Redis, 75%; if it is co-located with other services, 60% or even lower. The remaining space will also be consumed in no small part by the child process forked during BGSAVE doing copy-on-write.

3. Hands-on: build an observable cache step by step

Conclusion: data such as sessions must go through volatile-lru + enforced TTL, and there must be code-level eviction monitoring, so you do not have to wait until users are logged out to discover the problem.

The project below is called redis-memory-guard and contains three things: a session cache with TTL, a monitoring component that collects Redis memory metrics every 30 seconds, and an endpoint that exposes the metrics.

Project structure 

redis-memory-guard
├── docker-compose.yml
├── pom.xml
└── src/main
    ├── java/com/example/redisguard
    │   ├── RedisMemoryGuardApplication.java
    │   ├── monitor
    │   │   ├── RedisMemoryMonitor.java
    │   │   ├── RedisMemorySnapshot.java
    │   │   └── RedisMonitorController.java
    │   └── session
    │       ├── SessionCacheService.java
    │       └── SessionController.java
    └── resources/application.yml

Start a deliberately misconfigured Redis

First, start an instance with the kind of wrong configuration you are preparing to troubleshoot: a 128MB limit, allkeys-lru, to make it easy to reproduce the problem.

services:
  redis:
    image: redis:8
    container_name: redis-eviction-demo
    command:
      - redis-server
      - --maxmemory
      - 128mb
      - --maxmemory-policy
      - allkeys-lru
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"

Start it:

docker compose up -d

pom.xml 

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
​
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>4.1.2</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>
​
    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>redis-memory-guard</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    <name>redis-memory-guard</name>
    <description>Redis 内存淘汰监控示例</description>
​
    <properties>
        <java.version>21</java.version>
    </properties>
​
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
            <version>4.1.2</version>
        </dependency>
​
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis</artifactId>
            <version>4.1.2</version>
        </dependency>
​
        <!-- Lettuce 连接池需要，不引这个 pool 配置不生效 -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.apache.commons</groupId>
            <artifactId>commons-pool2</artifactId>
            <version>2.13.1</version>
        </dependency>
​
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
            <version>4.1.2</version>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
​
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>4.1.2</version>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

Note the commons-pool2 line. Many people write connection pool parameters in application.yml and find they don't take effect—this dependency is missing. Lettuce uses its own connection pool implementation, and Spring Boot only enables pooling configuration when commons-pool2 is present on the classpath.

application.yml 

server:
  port: 8080
​
spring:
  application:
    name: redis-memory-guard
  data:
    redis:
      host: 127.0.0.1
      port: 6379
      database: 0
      timeout: 2s
      lettuce:
        pool:
          enabled: true
          max-active: 16
          max-idle: 8
          min-idle: 2
          max-wait: 1s

timeout: 2s is the command timeout, not the connection timeout. The default is no timeout, and a slow command can hang a request thread indefinitely, so always set it explicitly in production.

Main Class 

package com.example.redisguard;
​
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.EnableScheduling;
​
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableScheduling
public class RedisMemoryGuardApplication {
​
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(RedisMemoryGuardApplication.class, args);
    }
}

@EnableScheduling is used by the monitoring component's scheduled task. If you miss it, the @Scheduled method will never execute, not a single log line will appear, and you'll think the monitoring code is wrong.

Session Cache Service 

package com.example.redisguard.session;
​
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
​
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
​
@Service
public class SessionCacheService {
​
    private static final String KEY_PREFIX = "session:";
    private static final Duration TTL = Duration.ofMinutes(30);
​
    private final StringRedisTemplate redisTemplate;
​
    public SessionCacheService(StringRedisTemplate redisTemplate) {
        this.redisTemplate = redisTemplate;
    }
​
    public void save(String sessionId, String userId, String nickname) {
        String key = KEY_PREFIX + sessionId;
​
        Map<String, String> data = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        data.put("userId", userId);
        data.put("nickname", nickname);
        data.put("loginAt", String.valueOf(System.currentTimeMillis()));
​
        redisTemplate.opsForHash().putAll(key, data);
        // putAll 不会带过期时间，TTL 必须单独设置
        redisTemplate.expire(key, TTL);
    }
​
    public Map<String, String> find(String sessionId) {
        String key = KEY_PREFIX + sessionId;
​
        Map<Object, Object> raw = redisTemplate.opsForHash().entries(key);
        if (raw.isEmpty()) {
            return Map.of();
        }
​
        Map<String, String> result = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        raw.forEach((field, value) -> result.put(String.valueOf(field), String.valueOf(value)));
​
        // 每次读都续期，做成滑动过期
        redisTemplate.expire(key, TTL);
        return result;
    }
​
    public void remove(String sessionId) {
        redisTemplate.delete(KEY_PREFIX + sessionId);
    }
​
    public long ttlSeconds(String sessionId) {
        Long ttl = redisTemplate.getExpire(KEY_PREFIX + sessionId, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        return ttl == null ? -2L : ttl;
    }
}

Two details are worth mentioning.

After putAll, calling expire separately is required. Redis's HSET command itself does not include an expiration time, and Spring Data Redis does not fold TTL into the putAll wrapper. If you miss this line, the key becomes permanent, and permanent keys are never evicted under volatile-lru—the cache only grows and never shrinks.

The renewal in find is sliding expiration: each access resets the 30-minute window. It suits sessions where the user stays active. If what you want is "must re-authenticate 30 minutes after login," then don't renew; use absolute expiration.

Session Endpoint 

package com.example.redisguard.session;
​
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.DeleteMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
​
import java.util.Map;
​
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/session")
public class SessionController {
​
    private final SessionCacheService sessionCacheService;
​
    public SessionController(SessionCacheService sessionCacheService) {
        this.sessionCacheService = sessionCacheService;
    }
​
    @PostMapping("/{sessionId}")
    public Map<String, Object> create(@PathVariable String sessionId,
                                      @RequestParam String userId,
                                      @RequestParam String nickname) {
        sessionCacheService.save(sessionId, userId, nickname);
        return Map.of(
                "sessionId", sessionId,
                "ttlSeconds", sessionCacheService.ttlSeconds(sessionId)
        );
    }
​
    @GetMapping("/{sessionId}")
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> get(@PathVariable String sessionId) {
        Map<String, String> session = sessionCacheService.find(sessionId);
        if (session.isEmpty()) {
            return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
        }
        return ResponseEntity.ok(session);
    }
​
    @DeleteMapping("/{sessionId}")
    public Map<String, Object> remove(@PathVariable String sessionId) {
        sessionCacheService.remove(sessionId);
        return Map.of("deleted", true);
    }
}

Memory Snapshot 

package com.example.redisguard.monitor;
​
public record RedisMemorySnapshot(long usedMemory,
                                  long usedMemoryRss,
                                  long maxMemory,
                                  long evictedKeys,
                                  long evictedDelta,
                                  String policy) {
​
    public static RedisMemorySnapshot empty() {
        return new RedisMemorySnapshot(0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, "unknown");
    }
​
    public double usedRatio() {
        if (maxMemory <= 0L) {
            return 0d;
        }
        return (double) usedMemory / maxMemory;
    }
​
    public double fragmentationRatio() {
        if (usedMemory <= 0L) {
            return 0d;
        }
        return (double) usedMemoryRss / usedMemory;
    }
​
    public String usedMemoryHuman() {
        return human(usedMemory);
    }
​
    public String maxMemoryHuman() {
        return maxMemory <= 0L ? "未设置" : human(maxMemory);
    }
​
    private static String human(long bytes) {
        if (bytes < 1024L) {
            return bytes + "B";
        }
        double kb = bytes / 1024.0;
        if (kb < 1024.0) {
            return String.format("%.1fKB", kb);
        }
        double mb = kb / 1024.0;
        if (mb < 1024.0) {
            return String.format("%.1fMB", mb);
        }
        return String.format("%.2fGB", mb / 1024.0);
    }
}

This is a record with immutable fields, suitable for passing between the monitoring thread and HTTP threads. evictedDelta is the "number of evictions added this round," which is much more useful than a cumulative value—a cumulative value only proves that "something was deleted," while a delta tells you that "deletions are happening now."

Monitoring Collection 

package com.example.redisguard.monitor;
​
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.data.redis.connection.RedisConnection;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.RedisCallback;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.Scheduled;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
​
import java.util.Properties;
​
@Component
public class RedisMemoryMonitor {
​
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(RedisMemoryMonitor.class);
​
    private final StringRedisTemplate redisTemplate;
​
    private volatile RedisMemorySnapshot latest = RedisMemorySnapshot.empty();
    private volatile long lastEvictedKeys = -1L;
​
    public RedisMemoryMonitor(StringRedisTemplate redisTemplate) {
        this.redisTemplate = redisTemplate;
    }
​
    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 30_000L)
    public void collect() {
        RedisMemorySnapshot snapshot = redisTemplate.execute(
                (RedisCallback<RedisMemorySnapshot>) this::read);
​
        if (snapshot == null) {
            log.warn("读取 Redis INFO 失败，本次采集跳过");
            return;
        }
​
        latest = snapshot;
​
        if (snapshot.evictedDelta() > 0L) {
            log.warn("Redis 正在淘汰 key：本轮新增 {} 个，策略 {}，已用 {} / 上限 {}，碎片率 {}",
                    snapshot.evictedDelta(),
                    snapshot.policy(),
                    snapshot.usedMemoryHuman(),
                    snapshot.maxMemoryHuman(),
                    String.format("%.2f", snapshot.fragmentationRatio()));
        }
    }
​
    private RedisMemorySnapshot read(RedisConnection connection) {
        Properties memory = connection.serverCommands().info("memory");
        Properties stats = connection.serverCommands().info("stats");
        if (memory == null || stats == null) {
            return null;
        }
​
        long used = parseLong(memory.getProperty("used_memory"));
        long rss = parseLong(memory.getProperty("used_memory_rss"));
        long max = parseLong(memory.getProperty("maxmemory"));
        long evicted = parseLong(stats.getProperty("evicted_keys"));
        String policy = memory.getProperty("maxmemory_policy", "unknown");
​
        long delta;
        if (lastEvictedKeys < 0L) {
            delta = 0L;
        } else if (evicted < lastEvictedKeys) {
            // Redis 重启过，计数归零，这一轮整体当作新增
            delta = evicted;
        } else {
            delta = evicted - lastEvictedKeys;
        }
        lastEvictedKeys = evicted;
​
        return new RedisMemorySnapshot(used, rss, max, evicted, delta, policy);
    }
​
    private long parseLong(String value) {
        if (value == null || value.isBlank()) {
            return 0L;
        }
        try {
            return Long.parseLong(value.trim());
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            return 0L;
        }
    }
​
    public RedisMemorySnapshot latest() {
        return latest;
    }
}

What this code does is simple: every 30 seconds it sends two INFO commands over the Redis protocol and parses the text results into a struct. Using RedisCallback instead of creating a new Jedis connection is to reuse Spring's connection pool and timeout configuration, and to route issues through unified exception handling.

serverCommands().info("memory") returns Properties, and the key names are exactly the field names in the INFO output, all lowercase with underscores. evicted_keys is only in INFO stats, so don't look for it in the memory section.

Metrics Endpoint 

package com.example.redisguard.monitor;
​
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
​
import java.util.Map;
​
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/admin/redis")
public class RedisMonitorController {
​
    private final RedisMemoryMonitor redisMemoryMonitor;
​
    public RedisMonitorController(RedisMemoryMonitor redisMemoryMonitor) {
        this.redisMemoryMonitor = redisMemoryMonitor;
    }
​
    @GetMapping("/memory")
    public Map<String, Object> memory() {
        RedisMemorySnapshot snapshot = redisMemoryMonitor.latest();
        return Map.of(
                "usedMemory", snapshot.usedMemoryHuman(),
                "maxMemory", snapshot.maxMemoryHuman(),
                "usedRatio", String.format("%.2f%%", snapshot.usedRatio() * 100),
                "fragmentationRatio", String.format("%.2f", snapshot.fragmentationRatio()),
                "policy", snapshot.policy(),
                "evictedKeysTotal", snapshot.evictedKeys(),
                "evictedKeysLastRound", snapshot.evictedDelta()
        );
    }
}

Run and Verify 

mvn spring-boot:run

Write a session:

curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/session/s-1001?userId=1001&nickname=lvdongbin"

Returns:

{"sessionId":"s-1001","ttlSeconds":1799}

Read it back:

curl "http://localhost:8080/session/s-1001"

{"userId":"1001","nickname":"lvdongbin","loginAt":"1792934400000"}

Check monitoring:

curl "http://localhost:8080/admin/redis/memory"

{"usedMemory":"1.2MB","maxMemory":"128.0MB","usedRatio":"0.94%","fragmentationRatio":"1.08","policy":"allkeys-lru","evictedKeysTotal":0,"evictedKeysLastRound":0}

To trigger eviction, just flood Redis with data:

docker exec redis-eviction-demo redis-benchmark -n 200000 -r 200000 -d 2048 -t set -q

This command uses Redis's built-in benchmarking tool to write 200,000 random keys, each value around 2KB, which can easily fill up 128MB. Once you push past the limit, check /admin/redis/memory again; evictedKeysLastRound will no longer be 0, and warnings about Redis 正在淘汰 key will also appear in the logs.

The value of this code is not in the monitoring itself, but in turning "eviction is happening" into a number you can receive a signal from. A drop in cache hit rate is lagging; the eviction count is real-time.

4. Pitfalls and Best Practices

Conclusion: 80% of Redis memory problems come from two things: "keys without TTL" and "maxmemory set too high."

Pitfall 1: HSET, LPUSH and then forgetting EXPIRE

Redis expiration is attached to the key, not to fields. If you keep adding fields to a Hash, the key's own TTL will not be reset by writes, nor will it be created automatically.

A real case: a project's user profile cache used opsForHash().putAll(key, map) in the code and never set an expiration. Three months after launch, this Hash had grown to more than 20 million keys and filled the entire instance. When the memory alarm went off, the first things killed by allkeys-lru were login sessions.

The fix is not to add memory, but to add one line, expire, where the write happens. For every method that writes to cache, TTL must be a required parameter and must not have a default value.

Pitfall 2: maxmemory set to 100% of physical memory

What happens when it fills up? used_memory indeed won't exceed the limit, but used_memory_rss will. The child process forked during BGSAVE performs copy-on-write and needs extra physical memory. Linux's OOM Killer will kill the Redis process, leaving a Killed in the logs, with no Redis error message of its own.

More insidious is swap. When physical memory is insufficient, the system swaps Redis pages to disk, and mem_fragmentation_ratio will drop below 1. At this point Redis can still run, but every access to cold data is disk I/O, and latency goes from 0.2 ms to 20 ms. Monitoring shows no errors, and it just feels like "Redis has gotten slower."

Pitfall 3: Looking only at used_memory, not at used_memory_rss

Redis freed 1GB of data, and used_memory drops immediately, but used_memory_rss does not necessarily drop. jemalloc does not always return memory to the operating system.

This does not count as a leak. As long as the fragmentation rate stays within 1.5, there is no need to worry about it. But if used_memory_rss keeps rising while used_memory does not increase, then it is real fragmentation. Enable activedefrag yes, or find an off-peak period and restart once.

Pitfall 4:volatile-lru configured with a bunch of keys without TTL

We covered the mechanism earlier; now let's look at the symptom. It goes like this: memory isn't full, yet write commands return OOM command not allowed. Ops takes one look at maxmemory, sees there's still headroom, and is completely baffled.

One command to troubleshoot:

redis-cli info keyspace

The output has two key columns per db: the total count keys and the number of keys with a TTL expires. If expires is 0 or far smaller than keys, then the volatile-* policy is basically equivalent to noeviction.

Best practices checklist:

  • Always use allkeys-lru for cache data, and give every key a TTL — belt and suspenders
  • When co-locating cache with "data that must not be lost," use volatile-lru, and also run a script periodically to scan for keys without a TTL
  • Put sessions, verification codes, and rate-limit counters in a separate instance or a separate db — don't let them compete with business cache for memory
  • With maxmemory, leave at least 25% of physical memory for fork, replication buffers, and client buffers
  • Enable lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes to avoid blocking the main thread when deleting large keys
  • Wire the growth rate of evicted_keys into alerting, with thresholds set per workload — for example, alert if more than 1000 are added within 5 minutes

The most critical item on the list is this one. The vast majority of Redis memory incidents are not due to a lack of monitoring, but because monitoring only looks at memory usage and not eviction rate.

V. Performance Comparison and Technology Selection

Conclusion: The CPU overhead differences between eviction policies are very small. The key to selection is "whether the data can be lost," not "which one is faster."

Comparison of eviction overhead across different policies:

PolicyExtra overhead per evictionHit rate performanceUse casenoevictionNone (directly rejects writes)Not applicableStoring data that cannot be lost, such as queues and configurationsallkeys-lruSamples 5 keys and compares timestampsGood for hotspot drift scenariosPure cache instancesallkeys-lfuSampling + counter comparisonBetter for stable hotspot scenariosRecommendation slots, leaderboardsallkeys-randomAlmost zeroWorst, not recommendedAlmost never usedvolatile-lruSame as allkeys-lruDepends on TTL coverageMixed deployment of cache and persistent datavolatile-ttlCompares remaining TTLModerateScenarios with clear time-based eviction

A few empirically measured rules of thumb:

maxmemory-samples Adjusting from 5 to 10 improves the hit rate by about 1~3 percentage points, while CPU overhead increases by less than 1%. It is worth tuning.

lazyfree-lazy-eviction Once enabled, the latency of evicting large keys drops from tens of milliseconds to the microsecond level, at the cost of delayed memory reclamation by a few seconds. It is recommended to enable it in high-concurrency write scenarios.

activedefrag Continuously consumes CPU (by default occupying one background thread). Do not enable it when the fragmentation rate is below 1.5.

For the decision order in technology selection, I suggest the following:

  1. Would losing this data cause a business failure? If yes → noeviction, use a separate instance.
  2. If not, but it is mixed with other data in the same instance? → volatile-lru, force all cache keys to have a TTL.
  3. Is the entire instance used as cache? → allkeys-lru, simple and direct.

Do not choose LFU just to be "more precise." The counter decay parameter in LFU is very difficult to tune. If it is not tuned well, "new hotspots can never get in" because the counters of old keys are too high. Unless you have a clear judgment that hotspots are stable, LRU is more reliable.

VI. Summary

Deleting keys after Redis memory is full is designed behavior, not a failure. The real questions to ask are three: which batch of keys is being deleted, why them, and will critical data be deleted next time.

maxmemory-policy determines the candidate pool. allkeys-* deletes permanent data along with everything else, while volatile-* only touches keys that have a TTL. Choosing volatile-* without setting a TTL on your keys turns the instance into noeviction, and every write request returns an error.

Don't push maxmemory all the way to your physical memory limit. Leave at least 25% for fork, replication buffers, and client buffers; otherwise the OOM killer will make a much harsher decision for you at some ungodly hour.

For monitoring, used_memory only tells you "almost full," while the growth rate of evicted_keys tells you "eviction has already started." Wiring the latter into your alerts is far more useful than staring at memory usage.

At the code level, a TTL should be a required field when writing to the cache, not an optional one. Only if you hold this line does volatile-lru mean anything.

  • INFO - Redis Docs
  • MEMORY USAGE - Redis Docs

title: How can non-engineers ship frontend changes as pull requests?
description:
Originally published on butterneck.com.

Short answer: have the non-engineer make and check the change on a live preview first, then let a developer turn the result into the pull request. The PR stays a code review step owned by someone who can read code. The non-engineer's job is to confirm the change looks and reads right before that PR exists.

Why not let them open the PR directly?

Some tools do open a PR for a PM or designer. That can work. But a PR is a poor place to iterate on small visual tweaks, and someone still has to own the code it contains. See AI PRs need an owner.

A workflow that works

  1. A developer connects a computer where the app already runs.
  2. The designer, PM or support lead opens a share link to the running app and types the change: "make this button say Start free", "move the price above the fold".
  3. The team's own coding agent edits the project on that computer. The preview updates on the same link.
  4. They check it and ask for tweaks until it's right.
  5. The developer reviews the diff in their own tools, then commits and opens the pull request. From there it goes through normal review and deploy.

This is how Butterneck works. Butterneck itself does not commit, push or open the pull request; the developer does.

See it before you set anything up: create a free account and try a request on a sample shop before connecting a computer. On your own project, the edit runs on your computer. Your team still decides what goes live.

What makes this go smoothly

  • Agree on which changes are in scope (copy, layout, styling, small fields). Our pilot proposal helps.
  • Read why a live preview before the pull request helps reviewers.
  • For other tools that do open PRs for non-developers, see AI tools that let non-developers change an existing web app.

FAQ

Can a designer open the pull request themselves?

They can if your Git setup allows it, but with Butterneck the developer opens it after reviewing the change. Butterneck doesn't open PRs.

Does the code have to be on GitHub?

No. Butterneck works on a project folder that runs on the developer's computer. Where the PR goes is up to your team.

Is there a free plan?

Yes. Starter is free for one developer and one requester. Pro is USD 19 per person per month. See pricing.

title: Tiny icons as data URIs — skip another network hop for chrome assets
description:
Chrome UI is full of tiny assets that should never fight the critical path: a 16×16 chevron, a mute glyph, a spinner frame, a toolbar mark that shows up before the rest of the page finishes deciding who you are.

I still see those shipped as separate /icons/*.svg or /icons/*.png requests. On a good day they ride HTTP/2 multiplexing and you barely notice. On a cold CDN edge, a flaky hotel Wi‑Fi, or a settings drawer that mounts before the icon sprite is warm, you get the classic flash of empty boxes.

For chrome icons — not hero art, not user avatars — I default to inlining as data URIs more often than I used to.

What I mean by "chrome assets"

Not the marketing hero. Not a product screenshot. The boring bits that make the shell feel finished:

  • Sidebar / toolbar glyphs under ~2–4 KB each
  • Empty-state illustrations that are basically icons with padding
  • Status dots and badges that are vector or tiny PNG
  • Favicon-sized marks reused inside the app chrome

If an asset is decorative, tiny, and shown before meaningful paint, a network hop is a tax. If it's large, user-generated, or rarely shown, leave it as a normal URL.

The network hop you forget about

A separate icon URL costs more than bytes:

  1. Priority / queue — competes with CSS, fonts, and your first API call
  2. Cache miss on first visit — every new deploy with hashed filenames resets the miss
  3. CORS / CSP footguns — SVG-as-<img> vs inline SVG vs background-image all behave differently
  4. Layout flash — width/height reserved late → CLS or empty toolbar buttons

Data URIs don't magically shrink bytes (base64 costs ~33%), but they remove a round trip and make the asset travel with the CSS/JS that needs it. For a 600-byte SVG that's often the right trade.

When data URIs win (and when they don't)

Prefer data URI when:

  • The icon is ≤ ~2–3 KB uncompressed (SVG preferred)
  • It appears in first paint / shell / authenticated chrome
  • You're already shipping a CSS or JS module that owns that surface
  • You don't need the browser to cache the same glyph across many unrelated pages independently

Prefer a normal URL (or sprite) when:

  • The asset is large or shared across many independent entry points
  • You need CDN edge caching and long-lived immutable URLs
  • Design iterates the icon weekly and you don't want CSS churn
  • You're shipping dozens of icons and a sprite / icon font / SVG sprite sheet is cleaner

I don't inline a 40 KB illustration. I do inline the 800-byte "copy" glyph next to every code block toolbar.

A workflow that doesn't fight the design handoff

Design still exports PNG/SVG. Engineering still needs a string you can paste into CSS:

.toolbar-copy {
  background-image: url("data:image/svg+xml,...");
  background-size: 16px 16px;
}

or:

const COPY_ICON =
  "data:image/svg+xml," + encodeURIComponent(`<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" ...>...</svg>`);

The friction is converting the export into a safe data URI without opening three tabs and hoping the encoder didn't mangle # / quotes.

Checklist I use:

  1. Prefer SVG over PNG when the mark is flat UI chrome
  2. Strip editor junk (id, unused defs, Illustrator cruft) before encoding
  3. Prefer encodeURIComponent for SVG (not base64) so the string stays readable in diffs
  4. Cap size — if the data URI is longer than the component that uses it, reconsider
  5. Keep width/height in CSS so you don't rely on intrinsic size for layout

Converting without another upload site

I don't want to POST a brand mark to a random "image to base64" site just to get a data: string. Same Offline litmus as other one-off transforms: if convert dies with DevTools Offline, it wasn't local enough for me.

When I need a quick tab for this, I've used Uwarp's image → data URI tool — drop the icon, get a data URI, paste into CSS/JS. Worth trying when the alternative is a desktop converter or an upload encoder you can't audit.

Roll your own if this is daily: a tiny Node script with fs.readFileSync + encodeURIComponent is fine. The point is the habit (inline tiny chrome) more than the tool.

Don't turn this into a religion

A few failure modes I hit:

  • Inlining everything → CSS balloons; first paint gets worse, not better
  • Base64 PNG for every glyph → you paid the 33% tax and still ship raster blur on retina
  • Inlining user avatars → privacy + size disaster; never do this
  • Forgetting dark mode → one data URI, one color; prefer currentColor SVG or dual tokens

Rule of thumb: if I can't justify the icon as "shell chrome under a few KB," it stays a URL.

Tiny habit

Next time you add a toolbar button and reach for /assets/icons/copy.svg, ask: is this a critical-path chrome glyph? If yes, inline it as a data URI (SVG + encodeURIComponent preferred). If no, leave the network hop alone.

Fewer empty boxes on first paint. Fewer "why is the mute icon late?" threads. Same design file — just a better shipping shape for the tiny stuff.

title: How to Plan a Small Brochure Website: Pages, Content and Launch
description:
A small brochure website has a simple job: help a visitor understand who you are, what you offer and how to reach you. It can be a single page with clear sections or a small collection of pages. The right choice depends on the services and questions you need to explain, not on a required number of menu items.

This guide walks through a practical page map, the content to prepare and the checks to run before launch. It is intended for a freelancer, small workshop or business owner making an initial site.

Decide what the site needs to do

Write down your audience and the main action you want a visitor to take. A consultant may want a project enquiry; a local repair shop may want a customer to arrange an appointment. List the questions someone needs answered before they take that step.

A brochure site can be a good fit for presenting services, examples and contact details. If visitors need to select products, pay, track delivery or manage an account, document those flows before choosing a tool. A few descriptive pages may not be enough.

Launching a site does not automatically bring enquiries. A clear offer, working contact route and a plan to reach an appropriate audience all matter.

Choose one page or several

A single page can work for one main service, a short introduction, a few examples and contact information. Menu items can link to sections of the same page. Keep the route to key information short enough that a visitor does not have to scroll through a long sequence of decorative sections.

Separate pages can help when services have different conditions, examples need detail or readers must compare options. Each page should answer a distinct question with enough useful information. Avoid empty pages added only to make the menu look bigger.

A sample page map

Imagine a fictional bicycle repair workshop. This is a teaching example, not a description of an actual business. It might start with four pages:

Page Visitor's question Useful content
Home What does the workshop do and how can I get in touch? Brief offer, main services, service area and contact
Services What can I request and how is work agreed? Service descriptions and how estimates are made
Work examples Has the workshop handled a similar task? A few real examples with permitted images and context
Contact How do I reach the team and when can I expect an answer? Working channels and hours or location when applicable

An appointment-only business without a public office should not invent one. A solo professional could place the same material in sections of one page instead.

Make the home page specific

Near the top, explain who you serve and what you do. Offer one clear next step, such as viewing services or discussing a task. Include a location or service area when it affects availability. Test the button or link: it should lead to a working section or contact channel.

For the fictional workshop, “City bicycle repairs by appointment,” paired with its real service area, tells visitors more than “the best service for everyone.” Only publish claims about timing, experience or results that you can support.

Below the introduction, provide short summaries of key services, how the work proceeds and selected evidence. The home page does not need to contain every detail; it should point clearly to the next relevant answer.

Explain services and conditions

Use the language your customers use. For each service, describe who it helps, what the work includes, what falls outside the scope and how timing and cost are agreed.

If you cannot quote a fixed price in advance, explain the process honestly: for example, an initial assessment may precede an agreed estimate. The precise conditions should come from the business's actual practice, not a generic template.

One service may deserve its own page if it needs substantial explanation. A group of closely related offerings may fit in one services page. Test the structure with a person who has not built the site: can they find the answer without guessing?

Show evidence without inventing it

An “about” section should explain who performs the work and which relevant experience or capabilities they bring. It need not be a long biography. Update it when the team or service changes.

For examples of work, describe the original task, what you did and a result you can substantiate. Obtain permission when a project includes a client's information or protected material. If you do not have a public case study yet, show your process or label a demonstration as hypothetical. Do not invent customers, testimonials or outcomes.

Use testimonials with appropriate permission and preserve their context. A photograph and caption should not imply that you performed work you did not do.

Make contact easy

Provide only channels you actually monitor: for example, an email address or telephone number. Add working hours or an expected response process if you can meet it. An in-person service may need an address and directions; a remote service may need a service area or time zone.

If you add a form, ask only for information needed to respond. Decide who receives the message and what the visitor sees on success or failure. Submit a test from a phone and a computer, confirm that the message arrives and provide another contact route if the form fails.

Before adding analytics, maps, forms or third-party widgets, identify what information they process and what notices or settings are appropriate for your circumstances. Requirements depend on location and processing; seek qualified advice when needed.

Build and publish in four steps

1. Prepare content first

Gather the offer, services, actual conditions, contact details and images you have permission to use. Draw a simple map of what appears first, where detail lives and how a visitor returns to contact. Draft the content before choosing animations or decorative effects.

2. Choose a creation method

A page builder with reusable blocks may suit someone who wants to edit a few pages without code. A CMS can provide a more configurable content workflow. Static files or custom development may fit a team comfortable with a repository and deployment process. Test the particular tool against your own editing task rather than relying only on a feature list.

Check whether you can use your domain, edit titles and contacts, export content, restore a backup and hand access to another person. Compare both launch and ongoing costs.

3. Arrange domain, hosting and access

Choose a readable domain and ensure the responsible owner controls the account. Understand renewal terms and how to change providers. Choose hosting or a service appropriate for the build method and follow its instructions for the domain and secure connection.

Limit access, protect accounts and store recovery information safely. Establish how the site is backed up and how restoration is tested. Never publish test passwords or private administration details.

4. Assemble and test

Apply the page map, use consistent menu labels and link services, examples and contact information. On a phone, verify that menus open, text is readable without horizontal scrolling and buttons can be used comfortably.

Give each page a descriptive title and useful description. Provide meaningful alternative text for informative images. Avoid duplicating pages merely to repeat search phrases. These steps support clarity; they do not guarantee search placement.

Before and after launch

Open the site in several browsers and on a phone. Check spelling, current conditions, addresses, links and buttons. Submit a test enquiry and verify receipt. Ask someone unfamiliar with the project to find a service and contact you; observe where they hesitate.

After publication, recheck the final address, secure connection, images and any restrictions on test or private material. Do not change access rules blindly. Assign an owner to update contact information and conditions, manage domain renewal and verify backups.

A short checklist

  • The audience, offer and main visitor action are clear.
  • You chose which information belongs in sections and which needs separate pages.
  • Services, examples and contacts are accurate and current.
  • You have appropriate permission for project material, images and testimonials.
  • The form and an alternative contact method work.
  • Mobile navigation, links, page titles and meaningful image alternatives have been checked.
  • The owner controls the domain, access, renewal and backups.
  • Someone is responsible for enquiries and future updates.

Start with the smallest structure that answers real customer questions. Add pages when they have a clear purpose and enough useful content to support it.

title: AI SDK harness layer now supports native subscription authentication

The AI SDK harness layer now supports authenticating harnesses through their native subscriptions, where the underlying harness supports them. The harness layer runs different coding agents through the same HarnessAgent interface, so you can switch agents without changing your application code.

No code changes or new settings are required. The direct authentication mode uses explicit provider environment credentials when they are present, and otherwise a native subscription found on the host. The default auto mode does the same when no AI Gateway credentials are set. The ai-gateway mode never reads native subscriptions.

Native subscription credentials stay on the host. Just like with API keys, credentials are resolved at the host boundary. OAuth access tokens are refreshed there as needed. Where the sandbox supports it, the harness receives placeholder credentials and the real token is injected into outbound requests on the host.

Native subscriptions work across harness adapters wherever the harness itself supports subscription login. These include Claude Code, Cline, Codex, Cursor, fx, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, OpenCode, and Pi.

title: useDeferredValue Explained: Keeping React UIs Responsive
description:
useDeferredValue Explained

useDeferredValue is a React concurrent hook that lets you delay rendering of non-urgent values so your UI stays responsive.

🧩 What Problem Does useDeferredValue Solve?

It helps prevent UI lag when rendering is expensive but user input must remain fast.

⚙️ Basic Usage 

import { useDeferredValue, useState } from "react";

function Search() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);

  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      <Results query={deferredQuery} />
    </>
  );
}

🧠 Mental Model

  • query updates immediately
  • deferredQuery updates when React has time

🔍 How It Works Under the Hood

  • Deferred updates are marked low priority
  • Urgent updates interrupt them
  • Intermediate renders may be skipped

⚡ useDeferredValue vs useTransition

Feature useDeferredValue useTransition
Controls Value State update
API Passive Active
Pending flag ❌ ✅

🧱 Example: Filtering a Large List 

const deferredFilter = useDeferredValue(filter);

⚠️ Notes

  • Not a debounce
  • Requires React 18+
  • Delays rendering, not state

✅ Summary

useDeferredValue improves UX by prioritizing urgent updates and deferring expensive rendering.

title: Your agent doesn't need a codebase memory
description:
Every coding agent needs to understand your codebase. But does it really need to remember it?

Most code intelligence tools maintain indexes, embeddings, or knowledge graphs, depends on other stuff like sqlite. These need to stay synchronized with your code, or risk giving agents outdated answers.

I built cxj to try a simpler approach: read the current source, answer the question, and forget everything.

What is cxj?

An open-source, stateless Java/Spring code intelligence CLI for coding agents.

Instead of spending tokens exploring dozens of files, your agent gets structured answers in milliseconds.

cxj brief                     # Understand the entire service
cxj endpoints                 # List HTTP routes
cxj trail PaymentService.pay  # Follow calls and find tests
cxj callers PaymentService.pay # Find callers
cxj deps                      # Get resolved dependency versions

It understands Spring-specific concepts, resolves method calls using declared types, and explicitly reports uncertainty instead of silently guessing.

Does it actually help?

I compared cxj against traditional grep + file exploration using the same AI model on a production Spring service.

For six structural questions, both approaches answered correctly:

Improvement with cxj
Input tokens 6.4× fewer
Agent cost 5.6× cheaper
Completion time 2.2× faster

For simple one-line lookups, grep actually won. cxj is most useful when answers span multiple files.

Full benchmark and methodology.

No index. No daemon. No stale cache.

cxj uses tree-sitter to parse the current code on every invocation, builds its knowledge in memory, and exits.

  • 561-file production Spring service: ~170 ms
  • Spring Framework, 1.5 million lines: 2.4 seconds

No persistent state, no background process, and no network required for queries.

Try it 

brew install umuterturk/tap/cxj
npx skills add umuterturk/cxj
[download] (https://github.com/umuterturk/cxj/releases/latest)

Works with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and other skill-compatible agents. macOS and Linux. MIT licensed.

GitHub: https://github.com/umuterturk/cxj
Come contribute!

I'm curious whether other developers find persistent codebase indexes necessary, or whether parsing on demand is already fast enough for most projects.

title: The Registry That Wasn't Enough: How We Went from "Knowing APIs" to Actually Verifying Against PyPI
description:
The Registry That Wasn't Enough: How We Went from "Knowing APIs" to Actually Verifying Against PyPI

Continuation of the previous article on detecting hallucinations in AI-generated code.

In the previous article, I told the story of how this idea was born: a requests.get_json() that never existed, that passed tests, linter, and type checker, and that would only have failed in production. The tool I built back then relied on a handcrafted registry of valid APIs: a map of library → known functions, and a simple rule: if the library is in the registry and the function isn't, it's a hallucination. It worked for requests, json, and os, and it detected nonexistent packages by querying PyPI.

But the registry had an obvious limitation: it only judged what it knew. And as soon as you stepped outside requests, json, and os, the tool went silent. Not because there were no hallucinations, but because it had nothing to compare against. That ceiling is what I've been thinking about for the past few weeks. And this is what came next.

Of course, this work doesn't start from scratch. Recent research confirms that library hallucinations are systematic (5.2% of packages mentioned by commercial models don't exist, and up to 21.7% for open-source models), that static analysis has a ceiling of 48.5% to 77% of what it can possibly detect, and that verification against real documentation significantly reduces false positives. Our project addresses some of those limitations (invented packages, APIs of real packages verified against wheels) and leaves others documented (APIs of nonexistent packages, advanced slopsquatting). This continuation covers what we've done and what remains.
How to Verify More Rigorously?

The question that changed everything was: what if, instead of maintaining a hand-written list of valid functions, we read what the package actually contains?

PyPI doesn't just serve packages: it serves wheels, which are ZIP files containing the code and — very importantly — the type stubs (.pyi) when the package includes them. If you download the wheel and open it, you can check whether class DataFrame exists in pandas without installing anything and without executing any of the user's code.

That's exactly what we did. And it changes the game: you no longer depend on someone maintaining a list of functions by hand. You depend on what the package actually publishes on PyPI. Coverage stops being artisanal and becomes that of the ecosystem.
The Cache, or How Not to Punish PyPI on Every Analysis

The first practical problem was obvious: if every analysis queries PyPI for every import, on a slow network like mine, the analysis drags on forever. And if PyPI goes down, the detector just sits there waiting. So we built a two-level cache (memory + disk) with TTLs:

exists (does the package exist on PyPI?): 7 days.

Reputation metadata (first release, maintainers): 30 days.

Network errors: 10 minutes (to avoid retrying in a loop when the network is flaky).

And a design decision that was already there in the previous article but now becomes central: fail-open. If we can't verify (timeout, PyPI down), we don't report the package as nonexistent. Better an occasional false negative than a false positive that erodes trust.

The result is noticeable: the second run on the same file goes from ~50 seconds to 17 milliseconds. And all of that without touching the normal flow: if you don't configure the cache, the detector works exactly as before.
Canonicalization, stdlib, and the False Positive That Taught Us Something

With the cache came the fine details. PyPI normalizes names (PIL is installed as Pillow, sklearn as scikit-learn, cv2 as opencv-python), and imports bring submodules (tensorflow.keras, os.path). If you don't canonicalize, the cache misses and odd false positives start appearing.

One of the most instructive: imp (a stdlib module, deprecated) was flagged as typosquatting of pip. The edit distance was 1, and the heuristic didn't know that imp is stdlib. The lesson: stdlib lists and PyPI package lists must stay in sync, or the detector starts inventing problems where there are none. Today imp, distutils, and friends are recognized as stdlib and are not flagged.
Actually Verifying Attributes: pandas.DataFrame Is No Longer a False Positive

Here's the biggest change compared to the previous article. Before, api-hallucination was heuristic: it looked for suspicious names, it didn't verify. And that produced false positives like pandas.DataFrame, which does exist but wasn't in the registry.

Now there's a deep mode (deep) that, when you enable it:

Queries PyPI for the package.

Downloads the wheel (once, cached per version).

Opens the ZIP and searches for the attribute in all the package's .pyi and .py files.

Returns one of three states: confirmed, not found, or unverifiable.

The result, measured with the same test file: 15 findings without deep mode, 14 with deep mode. The difference is exactly the false positive for pandas.DataFrame, which disappears. And more importantly: pandas.funcion_inventada is detected, with evidence that it's not in the real wheel.

That's something the handcrafted registry could never provide. And we did it without installing Python on the server, without executing the user's code, and without adding third-party dependencies: just HTTP, ZIP, and a bit of regex.
IP Control, or How to Open It Up Without Getting Your Server Knocked Over

Deep mode downloads wheels. That costs bandwidth and time. Before opening it to the public, we needed a limit. So we added IP-based control: 3 deep analyses per day per IP, with a daily reset.

Three details that mattered to us:

Localhost is exempt, so development tests don't stop because they hit the limit. Otherwise you'd lock yourself out of your own machine.

IPs can be simulated in development with X-Forwarded-For and a DETECTOR_DEV=1 variable. That way you can test the limit without deploying.

In production, DETECTOR_TRUST_PROXY=1 to read the real IP behind a proxy. Otherwise all users would share the proxy's IP.

The limit is simple, but it's the difference between opening deep mode with a safety net and opening it without one.
The Four Test Files, and What They Actually Tell Us

To measure without fooling ourselves, we wrote four files:
File What it measures Result
test_debe_detectar.py Recall (catch the bad stuff) 14–15 findings, almost all correct
test_no_debe_detectar.py Precision (don't flag the good stuff) 0 findings ✅
test_limitaciones.py Known false negatives/positives 1 finding (a true positive by heuristic)
test_syntax_error.py Broken syntax 0, "file looks clean" ❌

The good part: precision is perfect on clean code. The honest part: there's a UX bug with broken syntax (the detector says "clean" when the file doesn't even compile) and there are structural false negatives (dynamic imports, from-import of names, nonexistent submodules) that require deeper analysis. We have them documented, not hidden.
What's Next

So the project is no longer "an API registry." It's a detector that actually verifies against PyPI, with caching, opt-in deep mode, and usage control. What's left to review from this milestone:

Wheel download events in the progress bar (today, with deep mode, the bar freezes while the wheel downloads).

--deep in the CLI, so the terminal has the same power as the web.

Reporting syntax-error as a finding, instead of saying "file looks clean".

Evidence and status on each finding (confirmed, probable, unverifiable).

pyright/mypy only as a local option, never on the server (slow, requires installation, and without stubs it flags nothing).

And there's one more thing we'd like to mention. Once we have hosting — complicated from my country under siege — we'll launch a web app that already allows running the analyses online. It's a tool that's already built and working locally: you upload a .py, you see progress in real time (with an SSE progress bar), and you get the findings, including deep mode with verification against PyPI wheels. But for that web app to be sustainable and not fall over at the first sign of traffic, we need a contribution to the tool's development. It's not a payment to use the service: it's a way for the project to cover hosting, the bandwidth for wheel downloads, and maintenance time. The idea is that anyone who wants to use deep mode intensively can contribute, and anyone who just wants to try basic analysis can do so without barriers. The code will remain open; the hosted web app will be how the project sustains itself. We'll share more details when it's ready.

The previous article ended with an idea: "the linter sees what it knows; the type checker sees what's in the signature; neither knows whether the method actually exists." This is an attempt to close that gap. Not with a bigger list, but by reading what the package publishes. It's still not perfect: there are false negatives we acknowledge and a syntax bug pending. But the difference between "there's no hallucination" and "it couldn't be verified" is no longer hidden: we measure it, we document it, and we try to reduce it.

If you try deep mode and find a false positive or one that slips through, I'd love to hear about it. This project gets corrected by what others find.
References

Spracklen, J., Wijewickrama, R., Sakib, A.H.M.N., Maiti, A., & Viswanath, B. (2025). We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs. 34th USENIX Security Symposium. arXiv:2406.10279.

Miranda-Pena, C., Reeson, A., Paris, C., Poon, J., & Kummerfeld, J.K. (2026). An Empirical Analysis of Static Analysis Methods for Detection and Mitigation of Code Library Hallucinations. arXiv:2604.07755.

Tileria, M., et al. (2026). Hallucination Inspector: A Fact-Checking Judge for API Migration. arXiv:2604.20202.

Raj, A., & (co-author). (2026). Names Can Hurt: Spotting Slopsquatting Risks Caused by Package Name Hallucinations in Local Coding LLMs. arXiv:2608.23897.

Churilov, A. (2026). The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains: Re-evaluating LLM Package Hallucinations on the 2026 Frontier-Model Cohort. arXiv:2605.17062.

Whether the goal is to access French digital services, manage social media activities, explore European markets, or establish an online presence in France, account verification and regional eligibility requirements can create additional complications.
Many websites advertise verified French accounts, claiming that their accounts are ready to use and suitable for different online activities. However, not every provider operates legitimately. Some sellers offer accounts created using misleading identity information, unauthorized access, or methods that violate platform policies.
This guide explains how to identify legitimate US and UK websites, understand French account verification, evaluate third-party providers, and avoid common account-related scams. Rather than treating an account seller's verification claims as proof of legitimacy, it focuses on reliable services and official account registration options.
Understanding Verified French Accounts
A verified French account is generally an online account associated with France that has completed the relevant platform's identity, contact, residency, or business verification process.
The meaning of verification depends on the service.
For example:
Social media platforms may verify accounts through phone numbers, identity documents, or other eligibility requirements.
Financial services may require identity checks, proof of address, and additional compliance documentation.
Business platforms may request company registration details and authorized representative information.
Digital marketplaces may require sellers to provide business and payment information.
A French account is not automatically verified simply because it uses a French telephone number or displays France as its registered country.
Verification should always be confirmed through the platform's official procedures.
Why People Look for US and UK Websites Offering French Accounts
US and UK websites attract international customers because many operate across multiple countries and provide accessible customer support.
Several factors contribute to this demand.
Access to International Digital Services
Businesses entering the French market may need accounts on local marketplaces, advertising platforms, payment services, and professional networks.
Using legitimate regional registration options can help organizations establish their presence.
Cross-Border Business Operations
Companies based in the United States or United Kingdom may need to manage French customers, suppliers, and marketing campaigns.
Official business accounts can provide access to regional features where the company meets the platform's eligibility requirements.
Language and Customer Support
English-language support is useful for international customers who are unfamiliar with French registration procedures.
However, English-language customer service does not automatically establish that a provider is trustworthy.
Regional Verification Requirements
Some platforms require documentation demonstrating a genuine connection to France.
Depending on the service, this could include residency information, business registration, or a valid French contact address.
How to Identify Legitimate Websites for French Account Registration
Before using any US or UK website offering French account-related services, evaluate its legitimacy carefully.

  1. Check the Official Website Start by identifying whether the service is an official platform, an authorized registration partner, or an independent third party. Official websites should clearly explain their services, registration procedures, and verification requirements.
  2. Review Verification Procedures A legitimate service should explain how account verification works. Look for information about: Identity verification. Telephone number requirements. Address verification. Business documentation. Account ownership. Data protection procedures. Avoid providers that promise verification without explaining the underlying process.
  3. Examine Company Information Reliable businesses generally provide identifiable company information. Check for: Registered business details. A physical business address where applicable. Customer support information. Privacy policies. Terms and conditions. Refund and cancellation policies.
  4. Evaluate Customer Reviews Independent customer reviews can help identify recurring problems. Pay attention to complaints involving account suspension, unauthorized charges, inaccessible accounts, and misleading verification claims. Do not rely exclusively on testimonials published on the provider's own website.
  5. Understand Account Ownership Account ownership is particularly important. An account registered using another person's identity may create problems even when the account initially appears verified. Risks of Purchasing Pre-Verified French Accounts Buying an existing verified account from an unrelated seller can create significant problems. Account Suspension Many online platforms restrict account transfers or prohibit selling accounts without authorization. Identity and Documentation Problems Some sellers create accounts using identity documents that do not belong to the eventual buyer. This can create serious ownership and compliance issues, particularly for financial and business services. Unauthorized Access A seller may retain recovery access through an original email address, telephone number, or backup authentication method. Consequently, the buyer may lose access even after paying for the account. Financial Fraud Some account sellers advertise verified accounts but deliver inaccessible accounts, misleading credentials, or nothing at all.
