title: The desktop app you scrape updated overnight: a version watch that re-checks what you depend on, once per change
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the tool described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code. Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

Relaymote (MIT, Node.js) is a phone remote for Claude Desktop's Code-tab sessions. Desktop has no API for that, so Relaymote reads two things it does not own: the Code tab's sidebar (through the debugger port) and the session transcripts on disk. Both can change shape whenever Desktop or the Claude Code it bundles updates, and nobody sends you a changelog for the parts you scrape.

This post is about the small module that turns "it silently broke after an update" into one message on the day of the update: lib/claude-version-watch.js.

The failure that started it

One Desktop update (2.42304.2 to 3.1623.0) moved screen-reader-only status text inside each sidebar row's button. Relaymote read the row's text as the session title, so titles came out as " Awaiting input". 404 of 473 session titles were polluted before anyone noticed. Nothing crashed. Nothing logged an error. The data was just wrong.

The lesson is not "write a better selector". Selectors for someone else's UI will keep breaking. The lesson is: notice the update, run a live check of every surface you depend on, and say the result once.

Step 1: know the installed versions without asking the app

Both versions are visible on disk. Desktop installs into app-<version> folders and Claude Code into version-named folders, so the newest folder name is the installed version:

const cmpVer = (a, b) => {
  const x = String(a).split('.').map(Number), y = String(b).split('.').map(Number);
  for (let i = 0; i < Math.max(x.length, y.length); i++) {
    const d = (x[i] || 0) - (y[i] || 0); if (d) return d;
  }
  return 0;
};
const newest = (names) => names.filter(n => /^\d+(\.\d+)+$/.test(n)).sort(cmpVer).pop() || null;

Two details matter. Compare versions numerically, part by part: as strings, "3.999" sorts after "3.1623". And filter to names that look like versions, so a stray folder never becomes "the version".

Step 2: the live check names problems in plain sentences

check() does not compare against a stored snapshot of the UI. It asks questions whose answers must hold whatever the layout is:

  • Can we reach Desktop's debugger at all?
  • Did the sidebar read return any sessions? Zero rows means the session list moved.
  • Does any title match the known pollution pattern (/\s(Awaiting input|Unread response|Started (from|by) .*)$/)?
  • With 20 or more rows, does at least one show a status? If none do, the status labels changed.
  • Does the newest transcript parse, and does it contain record types we have never seen?

Each failure is pushed as a sentence someone can act on ("the Code tab sidebar read 0 sessions — Desktop changed its session list"), not as a stack trace.

Step 3: separate problems from notes

New transcript record types are common: Claude Code adds them regularly (api-request, cost-state and several others appeared between Claude Code 2.1.300 and 2.1.304). Relaymote skips unknown types safely, so a new type is a note, not a problem:

if (t.unknown.length)
  notes.push('new transcript record types (skipped safely): ' +
    t.unknown.map(([k, n]) => `${k}×${n}`).join(', '));

If every new record type raised an alarm, the alarm would be ignored by the second week. Keep "needs a fix" and "worth knowing" in different lists, and only the first makes the result not OK.

To find the types cheaply, it reads only the last 2 MB of the most recently modified transcript and drops the first (probably cut) line. That is enough to see what the current version writes.

Step 4: run on change, not on a schedule

The watch ticks every few minutes, but almost every tick is a no-op:

const was = load();
if (!was) { save({ ...now, at: new Date().toISOString(), checked: null }); return { first: true, now }; }
if (was.desktop === now.desktop && was.code === now.code && !was.pending) return null;
  • First sight only records. On a fresh install there is no "before", so there is nothing to report.
  • Same versions, nothing pending: return. The expensive live check runs only when a version actually changed.
  • One alert per change. After the check, the new versions are saved with the result, so the next tick is quiet again.

Step 5: don't blame the update for a restart

An update usually restarts Desktop, and for a minute the debugger is simply not up yet. Reporting "cannot reach Desktop" at that moment would be a false alarm on every single update. So if the only problem is the unreachable debugger, the change is parked as pending and retried, up to six ticks:

if (!r.ok && r.problems.every(p => /debugger link down/.test(p)) && (was.pendingTries || 0) < 6) {
  save({ ...was, pending: now, pendingTries: (was.pendingTries || 0) + 1 });
  return { waiting: true };
}

After six tries it reports anyway, because a debugger that never comes back is a real problem.

What the message looks like

One push notification, titled with what changed (Claude updated: Desktop <old> → <new>, Claude Code <old> → <new>, only the parts that changed) and a body that is either "everything it reads from Claude works" plus the notes, or the list of problems. The same line goes to the log. That is the whole output: no dashboard, nothing to open.

Takeaways

  • If you scrape or parse an app you don't own, its updates are your incidents. Detect them from the install on disk.
  • Check invariants ("some row has a status"), not a frozen copy of the UI.
  • Split problems from notes, or the alert becomes noise.
  • Run the expensive check once per version change, and record the result so it doesn't repeat.
  • Give a restart time to finish before calling it a failure, with a hard limit on how long you wait.

The code is in lib/claude-version-watch.js in the Relaymote repo, with its test in test/claude-version-watch.js. Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

title: Building a Zero-Dependency Key-Value Engine in 5 Languages (Rust, Go, TypeScript, Swift, Kotlin)
description:
Modern distributed software is polyglot. A cloud backend might have microservices written in Go, low-latency data pipelines in Rust, web APIs in TypeScript/Node, iOS clients in Swift, and Android/JVM services in Kotlin.

Yet, when working across different language ecosystems, caching semantics are wildly fragmented:

  • Eviction policies behave differently ($O(1)$ LRU vs probabilistic vs FIFO).
  • Concurrency models handle mutex contention and clock drift inconsistently.
  • Dependency bloat drags dozens of third-party packages into otherwise clean microservices.

To solve this, we engineered KVDock natively across 5 languages with zero external dependencies in core and unified memory/concurrency semantics.

Here is what we learned building high-performance key-value engines across Rust, Go, TypeScript, Swift, and Kotlin.

1. Rust (kvdock-rs): Monotonic Clocks & Zero Lock Contention

In systems programming, relying on wall-clock time (SystemTime) for TTL eviction is dangerous because NTP clock synchronizations or leap seconds can cause erratic cache expirations.

In kvdock-rs, we enforce TTL using monotonic Instant:

use kvdock_rs::{KVDock, MemoryAdapter};
use std::time::Duration;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let adapter = MemoryAdapter::new(10_000);
    let dock = KVDock::new(adapter).with_default_ttl(Duration::from_secs(60));

    // Single-flight stampede coalescing in Rust
    let session = dock.get_or_set("user:session:101", || async {
        fetch_user_from_db().await
    }).await;
}
  • Concurrency: Thread-safe KVDock<A> backed by read-write locks for sub-microsecond concurrent reads.
  • Eviction: True $O(1)$ LRU with doubly-linked intrusive pointers.

2. Go (kvdock-go): Generics & Singleflight Mutexes

Go 1.18+ generics revolutionized type-safe caching without interface{} type assertions:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "time"
    "github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock-go"
)

type UserSession struct {
    UserID string
    Role   string
}

func main() {
    dock := kvdock.New(kvdock.WithMemoryAdapter(10000), kvdock.WithTTL(60 * time.Second))

    // Generic type-safe get or set
    val, err := kvdock.GetOrSet[UserSession](dock, context.Background(), "user:101", func() (UserSession, error) {
        return queryUserFromDB()
    })
}
  • Concurrency: Combines atomic operational telemetry with internal single-flight deduplication to ensure concurrent Goroutines requesting the same missing key coalesce into a single execution.

3. TypeScript (kvdock): Zero Dependencies & Universal Runtimes

JavaScript runtimes are now fragmented across Node.js, Bun, Deno, and Cloudflare Workers:

import { KVDock, TieredDock } from "kvdock";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "kvdock/adapters/memory";
import { RedisAdapter } from "kvdock/adapters/redis";

const dock = new TieredDock({
  l1: new MemoryAdapter({ maxSize: 10_000 }), // In-memory L1 (< 0.05ms)
  l2: new RedisAdapter({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL }), // Distributed L2
  l1TTL: 15_000
});
  • Key Innovation: Zero runtime dependencies in core. Tree-shakeable dual ESM/CJS exports with single-flight promise coalescing that reduces database stampedes by 99.9%.

4. Swift (kvdock-swift): Swift 6 Concurrency & Actor Isolation

In modern Swift, data races are caught at compile-time using structured concurrency:

import KVDockSwift

let dock = await KVDock(
    adapter: MemoryAdapter(capacity: 10_000),
    defaultTTL: .seconds(60)
)

// Actor-isolated thread-safe access
let user = try await dock.getOrSet("user:profile") {
    try await fetchUserProfile()
}
  • Uses ContinuousClock for nanosecond monotonic TTL expiration.

5. Kotlin (kvdock-kt): Access-Order LRU & Coroutines

On the JVM and Android, coroutine compatibility and low memory overhead are paramount:

import com.kvdock.KVDock
import com.kvdock.adapters.MemoryAdapter
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.minutes

val dock = KVDock(MemoryAdapter(maxSize = 10_000), defaultTTL = 1.minutes)

val order = dock.getOrSet("order:7788") {
    fetchOrderFromDatabase()
}

The Polyglot Ecosystem on GitHub

Explore the source code, benchmarks, and architectures:

  • TypeScript Engine: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock
  • Rust Engine: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock-rs
  • Go Engine: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock-go
  • Swift Engine: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock-swift
  • Kotlin Engine: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock-kt

⭐ Star the repos & follow @zisam-glitch for deep dives into low-latency systems architecture!

title: Queueing Theory in Go: Understanding Latency, Throughput, and Saturation
description:
Your service handles 500 requests per second.

The CPU is not fully utilized. The database is responding normally. The average processing time looks reasonable.

Yet your p99 latency keeps increasing.

What is happening?

In many cases, the problem isn't how long requests take to execute. It's how long they spend waiting before execution even begins.

This is where queueing theory becomes useful.

Queueing theory gives us a way to reason about arrival rates, service capacity, concurrency, waiting time, and system saturation. It helps explain why a service can look healthy under moderate traffic and suddenly experience a dramatic increase in latency as it approaches its capacity.

In this article, we'll explore the fundamentals of queueing theory and apply them to practical Go backend systems.

We'll cover:

  • Arrival rate, service rate, and utilization
  • Little's Law and its practical applications
  • Why latency increases near saturation
  • The relationship between concurrency and throughput
  • Building bounded queues and worker pools in Go
  • Queue sizing, admission control, and overload behavior
  • Metrics and load-testing strategies

The goal isn't to turn every backend engineer into a mathematician. It's to make better engineering decisions using a few surprisingly powerful relationships.

1. Every Backend Service Is a Queueing System

Consider a typical HTTP service:

Client Requests
      |
      v
   HTTP Server
      |
      v
  Request Queue
      |
      v
  Worker Pool
      |
      v
 Database / API
      |
      v
   Response

Every request follows a similar lifecycle:

  1. It arrives at the system.
  2. It waits for an available resource.
  3. It gets processed.
  4. It leaves the system.

The important distinction is that processing time and waiting time are different things.

Imagine two requests:

Request Waiting time Processing time Total
A 5 ms 45 ms 50 ms
B 250 ms 45 ms 295 ms

Both requests require exactly the same processing time.

But Request B takes almost six times longer because it spends most of its lifetime waiting.

This is why optimizing database queries or application code alone doesn't always improve end-to-end latency.

Sometimes the queue is the bottleneck.

2. The Three Variables That Explain Queueing Behavior

Most basic queueing models start with three variables.

Arrival Rate (λ)

The arrival rate represents how frequently new requests enter the system.

For example:

λ = 500 requests/second

It describes incoming demand, not necessarily completed work.

Service Rate (μ)

The service rate describes how quickly a worker can process requests.

If a worker takes an average of 20 milliseconds per request:

μ = 1 / 0.020 = 50 requests/second

One worker can theoretically process 50 requests per second under that average service time.

With 10 equivalent workers, the theoretical aggregate service capacity becomes:

c × μ = 10 × 50 = 500 requests/second

Here, c represents the number of workers.

This assumes the workers can operate independently and that another shared resource doesn't become the bottleneck.

Utilization (ρ)

Utilization describes how much of the available service capacity is being consumed.

For a simple system with c equivalent workers:

ρ = λ / (c × μ)

Suppose:

  • Arrival rate: 400 requests/second
  • Service rate per worker: 50 requests/second
  • Number of workers: 10

Then:

ρ = 400 / (10 × 50) = 0.8 = 80%

The system is operating at 80% utilization.

That sounds reasonable.

But here's the important part: 80% utilization does not mean 20% of the system is freely available at all times.

Traffic is variable. Requests don't arrive at perfectly regular intervals, and processing times aren't identical.

A system can experience queueing delays even when its average utilization is below 100%.

And as utilization approaches capacity, those delays can grow rapidly.

3. Little's Law: The Most Useful Queueing Relationship

One of the most practical results in queueing theory is Little's Law:

L = λ × W

Where:

  • L = average number of requests in the entire system
  • λ = average arrival rate
  • W = average time spent in the entire system

In backend engineering, this gives us a direct relationship between throughput, latency, and concurrency.

For example:

Throughput: 200 requests/second
Average latency: 150 ms

Convert the latency to seconds:

W = 0.150 seconds

Then:

L = 200 × 0.150 = 30

On average, there are approximately 30 requests in the system.

This is incredibly useful because it allows us to estimate concurrency from production measurements.

Let's look at another example.

A service processes 1,000 requests per second, with an average time in the system of 80 milliseconds.

L = 1,000 × 0.080 = 80

The service has approximately 80 requests in flight on average.

This doesn't mean we should automatically configure 80 workers.

It means the observed workload has an average concurrency of approximately 80. Worker count, resource limits, queue capacity, and service time still need to be considered separately.

Queue length versus requests in the system

There's an important distinction here.

Little's Law can describe either the entire system or just the waiting queue, provided the measurements use matching definitions.

For the entire system:

L = λ × W

For the waiting queue:

Lq = λ × Wq

Where:

  • Lq = average number of requests waiting in the queue
  • λ = average arrival rate into the queue
  • Wq = average time spent waiting in the queue

The distinction matters when instrumenting a Go worker pool.

If we measure only queue depth, we shouldn't compare it directly with total request latency. We need to compare it with queue waiting time.

When should you use Little's Law?

It's useful for:

  • Estimating average in-flight requests
  • Understanding queue growth
  • Planning concurrency limits
  • Checking whether observed metrics are consistent
  • Estimating the waiting time implied by a queue
  • Identifying where work accumulates

However, Little's Law describes long-run averages in a stable system. It doesn't predict p99 latency or tell us how a system behaves during a sudden traffic spike.

For that, we need to understand utilization and variability.

4. Why Latency Explodes Near Saturation

Let's consider a simplified single-server queue.

Assume:

  • Requests arrive according to a Poisson process.
  • Service times are exponentially distributed.
  • There is one server.
  • The queue has unlimited capacity.

This is commonly called an M/M/1 queue.

For this particular model, the expected time in the system is:

W = 1 / (μ - λ)

And the expected waiting time in the queue is:

Wq = ρ / (μ - λ)

These formulas are model-specific. Real production systems often have multiple workers, correlated traffic, variable service times, and bounded queues.

But the model illustrates an important behavior.

Assume the server can process 100 requests per second.

Arrival rate Utilization Average time in system
50 req/s 50% 20 ms
70 req/s 70% 33.3 ms
80 req/s 80% 50 ms
90 req/s 90% 100 ms
95 req/s 95% 200 ms
99 req/s 99% 1,000 ms

Illustrative M/M/1 model, with a service rate of 100 requests per second.

The service rate never changes.

Yet the average response time increases from 20 milliseconds to one full second as utilization approaches 100%.

This is the queueing effect that makes operating a service continuously at maximum utilization dangerous.

The system doesn't necessarily become slower at processing individual requests. It becomes slower at getting requests to the point where processing can begin.

This also explains why a small traffic increase can cause a disproportionately large latency increase.

In real systems, variability can make the situation worse. Bursty arrivals, slow dependencies, garbage collection pauses, lock contention, and uneven request costs all contribute to queueing.

High utilization leaves very little room to absorb variability.

5. Concurrency Is Not the Same as Throughput

A common approach to improving performance is increasing concurrency.

If 10 workers aren't enough, why not use 100?

Because more concurrency doesn't necessarily produce more throughput.

Imagine a service that queries a database.

Go Service
    |
    v
100 Concurrent Requests
    |
    v
Database Connection Pool
    |
    v
20 Available Connections

Only 20 requests can use a database connection simultaneously.

The remaining requests may wait for a connection.

Increasing application concurrency from 100 to 500 doesn't increase database capacity.

It may simply move the queue from the application into the database connection pool.

This is an important principle:

Increasing concurrency can move the bottleneck without removing it.

A useful way to reason about concurrency is Little's Law:

L = λ × W

If throughput remains constant while the number of concurrent requests increases, the average time spent in the system must also increase.

For example:

Throughput: 100 requests/second
Concurrency: 100
Average time: 1 second

Now suppose concurrency increases to 300, but throughput remains 100 requests per second.

Concurrency: 300
Average time: 3 seconds

The system is carrying more work, but it isn't completing more work.

This is why measuring concurrency without measuring throughput and latency can be misleading.

6. Implementing a Bounded Worker Pool in Go

Let's move from theory to implementation.

A worker pool is a common way to control how much work executes concurrently.

But a worker pool alone isn't enough.

If the incoming queue is unbounded, the service can continue accepting work long after its processing capacity is exhausted.

A bounded queue provides an explicit limit.

Here's a simplified implementation using Go channels:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "sync"
)

var (
    ErrQueueFull  = errors.New("worker queue is full")
    ErrPoolClosed = errors.New("worker pool is closed")
)

type Job func(context.Context) error

type Pool struct {
    jobs chan Job

    ctx    context.Context
    cancel context.CancelFunc

    mu     sync.Mutex
    closed bool

    wg sync.WaitGroup
}

func NewPool(
    parent context.Context,
    workers int,
    queueSize int,
) *Pool {
    if workers <= 0 {
        panic("workers must be greater than zero")
    }

    if queueSize < 0 {
        panic("queue size cannot be negative")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(parent)

    p := &Pool{
        jobs:   make(chan Job, queueSize),
        ctx:    ctx,
        cancel: cancel,
    }

    p.wg.Add(workers)

    for i := 0; i < workers; i++ {
        go p.worker()
    }

    return p
}

func (p *Pool) Submit(job Job) error {
    if job == nil {
        return errors.New("job cannot be nil")
    }

    p.mu.Lock()
    defer p.mu.Unlock()

    if p.closed {
        return ErrPoolClosed
    }

    if err := p.ctx.Err(); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    select {
    case p.jobs <- job:
        return nil
    default:
        return ErrQueueFull
    }
}

func (p *Pool) worker() {
    defer p.wg.Done()

    for {
        select {
        case <-p.ctx.Done():
            return

        case job := <-p.jobs:
            if p.ctx.Err() != nil {
                return
            }

            if job != nil {
                _ = job(p.ctx)
            }
        }
    }
}

func (p *Pool) Close() {
    p.mu.Lock()

    if p.closed {
        p.mu.Unlock()
        return
    }

    p.closed = true
    p.cancel()

    p.mu.Unlock()

    p.wg.Wait()
}

The implementation demonstrates a few important ideas:

  • The number of workers is fixed.
  • The queue has a bounded capacity.
  • Submit rejects work immediately when the queue is full.
  • Worker execution receives a cancellation context.
  • Submission and shutdown are coordinated using a mutex.
  • Close cancels workers and waits for them to exit.

This is an intentionally small example, not a complete production job-processing framework.

In particular, it uses immediate cancellation rather than graceful draining. It also doesn't provide per-job results, panic recovery, retry handling, or error reporting.

Those behaviors should be designed explicitly for the workload.

Also remember that context cancellation is cooperative. A job that ignores its context can prevent Close from returning.

Why bounded queues matter

Consider a service with:

Workers: 20
Queue capacity: 500
Average processing time: 100 ms

Each worker can theoretically process:

μ = 1 / 0.1 = 10 jobs/second

Aggregate service capacity:

c × μ = 20 × 10 = 200 jobs/second

If all workers are busy and the queue contains 500 jobs, the approximate queue-draining time is:

Wq ≈ 500 / 200 = 2.5 seconds

This is a rough estimate assuming the workers continue processing at the same aggregate rate and no new jobs arrive.

If your API has a 500-millisecond response deadline, accepting work into this queue may be pointless.

The request might time out before a worker even starts processing it.

A queue is not automatically useful just because it can hold more work.

It should hold only the amount of work your system can reasonably process before that work becomes irrelevant.

7. Queue Capacity Is a Latency Decision

Developers often select queue capacity using arbitrary values:

make(chan Job, 1000)

But why 1,000?

Why not 100 or 10,000?

A better approach is to start with a latency budget.

Suppose:

Maximum acceptable queue waiting time: 500 ms
Aggregate processing capacity: 200 jobs/second

A rough initial queue capacity can be estimated as:

Queue Capacity ≈ Aggregate Service Capacity × Target Queue Waiting Time

Given:

  • Aggregate service capacity: 200 jobs/second
  • Target queue waiting time: 0.5 seconds

The calculation becomes:

Q ≈ 200 × 0.5 = 100 jobs

This suggests that a queue capacity around 100 jobs corresponds to approximately 500 milliseconds of waiting at the assumed completion rate, if the queue is full and no new jobs arrive.

This is not a worst-case guarantee.

Actual waiting time depends on worker availability, service-time distribution, traffic bursts, and the number of jobs already executing.

Still, it gives us a much more defensible starting point than choosing a large number without understanding its consequences.

Queue age is often more useful than queue depth

Imagine two systems:

System A:
Queue depth: 100
Oldest job: 10 ms

System B:
Queue depth: 20
Oldest job: 2 seconds

System B has fewer queued jobs, but its users may be experiencing a much worse situation.

Queue depth tells us how much work is waiting.

Queue age tells us how long that work has already been waiting.

For latency-sensitive systems, both metrics are important.

8. Admission Control: Decide Whether Work Should Enter

A bounded queue provides a capacity limit.

Admission control adds a policy for deciding whether incoming work should be accepted.

For example:

func HandleRequest(
    ctx context.Context,
    queue chan Job,
    job Job,
) error {
    if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    select {
    case queue <- job:
        return nil

    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()

    default:
        return ErrQueueFull
    }
}

This is a simplified non-blocking admission decision.

When the queue is full, the request is rejected instead of waiting indefinitely.

In a real HTTP handler, this could translate into an overload response such as:

HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
Retry-After: 1

The exact status and retry policy depend on the API contract.

There are several possible admission strategies:

Reject immediately

Useful when waiting is unlikely to produce a result within the request deadline.

Wait for a bounded period

Useful when short bursts are expected and a small amount of waiting is acceptable.

Prioritize work

Useful when critical operations should be processed ahead of background or low-priority tasks.

Apply load shedding

Useful when the system is overloaded and preserving the health of the remaining workload is more important than accepting every request.

The important part is to make overload behavior intentional.

9. The Connection to Backpressure, Load Shedding, and Adaptive Concurrency

Queueing theory provides the foundation for several resilience patterns we've discussed in this series.

They solve different parts of the same problem.

Pattern What it controls
Backpressure How quickly work enters the system
Load shedding Which work should be rejected
Bulkheads How resources are isolated
Retry budgets How much additional traffic retries generate
Adaptive concurrency How many requests execute simultaneously
Hedged requests How to reduce tail latency through controlled parallelism

These mechanisms become much more effective when we understand the queueing behavior behind them.

For example, an adaptive concurrency controller can reduce the number of in-flight requests when latency indicates that a dependency is approaching saturation.

A bounded queue prevents the service from accumulating unlimited waiting work.

Load shedding rejects requests that cannot be processed within a useful time window.

Together, these mechanisms help keep the system stable under changing traffic conditions.

10. What Should You Measure in Production?

Queueing theory is useful only when its variables can be observed.

At a minimum, I'd monitor the following metrics.

Metric Why it matters
Arrival rate Incoming demand
Completion rate Actual processing capacity
Queue depth Amount of waiting work
Queue age How long work has been waiting
In-flight requests Current concurrency
Queue wait duration Time spent waiting before execution
Service duration Actual processing time
Rejected requests Admission-control behavior
p95 / p99 latency User-facing latency distribution

A particularly useful metric is the difference between total request duration and processing duration.

Total request duration: 350 ms
Queue wait:              250 ms
Processing duration:     100 ms

If processing duration is stable but total latency increases, the queue is a strong candidate for investigation.

For Go services, you can expose these measurements through Prometheus.

Example metric names:

http_requests_total
http_request_duration_seconds

worker_pool_queue_depth
worker_pool_queue_wait_seconds
worker_pool_active_workers
worker_pool_jobs_rejected_total
worker_pool_job_duration_seconds

Use histograms for durations and counters for events. Queue depth and active workers are gauges.

Avoid putting unbounded values such as user IDs, request IDs, or raw URLs into metric labels. That creates unnecessary cardinality.

A practical diagnostic example

Suppose a production service starts showing the following behavior:

Arrival rate:          800 req/s
Completion rate:       790 req/s
Active workers:        100
Queue depth:           Increasing
Queue wait p95:        450 ms
Processing p95:        60 ms
HTTP latency p95:      520 ms

The first instinct might be to optimize the handler.

But the measurements tell a different story.

Processing time is relatively low compared with total latency.

The queue is accumulating work, and the service is completing slightly fewer requests than it receives.

Adding more workers may help only if the downstream resources have spare capacity.

Before increasing concurrency, investigate:

  • Database connection pool saturation
  • Downstream API latency
  • CPU and memory pressure
  • Lock contention
  • Uneven job execution times
  • Whether requests are arriving in bursts

The goal is to identify the actual bottleneck instead of simply increasing the number of workers.

11. Testing Queueing Behavior

A worker pool that works correctly with 10 requests may behave very differently with 10,000.

Load tests should examine more than maximum throughput.

I'd test at least four scenarios.

1. Normal load

Run below expected capacity and establish baseline latency, throughput, and resource usage.

2. Near-saturation load

Gradually increase arrival rate toward service capacity. Observe how queue wait and p99 latency change.

3. Burst traffic

Send a large number of requests in a short interval. Verify that the queue remains bounded and overload behavior is predictable.

4. Dependency slowdown

Artificially increase downstream service time. Observe whether concurrency, queue depth, and rejection rates remain controlled.

For a Go worker pool, also test:

  • Queue-full behavior
  • Cancellation before execution
  • Shutdown while workers are active
  • Jobs that ignore context cancellation
  • Worker panics, if panic recovery is part of the design
  • Concurrent submission during shutdown

A particularly important test is whether your service continues accepting work after its useful processing capacity has been exhausted.

A successful load test isn't necessarily one where every request is accepted.

Sometimes the better result is a system that rejects excess work quickly while keeping accepted requests within their latency objectives.

12. A Practical Checklist

Before deploying a queue-based Go service, ask:

  • Is the queue bounded?
  • Is the queue capacity based on a latency budget?
  • Do we measure queue wait time separately from processing time?
  • Can requests be rejected when the system is saturated?
  • Do jobs respect context cancellation?
  • Can shutdown stop workers without leaking goroutines?
  • Are downstream connection pools and concurrency limits understood?
  • Do we monitor queue depth and oldest-job age?
  • Have we tested burst traffic and dependency slowdown?
  • Are we optimizing useful throughput rather than simply maximizing accepted requests?

These questions help turn queueing theory into concrete engineering decisions.

Conclusion

Queueing theory explains something that's easy to overlook when building backend services:

A request doesn't need to be expensive to become slow. It only needs to wait.

Little's Law helps us reason about concurrency and latency. Utilization explains why waiting time increases rapidly near capacity. Bounded queues and admission control give us ways to prevent uncontrolled accumulation of work.

In Go, goroutines and channels make it relatively easy to build concurrent systems. But concurrency itself isn't a capacity-planning strategy.

The important questions are:

  • How much work enters the system?
  • How quickly can the system complete it?
  • How much work can wait?
  • How long can that work remain useful?
  • What happens when demand exceeds capacity?

A reliable service doesn't need to accept every request.

It needs to process accepted work predictably, protect its dependencies, and fail fast when it can no longer meet its latency objectives.

The goal isn't to keep every worker busy. It's to keep the system healthy and useful under load.

References

  • Little's Law as Viewed on its 50th Anniversary — INFORMS
  • MIT — Queueing Models and Little's Law
  • Amdahl's Law for Tail Latency — Communications of the ACM
  • Go Documentation — Context
  • Go Documentation — Go Memory Model

title: Solana RPC error -32015: why 4 in 10 transactions vanish from your app
description:
If your Solana code logs this:

Transaction version (1) is not supported by the requesting client.
Please try the request again with the following configuration parameter: "maxSupportedTransactionVersion": 1

your code asked the RPC for transactions up to version 0 and the one it wanted is version 1. The RPC refuses it instead of answering.

Why it matters now

Version 1 transactions went live on mainnet on 2026-09-15 (the first one we found is in slot 447,120,004). In sampled mainnet blocks they were 13.8% of non-vote transactions the week of Sep 14 and 41.9% from Oct 16 to 30 (44.4% of swaps). Whether you see one depends only on which wallet or SDK the sender used, so a payment can fail for one customer and work for the next.

We reported this bug in 30+ open-source projects. Six maintainers have already fixed it: Agent402, elizaOS, UltiMafia, rotki, taurvia and sol-parser-sdk-nodejs.

The fix 

// @solana/web3.js 1.99.0 or later (1.98.x throws on version 1 even with this setting)
const tx = await connection.getTransaction(signature, { maxSupportedTransactionVersion: 1 });

client.get_transaction(signature, max_supported_transaction_version=1)

let config = RpcTransactionConfig { max_supported_transaction_version: Some(1), ..Default::default() };

Same for getParsedTransaction(s) and getBlock.

Which library versions can read version 1

Tested on mainnet on 2026-10-30 against a real version 1 transaction:

  • @solana/web3.js 1.95.8 to 1.98.4: throw, even when asked correctly. 1.99.0+ works.
  • @solana/kit before 7.1.0 returns version as the bigint 1n, so version === 1 is false. 7.1.0+ works.
  • solana-py 0.30.2 to 0.41.0 works with max_supported_transaction_version=1.

Traps

  • getParsedTransactions / getTransactions throw for the whole batch when one entry fails: one version 1 payment hides 49 others.
  • Code that catches the error and returns null reports a paid transaction as "not found".
  • Raw version 1 bytes start with 0x81, so hand-written parsers break too.

Full page, with a live checker for any signature: https://solana-pulse-gateway-1021990235790.us-central1.run.app/fix/transaction-version-not-supported

title: SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control
description:
arXiv:2609.11752v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: For industrial content risk control, the real deployment constraint is not average accuracy but how much risk can be auto-handled under high precision and second-level latency. We present SIRF (Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model), which internalizes a platform's complex policies, synthesized without additional human annotation via EntiGraph, MAGA rewriting and account-level chain-of-thought (CoT), into the weights via continued pretraining (CPT), so rules are applied at high precision under an ultra-low-latency, verdict-only deployment. A controlled same-source comparison (Qwen3-8B-SFT vs. SIRF-8B-SFT, identical policy injection and verdict-only output form, differing only in policy-grounded CPT) attributes the gain to internalization: SIRF-8B-SFT reaches 71.3% Black Recall@P95, +15.1pp over the baseline, using only ~70M CPT tokens without harming general ability, and among included, logprob-available models under this interface it matches or exceeds far larger systems. SIRF is deployed as a tree-model adjudication layer (20% more mis-penalized samples recovered) and transfers to a freezing scenario at low cost (~70% relative mis-penalization reduction).

title: Why PostHog Left DuckDB at 2 PB (and How to Check Your DuckLake Catalog)
description:
At PostHog, writing to a single DuckLake table took more than three minutes. Most of that time went to statistics for tables that no longer existed.

That detail, from PostHog's post about moving their warehouse off DuckDB, is the most useful thing I've read about DuckDB's limits at scale this year. It also makes "DuckDB doesn't scale" look like a lazy takeaway, because the query engine held up fine. What broke was DuckLake's metadata layer, the one-machine sizing model, and the Postgres wire protocol, once all of them were serving a multi-tenant cloud product at 2 PB. PostHog is moving the warehouse to its own build of Trino.

I'll go through their numbers first. Further down are two SQL queries that tell you whether your own DuckLake catalog is heading the same way, and a checklist for when staying on DuckDB is still the right call.

Five months from DuckDB launch to Trino migration

On June 29, 2026, PostHog published Why we rebuilt our data warehouse on DuckDB over ClickHouse. They had sound reasons. Warehouse modeling queries can run for hours or days, which their shared ClickHouse cluster couldn't support. ClickHouse also has no cost-based optimizer, so you can't just hand it declarative SQL and trust the plan. Each org got its own DuckDB instance that slept when idle, a Postgres-wire endpoint, and DuckLake as the catalog on S3.

On November 2, 2026, the follow-up landed. They had been re-architecting without DuckDB for three months and were moving to their own build of Trino with a custom table format called HogLake.

So the DuckDB era lasted about five months, and Hacker News noticed. One commenter asked why you can't "foresee such issues" with mock data at the target size. Another called it a recruiting post. The author (roboben) gave a pretty candid answer: "we underestimated the problem and complexity of workloads our customers want to run," and admitted to some sunk-cost thinking.

Before anyone writes "PostHog dumps DuckDB", two things from the thread. The founder said the warehouse was "used by a handful of pilot customers", and ClickHouse "is serving all of our analytical queries." Only the warehouse product is moving.

2 PB, 15.3 million snapshots, 3-minute writes

At the point they moved, PostHog's own data in DuckLake was roughly:

Metric Value
Data ~2 PB
Rows ~1 trillion
Snapshots 15.3 million
Single-table write latency 3+ minutes
Catalog stats rows belonging to deleted tables over 99%
Speedup after cleaning those rows 30–50x faster writes
Customer pod size (from HN) 46 vCPUs / 360 GB, and they asked for more
Longest queries (from HN) 12 hours

The write latency is the number I keep coming back to. According to the post, "every commit re-read the statistics for the entire catalog." So commit cost scales with the whole catalog, not with the table you're writing to. Pile up dropped tables and millions of snapshots and every insert pays for the dead ones too.

PostHog cleaned the dead rows and got the 30–50x speedup. Then the rows grew back. When a cleanup job has to keep up with your catalog's own growth, I'd call that a design problem.

They listed three more DuckLake issues:

  • The catalog schema has to stay portable across SQL databases, which rules out engine-specific tuning on Postgres.
  • DuckLake opens a lot of connections to the metadata database, and on shared Postgres each one costs something.
  • They couldn't get changes upstream fast enough, so they ran a fork. Once you're on a fork, you've lost most of the community benefit you picked an open format for.

Where single-node DuckDB stops scaling

This is the part that's actually about DuckDB. A single-node engine has to be sized before the query arrives. PostHog couldn't predict CPU and memory per query, customers sent heavier queries than expected, and adding disks for spill would have made queries "too slow and expensive to be viable."

On one laptop or one big VM this doesn't matter, because you know your own workload. It does matter when you're a vendor holding thousands of tenants' unknown SQL and have to pick an instance size in advance. A distributed engine like Trino handles this by spreading work across workers, and you pay for that elsewhere: roboben also said on HN that "Trino is not made for fast response times." They plan to use it for long modeling jobs and nightly ETL.

Why DuckDB over the Postgres wire protocol hurt

The third issue had nothing to do with query speed. Exposing DuckDB over port 5432 meant dealing with missing reconnects, TTLs, idle connections, expensive long-lived sessions, and much thinner load-balancing tooling than HTTP has. HTTP headers let them route requests in Kubernetes. Every Postgres client also turned out to expect its own niche behavior, and "coverage never got good enough."

If you're thinking of putting a pgwire shim in front of an embedded engine so your BI tool can connect, read that paragraph again first.

DuckDB vs Trino vs ClickHouse: where each one wins

Even in the exit post, PostHog calls DuckDB "probably the best single-node tool for analyzing heaps of data," and says it "almost always finishes your query." I agree. Based on this case, this is how I'd split the three:

DuckDB (+ DuckLake) ClickHouse Trino
Shape Embedded, single node Server cluster Distributed MPP, coordinator + workers
Best at Analyst work, notebooks, local Parquet, CI jobs Fast queries over huge event tables Long, heavy joins over lake data
Optimizer Cost-based No cost-based optimizer (per PostHog) Cost-based
Breaks when Query size is unpredictable or bigger than one box Hours-long tenant queries share a cluster You need low-latency interactive answers
PostHog uses it for Nothing in the warehouse anymore All product analytics New warehouse (with HogLake)

Signs you've outgrown DuckDB (and how to check your DuckLake catalog)

Stay on DuckDB if you're one team on one machine, you roughly know your query sizes, and the data fits on one big box's disk plus S3 reads. That covers most people who argue about this online.

You're getting close to PostHog's wall if several of these are true:

  1. You're sizing instances for SQL other people write and you can't predict its memory use.
  2. Queries regularly spill to disk and spill time is now the slowest part.
  3. You run DuckLake with heavy table churn: lots of CREATE/DROP, frequent small commits, snapshot counts in the millions.
  4. Commit latency is rising even though the batches stay the same size.
  5. You're serving many clients over pgwire and spend more time on connection handling than on queries.
  6. You're carrying patches in a fork.

If item 3 or 4 sounds familiar, measure it before you panic. These queries run against your DuckLake metadata database (Postgres in PostHog's case) and use table names from the DuckLake spec:

-- how many snapshots are you carrying?
SELECT count(*) FROM ducklake_snapshot;

-- what share of column stats rows belong to tables with no live version?
SELECT round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE live.table_id IS NULL) / NULLIF(count(*), 0), 1) AS pct_dead
FROM ducklake_table_column_stats s
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT table_id FROM ducklake_table WHERE end_snapshot IS NULL) live
  USING (table_id);

Then set up the maintenance the DuckLake docs recommend instead of letting snapshots accumulate:

CALL my_ducklake.set_option('expire_older_than', '1 month');
CALL ducklake_expire_snapshots('my_ducklake', dry_run => true, older_than => now() - INTERVAL '1 week');
CALL ducklake_expire_snapshots('my_ducklake', older_than => now() - INTERVAL '1 week');
CALL ducklake_cleanup_old_files('my_ducklake', older_than => now() - INTERVAL '1 week');

Plus an occasional VACUUM on the Postgres catalog, which the docs say is likely enough there. The expire-snapshots docs say expiry also cleans up metadata for dropped objects, which is the kind of row PostHog was drowning in. Nothing in PostHog's post says expiry would have fixed their problem, though; they cleaned those rows and they came back. I'd still keep the snapshot count low. It costs you nothing, and 15.3 million is not a number you want to see in your own catalog.

My take

Picking DuckDB was defensible. The trouble started when PostHog used an embedded engine as a multi-tenant cloud service, put all of PostHog into a young metadata format at petabyte scale as the warehouse's first customer, and exposed it over the hardest-to-scale protocol available. You can get away with any one of those, but doing all three at once with 1 trillion rows is what broke.

What worries me more is the fix. HogLake is another in-house table format, and HN raised that right away ("making the same mistake again"). Roboben said Delta and Iceberg "had other downsides" for them but didn't explain what those were. I'd like that post more than this one.

So: how far have you pushed DuckDB before it broke? Was it memory, spill, DuckLake commits, or has it simply never broken for you? If you think PostHog should have stuck with ClickHouse on Iceberg, make the case in the comments.

Sources

  • Why we're moving our warehouse off DuckDB, PostHog, Nov 2, 2026
  • Why we rebuilt our data warehouse on DuckDB over ClickHouse, PostHog, Jun 29, 2026
  • Hacker News discussion
  • DuckLake recommended maintenance, expire snapshots, cleanup of files
  • DuckLake catalog specification
  • PostHog's DuckLake fork

title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
description:
arXiv:2610.41304v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

title: Why We Ditched Electron for Tauri 2 + Rust to Build an On-Device AI Canvas
description:
When building a desktop knowledge workspace that integrates local LLMs (Ollama) and on-device machine learning, the conventional shortcut is obvious: spin up an Electron wrapper, bundle an embedded Chromium runtime, and ship.

After all, almost every major desktop AI app in 2024–2026 is an Electron shell.

However, after running into severe memory ceilings and thermal throttling during heavy research sessions, we decided to build Knovum on a radically different stack: Tauri 2, Vue 3, and a compiled Rust backend.

Here is an honest engineering breakdown of what we gained, the hardest technical problems we had to solve (including running ONNX OCR on CPU without Python), and why we'll never go back to Electron.

1. The Real Cost of Electron: The 800MB Memory Baseline

Local AI introduces a resource constraint that web apps never faced:
Model weights live in physical memory (RAM / VRAM).

If a user runs a 7B or 8B parameter model via Ollama (e.g., Llama 3.2 or Qwen 2.5), that model demands 4.5GB–6GB of RAM. If the user is on an 8GB or 16GB MacBook or standard laptop, every megabyte of desktop overhead directly competes with the model's context window.

Metric Typical Electron AI Wrapper Knovum (Tauri 2 + Rust + Vue 3)
Idle RAM Usage 650MB – 950MB ~42MB – 48MB
Cold Boot Latency 2.8s – 4.5s ~350ms
Binary Installer Size 180MB – 250MB ~38MB compressed
IPC Serialization JSON stringify over IPC channel Zero-copy binary buffers & Rust channels

By delegating web rendering to the OS-native engine (WKWebView on macOS, WebView2 on Windows) and keeping the heavy lifting in compiled Rust, Knovum leaves 98% of your computer's memory free for local LLMs and vector math.

2. Solving On-Device OCR Without Bundling 4GB of Python

A major use case for desktop research is reading scanned PDFs, receipts, book pages, and whiteboard screenshots.

Most "local" OCR solutions either:

  1. Shell out to a cloud vision model (destroying user privacy and requiring subscription API keys).
  2. Bundle a full Python environment with PyTorch or PaddlePaddle, resulting in a multi-gigabyte installer and broken virtual environments.

In Knovum, we solved this by running PP-OCRv6 directly via the ONNX Runtime CPU worker in Rust:

  • Fixed & Pinned Model: We pinned the PP-OCRv6 ONNX weights with SHA-256 verification, downloaded once on first run.
  • Background Worker Priority: The text recognition job runs asynchronously on a dedicated worker pool with background scheduling priority, consuming zero GPU compute and avoiding any UI lag.
  • Locator Binding: Recognized text lines are bound directly to their physical locator (e.g. page: 3, line: 12 or image: whiteboard_1). When the local LLM generates an answer, its citations point directly to these coordinates.

3. In-Canvas PDF Reading with Highlight Anchors

When an AI quotes an 80-page document, the biggest UX failure is the "citation disconnect" — reading an abstract text chunk without being able to verify the original context.

We lazy-load an in-app pdf.js viewer directly onto the infinite 2D canvas:

  • When a user clicks a citation in an AI response, the viewer opens directly to the exact page and paints an active highlight over the quoted passage.
  • 48-Character Anchor Fallback: Because OCR text can occasionally drift by a character or two compared to layout text, we compute 48-character sliding anchor hashes. Even if whitespace or ligatures vary, the highlight reliably lands on the exact visual paragraph.

4. Open Standards: Why We Adopted JSON Canvas (.canvas)

SaaS knowledge tools love locking your notes into proprietary database blobs. If the startup shuts down or hikes pricing, your structured thoughts are trapped.

Knovum stores every visual board directly as an open JSON Canvas (.canvas) file on your local filesystem.

  • You can open the exact same canvas file in Obsidian Canvas.
  • Notes and relations live in clean, queryable local SQLite tables with numbered migrations.
  • Vector search runs locally via embedded LanceDB.

Summary & What's Next

Building with Tauri 2 and Rust requires disciplined architecture — there are no sloppy web shortcuts, and memory lifetimes must be handled deliberately. But the payoff is immense: a fluid, instant, 45MB desktop canvas that respects privacy and runs completely offline.

Knovum is source-available and free for personal & research use.

We’d love to hear your thoughts, feedback, and architecture critiques!

⭐ GitHub: https://github.com/madebyzan/knovum
📦 Releases (macOS DMG & Windows Setup): https://github.com/madebyzan/knovum/releases/latest

title: Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute, allowing connectors to reach providers with IP allowlists, such as Salesforce and Snowflake.

With Secure Compute routing enabled, Connect’s provider requests use the selected network’s dedicated static IP addresses instead of Connect’s shared IPs. Requests to obtain and refresh access tokens follow that route; your app’s direct API routing is unchanged by this setting. Credential management stays the same, so you don’t need to store long-lived provider secrets in your app or build OAuth flows yourself.

To enable Secure Compute routing for a supported connector and all projects that use it:

  • Open your connector’s Settings in the Vercel dashboard.

  • Under Secure Compute Routing, choose an existing network.

  • If your provider uses an IP allowlist, add the selected network’s displayed IP addresses to it in the provider’s settings.

  • Save your changes in Connect.

Requests for initial connector creation and all provider discovery requests bypass the selected network and connect directly to providers. If the selected network is unavailable, routed requests fail instead of falling back to Connect’s shared IPs.

Read the Secure Compute routing documentation for configuration details.

Read more

title: How many fields does an inquiry form need before sales can quote?
description:
A buyer types "please send price for 500 pcs" into a contact form late at night. The next morning a rep replies with a list of questions: which model, which country, when do you need it. The buyer answers two days later, or doesn't, and somewhere in between a competitor sent a number.

Making the form longer does not fix that, and neither does making it shorter. The useful question is narrower: which answers does a price depend on? Everything else can move into the reply.

Write the quote before you design the form

Get the person who actually quotes prices to produce three quotes for three recent inquiries, from scratch, without reopening the original email thread. Note every question they had to answer in order to reach a number. That list is your field list, and it is usually shorter than the form you already have.

It tends to come out as five items: what the item is, how many, where it ships, when it is needed, and an address that reaches a human. Everything else is comfort.

Give each candidate field a job

Question Can the quote be produced without it? First form?
Model or part number No Required
Quantity No Required
Delivery country and city No — freight and tax move with it Required
Rough timing Sometimes Dropdown, with an empty default
Working email address No — there is nowhere to send the quote Required
Company name Only if you sell to companies exclusively Required in B2B, optional otherwise
Contact name No Optional
Phone No Optional, never required
Free-text message No Optional, marked as optional
Budget No — and asking too early costs the inquiry Leave out
How did you hear about us No Leave out, or ask on the thank-you page
Tax or VAT number No, that is an onboarding step Leave out

The test for anything not on this list: if a blank answer would not stop the quote, it belongs in the reply, not on the form. Budget is the one field people insist on and buyers rarely answer honestly at first contact — if the number matters, ask after you have shown you understand the requirement.

Friction is rarely the field count

Six clean fields convert better than four bad ones. What kills inquiries:

A required phone number, on a form used by buyers in another country who do not want a call. A country dropdown with every territory in it, on a phone. A required company name when the buyer is an individual sourcing one sample. A field that only accepts uploads, which fail on mobile data and give no feedback when they do. Validation that clears the form on error. A blank thank-you page that does not say what happens next.

Every one of those is fixable without removing a question sales needs.

The form itself

Plain HTML, labels outside the inputs, input types that bring up the right keyboard on a phone:

<form action="/inquiry" method="post">
  <label for="email">Work email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required>

  <label for="company">Company <span>(optional)</span></label>
  <input id="company" name="company" type="text" autocomplete="organization">

  <label for="item">Model or part number</label>
  <input id="item" name="item" type="text" required>

  <label for="qty">Quantity</label>
  <input id="qty" name="qty" type="text" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="off" required>

  <label for="dest">Delivery country and city</label>
  <input id="dest" name="dest" type="text" autocomplete="address-level2" required>

  <label for="when">When do you need it?</label>
  <select id="when" name="when">
    <option value="">Not sure yet</option>
    <option value="2w">Within two weeks</option>
    <option value="1m">This month</option>
    <option value="1q">This quarter</option>
  </select>

  <label for="notes">Anything else <span>(optional)</span></label>
  <textarea id="notes" name="notes" rows="4"></textarea>

  <p class="hp" aria-hidden="true">
    <label for="website">Website</label>
    <input id="website" name="website" type="text" tabindex="-1" autocomplete="off">
  </p>

  <button type="submit">Get a quote</button>
</form>

<style>
  .hp { position: absolute; left: -9999px; }
</style>

Notes on the choices. Quantity is type="text" with inputmode="numeric" rather than type="number", because number inputs change value on a scroll wheel and reject the way people write quantities. The timing dropdown has an empty first option so nobody is pushed into a false answer. The honeypot replaces a captcha: reject the submission server-side if website is not empty, and skip the whole puzzle that real buyers fail on a train.

If a file matters — a drawing, a bill of materials, a photo of a damaged part — ask for it in the confirmation, not on the form. By then the buyer has committed, and a link is easier than a failing upload widget.

Keep the form to one column on every screen size. Preserve what was typed when a validation error fires, and put the error next to the field that caused it.

Say what happens after submit

The thank-you page is part of the form. Two things belong on it: what you will send and when, and the one or two details that would speed it up if they have them to hand. "We reply within one working day with a price and lead time. If you have a drawing or a target price, send it to this address and we will include it."

That single paragraph removes most of the second round trip without adding a field.

Read the messages for a fortnight

The free-text box is a research tool. Read every message that arrives for two weeks and count how often the same question appears — "do you ship to X", "is this the same as model Y". Anything asked repeatedly is either a missing field, a missing explanation on the product page, or a shipping restriction nobody wrote down. Fix the page before you fix the form.

What to measure afterwards

The share of inquiries where the first reply could be the quote itself, with no clarifying email. And the share that reach your order system without anyone re-keying or chasing a missing detail. If both stay flat after trimming fields, the problem is upstream of the form — usually the product pages do not state what the buyer needs to know to describe their requirement.

Hand this to whoever builds it

  • Required: model or part number, quantity, delivery country and city, email.
  • Optional and visibly marked optional: company, name, free text.
  • No required phone number, no required budget, no captcha, no required upload.
  • Timing as a dropdown with an honest "not sure yet" option.
  • Validation that keeps the typed values, with the error beside the field.
  • A thank-you page that states the reply time and asks for attachments by return.
  • Someone reads the free-text box weekly for the first month.

title: TypeSafe AI's Jev now available on AI Gateway
description:
Jev from TypeSafe AI is now available on AI Gateway.

Jev is a probabilistic decision model for software: state goes in, typed Choice, Score, and Boolean answers come out.

Regular language models generate text one token at a time, which the application then parses and validates. Jev evaluates all declared questions in parallel and returns typed answers plus probabilities directly. That removes unnecessary text generation and makes it straightforward to automate clear cases while routing uncertain ones to review.

TypeSafe reports Jev was up to 193.6x faster and 444.6x cheaper than LLMs on its workflow evaluations. Example use cases include:

  • Choosing the next tool or subagent in an agent loop

  • Deciding whether to continue, retry, ask the user, or stop

  • Scoring urgency or risk before an action

  • Verifying model outputs and enforcing guardrails.

AI SDK 7 exposes Jev through the experimental evaluate API. Choice selects an option, Score grades an ordered rubric, and Boolean estimates the probability of true. Install the current AI SDK (AI SDK 7.0.105 onwards supports the evaluate API):

Each evaluation specifies:

  • model: the evaluation model to call,

  • state: the shared string, object, or array to evaluate, and

  • questions: a map of named decisions to make about that state.

Call the model with typesafe-ai/jev. This example turns one support case into a queue, priority, and refund-review decision, with uncertain routing sent for manual review:

The result preserves question IDs and Choice keys. TypeSafe reports separate Choice and Score confidence in result.providerMetadata.typesafe.confidence. Calibrate probabilities and confidence against labeled examples from your workflow.

Jev supports Zero Data Retention and No Training, enabled per request in the example. Evaluation calls also appear in logs and custom reporting, count toward budgets, and accept other Gateway provider options in the same providerOptions.gateway object.

Read the documentation on evaluation models on AI Gateway for more details, discover practical use cases for Jev, and browse resources in the knowledge base.
