title: React Mastery Series — Part 1: React Fundamentals — From Zero to Components
description:
Welcome to the React Mastery Series!

This series is designed to take you from understanding the fundamentals of React to building modern, maintainable, and production-ready applications.

Whether you're a JavaScript developer exploring React for the first time or someone looking to strengthen your frontend fundamentals, this series will help you understand not only how React works, but also why it works the way it does.

In this first article, we'll focus on the foundations:

  • What React is
  • Why React was created
  • The problems React solves
  • Declarative vs. imperative programming
  • Understanding the DOM
  • Single Page Applications
  • The component-based architecture
  • Creating your first React application
  • Building your first components

Let's get started!

Table of Contents

  1. What Is React?
  2. Why Was React Created?
  3. The Problem with Traditional DOM Manipulation
  4. Declarative vs. Imperative Programming
  5. What Is the DOM?
  6. What Is a Single Page Application?
  7. React Is a Library, Not a Framework
  8. The Component-Based Architecture
  9. Understanding React's Rendering Process
  10. Setting Up Your React Environment
  11. Creating Your First React Application
  12. Understanding the Project Structure
  13. Your First React Component
  14. Component Composition
  15. Practical Example: Building a User Profile
  16. Understanding React's Mental Model
  17. Common Beginner Mistakes
  18. What We Learned
  19. What's Next?
  1. What Is React?

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces.

It was originally developed at Facebook, now Meta, and is used to create interactive web applications.

React allows developers to build interfaces using reusable pieces called components.

Instead of manually updating individual DOM elements whenever something changes, React lets us describe what the UI should look like based on the current data.

Consider a simple website:

Hello World

This is straightforward HTML.

Now imagine a dashboard containing:

  • A navigation bar
  • A sidebar
  • A profile section
  • A list of products
  • Notifications
  • Search functionality
  • Interactive filters

Managing all of these elements manually can become difficult.

React helps us organize the interface into smaller, reusable components.

For example:

function App() {
return (






);
}

Each component represents a specific part of the interface.

This makes applications easier to maintain, reuse, and scale.

  1. Why Was React Created?

To understand React, we first need to understand the problems developers faced when building complex interfaces.

Imagine you're building an online shopping application.

The interface contains:

  • A product list
  • A shopping cart
  • A total price
  • A checkout button

When a user adds a product to the cart, several things need to change:

  1. The cart contents update.
  2. The number of items changes.
  3. The total price changes.
  4. The UI reflects the new data.

Using traditional DOM manipulation, you might manually update each element.

const cartCount = document.querySelector(".cart-count");

cartCount.textContent = 3;

This works for simple applications.

However, imagine dozens of components depending on the same data.

Now you must carefully coordinate every DOM update.

This creates several problems:

  • UI logic becomes scattered.
  • DOM updates become difficult to maintain.
  • Bugs become harder to track.
  • Components become tightly coupled.
  • Reusing UI logic becomes more complicated.

React provides a different approach.

Instead of manually updating every affected element, you update the application state and describe the UI based on that state.

React handles the necessary rendering work.

  1. The Problem with Traditional DOM Manipulation

Let's build a small example using plain JavaScript.

0


Increment

JavaScript:

const countElement = document.getElementById("count");

const button = document.getElementById("increment");

let count = 0;

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
count++;

countElement.textContent = count;
});

This is perfectly valid JavaScript.

But notice what we are doing:

  • Keeping track of the count manually.
  • Finding the DOM element.
  • Listening for an event.
  • Updating the DOM manually.

For a small example, this is fine.

But imagine an application with hundreds of interactive elements.

You would need to manually synchronize:

  • Application data
  • DOM elements
  • Event handlers
  • UI states

This is where maintaining consistency becomes difficult.

React changes this approach by making the UI a function of data.

Conceptually:

Application State
↓
React Components
↓
UI

When the state changes, React determines what needs to be updated.

  1. Declarative vs. Imperative Programming

This is one of the most important concepts to understand before learning React.

Imperative Programming

Imperative programming describes how to perform a task.

You provide instructions step by step.

Example:

const heading = document.createElement("h1");

heading.textContent = "Hello React";

document.body.appendChild(heading);

We explicitly tell the browser:

  1. Create an element.
  2. Set its text.
  3. Add it to the document.

Declarative Programming

Declarative programming describes what the result should look like.

function App() {
return

Hello React

;
}

We describe the desired UI.

React handles the underlying DOM operations.

The difference

Imperative| Declarative
Describes how to do something| Describes what should happen
Requires manual DOM operations| React manages DOM updates
UI logic can become scattered| UI is described through components
Developer coordinates updates| React manages rendering

React's declarative model becomes especially powerful when the UI depends on changing data.

  1. What Is the DOM?

DOM stands for Document Object Model.

When a browser loads an HTML document, it creates a structured representation of that document.

For example:


Hello


Welcome to React



The browser represents this document as a tree.

Conceptually:

Document
|
└── html
|
└── body
|
└── div
|
├── h1
|
└── p

This structure allows JavaScript to interact with the document.

For example:

document.querySelector("h1").textContent = "Updated";

This changes the DOM.

React works with the browser DOM through its rendering system.

You usually don't need to manipulate DOM elements manually when building ordinary React interfaces.

  1. What Is a Single Page Application?

A Single Page Application, or SPA, is a web application that typically loads an initial HTML document and then updates its interface dynamically as users interact with it.

Traditional multi-page applications often navigate by requesting a new HTML document from the server.

In a typical SPA:

  1. The browser loads the application.
  2. JavaScript initializes the UI.
  3. User interactions update the interface.
  4. Navigation may happen without a full document reload.

For example:

User opens application
↓
Initial HTML loads
↓
JavaScript initializes
↓
React renders the UI
↓
User interacts
↓
UI updates

React is commonly used to build SPAs.

However, React is not limited to SPAs.

React can also be used with frameworks such as Next.js that support server rendering and other rendering strategies.

  1. React Is a Library, Not a Framework

This distinction is important.

React focuses primarily on building user interfaces.

It provides:

  • Components
  • Rendering
  • State
  • Hooks
  • UI composition

But React itself doesn't prescribe a complete solution for every application concern.

For example, React doesn't include a complete built-in routing system.

You may use additional tools:

Requirement| Common Solution
UI| React
Routing| React Router
Server rendering| Next.js or another framework
Client state| React state, Zustand, Redux Toolkit
Server state| TanStack Query
Forms| React Hook Form
Styling| CSS, Tailwind CSS, CSS Modules

You don't need all these tools when starting React.

Learn React fundamentals first.

  1. The Component-Based Architecture

Components are the foundation of React.

A component is a reusable piece of UI.

For example, a website might contain:

Application
│
├── Navbar
│
├── Sidebar
│
├── Dashboard
│ ├── Statistics
│ ├── Chart
│ └── RecentActivity
│
└── Footer

Each part can be implemented as a separate component.

This approach is called component-based architecture.

Why components?

Components help us:

  • Reuse UI
  • Separate responsibilities
  • Organize code
  • Maintain applications
  • Build complex interfaces from smaller pieces

Imagine building a dashboard without components.

You might end up with one enormous function containing hundreds of lines of JSX.

With components, each section can have its own logic and structure.

A component should have a clear responsibility

For example:

function Navbar() {
return

Navigation;
}

function Footer() {
return

Footer;
}

function App() {
return (
<>

Main content

</>
);
}

This is easier to understand than placing everything inside one component.

  1. Understanding React's Rendering Process

At a high level, React applications follow this pattern:

State or Props Change
↓
React Renders Components
↓
React Determines Necessary Updates
↓
React Commits Updates
↓
Browser Displays the UI

Let's simplify this.

Imagine a counter displaying:

0

The user clicks a button.

The state changes to:

1

React renders the component again using the new state.

React then determines what changes are necessary in the browser DOM.

The important idea is:

You describe the UI. React manages the rendering process.

Rendering a component does not necessarily mean that React changes the DOM.

React may render a component and determine that the resulting DOM is unchanged.

We'll explore rendering and reconciliation in more detail later in this series.

  1. Setting Up Your React Environment

Before creating a React application, make sure you have Node.js installed.

Node.js allows JavaScript tools to run outside the browser.

Check your versions:

node -v
npm -v

You should see version numbers.

If Node.js is not installed, download it from the official website:

https://nodejs.org

For modern React development, Vite is a common choice.

Vite provides:

  • A development server
  • Fast startup
  • Hot Module Replacement
  • Build tooling
  1. Creating Your First React Application

Let's create a React project using Vite.

Run:

npm create vite@latest react-mastery

Choose:

Framework: React
Variant: JavaScript

If you want TypeScript, choose the TypeScript variant instead.

Then:

cd react-mastery
npm install
npm run dev

Vite will start a development server.

You can open the local URL displayed in your terminal.

Your application should now be running.

What is Hot Module Replacement?

Hot Module Replacement, or HMR, allows Vite to update parts of your application during development without requiring a complete page reload in many situations.

This makes the development experience faster.

For example, when you change a component, Vite can update the application while preserving certain existing state.

  1. Understanding the Project Structure

A typical Vite React project looks like this:

react-mastery/
│
├── public/
│
├── src/
│ ├── assets/
│ ├── App.jsx
│ ├── App.css
│ ├── index.css
│ └── main.jsx
│
├── index.html
├── package.json
└── vite.config.js

Let's understand the important files.

App.jsx

This is usually where the main application component lives.

function App() {
return

Hello React

;
}

export default App;

main.jsx

This is the entry point that connects React to the browser DOM.

import { StrictMode } from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";

import App from "./App.jsx";

createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render(



);

index.html

Vite provides an HTML document containing a root element.

React renders the application inside this element.

  1. Your First React Component

Let's create a simple component.

function Welcome() {
return

Welcome to React!

;
}

export default Welcome;

This is a React function component.

Let's break it down.

function Welcome()

We define a JavaScript function named "Welcome".

return

Welcome to React!

;

The function returns JSX.

React uses this returned description to render the UI.

Now use the component in "App.jsx":

import Welcome from "./Welcome";

function App() {
return (




);
}

export default App;

Notice the syntax:

We use the component like a JSX element.

This is one of the fundamental ideas of React.

  1. Component Composition

Component composition means combining smaller components to create larger interfaces.

Let's create three components.

function Header() {
return

My Application;
}

function MainContent() {
return

Welcome to the dashboard;
}

function Footer() {
return

© 2026 My Application;
}

Now compose them:

function App() {
return (
<>




</>
);
}

The final interface is created from smaller components.

This approach makes your code easier to read and maintain.

Why not create one giant component?

A giant component often becomes difficult to:

  • Understand
  • Debug
  • Test
  • Reuse
  • Maintain

Breaking it into smaller components improves organization.

However, don't create a component for every single HTML element.

Components should represent meaningful pieces of UI or reusable behavior.

  1. Practical Example: Building a User Profile

Let's build a small React application using multiple components.

Step 1: Create the Profile component

function Profile() {
return (


src="https://placehold.co/100"
alt="User avatar"
/> 
  <h2>Hamed Farazi</h2>

  <p>Frontend Developer</p>

  <button>View Profile</button>
</div>

);
}

export default Profile;

Step 2: Create the App component

import Profile from "./Profile";

function App() {
return (


Team Members

  <Profile />
</div>

);
}

export default App;

The "App" component uses the "Profile" component.

Step 3: Reuse the component

function App() {
return (


Team Members

  <Profile />
  <Profile />
  <Profile />
</div>

);
}

Now we have three profile cards.

This demonstrates component reuse.

However, all three profiles currently display the same information.

In the next part of this series, we'll learn how to make components dynamic using Props.

  1. Understanding React's Mental Model

The most important thing to understand when learning React is its mental model.

React applications are built around a few fundamental ideas:

Components describe the UI

function Greeting() {
return

Hello

;
}

Props provide inputs

function Greeting({ name }) {
return

Hello, {name}

;
}

State represents changing data

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

React renders the UI based on these inputs

Conceptually:

Props + State
↓
React Component
↓
UI

When props or state change, React can render the component again.

This is the core mental model behind React.

Instead of manually updating the interface, you describe how it should look for the current data.

  1. Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Thinking React is HTML

JSX looks like HTML, but it is JavaScript syntax transformed into JavaScript.

const element =

Hello

;

This isn't ordinary HTML.

Mistake 2: Thinking React automatically makes everything faster

React helps manage UI rendering, but it doesn't guarantee that every application will be faster than manually written JavaScript.

Performance depends on architecture, rendering behavior, and implementation.

Mistake 3: Creating one massive component

Break your UI into meaningful components.

Mistake 4: Learning advanced hooks too early

Don't begin with "useMemo", "useCallback", or complex state management.

First understand:

  • Components
  • Props
  • State
  • Events
  • Rendering

Mistake 5: Memorizing syntax without understanding the mental model

The goal isn't to memorize every React API.

The goal is to understand how React describes and updates interfaces.

  1. What We Learned

In this article, we covered the fundamentals of React:

  • React is a JavaScript library for building UIs.
  • React uses a declarative programming model.
  • Components are reusable pieces of UI.
  • React manages rendering and DOM updates.
  • JSX allows HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript.
  • React applications can be built using Vite.
  • Components can be composed to create larger interfaces.
  • Props and state will help make components dynamic.

title: General-purpose foundation models surpass specialized ones on chemical property prediction tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.41899v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Foundation models (FMs) learn reusable representations from large collections of unlabeled data. In chemistry the corresponding data mainly consists of molecular structures, which are abundant, whereas experimental measurements are scarce. Chemical FMs such as ChemBERTa and MoLFormer were therefore trained on diverse molecular structures to enable fine-tuning on small experimental datasets (less than 100 datapoints in most realistic scenarios) and subsequent property prediction. At the same time, general-purpose FMs such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were trained on virtually all publicly available data, including knowledge of the humankind on molecular properties and laws governing them. Here we compare accuracies of chemical and general-purpose FMs on tasks from various areas of chemistry. Strikingly, general-purpose GPT-6 Astra outperforms the currently eligible chemical FMs on five physicochemical and quantum-chemical regression tasks when only 60 experimental datapoints are available. Only when provided 10x datapoints do the best chemical FMs reach performance of GPT-6 Astra: on 1,000 and 10,000 points they show performance on par with Astra on 60 and 1,000 points, respectively. Thus, counterintuitively, frontier general-purpose FMs are better suited for guiding chemical research in data-scarce areas than specialized chemical FMs, suggesting that learning relevant primitives (e.g. chemical structures) does not substitute training on relevant humankind knowledge.

title: Stop Updating Stock Quantities: Build an Inventory Ledger in Laravel
description:
Ask any ERP team what their most dangerous line of code is, and many of them will point at something like this:

$product->stock -= $line->quantity;
$product->save();

It looks harmless. It is also the reason so many small and mid-sized companies have a warehouse that says 42 while the shelf says 37, and nobody can explain where the other five went.

In this post I want to show a pattern I now use in every inventory module: stock is not a number you update, it is a ledger you append to. The current quantity is just a cached sum of that ledger. The code is Laravel, but the idea works in any stack.

The problem with a quantity column

A single stock column on the products table fails in three predictable ways.

1. It has no memory. When the number is wrong, you have nothing to audit. Was it the delivery note from Tuesday? The return that was posted twice? A manual correction someone did "just to fix it"? The column only knows the latest value.

2. It races. Two requests read stock = 10, both subtract 8, both save 2. You just sold 16 units of something you had 10 of. Read-modify-write in PHP is a classic lost update.

3. It cannot answer time questions. "What was our stock at the end of September?" is a normal question from finance. With a single column the honest answer is "we don't know", or a nightly snapshot job that someone eventually forgets to fix.

Accounting solved this a few centuries ago: you never overwrite a balance, you post entries, and the balance is the sum of entries. Inventory deserves the same treatment.

Step 1: The movements table (the source of truth)

Every change in stock becomes one row: a receipt, a delivery, a return, a transfer, an inventory count adjustment.

use Illuminate\Database\Migrations\Migration;
use Illuminate\Database\Schema\Blueprint;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schema;

return new class extends Migration
{
    public function up(): void
    {
        Schema::create('stock_movements', function (Blueprint $table) {
            $table->id();
            $table->foreignId('product_id')->constrained();
            $table->foreignId('warehouse_id')->constrained();
            $table->decimal('quantity', 18, 3);          // signed: + in, - out
            $table->string('type', 32);                   // receipt, issue, transfer_in, ...
            $table->string('source_type', 64);            // goods_receipt, delivery, count, ...
            $table->unsignedBigInteger('source_id');
            $table->unsignedInteger('line_no');
            $table->dateTime('occurred_at');              // business time, not insert time
            $table->foreignId('created_by')->nullable()->constrained('users');
            $table->timestamps();

            // One document line can only hit one warehouse once.
            $table->unique(['source_type', 'source_id', 'line_no', 'warehouse_id'], 'stock_movements_source_unique');
            $table->index(['product_id', 'warehouse_id', 'occurred_at']);
        });

        Schema::create('stock_balances', function (Blueprint $table) {
            $table->foreignId('product_id')->constrained();
            $table->foreignId('warehouse_id')->constrained();
            $table->decimal('quantity', 18, 3)->default(0);
            $table->timestamps();

            $table->primary(['product_id', 'warehouse_id']);
        });
    }
};

Two details matter more than they look:

  • The unique index is your idempotency key. If a queue job or a nervous user posts the same delivery note twice, the second insert fails instead of silently doubling the movement.
  • occurred_at is business time. A goods receipt typed in on Monday for a truck that arrived on Friday belongs to Friday. created_at stays as the audit trail of when it was entered.

stock_balances is not the truth. It is a cache that makes "how many do we have right now?" a primary-key lookup instead of a SUM() over millions of rows.

Step 2: Make movements append-only

If people can edit or delete movements, you are back to a column with extra steps. Enforce it at the model level:

namespace App\Models;

use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model;
use LogicException;

class StockMovement extends Model
{
    protected $guarded = [];

    protected function casts(): array
    {
        return [
            'quantity' => 'decimal:3',
            'occurred_at' => 'immutable_datetime',
        ];
    }

    protected static function booted(): void
    {
        static::updating(fn () => throw new LogicException('Stock movements are append-only. Post a correction instead.'));
        static::deleting(fn () => throw new LogicException('Stock movements are append-only. Post a reversal instead.'));
    }
}

This does not stop someone with a SQL client, but it stops the most common source of damage: well-meaning application code. If you want a database-level guarantee, revoke UPDATE and DELETE on the table for the application's DB user.

Mistakes are fixed the way an accountant fixes them: a reversal (the same lines with the opposite sign, pointing at the original document) and, if needed, a new correct posting. The history stays complete.

Step 3: One service that posts documents

All stock changes go through one class. Controllers, jobs and imports never touch stock_balances directly.

namespace App\Inventory;

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;
use RuntimeException;

final class InsufficientStock extends RuntimeException {}

final class StockLedger
{
    /**
     * @param  array<int, array{product_id:int, warehouse_id:int, quantity:string, type:string, line_no:int}>  $lines
     */
    public function post(string $sourceType, int $sourceId, array $lines, \DateTimeInterface $occurredAt, bool $allowNegative = false): void
    {
        // Always touch rows in the same order to avoid deadlocks between documents.
        usort($lines, fn ($a, $b) => [$a['product_id'], $a['warehouse_id']] <=> [$b['product_id'], $b['warehouse_id']]);

        DB::transaction(function () use ($sourceType, $sourceId, $lines, $occurredAt, $allowNegative) {
            foreach ($lines as $line) {
                if (! is_numeric($line['quantity']) || (float) $line['quantity'] == 0.0) {
                    throw new \InvalidArgumentException("Line {$line['line_no']} needs a non-zero numeric quantity.");
                }

                DB::table('stock_movements')->insert([
                    'product_id' => $line['product_id'],
                    'warehouse_id' => $line['warehouse_id'],
                    'quantity' => $line['quantity'],
                    'type' => $line['type'],
                    'source_type' => $sourceType,
                    'source_id' => $sourceId,
                    'line_no' => $line['line_no'],
                    'occurred_at' => $occurredAt,
                    'created_by' => auth()->id(),
                    'created_at' => now(),
                    'updated_at' => now(),
                ]);

                // Make sure the balance row exists before we update it.
                DB::table('stock_balances')->insertOrIgnore([
                    'product_id' => $line['product_id'],
                    'warehouse_id' => $line['warehouse_id'],
                    'quantity' => 0,
                    'created_at' => now(),
                    'updated_at' => now(),
                ]);

                // Let the database do the arithmetic and the check in one atomic statement.
                $query = DB::table('stock_balances')
                    ->where('product_id', $line['product_id'])
                    ->where('warehouse_id', $line['warehouse_id']);

                if (! $allowNegative) {
                    $query->whereRaw('quantity + ? >= 0', [$line['quantity']]);
                }

                // increment() accepts negative amounts and returns the number of affected rows.
                $affected = $query->increment('quantity', $line['quantity'], ['updated_at' => now()]);

                if ($affected === 0) {
                    throw new InsufficientStock("Not enough stock for product {$line['product_id']} in warehouse {$line['warehouse_id']}.");
                }
            }
        }, attempts: 3);
    }
}

Why it is written this way:

  • increment() compiles to UPDATE ... SET quantity = quantity + 12.500, so the arithmetic runs in the database. No PHP read-modify-write, so no lost updates. The row lock taken by the UPDATE serializes concurrent postings for the same product and warehouse until the transaction commits.
  • The negative-stock check is part of the same statement. If the condition fails, zero rows are affected, we throw, and DB::transaction() rolls back the movements already inserted for this document. A document posts completely or not at all.
  • attempts: 3 tells Laravel to retry the closure if the database reports a deadlock. Sorting the lines makes deadlocks rare; retrying makes the rare ones harmless.
  • Quantities are strings. Pass '12.500', not 12.5. Floats and stock do not mix (more on that below).

If you need to read a balance and make a decision in PHP before writing (for example, reserving stock across several warehouses), use lockForUpdate() inside the transaction, again in a consistent order.

A transfer is simply one document with two lines:

app(StockLedger::class)->post('transfer', $transfer->id, [
    ['product_id' => 10, 'warehouse_id' => 1, 'quantity' => '-30', 'type' => 'transfer_out', 'line_no' => 1],
    ['product_id' => 10, 'warehouse_id' => 2, 'quantity' => '30', 'type' => 'transfer_in', 'line_no' => 1],
], now());

Both warehouses change in the same transaction, so stock is never "in the air".

Step 4: Answer time questions for free

Because every movement has occurred_at, historical stock is a query, not a project:

$stockAtMonthEnd = DB::table('stock_movements')
    ->where('product_id', $productId)
    ->where('warehouse_id', $warehouseId)
    ->where('occurred_at', '<', '2026-10-01 00:00:00')
    ->sum('quantity');

The same table gives you a stock card per product (running list of movements with their source documents), turnover reports and "who changed this and why" in one place. When the table grows into the millions, add monthly closing snapshots and sum only the movements after the last snapshot.

Step 5: Reconcile the cache

A cache can drift: a manual SQL fix, a bug in an old import, a restore from backup. A scheduled check catches it early:

$drift = DB::table('stock_balances as b')
    ->leftJoin('stock_movements as m', function ($join) {
        $join->on('m.product_id', '=', 'b.product_id')
             ->on('m.warehouse_id', '=', 'b.warehouse_id');
    })
    ->select('b.product_id', 'b.warehouse_id', 'b.quantity', DB::raw('COALESCE(SUM(m.quantity), 0) as ledger_quantity'))
    ->groupBy('b.product_id', 'b.warehouse_id', 'b.quantity')
    ->havingRaw('b.quantity <> COALESCE(SUM(m.quantity), 0)')
    ->get();

If $drift is not empty, alert someone. Because the ledger is the truth, the fix is always the same: recalculate the balance from the movements.

Common pitfalls

Floats. 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in PHP. Use decimal columns, pass quantities as strings and let the database do the math. If you must compute in PHP, use integer base units (grams instead of kilograms) or a decimal library.

Units of measure. If you buy in boxes of 12 and sell in pieces, convert to one base unit before posting. A ledger that mixes boxes and pieces cannot be summed.

Editing posted documents. Users will ask for an "edit" button on a delivery note that already moved stock. The ledger-friendly version of that button is: reverse the old document, post the new one. Both stay visible.

Negative stock policy. Some businesses must allow it temporarily (goods sold before the receipt is typed in). Make it an explicit, per-warehouse setting, not an accident. That is what $allowNegative is for.

Backdated postings. A movement with an old occurred_at changes historical reports. Decide on a period lock (for example, no postings into a month that finance has closed) and enforce it in StockLedger.

Forgetting the cache in tests. Write at least one test that posts random documents and then asserts that every balance equals the sum of its movements. It catches more bugs than ten hand-written cases.

Summary

  • Stop updating a stock column. Append signed movements to a ledger and treat the balance as a cache.
  • Use a unique key on the source document line to make postings idempotent.
  • Post through one service, inside one transaction, with the arithmetic and the negative check in a single UPDATE.
  • Fix mistakes with reversals, never with edits or deletes.
  • Reconcile the cache on a schedule, and enjoy historical stock reports without snapshot jobs.

I first moved an inventory module to this pattern after a stock count that did not match anything. The next count matched, and when it didn't, the stock card showed exactly which document caused it.

How does your system handle stock today: a quantity column, a ledger, or something in between?

title: How we cut CDN metadata lookup latency by 91%
description:
Every request to Vercel passes through our CDN, which executes on average over 80 million routing instructions per second. Part of that work is looking up metadata to determine which paths exist and how to serve them. When that metadata isn’t cached, the CDN has to fetch it before it can serve the response.

We used to fetch and cache metadata one path at a time, retrieving only what each lookup needed. That seemed efficient at the time, but large deployments can contain hundreds of thousands of paths, each with its own cache entry. Every new deployment introduced fresh metadata, making cache misses a recurring cost for large sites that deployed frequently.

Fetching more metadata at once made these lookups faster. By grouping paths together, each fetch could populate the cache for many subsequent lookups. But fetching too much introduced its own costs. Through production experiments, we found a balance that cut P99 metadata lookup latency by 91% and made deployments faster along the way.

How the CDN finds the right route

The path in a request doesn’t always match the path of the content or function that serves it. Framework routing rules connect the two. A request for /blog/hello-world, for example, might resolve to the dynamic route /blog/[slug]. A request for that page’s React Server Component payload might resolve to /blog/[slug].rsc. As the CDN applies these rules, it may need to check several target paths to find the right response.

The framework describes those routes during a build. With framework-defined infrastructure, application code declares which outputs are static, which need Functions, and which responses can be cached or regenerated. Frameworks translate that intent into Build Output API outputs, and Vercel generates the routing metadata the CDN reads.

At request time, the CDN needs to determine which target paths exist and retrieve their metadata. The Bloom filters we added to global routing rule out paths that definitely don’t exist. Remaining paths need an exact metadata lookup.

Originally, we stored that metadata as a separate object per target path. The CDN fetched and cached each object independently. This worked well for smaller projects that deployed infrequently. But every new deployment created a fresh set of cache keys, so the first lookup for each path missed the cache.

Fetching metadata in groups

To reduce cache misses, we grouped metadata for many paths into files called shards. We bounded each shard’s size to control how much data a lookup had to fetch. Fetching a shard brought metadata for all of its paths into the cache, so later lookups for those paths could reuse it.

Each shard also included an index that let the CDN locate an individual path’s metadata without decoding, decompressing, or parsing the other entries. Each fetch warmed many paths, while each lookup still parsed only the record it needed.

Fetching more without parsing more

We built the shards using JSONL layouts already used for other large routing datasets at Vercel. JSONL stores one JSON value per line. We borrowed the sorted, alternating key-value records from Bulk Redirects and the directly addressable Base64 data structures we first built for our Bloom filters.

We kept the data layout separate from the lookup structures over it, so each workload can pick the properties it needs:

  • Inspectable, sorted key-value JSONL records with random access

  • Optional inline indexes for low-overhead binary search

  • Embedded Base64 data with offset-based decoding

  • Bounded shards that control transfer and cache costs

Each shard stores sorted target paths and their metadata as alternating JSONL records. An inline index records where each entry begins, so the routing process can jump directly to it. These positions are stored as fixed-width pointers. Each pointer is a whole number of six-bit Base64 characters, so any single pointer can be decoded in place without first parsing the index line as JSON or decoding the complete Base64 string.

As with Bulk Redirects, the first metadata fetch for a deployment already identifies which shard holds a given path, so selecting the shard adds no extra round trip.

Within that shard, the routing process uses the index pointers to binary-search the encoded paths. Finding a path takes O(log n) pointer reads and string comparisons. Once it finds a match, it parses the metadata value on the next line. The rest of the shard remains unparsed.

Finding the right shard size in production

We initially hoped the path metadata for most deployments would fit in a single shard. Because the index and binary search kept parsing cheap, we started with multi-megabyte shards.

Large shards only made sense if they stayed cached close to the request. Each routing process keeps a small least-recently-used (LRU) cache of recent shards in memory, in front of a larger cache shared by every process in the region. With only a few shards per deployment, we expected LRU hits most of the time, which would offset the cost of transferring larger shards.

In testing, the regional cache hit rate was high but the LRU hit rate was low, because requests were spread across many processes in each region. Transferring the multi-megabyte shards also cost more than we expected.

We settled on shards of about 200 KB, which kept the regional cache hit rate high and made LRU misses cheap to fill.

Production measurements showed lower average and P99 lookup latency:

Metadata lookup metric

Before: per-path metadata

After: indexed shards

Improvement

P99 latency

215.8 ms

19.1 ms

91% lower

Average latency

8.59 ms

1.81 ms

79% lower

Standard deviation

44.9 ms

19.0 ms

58% lower

Shrinking shards further wasn't worth the rollout

Putting fewer entries in each shard lowered transfer cost but raised the shard count. We also evaluated shrinking shards without increasing their number by encoding the same entries more compactly. We tested three approaches:

  • Front-coding the sorted paths so each stores only what differs from the last.

  • Splitting the shard into JSONL documents that deduplicate metadata.

  • Using a more compact custom serialization format.

Offline simulations measured both encoded size and lookup cost.

Each approach produced much smaller shards, but the simulations predicted only modest latency gains. We decided the extra encoding, compatibility, and rollout work wasn't worth it for this migration. When another workload makes more indexing or compression worth the effort, it will go into the shared library.

Changing routing safely

The CDN runs this lookup on requests to every deployment. If the sharded metadata disagreed with the per-path metadata, we would serve a stale route, a wrong status code, or a 404 for a path that exists.

We checked for that disagreement offline first, then in production. Offline, we built test deployments and ran a harness over them that looked up every path both ways and compared the answers.

In production, behind a feature flag, the routing system did both lookups on a random sample of requests while still serving the old result. It compared the new result against the old one in the background, and we watched for mismatches over several weeks without slowing production requests. We called this shadow mode.

Shadow mode found differences, and they were extremely rare. One was a bug in the old encoding, which packed paths into RFC 2047 encoded words to fit non-ASCII text into ASCII-only fields, and only showed up when an emoji was split across two words. The new format stores paths as plain UTF-8, so the bug can't happen there. Catching this edge case increased our confidence in the comparison, so we started letting the shards serve production traffic.

Faster builds

Once the shards were serving production, we went back to the build pipeline and removed the work they had made redundant:

  • Skipping the per-path metadata upload saves about 9.7 seconds.

  • Writing route group metadata into the manifest saves about 4.5 seconds.

  • Not uploading the files those two changes left empty saves about 2.4 seconds.

Together those save roughly 16.6 seconds. Across all deployments, the deploy step is about 10% faster, and for metadata-heavy deployments, where these steps dominate, we estimate closer to 25%.

Faster routing for your next deployment

Faster metadata lookups improved route resolution as a whole. For large sites, P99 route resolution is now roughly twice as fast. On our own marketing and docs sites, P99 metadata lookup latency fell from 203 ms to 31 ms. Median metadata lookup latency stayed around 0.7 ms.

The application’s Build Output API contract stayed the same. Frameworks still describe what the application needs, while Vercel improves how the CDN serves it.

Deployments built after July 17, 2026 already use the new metadata shards. For an older deployment, redeploy your project to pick up the faster lookups.

title: Retries Are Normal: Building an Idempotent Sync API
description:
In short: Networks retry, so any API that moves data or money receives some requests
twice. I built an idempotent sync API and hit three instructive bugs: a JSON mismatch that
failed without any error, deduplication that worked in tests but not over HTTP, and the
design change that made retries free. The pattern applies to payments, webhooks and message
queues alike.

When my laptop sends its changes to the VPS, the request can fail in the most annoying way
possible: the VPS receives it, applies it, and the response gets lost. From the laptop's
side that looks identical to "never arrived", so it sends the batch again.

Any network protocol that retries delivers messages at least once. The receiver has to
make the second delivery harmless. That property is idempotency, and getting it right took
three attempts.

Attempt 1: batch IDs

Each sync batch carries an ID. The receiver remembers IDs it has processed. If one arrives
again, it answers "accepted, nothing applied" instead of applying it twice:

{"accepted": true, "applied": 0, "skipped": 1, "message": "Duplicate batch ignored"}

A duplicate is accepted, not rejected. The sender did nothing wrong; it just can't tell
whether its first attempt landed. Returning an error would make it retry forever.

Unit tests passed. Then I tried it over HTTP.

The bug that returned no error

The sender encoded batches like this:

{"from_node": "laptop", "batch_id": "b-1", "mutations": [...]}

The receiver's Go struct had no JSON tags, so Go's decoder looked for keys named after
the fields: FromNode, BatchID, Mutations. Nothing matched.

Here's the part that cost me time: json.Decode doesn't treat unknown keys as an error. It
returned a perfectly valid, completely empty struct. The handler then correctly rejected an
empty batch as invalid. The handler did its job on garbage input; the bug was that the
encoder and decoder had two different ideas of what a batch looked like.

The fix was to put the tags on the one real type and have both sides use it:

type SyncBatch struct {
    FromNode  string         `json:"from_node"`
    BatchID   string         `json:"batch_id"`
    Mutations []SyncMutation `json:"mutations"`
}

One contract, used by both ends, can't drift apart. Two "equivalent" definitions eventually
will.

Attempt 2: deduplication that only worked in tests

With the wire format fixed, I sent the same batch twice to a running server and wrote down
my prediction first: second response, "Duplicate batch ignored". Actual result:

Accepted Applied Skipped Message
-------- ------- ------- -------
    True       1       0 Batch applied successfully
    True       1       0 Batch applied successfully

Applied twice. The cause was one line in the HTTP handler:

service := replication.NewSyncService() // inside the handler

A value created inside a request handler lives for one request. Every request got a
fresh service with an empty "seen batches" set, so no batch was ever a duplicate. The unit
tests reused one service across calls, so they never saw it.

The fix: create one service per node when the program starts, and share it with every
request (with a mutex, since requests run concurrently). The replay then returned
Applied: 0, Skipped: 1.

Attempt 3: IDs that make retries free

Where does a batch ID come from? A random ID works for network retries, but I wanted
something stronger: if the laptop sends the same contents again (say, after a restart),
the VPS should skip it without looking at a single change.

So the ID is a hash of the sender plus its contents:

func BatchIDFor(fromNode string, mutations []SyncMutation) string {
    hashes := make([]string, 0, len(mutations))
    for _, mutation := range mutations {
        hashes = append(hashes, HashMutation(mutation))
    }
    sort.Strings(hashes) // order-independent
    // ...sha256 of fromNode + hashes, first 8 bytes as hex
}

Could two different batches share an ID? Only if a machine's state returned to an
earlier version, and vector clocks only move forward, so it can't.

Two layers, and why the second one matters

Deduplication now happens twice:

  1. Batch ID seen before? Skip the whole batch. Fast.
  2. Otherwise, per change: compare vector clocks. A change the receiver already has compares Equal or older and is skipped.

The second layer let me fix a slow memory leak safely. The set of seen batch IDs grew
forever, so I capped it at 10,000 and forget the oldest. Is forgetting safe? Only because of
layer 2: a forgotten batch that arrives again is processed, and every change in it is
skipped anyway. I wrote a test that forgets a batch, replays it, and checks that nothing
changes.

A test checks one replay. Later I wrote a TLA+ specification of the protocol and stated the
property directly: delivering any message a second time, in any state any node can reach,
changes nothing. The model checker verified it across every interleaving of three machines
(see part 9). That's the real justification for forgetting batch IDs.

Where this shows up in real systems

  • Payment APIs. Stripe's idempotency keys are the best-known example: resending a charge request with the same key can't charge the customer twice.
  • Message queues. Kafka, SQS and most brokers deliver at least once by default. Consumers that aren't idempotent eventually process something twice.
  • Webhooks. Providers retry when your endpoint times out, even if you'd already processed the event. Every webhook handler needs the "accepted, nothing applied" path.
  • Contract drift between services. The silent JSON mismatch is the small version of a common integration failure: two teams' "equivalent" schemas that quietly disagree. Shared types or contract tests catch it; decoders that ignore unknown fields hide it.

What I took away

  • Design for the second delivery from the start. A retry isn't an edge case.
  • A decoder that ignores unknown fields can turn a schema mismatch into silent empty data. Keep one definition of every message.
  • Test through the real transport. Unit tests with a long-lived object hid a bug that the first real HTTP request exposed.
  • A fast path is fine to make lossy when there's a correct slow path behind it.

Next: How Two Computers Find Their Differences Without Sending Everything.

About this series: I'm learning distributed systems by building a real application, with an
AI assistant as coach and pair programmer. It explains, reviews and sometimes writes code; I
verify every claim against tests and measurements, and every bug and number here is real.

I write about building reliable software in Go, from the code up. If you're working on similar
problems, I'd like to hear from you: get in touch or connect with me on LinkedIn.

title: Audio-to-Text Transcription API for Invoice SaaS — GPU-Free Hosting in Go
description:
Short answer: an audio-to-text transcription API is the simplest way to avoid GPU hosting in a SaaS app. For logistics invoices, use AssemblyAI for transcription, keep extraction behind a Go interface, and treat the transcript as an input rather than as an accounting record. OpenAI, Deepgram, AWS Transcribe, and Google Cloud Speech-to-Text are real alternatives, but they make different trade-offs around portability and the rest of your platform.

There is one more boundary worth stating early. Infrai cannot currently serve ASR, so it belongs after transcription, not in the microphone-to-text hop. Its broad, self-describing REST surface can still be useful for later text work when a team wants one documented contract around several backend capabilities: one key, one REST contract, and a public discovery surface with runnable examples.

Should an audio-to-text transcription API avoid GPU hosting?

Yes, for most early and mid-sized invoice SaaS systems. A managed API removes model packaging, CUDA drivers, GPU capacity planning, and a class of inference-worker incidents. It does not remove your work. You still own secret rotation, rate limits, retention, retries, tenant isolation, and the accounting checks that decide if an extracted invoice is safe to post.

For supplier invoices, transcription is an input transformation. The business output is a typed record: supplier, invoice number, issue date, currency, line items, tax, and total. A bad transcript is an ASR failure. A fluent transcript that changes 8.50 to 85.00 is a validation failure. Those need different queues, alerts, and SLOs.

The provider boundary should be small enough to replace. Store the source audio privately, submit it to the selected API, persist the provider request ID and raw response, then pass normalized text to extraction. Do not let one vendor's response JSON become your domain model by accident.

Which providers fit the portability decision?

Option Best fit Portability cost Boundary to test
AssemblyAI A focused managed transcription workflow with extra processing options A separate extraction contract remains yours Transcript quality, numeric accuracy, and retry behavior
OpenAI audio APIs Teams already using OpenAI clients and model conventions A client-compatible surface can still tie later steps to one provider Audio formats, retention, and invoice-number accuracy
Deepgram A specialist transcription comparison Invoice extraction remains outside the service Accuracy on accents, silence, and long recordings
AWS Transcribe A pipeline already built around AWS storage, IAM, and queues AWS-specific integration can make migration larger Region controls and object-storage handoff
Google Cloud Speech-to-Text A pipeline standardized on Google identity and regions Cloud-specific policy becomes part of the move Data location and operational integration
Local model Strict deployment or data-control requirements GPU operations, updates, and paging are yours Capacity, model lifecycle, and recovery

AssemblyAI is the first trial I would run for this scenario because it provides a feature-rich transcription API without requiring a locally hosted GPU, and its documented processing options include summarization and sentiment analysis. OpenAI is attractive when an existing client and model workflow matter more than provider neutrality. Deepgram deserves a direct quality test as a specialist. AWS and Google are sensible when the surrounding cloud controls already carry the decision. For the later extraction step, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini are separate model-platform alternatives, not transcription substitutes; choose among them on schema control, regional policy, and the validation tests your invoice data requires.

Those are not benchmark results. Run the same anonymized invoice corpus through at least three candidates. Measure word errors, numeric-field accuracy, duplicate handling, retry behavior, and regional controls. A transcript that reads well but loses a decimal point fails the actual job.

How do you build the handoff and capacity plan?

Let A be average audio minutes per hour, P the provider's effective parallel capacity, and R the reserve for retries and replay. The worker needs room for upload bursts, slow jobs, and a recovery run after a provider incident. Define one SLO for accepted audio becoming extraction-ready and another for correct invoice totals. One number cannot describe both.

Keep queue messages small: private object key, tenant ID, content hash, and an idempotency key. A worker fetches the object, calls the provider, records the request ID, and writes one normalized transcript. Queues are generally at-least-once. Duplicate protection is part of the design, not a cleanup task.

Use exponential backoff and honor Retry-After on 429 responses. A 4xx body should go to review or a dead-letter path with enough context for an operator to fix the input. Retrying malformed audio forever is a capacity leak.

The extraction worker should reconcile line items against subtotal, tax, and grand total before publication. Keep that check independent from ASR so a provider swap does not silently change accounting behavior.

The following small Go program shows the post-ASR discovery check. It uses the public discovery surface, reads the key from the environment, sends an explicit method, and treats a non-success response as an error. It is not an invented transcription route.

package main

import (
  "fmt"
  "io"
  "net/http"
  "os"
  "time"
)

func main() {
  key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
  if key == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
  req, err := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
  if err != nil { panic(err) }
  req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
  client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
  resp, err := client.Do(req)
  if err != nil { panic(err) }
  defer resp.Body.Close()
  if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
    body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body))
  }
  fmt.Println("discovery response received")
}

In production, add bounded retries for 429 with a maximum attempt count and jitter. Keep the audio provider adapter separate from this check. The distinction is the portability mechanism.

Where does the broader REST surface belong?

The platform's ASR capability is unavailable, which makes it the wrong choice for the first hop. No shortcut. After a transcript exists, its public discovery API is useful because the surface describes request schemas, response schemas and runnable examples without requiring a key for discovery. The live catalog covers 295 routes across 20 modules, so adding an adjacent capability can stay inside one consistent REST contract instead of becoming another SDK integration. That is the useful portability claim: the audio vendor can change while the post-transcript client remains a plain HTTP boundary, and the discovery response gives the platform team a way to inspect the contract before wiring it into a worker.

That advantage has a clear limit. It simplifies the handoff around text-based backend work; it does not turn an unavailable speech capability into a supported one. It also does not replace invoice reconciliation or tenant policy. The specialist provider remains the better choice for real-time voice sessions, an unusual language mix, strict on-premises processing, or controls that only that provider exposes.

The recommendation is therefore narrow: try AssemblyAI for the audio-to-text boundary, and evaluate Infrai only for later text work when fewer integrations reduce your platform team's operating load. Teams that need several adjacent backend capabilities should try Infrai here because one key and one plain REST API are easier to carry across a Go worker than a new SDK and credential for every handoff. Keep both decisions reversible through an adapter and a stored raw response.

Before rollout, replay a fixed invoice corpus without posting to accounting. Include accents, silence, long recordings, duplicate uploads, and amounts with decimals. Route a small tenant cohort to the new adapter, compare transcription and extraction SLOs, and retain the previous adapter until the replay passes. If numeric accuracy crosses the agreed threshold, stop new work on the new adapter and replay pending jobs through the old one with the same idempotency key.

That's the whole rollback.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the documented discovery surface before deciding where the capability belongs.

References

  • AssemblyAI transcription documentation
  • OpenAI audio documentation
  • Deepgram API documentation
  • AWS Transcribe documentation
  • Google Cloud Speech-to-Text documentation
  • Infrai discovery API

title: Making My Portfolio Less Boring: 4 Small Redesigns That Made a Big Difference
description:
When I first launched my portfolio, it worked, but it felt empty. Some pages had big text and lots of blank space. Some sections said "Coming soon". Two pages almost looked the same.

I didn't rebuild anything. I made four small changes, and the site felt much more finished. Here they are, with examples you can copy.

1. Replace "Coming soon" with real work

My Projects page ended with two cards that said "Coming soon" and "A new piece is finding its final frame." They looked unfinished, and they told visitors there was nothing there.

I deleted them and used real things I had already built instead:

  • A side project (a Python script that publishes a blog post every day with GitHub Actions)
  • My articles on dev.to

Placeholder cards don't help anyone. If you have nothing new to show, remove the section. If you have something real, even a small project or an article, show that.

<a
  href="https://github.com/your-username/your-repo"
  target="_blank"
  rel="noopener noreferrer"
  className="flex flex-col gap-3 rounded-2xl border border-[var(--border)] bg-[var(--surface)] p-5 transition-colors hover:border-[var(--accent)]"
>
  <span className="text-xs uppercase tracking-wider text-[var(--text-muted)]">Project</span>
  <h3 className="text-lg font-semibold">Daily blog automation</h3>
  <p className="text-sm leading-6 text-[var(--text-muted)]">
    A Python script that writes and publishes a blog post every day.
  </p>
  <span className="mt-auto text-sm font-semibold text-[var(--accent)]">View on GitHub →</span>
</a>

2. Use the empty space next to a big heading

My Contact page had a huge heading on one side and nothing on the other. A visitor had to scroll to find out how to reach me.

I moved the contact options next to the heading as three clickable cards: Email, WhatsApp and LinkedIn. Under the heading, I added small chips for what I can help with.

<div className="grid gap-8 lg:grid-cols-2 lg:items-center">
  <div>
    <h1>Let's make something good.</h1>
    <p>Have a project in mind? I'd love to hear what you're thinking.</p>
  </div>
  <div className="flex flex-col gap-3">
    {/* three contact cards here */}
  </div>
</div>

The same idea worked on my Skills page: the empty right side now shows four small cards that link to the skill details below.

3. Turn a row of small links into cards

My "Find me online" section was a row of tiny text chips. They were easy to miss, and a visitor couldn't tell what each link was.

I changed them into larger cards with an icon, a name and one short line, such as "Articles on web development and automation". Now each link explains itself before anyone clicks it.

Keep each card focused on one job: an icon, a title, one line of description and one clear action.

4. Check your contrast

My "Let's Work Together" banner had white text on a light lavender background. On my laptop it looked fine, but it was hard to read on a phone, and the button text was also light.

The fix was simple:

  • Use a deeper purple for the banner background
  • Use white text on it
  • Make the button text the same deep purple on a white button

If you can barely read something when you squint, a visitor with a small screen and bright sunlight will not read it at all.

A bonus: make every page do a different job

My Home and About pages used the same hero, the same photo and the same story. I changed them:

  • Home: a short hero, a few skills and clear buttons
  • About: the full story, what I'm currently learning, and my profiles

When two pages say the same thing, a visitor sees no reason to open the second one. It can also confuse search engines.

My rules for every change

  1. Use only real content. No invented numbers, clients or promises.
  2. One change at a time. Then I look at the page on a phone-sized window and a laptop.
  3. Remove before adding. Often the best fix was to delete something.
  4. Check on a real phone. Some problems only show up there.

Wrapping up

None of these changes needed a new framework or a big rewrite. They only needed me to look at my own site the way a visitor does.

You can see the result here: ritika-rajput-portfolio.vercel.app. I also share videos on RitikaMoments.

What is one thing on your portfolio that you know looks unfinished?
