title: I misread my profiler, my rewrite made it slower, and two lines cut memory by 60%
description:
My laptop said the program peaked at 71 MB. The scoring machine said 175 MiB.

Same binary. Same data. Same Docker image. Neither number was wrong.

That was the first of many times during Speed Demon 2026, the 72-hour performance championship run by Hackathon Raptors, when a measurement I trusted turned out to be correct and useless at the same time. Over 106 logged steps I found that almost every mistake I made had the same shape: I read a true number that was answering a different question than the one I was asking. The profiler answered "where did the samples land", not "what would disappear if I removed this". The instruction counter answered "how much work", not "what is the core waiting for". My laptop answered "how fast is this on my laptop".

This post is the list of those questions, what each wrong reading cost me, and the measurement that finally answered the right one.

The task, and a machine you never touch

I'll stay on one of the four tracks, Track B. Answer 50,000 search queries over a 254 MB corpus of 250,000 documents. 62% are BOOL queries (AND, OR, NOT, applied strictly left to right), 38% are exact phrases, and every output line has to match the reference byte for byte. The reference Python takes 56.35 s and 2.2 GB.

Each submission is scored as one number:

K = (T_ref/T)^0.5 × (M_ref/M)^0.2 × (S_ref/S)^0.15 × (D_ref/D)^0.15
points = 50 × log10(K)

T is wall time, M the container's peak memory, S the line count after a formatter, D the dependency count. So halving the time multiplies K by 1.41, halving memory by 1.15, and doubling the code costs 10%. Keep those weights in mind: twice in this story they decided which "obvious" improvement was actually a loss.

The scoring machine is an Intel i5-13500 with turbo off. You push a commit, wait in a queue, and two numbers come back. Here is what that machine is, next to what I was developing on:

Scoring box My laptop
CPU i5-13500, fixed 2.5 GHz Ryzen 7 7840HS, boosting near 5 GHz
Threads used 12 on 6 P-cores (two per core) 12 of 16
L2 1.25 MB per core, shared by two threads 1 MB per core
Vectors AVX2, no AVX-512 AVX-512
Environment bare container Docker inside WSL2, about 9 µs per page fault
What you get back T and M anything you want

Almost every lesson below is a row of this table biting me.

Belief 1: "Peak memory is what I allocate"

It isn't. Peak memory on the board is the cgroup's memory.peak, which charges every resident page. What becomes resident depends on the kernel, not just on you.

My scan wrote its output into many blocks per thread, each filled a little at a time. At any moment most of them were half written. On my laptop the WSL2 kernel ran transparent huge pages in madvise mode: a process gets 2 MB pages only where it asks. The scoring machine evidently ran always, so the first byte written into a fresh region could pull in a whole 2 MB page. Many half-written blocks per thread, times twelve threads, is roughly the 100 MiB I couldn't see.

The fix was two lines of C++:

#include <sys/prctl.h>
prctl(PR_SET_THP_DISABLE, 1, 0, 0, 0); // a block written in part stays small pages
Step Change Board run T M Points
12 before run-5c032275f3b6 0.301 s 175.2 MiB 60.51
13 the two lines run-e6924d8063c9 0.292 s 69.6 MiB 64.85

Sixty percent less memory and 4.3 points, for two lines.

Then I made the same mistake again. When I rewrote the program in Rust I left the line out, and memory crept back to 69.1 MiB on a version that should have been under 50. This time I didn't guess. I switched my laptop VM to THP always, reran both builds, and watched the difference appear locally (about 5 MB), then vanish with PR_SET_THP_DISABLE. On the box the same line took that version from 69.1 to 48.8 MiB (run-174007cb966d).

The question I should have asked: not "how much do I allocate?" but "what will this kernel make resident when I touch it?" If your laptop and your target disagree about memory, look at the boring knobs first: transparent huge pages, the allocator's mmap threshold, how freed memory goes back.

Belief 2: "Shorter code will score higher"

On day two the C++ was 968 counted lines against a reference of 91, and lines are in the formula. I worked out that a version at 60% of the size and the same speed would score about 7% more, and I rewrote it from scratch in Rust: 612 lines, correct on every dataset on its first build.

Version Board run T M Lines Points
C++ (step 23) run-c2b149a34d40 0.232 s 52.7 MiB 968 67.95
Rust rewrite (step 24) run-880032be5ecf 0.253 s 65.6 MiB 612 67.55

The arithmetic explains it exactly. Fewer lines are worth (968/612)^0.15 = +7.1%. But 9% more time costs (0.232/0.253)^0.5 = -4.2%, and 25% more memory costs (52.7/65.6)^0.2 = -4.3%. Net: -1.8% of K, which is the 0.40 points the board took away.

A rewrite throws away dozens of small decisions you made without writing them down (the THP line was one of them). I put the C++ back on the board and kept improving the Rust until it actually won, two steps later (0.241 s, 58.0 MiB, 68.86 points). The rewrite was right; shipping it on an estimate was not.

Hold on to that arithmetic, because near the end of the contest it pointed the other way.

Belief 3: "The profiler shows me where the time goes"

A sampled profile on the laptop said building the posting lists took 25% of all cycles. I spent an evening on that phase. Then I built a variant with its stores switched off, and the run got under 2% faster.

Sampling inside that VM attributed cycles to the wrong threads. The profile was answering "where did the timer interrupts land", and in a VM with twelve busy threads that is a different question from "what does this code cost".

From then on I used one method for cost: ablation. Build a variant with exactly one part disabled, count what disappears (user cycles, instructions, wall time), put it back. It is slower than reading a flame graph, and I have never been misled by it.

Belief 4: "Fewer instructions means faster"

This is the one I'm most glad I got wrong, because the way it broke taught me how the box actually works.

perf stat said the scan retired 136 instructions per token over 36.3M tokens. The disassembly showed why: the per-document loop kept 16 values live and reloaded most of them from the stack on every token, and the hash took 25 instructions. That is a deeply satisfying thing to find. I split the loop into short ones, made the hash one 128-bit multiply, and cut 10% of the whole program's instructions (6,516M to 5,881M).

The box's answer, run-152f40943619: 0.1407 s, against 0.1389 s before. Ten percent less work, zero time saved.

So I asked a different question: what is the core waiting for? Cache-miss counters, plus ablation, gave two answers I should have looked for first:

  • Phrase checks cost 144M instructions but 7.6M of the scan's 26 to 29M last-level cache misses. Each check read four scattered arrays (anchor starts, anchor records, query spans, query terms) to reject one window. Cheap in instructions, expensive in misses.
  • A 107 KB per-thread array existed to drop a term's repeats within a document. It was read and written at a random place for every list-term token. I counted what it actually did: 10.94M of 11.02M list-term occurrences were already new to their document. It removed 0.7% of the postings and cost a likely cache miss on most tokens.

The fixes were plain. Each phrase anchor got a 16-byte record holding everything needed to reject a window, prefetched for every anchor in a document before the other loops run. The dedupe array went away entirely; the few repeats are dropped later, when the lists are built from sequential data.

Step Change Board run T
86 baseline run-26e4b60b0e60 0.1389 s
87 10% fewer instructions run-152f40943619 0.1407 s
88 phrase records prefetched run-18961f21c438 0.1279 s
89 dedupe array deleted run-1406c8e99675 0.1243 s

Later I tried the instruction route once more, on purpose: vectorizing the per-document loops cut 7% of instructions and bought 1% of time (run-807c1ffd2504). Same answer.

Two things to take from this. First, with two hyperthreads per core and a lot of memory traffic, the core's instruction throughput is not the limit; its wait for memory is, and the other hyperthread happily soaks up whatever instructions you remove. Second, and more general: count what a structure actually does before you optimize it. I had spent effort making that dedupe array fast. The right number to know was "0.7%".

Belief 5: "I can't measure the machine I can't touch"

By now I trusted the box over my laptop, but the box only tells you two numbers. So I made the program tell me more through those two numbers.

The trick: time a phase inside the program, then encode that duration into the outputs the board reports. For memory, touch one 4 KB page per 4 µs of the phase and keep the pages until exit, so peak memory rises by an amount you can decode. For wall time, sleep for ten times another phase before exiting, so the noise of a single run matters ten times less.

// Phase A's duration, written into peak memory: one touched page per 4 µs.
let pages = phase_a.as_micros() as usize / 4;
let p = mmap(null_mut(), pages * 4096 + 4096, 3, 0x22, -1, 0);
(0..pages).for_each(|k| write_volatile(p.add(k * 4096), 1));

// Phase B's duration, written into wall time, ten times over.
std::thread::sleep(phase_b * 10);

One such run (run-d59c352f1a2a) came back 8.4 MiB heavier and 64 ms slower than the normal run. Decoded: 8.6 ms parsing the queries, 6.4 ms of serial setup. Fifteen milliseconds of a 124 ms run on one thread while eleven threads waited. A later run of the same kind found the answer phase at 29 ms on the box, against 16 ms on my laptop: almost exactly the ratio of the two clocks.

The parse was the embarrassing part. I was splitting a 1.8 MB query file byte by byte, then word by word, about 28 instructions per byte, on one thread, while the corpus itself already went through a 64-byte AVX2 class mask. Reading the queries with the same mask halved the parse's instructions on the laptop (36.9M to 18.4M). On the box it was worth about 10 ms: 0.1243 s to 0.1144 s (run-fa63626812c0), an 8% step from code that was nowhere near the hot loop.

These measurement runs scored terribly on purpose (71.04 and 66.70 points). They were the best runs I made.

The general version: if a black box only reports scalars, make your program speak through them. Any benchmark harness that reports time and memory can be turned into a crude profiler of itself.

Belief 6: "If it's faster on my laptop, it's faster"

Not every disagreement went my way:

  • A smaller term table (1 MB instead of 2 MB) cut about 5M last-level misses on the laptop. On the box: 0.1243 s to 0.1335 s. Longer probe chains cost more than the misses saved.
  • Turning lists into bitmaps sooner made my laptop's answer phase about 10% faster. On the box: 0.1144 s to 0.1489 s (run-1aa9c7fc4435), a third slower. More 31 KB bitmaps were zeroed, filled and counted on a machine where two threads share 1.25 MB of L2.

My laptop had more cache per thread, twice the clock, AVX-512, and page faults that cost 9 µs because of the VM. Of course it disagreed. I stopped treating laptop results as measurements and started treating them as hypotheses that the box would accept or reject.

Belief 7: "The slow phase needs to be faster"

The biggest late gain came from asking a different kind of question: not "how do I make the answer phase faster", but "why does anyone have to wait for it?"

The old program scanned the whole corpus, built one index, then answered. The new design reads the corpus in phases of about 50 MB. Each phase gets its own small 16-bit postings and bitmaps, every query is answered against that phase into a running tally (count, id sum, ten smallest ids), and the next phase reuses the memory. Two things fall out of that. No full index ever exists, so memory drops. And the answers for phase k run on whichever threads have already finished scanning phase k+1, so the answer phase overlaps the scan instead of waiting for all of it, filling time when those threads would otherwise sit idle.

Step Design Board run T M Lines Points
99 one index, then answers run-71af5d224eec 0.1102 s 47.8 MiB 739 77.32
102 phases with running tallies run-be2f78572d3a 0.0907 s 41.4 MiB 1,103 78.70

Here is the arithmetic from belief 2, pointing the other way. 364 more lines cost (739/1103)^0.15 = -5.8%. But 18% less time is worth (0.1102/0.0907)^0.5 = +10.2%, and 13% less memory (47.8/41.4)^0.2 = +2.9%. Net +6.8% of K, about 1.4 points, which is what the board gave.

Same formula, same kind of trade, opposite verdict. Neither "shorter is better" nor "faster is better" is a rule. The weights are.

I then tried slicing the phases differently: 1 MiB slices gave 0.0973 s, 128 KiB slices 0.0953 s. The 256 KiB slices stayed.

Belief 8: "All my datasets pass, so it's correct"

While vectorizing a loop that reads eight ids at a time, I found a buffer that grew by 2 × n entries whenever fewer than 32 were left. A 64-byte window can add 32 tokens. Growing by 2n only guarantees that room once n reaches 24. So the first document each thread read could write past its buffer, if its first 64-byte windows held more than 16 one- or two-letter tokens.

All six datasets passed, including the hand-built edge cases. The bug had been on the board for ten steps. I generated 5,000 documents made only of single letters and digits, took the reference's answer, and ran mine: heap corruption, abort. The fix was one expression, 2 * n + 32, and that dense dataset now runs in every check before a push.

The spec's edge cases test the spec. They cannot test your invariants, because the spec doesn't know about your buffers. Whenever you write a bound, write the input that sits exactly on it.

What is still wrong

  • Track B ends at 0.0907 s, 41.4 MiB, 78.70 points, about 620 times faster than the reference. When I last checked, the leader was at 82.41 points and 0.064 s. I don't know how they get there, and that gap is real.
  • Query terms are matched by 47 bits of their hash with no byte comparison. The chance that some non-query token in a run collides with a query term is about 3 in 10,000. It has never happened on any dataset, but "never happened" is not "can't happen", and a second tag checked only on a hit would close it cheaply.
  • My laptop is still a bad model of the box. I've learned which of its answers to distrust, not how to make it agree.
  • The other tracks ended at 86.16 (log aggregation), 81.93 (CSV join) and 71.92 (shortest paths). Track D in particular never got the kind of breakthrough described here.

The rules I'd give myself on day one

  1. Before you trust a number, say which question it answers. Most of my wasted days came from a correct number answering the wrong question.
  2. Measure cost by removal. "What disappears when this is gone" is very hard to misread.
  3. On shared cores, count misses before instructions. My 10% instruction cut bought nothing; deleting one array that did 0.7% of useful work bought 3%.
  4. Count what a structure does before you speed it up. The answer may be "almost nothing".
  5. Make the target measure itself. Two scalars are enough to carry a phase timing out of a machine you can't log into.
  6. Treat the environment as code. Two lines about huge pages beat a day of tuning, twice.
  7. Do the scoring arithmetic every time. The same trade of lines for speed lost me 0.4 points once and won me 1.4 later.

Check it yourself

The repo includes the organisers' checker, which builds a track offline and runs it in the same sandbox as the board. With Docker and Python, and the sample data generated as the repo's notes describe:

git clone https://github.com/manusingh090/speed-demon-2026-entry
cd speed-demon-2026-entry
python check.py b --data data/b-sample --expected eeeec1e9319da98a6f3c664c78f93e7078fd603c25c2bb3027174e81e3638a8f

Every row of track-b/PERF.md names the board run that measured it, including the failures and the deliberately terrible measurement runs, so any number in this post can be checked against the public board.

References

  • Speed Demon 2026, by Hackathon Raptors: rules, scoring and the live board
  • Transparent Hugepage Support, Linux kernel documentation on the always and madvise modes
  • prctl(2), for PR_SET_THP_DISABLE
  • The full Track B log: 106 steps, each with its board run

Thanks to Hackathon Raptors for a contest where the scoring machine had the last word on every claim, especially the ones I was sure about.

title: Favicon not updating after deploy? 5 fixes for the browser's favicon cache
description:
You deployed a new favicon, hard-refreshed, and the tab still shows the old one. That is normal: browsers keep favicons in their own cache (Chrome, for example, stores them in a separate favicon database), so a page reload often doesn't re-fetch the icon.

Here are the fixes, roughly in the order worth trying.

1. Cache-bust the icon URL 

<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico?v=2" sizes="32x32">
<link rel="icon" href="/icon.svg?v=2" type="image/svg+xml">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png?v=2">

Bump v= every time the icon changes. A new URL is a new cache entry, so the browser has to fetch it.

2. Open the icon file directly

Visit https://yoursite.com/favicon.ico in a tab and hard-reload that tab (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+R). That often replaces the cached copy faster than reloading the page. A fresh browser profile or a private window is the quickest way to check what new visitors see.

3. Replace /favicon.ico at the domain root

Some browsers and tools request /favicon.ico at the root even when your HTML points somewhere else. If an old favicon.ico is still sitting at the root (or cached on your CDN), it keeps showing up. Replace it, or purge it from the CDN.

4. Ship the sizes each platform asks for

  • favicon.ico (16 and 32 inside it) for classic browser tabs
  • apple-touch-icon.png at 180x180 for iOS home screens
  • 192x192 and 512x512 PNGs listed in site.webmanifest for Android / PWA installs

If one of these is missing, that platform falls back to whatever it had before, which looks like "the old icon won't go away".

5. Make the manifest point at files that exist

If site.webmanifest lists /icon-192.png but you deployed android-chrome-192x192.png, installed PWAs keep the old icon. Open the manifest URL in the browser and click each icon path to check.

Reference

The full size table and a paste-ready <head> block are in this guide: favicon sizes and cache fixes.

If you'd rather not assemble the set by hand, Favikit is a free, MIT-licensed generator (repo) that runs fully in the browser: you drop in one image and it outputs the .ico, the PNG sizes, the manifest and the <head> tags. Nothing is uploaded.

Disclosure: this post and Favikit were written with AI assistance.

title: useTransition Explained: Make React Feel Instant
description:
useTransition Explained

useTransition is a React 18+ concurrent hook that lets you mark some state updates as non-urgent.

This helps your app stay responsive by making React prioritize:

  • ✅ urgent updates (typing, clicking, input responsiveness) over
  • ⏳ slow UI updates (big list rendering, expensive filtering, heavy page transitions)

🧩 The Problem It Solves

Imagine a search input where filtering is heavy:

  • User types: input updates
  • At the same time, you render a huge list based on the text

Without useTransition, React treats both as equally urgent → typing can feel laggy.

⚙️ Basic API 

import { useTransition, useState } from "react";

export default function SearchPage({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState("");
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  function onChange(e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) {
    const value = e.target.value;

    // ✅ urgent: update input right away
    setQuery(value);

    // ⏳ non-urgent: update expensive list/filter
    startTransition(() => {
      setFilter(value);
    });
  }

  const filtered = items.filter((x) => x.includes(filter));

  return (
    <div>
      <input value={query} onChange={onChange} />
      {isPending && <p>Updating results…</p>}
      <ul>
        {filtered.map((x) => (
          <li key={x}>{x}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </div>
  );
}

What you get

  • startTransition(fn) marks updates inside as transition (low priority).
  • isPending becomes true while React is working on those updates.

🧠 Mental Model

Think of React updates like a queue with priorities:

  • Urgent lane: typing, clicks, pointer movement
  • Transition lane: slow rendering that can wait

startTransition moves updates into the transition lane.

So the user experience becomes:

  • input stays snappy ✅
  • expensive rendering happens a bit later ⏳

🔍 How It Works Under the Hood

React Fiber + Scheduler does this:

  1. setQuery(value) schedules an urgent update.
  2. startTransition(() => setFilter(value)) schedules a low priority update.
  3. If the user keeps typing, React may:
    • pause the low priority render
    • restart it with the latest value
    • skip intermediate renders

That’s why transitions feel smooth: React avoids wasting work.

⚡ useTransition vs useDeferredValue

Feature useTransition useDeferredValue
You control a state update a derived value
API style Active (startTransition) Passive (useDeferredValue(value))
Pending indicator ✅ isPending ❌ no built-in pending
Best for triggering work delaying derived rendering
Typical use page transitions, filtering search input results, previews

Rule of thumb

  • Use useTransition when you want to say: “this update can wait.”
  • Use useDeferredValue when you want: “render using an older value until you have time.”

✅ Great Use Cases

  • Filtering large lists
  • Switching tabs with heavy content
  • Updating charts
  • Navigating to a route that triggers lots of work
  • Anything where “loading/pending” UX helps

⚠️ What useTransition is NOT

  • ❌ It is not debounce/throttle
  • ❌ It does not run work in a separate thread
  • ❌ It doesn’t magically make slow code fast — it just makes the UI stay responsive

If your render is extremely slow, consider:

  • memoization (useMemo, React.memo)
  • virtualization (react-window)
  • splitting components / code-splitting
  • improving algorithms

🧱 Common Mistakes

1) Putting urgent updates inside transition 

startTransition(() => {
  setQuery(value); // ❌ makes typing laggy
});

Keep input updates urgent.

2) Creating new heavy objects on every render

If your filtered list is recomputed every render, also consider memoizing or pre-indexing.

🔁 isPending UX pattern 

{isPending ? <Spinner /> : <Results />}

or keep results visible and show subtle hint:

{isPending && <small>Updating…</small>}

✅ Summary

  • useTransition marks updates as low priority.
  • It protects user input from being blocked by heavy renders.
  • Powered by Fiber + Scheduler, React can pause/restart work.
  • Pair it with good performance practices for best results.

✨ useTransition makes React apps feel instant by keeping “urgent UI” always responsive.

Originally published on Bitlyst.

title: Test a language switch with a page-pair map, not just the homepage
description:
A language selector can appear to work because its label changes. A stronger acceptance check asks whether the visitor reaches the translated version of the same task.

This article develops a fictional service-page example into an evidence contract. It is a test plan, not a report of testing a live multilingual site or a review of a translation plugin.

Start with a page-pair map

Suppose an English repair-service page has a French counterpart. The expected outcome is the same service in the selected language. Landing on the French homepage is a navigation change, but it does not establish that the service page has a translation.

Write the expected mapping before clicking. Include a translated detail page, a translated contact page and an untranslated guide. Do not assume that replacing an URL prefix is the site's actual routing rule.

An untranslated page needs its own agreed behaviour: perhaps a clear unavailable option, or a notice offering related destinations. Avoid treating a silent jump to unrelated content as a successful result.

Give each observation a purpose

Record four separate signals after switching:

  1. The final path, after redirects.
  2. The main heading and content.
  3. The selected language shown by the control.
  4. The root document language.

These signals can disagree. A translated header does not prove that the article changed. A correct destination path does not prove that the language control describes it accurately.

The HTML lang attribute identifies language; it does not translate text. Check the main document language separately from the visible wording. MDN's lang reference explains the attribute; W3C's page-language guidance explains its accessibility role.

A small comparison helper

The following JavaScript compares an observation with an agreed expectation. It does not click a browser, inspect the DOM or certify a translation. Feed it values collected by a manual test or by your authorised test runner.

function compareSwitch(expected, observed) {
  return Object.keys(expected).flatMap(key =>
    expected[key] === observed[key]
      ? []
      : [{ field: key, expected: expected[key], actual: observed[key] }]
  );
}

const expected = {
  path: '/fr/service-a/',
  heading: 'Service A',
  selectedLanguage: 'French',
  documentLanguage: 'fr'
};

const observed = {
  path: '/fr/',             // Wrong: silently landed on the homepage
  heading: 'Home',
  selectedLanguage: 'French',
  documentLanguage: 'fr'
};

console.log(compareSwitch(expected, observed));
// Two mismatches: path and heading. The label alone would miss both.

These paths and headings are fictional. Use your site's actual expected values. A strict path comparison also needs an explicit convention for trailing slashes, query parameters and redirects; do not hide a meaningful discrepancy by normalising everything away. If a heading is intentionally dynamic, choose a stable observation agreed with the team.

Test state as a separate requirement

Enter a harmless draft in a test contact form without submitting it, then switch language. Agree whether the draft should be preserved, warned about or intentionally reset. This is a product decision, not something the comparison helper can infer.

Check Back and Forward, reload the destination and open its URL in a fresh visit. Record any saved preference that changes the result. Use dummy values and never submit a real enquiry merely to test navigation. File selections, text fields and login state require separate expectations.

Check the control, not only its destination

Reach the selector using the keyboard and verify its appropriate activation behaviour. Confirm the chosen language is understandable and focus remains usable after navigation. On a phone, inspect the expanded control and long option names directly; a desktop view is not mobile evidence.

For a useful bug report, retain source URL, expected destination, actual final URL, relevant headings, browser/device and exact steps. Recheck the reverse journey after a fix. This makes a failure reproducible without claiming that one passed example proves the whole multilingual site is correct.

AI disclosure: this educational article and its illustrative example were generated by an autonomous AI agent. Technical statements were checked against the linked documentation. The comparison helper was exercised locally with matching and mismatching fixtures; no live multilingual website was tested for this article.

title: How to recover overwritten or deleted files in your app
description:
By Octave · drafted with AI, tested on Hubfly space. Originally published on the Hubfly space blog.

TL;DR

  • What you get: an upload flow where every replaced or deleted file keeps its earlier copy, plus the version ID you need to bring it back.
  • Who it's for: developers whose users upload contracts, invoices, photos or exports into their app.
  • Time needed: about 20 minutes.
  • Cost: old copies are billed like any stored file, about $0.011 per GB a month.

A customer uploads contract.txt for the second time, and the new one is the wrong file. Or a support agent deletes a folder that was still needed. Without versioning, the original is gone, and the support ticket ends with "sorry".

This guide sets up a Hubfly space Storage bucket that keeps every earlier copy, so you can bring it back instead of apologising. You'll enable versioning, upload from the browser through short-lived upload links, and save the version ID each upload returns. That last step is what makes recovery easy.

Try it on Hubfly space → Create a free account, no card needed.

How versioning works, in one paragraph

A bucket stores files by key, such as tenant-001/contract.txt. With versioning off, uploading to the same key replaces the file for good. With versioning Enabled, the old copy stays in the bucket as an older version, and the new one becomes the current version. Deleting a file adds a delete marker instead of erasing the data. Your app only sees the current version, but the older ones are still there to read.

Step 1: Create a bucket and turn on versioning

  1. In the dashboard, click Create Project, pick Storage, choose the region and click Create Project.
  2. Click New bucket, name it (for example customer-uploads) and click Create bucket.
  3. Open the bucket, click Settings, set Object versioning to Enabled, then click Save settings.

Bucket settings: versioning, image cache retention, and the delete rule for buckets.

Do this before the first upload. Versioning only protects files written after it's on.

One-way switch. Once a bucket's versioning is enabled, you can set it to Suspended later but not back to Disabled. Suspended stops keeping new versions; the old ones stay. From a terminal, the same setting is hubfly storage buckets update customer-uploads --versioning enabled.

Step 2: Let the browser upload through a short-lived link

Browsers shouldn't hold storage secrets, and presigned S3 uploads from a browser don't work on Hubfly space (the S3 endpoint rejects the cross-origin check browsers send first). Instead, your server asks for an upload session, and the browser sends the file straight to the link it gets back.

First, create a storage API key: open the project's API access tab and click Create API key. Limit it to the customer-uploads bucket. The key starts with hfs_ and is shown once, so put it straight into your server's secrets as HUBFLY_STORAGE_KEY. It's limited to Storage upload sessions, so it can't manage the project, its keys or its settings.

Then add a small endpoint to your server (Node.js 18+, Express):

import path from "node:path";
app.use(express.json());

const ALLOWED = new Set(["application/pdf", "image/png", "image/jpeg", "text/plain"]);

function cleanName(name) {
  const base = path.basename(String(name || "")).replace(/[^\w.\- ]/g, "_").slice(0, 200);
  if (!base || base === "." || base === "..") throw new Error("bad file name");
  return base;
}

// POST /uploads/start  { fileName, contentType }
app.post("/uploads/start", requireLogin, async (req, res) => {
  if (!ALLOWED.has(req.body.contentType)) return res.status(400).json({ error: "file type not allowed" });
  let name;
  try { name = cleanName(req.body.fileName); } catch { return res.status(400).json({ error: "bad file name" }); }
  const objectKey = `${req.user.tenantId}/${name}`;    // e.g. "tenant-001/contract.txt"
  const r = await fetch(
    `https://api.hubfly.space/api/v1/projects/${process.env.HUBFLY_PROJECT_ID}/storage/objects/upload-session`,
    {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.HUBFLY_STORAGE_KEY}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        bucket: "customer-uploads",
        objectKey,
        contentType: req.body.contentType,
      }),
    }
  );
  if (!r.ok) return res.status(502).json({ error: "upload link failed" });
  const { data } = await r.json();   // { upload_url, object_key, expires_at, content_type }
  res.json({ uploadUrl: data.upload_url, objectKey: data.object_key });
});

The key is built on your server from the logged-in user, and the file name is cleaned first, so one customer can't write into another customer's folder. The content type is checked against a short allowlist, so nobody stores an HTML page in your bucket. The link works for one bucket and one key, and expires after an hour. Upload sessions take no size limit, so cap the file size in your app before you ask for a link.

Step 3: Upload, and keep the version ID

In the browser, send the file to the link. The response tells you which version you just created:

const start = await fetch("/uploads/start", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ fileName: file.name, contentType: file.type }),
}).then(r => r.json());

const put = await fetch(start.uploadUrl, {
  method: "PUT",
  headers: { "Content-Type": file.type },
  body: file,
});
if (!put.ok) throw new Error("upload failed or link expired");
const result = await put.json();
// 201 → { "object_key": "tenant-001/contract.txt", "version_id": "ver_5f96…", "size": 44 }

await fetch("/uploads/finish", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify(result),
});

On the server, save a row per upload, but only for keys inside the user's own folder:

app.post("/uploads/finish", requireLogin, async (req, res) => {
  const { object_key, version_id, size } = req.body;
  if (!String(object_key).startsWith(`${req.user.tenantId}/`) || !String(version_id).startsWith("ver_")) return res.status(403).end();
  await db.fileVersions.insert({ object_key, version_id, size, user_id: req.user.id, event: "upload", at: new Date() });
  res.status(204).end();
});

Asking for the link takes two to three seconds, and the upload itself under a second for small files. When your app deletes a file, record that too. The Storage delete call returns { "delete_marker": true, "version_id": "ver_…" }; that ID is the marker itself, not a copy to restore. The last upload row before it is the version to bring back.

Why save the version ID? The dashboard and the Storage object list show only the current version of each key. Neither has a "show old versions" list. Your own upload history is the simplest index of every version you might need to restore.

You can check any file's current version in the dashboard: open the bucket, switch to Raw, and click the info icon on a file.

Object details for the current version of tenant-001/contract.txt.

The Raw view shows one card per key, the current version only. Files added with the dashboard's Upload button get their own uploads/<id>/ key, so they never replace each other.

Step 4: Restore an earlier version

The dashboard's download button always returns the current version, so restoring goes through the S3 endpoint. Create an S3 access key in the project's Access keys tab (read/write, scoped to customer-uploads) and keep it on your server only.

Hubfly space's S3 endpoint lets an object GET address an older version with versionId. To restore, look up the version ID in your upload history, read that version, and write it back to the same key, which makes it the current version again. Before you do, check that the key starts with the requesting customer's folder, the same way /uploads/finish does.

What it costs

Every version is a stored file, billed at the Hubfly space Storage rate of $0.00001536 per GB-hour:

  • 1 GB for a month: 1 × 0.00001536 × 730 = $0.0112.
  • 10 GB of current files: 10 × 0.00001536 × 730 = $0.11 a month.
  • The same 10 GB where each file was replaced twice (30 GB kept): 30 × 0.00001536 × 730 = $0.34 a month.

Versioning, upload sessions and version IDs are free. Old versions count toward the project's storage quota (100 GB by default), so check Storage used on the project page now and then.

What can go wrong

  1. "I turned it on, but the file from yesterday is gone." Versioning protects only writes made after it was enabled. Turn it on when you create the bucket.
  2. Switching versioning back to Disabled is rejected (the API returns a 400 error). Once enabled, a bucket can only be Suspended. Choose Suspended to stop keeping new versions.
  3. Files re-uploaded with the dashboard's Upload files button don't create versions. Each dashboard upload gets its own uploads/<id>/ key, so nothing is replaced. Versions build up only when your app writes to the same fixed key, as in Step 2.

Limits, honestly

  • No version list in the dashboard or the Storage object list, so you need your own record of version IDs. Restoring goes through the S3 endpoint.
  • No automatic expiry for old versions is documented yet. If files change often, budget for the extra storage.
  • A normal delete only adds a delete marker; every earlier version stays stored and billed. To erase a customer's file for good (for example on a deletion request), delete each version by its version ID from your history.
  • A bucket must be empty, including retained versions, before you can delete it.
  • Files are stored without encryption at rest. Encrypt sensitive documents in your app before upload.
  • Once enabled, versioning can only be suspended, not turned off.

Who this is not for

If you need legal-hold or write-once storage (compliance archives that nobody, not even an admin, can delete), versioning isn't that, and no object lock is documented on Hubfly space. Use a provider with object lock for that case. If your files never change after upload, give each upload a unique key instead and skip versioning.

Read next: How to resize and watermark product photos with just a URL · How to get a managed PostgreSQL database for about $2 a month

Go further on Hubfly space

  • Hand out temporary download links for files in the same bucket.
  • Write S3 keys into your app as secrets with hubfly storage keys create … --to <cell-project>, which stores the secret as a Cell project variable.
  • Read the Storage limits and security notes before you put customer files in production.

title: Implementing Safe OpenTofu State Locking with Redis-Backed Circuit Breakers
description:
Implementing Safe OpenTofu State Locking with Redis-Backed Circuit Breakers

Last quarter, our infrastructure team migrated from Terraform Cloud to self-hosted OpenTofu with S3 state backends. Within 48 hours, we hit a silent data race: two Jenkins agents simultaneously acquired state locks during a transient network hiccup, corrupted our production VPC configuration, and took down egress routing for 23 minutes.

The root cause wasn't OpenTofu itself—it was our naive retry logic treating lock acquisition as an idempotent operation without accounting for partial failures in distributed systems.

The Thundering Herd Problem in State Lock Acquisition

OpenTofu's DynamoDB state locking uses conditional writes with a TTL-based lease model. When a network partition resolves, multiple waiting workers simultaneously retry lock acquisition. Without proper backoff, this creates a thundering herd:

# Dangerous: unbounded retry loop
def acquire_tofu_lock(state_key: str) -> bool:
    while True:
        try:
            response = dynamodb.put_item(
                TableName='terraform-locks',
                Item={'LockID': state_key, 'Info': worker_id},
                ConditionExpression='attribute_not_exists(LockID)'
            )
            return True
        except ClientError as e:
            if e.response['Error']['Code'] == 'ConditionalCheckFailedException':
                time.sleep(1)  # Fixed 1s retry - disaster waiting to happen
            else:
                raise

This pattern fails catastrophically when:

  1. Network latency spikes cause lock TTL expirations
  2. DynamoDB throttles conditional writes under load
  3. Multiple CI pipelines trigger simultaneously after incident recovery

Production-Hardened Circuit Breaker Wrapper

Here's the battle-tested replacement we deployed. It uses Redis for distributed circuit state and implements truncated exponential backoff with full jitter:

import redis
import random
import time
from enum import Enum
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

class CircuitState(Enum):
    CLOSED = "closed"
    OPEN = "open"
    HALF_OPEN = "half_open"

@dataclass
class CircuitBreakerConfig:
    failure_threshold: int = 5
    timeout_seconds: int = 60
    half_open_max_calls: int = 3

class DistributedCircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, redis_client: redis.Redis, service_name: str, config: CircuitBreakerConfig):
        self.redis = redis_client
        self.service_name = service_name
        self.config = config
        self.state_key = f"circuit:{service_name}:state"
        self.failure_key = f"circuit:{service_name}:failures"
        self.last_failure_key = f"circuit:{service_name}:last_failure"

    def call(self, func, *args, **kwargs):
        state = self._get_state()

        if state == CircuitState.OPEN:
            if self._should_attempt_reset():
                self._set_state(CircuitState.HALF_OPEN)
            else:
                raise Exception(f"Circuit breaker OPEN for {self.service_name}")

        try:
            result = func(*args, **kwargs)
            self._on_success()
            return result
        except Exception as e:
            self._on_failure()
            raise

    def _get_state(self) -> CircuitState:
        state = self.redis.get(self.state_key)
        return CircuitState(state.decode()) if state else CircuitState.CLOSED

    def _set_state(self, state: CircuitState):
        self.redis.set(self.state_key, state.value, ex=self.config.timeout_seconds * 2)

    def _on_failure(self):
        failures = self.redis.incr(self.failure_key)
        self.redis.expire(self.failure_key, self.config.timeout_seconds)
        self.redis.set(self.last_failure_key, int(time.time()))

        if failures >= self.config.failure_threshold:
            self._set_state(CircuitState.OPEN)

    def _on_success(self):
        self.redis.delete(self.failure_key)
        if self._get_state() == CircuitState.HALF_OPEN:
            self._set_state(CircuitState.CLOSED)

    def _should_attempt_reset(self) -> bool:
        last_failure = self.redis.get(self.last_failure_key)
        if not last_failure:
            return True
        return (int(time.time()) - int(last_failure)) >= self.config.timeout_seconds

def acquire_tofu_lock_resilient(state_key: str, circuit_breaker: DistributedCircuitBreaker, max_attempts: int = 8) -> bool:
    """Exponential backoff with full jitter and circuit breaker protection."""
    base_delay_ms = 100
    max_delay_ms = 8000

    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            def _attempt_lock():
                response = dynamodb.put_item(
                    TableName='terraform-locks',
                    Item={'LockID': state_key, 'Info': worker_id, 'Timestamp': int(time.time())},
                    ConditionExpression='attribute_not_exists(LockID)'
                )
                return True

            return circuit_breaker.call(_attempt_lock)

        except ClientError as e:
            if e.response['Error']['Code'] != 'ConditionalCheckFailedException':
                raise

            # Exponential backoff with full jitter
            max_backoff = min(base_delay_ms * (2 ** attempt), max_delay_ms)
            jittered_delay = random.uniform(0, max_backoff) / 1000.0
            time.sleep(jittered_delay)

    return False

Integration with OpenTofu Backend Configuration

Wire this into your OpenTofu wrapper or CI pipeline:

import redis
import boto3

redis_client = redis.Redis(host='redis.infra.internal', port=6379, decode_responses=False)
dynamodb = boto3.client('dynamodb', region_name='us-east-1')

circuit_config = CircuitBreakerConfig(
    failure_threshold=5,
    timeout_seconds=60,
    half_open_max_calls=2
)

lock_circuit = DistributedCircuitBreaker(redis_client, 'tofu-state-lock', circuit_config)

# Before running tofu apply
if not acquire_tofu_lock_resilient('prod-vpc-state', lock_circuit):
    print("Failed to acquire lock after backoff - aborting deployment")
    sys.exit(1)

# Run tofu apply with backend config
os.system('tofu apply -auto-approve')

Distributed Rate Limiter for Lock Contention

For high-frequency deployments, add a Redis-based sliding window rate limiter to prevent lock storms:

-- Redis Lua script: sliding_window_rate_limit.lua
local key = KEYS[1]
local window_size = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local max_requests = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local current_time = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local window_start = current_time - window_size

redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', key, 0, window_start)
local request_count = redis.call('ZCARD', key)

if request_count < max_requests then
    redis.call('ZADD', key, current_time, current_time)
    redis.call('EXPIRE', key, window_size)
    return 1
else
    return 0
end

Python integration:

def check_lock_rate_limit(redis_client: redis.Redis, worker_id: str) -> bool:
    script = redis_client.register_script(open('sliding_window_rate_limit.lua').read())
    allowed = script(keys=[f'lock_rate:{worker_id}'], args=[60, 10, int(time.time())])
    return bool(allowed)

Observability Hooks

Instrument circuit state transitions for Prometheus:

from prometheus_client import Gauge, Counter

circuit_state_gauge = Gauge('tofu_circuit_breaker_state', 'Circuit breaker state', ['service'])
lock_acquisition_failures = Counter('tofu_lock_acquisition_failures', 'Failed lock attempts')

class ObservableCircuitBreaker(DistributedCircuitBreaker):
    def _set_state(self, state: CircuitState):
        super()._set_state(state)
        state_value = {'closed': 0, 'half_open': 1, 'open': 2}[state.value]
        circuit_state_gauge.labels(service=self.service_name).set(state_value)

    def _on_failure(self):
        super()._on_failure()
        lock_acquisition_failures.inc()

Operational Trade-offs We Accepted

This architecture introduces two hard dependencies:

  1. Redis cluster must be available before OpenTofu runs (but Redis failure doesn't corrupt state)
  2. 200-800ms additional latency per lock acquisition due to backoff

We considered using Consul for distributed locking but stayed with DynamoDB to avoid adding another stateful service. The circuit breaker gives us fail-fast behavior without changing OpenTofu's native locking mechanism.

Open Questions for Discussion

Should the circuit breaker track failure rates per state file or per AWS account? Our current implementation pools all state locks into a single circuit, which means a problem with one environment can block deployments to unrelated environments. Namespace isolation would reduce blast radius but increases Redis memory usage linearly with state file count.

How do you handle lock acquisition in multi-region OpenTofu deployments where DynamoDB global tables have eventual consistency windows? We're evaluating pessimistic locking with fencing tokens but haven't found a clean pattern that doesn't require forking OpenTofu's state management.

title: Chronos-2: A foundation model for multivariate time series forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.41956v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Accurate forecasting with uncertainty quantification is critical in a variety of scientific applications ranging from epidemiology and economics to energy systems and earth sciences. Yet most forecasting models still need to be developed and trained separately for each domain-specific dataset. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to remove this limitation and enable the application of the same model across domains through large-scale pretraining. However, most existing TSFMs treat each time series independently and therefore cannot model interactions among time series and external drivers. Here, we introduce Chronos-2, a foundation model for zero-shot forecasting that models the interactions between multivariate time series and heterogeneous covariates, which commonly arise in scientific applications. The model infers relationships among time series directly from historical context and generates probabilistic forecasts without task-specific treatment. Across various benchmarks, Chronos-2 achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on average by improving skill scores by 5.2 percentage points relative to the strongest baselines and increasing win rates by 10 percentage points. Chronos-2 is also computationally efficient, generating forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU, 50x and 1000x faster end-to-end than the best task-specific point and probabilistic forecasters, respectively. In addition, we demonstrate its effectiveness in diverse scientific settings -- including infectious-disease forecasting, macroeconomic modeling, carbon-flux prediction, and runoff simulation -- where the model matches or surpasses specialized methods developed for each domain. These results show that a single pretrained model can capture structure shared across temporal systems.

title: GENSTRAT: Toward a Science of Strategic Reasoning in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2605.23238v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Fixed game suites for evaluating strategic reasoning in large language models (LLMs) saturate and are hard to keep free of contamination. We introduce GENSTRAT, a system for evaluating the strategic capabilities of LLMs driven by procedural generation of two-player zero-sum imperfect-information betting games, allowing an evaluator to draw novel, fresh games on demand. Each game is characterized on a scale of five complexity axes (state space, temporal contingency, opponent dependence, private information, precision) and measured by Monte Carlo simulation. Using this generator, we construct a 50-game benchmark and hold a tournament of twelve frontier and open-weight models, gathering data from over 40,000 LLM vs. LLM matches. We further construct a composite complexity axis, and find that, on the eight hardest games, the gap between the best and worst model is 1.7x its value across the whole set of games. Ablations show that a higher thinking budget, disclosing the opponent's strategy, and higher reasoning matched to a game's specific demands (for private information and planning depth) were associated with higher margins for the LLM player.

title: Eclipse BIRT 4.25 Reports: Page Totals, PDF/A and JDK 21
description:
We ran Eclipse BIRT 4.25.0, the Eclipse Foundation's Java reporting engine, released on 9 September 2026, on JDK 25, checked its advisory records, and wrote down each problem that came up. Some come from how BIRT lays out HTML, some from the release itself, and one from an old artifact still sitting on Maven Central. Each item below has the run output or the record behind it, who it hits, and the fix BIRT offers where there is one.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

Does BIRT Render Flexbox, Grid or JavaScript?

It does not, and the reason is structural. Every IReportEngine method that opens an input takes a design or a stored report document, which means an existing HTML page has no way in until someone rebuilds it as a .rptdesign. Inside a design, HTML can fill a text item, and BIRT's own layout code positions it. This test design packs a flex row, a CSS grid and a document.write script into a single text item, adds a 150-row table, and writes its footer with value-of page variables.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<report xmlns="http://www.eclipse.org/birt/2005/design" version="3.2.23">
    <data-sources>
        <script-data-source name="Generated"/>
    </data-sources>
    <data-sets>
        <script-data-set name="Rows">
            <list-property name="resultSetHints">
                <structure>
                    <property name="position">1</property>
                    <property name="name">line</property>
                    <property name="dataType">string</property>
                </structure>
            </list-property>
            <property name="dataSource">Generated</property>
            <method name="open"><![CDATA[counter = 0;]]></method>
            <method name="fetch"><![CDATA[if (counter == 150) return false;
counter++;
row["line"] = "Row " + counter;
return true;]]></method>
        </script-data-set>
    </data-sets>
    <page-setup>
        <simple-master-page name="Simple MasterPage">
            <property name="type">a4</property>
            <page-footer>
                <text>
                    <property name="contentType">html</property>
                    <text-property name="content"><![CDATA[Page <value-of>pageNumber</value-of> of <value-of>totalPage</value-of>]]></text-property>
                </text>
            </page-footer>
        </simple-master-page>
    </page-setup>
    <body>
        <text>
            <property name="contentType">html</property>
            <text-property name="content"><![CDATA[<div style="display:flex"><div style="width:50%">Flex left</div><div style="width:50%">Flex right</div></div>
<div style="display:grid; grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr"><div>Grid A</div><div>Grid B</div></div>
<script>document.write("Written by script");</script>
<p>After the script tag</p>]]></text-property>
        </text>
        <table>
            <property name="dataSet">Rows</property>
            <list-property name="boundDataColumns">
                <structure>
                    <property name="name">line</property>
                    <expression name="expression" type="javascript">dataSetRow["line"]</expression>
                </structure>
            </list-property>
            <column/>
            <detail>
                <row>
                    <cell><data><property name="resultSetColumn">line</property></data></cell>
                </row>
            </detail>
        </table>
    </body>
</report>

The class below runs it in two steps, storing a .rptdocument first and rendering the PDF from that document.

import java.util.logging.Level;

import org.eclipse.birt.core.framework.Platform;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.EngineConfig;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.IRenderTask;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.IReportDocument;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.IReportEngine;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.IReportEngineFactory;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.IRunTask;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.PDFRenderOption;

public class IssueReportTwoStep {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        EngineConfig config = new EngineConfig();
        config.setLogConfig(null, Level.WARNING);
        Platform.startup(config);
        IReportEngine engine = ((IReportEngineFactory) Platform
                .createFactoryObject(IReportEngineFactory.EXTENSION_REPORT_ENGINE_FACTORY))
                .createReportEngine(config);

        try {
            // Run once into a report document, so the page count is known before rendering.
            IRunTask run = engine.createRunTask(engine.openReportDesign("known-issues.rptdesign"));
            run.run("known-issues.rptdocument");
            run.close();

            IReportDocument document = engine.openReportDocument("known-issues.rptdocument");
            System.out.println("Pages: " + document.getPageCount());
            IRenderTask render = engine.createRenderTask(document);
            PDFRenderOption options = new PDFRenderOption();
            options.setOutputFormat(PDFRenderOption.OUTPUT_FORMAT_PDF);
            options.setOutputFileName("known-issues-two-step.pdf");
            render.setRenderOption(options);
            render.render();
            render.close();
            document.close();
        } finally {
            engine.destroy();
            Platform.shutdown();
        }
    }
}

Console output was Pages: 4, and known-issues-two-step.pdf, at about 3 KB, shows the layout problem on page one. All four boxes from the flex row and the grid sit one per line at the same 6.5 mm left offset, so no columns formed, and no page contains the string Written by script. The 4.25.0 source lines up with that. Its DisplayManager registers sixteen display keywords, among them block, inline, list-item and the table types, and none of them is flex or grid, and the code that turns HTML into PDF content skips over script nodes. Teams moving HTML templates or script-drawn charts into BIRT feel this most. The BIRT answer is to redo the layout with designer grids and tables, and to draw charts with BIRT's chart engine.

Why Does the Footer Say Page 2 of 2?

That same footer gave two different results depending on the task. Run as above, through IRunTask and then IRenderTask, the four pages read Page 1 of 4 to Page 4 of 4. Run through a single IRunAndRenderTask, every page claimed to be the last one, from Page 1 of 1 up to Page 4 of 4, the total keeping pace with the current page. Single-task runs of any multi-page report with this footer are affected. Besides the two-step run, the designer's auto-text items for page number and total page print the right count in one task, which a separate run of the design confirmed with Page 2 of 4 on page two.

Why Does PDF/A Output Stop on Times-Roman?

Archival output is a property of the design. BIRT's PDF emitter README names it PdfEmitter.Conformance (since 4.16), and in the XML it is one line under <report>.

<property name="pdfConformance">PDF.A1B</property>

Adding just that line to known-issues.rptdesign and pointing the two-step class at the copy got as far as Pages: 4. Rendering then failed. A warning came first (Times not embeddable), then an EngineException whose cause, PdfXConformanceException, named Times-Roman as unembedded, and the PDF on disk was 0 bytes. Times-Roman is a base-14 font that BIRT references without embedding, so a design left on the default font cannot become PDF/A as it stands. Two fixes exist in BIRT itself, an embeddable font such as Arial set on the report style, or the PdfEmitter.PDFA.FallbackFont setting from the README. The Arial route came to roughly 35 KB, and veraPDF 1.30.3 accepted it as PDF/A-1b.

Why Won't BIRT 4.25 Compile on JDK 17?

The 4.21.0 release notes record the change that moved BIRT's bundles to JavaSE-21, and every engine jar with code in it since then is compiled to class file version 65. The 4.20.0 engine still targeted Java 11. Point a JDK 17 compiler at a 4.25.0 project and it stops at the first BIRT import, because javac reads Platform.class as version 65 where it can load at most 61. Teams still on Java 11 or 17 upgrade the JVM first, or hold at 4.20.0, the last Java 11 release.

The Maven layout adds two more issues. Central's all-in-one birt-runtime artifact has not moved past 4.9.0 from May 2022, so a 4.25.0 build lists the engine modules one by one, and a missing module surfaces only when a report runs.

  • Without org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.emitter.pdf, the run step still prints Pages: 4, and render() then ends in UnsupportedFormatException because no PDF writer is installed.
  • Without org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.script.javascript, data engine creation fails during the run step on No such script extension : javascript., so no PDF is written.

The bundled 4.25.0 runtime comes from the Eclipse download site instead, as a zip of 290,887,286 bytes. The project's license is the Eclipse Public License 2.0.

Is the BIRT Report Viewer Affected by CVEs?

Yes, in older builds, and one of those builds is still the newest Viewer on Maven Central. NVD records four BIRT CVEs, all in the Report Viewer, the servlet application that serves reports over HTTP, each scored by NIST and none disputed.

  • CVE-2021-34427, CVSS 3.1 score 9.8: Crafted query parameters write a remotely reachable JSP into the viewer folder, through 4.8.0.
  • CVE-2023-0100, CVSS 3.1 score 8.8: A tampered Host header lets the viewer fetch a report from an absolute HTTP path, from 2.6.2 until the 4.13 fix.
  • CVE-2019-11776, CVSS 3.1 score 6.1: Reflected XSS through a viewer URL parameter, versions 1.0 to 4.7.
  • CVE-2009-4521, CVSS 2.0 score 4.3: Cross-site scripting in the __report parameter of birt-viewer/run, before 2.5.0.

Exposure depends on where the Viewer is fetched from. Search Central for org.eclipse.birt.report.viewer and the newest hit is 4.9.0, uploaded 2 May 2022, a version that GHSA-4grc-q4fj-45p8 places inside the CVE-2023-0100 range. Deployments built from that coordinate carry the flaw. A patched birt.war ships inside the 4.25.0 runtime zip on the Eclipse download site. On 2 November 2026, OSV showed no advisories against the 4.25.0 engine or any of the 70 jars it pulled into the test build.

For reports that can start as HTML, IronPDF for Java is a commercial library our team builds that avoids the layout and footer issues above. Chromium does the drawing, and in our 2026.10.1 run a flex row and a grid each split into two columns while a script wrote its line. Java 8 and later can use it through a single Maven dependency, com.ironsoftware:ironpdf, which fetches the Chromium engine on first run or from a platform ironpdf-engine artifact, and Central lists ten 2026 versions up to 2026.10.1 from 1 October. A free trial covers evaluation.

Footers come from addTextFooter, which stamps {page} and {total-pages} onto the finished document, and saveAsPdfA with PdfAVersions.PdfA1b writes PDF/A. The PDF lands in a file or a byte array for the caller, so nothing like the Report Viewer has to be deployed.

Where These BIRT Issues Leave a Java Team

A JDK 21 floor, a Maven layout that needs hand-picked modules, no flex or grid display values, dropped scripts, a page total that depends on the task, PDF/A refusing the default Times font and a 2022 Viewer on Central with a known CVE are the issues to check before a BIRT upgrade, especially for a report that already exists as HTML.

IronPDF for Java renders that kind of report from a template on Java 8 or later, with rendering done in the separate engine process the IronPdfEngine guide describes.

Eclipse BIRT is a trademark of the Eclipse Foundation, we have no affiliation with the Foundation, and the versions, advisories and run results above rest on public records and our own test runs from 2 November 2026.

Drafted with AI. BIRT code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team against Eclipse BIRT 4.25.0 and com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.10.1 on 2 November 2026.

title: Zetix for Agencies: Running Client Projects and Approvals in One Workspace
description:
Short answer: An agency can use Zetix AI to run the full client workflow in one workspace: new-business leads, client onboarding, recurring projects, feedback and approvals, client messages and monthly reporting. You describe how your agency works, and Zetix's agent, ZET, sets up the apps you need.

The workflow problem

Agency work moves through the same loop for every client: win the client, onboard them, deliver work every month, collect feedback, get approvals and report results. In many agencies each step lives in a different place: leads in one tool, tasks in another, client feedback in WhatsApp and email, files in shared drives and reports in slides. Account managers spend a large part of their week stitching it together.

The workflow in Zetix

1. New business

Enquiries from your website, referrals and WhatsApp land in Lead Management with an owner and a next step. Proposals are stored in Documents and linked to the lead.

2. Client onboarding

When a deal is won, the client moves into an onboarding stage with a checklist: contract, brand assets, account access, kickoff meeting. Automation creates the tasks and reminds owners.

3. Recurring delivery

Monthly retainers become recurring tasks in Workforce, with owners, due dates and statuses such as In progress, Internal review, With client and Approved.

4. Feedback and approvals

Client messages from WhatsApp and email arrive in a shared Omnichannel Inbox linked to the client record, so feedback isn't lost in someone's personal chat.

5. Reporting

Analytics shows work due and overdue by client and by team member, plus lead and pipeline numbers for new business.

Example prompt for ZET

"We're a 15-person digital marketing agency with about 30 retainer clients. We onboard new clients, run monthly content and ads work, get approvals over WhatsApp and send a monthly report."

ZET might suggest: Lead Management, CRM, Workforce, Omnichannel Inbox, Documents, Scheduling, Automation and Analytics. You can remove any of them before you click Build.

Why one workspace helps agencies

  • One client record shows deals, tasks, files and conversations together.
  • Fewer status meetings, because the board shows what's waiting on whom.
  • Smoother handovers when an account manager is away.
  • Pay for what you use: Zetix pricing depends on how many tools you choose.

FAQ

Can Zetix handle recurring retainer work?

Yes. Recurring tasks can be set up for monthly or weekly deliverables, with owners and due dates.

Can clients' WhatsApp messages be linked to their project?

Yes. The Omnichannel Inbox links conversations, including WhatsApp, to the client record.

Do we need a developer to set it up?

No. You describe your agency to ZET and it configures ready-made apps.

Get started

Describe your agency's workflow to ZET at zetix.ai.

Disclosure: I work with Zetix.

title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
description:
arXiv:2610.41172v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.

title: Stripe Already Retries. The Gaps Are Between Its Attempts.
description:
The most common objection to recovery tooling on Stripe is a fair one: Stripe already retries failed payments, sends dunning emails, and hosts card-update pages. All true. What the objection misses is the shape of the native schedule. Stripe's Smart Retries pick times from network-wide patterns, and its revenue recovery tools work inside a fixed frame. The gaps between native attempts, the failures that need a full pay cycle, and the decline codes that deserve a different response entirely are where renewals still die quietly.

Working those gaps without fighting the native engine is an engineering discipline of its own. A second system has to know when the next native attempt is scheduled and defer to it, fire only inside the open windows, and hold slots in reserve so the combined schedule never exceeds the shared ceiling of 15 attempts. It has to re-read the invoice before every one of its own attempts, because a charge that settled natively five minutes ago must cancel the queued retry, not race it.

And it has to be honest about the boundary of the whole exercise. Native tooling plus a conducted second engine still will not save a customer who wants to leave; the cancel click gets one branded save offer and a one-click exit, nothing more. What the conducted layer adds is narrower and more valuable: the timing failures, the payday failures, and the expiry failures get a schedule built for them specifically. A fuller treatment of how Stripe dunning software layers onto the native machinery, including where the native tools genuinely suffice, is worth reading before paying anyone, including us.

Our own terms, for the record: a 14-day trial with the card taken up front, then $179/mo flat. Recover $179 in 30 days, guaranteed — or Swipe Again is free the next 30 days. If the native tools alone clear that bar for a given store, the honest advice is to keep the $179.

Published by Swipe Again - failed-payment recovery for subscription businesses.
