title: Idempotent Jobs & Exactly-Once Effects: Designing Safe Retries
description:
Durable execution, async LLM workflows and message-delivery debates keep showing up on DEV: MQTT QoS posts, local agent pipelines, tool-call cost control. The fancy orchestration only works if the boring layer underneath is honest about failure. Most SaaS queues deliver at least once. Your job will run again after a worker crash, a deploy, a lock timeout or a broker redelivery. If that job charges a card, sends a welcome email or decrements inventory, "just retry" becomes double billing. Part 1 of this series is the foundation every queue needs before you chase orchestration frameworks: idempotent jobs and exactly-once effects.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every example and claim myself against Laravel queue behaviour and common BullMQ patterns. I build Loop Origin, where we design and ship Laravel and Node SaaS systems for clients, and this post opens a new series on reliable queues and async work.

📚 Series Roadmap — Reliable Queues & Async Work in SaaS

  • Part 1 (This Post): Idempotent Jobs & Exactly-Once Effects: Designing Safe Retries
  • Part 2: Queue Backpressure, Fairness & Tenant Isolation in Multi-Tenant SaaS
  • Part 3: Dead Letter Queues, Poison Messages & Safe Replay Playbooks
  • Part 4: Delayed Jobs, Schedulers & Clock Skew Gotchas
  • Part 5: Observability for Async Work: Correlation IDs & Job Traces
  • Part 6: Choosing Redis, SQS or Database Queues for Laravel and Node SaaS

Earlier Loop Origin series: Production MCP servers · Multi-tier caching & stampede protection · Usage-based billing metering

How do you make queue jobs safe under at-least-once delivery?

Direct answer: Assume every job can run more than once. Give each logical unit of work a stable idempotency key, record successful side effects in a dedupe store before or atomically with the effect, and make retries no-ops when that key is already completed. Exactly-once effects are designed; exactly-once delivery from the broker is not something you should bet the business on.

At-least-once is the default

Brokers and workers fail independently. A worker may finish Stripe, crash before acking the message, and another worker will process the same payload. SQS visibility timeouts, Redis requeues after SIGKILL, and database queue reserved_at reclaim all produce the same shape: duplicate execution of a job you thought was done.

That is fine for pure recomputation (rebuild a cache entry, regenerate a report file). It is not fine for:

  • Sending email or SMS
  • Charging or refunding via Stripe
  • Mutating inventory or wallet balances
  • Creating external tickets or webhooks your partners treat as unique events

Those need an exactly-once effect built on top of at-least-once delivery. The same discipline shows up in metering pipelines from the usage-based billing architecture post: count once, bill once.

Idempotency keys

An idempotency key names the business operation, not the queue attempt.

Good keys:

  • invoice:{invoice_id}:finalize
  • user:{user_id}:welcome_email:v1
  • order:{order_id}:reserve_stock
  • Stripe-style keys you already send as Idempotency-Key on the API call

Bad keys:

  • Random UUIDs generated inside handle() (every retry looks new)
  • The queue job UUID alone (re-dispatch creates a new one)
  • Timestamps

Generate the key when the command is accepted (HTTP handler, domain service), store it on the job payload, and reuse it for every attempt.

Dedupe store patterns

You need a place that remembers "this key already completed" with clear semantics.

Approach Pros Cons Best for
DB unique constraint on idempotency_key Strong, transactional with business rows Needs a table; watch long transactions Payments, inventory
Redis SET key NX EX Fast, simple TTL Must choose TTL carefully; Redis loss risk Emails, notifications
Provider idempotency (Stripe) Effect-level guarantee at the vendor Only covers that vendor call Card charges
Outbox + unique event id Ties to durable domain events More moving parts Cross-service workflows

A practical pattern for side effects:

  1. Begin transaction / acquire lock for the key.
  2. If status is completed, return success (no-op).
  3. If status is in_progress and not stale, exit and let the other worker finish (or retry later).
  4. Perform the side effect (or call Stripe with the same Idempotency-Key).
  5. Mark completed and commit.

Order matters. Marking complete before the email sends can skip a real send after a crash. Marking complete only after a non-idempotent charge can double-charge if you crash between charge and write. Prefer vendor idempotency for money; for email, accept rare duplicates or use a provider-side dedupe id.


AI-generated image.

Laravel: unique jobs and explicit keys

Laravel can prevent overlapping duplicates while a job is on the queue, which is necessary but not sufficient for exactly-once effects:

use Illuminate\Contracts\Queue\ShouldBeUnique;
use Illuminate\Bus\Queueable;
use Illuminate\Contracts\Queue\ShouldQueue;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Bus\Dispatchable;
use Illuminate\Queue\InteractsWithQueue;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Mail;

class SendWelcomeEmail implements ShouldQueue, ShouldBeUnique
{
    use Dispatchable, InteractsWithQueue, Queueable;

    public function __construct(
        public int $userId,
        public string $idempotencyKey, // e.g. user:42:welcome_email:v1
    ) {}

    public function uniqueId(): string
    {
        return $this->idempotencyKey;
    }

    public function handle(): void
    {
        $claimed = DB::table('job_idempotency')->insertOrIgnore([
            'key' => $this->idempotencyKey,
            'status' => 'completed',
            'created_at' => now(),
            'updated_at' => now(),
        ]);

        if ($claimed === 0) {
            return; // already sent (or claimed)
        }

        $user = User::query()->findOrFail($this->userId);
        Mail::to($user)->send(new WelcomeMail($user));
    }
}

// At the HTTP edge — key is stable before dispatch
$key = "user:{$user->id}:welcome_email:v1";
SendWelcomeEmail::dispatch($user->id, $key);

ShouldBeUnique stops two welcome jobs sitting on the queue at once. The job_idempotency row stops a second send after the first succeeded and the unique lock released. For charges, call Stripe with the same key the job carries; Stripe will not create a second PaymentIntent for that Idempotency-Key.

If you are shaping Laravel services for production SaaS, the same boundaries show up in how we approach Laravel development work: commands accept idempotency keys at the edge, jobs never invent them.

Node / BullMQ equivalent 

// producer
await welcomeQueue.add(
  'welcome',
  { userId, idempotencyKey: `user:${userId}:welcome_email:v1` },
  {
    jobId: `user:${userId}:welcome_email:v1`, // BullMQ dedupe by jobId
    attempts: 5,
    backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 2000 },
    removeOnComplete: true,
  }
);

// worker
welcomeQueue.process(async (job) => {
  const { userId, idempotencyKey } = job.data;
  const set = await redis.set(`idem:${idempotencyKey}`, '1', 'EX', 60 * 60 * 24 * 30, 'NX');
  if (set !== 'OK') return; // already completed

  await sendWelcomeEmail(userId);
});

jobId gives you broker-level dedupe for identical enqueues. The Redis SET NX gives you effect-level dedupe across retries and re-dispatches after the original job record is gone. Mirror money moves with Stripe's Idempotency-Key header using the same string.

Cache stampede locks from the Redis/Valkey singleflight patterns are cousins of this idea: one winner does the work, everyone else observes the result.

Retry strategies compared

Strategy Behaviour Use when Risk if misused
No retry Fail once Non-critical, manually replayable Lost work
Fixed delay Retry every N seconds Simple internal APIs Thundering herd
Exponential backoff + jitter Growing delays Downstream 429/5xx Still doubles effects without keys
Unique / jobId dedupe One in-flight job per key Duplicate enqueues Does not cover post-success redelivery alone
Effect idempotency key Side effect runs once Email, payments, stock Key design bugs

Retries without idempotency keys multiply damage. Keys without retries leave users stuck on transient blips. You want both.

For broader product work that spans Laravel and Node services, the same queue contract applies across custom web application builds: define the key at command acceptance, not inside the worker.

Diagnostic checklist

  1. Can every critical job run twice without corrupting money, stock or messaging?
  2. Is the idempotency key created before dispatch and stored on the payload?
  3. Do you avoid random keys inside handle() / process callbacks?
  4. Is there a dedupe record (DB unique, Redis NX, or vendor key) for each side effect?
  5. Are Stripe (or similar) calls passing a stable Idempotency-Key?
  6. Does uniqueness middleware cover in-flight duplicates and a completed-state check?
  7. Are TTLs on Redis dedupe keys longer than any realistic late redelivery?
  8. Do poison retries go somewhere observable instead of silent infinite loops? (Part 3)
  9. Can you explain in one sentence what happens after a crash between side effect and ack?
  10. Have you load-tested duplicate delivery (replay the same payload) in staging?

FAQ

Is exactly-once delivery possible?

In general distributed systems, end-to-end exactly-once delivery is fragile. Design for at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handlers. That combination gives you exactly-once effects where it matters.

Should every job be idempotent?

Every job with an external side effect should be. Pure recomputation can be naturally idempotent if it overwrites the same artifact. Still guard expensive LLM or vendor calls; retries without caches burn money, which is why agent and tool-cost threads keep trending.

What TTL should Redis dedupe keys use?

Longer than your maximum job retention plus any manual replay window. Thirty days is a common starting point for emails; financial keys often live in Postgres forever.

Does Laravel ShouldBeUnique replace a dedupe table?

No. It mostly prevents concurrent duplicates while a job is queued or running. After success, a re-dispatch with a new attempt still needs a completed-state check.

How do I test this?

In staging, dispatch the same job payload twice, kill a worker mid-handler, and replay DLQ messages. Assert one email, one charge, one inventory row.

What about MCP and agent tool calls?

Treat each tool invocation that mutates state like a job side effect: stable ids, dedupe, and budgets. The production MCP server patterns for approval gates pair naturally with idempotent execution.

Next in this series, Part 2 covers queue backpressure, fairness and tenant isolation so one noisy customer cannot starve everyone else's workers.

title: TypeScript `@throws` JSDoc and Error Typing in 2026: Why Exceptions Are Still Untyped and What to Do About It
description:
TypeScript @throws JSDoc and Error Typing in 2026: Why Exceptions Are Still Untyped and What to Do About It

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers write try/catch blocks around TypeScript functions without knowing what exceptions those functions throw. The compiler stays silent when a function that throws NetworkError gets called without a handler, and the codebase ships with runtime crashes that static analysis should have caught. This happens because TypeScript treats exceptions as invisible to the type system.

Problem flow showing unhandled exception propagation in TypeScript

Languages with checked exceptions force developers to declare and handle throws behavior at compile time. TypeScript documentation includes a @throws JSDoc tag, but the tag has no enforcement mechanism. Engineers who write @throws {NetworkError} above a function signature get zero compiler feedback when callers ignore that annotation. The gap between documentation and verification creates a dangerous false confidence.

Solution flow showing explicit Result type error handling

Teams that need predictable error handling in TypeScript codebases must build their own type-safe patterns. Result types, discriminated unions, and explicit error boundaries provide the guarantees the language does not. The solutions require more code than a hypothetical throws keyword, but they work today without waiting for a language feature that may never arrive.

Key Takeaways

  • TypeScript does not type exceptions and likely never will due to JavaScript runtime semantics and the unchecked exception model.
  • The @throws JSDoc tag documents throw behavior but provides zero compiler enforcement or type safety.
  • Result types (Result<T, E>) and discriminated unions create verifiable error handling without language-level throw types.
  • Error discrimination patterns using instanceof and type guards allow safe exception handling in catch blocks when exceptions remain the chosen approach.
  • Teams must choose between exceptions with manual documentation (faster to write, harder to verify) and Result types (more verbose, compiler-verified).

Why TypeScript Still Doesn't Type Exceptions in 2026

TypeScript inherits JavaScript's unchecked exception model. Any function can throw any value at any time, and the runtime provides no compile-time guarantees about what gets thrown. Java and C# have checked exceptions where the compiler enforces throw declarations, but JavaScript does not, and TypeScript follows JavaScript semantics.

The language could theoretically add throw types as an optional static analysis layer. TypeScript already diverges from JavaScript in ways that require compilation (enums, namespaces before TypeScript 5.8's --erasableSyntaxOnly). Adding a throws keyword or enforcing @throws annotations would fit that pattern. The TypeScript team has chosen not to pursue this feature.

Three technical barriers prevent practical implementation of throw types in TypeScript:

Dynamic function references lose throw information under indirection. When a function gets assigned to a variable, passed as a callback, or returned from another function, TypeScript would need to preserve throw signatures through every layer of indirection. Higher-order functions and async operations create combinatorial explosion in the number of possible throw paths.

Third-party code has no throw annotations. The vast majority of npm packages ship without throw documentation. Even if TypeScript added throw types tomorrow, existing libraries would appear to throw nothing. The type system would require every developer to manually annotate every dependency, or accept a mass of implicit any exceptions that defeat the entire purpose.

JavaScript's throw accepts any type. Code can throw strings, numbers, null, or custom objects. A robust throw type system would need to model all possible thrown values, including edge cases where throw appears in expression position. The complexity of accurately representing JavaScript's throw semantics exceeds the benefit.

TypeScript 5.2 added decorator metadata (accessed via Symbol.metadata) that frameworks use to attach runtime information to classes. Decorator metadata does not extend to function throw signatures. TypeScript 5.8 introduced --erasableSyntaxOnly to restrict syntax to patterns that Node.js type-stripping can handle, but this targets import/export semantics and namespace elimination, not exception typing.

The official TypeScript handbook documents @throws in JSDoc but provides no mechanism to verify those annotations. The tag exists for human readers and documentation generators, not for the compiler.

The @throws JSDoc Tag: What It Provides and What It Doesn't

TypeScript recognizes the @throws JSDoc tag as valid documentation syntax. Developers write @throws {ErrorType} description above function declarations to document exception behavior. IDEs display this information in hover tooltips and generated documentation sites parse it. The compiler ignores it completely during type checking.

/**
 * Fetches user data from the API
 * @throws {NetworkError} when the request fails
 * @throws {ValidationError} when the response is invalid
 */
function fetchUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  // implementation
}

// This compiles without error despite missing try/catch
const user = await fetchUser("123");

The function signature carries throw information in JSDoc but the call site receives no type error. Developers who read the hover tooltip see the documented exceptions. Developers who skip the tooltip get no warning when they omit error handling. The pattern depends on discipline rather than verification.

JSDoc comments provide value for human communication. A well-documented codebase with consistent @throws annotations helps engineers understand error paths when reading code. Documentation generation tools like TypeDoc extract @throws tags into reference pages. These benefits matter for large teams maintaining complex systems.

The disconnect between documentation and enforcement creates a specific problem: stale annotations. When a function's throw behavior changes but the JSDoc comment does not get updated, the compiler never reports the mismatch. Callers continue seeing outdated throw documentation. Tests might catch the divergence if they cover error paths, but the type system provides no safety net.

TypeScript error handling documentation approaches

Some teams treat @throws annotations as required parts of their style guide and enforce them via linter rules. The eslint-plugin-jsdoc package includes a require-throws rule that demands JSDoc throw documentation on functions that contain throw statements. This catches missing documentation but does not verify that callers handle the documented exceptions.

The pattern works for teams that value documentation completeness and accept that verification happens during code review rather than compilation. For teams that need compiler-enforced error handling, different patterns become necessary.

Building Type-Safe Error Handling Without Language Support

Result types encode success and failure cases directly in return values. A function that can fail returns Result<T, E> where T represents success and E represents failure. Callers must explicitly unwrap the result to access the success value, forcing them to handle the error case.

type Result<T, E> = 
  | { ok: true; value: T }
  | { ok: false; error: E };

function parseConfig(data: unknown): Result<Config, ConfigError> {
  if (!isValidConfig(data)) {
    return { ok: false, error: new ConfigError("Invalid structure") };
  }
  return { ok: true, value: data as Config };
}

const result = parseConfig(rawData);
if (!result.ok) {
  // Compiler requires handling the error case before accessing value
  console.error(result.error);
  return;
}
// result.value is now safely typed as Config
processConfig(result.value);

The type system enforces error handling at compile time. Attempting to access result.value without checking result.ok produces a type error. The pattern eliminates silent failure propagation because every result must be explicitly unwrapped.

Rust and Go popularized this pattern in systems programming. The Rust standard library uses Result<T, E> as its primary error handling mechanism. Go functions commonly return (value, error) tuples. These languages prove that explicit result types scale to large production systems.

TypeScript libraries provide pre-built Result type implementations. The neverthrow package offers a chainable Result API with .map(), .mapErr(), and .andThen() methods for composing operations. The ts-results package provides similar functionality with a focus on zero-dependency size. Teams can adopt these libraries or implement their own Result type based on their needs.

import { Result, ok, err } from 'neverthrow';

async function fetchUserData(id: string): Promise<Result<User, NetworkError>> {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
      return err(new NetworkError(response.status));
    }
    const data = await response.json();
    return ok(data);
  } catch (e) {
    return err(new NetworkError(0, 'Connection failed'));
  }
}

// Chaining with automatic error propagation
const result = await fetchUserData('123')
  .andThen(user => validateUser(user))
  .andThen(user => enrichUserData(user));

if (result.isErr()) {
  handleError(result.error);
} else {
  processUser(result.value);
}

Result types add verbosity compared to exceptions. Every fallible operation returns a Result that must be unwrapped. Chaining multiple operations requires .andThen() calls or manual result checking. For teams working in exception-heavy codebases, converting to Result types represents a significant architectural shift.

The tradeoff favors type safety over brevity. Exception-based code can appear cleaner because errors propagate implicitly, but that implicit propagation creates the exact problem Result types solve. When error handling matters more than code conciseness, Result types deliver compiler-verified correctness.

Result Types vs Exceptions: The Practical Trade-Offs

Aspect Result Types Exceptions
Compile-time verification Required by type system Documentation only
Error propagation Explicit at every call Implicit through call stack
Refactoring safety Compiler catches all call sites Manual search required
Code volume Higher (wrapping overhead) Lower (implicit propagation)
Integration with existing code Requires conversion layer Works immediately
Performance overhead Negligible (return value) Negligible (modern VMs)
Team learning curve Moderate (new pattern) Minimal (familiar)

Result types force every error case to surface at the call site. When a function changes its error type from ConfigError to ConfigError | NetworkError, the compiler reports an error at every location that unwraps the result. This property makes large refactors safer because the type system identifies every affected call site automatically.

Exceptions propagate through intermediate callers without modification. A function that calls another function that might throw does not need to declare or handle the exception. The call stack unwinds until a catch block appears. This behavior reduces code volume because intermediate functions need no error-handling logic, but it also means errors can travel far from their source before getting caught.

Comparison of error propagation in Result types versus exceptions

Teams working in established codebases with thousands of exception-throwing functions face a migration challenge. Converting one function to return Result<T, E> requires updating every caller. Exceptions remain compatible with the existing architecture. For greenfield projects or isolated modules, Result types impose no integration cost.

Exception performance in modern JavaScript engines imposes negligible overhead under normal control flow. Throwing and catching exceptions costs more than returning a value, but the difference matters only in tight loops where exceptions occur frequently. Real applications rarely hit performance limits from exception handling. Result types have similarly negligible performance impact because they compile to plain object returns.

The learning curve for Result types affects teams differently based on their background. Engineers familiar with Rust, Go, or functional programming recognize the pattern immediately. Teams working exclusively in JavaScript/TypeScript need time to internalize the explicit error handling mindset. The pattern requires consistent adoption across a codebase to provide value.

Exception familiarity gives them an advantage for quick prototyping and small projects. Every JavaScript developer understands try/catch syntax. Result types require teaching the team a new pattern before they can use it effectively. For projects where time to market matters more than long-term maintainability, exceptions offer a faster path.

Error Discrimination Patterns That Actually Work in Production

Catching exceptions in TypeScript produces values typed as unknown. The type system provides no information about what gets thrown. Developers must narrow the caught value to specific error types before accessing error properties safely.

class NetworkError extends Error {
  constructor(public statusCode: number, message: string) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'NetworkError';
  }
}

class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(public field: string, message: string) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'ValidationError';
  }
}

function processRequest(data: unknown) {
  try {
    validateData(data);
    sendToServer(data);
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof NetworkError) {
      console.error(`Network failed with status ${e.statusCode}`);
      return;
    }
    if (e instanceof ValidationError) {
      console.error(`Validation failed on field ${e.field}`);
      return;
    }
    // Unknown error - rethrow or log
    throw e;
  }
}

The instanceof operator narrows the type of e within each conditional block. TypeScript understands that after e instanceof NetworkError passes, e has type NetworkError in that branch. This pattern works for class-based errors that extend Error or implement distinct prototypes.

Custom error classes should always extend Error and set a distinctive name property. This practice ensures stack traces remain accurate and error monitoring tools can distinguish error types. The built-in Error.prototype.name gets set automatically when using class syntax with extends Error.

Type guard functions provide an alternative to instanceof checks when errors do not share a common base class. A type guard returns a boolean and uses a type predicate to tell TypeScript what type the value has when the guard returns true.

interface APIError {
  code: string;
  message: string;
}

function isAPIError(e: unknown): e is APIError {
  return (
    typeof e === 'object' &&
    e !== null &&
    'code' in e &&
    'message' in e &&
    typeof (e as APIError).code === 'string'
  );
}

function handleResponse(response: unknown) {
  try {
    processResponse(response);
  } catch (e) {
    if (isAPIError(e)) {
      console.error(`API error ${e.code}: ${e.message}`);
      return;
    }
    console.error('Unknown error:', e);
  }
}

The type guard performs runtime validation that the caught value has the expected shape. This pattern works when integrating with third-party APIs that throw plain objects rather than Error instances. The guard must check every required property because unknown values can be anything.

Error discrimination flow using instanceof and type guards

Error discrimination patterns in TypeScript catch blocks

Some codebases throw string literals or plain objects instead of Error instances. These patterns work at runtime but complicate error handling. Catching a string provides no stack trace and no way to distinguish error types beyond string parsing. Modern code should always throw Error instances or subclasses.

The zod library provides a .safeParse() method that returns a discriminated union instead of throwing. This pattern bridges the gap between validation libraries that throw and Result-type error handling.

import { z } from 'zod';

const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  email: z.string().email(),
});

function validateUser(data: unknown) {
  const result = UserSchema.safeParse(data);
  if (!result.success) {
    // result.error is a ZodError with detailed validation failures
    console.error(result.error.format());
    return null;
  }
  // result.data is typed as { id: string; email: string }
  return result.data;
}

The .safeParse() API demonstrates how libraries can provide both throwing and non-throwing variants. The standard .parse() method throws a ZodError on validation failure. The .safeParse() method returns { success: true; data: T } or { success: false; error: ZodError } without throwing. This gives callers the choice between exceptions and Result types per call site.

Documenting Throws Behavior for Teams and Tools

Teams that continue using exceptions need documentation strategies that scale. JSDoc @throws tags work when combined with linting rules that enforce their presence and code review processes that verify accuracy. The pattern relies on human discipline but provides value when applied consistently.

/**
 * Connects to the database with retry logic
 * @throws {ConnectionError} when all retry attempts fail
 * @throws {AuthenticationError} when credentials are invalid
 * @throws {TimeoutError} when connection exceeds deadline
 */
async function connectDatabase(config: DatabaseConfig): Promise<Connection> {
  // implementation
}

The eslint-plugin-jsdoc package includes rules that enforce @throws documentation. The require-throws rule checks that functions containing throw statements have corresponding @throws tags. Configuration options control whether the rule applies to all functions or only exported ones. Related tooling context shows how modern linters handle JSDoc validation.

Code review checklists should include verification that @throws tags match actual throw behavior. When a pull request modifies a function's error handling, reviewers check that JSDoc comments get updated accordingly. This manual process catches most documentation drift but depends on reviewer attention.

Documentation flow for throw behavior in team workflows

TypeDoc and similar documentation generators parse @throws tags into generated reference documentation. The official TypeDoc documentation (accessed via npm package typedoc version 0.26.x) shows that @throws tags appear in a dedicated "Throws" section of function documentation. This makes error behavior visible in generated API docs but does not affect compilation.

Some teams encode error types in function names as a lightweight alternative to comprehensive JSDoc. Functions named fetchUserOrThrow signal explicitly that they throw on failure, while tryFetchUser suggests they return null or undefined. This convention provides no type safety but improves code readability.

Error boundaries in React applications demonstrate a practical exception-based pattern that works without type system support. A component wraps children and catches errors that propagate during rendering. Related distributed context explores how error tracking spans service boundaries.

class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component<
  { children: React.ReactNode },
  { hasError: boolean; error?: Error }
> {
  state = { hasError: false, error: undefined };

  static getDerivedStateFromError(error: Error) {
    return { hasError: true, error };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error: Error, errorInfo: React.ErrorInfo) {
    logErrorToService(error, errorInfo);
  }

  render() {
    if (this.state.hasError) {
      return <ErrorFallback error={this.state.error} />;
    }
    return this.props.children;
  }
}

Error boundaries rely on React's lifecycle methods rather than TypeScript's type system. The pattern works because React guarantees when componentDidCatch gets called, eliminating the need for static analysis to track throw behavior through the component tree.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why doesn't TypeScript just add a throws keyword like Java?

JavaScript has unchecked exceptions and no runtime enforcement of throw declarations. TypeScript follows JavaScript semantics and avoids features that require fundamental runtime changes. The complexity of accurately modeling JavaScript's dynamic throw behavior through function references, callbacks, and async operations exceeds the benefit.

Can I use a compiler plugin to add throw type checking?

No compiler plugin system exists in TypeScript that allows custom type checking logic. The TypeScript compiler architecture does not support plugins that extend the type checker. Teams must work within the type system's built-in capabilities or use external tools like custom linters.

Do Result types work with async/await?

Result types work with async/await when the Promise resolves to a Result. Functions return Promise<Result<T, E>> instead of throwing. Callers await the Promise and then unwrap the Result with the same patterns used for synchronous code. The neverthrow library provides .asyncMap() and similar utilities for async Result composition.

How do I convert an exception-throwing library to use Result types?

Wrap library calls in adapter functions that catch exceptions and return Results. The adapter provides a typed boundary between exception-based external code and Result-based internal code. This pattern contains the exception handling at the integration point without requiring changes to the library itself.

What happens to stack traces when using Result types?

Result types preserve stack traces when the error case contains an Error instance. Creating errors with new Error() captures the call stack at that point. Result types simply return the error rather than throwing it, so the stack trace remains intact and accessible through the error's .stack property.

What to Do Until (If Ever) TypeScript Gets Throw Types

TypeScript will likely never support throw types given the language's design constraints and JavaScript's runtime semantics. The core team has not signaled any movement toward this feature in recent releases. Teams building production TypeScript applications must accept that exception typing will remain outside the type system's guarantees.

Result types provide the strongest alternative for codebases that need verifiable error handling. The pattern requires architectural commitment and training investment, but it delivers compile-time verification that exceptions cannot match. New projects should consider Result types from the start when error handling matters more than code brevity.

Exception-based codebases should combine @throws JSDoc with linter enforcement and code review processes. This approach lacks type system verification but provides human-readable documentation that scales to large teams. The pattern works when the team values familiar exception syntax and accepts manual verification during review.

Error discrimination using instanceof checks and type guards makes exception handling safer when exceptions remain the chosen approach. Every catch block should narrow the caught value to specific error types before accessing properties. This pattern prevents runtime errors from assumed error shapes while working within TypeScript's type system.

The library architecture patterns that underpin maintainable TypeScript projects apply equally to error handling strategy. Choose one approach and apply it consistently across the codebase rather than mixing patterns that create confusion at boundaries. The consistency matters more than the specific choice between Results and exceptions for most applications.

title: Building an Authorization Gateway for AI Agents: A Practical Architecture
description:
AI agents are increasingly capable of interacting with external APIs and enterprise systems.

But consider this scenario:

You build an AI agent that can access Gmail, update Salesforce, and interact with cloud infrastructure.

How do you prevent it from performing an action that the requesting user was never authorized to perform?

A common mistake is to give the agent a service account with broad permissions.

That makes implementation easier, but it creates a significant security risk.

Let's explore a better approach: an authorization gateway for AI agents.

*1. The architecture
*
Instead of allowing agents to communicate directly with enterprise APIs, route actions through an authorization gateway.

User Request
|
v
AI Agent
|
v
Action Request
|
v
Authorization Gateway
|
+---- Identity Validation
|
+---- Policy Evaluation
|
+---- Permission Check
|
v
Enterprise API
|
v
Audit Event

The agent proposes an action. The gateway determines whether that action is authorized.

The agent should not be responsible for granting itself permission.

*2. Define an agent identity
*
An agent needs an identity that is independent of its LLM provider.

*Example:
*
{
"agent_id": "crm-agent-001",
"owner": "sales-platform",
"environment": "production",
"allowed_actions": [
"customer.read",
"customer.update"
]
}

In a production implementation, identity records should be maintained in a trusted registry rather than accepted directly from an agent request.

*3. Define an action request
*
Every action should carry enough information for the gateway to evaluate it.

{
"agent_id": "crm-agent-001",
"principal_id": "employee-123",
"task_id": "task-987",
"resource": "customer/456",
"action": "customer.update"
}

The principal_id must be established through a trusted authentication and delegation process. It must not simply be trusted because the agent included it in JSON.

*4. Implement a basic policy check
*
A simplified Python example:

AGENT_POLICIES = {
"crm-agent-001": {
"customer.read",
"customer.update"
}
}

def authorize_action(agent_id, action):
allowed = AGENT_POLICIES.get(agent_id, set())

if action not in allowed:
    return {
        "authorized": False,
        "reason": "Action not permitted"
    }

return {
    "authorized": True,
    "reason": "Policy allows action"
}

This demonstrates the basic decision, but it is not production-grade authorization.

A real gateway must also validate the authenticated principal, delegation, resource ownership, tenant boundaries, credential scope, and applicable contextual policies.

*5. Add a human approval boundary
*
Not every action should be treated equally.

*For example:
*

  • Action
  • Suggested policy
  • Read a customer record
  • Automatic if authorized
  • Update a customer record
  • Automatic with scoped permission
  • Send an external email
  • Approval based on policy
  • Delete a customer account
  • Explicit approval
  • Modify production infrastructure
  • Strong approval controls

Human approval should be enforced by the gateway, not merely requested through an LLM prompt.

*6. Add audit logging
*
Every authorization decision should produce an event.

{
"event_type": "agent.authorization",
"agent_id": "crm-agent-001",
"task_id": "task-987",
"action": "customer.update",
"resource": "customer/456",
"decision": "ALLOW",
"timestamp": "2026-11-02T12:00:00Z"
}

Production systems should also capture the authenticated principal, policy version, correlation ID, execution result, and relevant delegation metadata.

Avoid logging access tokens, secrets, or unnecessary sensitive customer data.

*7. What should a production implementation add?
*
The simplified example is a starting point. A real enterprise authorization gateway should include:

  • OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect integration.
  • Short-lived, scoped credentials.
  • Token exchange or equivalent delegated authorization.
  • Centralized policy management.
  • Resource-level authorization.
  • Agent identity registration and revocation.
  • Rate limits and execution budgets.
  • Tamper-resistant audit storage.
  • Human approval workflows.
  • Multi-tenant isolation.

It should also ensure that a delegated agent cannot obtain broader permissions than the original authorization allows.

*8. Why this matters
*
Agent frameworks will continue to evolve. LLM providers will change. New orchestration technologies will emerge.

But enterprise security cannot be tightly coupled to a particular model or agent framework.

An independent authorization layer creates a consistent security boundary across different agent implementations.

*The key architectural principle is simple:
*
An AI agent may decide what action it wants to perform, but a trusted authorization layer must decide whether it is allowed to perform it.

That separation could become one of the foundational requirements for enterprise agent infrastructure.

What approach are you taking to identity and authorization in your agent implementations?

About the Author

Ashwin Giridharan writes about Cloud & Enterprise Architecture, AI Infrastructure, Generative AI, and Agentic AI.

Website: https://ashwingiridharan.com/

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/ashwingiridharan7/

GitHub: https://github.com/giridharan-ashwin

Medium: https://medium.com/@gashwin7

Follow me for more discussions on enterprise architecture, AI infrastructure, and building production-ready AI systems.

title: I Built an Editable Timeline for AI Agents: Skills, MCP, and Transactional Video Editing
description:
An AI agent can generate an FFmpeg command. But what happens when the next request is: “Shorten the second shot, move the voiceover and its captions together, and give me a project I can keep editing”?

That is the problem I have been working on in Timeline Studio, an open-source, local-first browser video editor with an Agent Skill and a shared command layer.

  • Source code
  • Try the editor

This post focuses on the editing architecture: how an agent turns a request into an inspectable plan, how that plan changes project state, and where rendering still has explicit limits.

Start with an editable project

A rendered MP4 does not preserve the decisions needed for the next edit: clip identity, source ranges, timing, transforms, and caption/audio relationships.

Timeline Studio uses an editable .timeline project as the source of truth. In the local command workflow, the archive contains project.json and embedded media. Asset import probes necessary metadata, computes SHA-256 integrity information, and embeds the media bytes.

This gives both the user and the agent a concrete state to return to. The user can reopen the project in the editor. The agent can inspect it before making another change.

Separate editorial decisions from state changes

The model can decide that a voiceover should start at three seconds. The application should enforce whether the clip exists, whether the time is valid, and how linked captions follow it.

The architecture looks like this:

User request + media evidence
             |
     Skill: analyze and plan
             |
     Structured edit plan
             |
 CLI / local MCP / browser WebMCP
             |
 Shared command registry and reducers
             |
 Editable project + verified output

The transports have different environments. The CLI operates on local archives. The local STDIO MCP adapter exposes that command runner to an agent. Browser WebMCP, when exposed by the host, operates on the open editor and commits through its normal history.

The important constraint is to reuse editing rules rather than implement a separate editor for each transport.

An edit plan needs preconditions

Here is a simplified plan that moves an existing voiceover to project time 3s:

{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "project": "/projects/input.timeline",
  "baseRevision": 12,
  "dryRun": false,
  "operations": [
    {
      "id": "move-voice-001",
      "type": "timed.move",
      "track": "audio",
      "clipId": "voice-1",
      "start": 3
    }
  ],
  "output": {
    "project": "/projects/output.timeline"
  }
}

The revision and clip ID are illustrative: they must come from inspecting the actual project.

Each field has a job:

  • baseRevision checks the state on which the plan was based.
  • Operation IDs support idempotent handling of retries.
  • clipId identifies an existing project object.
  • type restricts the action to a supported operation.
  • output.project declares a new output artifact.

For this audio move, still-linked captions move by the same delta. That behavior belongs in the editing rules.

Preview a semantic diff before applying

The workflow is:

inspect -> plan -> validate -> diff -> apply -> inspect

The CLI exposes it directly:

npm run agent -- project.inspect /projects/input.timeline

node skills/edit-timeline-studio/scripts/validate_edit_plan.mjs \
  /projects/plan.json

npm run agent -- project.diff /projects/plan.json
npm run agent -- project.run /projects/plan.json

The standalone validator checks transport shape, finite time fields, and duplicate operation IDs. It does not prove that a plan is valid for a particular project.

project.diff is the project-aware dry run. It uses the same command registry and reducers as application, without writing an archive. It checks supported operations and preconditions, then reports project fields, clip additions/removals, changed fields, ordering, and duration changes.

This makes accidental scope expansion visible. A request to move narration should not quietly change the visual sequence duration.

Retries and concurrent edits are normal cases

Three mechanisms matter here.

Idempotency

If an operation completes but its response is lost, retrying the same operation ID should not insert the same clip twice. Previously applied IDs are treated as no-ops.

Revision checks

If the agent inspected revision 12 and the user subsequently edited the project, a stale plan containing new operations must fail with a revision conflict. The agent needs to inspect again and reconsider the plan.

Transactional application

A failed batch should not leave a partially edited output archive. Local CLI and MCP writes also require a new output path and reject overwriting the input or an existing output.

These are familiar application-engineering techniques. They become especially useful when the caller is an agent that may retry or reason from outdated state.

Video editing has more than one clock

A timestamp can refer to source media, a clip-local position, or the final project.

For a constant-speed clip:

sourceTime = sourceIn + (timelineTime - clipStart) * speed

With a speed curve, source-time mapping must accumulate the changing playback speed over time.

An agent identifying an action at source time 8s cannot assume that the cut belongs at project time 8s. Trimming, splitting, keyframes, thumbnails, and effect analysis all depend on maintaining that mapping.

Tracks also have different semantics. Main visuals form a contiguous sequence; narration, captions, and overlays have explicit timing. Whether a duration change shifts other tracks depends on ripple mode, links, and track locks.

These rules need to be explicit application behavior.

Skills and MCP serve different purposes

The Skill describes the workflow: inspect material, plan the edit, choose an execution path, and verify the result.

The MCP adapter exposes concrete tools, including:

timeline_project_inspect
timeline_track_inspect
timeline_clip_inspect
timeline_project_diff
timeline_project_apply
timeline_project_render

The local adapter is a thin transport over the existing command runner. It does not duplicate timeline editing logic.

To install the Skill:

npx skills add MartinDelophy/ai-video-editor \
  --skill edit-timeline-studio

To explore the repository and local MCP server:

git clone https://github.com/MartinDelophy/ai-video-editor.git
cd ai-video-editor
npm install
npm run mcp

Installing the Skill does not install the complete runtime. Local MCP needs the checkout and Node dependencies; media operations need their corresponding tools. The Skill includes a host dependency-check workflow.

An edited project is not yet a verified video

The current local project.render path supports the documented portable Visuals, Voiceover, and Music subset. It uses FFmpeg to produce H.264/AAC MP4 and ffprobe to check dimensions, duration, and audio-track presence.

It rejects unsupported composition features rather than silently dropping visible captions, overlays, transitions, or effects. Richer compositions require the browser renderer.

Verification needs several levels: inspect the project, reopen it and resolve archived media, check the output container, and actually play the important visual and audio boundaries. A valid project structure alone cannot prove that the final mix sounds right.

Where to read the implementation

Useful entry points in the repository:

  • src/lib/projectCommandEngine.js — shared project command engine
  • scripts/timeline-command.mjs — local archive operations and rendering entry point
  • skills/edit-timeline-studio/mcp/server.mjs — STDIO MCP adapter
  • src/hooks/useWebMcpEditor.js — browser editor integration
  • skills/edit-timeline-studio/SKILL.md — agent workflow

The command reference documents the current contract and limits.

The larger lesson for me is that agent reliability depends on the application interface: explicit state, constrained operations, reviewable changes, and verifiable outputs.

If you are building agent tools or working on browser media, I would welcome feedback on the architecture. Real editing failures and reproducible cases are particularly useful. You can explore the source, try the editor, or browse the editing handbook.

Writing disclosure: this article was drafted with AI assistance using the project's source code and documentation.

title: Green tests, dead tripwire
description:
Here is a failure I had not thought about until someone asked me the right question.

You write a PreToolUse hook. It reads the tool call, decides the command is dangerous, and blocks it. You write unit tests for it, because a guard with no tests is a wish. The tests pass. Months go by and the hook never fires, which you read as good news, because nothing bad has happened.

Then one day you find out the harness renamed a field in the payload eighteen weeks ago, your hook has matched nothing since, and every one of your tests is still green. They're green because the test builds the payload itself, in the shape you believed the harness sends. The test and the hook agree with each other perfectly. Neither of them has spoken to the harness in months.

Green tests, dead tripwire. The guard and its tests share a belief, so the tests cannot see the belief go stale.

This is the same shape as a bug I wrote about last time, where a redaction tool verified its own output using the same wrong geometry it had used to draw with. Different domain, identical structure: a check built from the same assumption as the thing it checks is not a check, it's a second copy of your belief.

Why "it hasn't fired" tells you nothing

A guard has two states that look identical from the outside. Working and quiet, because nothing tripped it. Broken and quiet, because it cannot match anything any more.

Nothing in your workflow distinguishes them. You don't get a weekly report of hooks that ran. The absence of refusals feels like safety, and in the broken case it is precisely the opposite: you've been running unguarded while believing you were covered, which is worse than having no hook at all, because you'd have been more careful without one.

Every guard that encodes a fact about an external world has this problem. The payload shape of your agent harness. The name of a tool. Whether CI still runs the check your hook assumes runs. Those facts change without telling you, and the guard goes quiet rather than loud.

Fail closed, but not everywhere

The obvious fix is to fail closed. If this is a tool I'm guarding and the field I need isn't there, that's an anomaly, not an allow. Most hooks, mine included, default to allowing anything they can't parse, which is exactly backwards.

The question I got asked, and did not have a good answer for at first, was whether that means failing closed everywhere, or only for guards on irreversible things.

I now think irreversibility is the wrong axis. The right one is what happens when the hook declines to decide. Three modes, three correct failures:

Block mode: fail closed. The hook is certain from the input alone that the call is wrong. If it can't read the input, refuse. The fallback is a retry or a question, both cheap, and the false block you eat on the day the harness changes is the thing that tells you the shape moved. That one annoying refusal is the monitoring you never set up.

Warn mode: don't fail closed, and say why. A warn hook exists because the rule is a heuristic that will fire on legitimate work, so turning an unparseable payload into a wall contradicts its own design. Emit the warning anyway. And the detail I'd have got wrong: the warning has to say precisely that it couldn't read the input, rather than printing its usual generic text. A warning that can't name the file or the command, but talks as if it can, teaches the model to discount every future warning from that hook.

Auto-allow mode: already fails closed, for free. This is the mode nobody discusses. Hooks that pre-approve read-only commands so they never surface a permission prompt. If one can't parse the input, it simply doesn't allow, and you land on the normal prompt. The fallback is a human, which is exactly where you want to be.

So the rule I'd write now: fail closed wherever declining costs a prompt. Don't, wherever declining costs a block on legitimate work.

The fixture that lies to you

The other half is contract tests, and there's a trap in them.

Recording one real payload from an actual session and replaying it against the hook catches the rename before it costs you anything. Writing that fixture by hand does not, because a hand-written fixture is your belief about the payload shape stored in a second file. You now have two copies of the same assumption and a false sense of coverage. If you can't capture a real one, log the raw input on every invocation and go read it occasionally. Dull, works.

My own setup, honestly: two hooks have real unit tests, one with a table of about thirty adversarial command variants, and both assert the deny path rather than only the happy one. Neither has a recorded fixture. I haven't fixed it yet.

What I still don't have

The thing I'd actually want is a canary. A scheduled job that deliberately issues a known-bad call and asserts it gets refused, so a dead guard announces itself instead of waiting to be discovered. That's a cron and an assertion, it isn't hard, and I haven't built it, which I suspect means most people running a dozen hooks haven't either.

Most of this post came out of the comments on my last one rather than from me. @build996 pushed on which refusals an agent can actually act on, @max_quimby on hooks quietly becoming an unversioned rulebook nobody remembers the reasons for, @syntaxwanderer_26 asked the question that produced the whole fail-closed taxonomy and then supplied the warn-mode detail, and @doriansotpyrc asked how a rule earns promotion from prose into a hook, which I answered as: once means write the sentence, twice means the sentence isn't carrying it.

So, the part I'm stuck on. How would you detect a guard that has been dead for a month? A canary is the only honest answer I've got, and it only covers the failures you thought to simulate. If you've found something better, or you've had a tripwire die quietly and only noticed by accident, I'd like to hear it.

title: Introducing Flat Rate CDN
description:
Over the past year, we have improved Vercel’s Pro pricing to better reflect how teams build, with expanded user roles, flexible credits, access to enterprise features, and more. But one area our customers continued to give us feedback on was CDN pricing.

CDN costs should be predictable, but viral launches, traffic bursts, or misconfigured routes sometimes turned an otherwise normal month into an unexpected bill. For teams building on Vercel, that uncertainty made growth feel like a problem at exactly the moment it should feel exciting.

Today, we are introducing Flat Rate CDN for Pro teams: a new way to pay for CDN usage with a predictable monthly bill, built-in spike protection, and service tiers designed for different traffic profiles.

What is Flat Rate CDN?

Flat Rate CDN is an alternative to usage-based CDN billing that provides you with a predictable monthly bill.

The model is designed around a simple idea: teams should be able to choose the CDN capacity that corresponds to their typical usage profile, pay a known amount monthly, and avoid surprise overages from temporary spikes.

Flat Rate CDN has several advantages over usage-based billing:

  • Fixed monthly price: Pay a fixed amount for Vercel CDN each month.

  • Covers traffic spikes: CDN Requests, Fast Data Transfer, and other resources are no longer billed directly, so spikes don't result in surprise bills.

  • No overages: Your bill will never increase because of temporary usage spikes.

Importantly, predictable pricing does not mean lower-quality bandwidth. Every request still runs on Vercel’s premium network, including private fiber that routes around congestion on the public internet, which can improve performance by up to 60%. Comparable routing is often sold as a premium add-on, but Vercel includes it by default for Pro teams, and performance isn't degraded during traffic spikes.

How it works

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default, and existing Pro teams can opt in. Usage is tracked at the team level and covers all projects, so you no longer need to manage capacity for them individually.

What’s included

On Flat Rate CDN, one fixed monthly fee covers:

  • CDN Requests

  • Fast Data Transfer

  • Blob Data Transfer

  • Observability events generated by CDN requests

The default tier is included with Pro. You can upgrade to a higher tier for increased request and data transfer capacity.

Your tier is fixed throughout any given billing period, so you never have to worry about charges from temporary traffic spikes.

What happens during a spike

The following team had a relatively normal usage profile that would fit comfortably in our $20/month Flat Rate CDN tier:

Only days after the above period, they experienced a viral product launch that generated a significant surge in traffic:

If the team had been on usage-based pricing, their CDN bill would have reached tens of thousands of dollars. On Flat Rate CDN, it stayed at $20 for the month.

No caps and no performance hit

Flat rate pricing from other infrastructure providers often places caps on usage when you reach your capacity, resulting in rapid performance degradation and request rejection. Flat Rate CDN is different in two ways:

  1. We recognize usage spikes and remove them when evaluating your CDN usage against capacity.

  2. We rightsize your Flat Rate CDN tier every month based on sustained usage.

This means we’ll never bring down your site when you’re going viral, and you don’t have to actively manage your tier when you’re growing quickly.

You can still monitor every covered resource on the Usage page or in the CLI, including traffic spikes absorbed by Vercel:

What we heard from customers during beta

Even though surprise bills are rare across our entire customer base, we’ve seen numerous stories from Pro customers about unexpected bills, many of which famously blew up on X. One team we interviewed was running hundreds of client sites and told us that CDN costs were “by far our largest line item, and the hardest to forecast,” especially when traffic spiked “from a client’s listing going viral, seasonal traffic, or bot traffic.”

In May, we released Flat Rate CDN to a small set of teams in limited beta. Over the last several months, it has changed how they operate on Vercel.

They worried less:

Flat Rate CDN eased our billing anxiety. With the recent increase in AI crawler traffic, we used to frequently check bot activity through Observability and monitor which bots were generating traffic. We now spend much less time doing that.

They built more:

Knowing that CDN usage is predictable makes us more willing to adopt caching-oriented approaches. We're now considering broader use of Cache Components and other caching strategies in our Next.js architecture, whereas previously we had to think more carefully about the potential cost impact of additional cache traffic.

This is exactly what we built Flat Rate CDN to do. No surprise bills, predictable pricing, and peace of mind to ship the next project.

Get started

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default. Existing Pro teams can opt in to the new plan:

  1. Select Billing in the navigation.

  2. Browse to Flat Rate CDN and toggle the setting to on.

  3. Choose a capacity tier that corresponds to your typical usage.

  4. Review your selection, which will show subscription costs if you chose a paid Flat Rate CDN tier.

  5. Select Enable to apply.

Learn more about Flat Rate CDN pricing in the documentation.

title: From Core Java to Spring Boot: When the Code Works, but the "Big Picture" is Still Loading
description:
Learning software engineering is an absolute ride. Some days you feel like your coding IQ is increasing exponentially; other days, you wish you were just born with all the skills already downloaded into your brain!

Lately, I’ve been making the transition from core Java OOP concepts into Spring Boot.

I get the concepts… but at the same time, I don’t quite get them yet. Funny, right?

💻 Where I’m At Right Now

I've been following along with structured literature, working through hands-on code examples line by line. Right now, I'm exploring Spring Context configurations, * lazy * initialization (*@lazy), *component stereotypes, and fetching beans dynamically via ApplicationContext.

🧠 The "Real-World Project" Gap

Even though the book examples run smoothly, I find myself pausing and asking:

"How does this actually map to a real, production-ready system?"

Because textbook exercises are isolated, it can be tricky to discern why a specific design choice is made until you’re building something substantial from scratch. I suspect the missing bridge is simply experience—I haven't built a massive end-to-end production application in Spring yet.

Despite the hurdles, the process has been genuinely fun. Watching how framework abstractions work after months of pure Java feels like discovering magic spells.

❓ To the Spring Devs out there: What was your turning point?

For anyone who has crossed this bridge before:

When did the "Spring Way" of thinking finally click for you? Was it during your first full project, or did a specific concept make it all fall into place?

What small starter project would you recommend for bridging the gap between textbook examples and real-world backend architecture?

If you're currently in the middle of learning Spring too, let me know how your journey is going in the comments below!
