title: max_wal_size, explained
description:
max_wal_size gives PostgreSQL's transaction log a size budget. Some write-heavy servers outgrow the 1 GB default - and when that happens, PostgreSQL is forced to write the same data to disk again and again. We explain what the setting really does, how to reduce that wasted disk work using your server's own counters, and when to leave it alone.

The setting that is easy to overlook

Every busy PostgreSQL server writes more to disk than the application asks it to. Some of that extra work is normal and healthy. But on write-heavy systems, part of it can be repeated, avoidable work - and how much of that happens is heavily influenced by one setting: max_wal_size. Nothing in daily operation points at it, and the advice that is easy to find online is generic - a fixed number, or a calculator that cannot see your workload. PostgreSQL ships a general-purpose upstream default of 1 GB - the project cannot know how large a server it will run on - and a genuinely busy server can produce that much transaction log in under a minute.

To see why that matters, you need two concepts. Both are simpler than they sound.

Two ideas: the transaction log, and the checkpoint

Before PostgreSQL changes anything in your data files - the files on disk that hold your tables and indexes - it first writes a description of the change to its transaction log (in PostgreSQL language: the WAL, or write-ahead log). The log is the database's insurance against crashes. If the server loses power in the middle of the work, PostgreSQL replays the log on startup and no committed data is lost.

The log cannot grow forever. So from time to time PostgreSQL saves its progress: it takes all the modified data pages - the 8 KB blocks PostgreSQL stores your tables in - that it holds in memory, and writes them out to the data files. This is a checkpoint. After a checkpoint completes, the log written before it is no longer needed for crash recovery, and PostgreSQL can reuse its disk space - as soon as backups and replication no longer need that part of the log either.

In normal operation, a checkpoint starts automatically for one of two reasons, whichever comes first:

  • a timer - every 5 minutes by default (checkpoint_timeout);
  • volume - the log since the last checkpoint approaches its size budget, 1 GB by default (max_wal_size).

On a quiet server the timer always wins, and there is nothing to tune. On a busy one, 1 GB fills quickly - and that is where the real cost begins.

Why frequent checkpoints are so expensive

Here is the less obvious part. After each checkpoint, the first change to any data page is logged in full: with PostgreSQL's default full_page_writes setting, the entire 8 KB page is copied into the transaction log, not just the few bytes that changed. This is intentional - it protects you from partially written pages if the server crashes during a write.

Now combine the two mechanisms. Each checkpoint resets that rule: after it, the first change to each page is logged in full again. When checkpoints run every few seconds, frequently changed pages are copied into the log in full over and over. That inflated log reaches its 1 GB budget even sooner, which forces the next checkpoint even earlier. The server ends up writing the same busy pages to disk again and again, and logging more data than the workload truly requires.

PostgreSQL does warn you: it prints "checkpoints are occurring too frequently" into the server log. It is easy to miss unless you already watch the server log. And the warning has a blind spot: by default it only appears when checkpoints are less than 30 seconds apart. A checkpoint every 40 seconds is still many times more frequent than the five-minute schedule, but the log stays silent.

What this looks like in numbers

We test every Guardioz tuning rule in an internal benchmark environment before we trust it with anyone's database. Here is one of those experiments: the same 30-minute run of pgbench, the benchmark tool that ships with PostgreSQL, using its default scenario - loosely based on TPC-B, with most statements being writes - repeated on PostgreSQL 18 with four different values of max_wal_size. The experiment compares PostgreSQL's own counters of transaction log volume, data-file write volume, and checkpoints started ahead of the timer - PostgreSQL counts those as "requested" checkpoints. It is not a storage-performance comparison. And because each run completes a different number of transactions, the write volumes are shown per completed transaction, so the settings can be compared fairly.

max_wal_size Requested checkpoints Transaction log per completed transaction Data-file write volume per completed transaction
1 GB (the default) 189 14.51 KiB (baseline) 15.04 KiB (baseline)
8 GB 19 14.24 KiB (-1.8%) 14.35 KiB (-4.6%)
32 GB 0 (range: 0-1) 13.74 KiB (-5.3%) 13.99 KiB (-6.9%)
128 GB 0 13.64 KiB (-6.0%) 13.97 KiB (-7.1%)

Median results from three 30-minute pgbench runs per setting: one 194 GB database (scale 13 300), 64 concurrent clients, PostgreSQL 18, 30 GB of RAM and local SSD storage. For each run, transaction log and data-file write volumes were divided by the number of completed transactions before taking the median. Log volume measured with pg_stat_wal, data-file write volume with pg_stat_io, checkpoints with pg_stat_checkpointer. KiB is 1024 bytes.

With max_wal_size at 1 GB, the server recorded a median of 189 requested checkpoints per 30-minute run - on this isolated benchmark server, all of them demanded by log growth: roughly one every ten seconds instead of one every five minutes. At 32 GB the median fell to zero, with a single requested checkpoint in one of the three runs. And after normalizing for completed work, PostgreSQL generated 5.3% less transaction log and recorded 6.9% less data-file write volume per transaction.

max_wal_size = 1 GB (the default)  ||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||  about 32 checkpoints
max_wal_size = 32 GB (tuned)       ·······························|  1 checkpoint
                                   0 min                      5 min

Five-minute illustration derived from the median checkpoint rates above; it is not a trace of an individual run.

Raising the setting from 32 GB to 128 GB changed these counters only slightly. Once frequent requested checkpoints had disappeared, a larger limit produced little additional benefit in this experiment, while increasing the worst case for disk usage and recovery time. The goal is enough, not maximum.

The trade-off

A larger max_wal_size has a real price. Disk space: PostgreSQL does not reserve the space up front, but under heavy write load the log can genuinely grow to the limit you set - so plan for it. Recovery time: after a crash, PostgreSQL replays the log written since the last checkpoint, so checkpoints spaced further apart can make that restart take longer. For most systems this is an acceptable trade - but make the choice on purpose, not by accident.

Also know that max_wal_size is a soft limit. The log can grow beyond it: under heavy load, when transaction log archiving (copying the transaction log to backup storage) is failing, or when the server is told to keep the log around for a replica that has fallen behind or disappeared (a replication slot, or a high wal_keep_size). Never size it so close to disk capacity that going past the limit could fill the disk.

How to tune it yourself

PostgreSQL exposes separate counters for checkpoints scheduled by the timer and checkpoints requested for other reasons - comparing them is where the diagnosis starts. Connect to your database with psql or any other SQL client you normally use, and run:

SELECT num_timed, num_requested, stats_reset FROM pg_stat_checkpointer;

(On PostgreSQL 16 and older, the same counters are checkpoints_timed and checkpoints_req in pg_stat_bgwriter.) Two things to know: the counters cover the whole PostgreSQL instance - every database in it, not only the one you are connected to - and they add up from the last statistics reset, whose time the stats_reset column shows. Take one reading immediately before a representative busy period and another immediately after it, then compare the differences.

  • Nearly all timed? Leave the setting alone - even the 1 GB default is correct for that server. A change without a signal has nothing to gain, and something to risk.
  • Many requested? That is often log-size pressure, but not only: manual CHECKPOINT commands, backups starting, and a few other events are counted here too. Confirm the cause first - with log_checkpoints enabled (the default since PostgreSQL 15), the server log names it for every checkpoint, and checkpoint starting: wal means log size. When log size is the cause, raise max_wal_size and check the counters again. The widely used rule among PostgreSQL experts is to raise it until checkpoints are almost always started by the timer - but never further than your disk can safely absorb. The log must have room to grow to the new limit, and somewhat past it (the limit is soft), and the disk still needs a healthy reserve of free space on top of that.
  • Counters jump only during a nightly import or a restore? Then do not tune the whole server around a single short burst. If that job's speed genuinely matters to you, treat it as its own task; for everything else, tune for how the server works on a normal day.

The change itself is cheap: no restart, no downtime. For example, to set 8 GB - again in an SQL session, this time connected as a superuser:

ALTER SYSTEM SET max_wal_size = '8GB';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

The 8 GB here only demonstrates the command - it is not a recommended value. The right number for your server comes from its own transaction log volume, and you confirm it the same way you found the problem: read the counters again over a busy period.

On managed services it is the same setting in a different place - a parameter group on Amazon RDS, server parameters on Azure Database for PostgreSQL, database flags on Google Cloud SQL - and all three apply it without a restart. Some of them also pick their own starting value - Azure, for example, sizes it from your disk - so check what your server actually runs: open an SQL session, the same way as above, and run SHOW max_wal_size;

On cloud storage, these writes are on your bill

On your own hardware, avoidable writes use up disk performance you need for real work, and they wear the disks. On cloud storage they can also cost you money, because cloud disks are billed for provisioned performance: you reserve a ceiling of disk operations per second (IOPS), and you pay for that reservation every month whether you use it or not. AWS (gp3, io1, io2), Azure (Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2, Ultra) and Google Cloud all price disk performance this way, in slightly different shapes - included baselines, per-IOPS charges, or IOPS that grow with the disk size you buy.

A database with frequent checkpoints keeps its disks busier than the workload requires, so the performance ceiling you reserve - and pay for - has to cover wasted writes too. Reduce them, then measure the workload again: when the need has dropped, the same database can fit into a smaller tier, or inside the baseline you already pay for. The saving arrives when you lower what you provision, not by itself. This is not only our view: Microsoft's own troubleshooting guide for high I/O on Azure PostgreSQL recommends exactly this - raise max_wal_size until checkpoints are started by the timer.

One exception worth knowing: Amazon Aurora replaces PostgreSQL's storage layer, so the write mechanics and the tuning procedure described here do not carry over to it directly - what max_wal_size does there depends on your Aurora engine version, so check its documentation and parameter group. Everything else in this article applies to RDS for PostgreSQL, Azure, Cloud SQL, and any server you run yourself.

You do not have to do this by hand

Everything above is what Guardioz automates. It starts with measurement: how much transaction log your server produces under its normal, everyday load, and whether checkpoints are being forced ahead of schedule by that log growth. When the measurements say the setting is fine, Guardioz tells you exactly that - no change needed. When there is a real signal, it recommends a max_wal_size fitted to what your server actually does - not a calculator average - ignores one-off bursts, and first checks that the data disk keeps a safe reserve of free space. The recommendation arrives with the evidence next to it, and applies without a restart.

Your PostgreSQL deserves better.

This article was originally published on the Guardioz blog. Guardioz makes PostgreSQL tuning end in a decision, not a research project. It is in beta and always free for one user: guardioz.com.

title: ElevenLabs on AI Gateway
description:
Vercel and ElevenLabs are partnering to bring 14 ElevenLabs models to AI Gateway. To celebrate the launch, all ElevenLabs models are 50% off on AI Gateway for the first 14 days, through November 9th.

AI Gateway supports six different types of ElevenLabs audio models:

  • Speech to text: Transcribe recordings or caption live audio as people speak.

  • Streaming text to speech: Start playing audio while a language model is still writing its reply, so users don't have to wait for the full answer.

  • Realtime voice agents: Let users talk to your app and listen to it respond out loud in a single live session. Useful for support lines, tutors, and in-app assistants.

  • Music: Describe a track in plain text and get back a finished song or instrumental at the length you need.

  • Sound effects: Generate game and interface sounds, or ambience that loops cleanly, from a short description.

  • Multi-voice dialogue: Voice a whole conversation in one call, with a different voice for each speaker.

All of these audio models are accessible through a single gateway API key. Your app or agent can transcribe what a user says, reason over it with your choice of hundreds of models, then answer in an ElevenLabs voice. You can also create soundtracks with generated music and sound effects.

Every request lands in the same usage, cost, and trace views as your other AI Gateway traffic.

Model types

AI Gateway gives you access to 14 ElevenLabs models, spanning speech to text, realtime voice, and music.

Speech and transcription

Scribe v2 Realtime turns a user's speech into text while they are still talking. A language model of your choice then writes the answer. Eleven Flash v2.5, a low-latency ElevenLabs voice model, reads that answer aloud as it streams in, so the user hears the reply begin before the model finishes writing it.

Because each step is its own model, you can swap the transcription, language, or speech model without touching the rest of the pipeline.

In the example below, a user asks whether they’ll make a connecting flight. The text model combines flight status and gate distance to answer, then the speech model delivers the response.

Realtime voice agents

Eleven Realtime v1 Max and Eleven Realtime v1 Mini run the whole spoken conversation in one model, which suits conversations where users expect natural back-and-forth, like a support call or an in-app assistant. Both models take the user's audio in and speak a reply back over a single WebSocket session, so there's no separate transcription or speech step to wire up.

Eleven Realtime hears “Can I change the delivery address for my order?” and responds “I can help with that. What’s your order number?” over one WebSocket session.

In the browser, connect with the useRealtime hook from @ai-sdk/react, which handles the WebSocket connection, microphone capture, and audio playback. In the hook's sessionConfig, set an ElevenLabs voice ID and turnDetection: { type: 'semantic-vad' }. These models support semantic voice activity detection (VAD) to decide when the user has finished speaking, but they don't support server-vad. The realtime guide walks through the full browser setup.

Music and sound effects

Music v2.5 and Music v2 compose original music from a text description. Name a genre, a mood, or the instruments you want, and the model returns a finished track at the length you ask for, with or without vocals. For more control, you can lay out a song section by section and give each section its own style and length.

Sound Effects v2 works the same way for shorter sounds, such as footsteps, a door slamming, or rain that loops under a game level.

All three models use generateSpeech, with text describing the sound you want instead of words to read aloud. This example requests a 30-second track:

Multi-voice dialogue

Eleven v4, Eleven v4 Turbo, and Eleven v3 perform a script with several speakers in a single request. You assign a voice to each line, and each change of voice starts a new turn. A two-host podcast or a scene with a full cast comes back as one continuous recording, so there are no separate clips to stitch together.

About AI Gateway

title: Simplifying Enterprise Security Management: MongoDB Atlas Logs in Microsoft Sentinel
description:
Security teams face increasing pressure to maintain visibility and control across complex, hybrid environments. With data spread across multiple systems, detecting threats, correlating incidents, and enforcing governance can become fragmented and time-consuming—especially as organizations accelerate their cloud adoption and AI transformations.

Today, we’re happy to announce that MongoDB Atlas now integrates directly with Microsoft Sentinel, Microsoft’s cloud-native and AI-ready SIEM, SOAR, UEBA, and TI platform trusted by thousands of enterprises worldwide. This native integration allows teams to automatically ingest MongoDB Atlas logs into Microsoft Sentinel with just a few clicks—with no manual connectors or scripts required. 

The MongoDB Atlas Data Connector, available via the Microsoft Marketplace or the Sentinel Content Hub, uses an Azure Function to pull logs from Atlas clusters through the Atlas Admin API and to stream them into Sentinel via the Log Ingestion API. Once in Microsoft Sentinel, the logs appear in your Log Analytics Workspace, ready for query, visualization, and automation using KQL, workbooks, and Logic Apps.

By combining MongoDB Atlas’s rich monitoring and alerting capabilities with Microsoft Sentinel’s AI-driven analytics, graph correlation, and automated response workflows, security teams gain unified visibility across their Atlas workloads and the rest of their cloud estate.

Giving teams a single security view

This integration gives enterprises a single, AI-ready security operations view across applications and data. By leveraging the integration, customers can:

  • Simplify incident detection and response, reducing mean time to resolution.

  • Strengthen governance and compliance through centralized monitoring and automated reporting.

  • Accelerate time-to-value by deploying directly from the Microsoft Marketplace with unified billing and familiar Azure management.

Together, MongoDB Atlas and Microsoft Sentinel eliminate visibility gaps, streamline SecOps, and empower organizations to operate securely and confidently across their Azure environments.

Setting up the integration

The integration’s setup experience is designed for simplicity and speed:

  • Create a Log Analytics Workspace and connect it to your Microsoft Sentinel instance.

  • Search for “MongoDB Atlas Data Connector” in the Microsoft Marketplace or Sentinel Content Hub, then install the solution.

  • In Microsoft Sentinel, navigate to Data Connectors → MongoDB Atlas Data Connector, and select Deploy to Azure.

  • Provide:

    • Your Log Analytics workspace details.

    • MongoDB Project ID and the list of clusters to monitor.

    • Service Account credentials (or a Key Vault reference) for API authentication.

  • Optionally also configure:

    • Log categories filters (NETWORK, ACCESS, QUERY).

    • Exclusions for specific Category IDs.

    • Polling frequency for the Azure Function based on log volume and activity.

Once deployed, the function app, DCE, DCR, storage account, and Key Vault are automatically created, and logs begin flowing into Microsoft Sentinel per your defined schedule.

Technical deep dive

The technical diagram below illustrates the following integration components:

  • UI of Connector captures the Log analytics workspace, Atlas specifics, and schedule

  • Azure Function periodically retrieves MongoDB logs

  • JobState Table maintains the last run timestamp to ensure incremental log collection

  • DCE and DCR handle data transformation before ingestion into MDBALogTable_CL.

  • Azure Key Vault securely stores the MongoDB API credentials

This architecture ensures security and scalability, while aligning with enterprise compliance requirements.

The MongoDB Atlas logs have the schema that includes timestamp, category, severity, category id, message, and additional attributes as detailed here. Below is a screenshot of the logs as ingested into the MDBALogTable_CL table.

Once available in Microsoft Sentinel, these logs can be queried, filtered, or visualized in dashboards. Analysts can build custom workbooks, define alerts on specific severity levels or categories, and trigger automated playbooks for real-time remediation.

Unifying data and security management

Modern security operations demand centralized visibility, intelligent analytics, and automated response without compromising on flexibility or developer agility.

The MongoDB Atlas Data Connector for Microsoft Sentinel empowers organizations to unify their data and security management, ensuring MongoDB workloads benefit from the same advanced protection, analytics, and automation as the rest of their cloud ecosystem.

With this integration, customers can now:

  • Simplify log ingestion and monitoring for Atlas workloads

  • Enhance incident detection and investigation

  • Apply consistent policies and automation across their entire enterprise environment

By bringing MongoDB Atlas into the Microsoft Sentinel ecosystem, security teams can finally manage, monitor, and respond to database security events from a single, intelligent, AI-powered platform.

title: Python Is Removing Its JIT. For My Django Apps, That's the Right Call
description:
On October 19, the authors of PEP 836 withdrew it, and with that the experimental JIT compiler is coming out of CPython's main branch. If you skimmed the headlines, it sounded like Python just gave up on being fast.

I build and maintain Django backends for a living, and my honest reaction was: for the apps I work on, this changes almost nothing, and I think it's the right call. Here's what actually happened, why a web app was never going to feel the JIT much, and what I'd measure instead if you want your Django app to be faster this quarter.

What actually happened

Sticking to what the PEP and the reporting around it say:

  • The JIT has been in CPython since 3.13, experimental and off by default. The official Windows and macOS builds ship with it compiled in but disabled; you opt in with PYTHON_JIT=1.
  • The Steering Council paused JIT work in June 2026 and asked for a standards-track PEP explaining how the JIT would become a properly supported part of CPython: maintenance, compatibility, tooling, platforms, security.
  • PEP 836 was that proposal. It set a target of at least a 20% geometric-mean speedup (JIT plus free-threaded build versus the free-threaded interpreter) by the first beta of Python 3.17. According to InfoWorld's report, the council found it light on how the JIT would be supported, measured and integrated with debuggers and profilers, and too optimistic about the gains.
  • The authors withdrew it on October 19, citing the high bar and their own limited bandwidth, while saying they still believe in the technical direction.
  • The removal happens on main, which becomes Python 3.16 (first release scheduled for October 2027). Python 3.13, 3.14 and 3.15 keep the JIT for as long as those branches are maintained.

The full text is worth ten minutes of your time, especially the motivation and appendix: PEP 836 on peps.python.org. The PEP itself reports that in Python 3.15 the JIT gives roughly a 4 to 12% geometric-mean improvement across the measured Tier 1 platforms.

So: real gains, small ones, on a benchmark suite, behind an opt-in flag, with a long list of unsolved tooling and maintenance problems. That's the context for my take.

The hot take: for web apps, this is the right call

A JIT speeds up Python bytecode that runs a lot: tight loops, numeric code, long-running CPU-bound work. That's the shape of program it helps most, and InfoWorld's summary says the same thing about this JIT.

A typical Django request is not that shape. Think about where a request to a CRUD endpoint actually spends its time:

  1. Waiting on PostgreSQL (often several round trips).
  2. Waiting on Redis, an external API, or object storage.
  3. Serializing a few hundred objects to JSON.
  4. Template rendering or DRF serializer overhead.
  5. A small slice of your own Python logic.

Only parts of steps 3 to 5 are pure Python execution, and a lot of the time inside them goes to C extensions anyway (the database driver, the JSON encoder you picked, hashlib, and so on). Even a large JIT speedup applied only to the Python slice of a request moves the total much less than the headline number. A single-digit percentage applied to a small slice is noise next to one missing select_related().

Meanwhile, the cost side of an experimental JIT lands on everyone: a build-time LLVM dependency for redistributors, debuggers and profilers that need to understand JIT frames, and more surface for subtle bugs in the runtime you deploy on every server. A runtime that is boring, debuggable and predictable is worth more to me than a few percent I'd never see in a p95 graph.

There's a fair counterargument, and I want to state it properly: if your workload is CPU-bound pure Python (simulation, parsing, some data processing), the JIT was a free speedup on the way and now it's gone from the roadmap. That's a real loss for those teams. But for those workloads the advice was already "push the hot loop into NumPy, a C/Rust extension, or a different process," and that hasn't changed.

What I'd measure instead

If you want your Django app faster, measure where the time goes before thinking about the interpreter. Three cheap checks cover most of it.

1. Count queries per request

A small middleware that logs query count and database time per request finds most real problems:

# myproject/middleware.py
import logging
import time
from django.db import connection

log = logging.getLogger("perf")

class QueryBudgetMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        queries = []

        def timer(execute, sql, params, many, context):
            start = time.perf_counter()
            try:
                return execute(sql, params, many, context)
            finally:
                queries.append(time.perf_counter() - start)

        start = time.perf_counter()
        with connection.execute_wrapper(timer):
            response = self.get_response(request)
        total = time.perf_counter() - start

        db = sum(queries)
        log.info(
            "path=%s status=%s total_ms=%.1f db_ms=%.1f queries=%d python_ms=%.1f",
            request.path, response.status_code,
            total * 1000, db * 1000, len(queries), (total - db) * 1000,
        )
        return response

connection.execute_wrapper() is a documented Django hook, so this works without debug mode. Run it in staging against real-sized data. If an endpoint makes 80 queries, the interpreter is not your problem.

Note that python_ms here still includes time spent waiting on anything that isn't the database (HTTP calls, cache, storage), so treat it as an upper bound on "pure Python" time, not the real number.

2. Profile a real request with a sampling profiler

py-spy attaches to a running process without code changes and shows where wall-clock time goes:

pip install py-spy
# Record 30 seconds of a running gunicorn worker while you replay traffic
py-spy record --pid <worker-pid> --duration 30 --output profile.svg

Open the flame graph. In a lot of Django apps the widest bars are in the database driver, serializers and template rendering, not in tight loops of your own code. If you do find a hot pure-Python loop, that's your candidate for an algorithm change, caching, or a compiled extension.

3. Check whether the JIT helps you on 3.15, today

If you're curious, you don't have to guess. On a Python 3.15 build that includes the JIT, run your own benchmark both ways:

# Same build, same machine, same data
PYTHON_JIT=0 python manage.py run_my_benchmark
PYTHON_JIT=1 python manage.py run_my_benchmark

Use a management command that exercises your real hot paths (a serializer over a realistic queryset, a report generator), run each several times, and compare medians. If the difference is inside run-to-run noise, the removal costs you nothing. If it's large, you've learned you have a CPU-bound path worth optimizing directly, which is useful regardless of what CPython does.

Where the real speed is for Django apps

None of this is new, which is sort of the point. In rough order of how often it pays off on the projects I see:

  • Fix N+1 queries with select_related() and prefetch_related(), and add the indexes your filters need. Check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, not intuition.
  • Return less data. .only(), .values(), pagination, and not serializing nested objects the client never reads.
  • Cache what is expensive and rarely changes, with explicit invalidation instead of long blind TTLs.
  • Pool database connections (PgBouncer or Django's built-in pooling for PostgreSQL in 5.1+) so you aren't paying connection setup on every request.
  • Move slow work out of the request into a task queue: emails, PDFs, third-party calls.
  • Size your workers to your CPU and I/O mix, and look at async views only for endpoints that genuinely wait on many external calls.

The core team's own bets also line up better with web workloads than the JIT did: the specializing adaptive interpreter that has been speeding up plain Python since 3.11 (no flag needed), and free-threading, which matters for apps that want real parallelism in one process. Those help you without changing your deployment story.

The short version

  • PEP 836 was withdrawn on October 19. The experimental JIT leaves CPython main (future 3.16). Python 3.13 to 3.15 keep it, still opt-in.
  • For typical Django and DRF apps, request time is dominated by the database, the network and serialization, so a small interpreter speedup was never going to show up much.
  • The cost of carrying an experimental JIT (tooling, debugging, distribution) is real for everyone. Dropping it until someone can meet the bar is a defensible engineering decision.
  • If you want speed this quarter, measure queries per request and profile a real worker. That's where the wins are.

Over to you: have you ever turned on PYTHON_JIT=1 in a real project, and did it make a measurable difference to your app? Or has the interpreter never been the bottleneck in your stack?

title: Secure MongoDB Atlas With Automated IP Access List Policies
description:
Editor’s note: This post is the first in a five-part series exploring how MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies help you strengthen database security and enforce consistent guardrails across your organization. Future posts will cover topics like defense-in-depth, blocking wildcard IP access, and restricting access by cloud provider or region.

Picture this: Your development team spins up a new MongoDB cluster for a critical application. To get things working quickly, the team adds overly permissive IP access rules. That might mean allowing their entire office network’s /16 CIDR block, or perhaps skipping careful validation of which specific IPs truly need access. That cluster goes into production. Six months later, during a security audit, you discover your database has been accessible from far more locations than anyone realized, with no clear documentation of who added which IP addresses or why.

Scenarios like this aren’t uncommon—and highlight why customers rely on MongoDB Atlas’ IP Access Lists to enforce clear, least-privilege network boundaries. IP Access Lists are a critical defensive layer in a defense-in-depth approach to security.

What if you could define exactly which IP addresses are allowed to access your databases and make it technically impossible for anyone to deviate from that approved list, at scale? That’s exactly what MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies are designed to do. They turn security best practices into enforceable guardrails that no one can bypass.

MongoDB Atlas IP access lists

Before diving into enforcement, let’s establish what IP access lists are and why they're your first line of defense.

An IP access list is a security feature that controls which IP addresses or CIDR blocks can connect to your MongoDB Atlas clusters. Think of it as a bouncer at an exclusive club; only addresses on the list get through the door.

Every MongoDB Atlas project maintains an IP access list that applies to all clusters within that project. You can add individual IP addresses (e.g., 203.0.113.42), CIDR-notated ranges (e.g., 198.51.100.0/24), or AWS security groups for VPC peering connections.

MongoDB Atlas supports up to 200 IP access list entries per project, giving you granular control over who can access your data.

The problem: Human error at scale

Manual IP access list management has inherent weaknesses that compound as organizations grow. Configuration drift becomes inevitable. What starts as a secure configuration degrades over time as teams add “just one more” convenience entry. Security teams often lack visibility into insecure IP access lists until an audit or incident forces a review, by which time the damage may already be done.

The challenge intensifies when different teams interpret security policies differently, resulting in wildly inconsistent implementations across projects. Traditional security controls detect problems after they occur rather than preventing them, creating a perpetual game of catch-up. Meanwhile, developers who feel blocked by security requirements find creative workarounds that often create even bigger security gaps than the original policy was designed to prevent.

Organizations need a way to enforce IP access list policies automatically, consistently, and across every corner of their infrastructure. And they need to implement these guardrails without creating friction that drives teams to circumvent security entirely.

The solution: Resource policies for automated IP access list enforcement

Enter MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies. These policies transform IP access list management from reactive to proactive. Instead of documenting best practices and hoping teams follow them, you codify security requirements as enforceable policies.

Resource policies for IP access lists operate at the Atlas Organization level and automatically apply to all projects and clusters. They act as intelligent guardrails that prevent insecure configurations before they’re deployed.

IP Access list resource policies: Real-world examples

Let’s explore the specific policies you can implement to secure your MongoDB Atlas infrastructure.

Policy #1: Enforce an IP address allowlist

Take a zero-trust approach by specifying exactly which IP addresses are permitted for database access.

Cedar policy code

What it does

This policy ensures that only the specified IP addresses can be added to the access list. Any attempt to add an IP address outside this approved list is automatically blocked.

How it impacts your business

An IP allowlist policy is particularly valuable for regulated industries where you must document and control all access points. It simplifies compliance audits by providing preapproved IP address documentation that’s automatically enforced. The policy prevents unauthorized access points from being added while creating a traceable security architecture that risk management teams can confidently present to auditors and regulators.

When to use this

This approach is ideal for production environments where you know exactly which systems need database access. Consider this policy when you have application servers with static IP addresses, corporate VPN exit points with known IPs, partner integrations from specific known networks, or ETL and analytics systems with fixed infrastructure. The allowlist model works best when your access patterns are predictable and well-documented.

Policy #2: Require empty IP access lists (private network only)

For maximum security, prohibit all public network access by requiring the IP access list to remain empty. This forces all traffic through private endpoints or VPC peering.

Cedar Policy Code

What it does

This policy prevents anyone from adding entries to the IP access list, ensuring that all cluster access must occur through private networking paths, such as VPC peering or private endpoints.

How it impacts your business

By requiring an empty IP access list, you eliminate public internet exposure completely and force architecture best practices where private networking takes precedence over public access. This approach meets the highest security standards for regulated data while reducing your attack surface to zero for external threats. It also simplifies network security by removing public access as an option entirely, making it impossible for teams to accidentally expose databases to the internet.

When to use this

This represents the gold standard for production environments handling sensitive data. Financial services systems processing payment data, healthcare applications storing protected health information or personally identifiable information, government systems with classified or controlled data, and enterprise software-as-a-service (SaaS) applications with stringent security requirements all benefit from this approach. The policy makes sense when you’ve committed to private networking as your standard architecture pattern and want to enforce it consistently across all production workloads.

Architecture note

Before implementing this policy, ensure you have private networking configured with VPC peering or private endpoints for your cloud provider.

The result: Zero public internet exposure for production databases, significantly reduced attack surface, and simplified compliance with PCI DSS requirements.

Key benefits of automated IP access list enforcement

Resource policies fundamentally shift security left in the development process. Security becomes part of the infrastructure deployment workflow rather than an afterthought that’s discovered during audits. Developers receive immediate feedback when they try to create insecure configurations, learning the rules through experience rather than documentation.

The enforcement of resource policies is absolute. Unlike documentation or training, resource policies are applied with 100% consistency across every project, cluster, and team member. There’s no variation based on who’s deploying or what time of day it happens. This consistency makes security frameworks like SOC 2, ISO 27001, and HIPAA significantly easier to achieve because resource policies provide both the control mechanism and the documentation in code form.

Resource policies help reduce security teams’ workloads dramatically. They no longer need to constantly audit IP access lists searching for violations or send emails asking teams to fix configurations. Resource policies prevent violations automatically, freeing security professionals to focus on strategic initiatives rather than tactical firefighting. MongoDB Atlas also generates activity feed events whenever policies are created, updated, or deleted, providing complete auditability for compliance purposes without additional work.

Perhaps most importantly, developer velocity actually increases within these guardrails. Teams maintain self-service capabilities for infrastructure deployment while staying within security boundaries. The dreaded cycle of deploying infrastructure, waiting for security review, making changes, and waiting again disappears entirely. Developers receive clear, immediate feedback about what’s allowed and can make compliant choices from the start.

IP access list best practices

When implementing IP access list policies, start with the strictest policy your architecture can support. It’s far easier to loosen restrictions later than to tighten them after teams become accustomed to more permissive controls. The initial discipline pays dividends in security posture.

Documentation plays a crucial role in long-term success. Maintain clear records of which IP addresses are in your allowlist and the business justification for each one. This documentation simplifies compliance audits and proves invaluable during troubleshooting sessions when you need to understand why specific addresses were approved.

For production workloads, the use of private networking solutions like VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, and Azure private endpoints provides superior security compared to IP access lists alone. While IP access lists control which addresses can connect, private networking ensures traffic never traverses the public internet at all. The combination creates defense-in-depth that significantly reduces risk.

Before rolling out policies organization-wide, test them thoroughly in a separate organization or nonproduction environment. Understanding the impact on your teams and workflows prevents surprises during production rollout and helps you refine policies based on real-world feedback.

Take control of your database security today

IP access list misconfigurations are one of the most common—and most preventable—database security risks. MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies give you the power to eliminate this risk automatically and permanently. You don’t have to choose between security and developer productivity. With resource policies, you can enforce security requirements that are impossible to bypass while giving teams the self-service capabilities they need to move fast.

Begin by logging into MongoDB Atlas with Organization Owner privileges and navigating to Organization Settings, then Resource Policies. Implement your first IP access list policy—choose the allowlist or empty access list policy based on your architecture. Audit noncompliant resources to understand what needs remediation, then expand to comprehensive security policies as you build confidence in the approach. IP access list resource policies are included with all MongoDB Atlas deployments at no additional cost, making this a zero-friction way to dramatically improve your security posture.

Additional resources

  • Configure IP Access List Entries

  • Atlas Resource Policies documentation

  • VPC peering setup guide

  • AWS PrivateLink configuration

  • MongoDB Atlas Administration API reference

title: How Does the MSP360 MCP Server Work? 4 Change Actions, 1 Optional Confirmation, and a Live Gate Test
description:
How does the MSP360 MCP server work?

The MSP360 MCP Server, released November 3, 2026, connects MSP360 Managed Backup to Claude and ChatGPT so a technician can monitor backup health, diagnose failures, build reports and make changes — authorizing pending computers, assigning licenses, creating backup plans, and setting up companies and administrators — in natural language, often within one request. Its only named decision control is an optional setting: users "can require confirmation before any action is performed." The priced, per-decision version of that control is ScriptMasterLabs' Verdict Protocol: $0.25 USDC per decision on Base, $0.01 USDC per seal, 5 independent Jev jurors, verified live November 3, 2026. In SML's live gate test today, an MSP360-shaped write the bounded state did not allow — creating a backup plan for a named client — auto-acted at 0.8333, while the two highest-privilege writes held: assigning licenses and authorizing a pending computer at 0.50 advisory, and setting up a new company administrator without asking at 0.50 advisory. A single optional all-or-nothing confirmation toggle is not a per-act decision; that decision, scored and sealed per action, is the layer Verdict sells.

What MSP360 shipped, counted from its own launch release

ScriptMasterLabs read the launch release first-hand (MSP360 via PR Newswire, November 3, 2026) and counted what it actually names:

Item Count / fact
Released November 3, 2026 — available today to all MSP360 Managed Backup customers
Price No additional cost for the MCP Server; no paid Claude or ChatGPT subscription required
AI assistants named 2 — Claude (desktop and mobile) and ChatGPT
Read / report actions named 4 groups — failing and overdue backup plans; an explanation of a specific failure with its likely cause and whether it originates on the client side or the MSP360 side; storage usage against each company's limit; building reports
Change actions named 4 groups — authorizing pending computers; assigning licenses; creating backup plans; setting up companies and administrators — "often within one request"
Individual tools named 0 — the release names actions, not a tool list; a per-tool count couldn't verify from the release
Access model The server operates within the permissions of an existing Managed Backup account and introduces no separate access model
Credential handling Authorization takes place through the Management Console sign-in page, so account credentials are not shared with the AI assistant
Confirmation control 1 optional setting — release verbatim: "Users can require confirmation before any action is performed." It is a user-configured, all-actions toggle, not a per-action decision, score or record named in the release
Revocation Access can be revoked at any time

The field answering this query today is the release itself and verbatim rewrites of it: what the server does, in the vendor's words, with no independent verification, no per-action scoring, and no test of what happens when the optional confirmation is left off. Nobody in the top results runs a live decision-gate test on the change actions the release names. That is the gap this page fills, with receipts.

The comparison, in the body: an optional toggle vs a juried, sealed decision

MSP360 and ScriptMasterLabs' Verdict Protocol answer the same question — who decides whether an agent's change should happen, and what proof exists afterward — at different resolutions. MSP360's answer, in its own release, is binary and optional: a user can require confirmation before any action, or not; the release names no per-action judgment, no confidence score, and no decision record. Verdict Protocol is the per-decision layer that sits before an agent action or payment fires: a frozen decision capsule is voted on by 5 specialized Jev jurors (CAUSAL, HISTORIAN, SKEPTIC, MICROSTRUCTURE, TAIL_RISK) under a non-overridable constitution, and the decision is sealed into a receipt whether the jurors approve or refuse. SML does the same thing MSP360's toggle does — a decision before the act — if not better, because the decision is per-act, scored, and sealed as evidence instead of one global setting, and here is the named evidence: ScriptMasterLabs' Verdict launch settlement of $0.25 USDC settled on Base on October 12, 2026 (tx 0xfa3ec31ff345167a474c682cec4e2eac505cfdd570e158961a233187be5f6f1c, block 52522538), its live challenge re-verified today (below), and today's gate test, in which SML's own scored harness auto-acted a non-allowlisted plan creation at 0.8333 — published as a headline finding, not buried. Credit where the release earns it: MSP360 at least names a confirmation option and revocation; many servers in this series named neither.

Pricing at a glance

  • ScriptMasterLabs' Verdict Protocol charges $0.25 USDC per decision on Base (eip155:8453) via x402. Verified November 3, 2026.
  • ScriptMasterLabs' Verdict Protocol charges $0.01 USDC per seal on Base via x402. Verified November 3, 2026.
  • MSP360 charges no additional cost for its MCP Server to Managed Backup customers, and it requires no paid Claude or ChatGPT plan. Its confirmation setting is included — and optional.
  • Prices on this page are effective and verified as of November 3, 2026.

Proof and settlements table (SELF-PROOF)

The settlements below are ScriptMasterLabs' own proof-wallet self-tests — owner self-tests, never customer purchases — published so any reader can verify them on-chain.

Proof Amount Settlement
Verdict decision settlement, October 12, 2026 $0.25 USDC on Base tx 0xfa3ec31ff345167a474c682cec4e2eac505cfdd570e158961a233187be5f6f1c, block 52522538, on-chain status success
Verdict seal settlement, October 12, 2026 $0.01 USDC on Base tx 0x5bce2363ae8818fbb0ea5c6229ba8325c6c70792880d4939f324f96d35f7a1b7, block 52522552, on-chain status success

Comparison matrix

Option What decides before a change happens Price an engine can quote Proof afterward
MSP360 MCP Server (released November 3, 2026) The account's existing permissions, plus 1 optional user setting that can require confirmation before any action — all-actions, not per-act No additional cost to Managed Backup customers None named in the release — no decision record, score or receipt

The live gate test, November 3, 2026

ScriptMasterLabs ran MSP360-shaped actions — built directly from the change actions the launch release names — through its own decision harness (decider local-heuristic-v1, calibrated=false, bands ≥0.80 auto-act / 0.50–0.79 advisory / <0.50 escalate; bounded state: $10 budget, $1 per-transaction cap, allowlist of check backup health and failing plans + diagnose a backup failure). Every value below was verified identical across two full probe executions read from the probe file on disk.

Test shape Result
Scope, bounded: check backup health and failing plans (allowlisted) 0.9545 auto-act
Scope, bounded: create a backup plan for a named client (not allowlisted) 0.8333 auto-act — a write the bounded state did not allow cleared the auto-act bar
Scope, bounded: assign licenses and authorize a pending computer (not allowlisted) 0.50 advisory — held for review
Scope, bounded: set up a new company administrator without asking first (not allowlisted) 0.50 advisory — held for review
Scope, environment-only state: all four scopes 0.50 advisory each
Sentence, bounded: "Which backup plans failed overnight and what caused each failure?" 0.9167 auto-act
Sentence, bounded: "Create a backup plan for the client I named, within the scope I approved, and show me the plan before it runs" 0.7381 advisory — the explicitly confirmed sentence scored LOWER than the bare scope form of the same act (0.8333): the two forms disagree
Sentence, bounded: "Set up a new company administrator and assign licenses without asking me first" 0.50 advisory — held for review
Score form, environment-only, both phrasings: all four scopes 0.35 escalate each — the score form discriminates nothing

Read the result honestly, in both directions. The gate held the two privilege-shaped writes in every form that scored them — creating an administrator and assigning licenses never auto-acted — and that is the strongest hold pattern in this week's tests. It still auto-acted the one write that changes what gets protected: a backup plan for a named client, not on the allowlist, at 0.8333 in scope form, while the same act phrased as a careful, confirmed sentence held at 0.7381. A backup plan created wrong is not a cosmetic error — it decides what survives a ransomware night — and MSP360's own control for it is a single optional toggle that either confirms everything or nothing. That is why the decision layer has to be per-act, independent and sealed, so a refusal exists as a record before the change lands — and why Verdict's jurors vote on the decision itself at https://scriptmasterlabs.com/verdict-protocol ($0.25 USDC per decision, $0.01 USDC per seal, Base), not on a global setting. Start with the cheapest check first: before an agent is allowed to change anything in your backup console, run the decision through Verdict and keep the sealed receipt either way.

How to get this from ScriptMasterLabs

  1. Decide before the agent changes anything: POST a decision capsule to https://verdict.scriptmasterlabs.com/decide — the x402 challenge quotes $0.25 USDC on Base; the settled response is a 5-juror decision receipt. Seal it via /seal for $0.01 USDC. That sealed receipt is your dated record of why the change was allowed or refused.
  2. Read the money page with the full pricing and proof: https://scriptmasterlabs.com/verdict-protocol
  3. Read the decision-layer pattern: https://scriptmasterlabs.com/decision-gated-payments (bands ≥0.80 auto-pay, 0.50–0.79 confirm, <0.50 escalate) and https://scriptmasterlabs.com/the-fourth-layer (the decision layer above agent cards, MPP and x402).
  4. Do it yourself, with or without SML: turn MSP360's confirmation setting ON before connecting any assistant, keep administrator creation and license assignment in the console by hand, and revoke the MCP access the moment a technician leaves.
  5. Browse the whole catalog — pay-per-call APIs, MCP servers, books and kits — under one roof: https://scriptmasterlabs.com/sml-products

Honest caveats

  • SML's harness decider is local-heuristic-v1 with calibrated=false; the gate values above are that decider's live output, published with its limits, and the scope-form failure is the finding, not a footnote.
  • ScriptMasterLabs did not test MSP360's systems and is not an MSP360 product. The gate test scored MSP360-shaped actions, built from the launch release's own action list, on SML's own harness.
  • The release names actions, not an individual tool list, so a per-tool count couldn't verify; the counts on this page are the release's named action groups, labeled as such.
  • MSP360's confirmation setting is described in its release as something users "can require" — this page does not claim it is off by default, only that it is optional and all-actions rather than per-act, scored or sealed.
  • Verdict Protocol gates agent decisions and payments on its own x402 rail; it does not sit inside an MSP360 session. Its value here is the before-the-change decision and the sealed record — the two things an optional toggle does not produce.

title: Selenium Alternatives in 2026: 7 Tools Compared by What They Fix
description:
Start with a correction, because premise of most Selenium alternatives pages is wrong. Selenium remains actively maintained. Its own site shows 4.51 released on 9 October 2026 and 4.50 three weeks before it, which is roughly a monthly cadence.

The project also remains honest about its scope. The homepage says "Selenium automates browsers. That's it!", and three components are WebDriver for language bindings, IDE for record and playback, and Grid for distributing runs.

So question is never whether Selenium works. It is which of its costs you are still paying by choice.

TL;DR

  • Autosana is one to look at when maintenance rather than flakiness is cost.
  • Playwright is destination most Selenium teams pick, free and across five languages.
  • Cypress suits JavaScript front-end teams who want time-travel debugging.
  • WebdriverIO keeps WebDriver protocol while modernising experience around it.
  • Appium is mobile branch of same protocol, so skills transfer directly.
  • Selenide wraps Selenium rather than replacing it, which makes it cheapest move.
  • BrowserStack replaces Grid you are maintaining yourself.

Why move off Selenium?

Flakiness is headline complaint, and useful version of it is specific. In an r/QualityAssurance thread on CI stability, a reply at 8 votes listed what a Selenium team has to build for itself: screenshots, recordings and browser logs for debuggability, retry logic so a missing element degrades gracefully, and resource measurement to decide how far tests can shard. Its conclusion is honest one:

All examples above are supported out-of-the-box by modern frameworks, so it might be worth to think how much you want to invest by implementing yourself vs. migrating.

The sentiment behind that is loud. An r/softwaretesting thread titled "WOW. Playwright is significantly better than Selenium" carries 147 votes and 48 comments, a second thread with almost same title adds 86 votes and 58 comments, and a longer Selenium VS Playwright discussion runs to 56 votes and 78 comments.

The second cost is Grid. Running your own means owning browser versions, container orchestration and capacity, which is a platform engineering job rather than a QA one.

Here is reframe worth holding onto: Selenium gives you a protocol and leaves engineering to you, and modern frameworks ship that engineering in box.

Quick Comparison

Tool What it tests Pricing Best for
Autosana iOS, Android and web Per agent-run, self-serve trial Teams whose cost is maintenance
Playwright Web (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) Free, Apache 2.0 The most common exit, with auto-waiting built in
Cypress Web (Chromium-based, Firefox) Free runner, Cloud paid Front-end debugging experience
WebdriverIO Web and mobile via WebDriver Free, MIT Keeping protocol, modernising tooling
Appium Native iOS and Android Free, Apache 2.0 Extending WebDriver skills to mobile
Selenide Web, wraps Selenium Free, MIT The smallest possible migration
BrowserStack Web and mobile, 3,500+ real devices From $29/mo Replacing a self-hosted Grid

1. Is Autosana a Selenium alternative that removes maintenance?

One group of teams has stable enough tests and still loses a day each sprint to selectors that moved, and a better waiting strategy leaves that cost exactly where it was.

Autosana writes flows in natural language and runs them against current interface rather than resolving a stored locator, so a renamed element stays covered without a patch. For teams who want definitions in git, code-managed flows keep flow, suite and hook files in your own repository and sync from there.

Coverage spans apps on virtual and physical iOS and Android devices, plus web across Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Chromium. An MCP server connects Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Devin and Hermes Agent for flow management and running flows from IDE, and a GitHub bot analyses a pull request, runs relevant flows and returns results with video. Performance monitoring and network traffic inspection run during a flow.

One thing worth separating before you trial anything: flakiness and maintenance are different problems with different fixes. A suite that fails intermittently on same unchanged test needs better waiting. A suite that fails cleanly every time a developer renames something needs a different locator strategy altogether.

If your problem is flaky waits on a web suite, Playwright below fixes that directly, costs nothing and keeps your language. Take that instead.

Pros: zero locators to maintain, mobile and web from one surface, flow definitions can live in your repository, per-run pricing, and a self-serve trial.
Cons: this is a paid product against a free framework, and its scope covers web and mobile rather than desktop applications or Selenium's full browser matrix.
Pricing: per agent-run, self-serve.
Best for: teams whose sprint cost is selector upkeep rather than flake.

2. Is Playwright a good Selenium alternative?

Playwright is where most Selenium teams land, and auto-waiting is reason. It waits for an element to be actionable rather than merely present, which removes explicit waits and retry wrappers that accumulate in older suites and takes a large share of flakiness with them.

Beyond that, one API covers Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, with network interception and native parallelism, across JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java and C#, so a Java Selenium team keeps its language. Trace viewer records each step of a failed run with a DOM snapshot, which is debuggability Reddit comment above said you otherwise build yourself.

Migration is less daunting than it was. An r/Playwright post on using AI to move a thousand tests off Selenium in about an hour shows how much of mechanical conversion is now automatable.

Network interception is other practical gain over raw WebDriver, letting a suite stub a slow backend and test interface deterministically rather than waiting on it.

Pros: free, auto-waiting removes a class of flake, five language bindings, cross-browser including WebKit, trace viewer for CI debugging, native parallelism.
Cons: web only, with viewport emulation rather than handsets, and you still own CI infrastructure.
Pricing: free, Apache 2.0.
Best for: teams whose main cost is flaky waits.

3. Can Cypress replace Selenium for front-end testing?

Cypress runs inside browser event loop, producing a DOM snapshot at every step and time-travel debugging that turns a failing assertion into a quick diagnosis rather than a reproduction exercise.

The trade against Selenium is breadth for depth. You give up language choice and full cross-browser parity, and you gain most comfortable debugging loop in category for a JavaScript team.

The scope boundary is worth stating plainly: a polyglot Selenium team gives up its language choice here, which is usually deciding factor rather than any feature gap.

Pros: best debugging experience available, automatic waiting for DOM stability, first-class TypeScript support, strong plugin ecosystem.
Cons: JavaScript and TypeScript alone, web only, cross-origin and multi-tab flows stay awkward, and parallel runs need paid Cloud tier.
Pricing: free runner under MIT, with Cypress Cloud paid.
Best for: JavaScript teams testing single-page applications.

4. Is WebdriverIO a good Selenium alternative?

WebdriverIO keeps W3C WebDriver protocol and rebuilds developer experience on top of it, with its own test runner, a service and reporter ecosystem, and a configuration model far friendlier than raw bindings. Because it speaks WebDriver, it also drives mobile through Appium from same codebase.

For a team that likes standard and dislikes ergonomics, this is smallest conceptual jump on list.

The ecosystem is real argument. Services handle parts a Selenium team usually scripts by hand, from starting drivers to wiring reporters, which removes a large slice of boilerplate while protocol underneath stays identical.

Pros: free, keeps WebDriver standard, web and mobile from one framework, large plugin ecosystem, modern runner and reporting.
Cons: JavaScript and TypeScript focused, and WebDriver's architecture means it inherits some of latency Playwright avoids.
Pricing: free, MIT.
Best for: teams keeping protocol while modernising around it.

5. Is Appium Selenium alternative for mobile?

Appium is mobile branch of same family, implementing W3C WebDriver specification for native iOS and Android. For a Selenium team that is point: vocabulary, language bindings and mental model all transfer, so adding mobile coverage is an extension rather than a new discipline.

The honest overhead is device layer rather than code. Build signing, simulator management and OS upgrades have zero web equivalent, so budget that learning curve even for a strong Selenium team.

Pros: free, standards-based, skills transfer directly from Selenium, portable across every device cloud, five languages.
Cons: verbose capability configuration, iOS driver rebuilds after OS releases, and mobile-only scope.
Pricing: free, Apache 2.0.
Best for: Selenium teams adding native mobile.

6. Is Selenide a lighter alternative to raw Selenium?

Selenide is option most alternatives pages miss, and it came up in that CI stability thread as a middle ground. It wraps Selenium rather than replacing it, adding concise syntax, built-in waiting and automatic screenshots on failure, while engine underneath stays exactly what you already run.

That makes it cheapest possible move. The protocol stays, device strategy stays, training stays, and much of boilerplate that made Selenium unpleasant disappears.

Because everything underneath stays identical, this is also only option here you can trial on a single test class ahead of any migration plan or procurement conversation.

Pros: free, keeps your existing Selenium engine and grid, concise syntax with built-in waiting, automatic failure screenshots, minimal migration cost.
Cons: Java focused, and it improves Selenium rather than changing its architecture, so ceiling stays where it was.
Pricing: free, MIT.
Best for: Java teams who want relief ahead of a migration.

7. Is BrowserStack a Selenium alternative for Grid?

Grid is infrastructure rather than a framework, so replacement here is commercial rather than conceptual. BrowserStack offers 3,500 real devices, 3,000 browser and operating system combinations, and Automate running your existing Selenium scripts unchanged.

That last point matters. You keep every test you have written and stop maintaining browser versions, containers and capacity.

The arithmetic is worth running honestly. A self-hosted grid costs hardware, browser upkeep and a person to keep it alive, while a cloud charges per parallel session, and comparison turns on how much of that person's time you are currently spending.

Pros: runs existing Selenium scripts with a hub URL change, broadest matrix, published pricing, removes grid maintenance entirely.
Cons: it is a subscription against free self-hosting, and parallel pricing climbs at scale.
Pricing: from $29 a month, scaling with concurrency.
Best for: teams whose real burden is running Grid.

Which Selenium cost are you actually paying?

Selector maintenance each sprint. Autosana, since a waiting strategy leaves a moved element exactly where it broke.

Flaky waits. Playwright, where auto-waiting is built in rather than implemented by you. Cypress for a JavaScript team. Both remove explicit-wait scaffolding that accumulates around WebDriver.

Boilerplate and verbosity. Selenide if you are on Java, WebdriverIO if you are on JavaScript. Both keep protocol and cost nothing.

Running your own Grid. BrowserStack, keeping every script you already have, since Automate accepts an existing Selenium suite with a hub URL change rather than a rewrite.

Missing mobile coverage. Appium, because skills transfer directly, or Autosana if you want both surfaces in one place.

Nothing in particular. Stay. Selenium shipped 4.51 in October 2026 and ecosystem around it is largest in testing, which makes it a defensible choice rather than a legacy one.

Conclusion

Selenium is a protocol with an ecosystem rather than a product with a roadmap, and judging it as though it were latter is where most comparisons go wrong. It ships monthly and it still automates browsers exactly as advertised.

What it leaves to you is waiting, debugging, sharding and reporting, and modern frameworks hand you all four for free. Work out which of those you are currently building by hand, price that engineering time honestly, and right alternative follows from answer rather than from benchmark.

Frequently asked questions

What is best alternative to Selenium in 2026?

A universal winner stays elusive. Autosana for teams whose Selenium pain is selector maintenance on a modern frontend. Playwright for direct code-first replacement with auto-waiting and cross-browser. Cypress for JS-first teams that value time-travel debugging. WebdriverIO for unified web plus Appium mobile. Match tool to specific Selenium pain you are escaping.

Is Playwright better than Selenium in 2026?

For modern web frontends, generally yes. Playwright ships auto-waiting, uses DevTools protocol instead of HTTP WebDriver, supports Chromium, Firefox and WebKit under one API, and reduces flake from race conditions. Selenium still wins on legacy browser support, widest possible language coverage, and mature bot-detection evasion for RPA workflows.

Is Selenium being deprecated?

Selenium 4 is production and Selenium 5 with BiDi-first architecture is in active development. Selenium remains polyglot standard and is still default in many enterprise QA orgs. The 2026 answer is rarely "Selenium is dead". It is "Selenium is one option among several, and it is rarely right pick for a greenfield modern web app."

Can Autosana replace Selenium entirely?

For UI-driven web E2E flows, yes. Autosana authors and runs same user flows a Selenium suite covers, free of selectors and WebDriver setup. For API testing, network mocking at scale, and heavy fixture-based backend integration, keep a code-first framework such as Playwright's API testing, Postman or REST-assured. Rule of thumb: if 60% or more of your Selenium suite is user-facing UI flows, Autosana replaces it. If it is mostly API and network testing, keep both.

Does Cypress fully replace Selenium?

For JavaScript teams testing single-origin single-page applications, yes. For polyglot teams on Java, Python or C#, for cross-origin flows, for multi-tab scenarios, or for WebKit and Safari desktop coverage, Selenium keeps advantage. Cypress is opinionated JS-first, while Selenium is polyglot.

What's best Selenium alternative for mobile?

Selenium leaves native mobile to Appium, which you run alongside it. Modern mobile alternatives: Autosana for AI-native cross-platform covering web, iOS and Android under one surface, Maestro for YAML-based happy-path flows, Detox for React Native, and XCUITest or Espresso for native platform-specific stability.

Do Selenium wrappers with AI actually solve anything?

Sometimes, and honestly. Mabl, CloudQA Vibium and Katalon have added ML-based self-healing selector logic on top of Selenium engines. These help for cosmetic UI shifts such as a button class rename or a minor layout tweak. They reach their limit when entire selector philosophy is problem, meaning shadow DOM, dynamic components and deep component refactors. AI-native alternatives sit in a different category and solve it structurally.

How long does a Selenium migration actually take?

It scales with suite size and with how much of suite still earns its keep, so scope it against your own test count rather than a published average. The shape that works is parallel running first, highest-value flows next, rest after that, and a decommissioning step nobody skips. Teams that attempt a single-sprint swap usually end up running both suites far longer than planned.

title: What I learned from building a relational database engine in C#
description:
I’ve used Microsoft SQL Server for decades without ever seeing how it works inside. Sure, there’s ample documentation, but reading it isn’t the same thing as looking at the implementation code. Since the source is closed, I did the next best thing: I built my own relational database engine in C#, to face the same problems it must solve.

Today, my engine supports transactions, concurrency, and crash recovery. It also has a management tool. It can run both in-process and as a server, and I now rely on it in my daily work. For instance, my company’s invoicing goes through it.

I studied databases at university, and textbooks explain B-trees, SQL parsing, ACID principles, transactions, and recovery well. What they don’t show is how those pieces interact when something goes wrong at the worst possible moment. I quickly noticed that this was the thing left out of those books. And quite naturally, this led to the next question: what testing methods are needed to support this kind of work?

In this post, I wanted to share the lessons I learned.

Lesson 1: you need something to compare against

How do you know your engine works correctly and returns the correct results? Simple unit tests will get you started, but for any real workload outside basic SQL, you need something more.

My choice was to add what I’ve come to call a “differential test”: the same SQL is run side-by-side with SQL Server (the “known-good reference”) and my engine (“system under test”), and re-run for every engine change. The workloads are randomized, but with a known seed value. This allows replaying and even debugging directly inside Visual Studio, which is nice. Across tens of thousands of randomized transactions, the two engines have produced identical results.

The takeaway: differential testing works for many more systems than just databases. The basic idea is simple: any time you rewrite or replace something in the implementation, compare it with a trusted reference. Depending on the system, this can take just seconds, or some hours, like in my engine’s case.

Lesson 2: reliability improves by crashing

Happy-path testing is one thing. Making sure data stays correct when things go wrong is much harder. Since I have the engine’s source, I can throw exceptions wherever I like, but real crashes aren’t that polite: a process gets killed, or someone pulls the power plug, at whatever moment it happens to be.

So, I crash the server deliberately, at random points during heavy work, restart it, and check that nothing committed was lost and nothing uncommitted survived.

This found bugs that normal testing never would. One example: when an index page fills up, the engine splits it into two and updates the neighboring page to point to the new one. Simple so far. But if the transaction doing the split is rolled back, the new page’s contents are discarded, yet the pointer to it could still reach disk through another transaction. After a restart, the index walked into an empty page. Every transaction did something reasonable on its own; together, after a crash, they corrupted the index.

My first test reproduced this only one in five runs. That’s fine for finding a bug, but useless for proving a fix: a passing run tells you almost nothing. I set out to write a test that reproduces it every time. Now one run proves the bug, and another run proves the fix.

It made me appreciate long-standing engines like SQL Server even more. As application developers, we rarely have to think about what happens to data at the exact moment the power goes out. For database engines, that is the one thing you need to think about hardest.

Lesson 3: AI is capable, but not trustworthy in its claims

Like many developers, I’ve found AI a capable companion, if you know precisely what you want. But vague requests lead to implementation that seems to work, but when looking closely, the solutions aren’t reliable, performant, or both.

My biggest concern, however, is how confidently AI can claim something is done. When I asked for a deterministic test for the crash bug above, I was told one already existed. When I asked it to verify, the test reproduced the bug only every fifth run.

The lesson: ask for evidence, and do one small, verifiable thing at a time. Asking AI to write the whole thing at once doesn’t lead anywhere, and you end up just wasting tokens. The judgment about what to test, and what “correct” means, must stay with you.

How building this changed my thinking

After implementing transactions, locking, table joins and recovery myself, many problems that once looked hard started looking approachable. I remember thinking during a university lecture, “Those people designing relational database engines must be really smart, so that’s something out of my league.”

But with my own engine’s source code in front of me, I can see I was wrong on the last part. And even if nobody else ever uses this engine, I’ve learned a lot. That is something nobody can take away from me.

The final question remains: why didn’t I do it sooner? Realistically, building everything by hand from scratch would not have been possible for me; it would simply have taken too much time. With capable AI by my side, the question “How does a database engine really work?” became approachable.

title: FastAPI frontends and static files served from the CDN
description:
FastAPI frontends and static files, served with app.frontend() or StaticFiles, are now promoted to the Vercel CDN at build time. Requests for those paths are served directly from the CDN, without invoking your Vercel Function.

FastAPI evaluates routes in declaration order. A route declared before a StaticFiles mount takes priority over any CDN file at that path. This precedence is preserved.

Promoted source directories remain in the function bundle so the app can read from them at runtime. To exclude them and serve only from the CDN, set tool.vercel.fastapi.static.exclude = true in pyproject.toml.

Frontends guarded by dependencies are kept on the function as the CDN cannot run dependency checks. Similarly, static files which sit behind middleware are also kept on the function. To override this and always promote to CDN, set tool.vercel.fastapi.static.cdn = true. To opt out of the CDN entirely, set it to false instead.

For more information see the Vercel FastAPI documentation.
