title: Shrink an SVG in the Browser: What the Optimizer Deletes and What It Leaves Behind
description:
I work on OnePassApps, the team behind the browser-local studios at app.onepassapps.com. The Icon Studio has an Optimize SVG tab, and the question that matters is not how small the file gets - it is what the tool throws away while making it small.

What the panel promises

The page opens with "Create icons and favicon assets on this device. Files stay in your active browser tab." and the tab itself is three steps:

  • 01 Source - "No SVG yet. Drop one on the stage or browse for it. SVG up to 5 MiB and 25,000 elements."
  • 02 What changes - three labelled rows: "Keeps" / "The viewBox and every visible shape", "Removes" / "Scripts, event handlers and external references", "Compares" / "The byte sizes before and after". This morning's run of the same tab recorded that same promise as one sentence: "The optimizer keeps the viewBox and every visible shape and removes scripts and external references."
  • 03 Result - "A smaller, safe SVG, with the file size before and after."

That is a promise about safety, not only about size, so I tested it against a deliberately dirty file instead of a tidy one.

The file I gave it

I hand-built a 128 x 128 SVG, 963 bytes, carrying everything an export tool leaves behind: an XML declaration, an editor comment, a metadata block, a title and a description, a script element, an onload event handler on the rectangle, an external image reference pointing at a tracker image on another host, an unused gradient, a group id, a no-op transform, and coordinates written out as 8.0000000.

The source stage named the file and its size - this morning's run recorded "probe-optimize-in.svg - SVG - 128 x 128 - 963 B". Later the same day the Source stage renders the loaded file as "hostile-probe.svg - SVG - 200 x 200 - 1.3 KiB" with a "Replace" and a "Remove" control beside the name - that was a deliberately hostile test file I used to probe the tab, and I did not finish the optimize run on it, so I make no claim about what it strips. Read the size off your own file.

What came out

The result stage read: "probe-optimize-in-optimized.svg - SVG - 612 B", with a Download SVG button and the line "SVG reduced by 351 bytes (36%)." The arithmetic matches the bytes on disk: 963 - 612 = 351.

I downloaded the optimised file and read it outside the browser. Removed - every one of them gone from the output bytes:

<script> element            0 occurrences
onload="alert(...)"        0 occurrences
xlink:href / any href      0 occurrences
example.com                0 occurrences
<metadata> block            0 occurrences
<!-- comment -->            0 occurrences
<?xml ...?> declaration     0 occurrences

Kept - still in the output bytes:

viewBox="0 0 128 128"      kept
<title>Probe</title>        kept
<desc>...</desc>           kept
<defs> with unused gradient kept (id="unused" and all)
<g id="layer1">            kept
transform="translate(0.0...)" kept
x="8.0000000"              kept, precision untouched
<image x="0" y="0" .../>    element kept, source gone

The three findings

The external reference is removed by dropping the attribute, not by deleting the element. The image tag survives with its x, y, width and height intact and no href at all, so the file still contains an image element that renders nothing. If that bitmap was doing work in your icon, the optimised file is a different drawing - check it before you ship it.

The unused gradient is not unused any more. The defs block, the gradient and its id all survive, even though nothing references them. The optimizer removes active content, not dead weight.

Precision is left alone. Coordinates written as 8.0000000 stay 8.0000000, and the no-op transform stays too. Part of the saving comes from somewhere else: colours are normalised on the way through. stop-color="#ff0000" came out as stop-color="red", "#0000ff" as "#00f", and fill="#58A0D6" as fill="#58a0d6".

So the byte saving is a mix of three different things - deleted metadata, shortened colours, and dropped attributes - and only one of them is what the panel advertised.

A second sample, so the number is not a one-off

I ran a second, smaller file through the same tab: 387 B in, 238 B out. The detail panel read "Before 387 B SVG, After 238 B SVG, Size change 38.5% smaller", the summary line said "SVG reduced by 149 bytes (39%)", and the run reported "Created in 0.3 s". The percentage tracks the file, not a fixed setting - read the number on your own file.

Where it runs

The page states "Processing stays in this browser." and the file you drop is never rewritten in place - you get a new file next to it, and "Your original stays untouched."

You can try it here: the Icon Studio. The other studios are listed on the guides page.

One membership covers all seven studios, and Standard is free right now: $0 a month, 100,000 credits every 30 days, no card required. The studios need no account and use no credits.

What I did not check

  • Signed-in behaviour - the studio was signed out in my browser.
  • Whether the output still renders identically in every SVG consumer. I read the bytes, not every renderer's parser.
  • Whether the optimizer ever touches the viewBox beyond keeping it.
  • Any other optimizer, so I make no comparison to other tools.

title: LEAF: Distillation of State‑of‑the‑Art Text Embedding Models
description:
At MongoDB Research, we’re exploring how to make cutting‑edge AI models smaller, faster, and more flexible.

In this blog post, we present LEAF (Lightweight Embedding Alignment Framework), a new knowledge distillation framework for text embedding models.

We’re also releasing two best‑in‑class embedding models trained with LEAF:

  • mdbr-leaf-ir—23M parameter model optimized for retrieval‑focused tasks like semantic search and retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG).

  • mdbr-leaf-mt—23M parameter model tailored for broader NLP applications such as classification, clustering, and sentence similarity.

These models are suitable for CPU-only deployments (no GPU), as well as IoT and mobile devices, with no internet connection required.

Note: We are publishing these models and the recipe used to train them as a contribution to the open source community. They have been developed by the ML team of MongoDB Research. The models are published under a permissive Apache 2.0 license and offered as is, without any explicit or implied support. At the time of writing, they are not used in any of MongoDB's commercial products or service offerings.

The challenges

Modern text embedding models have delivered huge gains in natural language processing tasks, from question‑answering to RAGs. But these gains come at a cost:

  • Model sizes are exploding. State‑of‑the‑art open‑weight embedding models can range from hundreds of millions to billions of parameters (e.g., 1B or 7B+). While these models can offer high accuracy, they typically need to run on GPU servers, making them impractical for many deployments.

  • Inflexible deployments. In information retrieval (IR) systems, the same large model is typically used for both document indexing and query encoding—even though these steps have very different performance requirements. Document indexing happens infrequently and tolerates high latency, while query-time embedding must meet strict latency targets—often expressed as P99 or tail latency—where even the slowest queries must return results within a few hundred milliseconds.

  • No easy swaps. Existing embedding models aren’t compatible with each other—even different sizes within the same family—so swapping models requires recomputing every document embedding from scratch.

These constraints make it hard to scale high‑performance retrieval systems, especially when operating at a large scale or under tight hardware and latency requirements.

How LEAF works

LEAF is a knowledge distillation technique that takes a larger "teacher" model and outputs a smaller version of it—a "student" model. 

What’s innovative about LEAF is that the student models it produces are compatible with their larger teachers, meaning that the text embeddings produced by the two are interoperable. 

This is achieved by a training scheme that has, as its sole goal, the objective of making the student model approximate the embedding space produced by the teacher model. Initial works [1] proposing distillation strategies attempted to maximize the number of internals of teacher and student models to be aligned. This included aligning attention matrices as well as hidden states of all the layers and all attention heads of the student. Later works [2, 3] realized that better results could be achieved by avoiding excessive alignment of all layers by, e.g., focusing on the last layer of the Transformer backbone only. We take this lesson further and propose to align only the outputs of the teacher and the student. Namely, we propose to use the following L2 loss on the approximation error between the student and teacher’s output embeddings:

Earlier this year, we published details about the model architecture, training data, and training regime in our technical report [4].

Model compatibility unlocks new flexible asymmetric architectures in which, for example, documents can be embedded with larger and more expensive models, while queries can be encoded by local, fast LEAF models, as shown in Figure 1.

Further key advantages of LEAF:

  • No need for labeled data. With LEAF, obtaining training data is extremely simple. This is in contrast to traditional training techniques based on contrastive loss, which require so-called judgments and hard negatives.
  • Modest training infrastructure requirements. While previous methods prefer or even require working with large batch sizes—meaning they need a cluster of GPUs to train—LEAF favors small batches. As a consequence, we were able to train our distillations on a single A100 GPU.
  • Automatic inheritance of advanced features. LEAF models automatically inherit properties like MRL and robustness to output quantization from the teacher, without explicitly training for them.

Below we demonstrate that LEAF can produce models retaining up to 97% of their teacher’s performance, while being 5×–15× smaller and 7×–24× faster.

Two models, two state‑of‑the‑art results

To demonstrate LEAF in action, we’re releasing two new compact, best-in-class text embedding models, both available on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. mdbr-leaf-ir is specifically designed for Information Retrieval (IR) tasks, such as the retrieval stage of RAG pipelines. It currently ranks #1 on the public MTEB leaderboards of the BEIR and RTEB benchmarks for models with ≤100M parameters. It has been distilled from snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v1.5.

mdbr-leaf-mt, on the other hand, excels at general purpose tasks like classification, clustering, sentence similarity and summarization. It currently ranks #1 on the public leaderboard for the MTEB v2 (Eng) benchmark for models with ≤30M parameters. It has been distilled from mxbai-embed-large-v1.

These models are an excellent choice in deployment scenarios where a GPU is not available or is not cost-effective. This includes CPU-only servers, as well as IoT and mobile devices. Since they run on your hardware, they do not require an internet connection.

Typical throughputs obtained on a 2vCPUs instance are 120 queries/sec and 20 docs/sec, respectively. The memory footprint of the full-precision versions is 87MB. Several quantizations are available to further increase throughput and reduce memory footprint.

Besides offering state-of-the-art retrieval performance for their size, both models are equipped with MRL and robustness to output quantization. They can be fine‑tuned on domain‑specific data to further boost performance.

They are well-suited to work with a vector DB (such as MongoDB Vector Search in Community Edition) to power your next AI-enabled application.

References 

  • [1] Xiaoqi Jiao, Yichun Yin, Lifeng Shang, Xin Jiang, Xiao Chen, Linlin Li, Fang Wang, and Qun Liu. TinyBERT: Distilling BERT for Natural Language Understanding. In Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP, 2020.

  • [2] Wenhui Wang, Furu Wei, Li Dong, Hangbo Bao, Nan Yang, and Ming Zhou. MiniLM: Deep self-attention distillation for task-agnostic compression of pre-trained transformers. Advances in neural information processing systems, 2020.

  • [3] Victor Sanh, Lysandre Debut, Julien Chaumond, and Thomas Wolf. DistilBERT, a distilled version of BERT: smaller, faster, cheaper and lighter. https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.01108, 2020.

  • [4] Vujanic, Robin, and Thomas Rueckstiess. "LEAF: Knowledge Distillation of Text Embedding Models with Teacher-Aligned Representations." arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.12539 (2025).

  • Hugging Face Models: mdbr-leaf-ir and mdbr-leaf-mt

*In throughput terms (documents or queries per second), measured on a EC2 i3.large instance. Details are in the technical report.

title: How to Estimate Cloud Cost Before Migration?
description:
Moving to the cloud without a cost estimate is how a simple migration turns into a surprise bill. The estimate does not need to be perfect. It needs to be honest, item by item, so you can compare providers, spot the expensive parts early, and decide what to move first.

What does cloud cost actually include?

Most teams only count virtual machines. A real cloud bill also includes storage, databases, data transfer, load balancers, backups, monitoring, and support. If you leave one of those out, your estimate will look low and your first real bill will look wrong.

Start with a simple inventory: how many services you run, what each one does, how much CPU and memory it uses at peak, how much storage it holds, and how much traffic it serves. That list is the base for every provider comparison that follows.

How do I estimate cloud cost on AWS, GCP and Azure?

Do not compare a single instance price. Compare the same workload on each provider: the same CPU and memory, the same storage type, the same region, and the same traffic pattern. Prices change by region and by storage class, so a like-for-like comparison matters more than a headline price.

A practical way to do this is with a free estimator that breaks the total down by service instead of giving you one lump sum. The ArkanOps Cloud Cost Estimator on the ArkanOps tools page does exactly that for AWS, GCP and Azure, with a breakdown and FinOps suggestions to review — you can find it at https://arkanops.com/tools/ alongside the other ArkanOps tools. Use it to test a workload, change one input at a time, and see which part of the bill moves most.

What is the biggest cost driver in a migration?

Usually it is not compute. It is storage that grows without cleanup, data transfer out of the cloud, and services left running after testing. A second driver is over-sizing: choosing the largest instance “to be safe” and never revisiting it.

Check these three questions before you migrate:

  1. Which services can be stopped outside working hours?
  2. Which storage can move to a cheaper tier after 30 days?
  3. Which old backups and test environments can be deleted?

Those answers often cut more from the estimate than switching providers does.

Should I use reserved capacity or pay as you go?

For a first migration, pay as you go is usually safer. You do not yet know your real usage pattern, and reserved capacity locks you into a size you may not need. Once a workload has run steadily for a few months, then look at reservations or savings plans for the stable part only, and keep the variable part on demand.

This is a general rule, not a saving claim: the right split depends on your workload, and no estimator can promise a percentage saving without your real usage data.

How much buffer should I add to a cloud estimate?

Add a buffer for the first month, and say so openly in your plan. Migrations bring extra traffic during cutover, duplicate running while old and new systems overlap, and extra logging while you check that everything works. A buffer is not waste — it is the cost of a safe cutover. After the first month, compare the estimate with the real bill, service by service, and adjust the next estimate from that gap.

What should I do after the estimate?

Use the estimate to decide the order of migration. Move a small, well-understood service first, measure its real cost for a month, and compare it with the estimate. Then move the next service with a better estimate. That loop — estimate, move, measure, adjust — is more reliable than one big estimate for everything at once.

If you want a starting point, run your current workload through the free Cloud Cost Estimator at https://arkanops.com/tools/ and keep the breakdown. It will not replace your own judgement, but it will show you where the money is going before you commit to a provider.

ArkanOps builds web and mobile products, AI automation and Dev-to-Production systems. More free engineering tools, including a Kubernetes Sizer and a CI/CD Pipeline Generator, are at https://arkanops.com/tools/.

title: Building a done-for-you website service as one React SPA: site, order flow, client portal and admin
description:
Written by the Take2 team. Disclosure: I'm a Take2 affiliate (Take2 Innovations Digital, a small web design shop).

Take2 Innovations Digital is a very small web design shop in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. We build websites for local businesses that don't have one yet, like diners, plumbers, salons, churches and lawn care crews. One person builds and one handles sales.

Before building anything for clients, we had to build the thing that sells and runs the service. That's this app: https://take2-innovations-digital.rork.app. This post covers what's in it, how it's put together, and what we'd do differently.

What we built

One app does four jobs:

  1. Marketing site. Home, Packages, Add-ons, Portfolio, Reviews, About, Contact and Legal pages.
  2. Order funnel. A multi-step order that ends in a signed agreement and a deposit.
  3. Client portal. After ordering, clients log in with a magic link to send content, track progress, request changes and pay the balance.
  4. Staff/admin area. Quotes, jobs, pricing overrides and stats.

The public pitch is simple: pick a package, tell us about your business, we build it, you approve it, and we keep it running every month. Setup is paid in two halves, half up front and half once the client is happy.

Stack

Frontend

  • Vite + React + TypeScript
  • Tailwind CSS with shadcn/ui (Radix primitives)
  • react-router-dom for routing
  • @tanstack/react-query for server state
  • react-hook-form + zod for the long order and quote forms
  • recharts for admin charts, jspdf for generating documents

Backend

  • A Cloudflare Worker with a Durable Object backed by SQLite, split into modules: billing, finance, jobs, portal, staff, store, stats and backup. Shared libs handle Stripe, email, push and crypto.
  • Stripe PaymentIntents for deposits and final payments, plus a /webhooks/stripe endpoint.
  • A small Supabase project that stores only analytics events (a site_events table and an export function).

The app is built and hosted on Rork, so the Worker runs on Rork's Cloudflare hosting.

API shape

Splitting routes by who's calling kept auth simple:

/public/{config, order, quote-request, contact, review, help}
/auth/{login, logout, magic, magic/verify}
/portal/*      # signed-in clients
/staff/*       # signed-in staff
/webhooks/stripe
/analytics/event
/stats/*

/public/config is the important one. It returns prices, feature flags and payment readiness, and the frontend renders from it. Defaults live in a pricing.ts file and an admin can override them without a deploy.

The order funnel

The order flow is a step machine:

Package → Your pages → About you → Your business → Web address → How we work → Sign & pay → Order placed → Client portal

Things that worked:

  • One zod schema per step. Each step validates on its own, so the user never gets a wall of errors at the end.
  • The agreement and deposit happen on one step. The client signs the terms and pays 50% together, which gives a clean record.
  • A parallel quote path. Not everyone wants to buy from a price list. Quote request → staff sends a quote → the client gets a quote link → quote checkout. It uses the same payment code with a different entry point.
  • Magic-link portal auth. Small business owners don't want another password. Email links fit the audience better.

Lessons learned

1. Run a funnel event on every step from day one

We log an analytics event per order step, which shows exactly where people stop. Our early numbers made it plain that most visitors look at packages and never reach the second step. Without per-step events we would only have known "nobody ordered."

2. A client-side SPA on a shared subdomain is close to invisible to search

The whole site is a single HTML shell rendered on the client. Every route has the same title and description, there's no sitemap.xml, no og:image and no LocalBusiness JSON-LD, and it sits on a platform subdomain. For a business that sells "get found on Google," that's the first thing we're fixing:

  • Prerender the marketing routes at build time
  • Give each route its own <title>, meta description and Open Graph tags
  • Add sitemap.xml and LocalBusiness structured data
  • Move to our own domain

3. Show samples before you have clients

A web shop with an empty portfolio is a hard sell. We put up sample designs for the kinds of businesses we serve, including a corner diner, a community church, lawn and landscaping, a local plumber, a hair salon, a barber shop, a roofer, auto repair, heating and air, a tire shop and a dry cleaner. Each one is labeled as a sample design. Labeling them keeps us honest, and visitors can still picture their own site.

4. Know your platform dependency

Building on a hosted platform got us from idea to a working site, portal and payments quickly. The trade-off is that the backend runs on someone else's hosting and is harder to move. Keep the data layer and Stripe logic in plain modules so you can migrate if you ever need to.

What's next

  • Prerendering plus per-page meta and a sitemap
  • A custom domain
  • Real client reviews to replace the empty Reviews page

If you're building a productized service, whether websites, design or bookkeeping, the pattern of a config-driven price list, a step-validated order flow, a magic-link portal and per-step analytics carries over well.

Sample work: https://take2-innovations-digital.rork.app/portfolio

Disclosure: written by the Take2 Innovations Digital team; we build websites for small businesses, and free quotes are available at https://take2-innovations-digital.rork.app.

title: Node 24 vs Node 26: Benchmarks, Breaking Changes and Should You Upgrade (2026)
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Node.js 26 became the Active LTS line on October 28, 2026 with v26.13.0 "Lithium", and Node 24 moved to Maintenance LTS on October 20. If you're deciding between Node 24 vs Node 26 for a production app, this post covers what changes, what breaks, and how the two compare on a few benchmarks I ran on the same machine tonight. The short version: Node 26 was faster at JSON serialization, async-heavy code and a plain node:http server, but slower in two places you might not expect, fetch() and inserting a million keys into a Map.

Node 24 vs Node 26 at a glance

Node 24 "Krypton" Node 26 "Lithium"
Version tested v24.22.2 v26.13.0
Status (Nov 2026) Maintenance LTS since Oct 20, 2026 Active LTS since Oct 28, 2026
End of life April 30, 2028 April 30, 2029
V8 13.6 14.6
Undici (powers fetch) 7.30.1 8.12.2
NODE_MODULE_VERSION 137 147
Bundled npm 11.19.1 11.20.0
Temporal global not available on by default

Dates come from the Node.js release schedule. Versions are what process.versions printed on each binary.

What's new in Node 26

From the Node 26.0.0 release notes and checked on v26.13.0:

  • Temporal is enabled by default. Temporal.Now.plainDateISO('Asia/Karachi') works with no flag. On Node 24, Temporal is undefined.
  • V8 14.6 brings Map.prototype.getOrInsert() / getOrInsertComputed() (the upsert proposal) and Iterator.concat().
  • Undici 8, so the global fetch() is a different major version of the HTTP client.
  • TypeScript type stripping still works out of the box for .ts files, as it does on Node 24. --experimental-transform-types was removed, so enums and namespaces that need transformation won't run without a build step. 
// Node 26 only
const counts = new Map();
for (const word of ['a', 'b', 'a']) {
  counts.set(word, counts.getOrInsert(word, 0) + 1);
}

const today = Temporal.Now.plainDateISO('Asia/Karachi');
console.log(today.add({ days: 30 }).toString());

const all = Iterator.concat([1, 2].values(), [3].values()).toArray(); // [1, 2, 3]

Breaking changes to check before upgrading

These are the ones most likely to hit a typical Node.js, NestJS or Next.js codebase:

  1. Native addons must be rebuilt. NODE_MODULE_VERSION went from 137 to 147. Anything with a compiled .node file (bcrypt, sharp, better-sqlite3, canvas) needs a fresh install on Node 26. Delete node_modules in your Docker build rather than copying it from a Node 24 stage.
  2. http.ServerResponse.prototype.writeHeader() is gone. It was a legacy alias. On v26.13.0 typeof res.writeHeader is undefined. Use writeHead().
  3. The _stream_* legacy modules are removed (_stream_readable, _stream_writable and friends). Old dependencies that require('_stream_readable') will crash at import.
  4. module.register() is runtime-deprecated. Running a loader that calls it prints DEP0205 DeprecationWarning: module.register() is deprecated. Use module.registerHooks() instead. It still works, but plan to move custom loaders to registerHooks().
  5. --experimental-transform-types is removed. If you run .ts with enums directly through Node, switch to erasableSyntaxOnly style code or keep a compiler step.

A quick way to find the first two in a codebase:

grep -rn "writeHeader(\|_stream_readable\|_stream_writable\|module.register(" src/ node_modules/.pnpm 2>/dev/null | head

Node 24 vs Node 26 performance: benchmark setup

I ran these on November 3, 2026 on one Linux VM with 8 vCPUs (Intel Xeon) and 16 GB RAM. The machine was shared with other work (load average around 1.5 before starting), so treat small differences as noise. To limit that:

  • Each benchmark process was pinned to one CPU with taskset.
  • Node 24 and Node 26 runs were interleaved over 5 rounds, and I report the median of the 5 rounds.
  • The HTTP load generator (autocannon, 100 connections, 10 s) always ran on Node 24 on separate CPUs, so only the server changed.
  • The fetch() test sent 20,000 requests with 50 concurrent loops to a fixed Node 24 server, so only the client changed.

The scripts are plain .mjs files: JSON.parse/JSON.stringify on a 20,000-item document, sorting 300,000 numbers, setting 1 million string keys in a Map, a global regex replace, SHA-256 over 16 MB, allocating 2 million small class instances, and 1 million sequential awaits.

Benchmark results

Lower is better for times, higher is better for requests per second. Median of 5 rounds.

Test Node 24.22.2 Node 26.13.0 Change
JSON.parse (20k items) 11.79 ms 10.46 ms 11% faster
JSON.stringify (20k items) 7.20 ms 4.53 ms 37% faster
Sort 300k numbers 54.6 ms 51.7 ms 5% faster
Map.set 1M string keys 396.7 ms 507.5 ms 28% slower
Regex replace 2.06 ms 1.72 ms 16% faster
SHA-256 over 16 MB 9.57 ms 9.17 ms 4% faster (within noise)
2M class instances 47.8 ms 35.0 ms 27% faster
1M sequential await 58.6 ms 35.0 ms 40% faster
node -e 0 startup 22.3 ms 20.7 ms 7% faster
RSS after startup 41 MB 41 MB same
node:http server, req/s 73,079 79,653 9% more
node:http p99 latency 3 ms 2 ms lower
fetch() client, req/s 8,442 7,601 10% fewer

What stood out:

  • JSON.stringify and await got much cheaper. Those two show up everywhere in API servers, so the 9% higher node:http throughput is consistent with them.
  • fetch() was slower in 4 of 5 rounds. Node 26 ships Undici 8. If your service makes lots of outbound HTTP calls, measure your own workload before and after.
  • Map.set with 1 million new string keys was slower in every round. The Node 24 numbers for this test varied a lot (336 to 513 ms), so the size of the gap is uncertain, but the direction was consistent. Code that builds very large maps in a hot path is worth profiling.

These are microbenchmarks on one VM. They tell you where to look, not what your app will do.

How to upgrade from Node 24 to Node 26 

# 1. Switch locally
nvm install 26 && nvm use 26     # or: fnm use 26 / volta install node@26

# 2. Reinstall so native addons rebuild against ABI 147
rm -rf node_modules && npm ci

# 3. Surface deprecations your code triggers
NODE_OPTIONS=--trace-deprecation npm test

Then update the places that pin the version:

# Dockerfile
FROM node:26-alpine AS deps

// package.json
{ "engines": { "node": ">=26" } }

Also update .nvmrc, your CI matrix and the Node version in your hosting panel. If you deploy Next.js in Docker, the multi-stage setup in my Next.js Dockerfile guide works the same with node:26-alpine as the base image.

Should you upgrade to Node 26 now?

  • New projects: start on Node 26. It's the Active LTS line and is supported a year longer than Node 24.
  • Existing Node 24 apps: there's no rush. Node 24 gets security fixes until April 30, 2028. Upgrade when you next touch your Docker base image, after rebuilding native addons and running your tests with --trace-deprecation.
  • Services that are mostly outbound HTTP: benchmark your own fetch() traffic first, because that was the one place Node 26 was clearly slower in my test.

If you're also weighing runtimes rather than versions, I compared Bun vs Node on real workloads earlier.

FAQ

Is Node 26 LTS?

Yes. Node 26 entered Active LTS on October 28, 2026 with v26.13.0, codename "Lithium". It stays Active LTS until October 20, 2027, then Maintenance LTS until April 30, 2029.

When does Node 24 reach end of life?

April 30, 2028. Node 24 has been in Maintenance LTS since October 20, 2026, which means security and critical fixes only.

Is Node 26 faster than Node 24?

In my benchmarks on one 8-vCPU VM, Node 26 was faster at JSON.stringify (37%), sequential await (40%) and as a node:http server (9% more requests per second). It was slower for the fetch() client (10% fewer requests per second) and for inserting 1 million keys into a Map (28% slower). Measure your own workload.

What breaks when upgrading from Node 24 to Node 26?

The common ones are native addons that need rebuilding (NODE_MODULE_VERSION 147), the removed res.writeHeader() alias, the removed _stream_* modules, the removed --experimental-transform-types flag, and a runtime deprecation warning for module.register().

Does Node 26 have Temporal?

Yes. The Temporal global is enabled by default in Node 26. In the official Node 24.22.2 binary, typeof Temporal is 'undefined'.

title: Vitest vs Jest vs node:test in 2026: Benchmarked on a Real TypeScript Project
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

I ran the same TypeScript test suite under Vitest 5.1, Jest 30.5 and Node's built-in node:test, and timed cold runs, warm runs, single files, watch mode and coverage. The suite is 39 test files and 183 tests against a small NestJS-style orders service, an HTTP API and an MCP server. The result surprised me: with default settings, Jest with @swc/jest was the fastest full run, and Vitest was the slowest of the three. Change one isolation setting and the order flips. Below are the numbers, the setup for each runner, and the TypeScript and ESM problems I hit along the way.

What I tested

Everything ran on November 3, 2026 on one Linux VM with 8 vCPUs (Intel Xeon) and 16 GB of RAM, on Node.js 24.22.1:

  • Vitest 5.1.0 (Vite 8.3.5), @vitest/coverage-v8 5.1.0
  • Jest 30.5.2 with @swc/jest 0.2.39 and @swc/core 1.16.21, and separately with ts-jest 29.4.15
  • node:test from Node 24.22.1, using Node's built-in type stripping (no loader)
  • TypeScript 6.0.3 for type checks. ts-jest 29.4.15 declares typescript >=4.3 <7, so it doesn't support TypeScript 7.0.2, the current latest on npm.

The code under test is real, not generated: money math with cent allocation, slugs, cursor pagination, an LRU cache, a token-bucket rate limiter, retry with backoff, a CSV parser, an event bus, Zod order schemas, a pricing service, an orders service with status transitions, a node:http JSON API, and the MCP server from my MCP testing guide. That's 387 lines of source and 501 lines of tests. The HTTP and MCP tests start real servers on random ports and call them with fetch and the official MCP SDK client.

To keep the suite identical, every test file imports describe, it and hooks from #t, a one-line shim that each runner maps to its own API, and asserts with node:assert/strict. Fakes are hand-written, so no runner-specific mocking runs inside the benchmark. I compare the mocking APIs separately below.

How I measured: a script ran each configuration 10 times in shuffled order. "Cold" means I deleted the runner's caches first (jest --clearCache, and node_modules/.vite plus node_modules/.vitest-cache for Vitest). "Warm" is the next run with caches in place. Times are whole-process wall clock, and I report the median. Every run had to exit 0 with all 183 tests passing.

One honest caveat: this VM is shared, and other jobs were running (load average between 3 and 13 on 8 cores). Absolute times are noisy, so read the ranking more than the decimals. I ran the main configurations in two separate batches, and Vitest, Jest and node:test each landed within about 0.1 s of their first-batch medians.

Results: the full suite

39 files, 183 tests, median of 10 runs:

Runner and config Cold Warm
Vitest 5.1, defaults (forks pool, isolated) 1.59 s 1.51 s
Vitest, --pool=threads 1.55 s 1.42 s
Vitest, --pool=vmThreads 0.91 s 0.91 s
Vitest, --no-isolate 0.75 s 0.68 s
Vitest, --fsModuleCache 1.63 s 1.52 s
Jest 30.5 + @swc/jest (CommonJS output) 0.99 s 0.81 s
Jest + @swc/jest, native ESM (--experimental-vm-modules) 1.19 s 1.01 s
Jest + ts-jest (type-checks every file) 4.30 s 3.13 s
Jest + ts-jest, isolatedModules: true 1.44 s 1.14 s
node --test (process per file) 1.23 s 1.24 s
node --test --test-isolation=none 0.52 s 0.51 s

The threads, vmThreads and --test-isolation=none rows come from the second batch. In that batch, the Vitest default, Jest + @swc/jest and node --test rows measured 1.52/1.40 s, 0.95/0.80 s and 1.14/1.23 s.

What the numbers say:

  • Isolation is most of the cost. Vitest's default forks pool starts a fresh child process for each test file, and its own summary told me so: "39 workers spawned, ~81ms startup each". node --test also runs each file in its own process. Jest isolates each file in a separate vm context but reuses its 7 worker processes. Turn isolation off and Vitest (0.68 s) and node:test (0.51 s) both beat Jest.
  • vmThreads is the middle ground for Vitest. It kept per-file isolation and cut the run from 1.51 s to 0.91 s. The catch is that it runs each file in a vm sandbox, like Jest does. Vitest's docs warn that this leaks memory on large suites (workers restart when they pass vmMemoryLimit) and that objects from Node APIs such as fetch's response.json() and structuredClone() have a different prototype. That's the same realm problem I hit with Jest below, and this suite only passed under vmThreads because I had already fixed those tests.
  • ts-jest with type checking costs about 2.3 seconds here. It was 3.13 s warm against 0.81 s for @swc/jest. With isolatedModules: true it skips the type checker and drops to 1.14 s. Running tsc --noEmit on the whole project separately took about 1.5 s (median of 5), so a separate type-check step is cheaper than type-checking inside Jest.
  • Caches barely mattered at this size. Cold and warm runs differ by 0.1 to 0.2 s for Vitest and Jest with SWC. Vitest 5 made fsModuleCache stable, but on a project this small it made no measurable difference. node --test has no transform cache at all, because type stripping is cheap.

Results at 4x the size

To see how the gap scales, I copied the test tree three more times: 156 files and 732 tests, same source. Median of 7 runs:

Runner and config Cold Warm
Vitest, defaults 5.15 s 5.03 s
Vitest, --pool=vmThreads 2.29 s 1.99 s
Vitest, --no-isolate 1.32 s 1.08 s
Jest + @swc/jest 1.75 s 1.52 s
node --test 4.32 s 4.26 s
node --test --test-isolation=none 1.08 s 1.10 s

The per-file process cost grows with the file count. Isolated Vitest went from 1.5 s to 5.0 s, while Jest went from 0.8 s to 1.5 s. Without isolation, Vitest and node:test stay around one second. On a busy machine, process startup is exactly the thing that gets slower, so your numbers on a quiet laptop may be closer together, but the direction should hold.

One file, the inner loop

Running only test/orders/service.create.test.ts (4 tests), warm, median of 7:

Runner Time
node --test 0.18 s
Jest + @swc/jest 0.39 s
Vitest 0.40 s
Jest + ts-jest 1.40 s

Node has nothing to boot except itself. Vitest and Jest each spend about 0.2 s more starting their runner.

Watch mode

I started each runner in watch mode, waited for the first run, then edited a source file and timed the rerun (median of 5). money.ts is imported by 3 test files. events.ts is imported by the shared test fixtures, so 18 files depend on it.

Watch command Edit money.ts Edit events.ts
vitest --watch 0.23 s, 3 files 0.97 s, 18 files
jest --watch (needs git) 0.25 s, 3 files 0.52 s, 18 files
jest --watchAll 0.66 s, all 39 files 0.61 s, all 39 files
node --test --watch 0.31 s, 3 files 0.94 s, 18 files

All three rerun only the affected test files. Vitest follows the module graph, and node:test did the same in my test. Jest's --watch uses git to find changed files, and outside a git repo it refuses to start ("--watch is not supported without git/hg, please use --watchAll"). Vitest's interactive watch UI is the nicest of the three (filter by name, rerun failed tests, the optional browser UI), but on raw rerun speed they're close.

Coverage

Full suite with coverage on, median of 5 runs after one warm-up:

Runner Time Lines reported
Vitest, @vitest/coverage-v8 1.99 s 97.38%
Jest + @swc/jest, default (Babel/Istanbul) 0.99 s 97.81%
Jest + @swc/jest, --coverageProvider=v8 1.66 s 98.44%
node --test --experimental-test-coverage 1.36 s 100% lines, 95.79% branches

Coverage added about 0.5 s to Vitest and less to Jest with Istanbul. The percentages aren't comparable between tools, because each counts lines, statements and branches differently. Node said 100% of lines while the others found a few uncovered lines in the same code. Pick one tool for your coverage threshold and stay with it. Node's coverage is still behind the --experimental-test-coverage flag on Node 24.

Setup for each runner

Vitest 

// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    include: ["test/**/*.test.ts"],
    coverage: { provider: "v8", include: ["src/**"] },
    // isolate: false,   // 0.68 s instead of 1.51 s, if your tests don't leak state
    // pool: "vmThreads", // keeps isolation, 0.91 s here
  },
});

That's all it needed. ESM, TypeScript, .ts extensions in imports, top-level await and import.meta all worked without extra config. The exception is decorators: a class with a legacy decorator and a constructor parameter property failed with "SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token" under my bare config, even with experimentalDecorators in tsconfig.json. Adding unplugin-swc 2.0.0 to the plugins, with experimentalDecorators and emitDecoratorMetadata in tsconfig, fixed it. If you're on NestJS 12, the Vitest config that nest new generates already handles this. I covered that in my NestJS 12 migration guide.

Jest with @swc/jest 

// jest.config.cjs
/** @type {import('jest').Config} */
module.exports = {
  testEnvironment: "node",
  testMatch: ["<rootDir>/test/**/*.test.ts"],
  transform: { "^.+\\.ts$": ["@swc/jest"] },
};

This works if SWC compiles your ESM TypeScript to CommonJS, which is what happens when you don't list .ts in extensionsToTreatAsEsm. It broke in three places:

  1. Top-level await and import.meta. My MCP server file had an if (import.meta.url === ...) block with a top-level await to start the server when run directly. As CommonJS, Jest failed to parse it: "await is only valid in async functions and the top level bodies of modules". I moved the entry point to its own main.ts, which is cleaner anyway, and used the same code for all three runners.
  2. Realm mismatches with node:assert. Jest runs each file in a vm context with its own Object.prototype. Objects created by Node's globals, like Response.json() from fetch or structuredClone(), come from the outer realm. assert.deepStrictEqual checks prototypes, so it failed with "Compared values have no visual difference". Jest's own expect().toEqual() and toStrictEqual() passed on the same objects. Vitest's default pool and node:test didn't have the problem. I changed those tests to JSON.parse(await r.text()) for all runners.
  3. jest.mock hoisting. With @swc/jest 0.2.39, a jest.mock() call wasn't hoisted when jest was imported from @jest/globals. The real module ran, and my "must not send email" guard threw. Using the global jest object fixed it, and so did ts-jest, which hoisted the same file correctly.

For native ESM, add extensionsToTreatAsEsm: [".ts"], tell SWC to keep ES modules, and start Node with --experimental-vm-modules. On Node 24.22, Jest 30.5 still printed "VM Modules is an experimental feature" for every worker. In this mode, module mocks use jest.unstable_mockModule() followed by a dynamic import().

// jest.esm.config.cjs, run with NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-vm-modules
module.exports = {
  testEnvironment: "node",
  testMatch: ["<rootDir>/test/**/*.test.ts"],
  extensionsToTreatAsEsm: [".ts"],
  transform: { "^.+\\.ts$": ["@swc/jest", { module: { type: "es6" } }] },
};

Jest with ts-jest

ts-jest uses the TypeScript compiler, so it type-checks your tests, which explains the 3.1 s run. It also brings tsconfig friction. My project tsconfig uses "module": "nodenext" and verbatimModuleSyntax in a "type": "module" package, and ts-jest's CommonJS mode failed every file with TS1295: "ECMAScript imports and exports cannot be written in a CommonJS file under 'verbatimModuleSyntax'". I needed a separate tsconfig.jest.json with "module": "commonjs", verbatimModuleSyntax: false, and a paths entry for the #t import (Node-style imports aren't resolved with node10 resolution). You also can't move to TypeScript 7 with ts-jest yet, because of the <7 peer range.

node:test 

{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "node --test \"test/**/*.test.ts\"",
    "test:watch": "node --test --watch \"test/**/*.test.ts\"",
    "test:cov": "node --test --experimental-test-coverage --test-coverage-include=\"src/**\" \"test/**/*.test.ts\""
  }
}

No dependencies and no config. Node 24 strips types by default, and the test runner finds .ts files from the glob. The price is that your TypeScript has to be erasable: Node removes types but doesn't compile anything. I checked each case on Node 24.22.1:

Syntax node file.ts --experimental-transform-types
enum Status { ... } ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX works
constructor(private readonly repo: Repo) ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX works
@Injectable() decorator ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX SyntaxError

So a NestJS codebase full of decorators and parameter properties can't run under plain node --test. My orders service is written NestJS-style, with constructor injection, but it assigns dependencies to private fields by hand instead of using parameter properties. That makes it erasable, and "erasableSyntaxOnly": true in tsconfig keeps it that way. You also need .ts extensions in relative imports (allowImportingTsExtensions plus noEmit for tsc) and import type for type-only imports (verbatimModuleSyntax).

Mocking APIs compared

The same two jobs in each runner: replace an ES module that sends email, and fake a 60-second timer. All three files below passed.

// Vitest: vi.mock is hoisted above the imports
import { vi, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { sendReceipt } from "./receipts.ts";
import { sendEmail } from "./mailer.ts";
vi.mock("./mailer.ts", () => ({ sendEmail: vi.fn(async () => ({ id: "msg_1" })) }));

it("mocks an ES module", async () => {
  expect(await sendReceipt("a@b.co", 7)).toBe("msg_1");
  expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith("a@b.co", "Receipt for order #7");
});
// timers: vi.useFakeTimers(); vi.advanceTimersByTime(60_000);

// Jest (CommonJS output): use the global jest object so jest.mock gets hoisted
import { sendReceipt } from "./receipts.ts";
import { sendEmail } from "./mailer.ts";
jest.mock("./mailer.ts", () => ({ sendEmail: jest.fn(async () => ({ id: "msg_1" })) }));
// timers: jest.useFakeTimers(); jest.advanceTimersByTime(60_000);

// node:test: needs --experimental-test-module-mocks, then a dynamic import
import { mock, it } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
const sendEmail = mock.fn(async (_to: string, _subject: string) => ({ id: "msg_1" }));
mock.module("./mailer.ts", { exports: { sendEmail } });
const { sendReceipt } = await import("./receipts.ts");

it("mocks an ES module", async () => {
  assert.equal(await sendReceipt("a@b.co", 7), "msg_1");
  assert.deepEqual(sendEmail.mock.calls[0].arguments, ["a@b.co", "Receipt for order #7"]);
});
// timers: mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout"] }); mock.timers.tick(60_000);

Vitest has the smoothest module mocking for ESM. Jest's is fine in CommonJS but needs unstable_mockModule and dynamic imports in ESM. Node's mock.module() works, but it's experimental: without the flag, mock.module is not a function. Node 24 also prints a deprecation warning if you use the older namedExports option instead of exports. Node's mock.fn(), mock.method() and mock.timers need no flag and covered everything else I needed. For most service code, constructor injection with hand-written fakes, like this suite uses, avoids module mocking altogether.

Which test runner should you use?

Pick Vitest for a new TypeScript or ESM project, a Vite or React frontend, or a NestJS 12 app. It needed the least configuration, handled ESM and top-level await without flags, and has the best mocking and watch experience. Its default per-file process isolation is the slowest option at scale, so try pool: "vmThreads" or isolate: false once your suite is stable. Those settings made it the fastest or close to it in my runs.

Keep Jest if you have a large, working Jest suite, especially CommonJS. With @swc/jest it was the fastest default configuration here, and moving to Vitest is mostly an API rename (jest.fn to vi.fn) that buys you little speed unless you also change isolation. Swap ts-jest for @swc/jest and run tsc --noEmit separately: that alone took this suite from 3.13 s to 0.81 s.

Pick node:test for libraries, CLIs and backend code written in erasable TypeScript, where zero dependencies matters. It had the fastest single-file runs (0.18 s) and the fastest full run without isolation (0.51 s). You give up a rich expect, snapshot ergonomics and stable module mocking, and decorator-heavy code won't run. If you're comparing runtimes too, I measured Bun against Node separately, and I covered what changes in TypeScript 7 for build tooling.

FAQ

Is Vitest faster than Jest?

Not with default settings in my test. On a 39-file TypeScript suite, Jest 30.5 with @swc/jest took 0.81 s warm and Vitest 5.1 took 1.51 s, because Vitest's default forks pool starts a process per test file. With isolate: false Vitest took 0.68 s, and with pool: vmThreads 0.91 s. At 156 files the default gap grew to 1.52 s for Jest against 5.03 s for Vitest.

Can node:test run TypeScript without a loader?

Yes, on Node 24 type stripping is on by default and node --test picks up .ts files from a glob. It only removes types, so enums, constructor parameter properties and decorators fail with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX. You also need .ts extensions in relative imports and import type for type-only imports.

Should I use ts-jest or @swc/jest?

Use @swc/jest and run tsc --noEmit as a separate step. In my runs ts-jest took 3.13 s warm because it type-checks every file, against 0.81 s for @swc/jest, while tsc on the whole project took about 1.5 s. ts-jest 29.4.15 also declares typescript below 7, so it doesn't support TypeScript 7 yet.

Does Jest support ESM in 2026?

Yes, but still behind Node's --experimental-vm-modules flag. Jest 30.5 on Node 24.22 ran my suite as native ESM in 1.01 s warm, but printed an experimental warning for every worker, and module mocks need jest.unstable_mockModule plus a dynamic import. Compiling to CommonJS with @swc/jest avoids the flag but breaks top-level await and import.meta.

Which test runner has the fastest watch mode?

They were close. After editing a file imported by 3 test files, Vitest reran in 0.23 s, jest --watch in 0.25 s and node --test --watch in 0.31 s, and all three reran only the affected files. jest --watch needs a git repository; jest --watchAll reruns every file.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: NestJS Explained: Node Backends With Structure Built In
description:
Node.js makes it easy to start a server and hard to keep one organised. A few routes become a few dozen, shared logic drifts into copy pasted handlers, and six months later nobody is sure where a feature lives. NestJS is a framework that gives a Node backend a deliberate shape from the first file, borrowing ideas from Angular and from enterprise frameworks in other languages.

The shape has three parts, and each has one job. Controllers receive HTTP requests and return responses, and they should do nothing else. Services hold the business logic, such as talking to a database or applying a rule. Modules group controllers and services that belong together, so a feature can be understood and tested as one unit. When you want to find where something happens, you already know which kind of file to open.

Here is the smallest complete example: a controller that answers a GET request by asking a service for a greeting.

import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppService } from './app.service';

@Controller()
export class AppController {
  constructor(private readonly appService: AppService) {}

  @Get()
  getHello(): string {
    return this.appService.getHello();
  }
}

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class AppService {
  getHello(): string {
    return 'Hello World!';
  }
}

The decorators do the wiring. @Controller marks the class as a request handler, @get marks the method as the answer to a GET request, and @Injectable marks the service as something NestJS can create and hand to whoever needs it. The controller never builds the service itself; NestJS injects it through the constructor, which is the dependency injection pattern. That one habit is what makes NestJS code testable: in a test, you can hand the controller a fake service and check its behaviour without starting a server or touching a database.

NestJS also standardises the pieces every real backend needs. Guards handle authentication, pipes validate incoming data, interceptors transform responses, and exception filters turn errors into consistent responses. Because these are framework concepts rather than one off middleware, a new developer joining the project meets the same patterns in every module.

TypeScript is not optional decoration here. Types on controllers and services catch mismatched shapes at build time, and the decorators only make sense with the type metadata TypeScript provides. If you dislike TypeScript, NestJS will feel like friction from day one.

The honest trade

NestJS trades freedom for consistency. You write more files and more boilerplate than you would with a minimal framework like Express, and the decorator heavy style can feel like magic until you learn what each piece does. For a small API with three endpoints, that structure is overhead. For a backend that will grow to dozens of endpoints, several developers, and years of maintenance, the structure is exactly what keeps the project readable. The wrong time to adopt NestJS is a weekend prototype; the right time is the moment a prototype starts turning into a product.

Structure you can grow into

Start with one module, one controller, and one service, exactly like the example above, and add a second module only when a second feature arrives. If the shape still feels helpful at five modules, it will still feel helpful at fifty.

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/nestjs-explained-node-backends-with.html

title: DupeLens after v1.0.0: what changed, and what’s next
description:
I joined the DEV community three years ago, but this is only my second post here. My first one introduced a small Java project I’d just released: DupeLens, a command-line tool for finding duplicate files.

That post didn’t get any responses. I’m sharing an update now because the project has continued to grow, with improvements from me and contributions from others.

DupeLens is a read-only Java CLI that finds files with identical contents and can create an offline HTML report. It shows you what it found without deleting or moving anything.

Since my first post, the project has grown in a few useful ways:

A simpler start: You can run it from source with Java 17 or newer. Maven is optional.

Safer scans: DupeLens groups files by size before hashing candidates with SHA-256. It skips symbolic links and reports unreadable files as warnings.

A portable report: The generated HTML works offline in a browser, with no server or external scripts.

More careful reporting: Results are sorted by redundant bytes, and the tool avoids overwriting an existing report.

Broader checks: The project now includes integration checks and GitHub Actions coverage across Java 17 and 21 on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

A quick example:

java -jar target/dupelens.jar ./your-folder --html report.html

Or run it directly from source:

java src/main/java/dev/dupelens/Main.java ./your-folder --html report.html

This is still a small tool, and there are limits: a scan isn’t an atomic snapshot, and DupeLens doesn’t compare file bytes after matching SHA-256 hashes. It’s designed to help you inspect duplicates while keeping control of your files.

Thanks to everyone who has contributed feedback, code, or time to the project. Open-source work gets better when people take a look and help shape what comes next.

The README lists exclusion patterns, machine-readable output, and scan cancellation as possible next steps. If one of those would be useful to you—or if you spot something I could improve—please open an issue or pull request.

Repository: https://github.com/illusionoftalha/dupelens

If you try DupeLens, I’d love to hear what worked, what didn’t, and what you’d like to see next.
