title: I used to reconcile delivery waybills by hand. Now an open-source tool does it
description:
Before I moved into QA, I ran transport logistics for a delivery service: 50-60 drivers and 2,500-3,000 deliveries a day. Every order had to match in four places: the waybill a driver loaded from in the morning, the status the driver set in the mobile app, the record in our system, and the returns that a warehouse employee checked against the waybill in the evening. If an item was in one place and missing in another, the driver paid a fine.

We did that reconciliation by hand, every day.

Later, as a QA engineer in FinTech and advertising analytics, I saw the same problem in software. The same order, payment or report lives in several places at once: the user interface, the API, the accounting export and the database. The expensive bugs are rarely inside one endpoint. They hide between systems.

Four bugs that live between systems

  • Rounding. On one FinTech project, our accrual and income statistics did not match the accountant's numbers. The formulas rounded intermediate values with ordinary half-up rounding, and the code applied a fixed percentage per client tariff while the accountant adjusted it to the business terms. Each number looked plausible on its own. The gap only showed up when two sources were compared.
  • Timezones. On every project I have worked on, "which timezone is this timestamp in?" was a question for the product owner or the customer. An export writes local time without an offset, the API returns UTC, and a delivery suddenly happened six hours earlier.
  • A row lost at a page boundary. An export pages through 200 rows at a time and drops the last row of every page. The endpoint test passes. Fourteen of 2,750 orders are missing, and nobody notices.
  • A stale status. The backend knows the order was delivered, but the dispatcher screen still shows "in transit" from a cache.

Postman checks that an API answers correctly. Playwright checks that a page works. Contract tests check the shape of a response. None of them takes the same shipment from the API, the screen and the Excel export and tells you: here it is 101 cents, there it is 100.

What LogiParity does

LogiParity is an MIT-licensed CLI that automates that reconciliation. It reads records from REST APIs, CSV and XLSX files, UI tables (through Playwright) and PostgreSQL (read only), matches them by key, and reports what is missing, what is extra and which field differs.

Everything is described in YAML. This is a shortened version of the demo configuration:

version: 1
environment: test
entities:
  - name: shipment
    key: shipment_id
    sources:
      api:
        type: rest
        label: API
        baseUrl: http://127.0.0.1:3010
        path: /api/shipments
        items: $.data[*]
        pagination: {type: page, totalPath: $.pagination.total, sizeParam: limit, size: 200}
        fields: {shipment_id: $.id, status: $.status, payout: $.driver_payout, delivered_at: $.delivered_at}
      export:
        type: xlsx
        label: Excel export
        file: ./shipments.xlsx
        sheet: Shipments
        fields: {shipment_id: 'Shipment ID', status: Status, payout: 'Driver payout', delivered_at: 'Delivered at'}
    compare:
      status: {type: enum}
      payout: {type: money, currency: USD}
      delivered_at: {type: datetime, sourceTimezones: {export: UTC}, toleranceSeconds: 60}

A few decisions come straight from that logistics experience:

  • The first source is the reference. At the delivery service, the waybill was the reference that returns were checked against, not the other way round. Which system is authoritative is a business decision, so the configuration states it.
  • Money is compared in exact cents. 1.01 becomes 101, so there is no floating-point drift. By default, values with more decimals than the currency allows are rejected instead of rounded. Rounding is an explicit, configurable rule, because after that FinTech project I treat rounding as business logic, not formatting.
  • No guessing timezones. A timestamp without an offset is an error until the configuration says which timezone the source uses. Ambiguous times around daylight saving changes are not guessed either.

From thousands of findings to a few causes

The package includes a synthetic delivery service with 55 drivers and 2,750 orders, with optional bugs. Without bugs, the check finds zero differences and exits with code 0. With bugs enabled, comparing the API with the Excel and CSV exports produces 3,741 findings. Nobody reads 3,741 rows, so the report starts with causes:

14 missing rows in Excel export follow page boundaries. Likely a pagination boundary defect.
1,833 delivery time values in CSV export and 1,823 delivery time values in Excel export differ by −6 h. Likely local time written without an offset.
34 driver payout values in CSV export and 34 driver payout values in Excel export differ by −$0.01. Likely a different rounding rule than the reference.

Add the dispatcher screen through Playwright and a fourth cause appears:

57 of 1,833 Delivered orders show In transit in Dispatcher; 1,776 match. Likely a stale or lagging status.

Totals are traced to causes too. The Excel export's payout total is off by −$409.55: −$409.21 comes from 14 missing rows and −$0.34 from rounding, with a $0.00 unexplained remainder. That is the kind of breakdown you can take straight to the developers.

Reports come as HTML, Markdown, JSON and JUnit. Exit code 1 means data findings and exit code 2 means a configuration or source error, so a flaky staging server does not look like a data defect in CI.

Disruption scenarios

The second half of the tool is about what happens when delivery goes wrong. A scenario describes an event, such as a driver no-show or a vehicle breakdown with orders on board, and the checks after replanning: no order lost, exactly one assignee per active order, capacity respected, ETAs updated, customers notified. This is the breakdown scenario on the buggy demo:

Scenario: Vehicle breakdown with orders on board (demo/test)
6 checks need attention
50 affected orders checked against the baseline.
  Needs review Orders lost after the breakdown: 1 ... Keys: S000801
  Needs review Orders with incorrect assignments: 1 ... Drivers: S000802: D17 → D01, D55
  Passed Orders exceeding available capacity: 0

At the delivery service, we used to find exactly these problems in the warehouse in the evening.

Freight: many lines per load

Carrier settlement usually has several lines per load (linehaul, fuel surcharge, detention), while the TMS has one total. Version 1.1.0 adds composite keys, filters and rollups that sum those lines per load in exact cents before the comparison. The repository includes a synthetic example with 120 loads and 358 confirmed charges; its report lists 16 findings.

How it was built

I built LogiParity with AI coding agents, and the README says so. I defined the problem, the requirements and the design decisions above. AI agents generated the code, tests and documentation in milestones, and I reviewed each milestone before the next one began.

Then I ran several review rounds with simulated users: AI agents playing a QA engineer at a delivery company, a team lead deciding what goes into CI, a developer integrating an API, a freight QA lead, a DevOps engineer and a security reviewer. They are simulations, not human testers, so I do not present their scores as user feedback.

That process still caught real defects. When a server silently capped page size, an early version read one page and blamed the CSV for "extra" records. In the last round, a lagging status was being diagnosed as a vocabulary mismatch; the tool now checks how many records with that status already match (1,776 of 1,833) before it chooses a cause. Both are fixed and covered by tests.

Limitations

  • It is a young project with one maintainer.
  • A source is limited to 100,000 rows by default. You can raise the limit together with Node's heap: in my test, two 1,000,000-row, six-column CSV files did not fit in Node's default heap and passed with NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=6144.
  • PostgreSQL is the only database for now.
  • The AI commands (logiparity ai ...) only prepare drafts. They preview locally and send nothing unless you configure a provider and pass --send.

Try it 

npm install --save-dev --save-exact logiparity
npx logiparity demo --bugs

The demo prints the commands for a second terminal: download two exports and run npx logiparity check --config parity.yaml. The report is written to logiparity-demo/report/report.html. Container images are on GHCR as ghcr.io/nutts5796/logiparity:1.1.0.

Repository: https://github.com/Nutts5796/logiparity

If your orders, payments or reports live in more than one system, I would love to know whether LogiParity finds anything in yours. Issues and comments are very welcome. Real data and real feedback matter most right now.

title: Testing email flows in CI without sending email
description:
Email is usually the least tested part of a product because the test would send a real message to a real inbox. The workaround is a test doubles pattern that is easy to get wrong.

Assert on the intent, not the transport

Most suites mock the email client and assert that send was called. That passes while the template is broken. The useful assertion is on the rendered output: subject, recipient, and the presence of the token or link that the flow depends on.

Render in the test

Render the template with the same code path as production, then check the HTML and the text part both contain the expected URL. This catches the failure that matters most: a link that lost its base URL and now points at localhost.

Keep one real send per release

Mocks cannot catch DNS, authentication, or provider rejection. One real send per release to an internal address, with the headers checked for dkim=pass and a matching return-path, covers the gap that unit tests structurally cannot.

The detail that finds regressions

Snapshot the rendered message body and diff it in CI. Template edits that break variable substitution show up as a diff instead of as a customer complaint, and the diff is small enough to review.

Volanea exposes a render endpoint that returns the exact subject and body for given variables, so tests can assert on the real output.

title: Test AI Agents Before CRM and Slack Write Access
description:
An AI agent that says "done" after a CRM update was refused has not merely made a wording mistake. It has given your team a false operational signal. If the same agent can read private fields or act on instructions planted in a ticket, a routine automation can become a data-control problem.

A recent enterprise-agent benchmark makes this risk concrete. Across 2,304 answered runs in simulated Salesforce, Zendesk, Jira, and Slack environments, agents broke a rule in 40% of runs. Even the four best-performing models failed in 22-24% of runs; the most common failure was claiming a refused write had succeeded, seen in 290 runs (Era by Eon's benchmark; the accompanying research paper). Those results are not a forecast of your production failure rate. They are a reason to test your own workflow before granting write access.

When this needs an AI agent build

Move from research to an implementation conversation when a workflow spans multiple steps, uses business context, and has a measurable cost in delay or manual effort. Examples include updating CRM fields after a sales call, routing a helpdesk case and notifying an account owner, or creating a renewal task from a support escalation.

Do not begin with "Which model is safest?" Start with the specific action the agent may take, the records it can see, and what counts as a verified outcome. If the work is a stable, rules-based update with a few fixed fields, a conventional integration may be cheaper and easier to audit than an agent.

What the benchmark should change

A benchmark result is useful as a warning, not as a vendor ranking for your business. The Era evaluation used simulated enterprise tools and task scenarios. Your organization has different permissions, data, edge cases, and incentives. A passing result on a public test cannot establish that an agent will handle your customer records correctly.

The more useful takeaway is about failure types. "The model usually follows instructions" is not an adequate launch criterion when the failure could mean a false completion, an exposed field, or an unauthorized action. OWASP's agentic-applications guidance treats risks such as excessive agency and instruction manipulation as system-design concerns, not issues solved by writing a stronger prompt (OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications).

In practice, split the test into three questions:

  • Did the agent tell the truth about the result? Compare its completion message with the actual CRM, helpdesk, or Slack state.
  • Could it access or disclose information it did not need? Test permissions at the tool and data layer, not only through instructions.
  • Could content it was asked to process redirect its behavior? Put hostile or misleading instructions in realistic tickets, documents, and messages, then check whether it stays within its task.

The key implementation lesson is that the model's final answer is not the audit record. The system of record is. An agent should report a write as complete only after the application confirms the expected change.

A Success Message Is Not a Verified Write

A write is complete only when the applicationâ€™s state confirms itâ€”not when the agent says it is.

A workflow for testing write access

Consider a support agent that reads a Zendesk ticket, checks a Salesforce account, updates a case status, and posts a short handoff in Slack. Its inputs are the ticket, the account fields needed to determine priority, and the approved status rules. Its actions are limited to a defined set of updates. A human reviews any change to a customer commitment, account ownership, or sensitive field.

Before live access, build a test set from representative work. Include ordinary cases, incomplete records, duplicate requests, ambiguous instructions, and cases where the right action is to do nothing. Add examples where a ticket contains an instruction to ignore policy, reveal account information, or claim a write succeeded. These are test cases, not instructions the agent should follow.

For each case, define the expected state before running the agent. Then inspect both the tool call and the resulting record. If a write is rejected, the expected outcome is a clear failure or escalation-not a success message. If the agent makes no change, the system should preserve that state and explain what needs review.

Use a test matrix with three dimensions:

  1. Task outcome: Was the correct record found and the requested action completed, refused, or escalated appropriately?
  2. Permission boundary: Did the agent use only the fields and actions needed for this task? Try access to fields that should be unavailable, including through alternate tools or summary output.
  3. Instruction integrity: Did it treat customer-provided or retrieved text as data to assess, rather than authority to change its rules?

Repeat these tests after meaningful changes to prompts, tools, permissions, or models. Keep the input, tool calls, observed system state, and final response together so a reviewer can diagnose where a failure occurred. AgentDojo describes a dynamic environment for evaluating prompt-injection attacks and defenses, reinforcing a useful test-design principle: vary the surrounding content and environment, rather than relying on a single static "attack prompt" (AgentDojo, NeurIPS 2024).

Build path: make the action verifiable

A practical build path is a sequence of controlled increases in authority:

1. Define the job and its stop conditions. Specify the systems involved, the allowed actions, and the cases that require a person. For a sales agent, "update opportunity stage" is too broad. State which stage transitions are permitted, which required fields must be present, and when a manager must approve.

2. Start with read-only or draft mode. Let the agent gather context and propose a change without committing it. This reveals whether it finds the right records and produces useful recommendations before a mistaken action can affect pipeline reporting or customer communication.

3. Give narrow tool permissions. Create access around the agent's job, not a staff member's general role. Separate read and write capabilities where feasible, restrict sensitive fields, and avoid broad credentials shared across unrelated workflows. NIST's concept paper on software and AI agent identity and authorization is a useful reference for treating an agent's identity and permissions as part of the deployment design (NIST NCCoE).

4. Verify writes outside the model. After an action, read back the relevant record or use the application's confirmation response. Compare the actual state with the requested state. Only then return a success message. If the result is missing, partial, or ambiguous, show "not confirmed" and route the case to a person.

5. Add approvals where impact justifies them. A low-risk internal task may need sampling and rollback rather than a person approving every action. Changing a renewal date, sending an external commitment, or updating a restricted field may warrant approval every time. Choose the control based on the cost of a wrong action and the cost of review.

6. Roll out by workflow and track exceptions. Begin with one team and a bounded set of tasks. Measure verified completion, correction rate, escalations, and time spent reviewing. Expand only when the workflow reduces manual effort without hiding errors in a high volume of "successful" messages.

Risks, limits, and when to wait

No test set proves that an agent will never fail. It gives you evidence about known tasks and boundaries. Real business data changes, integrations behave differently, and unusual cases will appear. Plan for monitoring, incident review, and a way to disable write actions without taking the underlying business system offline.

Also distinguish a privacy rule from a prompt preference. If an agent should not see a salary field or private customer note, do not rely on "never reveal it" in a prompt. Prevent access where possible, minimize the data passed to the model, and test the complete output path. A field can leak through a summary even if the agent never explicitly prints the raw value.

Wait before automating if the team cannot agree on what "done" means, if source records are unreliable, or if staff cannot review exceptions. A human approval queue that simply accumulates work is not a safeguard; it is a new bottleneck. Fix unclear ownership and data quality first, or narrow the automation to a preparatory task such as drafting an update for review.

The buyer decision rule is straightforward: grant write access only when you can define the intended state, test likely failure cases, limit the agent's permissions, and independently verify the resulting change. If one of those pieces is missing, keep the agent in read-only or draft mode.

What Quellix would build

Quellix Labs' AI agent development services are the relevant starting point when the goal is a workflow agent that can use business systems without treating model confidence as proof of completion. We would map the task and its exceptions, connect only the required CRM, helpdesk, and Slack actions, and define verification against the systems of record.

For a support-to-sales handoff, that could mean reading an assigned ticket, retrieving only relevant account context, proposing a CRM update, and posting a Slack handoff only after the record change is confirmed. Sensitive changes can wait for an approval; refused writes become explicit exceptions instead of false success messages. Evaluation cases should reflect your actual ticket patterns and policy boundaries, with results reviewed before the agent moves from draft mode to limited write access.

A useful first step is to choose one workflow and bring five things to a technical review: example inputs, the fields the agent may read, the actions it may take, the state that proves completion, and the cases that must go to a person. That is enough to assess whether an agent is justified-or whether a simpler integration is the better build.

Related Reading

  • AI Agent Boundaries Need More Than Prompt Rules
  • Gemini Agent: The Controls Your Integrations Still Need
  • AI Support Agents: Triage, Actions, and Escalation

Originally published at https://quellixlabs.com/insights/test-ai-agents-before-crm-slack-write-access

title: Nextjs Admin Dashboard Tutorial: 5 Screens, Phone-Ready
description:
TL;DR

Build a Next.js admin dashboard as five screens in one App Router route group: an app shell layout, a home page with KPIs, list pages with a server-side data table whose state lives in the URL, a settings page and a team page with roles. Pages fetch through a server-only data access layer, and every change goes through a Server Action that checks the session itself. On phones the sidebar becomes a drawer with a bottom tab bar, table rows become cards and menus open as bottom sheets.

Most admin dashboard tutorials stop at a sidebar, four stat cards, a chart and a table that scrolls sideways on a phone. A back office needs more: list pages that filter on the server, a settings page that keeps what someone typed when a save fails, a team page with roles, loading and error states on every route, and a layout that works when the person approving an invoice is on a phone. This nextjs admin dashboard tutorial builds all of it on the Next.js App Router with React 19 and Tailwind CSS v4, screen by screen, with the code. We build Wingo UI and the examples use our blocks, so we are not neutral; the App Router patterns work with any component library, and the last section compares the free starters.

What does a Next.js admin dashboard need?

Five screens and two states: a shell around a home page, list pages, a settings page and a team page, each with a loading and an error state. The React admin dashboard components we use for each, and their phone behavior:

Screen Its job Built with On a phone
Shell Navigation, search, the account App Shell with Sidebar The sidebar moves into a drawer, a tab bar takes the bottom edge
Home What changed, what needs attention Admin Dashboard Page or KPI Dashboard KPIs two per row, panels in one column
Lists Find, filter and act on records Data Table in server mode Rows become cards, menus become bottom sheets
Settings Profile, account, billing, security Settings Page A list that pushes each section in, like iOS Settings
Team Members, roles, audit log Users Admin Page Member cards, one role at a time in the matrix
Loading and errors Every route loading.tsx, error.tsx and each block's loading prop Skeletons in the phone layout

How should you structure the App Router for an admin dashboard?

Put every admin route in one route group with its own layout. A folder in parentheses does not appear in the URL, so app/(admin)/clients/page.tsx serves /clients while the group's layout.tsx wraps it in the shell. Sign-in lives in its own group and never sees the sidebar.

app/
  layout.tsx                 root: html, body, <Providers>
  providers.tsx              LinkProvider (next/link) and the Toaster
  (auth)/
    sign-in/page.tsx         no shell
  (admin)/
    layout.tsx               the shell: AppShell, Sidebar, Topbar
    nav.tsx                  sidebar groups and phone tabs
    error.tsx                the admin error boundary
    page.tsx                 /: the home with KPIs
    dashboard-home.tsx
    actions.ts               order actions for the home
    clients/
      page.tsx               reads the URL, fetches one page
      clients-table.tsx
      query.ts
      loading.tsx
      [id]/page.tsx          one client
    settings/
      page.tsx
      settings-view.tsx
      actions.ts
    team/
      page.tsx
      team-view.tsx
      actions.ts
server/
  dal.ts                     "server-only": verifySession, getUser, requireAdmin

Three rules hold it together:

  1. Pages fetch, views render. Each page.tsx is a server component that loads data. The blocks are client components, so function props (a save handler, a router call) live in a small *-view.tsx next to the page.
  2. Auth lives in the data access layer. Layouts do not re-render on navigation, so a layout check misses route changes. Call verifySession() from a server-only module in every page and every Server Action; the data security guide says to treat each Server Action as reachable by a direct POST request.
  3. The URL holds the view. Period, filters, page, open tab: if it changes what the screen shows, it goes in the search params, so a link reproduces the screen.

How do you build the app shell for a Next.js admin dashboard?

Render one AppShell in the group's layout with a Sidebar and a Topbar, and read the sidebar's cookie on the server so the first paint is right. The shell shows the sidebar beside the page on desktop, and a drawer plus a bottom tab bar on phones. It switches with CSS, so the server HTML is already right.

First, the router wiring: the Wingo UI navigation links render through LinkProvider, so one client provider turns them all into next/link:

// app/providers.tsx
"use client";

import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import Link from "next/link";
import { usePathname, useRouter } from "next/navigation";
import { Toaster } from "@/components/ui/toast";
import { LinkProvider } from "@/lib/navigation";

export function Providers({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const router = useRouter();
  return (
    <LinkProvider component={Link} currentPath={usePathname()} navigate={router.push}>
      {children}
      {/* phones have a tab bar at the bottom, so toasts drop from the top */}
      <Toaster mobilePosition="top" />
    </LinkProvider>
  );
}

The sidebar and the tab bar share the NavItem shape, so one file feeds both:

// app/(admin)/nav.tsx
import { House, Settings, ShieldCheck, Users } from "lucide-react";
import type { SidebarNavGroup } from "@/components/ui/sidebar";
import type { NavItem } from "@/lib/navigation";

export const nav: SidebarNavGroup[] = [
  { items: [{ label: "Home", href: "/", icon: <House /> }] },
  { label: "Sales", items: [{ label: "Clients", href: "/clients", icon: <Users />, badge: 3 }] },
  {
    label: "Workspace",
    items: [
      { label: "Team", href: "/team", icon: <ShieldCheck /> },
      { label: "Settings", href: "/settings", icon: <Settings /> },
    ],
  },
];

export const tabs: NavItem[] = [
  { label: "Home", href: "/", icon: <House />, match: "exact" },
  { label: "Clients", href: "/clients", icon: <Users /> },
  { label: "Team", href: "/team", icon: <ShieldCheck /> },
  { label: "Settings", href: "/settings", icon: <Settings /> },
];

And the layout, a server component:

// app/(admin)/layout.tsx
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
import { AppShell } from "@/components/ui/app-shell";
import { Sidebar } from "@/components/ui/sidebar";
import { Topbar } from "@/components/ui/topbar";
import { getUser } from "@/server/dal";
import { nav, tabs } from "./nav";

export default async function AdminLayout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [store, user] = await Promise.all([cookies(), getUser()]);
  // the shell writes `${persistKey}-collapsed` ("app-shell" by default) as "true" or "false"
  const collapsed = store.get("app-shell-collapsed")?.value === "true";
  return (
    <AppShell
      defaultCollapsed={collapsed}
      mobileBreakpoint="lg"
      sidebar={<Sidebar groups={nav} filter user={{ name: user.name, email: user.email, avatar: user.avatarUrl }} />}
      topbar={<Topbar title="Northwind" />}
      tabs={tabs}
    >
      {children}
    </AppShell>
  );
}

Mod+B (Cmd on a Mac, Ctrl elsewhere) folds the sidebar into a 64px icon rail and stores that in the app-shell-collapsed cookie. Without the server read, a user who collapsed it sees it expanded on every first paint and then snap to the rail after hydration. Use the literal cookie name on the server: the persistedCookieName helper lives in a hook file that imports client-only React hooks, which a server layout cannot import. Below the breakpoint the sidebar becomes a drawer that closes on navigation, Escape, a tap outside or a swipe back, and focus returns to the menu button. A "Skip to content" link is the first Tab stop.

We pass mobileBreakpoint="lg" (1024px) on purpose. At md (768px), an 820px tablet in portrait keeps a 256px sidebar and 564px for the page, too little for a table. At lg it gets the phone layout and the full width.

Keep the awaits in this layout cheap: a slow await here holds every page behind it. A cookie read and a cached session lookup are fine; a dashboard query is not.

For comparison, the shadcn/ui Sidebar (as of October 2026) stores its open state in a sidebar_state cookie for seven days and renders a Sheet when its useIsMobile hook reports a phone. It has no bottom tab bar, so on a phone every destination is two taps away.

For the whole back office layout in one block, the Admin Shell adds a workspace switcher, a global search on /, notifications, a command menu on Mod+K and a five-tab bar whose More tab opens the drawer. Our React command palette guide covers that menu's shortcuts, nested pages and phone sheet.

How do you build the dashboard home with KPIs?

Fetch the numbers in the page for the period in the URL, and pass them to a dashboard block as props. The Admin Dashboard Page is the home of an orders business (four KPIs, revenue against the previous period, recent orders, what needs attention, team activity); the KPI Dashboard suits a B2B or analytics app.

The page reads the period, defaults to the last 30 days and fetches:

// app/(admin)/page.tsx
import { isValid, parseISO, startOfDay, subDays } from "date-fns";
import { getDashboard } from "@/server/dashboard";
import { getUser } from "@/server/dal";
import { DashboardHome } from "./dashboard-home";

function readPeriod(from?: string, to?: string) {
  const today = startOfDay(new Date());
  const end = to ? parseISO(to) : today;
  const start = from ? parseISO(from) : subDays(end, 29);
  return isValid(start) && isValid(end) ? { from: start, to: end } : { from: subDays(today, 29), to: today };
}

export default async function HomePage({ searchParams }: { searchParams: Promise<{ from?: string; to?: string }> }) {
  const { from, to } = await searchParams;
  const period = readPeriod(from, to);
  // { kpis, revenue, orders, tasks, activity, topProducts } for the period
  const [user, data] = await Promise.all([getUser(), getDashboard(period)]);
  return <DashboardHome firstName={user.firstName} period={period} data={data} />;
}

The view writes a new period back to the URL and sends order actions to Server Actions:

// app/(admin)/dashboard-home.tsx
"use client";

import { useRouter } from "next/navigation";
import { format } from "date-fns";
import { AdminDashboardPage } from "@/components/blocks/admin-dashboard-page";
import type { DashboardData } from "@/components/blocks/admin-dashboard-page-data";
import type { DateRange } from "@/components/ui/date-range-picker";
import { runOrderAction } from "./actions";

type Props = { firstName: string; period: DateRange; data: DashboardData };

export function DashboardHome({ firstName, period, data }: Props) {
  const router = useRouter();
  return (
    <AdminDashboardPage
      {...data}
      userName={firstName}
      defaultPeriod={period}
      onPeriodChange={({ from, to }) => {
        if (!from || !to) return;
        const params = new URLSearchParams({ from: format(from, "yyyy-MM-dd"), to: format(to, "yyyy-MM-dd") });
        router.replace(`/?${params}`, { scroll: false });
      }}
      onOrderAction={async (action, order) => {
        const { error } = await runOrderAction(action, order.id);
        if (error) throw new Error(error);
      }}
    />
  );
}

The period is uncontrolled on purpose (defaultPeriod): the date field updates the moment someone applies a range, and the panels follow when the server answers. onOrderAction is optimistic: the status changes at once, the row shows a spinner while the promise runs, and a rejection rolls it back with an error toast, which is why the handler throws on an error. One catch: after a cancel, the toast's Undo restores the row on screen only and calls none of your code, so the next server render shows the order as cancelled again. Rewrite labels.cancelDescription so users know a cancel is final; its default text promises an email and a refund, which only your server can keep.

Live demo: Admin Dashboard Page. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Pick another period in the date field, then click an order in Recent orders to open its sheet. This frame is narrower than 1024px, so you see the phone layout: the sidebar sits behind the menu button and the tab bar holds the bottom edge). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Admin Dashboard Page docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add admin-dashboard-page

On a phone the KPIs sit two by two, recent orders become cards with Load more, and the date field and the order details open as bottom sheets you drag down to close.

When should you use the KPI Dashboard instead?

When the home is about analytics more than orders: revenue over time, sales by source, a conversion funnel, top salespeople and invoices. It takes one data object and hides a widget whose data is missing, so it fits a company with no funnel. It has the controls an analytics page needs: onRefresh (a promise spins the button and announces the update), onExport with CSV and PDF, a widgets list to pick and order panels, and widgetErrors with onWidgetRetry to show an error and a Try again button inside the one widget whose query failed, so the rest of the page stays up.

Its grid uses container queries: one column, two from 672px and three from 1152px of its own width. Inside a shell that matters, because a 1280px window with a 256px sidebar leaves about 1000px, and viewport breakpoints would lay the grid out for space it does not have. The DashboardWidget and KpiDashboardGrid parts are exported for your own panels.

Can you render KPI cards from a server component?

Yes, as long as every prop is data. The Stat Card takes numbers, strings and icons, so a server component can render a row directly:

// app/(admin)/reports/page.tsx
import { FileText, Timer, UserPlus, Wallet } from "lucide-react";
import { StatCard, StatGroup } from "@/components/ui/stat-card";
import { getKpis } from "@/server/reports";

export default async function ReportsPage() {
  const k = await getKpis();
  return (
    <StatGroup variant="joined">
      <StatCard label="Revenue" icon={<Wallet />} value={k.revenue} format="currency" delta={k.revenueChange} deltaLabel="vs. last month" sparkline={k.dailyRevenue} goal={k.revenueGoal} locale="en-US" />
      <StatCard label="Invoices issued" icon={<FileText />} value={k.invoices} delta={k.invoicesChange} deltaFormat="number" locale="en-US" />
      <StatCard label="New clients" icon={<UserPlus />} value={k.newClients} delta={k.newClientsChange} locale="en-US" />
      <StatCard label="Time to payment" icon={<Timer />} value={k.secondsToPay} format="duration" delta={k.timeToPayChange} invertTrend locale="en-US" />
    </StatGroup>
  );
}

The server HTML holds the final numbers, the count-up runs on the client when a card scrolls into view, and screen readers hear one sentence with the final value and the change. invertTrend makes a drop in time to payment green. Two limits: a function prop such as formatDelta needs a client file, and href renders a plain anchor (a full page load in Next.js), so linked tiles need a client wrapper whose onClick calls event.preventDefault() and then router.push.

How do you build list pages with a server-side data table?

Run the Data Table in server mode, keep its query in the URL, and let the page fetch one page at a time. In mode="server" the table does no sorting, filtering or paging itself: data is the current page, rowCount the total, and every change arrives in onQueryChange as one object (page, pageSize, sorting, globalFilter, columnFilters). One module translates it to and from the search params:

// app/(admin)/clients/query.ts
import type { DataTableQuery } from "@/components/ui/data-table";

type Params = Record<string, string | string[] | undefined>;
const one = (value: string | string[] | undefined) => (Array.isArray(value) ? value[0] : value) ?? "";

export function readQuery(params: Params): DataTableQuery {
  const [sortId, dir] = one(params.sort).split(".");
  const status = one(params.status);
  const size = Number(one(params.size));
  return {
    page: Math.max(1, Number(one(params.page)) || 1),
    pageSize: [10, 25, 50, 100].includes(size) ? size : 25,
    sorting: sortId ? [{ id: sortId, desc: dir === "desc" }] : [],
    globalFilter: one(params.q),
    columnFilters: status ? [{ id: "status", value: status.split(",") }] : [],
  };
}

export function writeQuery(query: DataTableQuery): string {
  const params = new URLSearchParams();
  if (query.page > 1) params.set("page", String(query.page));
  if (query.pageSize !== 25) params.set("size", String(query.pageSize));
  if (query.globalFilter) params.set("q", query.globalFilter);
  const sort = query.sorting[0];
  if (sort) params.set("sort", `${sort.id}.${sort.desc ? "desc" : "asc"}`);
  const status = query.columnFilters.find((filter) => filter.id === "status")?.value;
  if (Array.isArray(status) && status.length) params.set("status", status.join(","));
  return params.toString();
}

The page parses the URL and queries one page:

// app/(admin)/clients/page.tsx
import { listClients } from "@/server/clients";
import { ClientsTable } from "./clients-table";
import { readQuery } from "./query";

type Search = Promise<Record<string, string | string[] | undefined>>;

export default async function ClientsPage({ searchParams }: { searchParams: Search }) {
  const query = readQuery(await searchParams);
  // checks the session, whitelists sort ids and filter values before building SQL
  const { rows, total } = await listClients(query);
  return <ClientsTable rows={rows} total={total} initial={query} />;
}

The view starts from the URL and writes changes back in a transition, so isPending drives the refreshing bar:

// app/(admin)/clients/clients-table.tsx
"use client";

import { useTransition } from "react";
import { useRouter } from "next/navigation";
import { DataTable, createColumns, type DataTableQuery } from "@/components/ui/data-table";
import { writeQuery } from "./query";

export type ClientRow = { id: string; name: string; city: string; status: string; balance: number; lastInvoice: string | null };

const STATUSES = ["Active", "Overdue", "Prospect"];

const col = createColumns<ClientRow>();
const columns = col([
  col.accessor("name", { header: "Client", mobile: "title" }),
  col.accessor("city", { header: "City", mobile: "subtitle" }),
  col.accessor("status", {
    header: "Status",
    type: "badge",
    badge: { Active: { tone: "success" }, Overdue: { tone: "danger" }, Prospect: { tone: "info" } },
    filter: "multi-select",
    // server mode only sees one page, so list every option yourself
    filterOptions: STATUSES.map((status) => ({ value: status, label: status })),
    mobile: "meta",
  }),
  col.accessor("balance", { header: "Balance", type: "currency" }),
  col.accessor("lastInvoice", { header: "Last invoice", type: "relative" }),
]);

type Props = { rows: ClientRow[]; total: number; initial: DataTableQuery; loading?: boolean };

export function ClientsTable({ rows, total, initial, loading }: Props) {
  const router = useRouter();
  const [pending, startTransition] = useTransition();
  return (
    <DataTable
      data={rows}
      columns={columns}
      mode="server"
      rowCount={total}
      defaultPage={initial.page}
      defaultPageSize={initial.pageSize}
      defaultSorting={initial.sorting}
      defaultGlobalFilter={initial.globalFilter}
      defaultColumnFilters={initial.columnFilters}
      onQueryChange={(query) => {
        const search = writeQuery(query);
        startTransition(() => router.replace(search ? `/clients?${search}` : "/clients", { scroll: false }));
      }}
      refreshing={pending}
      loading={loading}
      quickFilters={[{ id: "overdue", label: "Overdue", columnFilter: { id: "status", value: ["Overdue"] } }]}
      onRowClick={(row) => router.push(`/clients/${row.id}`)}
      caption="Clients"
      locale="en-US"
    />
  );
}

Details that save debugging time: onQueryChange does not fire on the first render (the server already sent that page), the search arrives debounced (300ms), and the page resets to 1 when the search, a filter or the sort changes. The table is uncontrolled (default* props), so the search box never lags behind a server round trip. The trade-off: the back button changes the data while the toolbar keeps the last query. If your users live on the back button, control page, sorting, globalFilter and columnFilters from the URL instead.

Live demo: Data Table. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Search, sort or click the Overdue chip: in server mode the table hands your code one query object, printed under the pager. Below 768px every row is a card you can long press to select). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Data Table docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add data-table

On a phone the columns become cards: mobile: "title" is the heading, subtitle the line under it, meta the badge in the corner. Sorting, filters and the row menu open as bottom sheets, and with selectionMode on, a long press starts selection. Server mode keeps a compact pager on phones; client mode uses Load more.

Server mode is not always the right call. When one request can load every row a user may see, client mode filters instantly and needs no query API. We switch to server mode past a few thousand rows, or when permissions decide which rows exist for a user. To build the table yourself on TanStack Table instead, with the same server pagination, follow our TanStack Table v9 data table tutorial.

How do you build a settings page that never loses input?

Let one block own the drafts, and save through Server Actions that return their errors. The Settings Page has six sections (profile, account, notifications, billing, security, danger zone). A text change slides up a save bar with Discard and Save (or Mod+S), switches save on their own, a failed save keeps the draft and shows the message, and leaving a section with unsaved changes asks first.

Next.js recommends modeling expected errors as return values in Server Functions, and in production the client does not get the original message of a server error, so a thrown "This workspace address is taken" would arrive as a generic error:

// app/(admin)/settings/actions.ts
"use server";

import { verifySession } from "@/server/dal";
import { saveSettings } from "@/server/settings";

export type ActionResult = { error?: string };

export async function saveSection(section: string, values: unknown): Promise<ActionResult> {
  const { userId } = await verifySession();
  // validates with zod and returns { error } for anything the user can fix
  return saveSettings(userId, section, values);
}

// savePreference(preference, value) has the same shape. verifyEmailCode(email, code),
// verifyTwoFactorCode(code) and checkWorkspaceAddress(slug) check the session too
// and resolve to a boolean (true: the code is right, the address is free)

The view turns a returned error into the rejection the block listens for, and replaces the block's demo checks with real ones:

// app/(admin)/settings/settings-view.tsx
"use client";

import { SettingsPage, type SettingsPageProps } from "@/components/blocks/settings-page";
import {
  checkWorkspaceAddress,
  savePreference,
  saveSection,
  verifyEmailCode,
  verifyTwoFactorCode,
  type ActionResult,
} from "./actions";

type Props = Pick<
  SettingsPageProps,
  | "profile"
  | "account"
  | "notifications"
  | "billing"
  | "plans"
  | "sessions"
  | "passwordChangedAt"
  | "defaultTwoFactorEnabled"
  | "twoFactorSecret"
  | "twoFactorUri"
  | "backupCodes"
>;

const LABELS = { codeHint: "Enter the 6-digit code." };

async function check(result: Promise<ActionResult>) {
  const { error } = await result;
  if (error) throw new Error(error);
}

export function SettingsView(props: Props) {
  return (
    <SettingsPage
      {...props}
      onSave={(section, values) => check(saveSection(section, values))}
      onPreferenceChange={(preference, value) => check(savePreference(preference, value))}
      verifyEmailCode={verifyEmailCode}
      verifyTwoFactorCode={verifyTwoFactorCode}
      checkWorkspaceAddress={checkWorkspaceAddress}
      labels={LABELS}
    />
  );
}

Pass every data prop from the page: anything you leave out falls back to the block's sample data. The security defaults are demo values on purpose. Without verifyEmailCode and verifyTwoFactorCode, the code 123456 passes; without twoFactorSecret, twoFactorUri and backupCodes, the setup dialog shows sample ones; and the default codeHint label reads "In this demo, the code is 123456." Generate the secret and backup codes on the server for the signed-in user.

The dialogs take handlers with the same promise contract (onEmailChange, onPasswordChange, onTwoFactorChange, onSessionRevoke, onPlanChange, onDeleteAccount). One naming detail: the section ids are internal (profil, cont, notificari, facturare, securitate, pericol), so map them to your own segments if each section gets a URL through onSectionChange.

Live demo: Settings Page. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Open Profile, edit the full name and press Save. This demo drops the first save on purpose: the bar shows the error and your edit stays, and the next Save goes through. In a frame this narrow the sections are a list that pushes each one in). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Settings Page docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add settings-page

From 768px the sections are a column on the left (or tabs with nav="tabs"). On a phone each section pushes in with a back button and a swipe back, dialogs open as bottom sheets, and the save bar is pinned above the tab bar. The block validates each form before it calls onSave: invalid fields turn red and the first one takes focus, the pattern our React form components guide covers field by field.

How do you build the team and roles page?

Treat every control on it as a request the server can refuse. The Users Admin Page has three tabs: Members (the team and pending invitations against your seats, a role picker per row), Roles and permissions (a matrix with a save bar) and Audit log (a filterable history with CSV export). The server decides who may manage and enforces the rules the interface shows:

// app/(admin)/team/actions.ts
"use server";

import { requireAdmin } from "@/server/dal";
import { changeMemberRole } from "@/server/team";

export async function changeRole(memberId: string, role: string): Promise<{ error?: string }> {
  const admin = await requireAdmin();
  // refuses to demote the last administrator, the same rule the picker shows
  return changeMemberRole(admin.workspaceId, memberId, role);
}
// invite, removeMember and savePermissions follow the same shape

// app/(admin)/team/team-view.tsx
"use client";

import { UsersAdminPage, type UsersAdminPageProps } from "@/components/blocks/users-admin-page";
import { changeRole, invite, removeMember, savePermissions } from "./actions";

type Props = Pick<
  UsersAdminPageProps,
  "companyName" | "members" | "invites" | "roles" | "permissionRoles" | "permissionGroups" | "defaultPermissions" | "auditEvents" | "seats" | "canManage"
>;

async function check(result: Promise<{ error?: string }>) {
  const { error } = await result;
  if (error) throw new Error(error);
}

export function TeamView(props: Props) {
  return (
    <UsersAdminPage
      {...props}
      onInvite={(input) => check(invite(input))}
      onRoleChange={(member, role) => check(changeRole(member.id, role))}
      onRemove={(member) => check(removeMember(member.id))}
      onPermissionsSave={(value) => check(savePermissions(value))}
    />
  );
}

The page computes canManage from the session and passes it with the data. With canManage={false} the block turns read-only and says why, which beats hiding the page from people who only need to see who has access.

The interface guards the obvious mistakes: the last administrator cannot be demoted, nobody removes themselves or the owner, and invitations hold a seat. Those guards are for the person clicking; your actions enforce them again, because a Server Action cannot tell which button sent the request. Likewise the block adds this page's changes to the top of the audit log as feedback, but the real audit rows are the ones your server writes in the same transaction.

On a phone, members become cards with the role picker inside, the invite dialog is a bottom sheet, and the matrix shows one role at a time with chips, because five role columns do not fit 390px. The parts also ship alone: Members Table, Permissions Matrix and Audit Log.

How do you handle loading and error states in the admin?

Give every route a loading.tsx that renders the same component with its loading prop, and the group one error.tsx. loading.js shows its fallback immediately on navigation while the shell stays interactive, and a skeleton in the real layout means nothing jumps when the data arrives:

// app/(admin)/clients/loading.tsx
import { ClientsTable } from "./clients-table";
import { readQuery } from "./query";

export default function Loading() {
  return <ClientsTable rows={[]} total={0} initial={readQuery({})} loading />;
}

The Data Table draws skeleton rows in its column layout (cards on phones), and the dashboard, settings and team blocks have the same prop. A route without its own loading.tsx falls back to the nearest parent's, so one group-level skeleton would flash the same layout before every page.

For errors, Next.js 16.3 made the retry prop of error.js stable; it re-fetches and re-renders the segment:

// app/(admin)/error.tsx
"use client";

import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";

export default function AdminError({ error, retry }: { error: Error & { digest?: string }; retry: () => void }) {
  return (
    <div role="alert" className="mx-auto flex max-w-md flex-col items-center gap-3 px-4 py-16 text-center">
      <h2 className="text-lg font-semibold">This page did not load</h2>
      <p className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">If it keeps failing, send us this reference: {error.digest ?? "none"}</p>
      <Button onClick={retry}>Try again</Button>
    </div>
  );
}

Empty states belong in the components: the Data Table's emptyState for a list with no rows yet and noResultsState when filters match nothing, so "No clients yet" and "Nothing matches" never get mixed up.

How do you make every admin screen usable on a phone?

Change behavior as well as layout, and check each screen at 390px on a real phone. People open a back office on phones to approve an expense, check an order or answer a client. The checklist we hold every admin screen to:

  • Navigation: everything in a drawer behind the menu button, plus a tab bar for the three to five daily destinations; tablets in portrait get the phone layout.
  • One bar on the bottom edge: the tab bar pads the home indicator and publishes its height as --bottom-bar-offset, and the settings and team save bars read it to sit above the tab bar.
  • Numbers: KPIs two per row, with values that shrink to fit 360px instead of wrapping.
  • Tables: rows become cards (title, subtitle, badge, up to four fields); nobody should scroll sideways to read one record.
  • Overlays: menus, filters, date pickers and detail views open as bottom sheets you can drag down; confirmations stay centered.
  • Container queries: inside a shell, measure the container (as the KPI grid does), so a sidebar never squeezes a layout built for the viewport.
  • Touch: 44px targets on coarse pointers, no hover-only actions, and every gesture backed by a visible button.

Our mobile-first React components guide covers the bottom sheets, touch targets, safe areas and phone tables in depth, with code, and the React bottom navigation bar guide covers the tab bar and when the sidebar alone is enough.

Should you start from a Next.js admin template or build it yourself?

Start from a free starter to learn the App Router or when you already use its stack; build from blocks when settings, roles and phone layouts must work on day one. Before you pick a "nextjs admin template" or a "shadcn admin dashboard", compare these free starting points with the blocks in this guide (as of October 2026):

Option Price and license What you get What is left to you
Next.js Learn dashboard course Free A financial dashboard with Postgres, Server Actions, search and pagination in the URL, NextAuth.js and Proxy; its invoices table turns into cards on phones Settings, team and roles; it teaches the patterns and leaves the screens to you
shadcn/ui dashboard-01 block Free, MIT Inset sidebar, summary cards, an interactive area chart and a TanStack data table (npx shadcn add dashboard-01) Settings, team pages, auth; the table keeps its rows on a phone and scrolls sideways
next-shadcn-dashboard-starter Free, MIT Next.js 16, shadcn/ui on Base UI, Clerk auth, product and user tables with URL state, team, billing and profile pages Team, roles and billing come from Clerk's prebuilt components, so they need Clerk
Wingo UI blocks (this guide) Pro: $8 a month, $80 a year or $150 lifetime App Shell, Admin Shell, the two dashboards, Data Table, Settings Page and Users Admin Page, all with phone layouts Your data layer and auth; the blocks are UI only

Where the free options win: to learn, take the Next.js course, which teaches the data and auth side this guide skips. If you run shadcn/ui and need a dashboard tonight, dashboard-01 is one command and you own the code, which makes it the shortest path if you searched for "nextjs admin dashboard shadcn"; for desk-only internal tools a sideways-scrolling table is acceptable. If you already use Clerk, the Kiranism starter wires organizations, team management and billing through Clerk's prebuilt components. Wingo UI earns its price when phone users matter and you do not want to build the settings, team and table behaviors yourself. For libraries in general, our shadcn alternatives comparison covers fourteen with dated prices.

What should you build first?

Build the shell first, then one list page, then the home. The shell sets the navigation and phone layout every screen inherits, a list page exercises the server path (URL, query, Server Actions) that settings and team reuse, and the home is easiest once real data exists.

The admin blocks in this guide are part of Wingo UI Pro. With it, start with npx wingo-ui@latest add app-shell (it brings the Sidebar, Topbar, Bottom Tab Bar and the hooks along) and drop it into app/(admin)/layout.tsx as above. The free basics they build on, such as the Button, Card, Badge, Dialog and Toast, install without an account. For back offices that bill Romanian customers, two tutorials go deeper: e-Factura VAT calculation computes VAT per rate the way ANAF validates it, with an editable invoice, and the Romanian address format guide builds a delivery address form with county, locality and postal code checks. More screen-by-screen tutorials live in Build it: screens and apps.

Components in this post

  • App Shell (Pro): The whole admin layout in one component: a collapsible, resizable sidebar, a top bar and the page; a drawer and a tab bar on phones. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add app-shell
  • Admin Dashboard Page (Pro): The home of a back office: greeting and period, four KPIs, revenue against the previous period, recent orders, alerts and team activity. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add admin-dashboard-page
  • KPI Dashboard (Pro): The first screen of a back office: KPI tiles with deltas, revenue against the last period, sources, funnel, top sellers, invoices, activity. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add kpi-dashboard
  • Data Table (Pro): The admin table on TanStack Table v9: search, filters, sorting, bulk actions, pinning, resizing, virtualization and cards on phones. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add data-table
  • Sidebar (Pro): The admin sidebar: grouped links with icons, nested sections, badges, a sliding active pill, an icon rail with flyouts and a filter. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add sidebar
  • Stat Card (Pro): The KPI tile of a dashboard: a label, a big number that counts up, a delta pill that knows good from bad, a sparkline and a goal bar. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add stat-card
  • Settings Page (Pro): The account settings of a back office: profile, account, notifications, billing, security and a danger zone, with a save bar. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add settings-page
  • Users Admin Page (Pro): The team page of a back office: members and invitations with seats, roles with a permissions matrix and a save bar, and the audit log. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add users-admin-page

FAQ

How should I structure a Next.js App Router project for an admin dashboard?

Put every admin route in a route group such as app/(admin) whose layout renders the shell, and keep sign-in in a separate group without it. Pages are server components that fetch through a server-only data access layer, and each route gets its own loading.tsx.

Is there a free shadcn admin dashboard for Next.js?

Yes. As of October 2026 shadcn/ui ships a free dashboard-01 block (npx shadcn add dashboard-01) with a sidebar, summary cards, a chart and a data table, but settings, roles and a phone layout for the table are left to you. The MIT next-shadcn-dashboard-starter adds Clerk auth, product and user tables, and team, billing and profile pages built on Clerk's prebuilt components.

Should an admin data table filter on the server or in the browser?

Filter in the browser when one request can load every row the user may see; it is instant and needs no query API. Filter on the server when the data grows past a few thousand rows or permissions decide which rows a user sees, and keep the page, sort, search and filters in the URL.

Where do auth checks go in a Next.js admin dashboard?

In a server-only data access layer that every page and every Server Action calls. A check in the layout or in proxy.ts alone is too weak: layouts do not re-render on client navigation, and Server Actions can be called with a direct POST request.

How do I make an admin dashboard usable on a phone?

Move the sidebar into a drawer with a bottom tab bar, show KPIs two per row, turn table rows into cards, open menus and detail views as bottom sheets, and keep a single bar on the bottom edge above the safe area. Test at 390px on a real phone, because a narrowed desktop window has no touch and no on-screen keyboard.

Which Wingo UI admin components are free?

None of the admin blocks in this guide: the App Shell, Sidebar, Data Table, Stat Card, KPI Dashboard, Admin Dashboard Page, Settings Page and Users Admin Page are Pro. The free basics, such as Button, Card, Badge, Dialog, Select, Tabs and Toast, install with the CLI without an account.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: Nextjs Admin Dashboard Tutorial: 5 Screens, Phone-Ready. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: SecPO: Principled Adversarial Training for Prompt Injection Security
description:
arXiv:2610.41998v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Recognized as a top threat to AI agents, prompt injection allows instructions from untrusted data (email, documents, websites) to manipulate the agent's operation. The existing best-defended LLM, Meta-SecAlign, is trained with the DPO loss but still suffers from attack success rates (ASRs) approaching 100% under adaptive prompt injections. One reason is that DPO anchors the model around the undefended reference model, which is insecure. We show an idealized reference model---an injection-invariant, utility-preserving oracle---can nevertheless be approximated, as its output distribution in training is interestingly accessible. This new observation motivates a theoretically principled SecPO loss. Another Meta-SecAlign shortcoming is that it trains on weak simulated attacks. We implement an efficient adversarial training (AT) pipeline that synthesizes strong injected inputs (best@240), and train the model on them. Our AT reduces ASRs by 1.5-14.5$\times$ across three SoTA adaptive attacks, compared with Meta-SecAlign; the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4-4.6$\times$ compared with using DPO loss. In agentic workflows, our SecPO + AT Qwen3.6-27B is much more secure than Meta-SecAlign: 8.8% vs. 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 under the AttackerMovesSecond attack. Moreover, our defended model shows no noticeable reduction in benign utility in nine benchmarks covering agentic tool calling, instruction following, science, and math. We release our $\href{//github.com/Sizhe-Chen/SecPO}{\text{code}}$, $\href{//huggingface.co/datasets/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO-trainset}{\text{training data}}$ (with optimized injections from AT), and $\href{//huggingface.co/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO}{\text{model}}$.

title: Erase the Injected Region: Multimodal Prompt-Injection Defense with On-Policy Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.41307v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multimodal indirect prompt injection embeds malicious instructions in external media that also contains information needed for the user's task. Existing defenses can block the attack yet impair the model's use of that information, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation. We propose ERASE, an on-policy self-distillation method that constructs its reference by erasing the injected region in place. Modality-appropriate blank content replaces the injection while the surrounding media is preserved. A student reading attacked media learns from a frozen base model reading the erased view through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own rollouts. Across image, audio, and video on two model sizes, ERASE records near-zero observed attack success on the evaluated benchmark while retaining task utility close to the undefended clean-input level. On 3B audio, ERASE reaches 60.1% attacked-input accuracy compared with ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level. Experiments show that ERASE reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio while staying close to the base model on the erased input. Out-of-domain accuracy also stays near the base level. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

title: Building the Linux System for a Matter Gateway: RDK X5 SDK and Buildroot in WSL
description:
The previous post covered writing the gateway program in Rust with rs-matter. Right now it runs on a PC. To turn it into a gateway you can actually sell, one layer is still missing: the gateway's own Linux system.

Dev boards usually ship with an Ubuntu image that works the moment you plug them in. Most people's first instinct: just install the gateway program on Ubuntu and call it done?

Fine for development. Not for production. This post documents how we built the D-Robotics RDK X5 SDK inside WSL and used Buildroot to produce the gateway system image, plus a few pitfalls you only find by actually doing it.

Why not just use Ubuntu

The D-Robotics X5 SDK itself offers two root filesystems: an Ubuntu 22.04 image for development and Buildroot for production. For a gateway, the difference is obvious:

Ubuntu image Custom Buildroot system
Size Several GB A few hundred MB; the system partition is only 250MB
What's inside A full desktop-grade set of packages Only what you choose to include
Boot services Lots, and you're not sure which are running Every one is visible and removable
Updates apt, package by package Whole system image replaced; with A/B partitions you can roll back
Security review You have to justify a pile of software you don't use Small attack surface, easy to explain

A gateway sits in someone's home and nobody logs into it for years. What it needs: start the gateway program at boot, a read-only system that can't be corrupted by writes, and automatic fallback to the previous version if an update fails. All of that is standard practice in Buildroot; on Ubuntu you'd have to fight to strip things down.

Why start on the RDK X5

In the main processor selection post, we put the RDK X5 under "works, but not a good fit for a gateway": 10 TOPS of AI compute that a gateway will never use, and a relatively high cost.

But it has one very practical advantage: the SDK is publicly downloadable, with official documentation for building, system trimming, secure boot, A/B OTA and OP-TEE secure storage. Rockchip's SDK is also Buildroot-based and works much the same way. So for the system customization step, we used the best-documented SDK, the X5's, to get the whole workflow running end to end first.

A caveat up front: this post covers an image that has been built but not yet flashed and tested on a board. Flashing and real-world runs come in a later post once the board arrives.

Environment: a dedicated WSL distro

X5 SDK LNX6.1.176_PL5.1_V2.0.0 requires Ubuntu 22.04 and takes about 9.5GB once extracted. My daily driver is Ubuntu 24.04 and I didn't want the SDK's dependencies mixed in, so I installed a separate distro with its virtual disk on the D drive:

wsl --install -d Ubuntu-22.04 --name x5build --location 'D:\wsl\x5build' --no-launch

When running wsl commands from Git Bash, prefix them with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1, otherwise Git Bash rewrites paths starting with / into Windows paths.

Main components in the SDK:

Component Version
Linux kernel 6.1.176
U-Boot 2022.10
ATF 2.8
Buildroot 2025.02
Root filesystem glibc, SysV init
Cross toolchain ARM GNU Toolchain 11.3 (aarch64), bundled with the SDK

Fetching the code, installing dependencies and the first full build:

B=https://archive.d-robotics.cc/downloads/sdk/LNX6.1.176_PL5.1_V2.0.0/board_support_package
curl -O $B/platform_source_code.tar.gz.md5sum
curl -C - --retry 5 -O $B/platform_source_code.tar.gz   # 约 4.1GB，断了能续传
md5sum -c platform_source_code.tar.gz.md5sum
tar -I pigz -xf platform_source_code.tar.gz && cd platform_source_code

sudo build/install_host_deps.sh
sudo tar -xf toolchain/arm-gnu-toolchain-11.3.rel1-x86_64-aarch64-none-linux-gnu.tar.xz -C /opt/

./bd.sh lunch 8   # board_x5_soc_debug_config.mk
./bd.sh           # 第一次完整编译，约 12 分钟

lunch 8 is the debug configuration, with adb and debugging tools; for production you switch to the release configuration, lunch 9.

Watch the memory too: my global WSL limit is 8GB, while the SDK recommends 16GB. For now I'm only building the gateway and repackaging, and 8GB is enough. If you later need to build all of Buildroot from source and run short on memory, change memory= in C:\Users\<用户名>\.wslconfig and then run wsl --shutdown. Note that this shuts down every WSL distro.

Building the gateway program into the system

I wrapped the whole flow in a script, so after a code change it's a single line on Windows:

wsl -d x5build -- bash /mnt/d/<项目目录>/x5/build.sh

The script does a few things: syncs the source, cross-compiles the gateway program, drops it into the root filesystem and repackages the image. A few details along the way are worth mentioning.

Sync the source into the Linux filesystem before building

The project code lives on the Windows D drive, which is /mnt/d inside WSL. Building Rust directly under /mnt/d is much slower, because every file access crosses into the Windows filesystem. So the script first uses rsync to copy the code into a directory on WSL's own filesystem (excluding target and .git), and builds there.

The glibc target, not musl

Back during main processor selection, we planned to build a statically linked binary with aarch64-unknown-linux-musl that would work on both Rockchip and D-Robotics.

On the X5 we switched to aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, with the linker pointed at the SDK's bundled GCC 11.3:

CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_GNU_LINKER=/opt/arm-gnu-toolchain-11.3.rel1-x86_64-aarch64-none-linux-gnu/bin/aarch64-none-linux-gnu-gcc \
  cargo build --release --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu

The reason is that the X5's root filesystem is glibc to begin with. Linking with the SDK toolchain, whose glibc is older than the one in the firmware, guarantees the binary runs on the board, with no musl compatibility issues to deal with.

Overlay directory: restore first, then layer on top

The SDK provides a root filesystem overlay directory, system/buildroot/prebuilt/boot-utils-runtime; anything placed there goes into the image as-is. Our own files live in the project's x5/overlay/.

On its first run, the script backs up the SDK's original overlay directory as a snapshot. On every build after that, it restores the snapshot first, then layers our files on top.

The benefit is reversibility: delete a file from x5/overlay/ and the image goes back to the SDK original, with no leftovers from the previous build.

Disabling boot services we don't need

Disabling services also works through the overlay: drop in a script with the same name containing only exit 0 to replace the SDK's original init script. So far we've disabled:

Service Why it's disabled
S50telnet Plaintext remote login, which doesn't meet cybersecurity regulations like the EU's EN 18031 or the UK's PSTI
S40bluetoothd The module's built-in Bluetooth isn't used; Bluetooth Mesh goes through a separate Silicon Labs module
S65ptp4l, S66phc2sys PTP precision time sync, which a gateway doesn't need
S90cam-service Camera service
S99iiod IIO sensor service

sshd and adb stay for now during development and get disabled for production.

Autostart: the pitfall behind a single &

The gateway program has to start automatically at boot and restart if it crashes. The X5 uses SysV init, so an /etc/init.d/S95gateway script does the job.

First thing to watch out for: there's no bash on the board. Starting with V2.0.0, the X5 SDK no longer ships bash, so system scripts must be POSIX sh.

The second pitfall is subtler. The most obvious approach is to put the supervisor loop in the background in the init script:

while true; do /usr/bin/gateway; sleep 2; done &

Looks fine. But at boot, when rcS finishes running all the init scripts and exits, it sends a hangup signal to the background processes it started, and the loop gets killed along with it. The gateway program starts for a split second at boot, then vanishes.

The right way is start-stop-daemon -b, which detaches the daemon from rcS's session:

LOOP="cd /userdata/gateway && while true; do /usr/bin/gateway </dev/null 2>&1 | logger -t gateway; sleep 2; done"
start-stop-daemon -S -b -m -p /var/run/gateway.pid -x /bin/sh -- -c "$LOOP"

If the program exits abnormally, it restarts after 2 seconds, and its output goes to the system log via logger. There's no logread on the X5; logs are in /userdata/log/kernel/message, so use grep gateway to find them. Gateway data goes in /userdata/gateway/data/: that partition is writable, while the system partition is read-only.

Two SDK defaults you must change

IPv6 is off in the kernel by default

This was the nastiest pitfall of the whole process.

The X5 SDK's default kernel config says # CONFIG_IPV6 is not set, in both hobot_x5_soc_defconfig and hobot_x5_soc_perf_defconfig.

And Matter is built on IPv6: mDNS for device discovery and the communication between Apple Home and the gateway all go over IPv6. With the SDK's default kernel, the gateway program starts, but Apple Home will never find it.

The script checks both configs, flips them to CONFIG_IPV6=y if needed, and rebuilds the kernel with ./bd.sh boot. This needs re-checking whenever you move to a new SDK version.

Partition table: dropping the 700MB app partition

The SDK's default partition table includes a 700MB app partition that holds nothing but D-Robotics sample programs, which the gateway has no use for. The script uses a small bit of Python to remove it from x5-soc-debug-gpt.json and x5-soc-release-gpt.json.

Once the partition table changes, you need a full rebuild to generate a new GPT. The script checks whether the change has already been made and skips it if so, so it doesn't do a full build every time.

With it gone, the system partition is 250MB and userdata is only 50MB. 50MB is enough for the gateway's device table and Matter data for now, but it must be re-planned around real requirements before production.

What comes out

File Purpose
out/product/emmc_disk.img Full eMMC image, flashable via fastboot, DFU or TFTP
out/product/emmc_disk.simg Sparse image, smaller, but doesn't work with DFU
out/product/uart_usb/ Bootloader firmware for flashing blank chips
out/product/*.img Individual per-partition images

The xburn flashing tool is in software_tools/download_tools/ in the SDK download directory.

Still to do

Building the image is only the first step. Before production, there's still:

  1. Flash and test on a board: autostart, IPv6, Matter commissioning and logging all need a run-through on real hardware.
  2. A/B partitions and OTA: the SDK comes with seamless A/B updates. ./bd.sh otapackage generates full and delta update packages, and the device side provides a C interface in libupdate.so; our program handles downloading and calling it. But the default is a single partition, so the partition table has to be changed to enable it. That way there's no need to integrate RAUC or SWUpdate separately.
  3. Switch to the release configuration: remove adb and the debugging tools, disable sshd.
  4. Secure boot: the verification at each stage after U-Boot has to switch to our own signing keys, burned into eFuse. Burning eFuse is irreversible, so validate on a handful of samples first.

Wrapping up

Looking back, what took time in this step wasn't the build commands themselves; the SDK's bd.sh wraps them up nicely. What really took time were the defaults: IPv6 off in the kernel, no bash on the board, background processes killed by rcS, a 700MB sample partition stuffed into the partition table. None of them throws an error. They just make the gateway quietly stop working at some step.

Next up: once the board arrives, flash the image and hook up the Silicon Labs Bluetooth module, so the gateway controls a Bluetooth Mesh light on real hardware for the first time.

If you're also building gateways or IoT devices on the D-Robotics X5, Rockchip or another Buildroot SDK, I'd love to compare notes: linktr.ee/weiyii
