title: From One VM to a Three-Tier App, With an AI that Wouldn't Let Press Apply
description:
Last week I built infrastructure by clicking through consoles and running commands. This week I wrote it down as code, built it again, destroyed it, and built something bigger. Five assignments, two clouds, and one rule that mattered more than any of the code: a human reviews every change before it touches the account.

Here's how the week actually went, including the apply that failed halfway.

Part 1: One file, six resources

The first assignment was the smallest: an Azure Linux VM defined entirely in Terraform. A resource group, virtual network, subnet, public IP, network interface, and the VM, all in a single main.tf.

What struck me was how little I had to describe. The NIC points at the subnet, and the VM points at the NIC. Terraform works out the build order from those references, and terraform plan showed me exactly what would be created before anything existed. That preview is the safety net the portal never gave me.

Two habits started here and stayed all week:

  • The VM password lived in a variable marked sensitive, supplied through the environment, so it never appeared in the file or in a screenshot.
  • Every build ended with terraform destroy. Create, verify, destroy.

Part 2: The same ideas on AWS

The second assignment rebuilt the pattern on AWS: a custom VPC with a public and a private subnet, an internet gateway, a public route table, a security group, and an EC2 instance that installs Nginx at boot.

It also taught me about permissions. My IAM user was read-only from an earlier audit assignment, and Terraform needs to create things. A harmless dry run caught it before I wasted any time:

aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.99.0.0/16 --dry-run

UnauthorizedOperation meant missing permission. DryRunOperation ... would have succeeded meant I was good to go. I attached the EC2 policy and moved on.

Part 3: A React app that deploys itself

The third assignment used Azure custom_data (cloud-init) to turn an empty Ubuntu VM into a running React site: install Node and Nginx, clone the repository, build it, and serve the build folder.

Two details nearly tripped me up. A script saved with Windows line endings fails silently at boot, because the first line becomes #!/bin/bash\r. And a small VM can run out of memory during npm run build, so the script creates a swap file first. Neither shows up in a tutorial, and both would have cost me an evening.

Part 4: Modules, and an apply that half-worked

The fourth assignment split an AWS build into reusable modules: network, EC2, and RDS. The root file calls each module and passes outputs between them, so the database gets its subnets and security group from the network module without anything being copied by hand.

My first apply created twelve of thirteen resources and then failed on the database. RDS rejected my master password, because it forbids characters like /, @, ", and spaces. Terraform had recorded everything it had already built, so after fixing the password, the second apply created just the one missing resource. That was my first real lesson in why state matters.

Then I connected from the EC2 instance to the private database, imported the schema, and tested a cart action in the browser to see the matching row appear in RDS.

Part 5: The capstone, with Claude Code in the loop

The capstone was a production-style three-tier deployment of a Book Review app: a VPC across two Availability Zones with six subnets, a public load balancer, a web tier running Nginx and Next.js, an internal load balancer, a private Node.js API tier, and a Multi-AZ RDS MySQL database with a read replica. Sixty-three resources in the first apply.

The assignment's real subject was the workflow. I set up Claude Code with:

  • a CLAUDE.md holding the architecture, CIDR plan, security rules, and approval rules;
  • a Terraform engineer subagent that proposes a design, reads the current provider docs through the Terraform MCP server, and then builds one phase at a time;
  • a read-only reviewer subagent that checks each phase and reports PASS, WARN, or FAIL;
  • hooks that block auto-approved changes and format code after every edit.

Claude could validate and plan. Applying and destroying were reserved for me.

The review loop earned its keep. The reviewer caught a bootstrap script that could fail before Nginx was configured, missing validation on the admin SSH range, and a subtle risk I'd have walked into: with load balancer health checks and a manual deployment, the Auto Scaling group would eventually terminate my unhealthy instances and delete my hand-deployed work. I stretched the grace period and suspended the replacement process while I deployed.

The failure no review could catch

The first capstone apply failed on the read replica:

Creating read replicas for source instance with engine mysql where ManageMasterUserPassword is enabled is not supported.

Every plan, every review, and every doc lookup had passed. Only AWS knew that rule. I gave Claude the real error and we compared options: drop the replica (the assignment required one), or generate the password in Terraform with a write-only argument and store it in Secrets Manager, so it never lands in state or outputs. The plan showed the primary updating in place, and the second apply finished the replica.

It's a clean illustration of what the Terraform MCP server is and isn't. It serves documentation. It can't query my account, so it couldn't predict this.

I also said no to a recommendation. Claude suggested an instance refresh for the change, but nothing was deployed yet, so the refresh would have waited on replacements that couldn't become healthy. I replaced the two App instances myself with one command instead.

Deploying by hand, then proving it

User data only installed software, so I deployed the apps myself: the backend through a systemd service that fetches its database password from Secrets Manager at start, and the frontend built on each web instance. Both target groups went healthy, I registered a user, wrote a review, and then read both rows back from the private database. The credentials came from the instance's IAM role, so no password ever appeared in a terminal.

Then terraform destroy. A NAT gateway, two load balancers, and three database instances bill by the hour, and the most important command of the week was the last one.

What I'm taking away

  • State is the memory. A failed apply isn't a disaster, because Terraform resumes from what it recorded. Guard the state file, and never delete the project folder before you destroy.
  • AI is a fast engineer and a careful reviewer, but it can't see your live account. The best results came from a loop: plan, research, build, validate, review, then a human decides.
  • Keep secrets out of everything. Sensitive variables, write-only arguments, Secrets Manager, and a rule that nothing credential-shaped goes into user data or outputs.
  • Test each layer in order. Every deployment problem this week was solved by checking one hop at a time, not guessing.
  • Treat cost as part of the design. A single NAT gateway and a short-lived environment were deliberate tradeoffs, and I could explain every one of them.

P.S. This post is part of the DevOps Micro Internship (DMI) with Agentic AI, Cohort 3, by Pravin Mishra.
You can follow my graded progress throughout the cohort.

title: Jev is the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history
description:
Within 24 hours of launching on AI Gateway, Jev from TypeSafe AI reached more than twice as many paid teams as any previous model launch, making it the fastest-adopted model in gateway history.

Jev passed every other comparison model in its first twelve hours and continued to widen its lead for the rest of the day. By hour 24, nearly 13% of paid teams were using it. That's 2x the GPT-5.6 family and more than 6x Fable 5.1's share.

Jev’s launch shows how quickly a specialized model can find a place in production. Its first-day adoption was unmatched among recent launches; the next test is whether that early adoption lasts.

About Jev

Jev was introduced on September 15 as a probabilistic decision model designed to support structured decision-making within software. An application sends it context and a set of questions. Jev evaluates those questions in parallel and returns typed choices, scores, or true-or-false answers, along with probabilities.

Unlike the text produced by a general-purpose language model, Jev’s answers come in a format the code can use directly. Developers can use it to:

  • choose an agent’s next tool or subagent

  • decide whether a workflow should continue, retry, ask the user, or stop

  • score urgency or risk before taking an action

  • verify model outputs, enforce guardrails, or send uncertain cases for human review

In its own workflow evaluations, TypeSafe AI reports that Jev was up to 194 times faster and 445 times cheaper than language models.

See the September AI Gateway Production Index for more model usage data, or try Jev through AI Gateway and build with the AI SDK.

title: Node.js Marketing Consent API: Evidence per User During Support Login Migration
description:
Record marketing consent separately from login state, preserve its category-specific history, and check the current grant immediately before each send. For a customer support application migrating email-and-password authentication off a managed provider, the deciding constraint is continuity of consent evidence across the identity transition. A valid server-side session identifies the user; it does not establish permission to send marketing.

TL;DR: Move identities without turning session snapshots or sampled logs into the consent authority. Keep transactional and marketing categories distinct, retain evidence of grants and revocations, and make every marketing delivery consult the current category decision. For a GDPR-oriented implementation, the engineering mechanism and the policy governing evidence retention need separate review.

This decision record examines the evidence footprint of that migration. The useful optimization is a smaller diagnostic stream surrounding a complete consent history. Counting bytes cannot justify losing the record that explains why a message was permitted.

How should an API track marketing consent per user during migration?

The application lets support customers sign up and sign in with email and password. Its migration changes the authentication provider, while existing customers may still have active sessions and previously recorded marketing preferences. Those are separate concerns. A support password reset must remain possible after the same customer withdraws marketing permission; granting one category must not silently authorize another.

Preserve three invariants: an unambiguous relationship between the authenticated account and its consent records, an ordered history of category decisions, and a current decision checked at send time. Treat those as migration acceptance criteria, rather than assuming that a successful login proves the migration is complete. The historical record matters because a present-day denial cannot explain whether an earlier message had permission. Conversely, a past grant cannot authorize the next message after withdrawal.

History answers when.

Current state answers whether. The application needs both, even if their storage and access patterns differ. A grant history is evidence; an operational log saying that a worker ran is diagnostic context. Collapsing those records into one sampled stream makes their retention policies inseparable and encourages a particularly costly mistake: keeping verbose request bodies to compensate for missing structured evidence.

For this design, bind every authenticated action to the mapped account on the server. A user identifier supplied by a browser is not sufficient authorization to inspect or change another account's consent. OWASP's authentication guidance is a useful review reference for the surrounding login boundary, but the consent boundary requires its own acceptance tests and data review.

Decision: separate evidence from diagnostic volume

Choose a consent authority whose current decisions and history can remain meaningful after the managed authentication provider is removed. Record the category and the evidence needed to establish the grant, then preserve subsequent withdrawal history. Determine the exact evidence fields and retention policy before migration. Do not infer an undocumented provider schema or assume that a preference copied into user metadata constitutes a complete history.

An illustrative capacity model makes the distinction concrete. Suppose a support application has 40,000 accounts, 3 consent categories, and 2 delivery outcomes. Using account, category, and outcome as metric labels permits up to 240,000 label combinations before adding worker, region, or deployment labels. These are planning assumptions, not measured traffic. Removing the account dimension leaves 6 category-and-outcome combinations. Keep the account association in access-controlled evidence records, where it serves a specific purpose.

Count combinations first.

Retention has a similarly direct effect. At an assumed 80,000 diagnostic events per day and 300 bytes per event, a 14-day window contains 336,000,000 bytes of raw event payload. That calculation excludes indexes, replication, and storage overhead; it is a capacity estimate, not a bill. Keeping the same stream for 28 days doubles the raw payload. The evidence history needs a separately justified retention period, rather than inheriting either window because it happens to be the logging default.

Sampling belongs on the diagnostic side. Sampling 1 in 10 successful checks can help investigate normal behavior with less volume, but it cannot establish a complete history of consent changes or prove the disposition of every delivery. Preserve consent changes without sampling. Decide separately whether individual delivery-decision evidence is required, and retain that evidence explicitly if it is. Aggregate counters can describe volume without copying email addresses, session identifiers, authorization headers, or full request bodies into ordinary logs.

The trade-off is deliberate: less diagnostic detail means some investigations will have fewer examples. It does not have to mean less consent evidence. Consider a hypothetical account that grants marketing, signs in, withdraws marketing, and then receives a password reset. The evidence must distinguish those actions without treating the reset as renewed permission. A complete HTTP access log might show that four requests occurred yet omit the category decision that matters; conversely, a carefully scoped history can retain the relevant changes without retaining every diagnostic header. This is why diagnostic completeness and consent completeness need separate definitions in the migration review, separate retention decisions, and separate checks during rehearsal.

Keep less deliberately.

Compare the destination by the evidence it must preserve

The migration review should include Auth0, Firebase Authentication, and Supabase Auth, alongside a plain HTTP alternative. Their authentication documentation provides a starting point for evaluating account migration. It does not, by itself, establish that any candidate meets this application's category history and send-time decision requirements. The table separates a reasonable use case from the proof the migration team still needs.

Option Reason to retain it in the comparison Migration boundary to establish
Auth0 Consider it when retaining a managed identity boundary remains acceptable. Demonstrate how the target design preserves category history and maps accounts without relying on an old session preference. Moving to another managed provider changes the destination, while retaining that operating model.
Firebase Authentication Consider it when evaluating authentication as part of a Firebase application. Validate account mapping and the consent authority together. Selection around the wider application ecosystem still leaves consent history and delivery authorization as separate acceptance criteria.
Supabase Auth Consider it when evaluating the Supabase authentication ecosystem. Establish identity mapping, evidence retention, and decision ownership. The authentication component alone is insufficient evidence that the consent migration is complete.
Plain REST alternative An HTTP boundary fits a migration that should not introduce a provider SDK into the Node.js application. Validate the consent contract, historical evidence, and account authorization independently of the transport choice.

Infrai is a plain REST API with one key and one bill across 295 routes and 20 modules, including authentication and communications. Node.js can send HTTP requests without an SDK to install or a client library version to maintain. When support login and message delivery move together, a single API key replaces separate service-key handoffs, and consolidated billing gives the observability owner one invoice to reconcile for these backend calls. This breadth is a different advantage from HTTP transport; it matters when the migration includes adjacent backend services. A shared credential concentrates responsibility, so keep it on the trusted backend and review its access carefully. Public, self-describing discovery exposes request and response schemas without a key, allowing contract review before a worker receives credentials. Select this option when that shared boundary fits, while validating the consent contract and preserving historical evidence independently.

There is no universal winner here. A team seeking a different managed provider has a different constraint from a team requiring an independently owned consent authority. For this support system, selection should turn on whether the next marketing message observes withdrawal and whether earlier permission remains explainable after identity migration. Vendor familiarity is useful, but insufficient. The comparison deliberately makes no claim that an authentication product automatically supplies the required consent history.

Critical path: read the current category before delivery

Run the check from the trusted backend or delivery worker. The following curl request illustrates the read on that path; it does not send a message or create a grant. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the service's HTTPS API origin without a trailing slash or version path, INFRAI_API_KEY to its server credential, USER_ID to the mapped account identifier, and CONSENT_CATEGORY to the configured category. The identifier and category must be valid, URL-safe path segments.

curl --request GET \
  --url "${INFRAI_BASE_URL:?Set the HTTPS API origin}/v1/auth/consent/check/$USER_ID/$CONSENT_CATEGORY" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${INFRAI_API_KEY:?Set the server API key}" \
  --fail-with-body \
  --show-error \
  --retry 4 \
  --retry-max-time 60

The request uses an explicit method and bounded retries. Curl backs off for retryable responses, including HTTP 429, and honors Retry-After when supplied. The 4 retries and 60-second retry budget are example settings, not service limits. Because this request reads state, retries cannot duplicate a grant or withdrawal. Writes need a separate idempotency decision.

A successful HTTP response is not sufficient permission to send. Interpret the documented response schema and require an affirmative decision for the requested category. This command prints the response for contract inspection; it is not a complete delivery worker. A Node.js integration must implement the documented decision parsing and error handling before it can authorize delivery. Guessing a response field here would conceal the most consequential integration boundary.

Place the check after a queued marketing job becomes eligible for delivery, immediately before handing the message to the sender. A check performed when the campaign is queued leaves a withdrawal gap while the job waits. Reading consent from a session created yesterday has the same defect: session validity and marketing permission evolve on different timelines. If the check fails or its result is ambiguous, hold the marketing delivery for reevaluation. Do not reinterpret an unavailable decision as a grant.

There is still a failure boundary between a successful check and the actual handoff. A withdrawal that occurs during that interval cannot retract a message already handed to a sender. State that boundary accurately in the design review. Keep the interval narrow, and recheck when a delayed job attempts delivery again. Checking at send time makes withdrawal relevant to the next delivery decision, without pretending that a check and an external send form one atomic operation.

Rejected option: authorize marketing from a session snapshot

Reject a consent flag copied into the server-side session as the authority for marketing delivery. It describes an earlier decision. During migration, it also couples the lifetime of a marketing preference to the lifetime of an authentication record, making session cleanup appear to solve a consent problem that persists in queued work.

A snapshot still has a valid use: displaying a previously loaded preference while the settings page refreshes its authoritative state. That convenience must not authorize a send. Similarly, sampled request logs remain useful for diagnosing check failures; they cannot replace an unsampled grant and withdrawal history.

Before cutting over, rehearse the sequence that defines success: an account grants marketing, remains signed in, withdraws marketing, and then becomes eligible for a queued campaign message. The worker must decline that marketing delivery while a separately categorized support password reset remains possible. Also confirm that the account's earlier grant remains explainable after the old identity provider is removed. These are proposed acceptance criteria, not reported test results.

The migration is ready when identity mapping, current category decisions, and historical evidence survive together. Smaller diagnostic retention is compatible with that result. Losing the evidence is not.

References

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • Auth0 documentation: https://auth0.com/docs
  • Firebase Authentication documentation: https://firebase.google.com/docs/auth
  • Supabase Auth documentation: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth
  • GDPR Article 7, conditions for consent: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj
  • curl manual, retry behavior and error handling: https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html

title: October 22, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 22, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-7).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
573663408 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the ingress gateway to patch security vulnerabilities.
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
568535165 Skip main_task_wait_time and nio_task_wait_time metrics for the first 12 Prometheus scrapes during Message Processor startup warmup.
573602919 Fix generated OpenAPI specs' servers[] to carry the Apigee envgroup hostname instead of the backend target host.
562964081 The sgpUserIntentMatchingMode verdict-log field is now always present, including on dry-run policy records, and shows the mode used for the evaluation, including when sgpUserIntentMatching isn't set (CONSTRAINTS_AND_INTENT, or INTENT_ONLY when no policies match the tool call).
524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.
572025634 Responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact instead of returning a corrupted body.
549078690 If no SGP policy is attributed for a denial, a customer sees the generic fallback message. This fix short-circuits to show the rationale instead when no matched policy has a configured denial message.
492041991 VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken now set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables only from the LLM operation(s) that matched the request; they are no longer set from unmatched LLM operations or for requests that match no LLM operation.
567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.
567244615 Semantic Governance no longer evaluates a request or response with a field it cannot read when a tool call is involved. It records verdict ERROR naming the field, with status MODEL_ERROR. The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.
560272924 Added continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming support for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Model Armor policies now honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: with it set, Model Armor callouts bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic. Streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
158204922 VerifyJWT now rejects a JWT whose header contains "b64":false, with fault steps.jwt.InvalidToken, as RFC 7797 section 7 requires. Previously, such a token could be accepted if KnownHeaders listed b64, IgnoreCriticalHeaders was true, or the header had no crit.
158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.
158204922 VerifyJWS verifies RFC 7797 unencoded-payload JWS (b64:false), attached or detached. b64 in crit no longer needs a KnownHeaders entry. VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.
575439485 JavaCallout policies that run remotely (per-contract offload) can now pass every value type allowed by the GCP-2025-023 setVariable restriction between policies (collections, maps, arrays, primitive wrappers including Character, Date, BigDecimal, UUID, java.time, atomics, JDK enums, Optional), with their types preserved, instead of failing with steps.remotepolicy.NonSerializableVariable.
575439485 Remotely executed (per-contract offload) JavaCallout policies with continueOnError="true" now continue the flow when the callout faults, instead of returning HTTP 500.
567244901 In enforce mode, Semantic Governance now blocks a tool call when the governance check cannot be completed, instead of letting it through.
573622417 Fixed an issue where istio-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571679067 removes old version of ApigeeTelemetry CRD.
571378258 The Apigee Redis container is now built from the Valkey engine (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) at version 8.1.10. Wire protocol is unchanged (RESP2) and the redis-server/redis-cli binary names are preserved.

title: InfluxDB vs TDengine: MIT single-node or AGPL with clustering and tag-count prices
description:
InfluxDB and TDengine are both open-source time-series databases used for plant and sensor data, but the open-source deal and the pricing unit differ. InfluxDB 3 Core is permissively licensed (MIT or Apache-2.0) and single-node, with HA and clustering in the CPU-priced Enterprise edition. TDengine's open-source core is AGPL-3.0 and includes clustering; its commercial All-in-One adds industrial connectors and a data platform, priced by tag count and free up to 5,000 tags.

Every row below is taken from the vendors' own public pages.

Open-source license

  • InfluxDB 3 Core: MIT or Apache-2.0, at the user's choice. Core is a single node with no high availability; HA, read replicas, historical query capability and single-series indexing are Enterprise additions.
  • TDengine OSS: AGPL-3.0 (copyleft). The open-source edition is a full-featured database including clustering; Enterprise and Cloud are built on the same code base.

Commercial pricing (public pages, checked Oct/Nov 2026)

  • InfluxDB: Enterprise is custom-priced by CPU configuration (30-day trial). Cloud Dedicated is also custom-priced; Cloud Serverless is usage-based. There is also Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB.
  • TDengine All-in-One is priced by tag count: free to 5,000 tags (including small production use); 10,000 tags cost US$15,500/year or US$38,750 perpetual; high availability adds +30%. Cloud starts from US$970/month for 5,000 tags.

Plant-floor collection

  • InfluxDB collects via InfluxData's Telegraf agent (400+ plugins), including OPC UA and MQTT input plugins.
  • TDengine commercial plans include zero-code connectors for MQTT, Kafka, OPC and PI System, plus edge-to-cloud replication.

Querying and built-in processing

  • InfluxDB is built for fast recent-data queries (vendor docs cite under 10 ms for last-value queries) and ships an SQL editor in InfluxDB 3 Explorer, plus an embedded Python VM for plugins and triggers.
  • TDengine extends SQL for time series (interpolation, downsampling, time-weighted averages) and includes caching, stream processing, Kafka-like data subscription and the TDgpt AI agent.

Managed cloud and platforms

  • InfluxDB: Cloud Serverless, Cloud Dedicated, or Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB. Core runs on Linux, macOS and Docker.
  • TDengine Cloud runs on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud. Self-hosted packages cover Linux and Windows, plus Docker and Kubernetes.

Quick fit check

Pick InfluxDB if you want a permissive MIT/Apache license and a large Telegraf ecosystem, and you can live with a single node or pay for Enterprise HA — or you prefer usage-based cloud pricing or AWS-managed Timestream for InfluxDB.

Pick TDengine if you want clustering in the open-source edition and are comfortable with AGPL-3.0 obligations, or you want historian-style tag-count pricing with OPC, MQTT and PI System connectors in the box (free under 5,000 tags).

The full side-by-side table with every source link is on PlantWired: InfluxDB vs TDengine. Related: Canary Historian vs TDengine, Factry Historian vs InfluxDB, the TDengine profile, the InfluxDB profile, and Choosing a process historian.

Prices and licensing terms change, and our data comes from public vendor pages, so it surely has gaps. If you run either in production and something's wrong, tell us in the comments and we'll fix it.

PlantWired is a free, vendor-neutral map of factory software. A short weekly brief on new integrations is at plantwired.vercel.app/newsletter.

title: Marketplace Cohort Debugging: Capture and Resolve Node.js API Errors with Event Code
description:
Short answer: capture an API error as a small, typed incident record, then attach the experiment key, tenant cohort, request identifier, and trace context before you send it anywhere. Resolve it by comparing the same record across cohorts and by proving recovery with a later successful signal. A stack trace alone cannot reconstruct a marketplace rollout.

Here is the decision rule I use for a marketplace experiment: choose the event model that can answer “what did this tenant see, under which variant, and what happened next?” without joining five unrelated logs. The collector, dashboard, and alert channel are secondary. The join key is the product.

Option Incident reconstruction Operational cost Best fit
One error event with request context Fast for a single failing request Low Small services and early experiments
Error event plus trace and metric signals Strong across retries, dependencies, and cohorts Medium Marketplace rollouts with multiple services
Logs only Possible, but depends on exact field consistency Low at first, high during an incident Temporary diagnostics

My default is the middle row. Keep the error event useful on its own, then add standard trace context and low-cardinality metrics. That gives an operator a narrow path from a tenant-level failure to the request span, without turning every arbitrary tenant ID into a time-series label.

Start with the join key.

What does a marketplace API error need to prove?

An incident is a sequence, not a row in an error table. A buyer request enters the marketplace API, receives an experiment assignment, calls inventory or checkout, retries or fails, and may succeed after the assignment changes. The reconstruction needs those transitions in order.

The event should contain stable dimensions: service name, route template, deployment revision, experiment name, variant, tenant cohort, normalized error type, request ID, timestamps, duration, HTTP status, and a redacted dependency name. Do not put raw email addresses, authorization headers, payment details, or full request bodies into an error payload. Those fields make debugging riskier without making causality clearer.

There is a useful distinction here. tenantId is valuable for inspecting one incident, but it is usually a poor metric label because a marketplace can have many tenants. Record it on the event or trace. Aggregate metrics by cohort, experiment, route, and error class instead. OpenTelemetry describes metrics as measurements that are aggregated over time; that aggregation is exactly why high-cardinality identifiers belong elsewhere. See the metrics signal model in the References.

The same rule applies to error messages. “Inventory service timed out after 2000ms” is readable, but a changing item ID inside the message creates unstable groups. Store a normalized errorType such as DependencyTimeout and retain the short message as bounded detail. Grouping should be deterministic enough that the same failure does not become a new incident every time a request parameter changes.

How do you reconstruct the failure without guessing?

Start with one event schema. The schema below is deliberately boring. Boring schemas survive incident pressure.

Keep it boring.

type Cohort = "new-tenants" | "existing-tenants" | "high-volume";

type ApiErrorEvent = {
  occurredAt: string;
  service: "marketplace-api";
  route: string;
  requestId: string;
  traceId?: string;
  revision: string;
  experiment: string;
  variant: string;
  cohort: Cohort;
  errorType: "DependencyTimeout" | "UpstreamRejected" | "Unexpected";
  status: number;
  durationMs: number;
  dependency?: string;
  recoveredAt?: string;
};

The variant and cohort values are not interchangeable. A variant describes the treatment. A cohort describes the population receiving it. During a rollout, the same variant may behave differently for new tenants because their catalog state or request volume differs. Keeping both fields is what lets an operator separate treatment damage from population-specific behavior.

In Node.js, the error boundary should enrich the event once, at the point where the request still has its context. It should then hand the record to a generic transport. The transport can write to a self-hosted collector, a queue, or an internal endpoint; the application should not know which one.

type EventSink = (event: ApiErrorEvent) => Promise<void>;

type RequestContext = {
  requestId: string;
  traceId?: string;
  revision: string;
  experiment: string;
  variant: string;
  cohort: Cohort;
};

function classify(error: unknown): ApiErrorEvent["errorType"] {
  if (error instanceof Error && error.name === "TimeoutError") {
    return "DependencyTimeout";
  }
  if (error instanceof Error && error.name === "UpstreamRejectedError") {
    return "UpstreamRejected";
  }
  return "Unexpected";
}

async function captureApiError(
  error: unknown,
  context: RequestContext,
  sink: EventSink,
  startedAt: number,
): Promise<void> {
  const event: ApiErrorEvent = {
    occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    service: "marketplace-api",
    route: "/v1/errors/events/{error_group_id}",
    requestId: context.requestId,
    traceId: context.traceId,
    revision: context.revision,
    experiment: context.experiment,
    variant: context.variant,
    cohort: context.cohort,
    errorType: classify(error),
    status: 502,
    durationMs: Date.now() - startedAt,
    dependency: "inventory",
  };

  await sink(event);
}

The example makes one opinionated choice: route is a template, not a literal path. That keeps groups and metrics stable. It also makes the status code explicit rather than deriving an error category from a free-form message. In a real service, the boundary should map known failures to their actual response status instead of treating every exception as a bad gateway.

Do not block the customer response on a remote error collector. Put a bounded event on a local queue, apply a timeout, and count dropped telemetry separately. Telemetry loss is a visibility problem; it should not become a marketplace outage. The queue needs a size limit, a redaction step, and a shutdown policy so a process cannot retain unbounded failed requests.

Which signals make the cohort comparison trustworthy?

One error event tells you that a request failed. It does not tell you whether the experiment caused the change. For that, emit a counter and a latency measurement with dimensions that can be aggregated: experiment, variant, cohort, route, status class, and normalized error type. Keep tenant identity in the event and trace, where it can be inspected for a bounded sample.

The useful comparison is not “errors increased.” It is closer to this:

type CohortWindow = {
  experiment: string;
  variant: string;
  cohort: Cohort;
  route: string;
  requests: number;
  failedRequests: number;
  dependencyTimeouts: number;
  p95DurationMs: number;
};

function failureRate(window: CohortWindow): number {
  return window.requests === 0
    ? 0
    : window.failedRequests / window.requests;
}

function shouldPause(candidate: CohortWindow, baseline: CohortWindow): boolean {
  const candidateRate = failureRate(candidate);
  const baselineRate = failureRate(baseline);
  const relativeIncrease = baselineRate === 0
    ? candidateRate > 0
    : (candidateRate - baselineRate) / baselineRate;

  return relativeIncrease >= 0.25 ||
    candidate.dependencyTimeouts > baseline.dependencyTimeouts * 2;
}

Those thresholds are decision examples, not universal safety limits. Choose them from the experiment's traffic and harm model, and record the decision in the rollout policy. A 25% relative increase at two errors is not the same operational event as a 25% increase across 100,000 requests. Absolute counts, exposure, and time windows must travel with the comparison.

For reconstruction, preserve the trace identifier through the API boundary. W3C Trace Context defines the traceparent header format used to propagate trace identity between services. If a dependency call starts a new trace accidentally, the error record can still be found, but the causal chain is broken. That is the sort of small integration defect that costs more than adding another dashboard.

I also want a recovery signal. When the same request path succeeds after a failed attempt, associate the recovery with the request or trace where that is safe, and keep a separate success metric for the cohort. A retry that hides a dependency timeout is not the same as a clean request. Track both.

Where do common tracking choices stop helping?

Hosted error trackers and self-managed telemetry systems expose different boundaries. Sentry documents event capture, issue grouping, and tracing as separate concepts; that is useful when a team needs rich exception inspection but still needs a metric design for cohort rates. Rollbar documents occurrence grouping around item fingerprints and payload metadata; teams must choose those fields carefully or grouping will reflect changing request data. Bugsnag exposes error events and stability-oriented reporting, while cohort comparison still depends on the dimensions the application sends.

None of those boundaries removes the application design problem. A collector cannot infer that new-tenants is a population cohort, that variant-b is a treatment, or that two timeout messages represent one dependency failure. A platform can store, group, and query evidence. It cannot manufacture the missing causal fields.

That is why I measure time-to-first-call for the instrumentation itself. The first useful test should be a failed request in a local environment: does it produce one bounded event, with a stable group key, a trace identifier when available, and no credential material? If the answer requires a large configuration file or a custom adapter for every route, the design has already lost. Config bloat is an operational bug wearing a setup costume.

What should the resolution loop record?

Resolve the incident as a small experiment in reverse. First, identify the affected route, revision, variant, and cohort. Next, inspect representative traces, not just the aggregate rate. Then compare dependency timeout counts and duration against the control cohort for the same time window. Finally, record the intervention: pause exposure, roll back the revision, repair the dependency, or accept the signal as expected behavior.

The system should make that decision auditable. Store the event schema version, deployment revision, and experiment assignment at capture time. Keep raw payload retention short and aggregate metrics longer where policy permits. Redaction belongs before persistence, not in a dashboard query.

The runner-up approach is logs only. It can be the right choice for a tiny internal service, especially when a structured logger already carries request and trace fields. Its limitation is cross-cohort analysis: every consumer must agree on parsing, aggregation, and time windows. It becomes a poor fit when the marketplace needs a defensible treatment comparison. The more services join the incident, the more valuable a typed event and standard trace context become.

There is a second tradeoff. A hosted error tracker can reduce the time needed to inspect one exception, but it adds a service boundary, retention rules, and another event schema to govern. A self-managed collector gives more control over residency and routing, but it requires ownership of upgrades, storage, and on-call behavior. Neither option is universally better; pick hosted inspection for a small team with low integration surface, and self-managed telemetry when control and cross-service consistency outweigh setup time.

The final test is practical: can an engineer start from a cohort-level spike, open one failed request, follow its dependency edge, and see whether the same tenant later recovered? If not, add the missing field or propagation step before adding another alert. The useful tracking system is the one that shortens the path from a rate change to a defensible decision.

References

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/traces/
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/
  • https://nodejs.org/api/errors.html
  • https://docs.sentry.io/product/issues/
  • https://docs.rollbar.com/docs/grouping-occurrences
  • https://docs.bugsnag.com/product/errors/

title: GPU-Free Audio-to-Text Transcription API Architecture for Fintech Moderation Reports
description:
TL;DR: For a SaaS application that classifies fintech moderation reports before human review, the simplest GPU-free transcription design is an asynchronous, provider-neutral adapter. Persist the original audio and a job record, submit through one narrow interface, receive a transcript or a typed failure, and let moderation consume a versioned text artifact. Keep provider choice behind that boundary. It preserves portability and makes delivery failures visible instead of turning them into mysterious moderation gaps.

The important decision is not which transcription brand has the shortest integration guide. It is where the system owns the contract. Audio uploads, retries, webhook authentication, transcript quality, retention, and review escalation all outlive an individual API.

What must stay true when the provider changes?

I would record these invariants before writing an adapter:

  • The original audio is immutable and addressable by an internal job ID.
  • A report is never marked ready for moderation merely because submission succeeded.
  • Every transcript carries a source, schema version, language hint, and completion timestamp.
  • A timeout, rejected format, empty transcript, and provider outage are different states.
  • Human review remains the destination for low-confidence or incomplete text.

This separation matters in fintech. A clipped voice report can contain a disputed transaction, an account identifier, or a complaint about access. Losing the text silently is a workflow defect; showing an incomplete result as authoritative is a review defect. The adapter should make both states hard to confuse.

The portability boundary is small:

Boundary Application owns Adapter owns
Input job ID, audio reference, policy metadata request serialization
Processing state machine, retry policy, retention provider request and response mapping
Output transcript artifact and moderation handoff provider-specific fields and errors
Operations audit trail, metrics, escalation request correlation and raw response handling

A provider can be replaced without rewriting report classification, audit queries, or the reviewer queue. That is the useful form of portability: a stable internal contract, not a promise that every provider behaves identically.

Should an audio-to-text transcription API avoid GPU hosting?

The critical path should be boring. Boring is good here. The upload path records intent; a worker performs transcription; a separate step publishes text to moderation. The worker must be idempotent because a retry can happen after a network timeout even when the remote service accepted the request.

Here is the shape of the application-facing interface. The endpoint is deliberately pseudonymous; it keeps the integration testable and prevents the domain model from learning a vendor's nouns.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TranscriptionResult:
    status: Literal["completed", "retryable", "rejected"]
    text: str | None
    error_code: str | None
    provider_request_id: str | None


class TranscriptionAdapter:
    def submit(self, *, job_id: str, audio_url: str, language: str | None) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def fetch(self, *, remote_job_id: str) -> TranscriptionResult:
        raise NotImplementedError


def advance_transcription(job, adapter: TranscriptionAdapter) -> None:
    if job.status == "completed":
        return

    if job.remote_job_id is None:
        job.remote_job_id = adapter.submit(
            job_id=job.id,
            audio_url=job.audio_url,
            language=job.language,
        )
        job.status = "submitted"
        return

    result = adapter.fetch(remote_job_id=job.remote_job_id)
    if result.status == "completed" and result.text:
        job.save_transcript(text=result.text, provider_request_id=result.provider_request_id)
        job.status = "ready_for_moderation"
    elif result.status == "retryable":
        job.schedule_retry()
    else:
        job.status = "needs_human_review"

The exact SDK call belongs inside the adapter. The state transition belongs here. That distinction is where most of the long-term maintenance value sits.

One trap I initially underestimated was treating an empty successful response as a completed transcription. Later I found the safer rule: completion needs a non-empty artifact, while an empty artifact goes to a visible review state with the audio still attached. The system can tolerate a slow case. It cannot audit a missing one.

Which failure boundary should become a human-review boundary?

Do not collapse every exception into “retry.” Retrying a malformed file wastes capacity and delays a reviewer. Refusing to retry a transient timeout loses throughput. Use a small error taxonomy: invalid input, authentication or policy rejection, transient transport failure, provider processing failure, and contract mismatch. Only the transient categories should enter bounded retry with backoff. The trade-off is deliberate: cap a transient job at 3 attempts, then send it to human review with its last error instead of creating an invisible queue loop.

The job record should retain attempt count, last transition, correlation ID, and the reason for escalation. Retention rules should apply to raw audio, provider responses, and normalized text separately. Those artifacts have different operational value and different exposure risk.

Observability needs two views. The engineering view measures queue age, completion latency, retry rate, and adapter errors. The operations view measures how many reports reached moderation, how many became human-review cases, and how often text was empty or incomplete. A healthy API metric does not prove a healthy moderation workflow.

For tests, use a fake adapter that returns each typed result, then add contract tests against the chosen provider adapter. Keep audio fixtures short, synthetic, and representative of the accepted input rules. Test duplicate worker delivery explicitly. The idempotency test is worth more than a happy-path screenshot.

When is a local GPU actually the simpler choice?

A remote API is not automatically the simplest architecture. The limitation is data movement: a local runtime can be reasonable when data cannot leave a controlled environment, when predictable offline operation is a hard requirement, or when sustained volume justifies owning model serving. It adds model packaging, compute scheduling, capacity planning, upgrades, and quality evaluation to the team’s responsibilities.

For a SaaS team whose primary decision axis is provider portability, an adapter still helps even if the first implementation is local. Define the same submit/fetch/result contract and keep moderation independent of the runtime. Then a controlled local deployment and a hosted API are replaceable execution choices, not competing application designs.

That is the architecture decision record I would approve: asynchronous processing, explicit states, immutable source audio, a normalized transcript artifact, and a narrow adapter. It avoids GPU hosting without pretending transcription is a single synchronous call.

References

  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector

title: Agentic E2E Testing in CI: Auto-Healing & MCP Verification
description:
As AI coding assistants accelerate code generation, continuous integration testing has become the primary operational bottleneck. Integrating autonomous QA agents directly into CI loops using Model Context Protocol allows platforms to generate and repair end-to-end test flows alongside feature code.

However, unconstrained test self-healing presents a serious reliability risk. Silent runtime repairs that patch over broken user paths can easily mask genuine UI regressions. The optimal platform architecture uses runtime adaptation to unblock CI builds while emitting declarative YAML patches for mandatory developer code review.

Balancing autonomous test execution with explicit knowledge bases and parallel execution ensures high build velocity without sacrificing software quality.
