title: NDIS Funding Changes 2026: What Participants Need to Know
description:
The National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) is undergoing significant changes in 2026. These reforms are intended to improve the long-term sustainability of the scheme while changing how certain support budgets are calculated and managed.

For participants, families and carers, understanding these updates is important when preparing for a plan reassessment, reviewing support arrangements or choosing a disability support provider.

One of the most important developments is the funding reset that began on 1 October 2026. However, the changes do not affect every NDIS support category. Essential day-to-day assistance remains protected under the announced funding adjustments.

This guide explains the key NDIS funding changes in 2026, what participants should review and how to maintain continuity of everyday support.

What Are the Major NDIS Changes in 2026?

The Australian Government passed the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Securing the NDIS for Future Generations) Act 2026 in August 2026.

The reforms introduce changes to funding, plan reassessments, provider compliance and the way the scheme operates.

One of the most significant changes is the reset of funding allocations for two support categories:

  • Social, Economic and Community Participation.
  • Improved Daily Living Skills.

The announced budget reset includes a 50% reduction in allocations for Social, Economic and Community Participation and a 10% reduction for Improved Daily Living Skills.

These are changes to budget allocations, not an automatic reduction in every participant's actual spending or all their NDIS funding. The impact will depend on individual circumstances and the supports included in a plan.

When Will the NDIS Funding Changes Apply?

The funding changes are being introduced progressively over 12 months.

The new allocations apply:

  • From 1 October 2026 when a new plan is approved or an existing plan is reassessed.
  • From 1 February 2027 when plans are renewed.

Participants do not all experience the changes on the same date. Existing participants can continue using their current plans and supports until their plans are reassessed or renewed.

This makes it important to understand your plan's dates rather than assume that every funding change applies immediately.

Which NDIS Supports May Be Affected?

The funding reset applies to the two identified budget categories.

1. Social, Economic and Community Participation

This category can include eligible supports that help participants access community activities, develop social connections and participate in everyday community life.

Participants who rely on these supports should review their current arrangements and consider how their goals can be achieved within the revised budget.

2. Improved Daily Living Skills

This category can include eligible capacity-building supports that help participants develop skills and greater independence.

Examples may involve therapy and assessment services, depending on the participant's plan and the applicable support rules.

Participants should check how their funded services are classified rather than assuming that every daily living service is affected.

Are Essential Daily Living Supports Still Funded?

Yes. The October 2026 budget reset does not automatically reduce all essential daily living supports.

The Government has identified several day-to-day supports that are not affected by these particular budget reductions, including assistance with:

  • Eating and drinking.
  • Dressing and toileting.
  • Laundry and cleaning.
  • Medication assistance and nursing care.
  • Home and vehicle modifications.
  • Personal mobility equipment.

This distinction is particularly important for participants who depend on regular support to manage everyday activities at home.

Eligible personal care services Melbourne participants use and assistance with daily living NDIS Melbourne services should be considered according to the participant's plan, support needs and applicable funding rules.

What Should NDIS Participants Do Now?

Understanding your funding is the first step. Participants can take practical steps to prepare for changes.

Review Your Current NDIS Plan

Check the funding categories, allocated budgets, plan dates and supports you currently use.

Identify which services fall under Social, Economic and Community Participation or Improved Daily Living Skills.

Discuss Your Support Requirements

Speak with your support coordinator, plan manager or my NDIS contact about any concerns.

If you expect your plan to be reassessed or renewed, discuss how the revised budget allocations may affect your arrangements.

Keep Relevant Documentation

Maintain reports, assessments and records that explain your disability-related support needs.

Documenting how assistance contributes to daily routines, safety and independence can help when discussing your support requirements.

Review Your Service Provider

Choosing reliable ndis providers melbourne participants can communicate with is important during periods of change.

Look for providers that explain services clearly, respect participant choices and understand the importance of consistent support.

Choosing the Right NDIS Support Provider in Melbourne

Funding changes can make it more important to understand how your services are delivered and how they relate to your goals.

When comparing ndis support providers melbourne participants should consider:

  • Whether the provider understands their individual support requirements.
  • Whether services are explained clearly.
  • Whether workers respect privacy, dignity and personal preferences.
  • Whether support encourages independence rather than unnecessary dependence.
  • Whether communication is consistent with participants and their representatives.

Sahima Care Services provides disability support services designed around individual needs and everyday routines.

Explore our NDIS support services to learn more about the assistance available.

You can also learn about Sahima Care Services and the areas we serve through our Melbourne service areas.

How Sahima Care Services Supports Everyday Independence

Every participant has different goals, preferences and support requirements.

Sahima Care Services focuses on practical assistance that can help eligible participants manage everyday activities, maintain routines and work towards greater independence.

Depending on individual needs and plan funding, support may include personal care, assistance with daily living, household tasks, transport and community participation.

The aim is to provide respectful support that considers what matters to each participant.

Visit Sahima Care Services to learn more about available services.

Final Thoughts

The 2026 NDIS reforms introduce important changes, but they do not mean that every participant will lose funding for essential daily support.

Understanding which budget categories are affected, checking plan dates and reviewing individual support requirements can help participants prepare.

If you are looking for ndis care providers melbourne participants can approach for practical disability support, take time to understand the services offered and how they align with your needs.

Need help understanding your everyday support options? Contact Sahima Care Services to discuss your support requirements.

Disclaimer: This article provides general information about NDIS reforms as at 3 November 2026. Funding eligibility and individual plan decisions are determined by the NDIA. Participants should refer to official NDIS guidance for current information.

title: The Reconciliation Tool I Almost Didn't Finish
description:
I want to tell you about the night I decided to build this. It wasn't when I
sat down to write code — it was three hours into an Excel reconciliation for a
client, at 11pm, when I noticed the sum of a column was off by ₦0.02 and spent
45 minutes finding out why.

The answer: floating-point arithmetic. Excel was storing ₦5,000.00 as
5000.0000000000003 because of the way it handles decimals, and my VLOOKUP was
failing because the two sides of the match had slightly different underlying
values. The ₦0.02 wasn't real money. It was the way Excel represented the
money.

I closed the spreadsheet, opened a blank Python file, and wrote:

from decimal import Decimal

That was the first line of reconcile. It's been the most important line I
wrote all week.

The first decision I made, and why it stuck

I knew within five minutes of starting that the tool needed Decimal, not
float. Not because I'm disciplined about types — I'm not. But because I'd just
spent 45 minutes of my life on a bug that existed only because float arithmetic
rounds in ways a spreadsheet hides.

Money in float is a lie. 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 in float math. For
a chart, that doesn't matter. For reconciliation, it's the entire bug class I
was trying to escape. Decimal doesn't have the problem. Decimal stores
5000.00 as exactly 5000.00.

I made that decision in the first five minutes and never reconsidered it. That's
rare for me. Normally I'd write the code with float, hit the bug, and rewrite.
This time I'd already hit the bug — in Excel, at 11pm — and I knew what the fix
was going to look like.

The lesson I didn't fully articulate at the time: the first decision sets the
tone for the whole project. Getting the type right on Day 1 meant I never had a
rounding bug on Days 2, 3, 4, or 5. The bug was pre-empted, not debugged.

The second decision: three sections, not one number

My first instinct for the report was a single line: "N transactions matched, M
didn't." That would be easier to write. It would also be useless.

The question I wanted the tool to answer wasn't "did everything match" — it was
"what didn't match, and what should I do about it?" A count of 47 matches
doesn't tell you the three things that need fixing.

So the report became three sections. Matched so you can verify the good
ones. Unmatched processor rows — the transactions the processor says
succeeded but that aren't in the bank. Those are the ones you chase. Unmatched
bank rows — bank entries with no matching processor transaction. Those are the
ones you investigate. Are they refunds? Chargebacks? A different client paying
into the same account?

That decision added about 30 lines of output-formatting code on Day 2. Worth
every line.

The instinct I had to resist was "make it as simple as possible." A
single-number report would have been simpler to build and harder to use. The
simplest thing the user needs is not the simplest thing the code can produce.

The first thing that went wrong

On Day 2, I wrote the matcher. The exact-match version. The one that compares
reference column to reference column, amount column to amount column.

I ran it on the fixtures and got zero matches. All rows unmatched on both
sides.

The reason: the processor's reference is ORD-001. The bank's description is
TRF/ORD-001/PAYSTACK. Different formats. The column I thought I was comparing
was actually a free-text description that contained the reference somewhere
inside it.

This is the kind of bug that doesn't show up in a mental model. I knew
references wouldn't be exact matches — that's why I'd built in fuzzy matching
for Day 3. But I wrote the exact-match version first anyway, because Day 2's job
was the simplest possible thing. Simplest possible thing, it turned out, matched
zero rows.

The fix was a regex on Day 3. [A-Z]+-\d+, extract ORD-001 from
TRF/ORD-001/PAYSTACK, case-insensitive comparison. Ten lines of code.

Should this have been on Day 2? Probably. I could have designed the fixture
files to have exact-matching references and saved normalization for Day 3. But
the fixtures I picked reflected what real bank statements actually look like,
and the real problem was always going to need extraction.

The bug you find on Day 2 is often the bug you should have designed for on Day

  1. That's not a failure. That's what the process looks like.

The thing I almost shipped but didn't

There was a moment on Day 3, after the fuzzy matching worked, where I thought:
"Let me add a --verbose flag to the CLI." The output was one line per match,
and I wanted a flag that showed more detail for each row.

I sat with it for five minutes and killed it.

The reason: the output already showed everything. Adding --verbose would let
the user choose to see less. But the tool's entire purpose was showing the
full picture. A user who runs reconcile wants to see the three sections. A
user who wants one line of output wants a different tool.

This is the difference between "a feature I could add" and "a feature the
product needs." I default to adding. This time I didn't.

The rule I'd carry forward: if you're adding a flag to hide what's already
there, you're probably building a different tool than the one you set out to
build.

The 5-day build, honestly

Here's what actually happened, not the polished version.

Day 1 (2 hours): models.py, cli.py, print row counts. The CLI reported "4
processor rows, 3 bank rows" and I closed the laptop.

Day 2 (3 hours): matcher.py with exact match, two tests. Got zero matches
first, realized the reference-extraction problem, added a regex that probably
belonged on Day 3. Tests passed eventually. Went to sleep at 1am.

Day 3 (3 hours): fuzzy matching — amount tolerance, date window,
case-insensitive reference — plus 7 more tests. 9 tests total. Felt like the
hard part was done.

Day 4 (1.5 hours): README, LICENSE, CI, push. Most of this day was
writing, not coding. Also spent 30 minutes fighting a Python PATH issue when
reconcile.exe wasn't found. The fix was python -m reconcile instead of
reconcile. Six minutes of work, 30 minutes of not realizing it was six
minutes of work.

Day 5 (2.5 hours): reconcile-demo. FastAPI wrapper, HTML form, Render
deploy. First deploy failed. Second deploy worked. Total: 12 hours, five
calendar days, most of it in 2-hour sessions.

The honest part: every single day had a "this isn't working" moment. Day 2's
was the zero-match. Day 3's was a test failing because the date math was off by
one day — weekends don't post the same way weekdays do, and I hadn't thought
about that. Day 4's was the PATH issue. Day 5's was ModuleNotFoundError for
the reconcile package because the temp files were being read incorrectly.

Every day, something didn't work on the first try.

The reason I finished anyway: each of those moments was a specific error message
pointing at a specific line. None of them were "I don't know where to start."
They were all "this one thing is wrong." And each one was fixable in under 20
minutes once I stopped trying variations of the same command and actually read
what the error was saying.

What's still not done, and why

Things I deliberately cut because they weren't part of the finish line:

  • No support for Xero or QuickBooks exports. Only the two CSV formats in the README.
  • No CLI flags for tolerances. Change FuzzyMatchConfig in code if you need different tolerances.
  • No JSON output. Text only.
  • No CI test for the pip installed command. Works locally; not tested on CI.
  • No partial refunds, chargebacks, or multi-currency settlement.

Each one is in the README's "Limitations" section. The point of that section
isn't to apologize — it's to make the boundary visible. Anyone using the tool
knows exactly what it does and doesn't do.

What I'd do differently

One thing. I'd write the fixture files before the matcher.

I wrote models.py first, then the matcher, then the fixtures. Then on Day 2 I
discovered the fixtures needed a specific format the matcher didn't expect. If
the fixtures had come first, they'd have shown me the reference-extraction
problem before I wrote code that assumed it away. The matcher would have been
written correctly on the first try.

The rule I'll carry forward: write the test data before the code that uses it.
The data tells you what the code needs to handle, and it's cheaper to change the
data than to change the code.

If you're doing this in Excel right now

Everything above is about a specific 12-hour project. The part that matters to
you is whether Excel is the right tool for your situation.

The honest answer: for fewer than 20 transactions a month with fewer than 3
clients, Excel is fine. The manual process takes 20 minutes and the
discrepancies are rare enough that a tool is not the bottleneck.

For 20+ transactions a month with 3+ clients, no bookkeeper, and no
spreadsheet discipline — Excel is losing money for you. Not visibly. Not in a
way you can point to a line and say "that's what Excel cost me." But every
₦15,000 missed payment that goes uncaught is real, and the same missed payment
every month for a year is ₦180,000 that went to a bank's reconciliation queue and
never came back.

You can try the tool in the browser
without installing anything. Upload any two CSVs and see what it does. If it
doesn't help, you've lost nothing. If it does, the source is at
github.com/Agenda-X-PR/reconcile
and you can run it locally.

Either way, you now know why your Excel is lying to you.

title: LLM JSON Parsing Always Fails? Java Structured Output in Practice
description:
A week after the customer service ticket extraction feature launched, the logs were full of JsonParseException. Sometimes the model wraps JSON in a Markdown code block; sometimes it prepends a line like "Sure, here are the results"; and the field name can even change from orderNo to order_no. Adding regexes, truncating strings, and tweaking prompts holds up for a couple of days before it breaks again. This article explains LangChain4j's structured output: how to push format constraints down to the protocol layer, and how to add business validation that the schema cannot handle. The code is a complete project; copy it and it runs.

1. What This Problem Actually Is: Why Does JSON Returned by LLMs Always Break

JSON parsing failures are not because the model is "disobedient"; they happen because you only ask it with prompts and do not constrain it at the protocol layer.

The five most common ways of asking a model to return JSON go wrong:

  • Wrapped in a code block: it returns a json block wrapped in three backticks, and Jackson immediately reports "Unexpected character '`'".
  • Prefixes and suffixes: "Sure, I've organized it for you as follows:" followed by JSON. You slice from { to }, and it breaks again when curly braces appear inside string values.
  • Field drift: this time orderNo, next time order_no, and the time after that order_number.
  • Type drift: the amount should be a number, but the model gives you "399 元", and parsing BigDecimal blows up immediately.
  • Enums improvising: you define REFUND and LOGISTICS, and it returns "退款" and "refund_request".

Many people's first reaction is to change the prompt: add "must return pure JSON", add "do not explain", add few-shot examples. It works in the short term, then breaks again a couple of days later. The reason is no mystery:

  1. Prompts are soft constraints. When generating each token, the model can still choose any word.
  2. As context grows longer, earlier format requirements get diluted. Ticket conversations are often thousands of words long, so the model is more likely to "casually" add an explanation.
  3. Different models understand "JSON" differently. Some think code blocks count as JSON; some write numbers as strings.
  4. Even low temperature is not zero probability. As long as one token goes off track, the whole response is ruined.

Some people also think that setting temperature to 0 makes things stable. Temperature only affects the sampling distribution; it does not guarantee that the same input always produces the same output: server-side batching, model version canary releases, and changes in context length can all make results drift. What is more troublesome is "half-correct" output—four out of five fields are correct, parsing succeeds, and bad data is silently written to the database. A total failure at least triggers an alert; a half-correct result quietly pollutes reports.

Hand-written cleanup code is equally unreliable. Regexes can only cover the failure modes you have seen; substring(indexOf("{"), lastIndexOf("}")) truncates the JSON when } appears inside a string value; worse, swallowing parse exceptions and returning null pushes the null pointer to the business layer and doubles the debugging cost.

Cleanup code also has a hidden cost: it mixes "format problems" and "business problems" together. When parsing fails, you add a regex; when a field is wrong, you add if; six months later nobody dares to touch that code, because nobody knows which line is compensating for which model's which quirk. Structured output pulls this back into the type system: if something breaks, it is a compile error or a parse exception, and the boundary is clear.

Here the problem needs to be split into two layers:

LayerSpecific problemWho can solve itShapeIs it valid JSON, are the field names correct, are the types correct, are the enum values validJSON SchemaSemanticsIs the amount a refund amount or an order amount, is the classification correct, is the order number the one for this orderBusiness validation

The schema can guarantee that amount is a number, but it cannot guarantee that the number comes from "refund 399 yuan" rather than "original price 599 yuan". The schema can guarantee that category is one of the four enums, but it cannot guarantee that the model did not classify a logistics issue as a refund.

In one sentence: leave format to the schema, facts to validation, and failures to bounded retries.

2. How the Underlying Mechanism Actually Works: How JSON Schema Constrains LLM Output

Structured output compiles Java types into a JSON Schema, sends it to the model with the request, constrains the generation phase with the schema, and then deserializes the returned text back into an object.

The whole chain has three steps.

Step 1: Translate Java Classes into a Schema

LangChain4j uses reflection to read your return type and generates the schema field by field:

  • String → "type": "string"
  • int / Integer → "type": "integer"
  • BigDecimal / double → "type": "number"
  • enum → "type": "string" plus the enum whitelist
  • List<T> → "type": "array" plus items
  • Nested objects → "type": "object"; recursive structures are closed off with $defs and $ref

The @Description on a field gets written into the schema's description. Don't underestimate this one line of text — it's mainly what the model relies on to decide "what should go in this field." The @JsonProperty(required = true) on a field goes into the required list.

This translation is recursive. List<TicketItem> produces an array, and the element objects get expanded in turn; self-referencing types don't recurse infinitely — once LangChain4j detects a cycle, it switches to $ref pointing at $defs. So you can put tree structures in your DTO and still get a valid schema, it's just that the deeper the nesting, the higher the odds the model fills something in wrong.

A schema generated from a ticket class looks roughly like this:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "orderNo": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "订单号，格式为 ORD- 加 8 位数字"
    },
    "category": {
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["REFUND", "LOGISTICS", "INVOICE", "OTHER"]
    },
    "amount": {
      "type": "number",
      "description": "涉及金额，单位元；对话里没提金额就填 0"
    }
  },
  "required": []
}

Note that required here is empty. Only fields marked @JsonProperty(required = true) make it in. Before sending to OpenAI, strict mode does another rewrite pass: it stuffs all the keys into required and turns the types of fields not marked required into nullable forms, such as ["string", "null"] and ["number", "null"]. So "required" under strict mode only guarantees the key is present, not that the value is non-null. I'll dig into this trap later.

Step 2: Put the Schema into the Request

The request carries the schema via ResponseFormat:

ResponseFormat.builder()
        .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
        .jsonSchema(schema)
        .build();

The OpenAI adapter layer translates it into response_format: {"type": "json_schema", ...}.

If strict is enabled, the server enforces the constraint at the decoding stage: for every token generated, candidates that violate the schema get masked out outright. The model isn't "trying its best to get it right" — it "can't write it wrong." That's a whole different thing from asking it nicely in a prompt.

Capabilities vary widely across vendors:

  • OpenAI's Structured Outputs supports a common subset of JSON Schema, with hard constraints in strict mode.
  • Inference frameworks like vLLM use guided decoding and can also mask tokens according to the schema.
  • Plenty of OpenAI-compatible services only support json_object. It only guarantees "the whole thing is valid JSON" — field names, types, and enums are all ignored.
  • Some services just ignore response_format entirely — whatever you pass, they act like they never saw it.

json_object and json_schema often get conflated. The former only guarantees syntax; the latter governs field names and types as well. A concrete example: you ask it to extract {"amount": 399}, and json_object mode might return {"退款金额": "399元"} — perfectly valid syntax, and your DTO still can't handle it. Schema mode won't even let the key name amount be changed.

LangChain4j uses capability flags to decide which path to take. Only if the model's supportedCapabilities() includes RESPONSE_FORMAT_JSON_SCHEMA does it go with native schema; otherwise it appends the format instructions to the user message. The fallback mode isn't completely useless — it pastes the schema and field descriptions into the user message, so the structure the model sees is accurate, and most of the time it gets it right. The difference is between "most of the time" and "always."

There's a well-hidden trap here: OpenAiChatModel doesn't declare this capability by default. You have to explicitly declare .supportedCapabilities(RESPONSE_FORMAT_JSON_SCHEMA) for it to turn the capability flag on. Without that line, AiServices will still convert the result into an object, but under the hood it's "pasting a format requirement into the prompt," and stability drops off immediately. A lot of people say "I'm using AiServices, so why does it still fall over?" — and the answer is usually right here.

Step 3: Turn the Returned Text Back into an Object

After AiServices gets the response, it hands it to PojoOutputParser. The parser doesn't just readValue right away — it first tries the whole string; if that fails, it scans backwards for the last } or ], then matches braces going backwards, skipping over braces that sit inside strings. So code fences and surrounding chatter all get rescued.

This leniency is a safety net, not a design goal. If field names or types are wrong, it can't save you either — it just throws OutputParsingException.

There's another case it can't do anything about: the response gets truncated by max_tokens. The JSON is missing a closing brace, brace matching fails, and it throws an exception outright. You can catch this kind of failure early by checking finishReason — don't wait for Jackson to blow up. Setting max_tokens comfortably above your normal output size is a cheap and effective fix.

Three Things Schema Can't Cover

Semantics. Schema governs shape. Whose amount it is, whether the category is right, whether the order number belongs to this order — it doesn't concern itself with any of that.

Unknown values. The OpenAI adapter's strict mode puts all properties into required and also changes the types of fields not marked required into nullable form. The key must be present, and the value can be null. When the model encounters "the amount isn't mentioned in the conversation," it is more likely to give you null than to make up a number. So in the DTO, use wrapper types to receive it. If you use int, Jackson will silently turn null into 0, and validation sees fake data; if the business does not accept nulls, check it in validation, or add UNKNOWN to the enum and agree on 0 for the amount.

Cross-field rules. A constraint like "the refund amount cannot be greater than the order amount" can be written with conditional expressions in JSON Schema, but support varies widely among model vendors. Don't pin business rules on the schema; just write Java validation.

3. Hands-On: Writing LangChain4j Structured Output Code Step by Step

A minimal working project consists of four parts: dependencies, DTOs, the AI Service interface, and validation plus retry. The three examples below go from simple to complete, and each one is a full class.

Dependencies 

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
​
    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>structured-output-demo</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
​
    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>
​
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>dev.langchain4j</groupId>
            <artifactId>langchain4j</artifactId>
            <version>1.22.0</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>dev.langchain4j</groupId>
            <artifactId>langchain4j-open-ai</artifactId>
            <version>1.22.0</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
            <version>2.22.4</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
            <artifactId>slf4j-simple</artifactId>
            <version>2.0.20</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
​
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.16.0</version>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

Example 1: AiServices Automatically Generates the Schema

This is the least effort approach. Define an interface, set the return type to a DTO, and LangChain4j handles schema generation, request sending, and result parsing.

package com.example.structured;
​
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.ChatModel;
import dev.langchain4j.model.openai.OpenAiChatModel;
import dev.langchain4j.model.output.structured.Description;
import dev.langchain4j.service.AiServices;
import dev.langchain4j.service.UserMessage;
​
import java.math.BigDecimal;
​
import static dev.langchain4j.model.chat.Capability.RESPONSE_FORMAT_JSON_SCHEMA;
​
public class TicketExtractionDemo {
​
    public enum Category {
        REFUND, LOGISTICS, INVOICE, OTHER
    }
​
    public static class Ticket {
        @Description("订单号，格式为 ORD- 加 8 位数字")
        public String orderNo;
​
        @Description("问题分类：REFUND 退款、LOGISTICS 物流、INVOICE 发票、OTHER 其他")
        public Category category;
​
        @Description("涉及金额，单位元；对话里没提金额就填 0")
        public BigDecimal amount;
​
        @Description("优先级，1 最低，5 最高；催得急或涉及投诉填 4 以上")
        public Integer priority;
​
        @Description("用户诉求摘要，不超过 30 个字")
        public String summary;
    }
​
    public interface TicketAssistant {
        @UserMessage("""
                从下面的客服对话中抽取工单信息。
                只抽对话里明确出现的内容，不要推测。
​
                对话：
                {{it}}
                """)
        Ticket extract(String dialogue);
    }
​
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ChatModel model = OpenAiChatModel.builder()
                .apiKey(System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
                .modelName("gpt-4.1-mini")
                // 这两行决定走原生 JSON Schema，而不是在 prompt 里贴格式说明
                .supportedCapabilities(RESPONSE_FORMAT_JSON_SCHEMA)
                .strictJsonSchema(true)
                .temperature(0.0)
                .build();
​
        System.out.println("模型能力: " + model.supportedCapabilities());
​
        TicketAssistant assistant = AiServices.builder(TicketAssistant.class)
                .chatModel(model)
                .build();
​
        Ticket ticket = assistant.extract("""
                用户：我上周买的耳机，订单 ORD-20261012，到现在还没发货。
                客服：我帮您查一下物流。
                用户：不用查了，直接退款，399 元，太慢了。
                """);
​
        System.out.println("订单号: " + ticket.orderNo);
        System.out.println("分类: " + ticket.category);
        System.out.println("金额: " + ticket.amount);
        System.out.println("优先级: " + ticket.priority);
        System.out.println("摘要: " + ticket.summary);
    }
}

Let's break down the key behaviors:

  • {{it}} in @UserMessage is a placeholder corresponding to the method's only parameter. You don't need to manually concatenate strings.
  • The return type is Ticket, not String. This single signature tells LangChain4j to generate a schema and deserialize the result.
  • @Description is not a comment; it goes into the schema. The more abstract the field name, the clearer the description must be. For example, if priority doesn't say '1 to 5', the model will happily give you 10.
  • temperature(0.0) reduces randomness, but don't expect it to replace the schema.
  • System.out.println(model.supportedCapabilities()) is for troubleshooting. If the output lacks RESPONSE_FORMAT_JSON_SCHEMA, you're in prompt fallback mode.

Example 2: Hand-Write the Schema Without Going Through the Interface Proxy

Some scenarios are not suitable for AiServices: the schema is assembled at runtime, you need to reuse a ChatModel, or you want to see exactly what request was sent. In these cases, construct ChatRequest directly.

package com.example.structured;
​
import dev.langchain4j.data.message.SystemMessage;
import dev.langchain4j.data.message.UserMessage;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.ChatModel;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.request.ChatRequest;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.request.ResponseFormat;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.request.ResponseFormatType;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.request.json.JsonObjectSchema;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.request.json.JsonSchema;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.response.ChatResponse;
import dev.langchain4j.model.openai.OpenAiChatModel;
​
import java.util.List;
​
import static dev.langchain4j.model.chat.Capability.RESPONSE_FORMAT_JSON_SCHEMA;
​
public class RawSchemaDemo {
​
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ChatModel model = OpenAiChatModel.builder()
                .apiKey(System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
                .modelName("gpt-4.1-mini")
                .supportedCapabilities(RESPONSE_FORMAT_JSON_SCHEMA)
                .strictJsonSchema(true)
                .temperature(0.0)
                .build();
​
        JsonSchema schema = JsonSchema.builder()
                .name("Ticket")
                .rootElement(JsonObjectSchema.builder()
                        .addStringProperty("orderNo", "订单号，格式为 ORD- 加 8 位数字")
                        .addEnumProperty("category", List.of("REFUND", "LOGISTICS", "INVOICE", "OTHER"))
                        .addNumberProperty("amount", "涉及金额，单位元，没有就填 0")
                        .addIntegerProperty("priority", "优先级，1 到 5")
                        .addStringProperty("summary", "用户诉求摘要，不超过 30 个字")
                        .required("orderNo", "category", "amount", "priority", "summary")
                        .additionalProperties(false)
                        .build())
                .build();
​
        ChatRequest request = ChatRequest.builder()
                .messages(
                        SystemMessage.from("你是客服工单抽取器，只输出 JSON。"),
                        UserMessage.from("订单 ORD-20261012 一直没发货，我要退款 399 元。"))
                .responseFormat(ResponseFormat.builder()
                        .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
                        .jsonSchema(schema)
                        .build())
                .build();
​
        ChatResponse response = model.chat(request);
        System.out.println(response.aiMessage().text());
    }
}

JsonObjectSchema.builder() provides a series of convenience methods; addStringProperty, addEnumProperty, and addNumberProperty all take two parameters: "name + description." required specifies which fields must be present, and additionalProperties(false) prevents the model from adding extras.

The advantage of hand-writing the schema is control: field names, enum values, descriptions, and required fields are all in your hands. The downside is that it easily drifts out of sync with the DTO. Change one side and forget the other, and parsing will still break. My advice: for scenarios the interface proxy can cover, prefer Example 1; only hand-write when the schema needs to be generated dynamically.

Example 3: Business Validation + Limited Retry

The first two examples solve shape; this one solves semantics. Core idea: after parsing succeeds, don't return immediately—run the rules first. If there's a problem, feed "which rule failed" back to the model and have it rewrite. Retry at most twice.

package com.example.structured;
​
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import dev.langchain4j.data.message.SystemMessage;
import dev.langchain4j.data.message.UserMessage;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.ChatModel;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.request.ChatRequest;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.request.ResponseFormat;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.request.ResponseFormatType;
import dev.langchain4j.model.chat.response.ChatResponse;
import dev.langchain4j.model.openai.OpenAiChatModel;
import dev.langchain4j.model.output.structured.Description;
import dev.langchain4j.service.output.JsonSchemas;
​
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;
​
import static dev.langchain4j.model.chat.Capability.RESPONSE_FORMAT_JSON_SCHEMA;
​
public class ValidatedExtractor {
​
    private static final Pattern ORDER_NO = Pattern.compile("^ORD-\\d{8}$");
    private static final ObjectMapper MAPPER = new ObjectMapper();
    private static final int MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3;
​
    private final ChatModel model;
​
    public ValidatedExtractor(ChatModel model) {
        this.model = model;
    }
​
    public static class Ticket {
        @Description("订单号，格式为 ORD- 加 8 位数字")
        public String orderNo;
​
        @Description("问题分类：REFUND 退款、LOGISTICS 物流、INVOICE 发票、OTHER 其他")
        public String category;
​
        @Description("退款或涉及金额，单位元；没有就填 0")
        public BigDecimal amount;
​
        @Description("优先级，1 最低，5 最高")
        public Integer priority;
​
        @Description("用户诉求摘要，不超过 30 个字")
        public String summary;
    }
​
    public Ticket extract(String text) {
        ResponseFormat format = ResponseFormat.builder()
                .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
                .jsonSchema(JsonSchemas.jsonSchemaFrom(Ticket.class).orElseThrow())
                .build();
​
        List<String> problems = List.of();
​
        for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= MAX_ATTEMPTS; attempt++) {
            String userText = text;
            if (!problems.isEmpty()) {
                userText = text
                        + "\n\n上一次输出有以下问题，请逐条修正后重新输出：\n- "
                        + String.join("\n- ", problems);
            }
​
            ChatRequest request = ChatRequest.builder()
                    .messages(
                            SystemMessage.from("只做信息抽取。不确定的字段按默认值填，不要编造。"),
                            UserMessage.from(userText))
                    .responseFormat(format)
                    .temperature(0.0)
                    .build();
​
            ChatResponse response = model.chat(request);
            String raw = response.aiMessage().text();
​
            try {
                Ticket ticket = MAPPER.readValue(raw, Ticket.class);
                problems = validate(ticket);
                if (problems.isEmpty()) {
                    return ticket;
                }
                System.out.println("第 " + attempt + " 次校验失败: " + problems);
            } catch (Exception e) {
                problems = List.of("输出不是合法 JSON：" + e.getMessage());
                System.out.println("第 " + attempt + " 次解析失败，原始输出：" + raw);
            }
        }
​
        throw new IllegalStateException(
                "连续 " + MAX_ATTEMPTS + " 次没有拿到合格结果，最后的问题：" + problems);
    }
​
    private List<String> validate(Ticket t) {
        List<String> problems = new ArrayList<>();
​
        if (t.orderNo == null || !ORDER_NO.matcher(t.orderNo).matches()) {
            problems.add("orderNo 必须是 ORD- 加 8 位数字，当前是 " + t.orderNo);
        }
        if (t.category == null
                || !List.of("REFUND", "LOGISTICS", "INVOICE", "OTHER").contains(t.category)) {
            problems.add("category 只能是 REFUND、LOGISTICS、INVOICE、OTHER");
        }
        if (t.amount == null
                || t.amount.signum() < 0
                || t.amount.compareTo(new BigDecimal("100000")) > 0) {
            problems.add("amount 必须在 0 到 100000 之间");
        }
        if (t.priority == null || t.priority < 1 || t.priority > 5) {
            problems.add("priority 必须在 1 到 5 之间");
        }
        return problems;
    }
​
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ChatModel model = OpenAiChatModel.builder()
                .apiKey(System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
                .modelName("gpt-4.1-mini")
                .supportedCapabilities(RESPONSE_FORMAT_JSON_SCHEMA)
                .strictJsonSchema(true)
                .temperature(0.0)
                .build();
​
        ValidatedExtractor extractor = new ValidatedExtractor(model);
        Ticket ticket = extractor.extract(
                "订单 ORD-20261012 一直没发货，我要退款 399 元。");
​
        System.out.println(MAPPER.writerWithDefaultPrettyPrinter().writeValueAsString(ticket));
    }
}

There are several design points in this code worth explaining.

The schema only declares the shape; validation rules are written in Java. category in Ticket deliberately uses String instead of an enum. In native schema mode, it is an enum whitelist; when third-party compatible services ignore the schema, it is just a free-form string. Validation catches both cases.

Feed the failure reason back. Just saying "regenerate" is useless; the model doesn't know what went wrong. Tell it "orderNo must be ORD- followed by 8 digits, and the current value is 20261012," and the second attempt will basically get it right. This is what separates effective retries from ineffective ones.

Cap the retries. If it still fails after three attempts, the input itself is the problem, and continuing to burn tokens is pointless. Throw an exception directly and hand it off to a human or a dead-letter queue.

The raw output must be logged. When parsing fails, raw is the only clue. In production, wiring this log into alerting is far more useful than guessing afterward why the model went off the rails.

One retry is one full call. Every retry resends the system prompt, the user's original text, and the schema, so the cost is very real. Therefore, list all validation rules at once; don't drip-feed them one by one.

4. Pitfalls and Best Practices: The 8 Places Where Structured Output Most Easily Goes Wrong

Eighty percent of structured output pitfalls aren't in schema syntax; they're in "assuming it works as soon as you configure it."

  1. Just writing "return JSON". That's not a constraint. Either use ResponseFormat + JsonSchema, or accept that it'll add code blocks whenever it feels like it.
  2. Assuming AiServices will always use the native schema. If the model doesn't declare RESPONSE_FORMAT_JSON_SCHEMA, the framework falls back to prompt mode. For OpenAI models, remember to add .supportedCapabilities(RESPONSE_FORMAT_JSON_SCHEMA), and print supportedCapabilities() once before going live to confirm.
  3. You also want optional fields in strict mode. OpenAI’s strict mode puts every property into required, while fields not marked as required allow null. The keys are always there; the values may be empty. On the Java side, use wrapper types (Integer, BigDecimal). If you use int, Jackson will silently convert null to 0, so validation ends up with fake data—harder to track down than an error. If you really don’t want nulls, add UNKNOWN to enums, agree on 0 for amounts, and handle it in validation.
  4. For amounts, use double. Floating-point errors in monetary amounts are a disaster. Use BigDecimal in the DTO and number in the schema, and Jackson can convert them correctly.
  5. Use date fields directly as LocalDate. When generating the schema, LocalDate isn't treated as string; instead, it gets translated into an object with no fields, leaving the model to fill it in blindly. The ObjectMapper on the parsing side also isn't guaranteed to have JavaTimeModule registered. Accept String in the DTO, then convert it to LocalDate in the business layer. Two extra lines save you an afternoon of debugging.
  6. The prompt and the schema each say something different. The prompt pastes the field structure again, so the model may output according to the old version in the prompt. The prompt should only cover the business rules (what counts as a refund, how priority is determined), and leave the structure to the schema.
  7. The DTO is both wide and deep. Twenty fields and three levels of nesting — the schema alone takes up several hundred tokens, and the model also tends to miss fields. Split it into two extractions: first extract the order number and category, then extract the details as needed. Both accuracy and cost improve.
  8. Retries with no cap and no idempotency. Retrying endlessly on validation failure means that with input that never passes, the bill can go up tenfold. Cap it at two or three attempts, log the raw output and issue list for each attempt, and make writes idempotent.

A few more that are less common but potentially fatal:

  • Field names are too casually chosen. With names like a, b, and tmp, the model can only guess. Use semantic English names such as orderNo and refundAmount, and add @Description to fill in the details.
  • Forgot additionalProperties(false). The model can add arbitrary fields to the object. These fields cannot enter the DTO, waste output tokens for nothing, and also show that it did not strictly follow your structure. Turn it off when writing the schema by hand.
  • Streaming output paired with a POJO return value. The streaming method in AiServices returns TokenStream and cannot directly return a DTO. If you want structured results, do not enable streaming, or parse the result yourself after streaming is complete.
  • Third-party compatible services silently ignore response_format. It does not report an error and still returns a passage of prose. So validation and parsing fallbacks are not optional; they are mandatory.

After launch, monitor three metrics: parse success rate, validation failure rate, and average retry count. If the parse success rate is low, check the model's capability flags and max_tokens first; if the validation failure rate is high, the business rules in the prompt aren't clearly defined; if retry counts rise, it's usually because the model version changed or the input distribution shifted. These three metrics are far more useful than "it feels less accurate lately."

5. Performance Comparison and Technology Selection: JSON Mode, JSON Schema, or Function Calling

For extraction tasks in production, prefer JSON Schema; use Function Calling only when you want the model to decide whether to call a tool.

Approach What it guarantees Extra overhead Suitable scenarios
Plain text + custom parsing Guarantees nothing None One-off scripts, toy demos
JSON mode The output as a whole is valid JSON Very small Older models; compatible services that only support json_object
JSON Schema Field names, types, enums, required fields The schema consumes input tokens; decoding is slightly slower Production extraction; the preferred choice
Function Calling Tool parameter structure, and the model decides whether to call a tool Tool definitions consume tokens Agents, where the model needs to choose actions autonomously

The bulk of the latency is always output tokens and network round trips. The overhead from constrained decoding is barely perceptible on outputs of a few hundred tokens, like ticket extraction. What really sends costs out of control is retries: one failed retry means double the tokens and double the latency. So get the schema right the first time, and list every validation rule up front.

Schemas aren't free. They ride along with every request — the more fields and the deeper the nesting, the higher your input token count. Keeping it to ten fields per DTO and no more than two levels of nesting is a comfortable range. Beyond that, consider splitting the call rather than cramming everything in.

Choosing is simple:

  • Internal systems doing information extraction, classification, or scoring: JSON Schema + Java validation, no hesitation.
  • Hooking up to a third-party OpenAI-compatible service: first probe whether it supports response_format; if not, fall back to JSON mode — and not a single line of validation logic can be skipped.
  • The model needs to decide which tool to call based on user intent: Function Calling. At heart it's also structured output, except what gets structured is "actions."
  • You just want nicer-looking logs: don't bother — regex extraction of key fields is enough.

6. Summary

Structured output comes down to three sentences:

Shape goes to the schema. Use ResponseFormat with JsonSchema to push the constraints down to the protocol layer; returning a POJO from AiServices auto-generates the schema, but make sure the model actually declares the capability.

Facts go to validation. The schema guarantees amount is a number; it can't guarantee it's a refund amount. Order number format, amount ranges, enum whitelists, cross-field relationships — hard-code all of it in Java.

Failures go to bounded retries. Feed back to the model exactly which rule failed, at most two or three times, and log the raw output. Past that, give up — don't burn tokens out of spite.

The implementation checklist is six items: narrow the DTO, turn on the schema, think through strict mode, always write validation, cap the retries, keep the raw logs complete.

When should you not use structured output? Open-ended copywriting, long-form summarization, brainstorming. These tasks have no stable fields; forcing a schema on them just ties the model's hands and leaves the output flat. Structured output is good for "moving information around," not for "creating content."

One more note for anyone about to ship: build a regression set from twenty real tickets and run it every time you swap models, tweak prompts, or touch the schema. Models aren't compilers — an upgrade won't tell you what's incompatible.

The model writes the answers; the code grades the paper. If the grading rules aren't clear, no model — however large — will save you.

References

  • LangChain4j docs: Structured Outputs
  • LangChain4j docs: AI Services
  • JSON Schema official guide: Understanding JSON Schema
  • Maven Central: dev.langchain4j:langchain4j

title: The Next Era Of Ai Isnt about Chatbots...
description:
The “chatbot” phase is starting to feel like old news. We’re now moving into what you could call the Agentic Layer, where models stop being just chat interfaces and start acting as the brains behind autonomous workflows (Agents).

Here’s what’s changing:

From Inference to Orchestration
The hard part isn’t “getting a response” anymore. It’s keeping track of state, context, and which tools to call when. Instead of relying on a single, general-purpose model, we’re moving toward swarms of specialized agents working together in parallel, each handling a specific part of the job.

The New State of the Art
We’re seeing a wave of frameworks built to act as the “manager” on top of all this: coordinating agents, routing tasks, and keeping everything from spiraling into endless loops or redundant work. These systems are focused on robust workflows, not just clever prompts.

The Last Mile: Reliability
The real push now is around verification and self-correction. Production-ready agents can’t just sound confident, they need to check their own work, correct mistakes, and safely interact with the real world: APIs, databases, codebases, and more, without a human babysitting every step.

The Bottom Line
We’re shifting away from simply talking to models toward deploying agents that actually execute tasks and deliver outcomes. The future isnt chat, its getting things done.

title: WordPress Core flaw: interpreting 62.969 blocked attack attempts
description:
Wordfence reported blocking 62.969 attack attempts in 24 hours targeting a WordPress Core vulnerability. This measures attempts Wordfence says it blocked, not successfully compromised websites. The cited data does not establish an exploitation success rate.

The vulnerability affects WordPress Core versions 4.7 through 7.1.3, has a CVSS score of 8,1, and has no CVE identifier. A patch was released on 28 October 2026. TMGS recommends updating affected installations to 7.1.4.

Why the upgrade window matters

During a Core update using a full package, affected versions extract files into a predictable directory under wp-content/upgrade. On many servers, this staging area is accessible through the web. An unauthenticated attacker reaching it at the right moment could interact with the staged WordPress installation and progress to PHP code execution on the server.

Wordfence emphasizes that successful exploitation requires hitting a very narrow window while the full Core update is being extracted. That condition limits what can be inferred from the attempt count. TMGS assesses that the short window does not justify lowering remediation priority when attack attempts have already appeared.

TMGS defensive recommendations

TMGS recommends inventorying WordPress websites, identifying affected versions, and prioritizing updates to 7.1.4. Prepare backups, recovery options, and post-update operational checks.

TMGS also recommends:

  • Verify the running version after updating and record it in the asset inventory.
  • Review suspicious requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade, focusing on activity before, during, and after the upgrade.
  • Correlate requests with error logs and file changes before concluding that a compromise occurred.
  • For outsourced website management, assign clear responsibilities across content administrators, hosting providers, and security teams. Record the final version, upgrade time, and contact responsible for access logs.

Read the full analysis on TMGS: https://tmgs.vn/tin-tuc/wordpress-doc-dung-62-969-luot-tan-cong-bi-chan-i.d487a618-e176-4ef5-b74a-5dd1345f7d37

title: Suppression is a compliance surface, not a checkbox
description:
Most teams add a suppression list after their first complaint. The list is a table of addresses, and within a month nobody remembers why half of them are on it. That is a compliance problem, not a tidiness problem.

Every entry needs a reason and a scope

A hard bounce, a spam complaint, a manual block and an unsubscribe are four different facts with four different lifetimes. A hard bounce is permanent for that address. An unsubscribe is permanent for that channel but may not cover a transactional password reset somebody explicitly requested. A complaint usually means permanent for marketing and a manual review before anything else.

If the table only has (address, created_at) you cannot answer 'why is this blocked' in a support ticket, and you cannot safely unblock anything.

Normalise before you compare

Local parts are case sensitive in theory and case insensitive in practice for every provider your customers actually use. Lowercase the whole address for the suppression lookup, but store the address as the customer wrote it so the UI is not confusing. If you support plus-addressing, decide whether a suppression on user+tag@example.com blocks user@example.com. Most senders say yes and most customers expect no.

Check at send time, not at enqueue time

A message can sit in a queue for an hour. If suppression was checked when the job was created, an unsubscribe that arrived in between is ignored. Re-check immediately before the SMTP conversation, and treat the check as part of the send transaction.

Volanea keeps suppression scoped per project with the reason attached, and re-checks it at delivery time rather than at enqueue.

title: T3 Code: A Free, Open-Source Control Panel for Claude Code, Codex and Other Coding Agents
description:
If you use AI coding agents every day, you have probably hit this wall: three terminals running Claude Code, one running Codex, all poking at the same repo, and no single place to see what each one is doing or what it changed.

T3 Code is an attempt to fix that. It comes from Theo Browne's team (the people behind the T3 Stack and T3 Chat), it is MIT licensed, and it costs nothing. In this post I will cover what it actually is, how to get it running, what you need to watch out for, and how it stacks up against the free and paid alternatives.

TL;DR

  • T3 Code is not a coding agent and has no model of its own. It is a GUI and control layer that drives the agent CLIs you already have installed.
  • It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode and Google Antigravity, using your existing subscriptions.
  • You get a desktop app (macOS, Windows, Linux), a web app, and iOS/Android apps for checking on agents remotely.
  • Each task is a thread that can run on its own Git branch or worktree, with an inline diff and a one-click PR flow.
  • It is very early software (v0.0.x). New threads default to Full access, which means no approval prompts. Change that first.

What T3 Code actually is

The project describes itself as an "agent harness control surface". In plain terms:

 You (desktop / web / phone)
          |
          v
   T3 Code server  <-- owns processes, terminals, Git, project files
          |
   +------+-------+-----------+----------+
   |      |       |           |          |
 Claude  Codex  Cursor CLI  OpenCode   Grok / Antigravity
  Code    CLI

A server process on your machine owns everything that runs: the agent processes, terminals, Git operations and project files. The desktop, web and mobile apps are thin clients that connect to that server. The desktop app bundles its own server, so on a single machine you do not have to think about this split at all.

Because T3 Code drives the official CLIs, it signs in through each CLI's own login. It does not resell API keys or add its own usage quota. Whatever you pay Anthropic, OpenAI or Cursor today is what you keep paying. T3 Code itself is $0.

Why developers are paying attention

One window for many agents. Run Claude Code and Codex side by side, compare their approaches on the same problem, and switch models in the middle of a thread.

Branch per thread. Each thread can work on its own branch or Git worktree. A worktree is a second checkout of the same repo on a different branch, so two agents can edit files at the same time without stepping on each other.

Diff review and PRs in the same place. You see the diff as the agent works, then commit, push and open a pull request from the app. The PR gets a generated title and body.

Remote control. Leave the agents running on your workstation and check on them from your phone or laptop.

An MCP server. Other agents (Claude Code in a terminal, Codex, ChatGPT) can connect to T3 Code over MCP to read threads and start new ones. That makes a "coordinator agent" pattern possible without writing your own plumbing.

Getting started

Step 1: Install and log in to at least one agent CLI

T3 Code cannot do anything without an agent behind it. Set up at least one of these first:

# Claude Code
claude auth login

# Codex
codex login

# Cursor CLI
agent login

# OpenCode
opencode auth login

# Grok Build
grok login

Google Antigravity is the exception: you enable it inside T3 Code's settings and sign in with Google. No CLI needed.

Step 2: Install T3 Code

Pick whichever fits your workflow.

Try it once without installing anything permanent:

npx t3@latest

Install the CLI (server plus local web app):

# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://t3.codes/install.ps1 | iex

Then:

t3                   # start the server and open the local web app
t3 service install   # keep it running in the background
t3 update            # move to a newer release
t3 --help            # full reference

Install the desktop app:

# macOS
brew install --cask t3-code

# Windows
winget install T3Tools.T3Code
# or
scoop install extras/t3code

# Debian / Ubuntu (download the .deb from GitHub Releases first)
sudo apt install ./T3-Code-*.deb

# Arch Linux
yay -S t3code-bin

Step 3: Change the default permission mode

Do this before your first real task. See the next section for why.

Step 4: Open a project and start a thread

Add your repo as a project, start a thread, choose the agent and whether it should run in a new worktree, and give it a task. When it finishes, review the diff and decide whether to open a PR or throw the branch away.

Permission modes: the setting that matters most

Every thread has a permission mode that decides how much the agent can do without asking you:

Mode What it does When to use it
Supervised Asks before commands and file changes. Work outside the workspace is restricted. Important repos, unfamiliar tasks
Auto-accept edits File edits go through, commands still need approval Refactors where you mainly care about shell commands
Auto Routine actions run, risky ones still ask Day-to-day work with providers that support it
Full access No prompts at all for commands or edits Throwaway worktrees and sandboxes only

Two things to know:

  1. Full access is the default for new threads. The agent can run any command and edit any file without asking. For a tool designed to run several agents at once, that is a risky default. Change it in Settings to Supervised or Auto.
  2. Auto mode depends on the provider. Codex hands routine approvals to an AI reviewer and Claude uses its own auto permission mode. Providers without an equivalent, such as OpenCode, fall back to asking every time, like Supervised.

The mode is set per thread, so changing it in one thread does not affect others.

Remote access in practice

The machine running T3 Code does the work. Your phone or laptop is just a remote. That means the host has to stay awake and reachable.

You have three main ways to connect:

LAN or Tailscale (traffic stays on your network):

t3 serve --host <your-lan-or-tailnet-ip>
t3 pair            # prints a QR code and a one-time pairing link

For HTTPS over Tailscale:

t3 serve --tailscale-serve

T3 Connect (no router or VPN setup):

t3 connect

This needs a T3 account and routes the connection through T3's relay. Convenient, but be aware of that trade-off if your company has rules about where code-related traffic goes.

SSH from the desktop app: add an SSH host in Settings, and T3 Code starts a server there and forwards the port for you. Projects, credentials and agent work stay on the remote machine. The remote host must be Linux or an Apple Silicon Mac.

Treat pairing links and codes like passwords. Keep them out of screenshots, logs and bug reports.

Letting other agents drive T3 Code (MCP)

Every T3 Code environment exposes an MCP endpoint at https://<environment-address>/mcp. For example, to connect Claude Code running in a terminal:

claude mcp add --transport http t3 https://<environment-address>/mcp
claude mcp login t3

For Codex:

codex mcp add t3 --url https://<environment-address>/mcp
codex mcp login t3

A new agent gets Read only access by default. You can raise it to Supervised or higher so it can start, message and stop threads. The address must be HTTPS (or localhost on the same machine), and sign-ins expire after 30 days.

What to know before you adopt it

It is early. The README says to expect bugs, and stable releases are still on v0.0.x with nightly builds shipping several times a day. Stick to the stable channel for real work.

Contributions are mostly closed. The team says small fixes may be considered, but big features will not be accepted for now. Feature ideas go to GitHub Discussions. If you need something specific, the MIT license lets you fork.

Docs live in the repo. There is no docs site yet. Everything is under docs/, and it is genuinely useful.

Your existing agent config still applies. Because T3 Code runs the real CLIs, things like your CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, hooks and MCP servers configured for each CLI should keep working.

The PR flow assumes a Git and GitHub-style workflow. If your work is not branch-and-PR shaped, you will get less out of it.

Costs still exist, just not here. Running four agents in parallel burns through your Claude or ChatGPT plan limits four times faster.

How T3 Code compares to other tools

There are two broad groups to compare against: orchestrators (tools like T3 Code that sit on top of agents) and AI editors and first-party agent apps (tools that come with their own model access).

Orchestrators and agent managers

Tool Price License Platforms Agents supported Interface Mobile / remote
T3 Code Free MIT macOS, Windows, Linux, web Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build, Antigravity Desktop + web GUI Yes: iOS, Android, web
Conductor Free local plan; paid Pro for cloud workspaces Closed source macOS only Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode Native Mac app Cloud workspaces on paid plan
Claude Squad Free AGPL-3.0 macOS, Linux (Windows via WSL) Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Aider, others Terminal UI (tmux) Via SSH
Vibe Kanban Free Apache-2.0 Cross-platform (runs via npx) 10+ including Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Amp, Cursor, OpenCode Kanban board in browser Self-host and tunnel

Quick notes on each:

  • Conductor is the closest competitor and the most polished Mac experience. It uses Git worktrees per workspace, like T3 Code. Its free plan covers local workspaces; reviews list Pro at around $50/month for cloud workspaces that keep running when your laptop is closed. If you are not on a Mac, it is not an option.
  • Claude Squad is a lightweight Go binary built on tmux and worktrees. It is great if you live in the terminal and do not want a GUI at all. No phone app.
  • Vibe Kanban frames agent work as kanban tickets, which suits people who like to plan a backlog first. Its original company, bloop, shut down in 2026 and the project continues as a community-maintained open-source tool, which is worth weighing for long-term support.

AI editors and first-party agent apps

Tool Price What you get Difference from T3 Code
Cursor Free Hobby tier; Pro $20/mo, Pro+ $60/mo, Ultra $200/mo, Teams $40/user/mo Full AI code editor with bundled model usage It is an editor with its own billing. T3 Code is a control layer and can even drive the Cursor CLI.
Codex app Included with ChatGPT plans OpenAI's own app for Codex Codex only
Claude Code / Claude desktop Included with Claude plans Anthropic's own agent, with built-in worktree support Claude only

The key difference: Cursor, Codex and Claude Code are where the model access and billing live. T3 Code does not replace them. It sits on top and lets you run several of them from one place.

Which one should you pick?

  • You use more than one agent and want a GUI on any OS: T3 Code.
  • You are on a Mac, want the most polished experience, and are fine with closed source: Conductor.
  • You prefer staying entirely in the terminal: Claude Squad.
  • You want to plan agent work as tickets on a board: Vibe Kanban.
  • You only use one agent and are happy with it: Its own app or CLI is probably enough. Claude Code and Codex both support parallel work on their own.
  • You want an editor with AI built in, not an agent manager: Cursor.

Wrapping up

T3 Code is not trying to be another AI model or another editor. It is a free, open control layer for the agents you already pay for, with worktrees, diffs, PRs and a phone app in one place. It is rough around the edges and changing fast, so treat it as early-adopter software and lock down the permission defaults. But if you already juggle several coding agents, it is one of the more interesting open-source projects to try right now.

Links:

  • GitHub: pingdotgg/t3code

Pricing and feature details were checked in early November 2026. These tools change quickly, so verify on each project's site before making a decision.
