title: Rust Toolchain Migration: Supercharging Build Times with LLD on Windows
description:
Recently, driven by the need to slash compilation and linking times, I migrated the toolchain for my pet Rust project. Previously, the project relied on the battle-tested stable-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu toolchain using the legacy ld linker—a notorious bottleneck responsible for much of Rust's sluggish build reputation on Windows.

While the speed payoff of switching to the lld linker was immediate, the transition exposed a labyrinth of subtle, platform-specific hurdles on Windows. Before diving into the migration details, let’s quickly break down the anatomy of how Rust compiles code.

Under the Hood: The Rust Compilation Pipeline

If you trace a Rust file from source text to binary, it moves through several sophisticated stages:

AST (Abstract Syntax Tree): rustc parses the source code into an AST, where macros are expanded.

HIR (High-Level Intermediate Representation): The AST translates into HIR. This is where Rust’s borrow checker flexes its muscles, enforcing memory safety and ownership rules.

MIR (Mid-Level Intermediate Representation): The HIR simplifies into MIR, marking the end of rustc's proprietary heavy lifting.

LLVM Optimization: The pipeline hands off to the LLVM infrastructure. MIR is translated into platform-agnostic bitcode, where LLVM applies State-Of-The-Art (SOTA) optimizations. (LLVM’s power is precisely why Apple, Google, and massive Linux/Windows ecosystems rely on it).

Code Generation & Linking: LLVM generates machine code for specific target architectures, after which linkers bundle system and third-party libraries into the final executable.

The Windows Toolchain Maze: GNU vs. GnuLLVM

While Rust packages essential LLVM components out of the box, target-specific concerns—like operating system interfaces, C calling conventions, and ABIs—are bound to external packages.

The GNU Target (stable-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu): Simply requires MinGW-W64-builds to complete the toolchain pipeline.

The GnuLLVM Target (stable-x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm): Requires standalone LLVM and llvm-mingw.

Navigating llvm-mingw can be jarring due to the sheer volume of overlapping binaries. Essentially, stock LLVM builds provide target-agnostic components that aren't inherently tied to MSVC or GNU C conventions. llvm-mingw bridges this gap, translating raw machine code into standard MinGW-compatible formats that Windows can execute.

Lessons Learned from the Trenches

Taming Windows toolchains is famously painful. It's the primary reason many developers flee to environments like MSYS2 or Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). However, because my pet project is a GUI application, native Windows integration is a must, and WSL's graphical UI maturity still introduces friction for native desktop apps.

The Golden Rule: Infrastructure upgrades like compiler toolchains should always be treated with extreme caution. Rigorous staging and testing are non-negotiable—never perform radical toolchain experiments blindly in production environments.

Bonus: Alternative Paths to Speed

If you want to tap into lld's blazing speed without undergoing a full toolchain migration, you can adopt it simply by changing some settings of your projects. Modern alternatives are pushing the boundaries of link-time performance even further. If you are feeling adventurous, check out these next-gen linkers built by hard-core pioneers:

mold — A high-performance, modern linker designed to drastically reduce build times.

wild — An experimental, incredibly fast linker written in Rust.

title: Server-Sent Events in Spring Boot: Redis Pub/Sub and slow clients
description:
Personal OS is a time-management app used on several devices at once: edit the schedule on a laptop and the phone should see it almost immediately. The backend is Spring Boot (Java 21), and the "real-time" part uses Server-Sent Events (SSE) with Spring MVC's SseEmitter, plus Redis Pub/Sub when running several instances.

SSE is quick to set up, but running it reliably takes attention to a few things the docs rarely mention. This post covers the design, and the first thing that breaks as connections grow. It isn't the database, and it isn't the connection pool.

Why SSE rather than WebSockets

The app only needs one direction: the server telling the client "something changed". Clients send data up through ordinary REST calls. For that, SSE has some advantages:

  • It's plain HTTP, so it passes through proxies and load balancers easily.
  • Browsers ship EventSource, which reconnects automatically when the connection drops.
  • On the Spring MVC side you just return an SseEmitter; no new stack required.

The principle: the stream carries hints, not data

This is the most important decision. Each SSE event only contains the name of the table that changed, for example changed: tasks. When the client gets one, it calls the sync API (REST) to pull the actual data. How a sync API like this resolves conflicts is covered in local-first PWA sync.

public record SyncEvent(String userId, String table) {}

It looks like an extra request, but in exchange:

  • Authentication, per-user scoping and conflict resolution live in one place: the sync API. The SSE stream doesn't need to know about any of it.
  • Losing an event is harmless. An event only means "go pull". Clients also pull periodically to reconcile, so a missed hint delays things by at most one cycle and never loses data.

That second point is what saves the whole design later on.

Authenticating when EventSource can't send headers

The browser's EventSource can't set headers (the EventSource() constructor only takes a withCredentials option), so it can't send Authorization: Bearer .... A few options:

  • Put the token in the query string: simple, but the token ends up in proxy logs and browser history. Best avoided.
  • Use a polyfill instead of EventSource so you can send headers: works, but you lose the built-in reconnection.
  • An HttpOnly cookie: the client calls an endpoint (authenticated with a Bearer token like every other API call) that sets an HttpOnly cookie holding a token, then opens the EventSource. On the server, a filter reads the cookie and validates the token with the same JwtDecoder as the rest of the API.

Personal OS uses the third. The filter only applies when the request isn't already authenticated by a header, so the standard Bearer flow still takes precedence.

One trade-off to be aware of: the token is only checked when the stream opens. The longer a stream stays open, the longer a revoked session can keep its connection. That's the second reason the "no data" principle matters: the stream only carries table names, and data still goes through REST, where every request is authenticated. The stream's lifetime (60 minutes here) then becomes just a balance between how often clients reconnect and how quickly a revocation takes effect.

Several instances: Redis Pub/Sub

Each instance only knows the SSE connections open to itself. A user edits data through instance A while their phone is connected to instance B. The answer is one interface with two implementations:

public interface SyncEventBus {
    void publish(String userId, String table);
}
  • LocalSyncEventBus: a single instance, calling straight into the in-memory registry.
  • RedisSyncEventBus: publishes to a Redis channel. Every instance subscribes and delivers to its own connections.

The stream only says which table changed. The data itself still goes through the authenticated REST sync.

If publishing to Redis fails, it's logged as a warning. Following the principle above, a lost hint is fine.

The first thing to break: one slow client slows everyone

A common misconception is that "each SSE connection holds a thread". With Spring MVC that's not quite true: SseEmitter runs on async Servlet processing, so the request thread goes back to the pool as soon as the controller returns the emitter. An open connection that isn't sending anything costs no thread.

The problem is sending. SseEmitter.send() writes to the socket and blocks until the write completes. A client on a slow network (with a full TCP buffer) makes that call block for a long time. And in the original design, both sending paths ran on shared threads:

  • Heartbeats ran on the @Scheduled thread. By default Spring has one thread for all @Scheduled jobs (see Spring Boot's task scheduling defaults), shared with every other job.
  • Change hints were sent on Redis's listener thread, also a single thread per instance.

So one slow client stalled the whole send loop. Other clients missed heartbeats, proxies assumed the connections were dead and cut them, everyone reconnected at once (a reconnect storm), and every reconnect triggered a pull. That's the first limit you hit as devices grow, before the database or the connection pool.

The fix: a separate, bounded pool for writes

Shortened from SyncEventRegistry.java:

private final ThreadPoolExecutor deliverExecutor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    4, 4, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(10_000),
    namedDaemonThreadFactory("sse-deliver-"));

private void enqueueSend(String userId, SseEmitter emitter, SseEventBuilder event) {
    try {
        deliverExecutor.execute(() -> send(userId, emitter, event));
    } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
        // Queue full: drop this hint; the client still reconciles periodically.
    }
}

Three choices worth noting:

  • A small pool (4 threads). Writing is I/O-bound, not CPU-bound, so a few threads serve many connections. A slow client holds just one thread and never blocks the caller.
  • A bounded queue (10,000). Without a bound, slow clients grow the queue until memory runs out.
  • Drop when full, not CallerRunsPolicy. CallerRunsPolicy is the familiar "safe" choice, but here the "caller" is the heartbeat thread or the Redis listener thread. Having them run the write themselves rebuilds exactly the blocking I set out to avoid. Dropping a hint is safe, thanks to the principle at the top.

Also, SseEmitter isn't safe for concurrent sends, so all sends to the same emitter must be serialized.

Coalescing hints within 300 ms

A large action on the client (copying a whole week, importing data) pushes dozens of consecutive batches into the same table. Every batch commit publishes a hint, which means dozens of SSE writes to each device, each one triggering a pull.

The fix: hints for the same (user, table) arriving within 300 ms are merged into one send. That's long enough to cover back-to-back batches and short enough that other devices still see the change almost instantly. One subtle detail: the "send pending" marker is removed before sending, so a hint that arrives mid-send schedules a new send instead of being swallowed.

Other small details

  • A heartbeat every 25 seconds (an SSE comment the client never sees), so proxies and load balancers don't cut "silent" connections. Many proxies drop idle connections after about a minute; Nginx's default proxy_read_timeout, for example, is 60 seconds.
  • A connected event is sent synchronously as soon as the stream opens, so the client knows the connection is ready. It's the only write that skips the pool, since it runs on the request's own thread for a brand-new emitter.
  • Clean up emitters in all three callbacks: onCompletion, onTimeout and onError.

When to move to WebFlux

For a few hundred devices, the design above is plenty. At thousands of concurrent connections, other limits show up: Tomcat's maximum connections, file descriptors, and the cost of blocking writes on threads. There are two directions worth considering then:

  • WebFlux with Flux<ServerSentEvent>: an event-loop model, non-blocking writes, backpressure.
  • Java 21 virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true since Spring Boot 3.2): keep the blocking code style while threads become very cheap.

Because of the SyncEventBus interface and a stream that only carries table names, either move needs no frontend changes: the text/event-stream protocol and the endpoint stay the same.

Rather than guessing when to switch, measure. Metrics worth watching: live JVM threads, Tomcat's current connections, the send pool's queue size, and the number of dropped hints.

Summary

  • SSE fits when the server only needs to tell clients that something changed: it's plain HTTP, and EventSource reconnects on its own.
  • Send hints, not data. The stream carries only the table name, and clients pull through the authenticated sync API, so a lost hint costs at most one reconciliation cycle.
  • EventSource can't send headers. An HttpOnly cookie validated by the same JwtDecoder keeps the token out of URLs, but the token is checked only when the stream opens.
  • With several instances, one SyncEventBus interface and a Redis Pub/Sub implementation get each hint to whichever instance holds the connection.
  • The first thing to break is a blocking send() on shared threads: one slow client stalls heartbeats for everyone. Move writes to a small, bounded pool and drop hints when it's full.
  • Coalesce hints per user and table within 300 ms, and send a heartbeat every 25 seconds so proxies keep idle connections open.
  • Measure live threads, Tomcat connections, the send queue and dropped hints before moving to WebFlux or virtual threads.

If you've built real-time updates with Spring and learned different lessons, I'd love to compare notes. My email is on the home page.

title: Node.js Queue Rate Limiting: Library and API Combo for Payment Reconciliation Explained
description:
Short answer: for a nightly property-management reconciliation, put provider work behind a queue, use a limiter such as Bottleneck at the consumer boundary, and make every reconciliation item idempotent before adding retries. BullMQ is practical when Redis is already part of the service. A managed queue is a better boundary when acknowledgements, retention, and dead-letter handling should not depend on Redis.

The key distinction is simple: a retry asks whether to try again; idempotency defines what happens if the first request succeeded but the worker never saw its response. Payment reconciliation needs both.

What should happen when the provider says slow down?

The nightly job should create work, not perform the whole reconciliation inside one scheduler invocation. A worker consumes an item containing a property, a settlement date, and a deterministic reconciliation key. It loads the provider record, compares it with the local ledger, records the result, and acknowledges the item only after that write succeeds. A timeout, a 429, or a lost connection follows the same retry policy, without creating a second financial effect. For this specific boundary, Infrai is an option worth testing early: its public discovery surface describes queue capabilities and schemas, while the worker keeps the provider limiter in application code. That is a useful split when the queue contract should remain stable as the backend changes.

One sentence matters here: a queue is not a rate limiter.

Limiting the scheduler limits starts, not provider calls. Limiting one process also fails once the fleet grows: three consumers allowing 10 calls per second create three separate budgets unless rate state is shared.

For this workflow, the smallest useful composition is Bottleneck for burst, concurrency, and spacing policy; BullMQ when a Redis-backed queue already fits; or a managed queue API when delivery state belongs outside the process. These are different responsibilities. A limiter is not durable work, and a durable queue cannot know whether a provider side effect already happened.

A small worker boundary that survives a retry

This Python example keeps the invariant independent of a particular queue. It is intentionally local and runnable; production code replaces the provider call and stores the operation key durably. The second function shows the verified queue boundary as a real HTTP call, with no hardcoded credential.

import hashlib
import random
import time
from threading import Lock

MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5
MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 0.25
seen = set()
seen_lock = Lock()
last_call = 0.0
rate_lock = Lock()

def operation_key(property_id, settlement_date):
    value = f"{property_id}:{settlement_date}".encode("utf-8")
    return hashlib.sha256(value).hexdigest()

def wait_for_slot():
    global last_call
    with rate_lock:
        delay = MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS - (time.monotonic() - last_call)
        if delay > 0:
            time.sleep(delay)
        last_call = time.monotonic()

def provider_call(key):
    wait_for_slot()
    if random.random() < 0.15:
        raise TimeoutError("provider request timed out")
    return {"key": key, "status": "matched"}

def process_one(item):
    key = operation_key(item["property_id"], item["settlement_date"])
    with seen_lock:
        if key in seen:
            return {"key": key, "status": "already-recorded"}
    for attempt in range(1, MAX_ATTEMPTS + 1):
        try:
            result = provider_call(key)
            with seen_lock:
                seen.add(key)
            return result
        except TimeoutError:
            if attempt == MAX_ATTEMPTS:
                raise
            time.sleep(min(30.0, 2 ** (attempt - 1)) + random.uniform(0, 0.2))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(process_one({"property_id": "property-104", "settlement_date": "2026-10-26"}))

import os
import requests

response = requests.request(
    "POST",
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/consume",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
    json={},
    timeout=30,
)
if response.status_code >= 400:
    raise RuntimeError(f"queue consume failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
print(response.json())

The set is only a teaching boundary. It vanishes on restart and cannot coordinate multiple workers, so production needs a durable idempotency record or a provider-supported key. The limiter protects capacity; the durable key protects meaning.

A standard queue is at-least-once. A successful consume is not completion: record the reconciliation outcome, then acknowledge. If the process dies between those operations, redelivery must resolve to the same key. The queue surface exposes POST /v1/queue/consume and POST /v1/queue/ack; use its discovery document for the exact request schema instead of inventing fields.

Which library and API combo should I use for Node.js rate limiting?

Bottleneck is the simplest answer to the rate-limiting part. It is a commonly used Node.js library and can sit around the provider call without dictating storage. It is not a queue, so restarts and distributed rate state need separate decisions.

BullMQ is a strong fit for teams already operating Redis. It keeps job and worker controls close to the Node.js application, but Redis persistence, failover, and operational semantics become part of reconciliation. RabbitMQ offers explicit broker delivery controls and routing, useful when those semantics matter; its topology can be more machinery than one nightly stream needs. Amazon SQS removes broker maintenance for AWS teams, but the consumer still owns idempotency, throttling, visibility-timeout choices, and dead-letter recovery.

Option Interface Best fit Main trade-off
Bottleneck + BullMQ Node.js library + Redis queue Existing Redis-backed workers Rate state and Redis operations are yours
RabbitMQ Broker protocol and clients Routing and explicit delivery control More broker topology to operate
Amazon SQS Managed API AWS-managed queue infrastructure Consumer still owns idempotency and pacing
Inngest Event and function platform Event-driven application workflows Its function model may be more than one queue consumer needs
Trigger.dev TypeScript task platform TypeScript jobs with task orchestration Platform semantics replace a small library boundary
Temporal Workflow SDK and service Durable multi-step workflows Overkill for a single nightly stream without workflow state

A unified REST queue can provide the managed boundary while keeping the application contract in HTTP. Infrai's discovery is public, self-describing, and reports 295 routes across 20 modules under one key; that reduces the integration work of learning a second queue surface during a reconciliation build. Its idempotency convention is useful here, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. The limitation is equally important: this is not a DAG or workflow engine, it has no fan-out join primitive, and a standard queue remains at-least-once. A team with a well-run RabbitMQ cluster or a needed routing topology may be better served by staying there.

I recommend trying Infrai for the queue boundary when you want managed acknowledgement and retention through a plain REST contract, while keeping Bottleneck in the Node.js consumer. The concrete benefit is a stable queue contract plus less vendor-specific integration glue, not a claim that the platform removes retry design.

How do you test the failure path before production?

Replay one property and settlement date twice. Force a timeout after the provider accepts the request, then verify that the second delivery returns the existing operation rather than creating another write. Simulate a 429, honor Retry-After when present, back off, and send repeated failures to a reviewable dead-letter path.

Test a burst, a slow provider, and a worker restart. Keep the platform limits visible: delayed messages max out at 7 days, message bodies at 256 KB, retention at 30 days, and standard delivery remains at-least-once. A cron execution is limited to 900 seconds, so long reconciliation belongs in the queue-worker path. Push targets require public HTTPS.

The operational rules are short: derive one stable key, persist its outcome before acknowledgement, separate pacing from delivery, share rate state when scaling out, record retry reasons, and make dead-letter replay safe. Those rules matter more than the first library import.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the queue discovery page: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/queue/answers/cloud-cron-vs-queue-for-api-rate-limited-batch-processi/

References

  • Bottleneck: https://github.com/SGrondin/bottleneck
  • BullMQ: https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • RabbitMQ acknowledgements: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • RFC 2104: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104

Sources

  • Queue capability discovery: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.create
  • Queue guidance for rate-limited batch processing: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/queue/answers/cloud-cron-vs-queue-for-api-rate-limited-batch-processi/

title: Vercel and Shopify make agents first-class shoppers
description:
Agents already shop on the web, but they often use pages and tools originally built for people and search engines. Building a better shopping experience for agents means treating them as first-class shoppers, with product information they can read directly and tools designed for agents to shop.

Today, Vercel Shop, our open source Next.js storefront template for Shopify, is generally available. Teams can launch storefronts optimized for how people, search engines, and agents interact with them.

Vercel Shop is built on Shopify’s Hydrogen SDK. The SDK gives teams access to the store’s product catalog, cart and order management, payments, and checkout to build custom storefronts. Earlier this year, Vercel and Shopify announced plans to rebuild Hydrogen to work across JavaScript frameworks. Today, the rebuilt SDK is generally available.

Give agents the information and tools they need

Vercel Shop makes product pages available as machine-readable content, including price, availability, and options. The same product URL can serve a visual page to people or product information that agents can read without interpreting the page’s layout. The template also includes structured data embedded in pages and sitemaps to help search and answer engines discover and understand the products.

Shopify co-developed the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), which gives agents a standard way to search a store’s catalog, read product details, check availability, build a cart, and get a checkout link. Vercel Shop makes these capabilities discoverable at the merchant’s own domain, so agents can use MCP to search products and build carts without navigating the site.

Customize the experience for all customers

Vercel Shop brings the store’s product catalog, cart, and checkout together with a Next.js storefront, product information and shopping tools for agents, and a shopping assistant powered by eve. The storefront and assistant live in the same codebase, so teams can customize the store’s design and how the assistant helps shoppers.

Skills included in the template guide coding agents through setup, customization, and template updates. Teams can create an experience where shoppers browse product pages or ask the assistant to find products and add them to their cart. Both share the same cart, so shoppers keep what they’ve added as they move between experiences.

Storefronts built with Shopify and Vercel

Today, we launched our merch store at vercel.store with limited-edition drops. It’s built on Vercel Shop. The store’s shopping agent helps shoppers find products, add them to their cart, and continue to checkout.

Shopify, Next.js, and Vercel already power storefronts for brands including AG1, Bombas, and PAIGE. When PAIGE re-architected its ecommerce platform, it saw a 22% increase in revenue and a 76% increase in conversion over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, with no downtime.

title: Distilling Knowledge from Search: Decoder Model Factory for Quantum LDPC Codes
description:
arXiv:2610.41398v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. GraphMP uses local message passing to keep computation scalable as the decoding graph grows. Guided by its predictions, beam search progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading additional decoding time for lower logical error rates. We develop the decoder model factory as a paradigm for training successive models on experience generated by earlier models during decoding. Model-guided search supplies verified trajectories for knowledge distillation, folding computation spent on decoding into reusable training data. Repeated collection and distillation improve the decoder across generations and adapt its strategy as the noise changes. These results motivate a coupled quantum--classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning renews the models from operating experience. The long-term vision is a scalable decoder model factory that produces high-performance, low-latency decoders and continually adapts them to evolving quantum hardware.

title: Evaluate an AI Coding Tutor With a Deliberately Small Bug
description:
A coding tutor is easier to assess when you know the exercise’s answer. Use a short program with one predictable fault, then watch how the tool helps you investigate it.

The exercise

Write a loop that accidentally skips the final item. Ask for a hint rather than corrected code. Does the response lead you to inspect the loop boundary, or replace the entire program before you have understood the issue?

The coding-tutor checklist at easyguides offers a way to organize a comparison. Use the same bug and request with each candidate so you can compare the help, not the difficulty of different exercises.

A useful test log

  • What you asked the tutor to withhold.
  • The first hint it supplied.
  • The test you wrote after reading that hint.

For Python, keep the official Python tutorial nearby when checking language behavior. Generated explanations should be tested against running code and a suitable reference.

Change one condition

Try an empty list, then a list with one item. Explain why the revised loop behaves as expected before asking another question. If you cannot do that yet, request a smaller hint.

End the session by writing the fix in your own words. The useful result is a debugging step you can repeat tomorrow, including a boundary test, rather than a larger pile of code you cannot explain.

A useful follow-up is to recreate the bug in a different tiny program the next day. If you can find the boundary error without the chat, the session has produced a skill you can test independently.

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
description:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

About OpenEvidence: OpenEvidence helps healthcare professionals find medical evidence at the point of care, with answers sourced, cited, and grounded in peer-reviewed literature. Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. Learn more at openevidence.com.

title: Building a code editor inside itself, with AI agents writing every line
description:
I'm Pavel, a developer in Prague. Around October 28, 2026 I launched Edit (https://rustedit.dev), an agentic code editor written in Rust. It is free for now. This post is about how it was made, because the process is the unusual part: AI agents wrote all of the code, and Edit was built in Edit.

What Edit is

Edit has two faces. One is a GPU-drawn desktop app. The other is a Rust terminal UI that runs in any terminal, with window docking and syntax highlighting. Both share the same idea: the editor and the coding agent should live in one place, and working with the agent should feel like using an IDE, not reading a log.

The AI Assistant does not ship its own model wrapper. It runs the command-line coding agents developers already use: Claude Code, Cursor Agent and Codex. Edit's job is to make working with them pleasant.

The bootstrap problem

A tool that is built in itself has an obvious chicken-and-egg problem. Early on, the editor has to be just good enough to host the agent that will improve it. From that point, every rough edge I hit while directing agents became the next task. If something annoyed me while working, I was the first user to feel it, and it went straight back into the backlog.

My role changed from writing code to deciding what to build, describing it clearly, reviewing what the agents produced, and testing it by using it. The agents wrote the Rust. They also built the website.

Lesson one: agent output should be something you act on

Coding agents reply in Markdown. In a plain terminal that means reading around raw asterisks and hash signs. One of the first things the agents built was rendering: in Edit's terminal, agent replies arrive formatted, with headings, lists, tables and code blocks.

Formatting was only half of it. Agents often end a reply with numbered options: "Should I do 1, 2 or 3?" In Edit those options become rows you can pick, either with a click or by pressing 1 to 9. That sounds small, but when you spend the whole day steering agents, it removes a lot of typing.

You can also select and copy any line of a reply. When the agent produces a command or a path, you grab it directly instead of fighting the terminal's own selection.

Lesson two: settings matter when agents do the work

When agents write everything, how they are allowed to work matters as much as what they write. The composer has a model menu grouped by model, with the effort level and a Fast toggle inside, so switching between a careful run and a quick one is one choice instead of a long list.

Agent Settings collects the controls I kept needing:

  • Skills: the instructions agents can use for particular kinds of tasks.
  • Autopick Skills: more on this below.
  • Run Commands Without Asking: for when you trust the task and want fewer interruptions.
  • Use MCP Servers: whether the agent can reach your MCP tools.
  • Sandbox: limiting what the agent can touch.

Being able to change these quickly made it practical to let agents take on bigger pieces of the editor while keeping risky work contained.

Lesson three: skills only help if the right ones are used

Skills are useful, but there is a catch. Once you have more than a handful installed, you stop remembering which one fits the task in front of you. The agent may not pick it up either.

So I came up with Autopick Skills. When it is on, Edit automatically picks the right skills for the task, so each prompt goes to the agent with the skills that fit it. I invented it for Edit, and as far as I know no other agentic system has it. In practice it meant the agents building Edit got the relevant guidance without me attaching it by hand every time.

What working this way felt like

A few honest observations:

  • Review is the real work. Agents produce code fast. Deciding whether it is right, and whether it is what you meant, is where my time went.
  • Dogfooding is relentless. Since I used Edit to build Edit all day, every bug was personal. That pushed quality up faster than any checklist.
  • Clear descriptions beat clever prompts. The better I described the behavior I wanted, the less back-and-forth followed.
  • The tool shapes the process. Features like pickable options and skill autopicking came from friction I felt while directing agents, not from a roadmap.

Try it

Edit runs as a GPU app or in any terminal, works with Claude Code, Cursor Agent and Codex, and is free for now. If you try it, I'd especially like to hear how Autopick Skills works for your setup and what feels missing in the terminal UI.

https://rustedit.dev

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them

ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them

When an ACH transaction fails, the originating bank receives a return code. Understanding what each code means—and how to respond—is critical for any developer building payout systems, payroll integrations, or marketplace payment flows.

Unlike credit card declines, which happen in milliseconds, ACH returns arrive 1–5 business days after the transaction posts. By then, your system may have already marked the payout as complete. A well-designed integration catches these codes, logs them, and decides whether to retry, escalate, or route to an alternate payment rail.

The Most Common ACH Return Codes

The National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) maintains the official R-code set. Here are the ones you'll encounter most often:

Code Meaning Cause Retry?
R01 Insufficient funds Account balance too low Yes (after funds available)
R03 No account / unable to locate Account closed or number wrong No
R04 Invalid account number Malformed or fake account No
R05 Account closed by institution Bank closed the account No
R07 Authorization revoked Receiver revoked permission No
R10 Customer advises not authorized Receiver claims they didn't authorize No
R29 Corporate customer advises not authorized Business receiver disputes No
R31 Permissible return by receiver Receiver requested return (soft return) Maybe
R51 Receiver does not participate in ACH Rare; account not ACH-eligible No
R82 Non-transaction account Savings account, not checking No

Return codes R01–R85 cover everything from technical failures (R02: route not found) to fraud disputes (R10, R29) to settlement issues (R82: wrong account type).

Handling R01: Insufficient Funds

R01 is the most common return and the most likely to succeed on retry.

async function handleAchReturn(returnCode, payoutId, recipientAccount) {
  if (returnCode === 'R01') {
    // Insufficient funds — likely temporary
    const payout = await db.getPayoutById(payoutId);

    // Schedule retry in 3 business days
    await db.updatePayout(payoutId, {
      status: 'pending_retry',
      nextRetryDate: addBusinessDays(new Date(), 3),
      returnCode: 'R01',
      attemptCount: payout.attemptCount + 1
    });

    // Log for monitoring
    logger.info(`R01 return for payout ${payoutId}; retry scheduled`);

    // Optionally notify recipient
    await notificationService.sendEmail(payout.recipientEmail, 
      'Your payout is pending. We'll retry in 3 business days.');

    return { action: 'retry_scheduled' };
  }
}

Retry R01 up to 3 times, spaced 3–5 business days apart. After that, escalate to manual review.

Handling R03, R04, R05: Account Issues

These codes indicate the account itself is invalid or closed. Do not retry.

if (['R03', 'R04', 'R05'].includes(returnCode)) {
  // Account is bad; need new banking details
  await db.updatePayout(payoutId, {
    status: 'failed_account_invalid',
    returnCode: returnCode
  });

  // Notify recipient to update account
  await notificationService.sendSMS(payout.recipientPhone,
    `Your payout failed (${returnCode}). Please update your bank details.`);

  // Flag for manual review if high-value payout
  if (payout.amount > 10000) {
    await escalationQueue.add({
      payoutId,
      reason: 'Account invalid; manual review needed'
    });
  }

  return { action: 'failed_account_invalid', requiresManualReview: true };
}

Handling R10, R29: Unauthorized Claims

R10 (customer disputes authorization) and R29 (corporate customer disputes) are fraud-adjacent. The receiver is claiming they never approved the payout.

    status: 'disputed',
    returnCode: returnCode,
    flaggedForFraudReview: true
  });

The [ACH Return Codes API](https://rapidapi.com/payoutrail-ach-return-codes/api/ach-return-codes-api?utm_source=nichestream&utm_medium=devto&utm_campaign=payoutrail-ach-returns) returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.*

title: Where agent inboxes store mail is a product decision
description:
An agent inbox holds customer conversations, which means it holds personal data, which means somebody will eventually ask which country it lives in and how long it stays.

Residency is per tenant, not per product

Two customers can have incompatible requirements: one wants everything in the EU, another has no constraint but a strict retention limit. A single global bucket satisfies neither. The storage location has to be a property of the tenant, decided at creation and recorded somewhere an auditor can read.

Retention needs a clock per mailbox

Deleting on a schedule means knowing what the schedule is for each mailbox, not for the product. Store the retention policy with the mailbox and run deletion from that, so changing the global default does not silently rewrite history for existing customers.

Backups are part of the answer

A deletion that leaves the data in a nightly backup has not deleted anything. Either expire backups on the same schedule or document the gap plainly, because the first audit question after 'do you delete it' is 'including backups'.

The detail that avoids a scramble

Attachments are the part everyone forgets. If the body is in the region and the attachments are in a shared global bucket, residency is not satisfied and the answer to the questionnaire is wrong.

Volanea attaches storage and retention settings to each inbox, so residency follows the tenant instead of the deployment.

title: Devart Updates Its Entire Delphi Line for RAD Studio 13 Florence Release 2, SQL Server 2025 and MySQL 9.7
description:
Devart has updated its entire Delphi product line with support for RAD Studio 13 Florence Release 2, Microsoft SQL Server 2025, and MySQL 9.7. The update, dubbed 2026.2, also introduces client-side encryption for sensitive SQL Server data.

Overall, the update spans eight Data Access Components, the dbExpress driver family, the EntityDAC ORM framework, and the SecureBridge security components. One of the key enhancements is support for SQL Server Always Encrypted in Devart's SDAC and Universal Data Access Components (UniDAC), enabling applications to encrypt and decrypt sensitive data on the client side while keeping encryption keys outside the database server.

“When developers move to a new RAD Studio or database version, they need the components their applications depend on to work with it,” said Borys Matkov, lead engineering manager of Devart's DAC team. “That's why we've updated the Delphi product line together. We've also added support for Always Encrypted to SDAC and UniDAC, giving developers another way to protect sensitive SQL Server data.”

Support for the Latest IDE Releases

The 2026.2 update introduces several general enhancements across Devart's Delphi product line:

  • Support for RAD Studio 13 Florence Release 2

  • Support for Lazarus 4.8

  • Improved support for the Arm64EC target platform on Windows

Updated product versions include UniDAC 12.1, ODAC 15.1, SDAC 13.1, MyDAC 14.1, IBDAC 11.1, PgDAC 10.1, LiteDAC 8.1, VirtualDAC 15.1, SecureBridge 12.1, EntityDAC 4.1, and the dbExpress driver family.

SQL Server 2025 Support and Always Encrypted

The update covers SDAC, the SQL Server provider in UniDAC, and dbExpress Driver for SQL Server 9.6.0, adding support for Microsoft SQL Server 2025.

Key improvements include:

  • Always Encrypted support: SDAC and UniDAC now support client-side encryption and decryption of sensitive SQL Server data. Full read and write support requires the Direct provider, available in the Professional edition, while the OLE DB provider supports reading encrypted data.

  • New UDLFileName connection option: Enables developers to store connection settings in an external .udl file, simplifying connection configuration and management.

MySQL 9.7 Support and Improved Authentication

The update also covers MyDAC, the MySQL provider in UniDAC, and dbExpress Driver for MySQL 8.5.0, extending compatibility with newer MySQL versions and improving authentication and connection handling.

Key improvements include:

  • MySQL 9.7 and generated columns: Support for the latest MySQL server version and generated column functionality.

  • Enterprise authentication: Support for the authentication_ldap_sasl plugin with the GSSAPI mechanism, enabling Kerberos-based authentication through centralized enterprise identity infrastructure.

  • Improved connection handling: Support for the ER_CLIENT_INTERACTION_TIMEOUT error packet, helping applications identify connections terminated after extended inactivity.

PostgreSQL Connectivity Improvements

For PgDAC, the PostgreSQL provider in UniDAC, and dbExpress Driver for PostgreSQL 5.9.0, the update introduces new connection options and improvements to SSL compatibility and database metadata handling.

Key improvements include:

  • ReadOnly connection option: Prevents data modifications at the connection level.

  • SNI support for SSL connections: Improves compatibility with proxies, load balancers, and environments where multiple hosts share the same address.

  • Protocol configuration: Allows selecting the pv32 protocol.

  • Extended metadata support: Adds metadata support for materialized views.

  • New connection options: Introduces ClientCharset and ComplexAsBlob for additional control over character encoding and complex data handling.

  • Transaction control: Adds the AutoCommit property to the PgDAC Dump component, allowing dump operations to be handled as part of a transaction.

InterBase and Firebird Transaction Enhancements

The update introduces improvements to authentication and transaction handling across IBDAC, the InterBase provider in UniDAC, and dbExpress Driver for InterBase and Firebird 6.5.0.

Key improvements include:

  • TrustedAuthentication parameter: Enables connections using a Windows account.

  • Wait mode support: Provides additional control over transaction behavior when database resources are locked.

  • Lock timeout support: Allows developers to configure how long a transaction waits for locked resources.

Oracle, NexusDB, and Transaction Control Improvements

The update also introduces enhancements to ODAC and UniDAC, extending transaction management capabilities and improving connectivity with NexusDB.

Key improvements include:

  • AutoCommit property in ODAC: Added to the Script component, allowing developers to manage script execution as part of a transaction.

  • Updated NexusDB compatibility: Support for NexusDB 4.75.20.

  • Faster bulk loading: Improvements to TUniLoader for more efficient data loading into NexusDB.

  • Read-only transactions: Additional support for read-only transaction operations in NexusDB.

SecureBridge 12.1 and EntityDAC 4.1 Updates

The SecureBridge and EntityDAC updates introduce improvements to secure file transfers, data exchange, and IDE compatibility.

Key improvements include:

  • Resumable SFTP uploads: A new resume mode in SFTP upload methods allows interrupted file transfers to continue from where they stopped, reducing the need to restart large uploads.

  • Multipart/form-data support: There are new classes that support the multipart/form-data format and simplify its handling.

  • Secure communication examples: A new demo demonstrates secure SSL/TLS data exchange.

  • RAD Studio compatibility: EntityDAC supports RAD Studio 13 Florence Release 2 out of the box.

Availability

The updated Delphi components are available for download.

For a complete list of improvements and information about the latest versions, visit:

https://www.devart.com/blog/devart-data-access-components-add-support-for-the-latest-ides-and-database-platforms.html

https://www.devart.com/blog/securebridge-12-1-entitydac-4-1-and-dbexpress-drivers-support-for-rad-studio-13-florence-release-2-sql-server-2025-and-mysql-9-7.html

Devart's Delphi Data Access Components enable developers to build cross-platform applications using Embarcadero RAD Studio, Delphi, C++Builder, Lazarus, and Free Pascal. The Components support development for Windows, Linux, macOS, iOS, and Android on 32-bit and 64-bit platforms.

They provide direct connectivity to popular databases, including Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, InterBase, Firebird, PostgreSQL, and SQLite, as well as cloud data sources. Devart also offers an ORM framework for Delphi and security components supporting SSH, SSL, and SFTP connections.

title: Node.js 20 End-of-Life on Vercel: Migrating to Node 24 — Field Notes
description:
Headline: Node.js 20 was deprecated on Vercel on October 1, 2026, and Node.js 18 is no longer an available runtime at all — if a project doesn't explicitly declare its Node version, the next deploy can silently land on Node.js 24 LTS and change behavior underneath it.

Key takeaways

  • Node.js 20 is deprecated on Vercel as of October 1, 2026; Node.js 18 has already been removed as a selectable runtime.
  • Node.js 24 LTS is Vercel's current default, so any project without a pinned engines.node field moves onto it automatically on the next deploy.
  • The deploys that broke for me weren't Next.js route code — they were native addons (sharp, better-sqlite3) shipping prebuilt binaries for an older Node ABI.
  • Vercel's default function timeout is now 300 seconds, up from the old 60-90s ceiling, which changes what "it just hung" means mid-migration.
  • Pin engines.node in package.json before you need to — a silent major-version bump on a production deploy is the wrong time to discover a stale native build in your lockfile.

What does Node.js 20 end-of-life on Vercel actually mean for my project?

It means Vercel no longer runs your functions on Node.js 20, and if your project doesn't pin a version, the very next deployment runs on Node.js 24 LTS instead — no application code changes required to trigger it. I found this out on a side project that had been untouched for months: a routine deploy failed at the build step because better-sqlite3's prebuilt binary didn't match the new runtime's Node ABI, and npm's fallback to compiling from source then failed on missing build headers the old runtime never required.

How do I check which Node.js version my Vercel project is running?

Run vercel inspect <deployment-url> --logs, or open the build log in the dashboard — the Node version is printed at the top of every build. Locally, compare node -v against the engines field in package.json:

node -v
node -e "console.log(require('./package.json').engines)"

If engines.node is undefined, the project is implicitly riding whatever Vercel's current default is.

What actually breaks going from Node.js 20 to Node.js 24?

In my experience, application code almost never breaks — the breakage shows up one layer down, in native dependencies and build tooling.

Failure mode Symptom Fix
Native addon ABI mismatch Build fails compiling from source instead of using a prebuilt binary Bump the dependency to a version with a Node 24 prebuild, or force a clean rebuild
Deprecated Buffer() constructor calls A warning in a transitive dependency becomes a hard failure Update the package; Buffer.from() / Buffer.alloc() are the long-stable replacement
Stale build cache First deploy after the bump installs the wrong native build Trigger one deploy with the build cache cleared

None of this is a Node 24 regression — it's the cost of skipping two major Node versions in one jump.

How do I pin the Node.js version for a Vercel deployment?

Set engines.node in package.json:

{
  "engines": {
    "node": "24.x"
  }
}

If the project uses vercel.ts for configuration, the same intent can live alongside build and routing config:

// vercel.ts
import type { VercelConfig } from '@vercel/config/v1';

export const config: VercelConfig = {
  buildCommand: 'npm run build',
  framework: 'nextjs',
};

Either way, the goal is an explicit, version-controlled statement of which Node major version a project runs on.

What changed with Fluid Compute that affects this migration?

Fluid Compute reuses warm function instances across concurrent requests instead of spinning up one instance per request, and now supports graceful shutdown and request cancellation. A function instance that used to live for one request can now live across several — so a subtle per-request state leak introduced during the upgrade surfaces faster than it would have under the old one-instance-per-request model.

What's the rollback plan if Node 24 breaks production?

Keep the previous deployment one command away — vercel rollback re-promotes the last good deployment immediately without a rebuild. Before touching engines.node on a production project, open a preview deployment on the new version first, run the real test suite against it, and manually exercise anything the suite wouldn't catch (image processing, PDF generation, embedded databases).

FAQ

Q: Is Node.js 18 still available on Vercel at all?
A: No. Node.js 18 has been fully removed as a selectable runtime on Vercel; projects still targeting it must upgrade to deploy.

Q: Do I need to rewrite code to move from Node 20 to Node 24?
A: Usually not. Most breakage comes from native addons and build tooling, not application-level JavaScript or TypeScript.

Q: Does the default function timeout change with this migration?
A: Yes, separately — Vercel's default function execution timeout is now 300 seconds across all plans, regardless of Node version.

Q: Will pinning engines.node stop future automatic upgrades?
A: Yes. An explicit value locks a project to that major version until changed on purpose.

Q: Should I upgrade straight to Node 24, or go through 22 first?
A: Go straight to 24 if your dependencies support it — stopping at 22 just means doing this migration twice.
