title: Seed the Chaos: Making Random Bugs Reproducible
description:
Every game that shuffles, spawns or rolls dice has a quiet problem: the bug that happened once and never again.

A tester sees the shop hand out the wrong reward. Nobody can make it happen twice. Without a way back to that exact run, the report is stuck: someone saw something, and nobody can prove what.

Randomness feels like the enemy of testing. It does not have to be. The same generator that makes a run unpredictable can make it exactly repeatable, if you keep one small piece of information: the seed.

A seed is a recipe, not a recording

Most engines let you set the starting seed of their random number generator. Godot's RandomNumberGenerator does. Give two runs the same seed and the generator produces the same sequence of numbers in both.

That gets you most of a replay, not all of it. An exact replay needs the same seed, the same code, the same engine version and the same inputs in the same order. Change any of them and the same seed tells a different story. A seed is the recipe for the randomness, not a recording of the run.

Two habits make seeds useful. Log the initial seed at the start of every run, meaning the seed the run began with, not the generator's later state. And log the build with it, so "cannot reproduce" at least means "cannot reproduce on this version".

Chaos, but on a schedule

Once every run has a seed, testing stops needing luck.

The practical setup is simple: an automated job plays seeded games and writes one line per failure - the seed it started from, the build, and the assertion that broke. The review comes down to three questions. Did anything fail? Does it fail again on the same seed and the same build? Is the failing state a real defect, or an expectation that aged?

On a quiet day the answers take minutes. On the day that matters, there is a reproduction already in hand instead of a theory.

The honest limits

Determinism covers logic. It does not cover timing, floating-point differences across devices, or the physics of a real thumb. A seeded replay can prove the shuffle behaved for that seed on that build. It cannot prove the game felt fair, any more than a passing screenshot proves a player understood the screen. I wrote about that boundary in an earlier piece (https://dev.to/kfiradut/a-test-report-should-say-what-it-cannot-prove-3i0i); it applies here with full force.

And some real defects stay intermittent even with seeds: race conditions, memory pressure, hardware quirks. A seed does not solve those. It gives every report somewhere concrete to start, instead of a shrug.

Why it is worth it

Reproducible randomness is not only for debugging. It is a design tool.

Balance questions stop being arguments from one lucky session. You can run a difficulty change across the same thousand seeds as the old one and compare what actually moved. The randomness becomes a fixed laboratory instead of weather.

Chaos is fine. Seed it first.

In my game projects, Instinct does much of the implementation and testing. I stay responsible for direction and for the decision to ship.

References:

  • RandomNumberGenerator - Godot Engine documentation: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_randomnumbergenerator.html
  • Random number generation - Godot Engine documentation: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/math/random_number_generation.html

title: Build a Web Research Agent With Google ADK and Zenrows
description:
This article was originally published on the Zenrows blog.

Your research agent might be reading fake pages. When a target sits behind Cloudflare, a plain requests call returns a 403 and a "Just a moment..." challenge page in place of the content. Unless the tool checks for that, the agent can treat the challenge markup as the answer and report on a page it never saw.

In this tutorial, you'll see how that happens and how to fix it in a Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) agent. You'll give the agent a web tool that routes each fetch through Zenrows Fetch and returns the page as Markdown, then connect a second agent to the hosted Zenrows MCP server with no function code. You'll need Python 3.10 or later, a Google AI Studio API key, and a Zenrows API key. The free plan includes 5,000 credits a month. The complete code is on GitHub.

What You'll Build

  • You'll register a function tool, fetch_protected_page, on a Gemini-powered ADK agent.
  • You'll write a comparison script that fetches one URL with plain HTTP and with Zenrows.
  • You'll add a second agent that loads the Zenrows MCP tools through ADK's MCPToolset.

1. Set Up the Project 

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

The pinned requirements.txt installs google-adk 2.9.2 with its MCP extra.

google-adk[mcp]==2.9.2
mcp==1.30.0
python-dotenv==1.2.3
requests==2.34.2
pytest==9.1.1
ruff==0.16.8
-e .

Copy the environment template and add your keys. The .gitignore excludes .env.

cp .env.example .env

GOOGLE_API_KEY=your_google_api_key
ZENROWS_API_KEY=your_zenrows_api_key

Here's the project layout.

google-adk-zenrows-research-agent/
├── scripts/
│   ├── compare_fetch.py
│   └── list_mcp_tools.py
├── tests/
│   ├── test_agent.py
│   ├── test_mcp_agent.py
│   └── test_web.py
├── zenrows_mcp_agent/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── agent.py
├── zenrows_research_agent/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── agent.py
│   └── web.py
├── .env.example
├── .gitignore
├── LICENSE
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
└── requirements.txt

2. Write the Fetch Function

Create zenrows_research_agent/web.py.

"""Web retrieval tools used by the Google ADK agent."""
import os
import requests
ZENROWS_ENDPOINT = "https://api.zenrows.com/v1/"
DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 180
MAX_TOOL_CONTENT = 12_000
def fetch_with_http(url: str) -> dict:
    """Fetch a public URL with a standard HTTP request for comparison."""
    try:
        # send the request without a protected-site access service.
        response = requests.get(
            url,
            headers={"User-Agent": "google-adk-research-agent/0.1"},
            timeout=20,
        )
    except requests.RequestException as exc:
        return {"status": "error", "url": url, "error": str(exc)}
    return {
        "status": "success" if response.ok else "blocked",
        "url": url,
        "status_code": response.status_code,
        "content": response.text[:2_000],
    }
def fetch_protected_page(url: str) -> dict:
    """Fetch a protected or JavaScript-rendered page through Zenrows.
    Args:
        url: The complete public URL the research agent needs to read.
    Returns:
        A dictionary containing the request status, source URL, and page content.
    """
    api_key = os.getenv("ZENROWS_API_KEY")
    if not api_key:
        return {
            "status": "error",
            "url": url,
            "error": "ZENROWS_API_KEY is not configured.",
        }
    # let Adaptive Stealth Mode select the request configuration.
    params = {
        "apikey": api_key,
        "url": url,
        "mode": "auto",
        "response_type": "markdown",
        "original_status": "true",
    }
    try:
        # give Adaptive Stealth Mode enough time to retrieve the page.
        response = requests.get(
            ZENROWS_ENDPOINT,
            params=params,
            timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT,
        )
        response.raise_for_status()
    except requests.RequestException as exc:
        # remove the API key from the error text before it reaches the model.
        error = str(exc).replace(api_key, "[REDACTED]")
        return {"status": "error", "url": url, "error": error}
    # do not return a successful result without page content.
    if not response.text.strip():
        return {
            "status": "error",
            "url": url,
            "error": "Zenrows returned an empty response.",
        }
    return {
        "status": "success",
        "url": url,
        "content": response.text[:MAX_TOOL_CONTENT],
    }

fetch_protected_page sends the URL to Zenrows with mode=auto, which turns on Adaptive Stealth Mode. It starts with the lightest configuration likely to work and escalates only when the target needs it. A few safeguards keep the agent honest.

  • response_type=markdown returns readable text in place of raw HTML.
  • original_status=true passes through the target's status code, so an error page from the target counts as an error.
  • The 180-second timeout gives mode=auto room to finish on protected targets.
  • Content is capped at 12,000 characters, and an empty response is reported as an error.
  • The API key is redacted from any error text before it reaches the model. fetch_with_http is a plain request used only for the comparison. ## 3. Register the Function as an ADK Tool Create zenrows_research_agent/agent.py. 
"""Google ADK agent configuration."""
from pathlib import Path
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from google.adk.agents import Agent
from .web import fetch_protected_page
# load the API keys stored in the project environment file.
load_dotenv(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / ".env")
# register the Zenrows retrieval function as an ADK tool.
root_agent = Agent(
    model="gemini-3.6-flash",
    name="web_research_agent",
    description="Researches public web pages that ordinary HTTP tools cannot read.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a web research agent. Use fetch_protected_page whenever a task "
        "requires content from a supplied URL. Base the answer only on returned "
        "page content, mention the source URL, and state clearly when retrieval "
        "fails or the page does not contain the requested information."
    ),
    tools=[fetch_protected_page],
)

ADK builds the tool schema from the function's name, type hints, and docstring, so the model only has to supply a URL.

4. Compare Plain HTTP With Zenrows

Create scripts/compare_fetch.py.

"""Compare standard HTTP access with Zenrows access."""
import json
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from zenrows_research_agent.web import fetch_protected_page, fetch_with_http
TARGET_URL = "https://www.scrapingcourse.com/cloudflare-challenge"
def summarize(result: dict) -> dict:
    """Reduce a fetch result to fields that are safe to print."""
    return {
        "status": result["status"],
        "url": result["url"],
        "status_code": result.get("status_code"),
        "content_preview": result.get("content", "")[:300],
        "error": result.get("error"),
    }
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # load the Zenrows API key from the project environment.
    load_dotenv()
    # retrieve the same URL through both access methods.
    comparison = {
        "standard_http": summarize(fetch_with_http(TARGET_URL)),
        "zenrows": summarize(fetch_protected_page(TARGET_URL)),
    }
    # print the comparison without exposing the API key.
    print(json.dumps(comparison, indent=2))

python scripts/compare_fetch.py

{
  "standard_http": {
    "status": "blocked",
    "url": "https://www.scrapingcourse.com/cloudflare-challenge",
    "status_code": 403,
    "content_preview": "<!DOCTYPE html><html lang=\"en-US\"><head><title>Just a moment...</title><meta http-equiv=\"Content-Type\" content=\"text/html; charset=UTF-8\"><meta http-equiv=\"X-UA-Compatible\" content=\"IE=Edge\"><meta name=\"robots\" content=\"noindex,nofollow\"><meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width,initial-scal",
    "error": null
  },
  "zenrows": {
    "status": "success",
    "url": "https://www.scrapingcourse.com/cloudflare-challenge",
    "status_code": null,
    "content_preview": "[![](https://www.scrapingcourse.com/assets/images/logo.svg) Scraping Course](http://www.scrapingcourse.com/)\n\n# Cloudflare Challenge\n\n![](https://www.scrapingcourse.com/assets/images/challenge.svg)\n\n## You bypassed the Cloudflare challenge! :D",
    "error": null
  }
}

The plain request got a 403 and the challenge page. Zenrows returned the page heading and the verification message. The Zenrows status_code reads null because the function doesn't return it.

5. Run the Agent 

adk run zenrows_research_agent

Submit this task.

Fetch https://www.scrapingcourse.com/cloudflare-challenge and report the page title, whether the challenge was passed, and the visible verification text. Cite the source URL.

[web_research_agent]: Based on the content retrieved from [https://www.scrapingcourse.com/cloudflare-challenge](https://www.scrapingcourse.com/cloudflare-challenge):
* **Page Title / Main Heading:** Cloudflare Challenge
* **Challenge Status:** Passed / Bypassed
* **Visible Verification Text:** "You bypassed the Cloudflare challenge! :D"
* **Source URL:** `https://www.scrapingcourse.com/cloudflare-challenge`

Run adk web if you'd prefer to test in ADK's browser UI.

6. Connect the Zenrows MCP Server

Create zenrows_mcp_agent/agent.py.

"""Google ADK agent that uses the hosted Zenrows MCP server."""
import os
from pathlib import Path
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from google.adk.agents import Agent
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool import MCPToolset, StreamableHTTPConnectionParams
# load the API keys stored in the project environment file.
load_dotenv(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / ".env")
# connect to the hosted Zenrows MCP server with the API key as a bearer token.
zenrows_toolset = MCPToolset(
    connection_params=StreamableHTTPConnectionParams(
        url="https://mcp.zenrows.com/mcp",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.getenv('ZENROWS_API_KEY', '')}"},
    )
)
# the agent chooses between the Zenrows scrape and browser tools on its own.
root_agent = Agent(
    model="gemini-3.6-flash",
    name="web_research_mcp_agent",
    description="Researches public web pages through the Zenrows MCP server.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a web research agent. Use the Zenrows tools whenever a task "
        "requires content from a supplied URL. Base the answer only on returned "
        "page content, mention the source URL, and state clearly when retrieval "
        "fails or the page does not contain the requested information."
    ),
    tools=[zenrows_toolset],
)

MCPToolset connects to https://mcp.zenrows.com/mcp with your API key as a bearer token, and ADK loads the server's tools. Check which ones arrived with scripts/list_mcp_tools.py.

"""Check which Zenrows MCP tools Google ADK loads for the MCP agent."""
import asyncio
from zenrows_mcp_agent.agent import zenrows_toolset
RESEARCH_TOOLS = ["scrape", "extract", "crawl_create", "batch_create", "browser_navigate"]
async def main() -> None:
    # ask the hosted Zenrows MCP server which tools it exposes.
    tools = await zenrows_toolset.get_tools()
    await zenrows_toolset.close()
    names = {tool.name for tool in tools}
    # confirm the tools a research agent relies on are loaded.
    print(f"Loaded {len(names)} Zenrows tools")
    for name in RESEARCH_TOOLS:
        print(f"{name}: {'available' if name in names else 'not loaded'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

python scripts/list_mcp_tools.py
adk run zenrows_mcp_agent

Loaded 62 Zenrows tools
scrape: available
extract: available
crawl_create: available
batch_create: available
browser_navigate: available

ADK prints experimental-feature warnings before that output.

Function Tool or MCP Server

Function tool Zenrows MCP
What the agent calls fetch_protected_page, one typed function scrape, extract, Crawl, Batch, and browser tools
Request settings Fixed in code (mode=auto, Markdown) Chosen by the MCP server per task
Code you maintain The function and its tests One MCPToolset block
Pick it when You want one fixed, typed request You want the agent to choose among scraping, crawling, and browser actions

Wrapping Up

Your ADK agent now reads protected pages as Markdown through a typed function, and a second agent reaches the full Zenrows toolset over MCP. Change the URL and the prompt to point it at your own research tasks.

What's Next

  • Use Extract with extract=auto when you need structured JSON fields.
  • Discover linked pages with Crawl or run large URL lists as one job with Batch.
  • Build the same idea with Agno and Zenrows or as a multi-agent system with AG2.

title: MySQL LIMIT and OFFSET Explained with Simple Examples
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

In MySQL, LIMIT controls how many rows a query returns, and OFFSET controls how many rows to skip before returning them. Together they answer questions like "show me the first 10 students" or "show me page 3 of the results, 10 per page". If you have ever seen a website split a long list into pages, this simple pair of clauses is almost certainly doing the work behind the scenes.

Why Limit Rows at All?

A table can hold ten rows today and ten lakh rows next year. A query with no limit happily returns all of them — slowly, and in no useful order for a human reader. Limiting rows keeps queries fast, keeps pages light, and gives users results in digestible chunks. It is the database version of asking a librarian for the first shelf of books instead of having the whole library dumped on your desk. MySQL itself rewards this habit: the official manual explains that when you need only a specified number of rows, using a LIMIT clause is better than fetching the whole result and throwing the extra data away. The MySQL Reference Manual page on LIMIT query optimisation goes into how MySQL can even stop early once it has found enough rows.

LIMIT: The Basic Form

Start with a simple students table. To fetch only the first five rows, add LIMIT 5 at the end of your query:

SELECT id, name, marks
FROM students
LIMIT 5;

That returns at most five rows — fewer if the table is smaller, which is perfectly normal and not an error. One warning that surprises every beginner sooner or later: without an ORDER BY, "first five" means "any five the database happens to reach first". The order is not promised, and it can change. If order matters — and for humans it almost always does — always sort first, as the next section shows.

ORDER BY + LIMIT: Top 10 Lists

The most famous use of LIMIT is the top-N list: the ten highest marks, the five newest posts, the three cheapest products. The pattern is always the same — sort by the column you care about, then limit.

SELECT id, name, marks
FROM students
ORDER BY marks DESC
LIMIT 10;

Here DESC sorts from highest to lowest, so the limit keeps the top ten scorers. Flip it to ASC and you get the ten lowest instead. The full syntax of the statement, including every clause order, is documented on the official MySQL SELECT syntax page — a dry page, admittedly, but the final word when a query behaves strangely.

The official MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual page on LIMIT query optimisation on dev.mysql.com.

OFFSET: Skipping Rows for Pagination

OFFSET skips rows before the limit applies. LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10 skips the first ten rows and returns the next ten — in other words, page two, if each page shows ten rows. The maths for any page is simple:

Page Rows per page OFFSET Query ending
1 10 0 LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0
2 10 10 LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10
3 10 20 LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20
5 10 40 LIMIT 10 OFFSET 40

The formula is: offset = (page − 1) × rows per page. MySQL also offers a shorter two-number form, LIMIT 20, 10, which means "skip 20, take 10" — the same as LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20. Both forms are correct; the long form with the OFFSET keyword is easier for beginners to read six months later, which is a perfectly good reason to prefer it.

-- Page 3, ten rows per page
SELECT id, name, marks
FROM students
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

Notice the ORDER BY id. For pagination it is not optional decoration: pages must be slices of one stable order, otherwise the same row can appear on two pages, or vanish between them, like a book whose pages shuffle themselves while you read.

Using LIMIT in a Real PHP Page

In a real website, the page number arrives from the URL, and PHP turns it into an offset. That is exactly the technique behind our tutorial on adding search and pagination to a PHP and MySQL listing page, which builds the full feature with page links. The core idea fits in a few lines:

$page = max(1, (int)($_GET['page'] ?? 1));
$perPage = 10;
$offset = ($page - 1) * $perPage;

$stmt = $pdo->prepare(
    "SELECT id, name, marks FROM students
     ORDER BY id LIMIT :limit OFFSET :offset"
);
$stmt->bindValue(':limit', $perPage, PDO::PARAM_INT);
$stmt->bindValue(':offset', $offset, PDO::PARAM_INT);
$stmt->execute();

Two details matter here. First, cast the page number to an integer — never trust URL input as-is. Second, bind the limit and offset as integers, not strings; MySQL is picky about that, and many a beginner has lost an evening to this exact quirk. If the language-versus-software distinction still feels fuzzy, our explainer on SQL vs MySQL clears it up in a few minutes.

One More Everyday Pattern: The Latest Five

Blogs, shops and dashboards all share one favourite query: "show the latest five". Latest means sorted by date or by ID, highest first, limited to five — the same top-N pattern, just wearing a different shirt.

SELECT id, title, created_at
FROM posts
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 5;

Try it with different numbers and orders until the pattern feels automatic: newest five posts, oldest three comments awaiting moderation, the two most recent orders for one customer (add a WHERE customer_id = 7 before the ORDER BY). Notice how WHERE filters first, ORDER BY sorts what remains, and LIMIT trims the sorted result last. That clause order — filter, sort, trim — is the mental model that makes almost every reporting query fall into place. Once it clicks, you will find yourself reading other people's queries and understanding them at a glance, which is a quietly satisfying milestone on the road from beginner to working developer.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

First, forgetting ORDER BY, as covered above — the classic. Second, off-by-one page maths: page 1 must use offset 0, not offset 10, or your first ten rows will never be seen by anyone. Third, huge offsets on very large tables: OFFSET 100000 still makes MySQL walk past those rows, so deep pages get slower. For ordinary student and small-business projects this is fine, but if you ever build something huge, look up keyset pagination, which jumps by the last seen ID instead. Fourth, limiting without thinking about totals: a page footer that says "Page 2 of 9" needs a separate count query, because LIMIT deliberately does not tell you how many rows exist in total.

What is the difference between LIMIT and OFFSET?

LIMIT says how many rows to return. OFFSET says how many rows to skip first. Page 1 uses an offset of 0; every later page increases it.

Does LIMIT make my query faster?

Often, yes. MySQL can stop once it has enough rows, especially with a matching index and ORDER BY. But a very large OFFSET still costs time, because the skipped rows must be counted past.

What does LIMIT 5, 10 mean?

It is the short form: skip 5 rows, then return 10. That is the same as LIMIT 10 OFFSET 5. The first number is the offset, the second is the count.

Can I use LIMIT with UPDATE or DELETE?

Yes, MySQL allows a simple LIMIT on those statements too, for example deleting only the oldest 100 rows at a time. There is no OFFSET in that form, so use it carefully and always with a clear ORDER BY.

Conclusion

LIMIT decides how many rows come back, OFFSET decides where the window starts, and ORDER BY keeps the whole thing honest. Memorise the page formula — offset equals page minus one, times rows per page — and you can build top-10 lists, paginated tables and tidy reports in any project. It is a small clause with an outsized effect on how professional your application feels.

title: Empowering AI Agents with agent-desktop
description:
A New Approach to the Problem

The agent-desktop repository addresses the challenge of enabling AI agents to effectively interact with desktop applications across different operating systems. By leveraging the OS accessibility tree, it allows agents to read and operate applications without pixel matching, which is often unreliable.

What is it and How it Works

agent-desktop is a CLI and C library developed for macOS, Windows, and Linux. It creates snapshots of the desktop environment, returning JSON representations of all elements an agent can interact with. The agent executes actions on these elements and verifies changes without requiring pixel recognition. Each CLI call operates in its own process, ensuring that headless calls do not interfere with the foreground application.

Key Features:

  • Cross-Platform Compatibility: Works on macOS, Windows, and Linux.
  • Snapshot Functionality: Returns a JSON object with references for every interactive element, allowing agents to perform actions and verify their results.
  • No Pixel Matching Required: The system uses the accessibility API, which is more reliable than pixel-based methods.
  • Privacy Considerations: Snapshots and outputs may contain sensitive data; users should manage this information carefully.

Key Capabilities & Developer Onboarding

Installation is straightforward via npm, Bun, Yarn, or pnpm:

npm install -g agent-desktop
agent-desktop version

For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, users can download the native archive from GitHub Releases and keep its helper beside the executable.

Here’s a quick start example showing how to interact with the Finder app on macOS:

agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i      # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8            # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i      # observe again to verify

The JSON response includes details about the application state, making it easier for developers to understand the environment.

Who Should Use It & Integration Scenarios

agent-desktop is ideal for developers building AI agents that need to automate desktop tasks across multiple operating systems. It is particularly useful for applications requiring interaction with GUI elements without direct user input. However, it may not be suitable for scenarios demanding real-time visual feedback or where pixel precision is critical.

Limitations & Trade-offs:

  • Platform-Specific Permissions: On macOS, accessibility permissions are required, which can add complexity to deployment.
  • Headless Operation Constraints: Although the system is headless by default, it requires a graphical session on Linux, which can limit usability in certain environments.
  • No Foreground Activation: Actions performed do not activate the foreground application, which may not align with all automation needs.

Community Pulse: What Developers Are Saying

Community discussions indicate a growing interest in the agent-desktop project, especially following the recent release of version v1.0.2 on October 30, 2026, which introduced various documentation improvements and clarified installation permissions. Users appreciate the simplicity of the API and the potential for integrating AI-driven workflows into desktop environments.

Our Read

Overall, agent-desktop presents a compelling solution for AI agent interactions with desktop applications, emphasizing cross-platform compatibility and privacy considerations. While it offers significant capabilities, potential users should be mindful of its limitations, particularly regarding permissions and headless operation constraints.

title: Building a 3D yoga anatomy viewer for the web, with 222 poses and no giant animation download
description:
I'm building a free web tool that shows which muscles contract, lengthen, or stabilize in each yoga pose. You rotate the model and click a muscle to see its name and role. The live version is here: 3D Yoga Anatomy.

This post isn't a feature tour. It covers the four technical problems that took the most work:

  1. Switching poses quickly without downloading every animation.
  2. Draco reordering vertices, which breaks per-vertex corrections.
  3. Picking the right muscle on a SkinnedMesh.
  4. Audio going silent because a proxy cached a 206 response.

Stack: React, React Three Fiber, three.js, Draco, three-mesh-bvh, and gltf-transform. The model is processed with Blender and Python, and the site is deployed on Vercel. Most of the code and the model pipeline was written with Claude Code.

The model pipeline

The source data is Z-Anatomy and BodyParts3D, an open anatomy atlas. The pipeline looks like this:

Z-Anatomy (.blend)
  → keep 50 muscles + the skeleton, normalize names
  → auto-rig and bake each pose in Blender
  → export one GLB containing every clip
  → split into base.glb + one small pack per clip
  → React Three Fiber viewer

Teaching data, such as each muscle's state in each pose, lives in separate JSON files. A muscle is active, lengthened, or stabilizing.

1. Don't put 335 clips in one GLB

There are 222 poses and 335 clips, because asymmetric poses have a clip for each side. In a single GLB, viewing one pose would mean downloading all of them.

So I split it:

File Actual size
base.glb: rigged model, Draco-compressed, no animation 3.4 MB
Each <clip>.pose.bin pack 176 KB on average, 401 KB at most
All 335 packs, if you had to download them about 58 MB

Pack sizes are before brotli. The viewer only fetches the pack for the current pose.

What's in a pack?

Bone rotation alone (skinning) tends to collapse joints and make muscles look wrong in deep bends. So each pose also has corrective shape keys: offsets for the specific vertices that need fixing. This data is very sparse, so most vertices don't need an entry.

The current format:

"YPK2" | header length (u32 LE) | header JSON | varint body

header: { clip, scale, tracks, entries }
  tracks  = the static pose of the bones
  entries = corrected regions, per primitive

body, for each entry:
  - vertex ids: LEB128 gaps from the previous id (ascending)
  - x, y, z: one stream per axis, zigzag varints of the delta to the previous vertex

Offsets are quantized to 0.25 mm, so the maximum error is 0.125 mm. A vertex that rounds to zero on all three axes is dropped.

Three things add up:

  • Store differences, not values. Neighboring vertices tend to move by similar amounts, so the numbers stay small.
  • Keep each axis in its own stream. Similar small numbers sit next to each other, which brotli compresses well.
  • Let Vercel serve the files with brotli. In my tests this compressed about twice as well as the previous format, which used raw Int16.

GPU memory doesn't grow with the pose count

If each pose were its own morph target, memory would grow with every pose viewed. I keep exactly two slots instead, as cs0 and cs1 attributes on each mesh:

for (const name of ['cs0', 'cs1']) {
  if (g.attributes[name]) continue;
  const a = new THREE.BufferAttribute(new Float32Array(n * 3), 3);
  a.setUsage(THREE.DynamicDrawUsage);
  g.setAttribute(name, a);
}

When the pose changes, the new data goes into the free slot. The old pose fades out and the new one fades in over 0.8 seconds, and each slot's weight follows its animation. The next change uses the other slot. Only the changed ranges of the buffer are uploaded, not the whole attribute.

2. Draco reorders vertices

A pack says "vertex 1234 moves by this much". But Draco reorders vertices when it compresses, so after decoding, vertex 1234 is a different vertex. If you don't handle this, muscles deform at random.

The fix is to give each primitive a _VID attribute holding the original vertex id. At runtime, the viewer builds a reverse lookup:

private vidToIndex(g: THREE.BufferGeometry): Int32Array {
  let inv = this.inverse.get(g);
  if (!inv) {
    const vid = g.attributes._vid;
    const n = g.attributes.position.count;
    inv = new Int32Array(n).fill(-1);
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) inv[vid ? vid.getX(i) : i] = i;
    this.inverse.set(g, inv);
  }
  return inv;
}

The part I'd recommend most is checking this at build time. The packing script decodes the file it just wrote, uses _VID to compare against the original vertex positions, and fails the build if the error passes a threshold. That way the bug shows up on the build machine, not on a user's screen.

3. Picking muscles on a SkinnedMesh

The default three.js raycast on a SkinnedMesh has two problems:

  • Bounds are computed once, in the first pose. After the figure bends over, some clicks miss or hit a muscle behind the one you meant.
  • Every tested triangle is skinned again on the CPU, so just moving the mouse can freeze the page.

My approach: once a pose has settled, snapshot each mesh's deformed positions into a static mesh with a BVH, and raycast against that.

function makeProxy(src: THREE.Mesh): THREE.Mesh {
  src.updateWorldMatrix(true, false);
  const geo = new THREE.BufferGeometry();
  geo.setAttribute('position', new THREE.BufferAttribute(deformedWorldPositions(src), 3));
  if (src.geometry.index) geo.setIndex(src.geometry.index);
  geo.boundsTree = new MeshBVH(geo) as unknown as typeof geo.boundsTree;
  geo.computeBoundingBox();
  const proxy = new THREE.Mesh(geo);
  proxy.raycast = acceleratedRaycast;
  proxy.userData.source = src;
  proxy.updateMatrixWorld(true);
  return proxy;
}

deformedWorldPositions does on the CPU what the GPU does, in the same order: morph, then skinning, then world space.

A few details keep the UI smooth:

  • Build in small steps. Each frame only spends a few milliseconds on the snapshot. If the user clicks before it's done, the rest is finished right then.
  • Keep the old snapshot until the new one is ready. It's only swapped once fully built. If the pose changes midway, the build in progress is dropped.
  • Limit hover. At most one ray per frame, and dragging to rotate the camera doesn't count as a click.
  • Pick what the user can see. Dimmed muscles are skipped, and nothing is picked if a bone is in front.

4. Silent audio from a cached 206

This has nothing to do with 3D, but it's useful to know if you proxy through Next.js on Vercel.

The tool lives at 3d.yogaway.vn and is proxied to yogaway.vn/giai-phau-3d/ with rewrites. At one point, clicking a pose or muscle stopped playing its spoken name.

The cause: when playing <audio>, the browser may first ask for Range: bytes=0-1. The proxy received a 2-byte 206 response, and the shared cache stored that fragment under the key for the whole file. Everyone after that got 2 bytes.

The fix was to keep media files off the proxy and redirect them straight to the origin, which handles Range correctly:

async redirects() {
  return [
    {
      source: "/giai-phau-3d/:path(.*\\.(?:mp3|m4a|ogg|wav|mp4|webm))",
      destination: "https://3d.yogaway.vn/:path",
      permanent: false,
    },
  ];
}

My takeaway: when a proxy caches responses, always test requests with a Range header separately.

What isn't good yet

Mobile performance is still modest. Pose pages show static text and a WebP image first, then build the 3D scene when the browser is idle. In a Lighthouse run on October 18, 2026, the mobile score went from 29 to 49 with a CLS of 0, but lab LCP was still 3.7 seconds because setting up three.js is expensive. Deferring the 3D until the first tap would score higher, but I chose to load it automatically because it's what people come to see.

Getting poses right is still the hardest part. The solvers can place the joints, but a yoga teacher spots mistakes quickly: an arm through a thigh, a foot sunk into the floor, a wrist bent sideways. I wrote automated checks for these:

- Parts that should touch the floor: within about 1.5 cm of z=0; nothing below -1.5 cm
- Arm vs. thigh or shin: axes at least 9 cm apart, unless the pose intends contact
- Wrist side deviation: at most 30°
- The left side must mirror the right side within 1 cm

These catch a lot, but they don't replace someone looking at the result. The poses are still being reviewed and fixed, so if you spot one that looks wrong, I'd like to hear about it.

Licensing: read it before you use open data

Z-Anatomy and BodyParts3D use CC BY-SA licenses, so derived files such as .blend and .glb must also be released under CC BY-SA 4.0 with full attribution. A few parts of Z-Anatomy, such as Inner Ear and Kidney, carry a non-commercial license, so my pipeline removes them automatically from a list in its config file.

If you plan to use an open atlas in a real product, check the license of each part at the start, not after the build is done.

Wrapping up

The biggest lesson for me was to separate data early: the model, the poses, and the teaching content all live apart. Because of that, going from 10 to 222 poses only grew the base model slightly, from about 3.2 MB to 3.4 MB.

You can try it at 3D Yoga Anatomy. If you've built a large 3D viewer for the web, I'd like to hear how you handled three.js setup time on phones.

The anatomy model is derived from Z-Anatomy (CC BY-SA 4.0; Gauthier Kervyn, Marcin Zielinski) and BodyParts3D (© The Database Center for Life Science, CC BY-SA 2.1 Japan). This tool is for learning anatomy and isn't a substitute for medical advice.

title: The Server Action That Ran Twice, but Only on localhost
description:
Picture a "mark as read" feature. Open a notification, and a Server Action flips it to read in the database and bumps a counter. You add a console.log to the action to watch it work, open the page in next dev, and the terminal prints:

[markAsRead] call #1
[markAsRead] call #2

One page load, two calls. Every time.

I rebuilt that exact setup on this blog's codebase (Next.js 16.4, React 19) as a ten-line test page, and got the same thing: two POST requests with the same next-action id in the network tab, two log lines on the server.

The wrong turn: blaming Next.js

Two calls from one load looks like a framework bug. Maybe Next.js retries actions. Maybe the page renders twice on the server and each render fires the action. Maybe HMR left an old copy of the component mounted.

None of those hold up. Here's the whole client component:

"use client";

import { useEffect } from "react";
import { markAsRead } from "./actions";

export function Notification({ id }: { id: string }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    markAsRead(id);
  }, [id]);

  return <p>…</p>;
}

Server Actions never run during rendering. They run when the browser calls them, and the only thing calling this one is useEffect. So the real question is: why does the effect run twice?

The reveal: React mounts everything twice in development

Next.js turns on React Strict Mode by default in the App Router (the reactStrictMode docs say so: it's been true by default since Next.js 13.5.1). In development, Strict Mode deliberately stress-tests every component when it first appears:

What Strict Mode does with your effect in development

1. Mount              — The component appears on the page
2. Run effect         — useEffect fires: first call to markAsRead
3. Simulated unmount  — React pretends the component left the page
4. Run cleanup        — Your cleanup function runs, if you returned one
5. Mount again        — React puts it back, keeping the same state
6. Run effect again   — useEffect fires again: second call to markAsRead

In production the middle steps don't exist, so the effect runs once.

That's why it only happens on localhost. In a production build there's no simulated remount. I checked this on a production build of the blog too: its view counter, which posts from a useEffect, sent one POST under next start and two under next dev (the first one cancelled by its cleanup).

React does this on purpose. A real user can make a component unmount and mount again: navigate away and back, or a parent that hides and shows it. Strict Mode makes that happen immediately, so you find out now whether your effect survives it.

Strict Mode isn't calling your action twice. It's showing you that your code would call it twice if the component ever remounted.

The fix: decide what the call is for

There are two kinds of "call an action when this shows up," and they get different fixes.

It's caused by something the user did. Marking as read, liking, saving, buying. These belong in an event handler or a form, not an effect. The click is the cause, so the click should make the call:

// before: fires whenever the component mounts
useEffect(() => {
  markAsRead(id);
}, [id]);

// after: fires once per click
<button onClick={() => markAsRead(id)}>Open</button>

// or with a form, which also works before JavaScript loads
<form action={markAsRead.bind(null, id)}>
  <button>Open</button>
</form>

It's caused by the component being shown. Page views and analytics are the classic case. Here the effect is the right place, so make the server safe to call twice. This blog's view counter does exactly that: the POST handler counts one read per visitor per post per day, so a second request changes nothing.

There's also the trick you'll find on Stack Overflow, a ref that remembers it already ran:

const ran = useRef(false);

useEffect(() => {
  if (ran.current) return;
  ran.current = true;
  markAsRead(id);
}, [id]);

It works: my test page logged one call with it instead of two. But the React docs advise against it, because it silences the warning without fixing the cause. The day the component really remounts, the ref starts over at false and you get a second call in production anyway.

The rule

If an action changes data because of something the user did, call it from the event that caused it. If it has to run from an effect, make the server handle it arriving twice.

TL;DR

  • Next.js enables React Strict Mode by default in the App Router, and in development Strict Mode mounts, unmounts and remounts every component.
  • So a Server Action called from useEffect runs twice in next dev and once in production.
  • In a test page on this blog, the action logged two calls in dev; a production build of the view counter sent one request.
  • Move user-caused mutations (read, like, save) into event handlers or <form action>.
  • For effects that must call the server, like view tracking, make the endpoint idempotent instead of hiding the second call with a ref.

Originally published on Bitlyst.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI functions and improvements are available in Preview:

  • The ai.extract function lets you extract structured data from unstructured text directly within your database queries without needing external extraction pipelines. For more information, see Extract structured data.

  • The ai.classify function lets you categorize unstructured text into predefined labels directly within your database queries. For more information, see Classify text.

  • Parameter names and signatures for AI query engine functions (ai.analyze_sentiment, ai.summarize, and ai.agg_summarize) are updated. For more information, see Model endpoint reference.

    • The prompt and prompts parameters are renamed to input and inputs in scalar and batch functions respectively.

    • An optional additional_instructions parameter is added to ai.summarize and ai.agg_summarize to provide custom instructions to guide summary formatting, length, and tone.

    • In cursor-based versions of ai.analyze_sentiment and ai.summarize, the prompt parameter is removed.

    • ai.agg_summarize supports multiple positional signatures, including passing optional additional instructions and specifying model IDs.

Apigee X

Feature

The Apigee API Health & Availability dashboard is now generally available in Cloud Monitoring to help you monitor the health, performance, and availability of your Apigee API proxies in real time:

  • Golden signal scorecards: track aggregate Traffic (requests per second), Error Rate (5xx), and Latency (p95) scorecards.
  • Status code and error trends: visualize the Request Rate by Status Code chart over time and identify problematic APIs using the dedicated 5xx Error Rate by Proxy and 4xx Error Rate by Proxy charts.
  • Granular filtering: filter telemetry by project_id, location, and proxy_name to troubleshoot specific regions or proxies.

For more information, see API Monitoring.

You can manage and version control SQL scripts and notebooks with BigQuery Studio Git repositories, which provide a streamlined, folder-based integration with remote Git repositories. This feature is generally available (GA).

This feature is generally available (GA).

This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

Feature

Regular expression URL rewrites (regexRewrite) for route rules in URL maps are now generally available (GA) for Application Load Balancers.   • Cross-region internal Application Load Balancers

  • Regional internal Application Load Balancers

For more information, see Regular expression URL rewrites for route rules.

title: An Open-Source Scanner That Tells You Exactly How to Get Quantum-Ready
description:
Hackers Are Already Stealing Your Data — They Just Can't Read It Yet

October 2026 was brutal. Sony Network Communications leaked 2.5 million customer records. Hackers exploited a VMmanager zero-day at FirstVDS to walk out with passwords, cloud credentials, and crypto wallet files. The University of Copenhagen exposed 525,000 people through a compromised test environment. Japan Airlines bled 92,000 customer records through Amadeus. CISA issued an emergency directive after attackers chained an Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day to exfiltrate credentials at scale.

That's one month. And every byte of that stolen data was encrypted in transit with classical TLS.

Here's the part most teams haven't internalized: attackers don't need to break your encryption today. They just need to copy the ciphertext. State-backed groups are already intercepting and stockpiling encrypted traffic to decrypt later once quantum computers can break RSA and ECC. The U.S. Department of State has confirmed that nation-state actors "sit at our boundary, collect encrypted information to decrypt later." Thales reports that harvest-now-decrypt-later is now the leading quantum-related concern, cited by 61% of organizations.

If your data has a shelf life longer than a decade — trade secrets, infrastructure credentials, health records, customer PII — the window to protect it is now, not when quantum computers arrive. Every day your traffic moves over classical-only TLS is another day of exposure to a future adversary who's already recording.

The good news: the tools to fix this exist today. The hard part is knowing where to start.

Q-Day Is a Migration Problem, Not a Research Problem

The post-quantum algorithms are standardized (FIPS 203/204/205). OpenSSL 3.5, Node 22, and .NET 10 already ship ML-KEM support. The cryptography isn't the bottleneck anymore — knowing what to change, where to change it, and in what order is.

Most teams stall out on the same questions:

  • Where does TLS actually terminate — my code, a library, or the load balancer in front of it?
  • If I upgrade a dependency, does that even change the negotiated crypto?
  • What's the smallest, safest change I can make right now?

pqmap is an open-source CLI that answers all three. Scan your codebase, get a readiness score, and receive a concrete remediation plan — pointed at the right layer, not guesswork.

Built for the Languages and Frameworks You Actually Use

pqmap ships with a data-driven catalog covering 50+ frameworks across seven languages, and adding more is just adding TOML rows — no Rust compilation required.

Currently supported:

Language Clients Servers
JavaScript / TypeScript fetch, axios, got, undici, node-fetch Express, NestJS, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, Nuxt
C# / .NET HttpClient, IHttpClientFactory, gRPC ASP.NET Core (Kestrel), HttpSys
Python requests, httpx, aiohttp, urllib3, grpc FastAPI, Flask, Django, uvicorn, gunicorn
Java HttpClient, OkHttp, gRPC Spring Boot, Tomcat, Jetty
Go net/http, grpc-go http.Server, ServeTLS
Rust reqwest, hyper, tonic axum, rustls

pqmap doesn't grep for string patterns. It resolves imports, aliases, and dependency-injection wiring (AddHttpClient<T>() in C#, axios.create({baseURL}) in JS, RestTemplate in Java) to trace each network call back to its actual TLS owner.

The Key Insight: Your Code Probably Doesn't Terminate TLS

In most production deployments, an ALB, CloudFront distribution, nginx reverse proxy, or Envoy sidecar terminates TLS before your application code ever sees the request. Upgrading your Python library to support ML-KEM does nothing if AWS ALB is the actual TLS terminator — and ALB is still classical-only.

pqmap catches this. It parses your infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, CDK, CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests) and maps each code-level network edge to its outermost TLS terminator. When your code says one thing and your infrastructure says another, pqmap flags it as a misleading code finding — so you don't waste time fixing the wrong layer.

Architecture: Clean Enough to Contribute To

pqmap is a Rust workspace split into six focused crates. Each one has a single job and a clear boundary:

pqmap/
├── core/       # The data model — NetworkEdge, EndpointGraph, PqAssessment
├── kb/         # Crypto-capability matrix (TOML with provenance per row)
├── analyzers/  # Language-aware scanners + infrastructure detection
├── scoring/    # Two-axis scoring engine + remediation ladder
├── probe/      # Built-in TLS handshake verification (rustls + ML-KEM)
└── cli/        # The five commands you actually run

This separation matters for contributors. Want to add Django REST Framework detection? You only touch analyzers/ and a TOML catalog file. Want to add a new infrastructure provider? Same pattern. The core data model stays stable while the detection surface grows.

The Knowledge Base Is the Moat

The most valuable part of pqmap is the crypto-capability matrix — a curated TOML dataset mapping runtimes, libraries, and infrastructure to their actual PQ support:

[[crypto]]
row_id      = "openssl-3.5-linux"
runtime     = "openssl"
version_min = "3.5"
pq_kem      = true
pq_sig      = false
source_url  = "https://www.openssl.org/news/changes.html#OpenSSL-3.5.0"
as_of       = "2025-09-10"

[[infra]]
row_id     = "aws-alb"
name       = "aws-alb"
pq_kem     = false
source_url = "https://docs.aws.amazon.com/..."
as_of      = "2025-06-01"

Every claim carries a source URL and date. Stale rows degrade to unknown — never a stale true. This is the kind of shared knowledge that gets better with more contributors: if you know when GCP Cloud Load Balancing adds ML-KEM support, that's a one-line PR that helps everyone.

Scan, Score, Fix — a Closed Loop 

pqmap scan /path/to/repo          # Build the relationship graph
pqmap score --graph pqmap.json    # Two-axis quantum readiness report
pqmap fix --dry-run               # See the remediation plan
pqmap probe --graph pqmap.json    # Live-verify what's actually negotiated

Honest Scoring

pqmap scores two axes independently because post-quantum readiness isn't a single boolean:

  • Confidentiality (key agreement) — protects against harvest-now-decrypt-later. ML-KEM is mature and deployable today.
  • Authentication (signatures) — protects against future identity forgery. The ecosystem is early; most of the industry is honestly a C here.

If pqmap can't determine the cryptography for a connection, it grades it N (unknown) — which never inflates your score. You see exactly what's known, what's not, and what needs investigation.

Fixes Pointed at the Right Layer

Detection without actionable remediation is a report that gathers dust. pqmap generates a four-rung remediation ladder and proves which rung applies before recommending it:

Rung What It Means Example
1 Dependency upgrade Node 20 → 22 (gets OpenSSL 3.5 + ML-KEM)
2 Configuration change ssl_conf_command Curves X25519MLKEM768 in nginx
3 Infrastructure change Put CloudFront in front of a classical-only ALB
4 PQC gateway/sidecar Reverse proxy with ML-KEM termination

The system won't recommend a dependency bump (Rung 1) when your TLS is terminated at the ALB — that change wouldn't affect the negotiated crypto. It'll tell you to fix the infrastructure (Rung 3). This is the difference between a useful tool and a checkbox exercise.

Why Open Source

Post-quantum migration is an industry-wide problem. No single vendor has visibility into every runtime, every framework, and every infrastructure provider's PQ rollout timeline. The knowledge base that powers pqmap — which runtimes support ML-KEM, which load balancers negotiate PQ groups, which versions introduced support — is inherently community-scale knowledge.

pqmap is designed so that the most impactful contributions don't require writing Rust:

  • Add framework detection: edit a TOML catalog file
  • Update PQ capability data: edit the knowledge base with a source URL
  • Add test fixtures: drop a sample project into fixtures/

The architecture is intentionally simple and data-driven so the barrier to contribution is low. The more runtimes and infrastructure the KB covers, the more useful the tool is for everyone.

Get Started 

cargo install pqmap
pqmap scan .

pqmap is:

  1. A single binary
  2. Runtime independent
  3. Offline
  4. Fast

The quantum clock is ticking, but the migration path doesn't have to be murky. Scan your project, see where you stand, and fix the thing that actually matters first.

Star the repo, file issues, contribute KB rows for your runtime or infrastructure. This is better when it's shared.

title: AI Strategy Training for CISOs: Write the Stop Rule First
description:
Most documents titled "AI strategy" in a security organization are shopping lists: a copilot for the SOC, an AI email gateway, maybe an agent that closes tickets. A shopping list is not a strategy. A strategy says which problems get money, how you will know each bet failed, and what each one adds to your attack surface. AI strategy training for CISOs and security leaders is worth paying for if it leaves you able to write that document for your own program. Below is what the document looks like, with a script that pressure-tests it.

The direct answer: four decisions, not a framework tour

A security leader's AI strategy comes down to four decisions:

  • Where AI goes. Pick problems where you can measure the current process and you have labeled outcomes. No baseline, no way to show improvement. No labels, no way to evaluate the model.
  • What it adds to the attack surface. Any model that reads email bodies, ticket comments, or process command lines is reading attacker-controlled text. MITRE ATLAS tracks this as AML.T0051.001, indirect prompt injection.
  • What ends the bet. A stop rule, written before the pilot, with a date on it.
  • Who runs it. The skills to evaluate a model on your own data, which is a different job from buying one.

Frameworks support those decisions. They do not make them. The NIST AI RMF (AI 100-1) asks you to document intended purpose and context (MAP 1.1) and to have a way to disengage a system that underperforms (MANAGE 2.4). It does not tell you whether phishing triage or endpoint auto-isolation should get this year's budget.

A worked example: the portfolio file

Write each candidate use case as a structured entry that a peer can argue with. Here are two, the first fundable and the second not:

# ai_portfolio.yml  (illustrative numbers)
use_cases:
  - name: phishing-report-triage
    problem: user-reported phishing queue sits too long before first touch
    baseline: {median_hours_to_first_touch: 9}
    labeled_positives: 412          # reports closed as malicious, last 12 months
    reads_untrusted_text: true      # the email body is attacker-written
    acts_without_approval: false    # model ranks the queue; analysts decide
    attack_surface: [AML.T0051.001]
    kill_rule: >
      median time to first touch not under 4h by day 60, or any confirmed
      malicious report ranked in the bottom 20% of the queue
    review: 2027-01-15

  - name: auto-isolate-endpoints
    problem: containment is slow on high-severity EDR alerts
    baseline: null                  # nobody has measured time to contain
    labeled_positives: 18
    reads_untrusted_text: true      # command lines, file names, hostnames
    acts_without_approval: true     # isolates hosts on its own
    attack_surface: [AML.T0051.001, OWASP-LLM06]
    kill_rule: null
    review: null

The second entry is the one vendors pitch hardest, and it fails on every line. Nobody measured containment time, so nobody can show it improved. Eighteen confirmed cases cannot support an evaluation. And a model that reads attacker-written command lines and then takes action without a human is the pattern OWASP calls LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency. An attacker who can name a file can try to write instructions into the name.

Score the portfolio before anyone buys anything

A few gates catch most bad bets. This is short enough to run in the meeting where the strategy is debated:

import yaml

GATES = [
    (lambda u: u["baseline"] is None,
     "measure the current process for 30 days before buying anything"),
    (lambda u: u["labeled_positives"] < 30,
     "cannot be evaluated; fund labeling or pick another problem"),
    (lambda u: u["reads_untrusted_text"] and u["acts_without_approval"],
     "require human approval on every action (OWASP LLM06)"),
    (lambda u: not u.get("kill_rule"),
     "not a strategy item until it has a stop rule"),
]

with open("ai_portfolio.yml") as f:
    portfolio = yaml.safe_load(f)["use_cases"]

for u in portfolio:
    problems = [msg for test, msg in GATES if test(u)]
    print(f"{u['name']:<28} {'HOLD' if problems else 'FUND PILOT'}")
    for msg in problems:
        print(f"    - {msg}")

Output for the file above:

phishing-report-triage       FUND PILOT
auto-isolate-endpoints       HOLD
    - measure the current process for 30 days before buying anything
    - cannot be evaluated; fund labeling or pick another problem
    - require human approval on every action (OWASP LLM06)
    - not a strategy item until it has a stop rule

The threshold of 30 is not arbitrary. If a model catches all 18 of 18 malicious cases, the rule of three still puts the 95 percent upper bound on its miss rate near 3/18, about 17 percent. You cannot distinguish that model from a coin that got lucky. Our post on proving SOC automation works covers building the labeled set itself.

The gates also push you toward classical ML more often than the pitch decks suggest. A ranking problem with 412 labeled examples is a gradient-boosted classifier as much as it is an LLM problem, and it is cheaper to evaluate. We cover that tradeoff in classical ML vs. generative AI in the SOC.

The other half: the AI you have to secure

A security AI strategy has a second column: the AI the rest of the company deploys, which your team inherits. That column starts with an inventory, not a policy. The proxy log exercise in where CISOs learn about AI security builds the first version in an afternoon. Give each system found there the same fields as above, with attack_surface and kill_rule filled in. A business unit's customer chatbot needs a stop rule as much as your SOC copilot does.

How to judge a strategy course

Bring the portfolio file to the vendor conversation. Ask whether the course has you score your own candidate use cases, or only walks through capability demos and framework summaries. Ask whether it covers classical ML or treats "AI" as a synonym for LLMs. And ask whether you leave with a draft document your deputy can poke holes in on Monday. Training that sends you home with a maturity model and a vocabulary list is cheaper to deliver than training that makes you defend a budget line. That is why there is more of it.

When this approach is overkill

If your AI footprint is a vendor feature you cannot turn off, such as an assistant built into your EDR console, the portfolio has one row and the work is contract review: data retention, whether your telemetry trains the vendor's model, and whether the feature can be disabled per tenant. And the gates are a filter, not proof. A use case that passes all four still needs a pilot with real measurement; the vendor POC guide covers that step.

We built A Cyber Executive's Guide for Artificial Intelligence around judgment rather than implementation: ROI evaluation, vendor assessment, governance, and what AI can and cannot do in a security program. It runs as a one-day course and as a private executive briefing for a leadership team.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Meta-Policies for Temporal Knowledge-Graph Memory under Partial Observability
description:
arXiv:2607.18368v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Partially observable reinforcement learning requires deciding what to retain, retrieve, and forget over time. We introduce a neuro-symbolic meta-policy that learns which symbolic memory heuristic to apply at each decision point while keeping execution symbolic. Our setting uses temporal knowledge-graph memory in RoomKG, where hidden state and observations are represented as Resource Description Framework (RDF) graphs and memory is augmented with temporal RDF triple annotations. The model combines knowledge-graph encoding of memory contents with value heads for question answering, exploration, and forgetting, yielding a controller that is both adaptive and inspectable. This gives the work a direct Semantic Web grounding through RDF-based representation, annotation-compatible graph semantics, and graph-based symbolic operations over explicit memory state. On train/test room splits at long-term memory capacity of 512, the qualifier-aware StarE-GNN configuration achieves the best held-out performance among the compared symbolic, neural, and neuro-symbolic systems while preserving step-level traceability of memory-management decisions.

title: Deduplicating contacts when the same person has three identities
description:
The same customer appears as an email address, a user id, and a Stripe customer. Merge them badly and you send three copies of the same onboarding email; merge them lazily and you cannot answer 'who is this'.

Pick the strongest key and never change it

The email address is the natural key for email, but it is mutable: people change addresses and teams reassign aliases. The durable key is your internal contact id. Everything else — email, external ids, phone — is an attribute that can be added or retired without breaking history.

Keep an identity table, not a wide row

One table of (contact_id, kind, value, verified_at) lets one contact hold two email addresses, an external CRM id, and a phone number without schema changes. Looking up which contact owns an address becomes a single indexed query, which is the only thing the send path actually needs.

Decide what a merge does to history

If two contacts are merged, their events should not be silently reattributed. Keep the event's original contact id and add a pointer to the surviving contact. Otherwise a merge rewrites analytics and any number you reported last month changes retroactively.

The detail that prevents duplicate sends

Deduplicate at the point of enqueue with a key composed of (contact_id, template_id, dedupe_window). Two features firing the same welcome email within five minutes then produce one message, and the rule lives in one place instead of in every caller.

Volanea keys contacts by id with verified identities attached, so a second address for the same person does not create a second contact.

title: Next.js Middleware to Proxy: How to Migrate middleware.ts to proxy.ts in Next.js 16
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

In Next.js 16, middleware.ts is deprecated and renamed to proxy.ts. Your existing middleware still runs, but every build now prints a deprecation warning, and a few things behave differently: the function name changes, Proxy always runs on the Node.js runtime, and having both files in a project fails the build. This guide covers the Next.js middleware to proxy migration step by step, with the exact warnings and errors I got from Next.js 16.4.5 on a small test app, so you know what to expect before you run the codemod.

Next.js middleware vs proxy: what actually changed

The behavior is the same feature under a new name. From the Next.js proxy docs:

middleware.ts (Next.js 12–15) proxy.ts (Next.js 16+)
File name middleware.ts proxy.ts
Exported function middleware (or default) proxy (or default)
config.matcher same same
NextRequest / NextResponse same same
Runtime Edge by default, Node.js opt-in since 15.5 Node.js only; runtime config throws
Status in 16.x deprecated, still runs with a warning recommended

The Next.js team says they renamed it because "middleware" was getting confused with Express-style middleware and encouraged using it for too much. "Proxy" describes what it is: a layer in front of your routes that can redirect, rewrite, set headers or return a response.

Step 1: see the deprecation warning

I started with a typical auth-redirect middleware on Next.js 16.4.5:

// middleware.ts
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'

export function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  const session = request.cookies.get('session')?.value
  if (!session) {
    const url = new URL('/login', request.url)
    url.searchParams.set('next', request.nextUrl.pathname)
    return NextResponse.redirect(url)
  }
  const headers = new Headers(request.headers)
  headers.set('x-user', session)
  return NextResponse.next({ request: { headers } })
}

export const config = {
  matcher: ['/dashboard/:path*'],
}

next build succeeds, but prints:

⚠ The "middleware" file convention is deprecated. Please use "proxy" instead.

  To migrate automatically, run:
  npx @next/codemod@canary middleware-to-proxy .

The route table already labels it ƒ Proxy (Middleware).

Step 2: run the middleware-to-proxy codemod 

npx @next/codemod@canary middleware-to-proxy .

On my test app the codemod renamed middleware.ts to proxy.ts and the exported function from middleware to proxy. Nothing else changed:

- // middleware.ts
- export function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
+ // proxy.ts
+ export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {

After that, next build ran with no deprecation warning. I checked it with next start: /dashboard without a cookie returned a 307 to /login?next=%2Fdashboard, and with session=waseem the page rendered the x-user header the proxy set.

Commit the codemod change on its own so the diff stays easy to review.

Step 3: migrate by hand (if you can't run the codemod)

It's two edits:

  1. Rename middleware.ts to proxy.ts, in the same place (project root, or src/ if you use it).
  2. Rename the exported function to proxy, or use a default export. 
// proxy.ts
import type { NextProxy } from 'next/server'

export const proxy: NextProxy = (request, event) => {
  // same logic as before
}

The NextProxy type infers request as NextRequest and event as NextFetchEvent, so event.waitUntil() for background logging still works. If you customized pageExtensions, the file name follows it, for example proxy.page.ts.

Errors you may hit during the migration

"Both middleware file and proxy file are detected"

If the old file is still there after you create proxy.ts, the build fails:

Error: Both middleware file "./middleware.ts" and proxy file "./proxy.ts" are detected.
Please use "./proxy.ts" only.

Delete middleware.ts. This one bites when a merge brings the old file back from another branch.

"Proxy does not support Edge runtime"

Proxy always runs on Node.js. If your old middleware had runtime: 'edge' in its config and you carry it over, the build fails:

Error: Next.js can't recognize the exported `config` field in route.
Proxy does not support Edge runtime.

Remove runtime from the config. For context, keeping middleware.ts with runtime: 'edge' on 16.4.5 also failed, asking for 'experimental-edge', and that value builds but warns that the Edge Runtime is deprecated. Either way, the direction is Node.js.

Running on Node.js is mostly good news: you can use Node APIs and regular npm packages (database clients, jose, crypto) in Proxy. The cost is that you can't rely on Edge-only behavior, so if you self-host behind your own server this changes nothing, and on platforms that ran middleware at the edge you should check where Proxy runs.

What doesn't change

  • Matchers. config.matcher strings, arrays, regex and has / missing conditions work the same. Matchers must still be constants.
  • Execution order. Proxy runs after headers and redirects from next.config.js and before filesystem routes.
  • Request header pattern. Use NextResponse.next({ request: { headers } }) to pass data to your app. NextResponse.next({ headers }) sends them to the browser instead.
  • Config flags. skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize is now skipProxyUrlNormalize. skipTrailingSlashRedirect is unchanged.
  • Testing helpers. The current docs show unstable_doesProxyMatch, but the 16.4.5 package I installed still only exports unstable_doesMiddlewareMatch from next/experimental/testing/server, so check your installed version before renaming it in tests.

Don't use proxy.ts as your only auth check

The Next.js docs point out that Server Functions are handled as POST requests to the page that uses them, so a matcher that excludes a path also skips Server Function calls on that path. Moving a Server Function or changing a matcher can silently remove Proxy coverage. Treat Proxy as the fast redirect for signed-out users, and check the session again inside each Server Action, Route Handler and data function.

I go through that pattern with a real auth library in Better Auth with Next.js, and the October Next.js patches in this security update post are a good reminder of why defense in depth matters.

Migration checklist

  • [ ] Run npx @next/codemod@canary middleware-to-proxy . or rename the file and function by hand
  • [ ] Delete any leftover middleware.ts
  • [ ] Remove runtime: 'edge' from the Proxy config
  • [ ] Rename skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize to skipProxyUrlNormalize in next.config (the old name is marked @deprecated in 16.4.5's types)
  • [ ] Re-run next build and confirm the warning is gone and the route table shows Proxy
  • [ ] Re-check auth inside Server Actions and Route Handlers, not only in Proxy

FAQ

Is Next.js middleware deprecated?

Yes. In Next.js 16.0.0 the middleware file convention was deprecated and renamed to proxy. On 16.4.5, middleware.ts still runs, but next build prints a deprecation warning that points to the codemod.

What is the difference between middleware.ts and proxy.ts in Next.js?

The file name and the exported function name. The API (NextRequest, NextResponse, config.matcher) is the same. The one behavior change is that Proxy always runs on the Node.js runtime and setting runtime in its config is an error.

How do I migrate from middleware to proxy in Next.js 16?

Run npx @next/codemod@canary middleware-to-proxy .. It renames middleware.ts to proxy.ts and the middleware function to proxy. Then delete any leftover middleware.ts, remove runtime: 'edge' if present, and rebuild.

Can I keep both middleware.ts and proxy.ts?

No. On Next.js 16.4.5 the build fails with "Both middleware file and proxy file are detected. Please use ./proxy.ts only."

Does Next.js proxy run on the Edge runtime?

No. Proxy uses the Node.js runtime, and the build fails with "Proxy does not support Edge runtime" if you set runtime: 'edge' in its config.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: There Is No Free Loop: When Does Looping a Trained Model Pay for Its Inference Compute?
description:
arXiv:2610.42030v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Looping re-applies a block of layers so that each token passes through the block more than once. Adding a loop to a trained model is attractive because it leaves the parameter count, and hence the disk size, the memory footprint and the training cost unchanged. Unfortunately, every generated token pays for the loop. Re-applying m of N layers makes each token about (N+m)/N times as expensive. Loops that a model learns during large-scale pretraining justify this price, but whether loops added after pretraining justify this cost remains unclear. We compare a looped model with two simple baselines. We first compare it with the same model trained identically without the loop (equal parameters). Secondly, we compare it with the best unlooped use of the same inference floating-point operations (equal FLOPs). Across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models from 0.8B to 9B parameters, only the looped 0.8B model beats both baselines. At 4B and 9B, the looped model does not beat the first baseline, i.e. the same model trained without the loop. This is not because the benchmarks are too easy, since on the same benchmarks the unlooped 9B model still scores up to 13 points higher than the 4B model, showing that there is ample room for improvement. Introducing loops in an already pretrained model therefore only pays for small models with a fixed parameter budget.
