title: AI Risk Management Training for Executives: Put a Number on It
description:
Ask a security leadership team to rank "prompt injection in the corporate AI assistant" against "ransomware on the file servers" for next year's budget, and most will answer with a color. Amber, probably. Then the CFO asks how much amber costs, and the conversation stalls.

That stall is the gap that AI risk management training for security executives should close. Most courses spend the day on frameworks (NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act) and send leaders home able to classify a risk but unable to price it. Classification decides whether something goes on the register. Price decides whether it gets money. If a course does not teach the second skill, the register entry sits in amber forever.

Why the heat map fails for AI risk

The problem with risk matrices is not new. Louis Anthony Cox Jr. laid it out in "What's Wrong with Risk Matrices?" (Risk Analysis, 2008): coarse likelihood and impact bins can assign identical ratings to risks that differ by orders of magnitude, and in some cases rank a smaller risk above a larger one. Douglas Hubbard and Richard Seiersen made the security-specific version of that argument in How to Measure Anything in Cybersecurity Risk.

AI makes it worse. "Likelihood: medium" for prompt injection hides the one number you can actually measure, which is how often an attack succeeds against your deployment. Throwing that measurement away to pick a bin is a bad trade.

Decompose one scenario with FAIR

The Open Group's Open FAIR standards (O-RT for the taxonomy, O-RA for the analysis) split risk into loss event frequency and loss magnitude. Loss event frequency is threat event frequency times susceptibility: how often an attacker tries, and what fraction of tries succeed.

Take one concrete scenario. An external sender plants instructions in an email or shared document, your assistant retrieves it while answering an unrelated question, and the model leaks internal data through a rendered link. MITRE ATLAS calls the technique AML.T0051.001, indirect prompt injection, and the outcome AML.T0057, LLM Data Leakage. EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) in Microsoft 365 Copilot followed this exact path; our AI incident tabletop post walks through it as an exercise.

Three inputs, and they come from three different places:

  • Attempt frequency (estimated). How many crafted payloads reach the retrieval index per year. You will not know this. Give a calibrated 90 percent range instead, say 2 to 20, and write down why.
  • Susceptibility (measured). The fraction of attempts that succeed. This is where AI risk differs from most FAIR work: your red team can run the attack 60 times against your own tenant with PyRIT or garak and count. Seven successes in 60 trials is evidence. "The vendor says it is mitigated" is not.
  • Loss per event (estimated with finance and legal). Response hours, notification, counsel, regulatory exposure. For a sense of the upper end, IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 puts the global average breach at US$4.44 million, and GDPR Article 83 allows fines up to 4 percent of worldwide annual turnover. A range of $50,000 to $2 million per leak event is a defensible starting point for most mid-sized firms; yours may differ.

The simulation

About twenty lines of NumPy turn those inputs into a loss distribution. Ranges become lognormals, red team counts become a Beta distribution, and attempts become Poisson draws.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
N = 100_000

def lognormal_from_ci(low, high, size):
    # treat (low, high) as a calibrated 90% interval
    mu = (np.log(low) + np.log(high)) / 2
    sigma = (np.log(high) - np.log(low)) / (2 * 1.645)
    return rng.lognormal(mu, sigma, size)

def simulate(successes, trials):
    attempts = rng.poisson(lognormal_from_ci(2, 20, N))            # payloads reaching retrieval per year
    p_success = rng.beta(1 + successes, 1 + trials - successes, N)  # red team result
    events = rng.binomial(attempts, p_success)                       # loss events per year
    return np.array([lognormal_from_ci(50_000, 2_000_000, k).sum() for k in events])

before = simulate(successes=7, trials=60)   # current config
after = simulate(successes=0, trials=60)    # external mail excluded from retrieval, link allowlist on

for name, ale in [("before", before), ("after", after)]:
    print(f"{name}: mean ${ale.mean():,.0f}  P90 ${np.percentile(ale, 90):,.0f}  "
          f"P(loss > $1M) {np.mean(ale > 1e6):.1%}")

You can sanity-check the means without running anything. The 2 to 20 attempt range has a mean of about 8. The Beta posterior for 7 of 60 has a mean of 8/62, about 13 percent. The $50,000 to $2 million loss range has a mean near $590,000. Multiply them: roughly $620,000 a year in expected loss before the fix. After the fix, the success rate drops to a posterior mean of 1/62, and expected loss falls to about $80,000.

That difference, around $540,000 a year, is the number to put next to the cost of the control. It is also the number that tells you the control does not get you to zero. Zero successes in 60 trials still leaves a 95 percent upper bound of about 5 percent (the rule of three: 3/n), and the simulation carries that uncertainty instead of rounding it away.

The P90 and P(loss > $1M) lines matter more than the mean for a board. "One year in ten, this scenario costs us more than X" is a sentence directors can act on. NIST's AI RMF asks for this work without naming a method: MAP 5.1 covers documenting likelihood and magnitude of impacts, and MEASURE 2.7 covers evaluating security and resilience. A script an auditor can rerun meets both. If you want a packaged version, pyfair implements the FAIR ontology in Python.

What a course should make you do

Judge any AI risk management course by one exercise: does each participant leave having priced a scenario from their own environment, with at least one measured input? Lectures on likelihood scales do not count. Neither does a vendor's risk calculator with the inputs pre-filled.

The measured input is the part executives tend to skip, because it requires asking the red team for trial counts instead of a pass/fail verdict. Our post on counting trials in AI red team work explains what to request. Calibration is the other piece: Hubbard's equivalent-bet test (would you rather bet on your range containing the answer, or on a spin with a 90 percent chance of winning?) takes twenty minutes to teach and fixes most overconfident ranges.

Where quantification breaks

It needs an inventory first. You cannot price a scenario for an assistant nobody knew was connected to the mail server; our CISO post covers finding those through proxy logs. It also decays. A measured success rate describes one model version under one system prompt, and SaaS vendors swap models without notice, so the red team rerun belongs on a schedule (quarterly, and after any vendor model change). And it handles the tail poorly. A regulator deciding to make an example of the first AI leak in your sector is not well described by a lognormal; say that out loud rather than letting the P90 imply more precision than it has.

None of this replaces judgment. It gives judgment something to argue with.

GTK Cyber's A Cyber Executive's Guide for Artificial Intelligence covers AI risk and governance frameworks and ROI evaluation for AI security tools, and we deliver it privately for leadership teams through an executive briefing.

title: Retry policy mistakes that turn a blip into an outage
description:
A sound retry policy needs jitter, caps, idempotency, a read of Retry-After and a budget. Here is each piece, and the storms that follow when one is missing.

A correct retry policy repeats only calls that can safely be repeated, only after errors that can change, with a wait that grows and carries a random part, under a hard limit on tries and on total time, and with a shared budget so that a sick dependency is not buried under its own clients. Each piece guards against a different failure. Leave one out and a ten-second blip can become an hour-long outage, because the retries themselves are traffic. The rest of this page goes through the pieces in the order a request meets them, then the storms you get when they are missing.

Read the full report on AISkills402: https://aiskills402.com/blog/retry-backoff-mistakes?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social

title: How our agents build on-brand pages with design.md
description:
Across Vercel, we use coding agents to design and build pages that have to look and feel like Vercel. The typography, color, and composition all need to carry the same judgment that we put into the pages we already ship ourselves.

We recently wrote about product-design, our skill that teaches agents how we design when they work in our codebases. The skill lives in each repository alongside the code that it governs, explaining how agents can find and understand our design system as well as product guidelines for whatever they are building.

This works great when agents are working in our codebases, where everything the skill needs is right there. But what about reports, proposals, and the one-off pages that still have to look like Vercel but get made in tools that can't read any of those files? For us, the answer was design.md, one public file any agent can load.

How we approached building design.md

What made product-design work well was that the design system and product guidelines were sitting right there in the repository for agents to read. We needed a way for agents and tools outside that environment to reach the same knowledge, so that the pages coming out the other end would still look like something we designed ourselves. That set two requirements:

  • A single public URL that anyone can point their agents at, regardless of the environment they run in.

  • Guidance covering everything that made product-design useful in the first place, from brand, layout, and copywriting to the design system, responsiveness, and information architecture.

The naive approach we tried first was to simply port product-design into a public prompt, collapsing the skill's reference files into one file any agent could read from a URL. The problem we found was that while the prompt described our visual language just fine, every model reading it interpreted that description differently, generating vastly different pages from the same guidance.

Part of this comes from the fact that design language is subjective. Phrases like "keep the layout clean" can really mean anything. What is "clean"? Beyond that, the bigger problem was everything else the prompt left behind. Inside our codebases, an agent reads product-design surrounded by real components and shipped examples of the things it describes. But a public prompt includes none of that, leaving every model to rebuild our style from just words alone.

So what we needed to do was distill what that environment provided into a single file, and the only way to know whether we were getting closer was to look at the pages coming out. We set the port aside and started writing a new file from scratch, this time testing every change against a repeatable set of eval prompts.

We wrote seven of them, pulled from real use cases and paired with mock inputs:

  • Usage and performance report

  • Renewal proposal

  • Benchmark report

  • Interactive planning page

  • Build-versus-buy brief

  • Security governance brief

  • Presentation deck

The prompts stayed fixed while the file changed, so any difference in the output traced back to the guidance.

The first comparison

These evals gave us a way to measure both what the file was actually doing and how it was being interpreted by different agents. For our first test, we wanted to know whether design.md would actually change what a model produced at all. We ran the renewal proposal eval twice in the same environment with the same model, once without design.md and once with it loaded, keeping the prompt, data, and viewport identical in both runs.

Without design.md, the model generated a generic SaaS dashboard. But with it, the page led with the renewal recommendation itself, pulled the commercial evidence into one grid, put peer values on a single scale so they could actually be compared, and kept supporting detail available without letting it compete with the summary. This allowed us to conclude that the file changed the page’s structure and hierarchy as well, not just the styling like we originally found, giving us enough signal to keep building the guidance like this, one rule at a time.

The three parts that make the system work

As we tested and rebuilt design.md, the scope evolved into a three-part system that made the entire thing work:

  • design.md supplies guidance that shows agents how to frame the reader's job, structure evidence, and choose a composition.

  • A public stylesheet that defines a bounded, documented vocabulary of classes and tokens.

  • An evaluation loop turns repeated human feedback into better guidance and deterministic checks.

Each of these layers covers a different slice of the work that creates a high-quality, on-brand Vercel page. The judgment that gets encoded in design.md gives agents guidance on:

  • Shaping a page for both a quick executive read and a detailed audit.

  • Writing copy with concrete claims and honest caveats.

  • Composing hierarchy, typography, and color so that evidence and prose support each other.

  • How to publish as Vercel, down to the asset rules for our wordmark and the triangle logo.

design.md also names the recurring generated-design patterns that we never want to see, allowing agents to recognize and avoid them far more reliably by giving the patterns names.

We created a stylesheet because agents kept inventing their own typography, spacing, and layout, so we took those decisions away from the model entirely. The stylesheet packages our design system's primitives, such as headers, tables, stat strips, and chart styles, as CSS that any page can use via a public URL. Then design.md documents the class names and tokens that the stylesheet provides, allowing the agent to build the page with those names in the HTML instead of reinventing them.

Another benefit to this is that the agent never actually reads the stylesheet itself. The stylesheet loads when the page renders in your browser, so none of the code enters the model's context, saving more room for design guidance instead.

Last, the evaluation loop is what helps make the other two pieces work. Deterministic checks are used to help catch mechanical failures, such as a table that ignores the width available to it, while people judge the subjective parts that can't be automated, like hierarchy, composition, and whether the page actually gives the reader what they came for.

How guidance made it into the file

Every line of guidance in design.md earned its place through the eval loop. We generated pages from fixed scenarios, reviewed what came back, encoded the corrections we accepted, and reran the scenarios to see whether each change stuck, since a change that helped one artifact could quietly hurt another. Nothing got in any other way.

Scenarios and rounds

Each of the seven prompts becomes a scenario, meaning the prompt is frozen together with its mock inputs and render settings. The renewal proposal, for example, always runs with the same fake customer data with the same viewport settings, keeping design.md as the only thing that changes between runs. A round means generating a fresh page from every scenario against the current version of the file. Full rounds cover all seven scenarios on both Claude Opus 4.8 and Codex with GPT-5.5.

If we want to investigate something specific, such as a rule change that only affects tables, we can rerun the affected scenarios or a single model, keeping iteration loops tight.

Generating all seven pages together also made them easy to compare side by side, and what stood out was that design.md wasn't pushing every page toward one template. The interactive planning page put its controls front and center, because someone opens a planning page to change the numbers and see what happens. The renewal proposal instead led with the recommendation and the commercial comparison behind it, because its reader is deciding whether to renew. Every page used the same Vercel typography, color, and spacing, but each one was structured around what its reader came to do.

Reviewing every run

To review the pages each round produced, we built a local app that displays full-page renders and runs blind A/B comparisons. This app eventually became our eval harness, running each scenario and storing the results. Each stored run keeps the prompt, inputs, model configuration, the version of design.md it used, the screenshots, and whatever feedback the reviewer left about it. Reviewers record every correction against the exact run that produced it.

Turning corrections into rules and checks

Each correction a reviewer records gets landed in the narrowest place that can consistently enforce it. Judgment changes go into design.md as prose, reusable mechanics go into the stylesheet, and anything that we can check mechanically becomes a deterministic check in code. Problems with the harness itself stay in the harness, and when a single model fails in a way the others don't, we keep it out of the rules until it repeats.

Take one of the early renewal proposals. Its commercial terms table came back squeezed to the same width as the prose, even though the page had room for the table to be twice as wide.

During review, we flagged that evidence tables should use the full width available to them. But when looking through previous outputs, we found this same failure everywhere. So this correction ended up going into two places:

  • A rule in design.md stating the intended behavior.

  • A deterministic check in code that catches the same layout failure the next time it appears.

Once this landed, later renewal proposal prompts resulted in pages with correct full-width tables. To verify changes like this one, we reran the affected scenarios after encoding them. At milestones we went further, running blind A/B rounds that put the updated design.md against an earlier version of the file to decide whether to keep, revise, or revert each change.

Measuring whether it worked

Building the file had taken well over 200 runs, counting full rounds, targeted checks, dry runs, and all of the dead ends. Alongside the human reviewers, a model judge wrote critiques for each round, and every round's feedback went into improving the next run.

After all of those runs, we wanted to know whether the corrections we had encoded were actually preventing the failures they were written for. So we picked three desktop scenarios, and for each one we had Codex with GPT-5.5 generate the page twice, once with design.md loaded and once without. We kept the first attempt from every generation, with no re-rolls. Then we ran our deterministic checks over all six pages and counted how many times a known failure, like a table that ignores its available width, showed up in each set. The pages generated with design.md had 39 of those failures. The pages generated without it had 91, which works out to 57% fewer in this test.

Those numbers come with two caveats. The checks can only catch failures we have already seen and written down, so this test says nothing about whether a page is well designed overall. Six pages is also far too small a sample to make claims about quality or reliability, and every one of them, with or without the file, still had at least one failure serious enough to block shipping. But what the test does well is tell us that once we name a failure and encode it, that failure tends to stay gone.

How design.md stays current

The eval loop got the file shipped, but what keeps it current is real usage. Inside our Slack, that usage comes through @design-agent, an agent built on eve that we use for anything from design critiques and copy alternatives to icon recommendations and report sites built from pasted data. Instead of setting up a prompt or hunting down source files, you just mention the agent in a thread. For website requests, it loads the current design.md, builds the page against the published stylesheet, and posts a full-page screenshot and deployment URL back to the thread. Unlike our fixed scenarios, each of these threads captures a real request, a real output, and whatever feedback or steering followed, showing us how the guidance performs out in the wild.

Every week, we gather all of that feedback in one place, the Slack threads along with comments from GitHub reviews and Figma. Automation groups the comments that keep repeating, and each repeated complaint becomes a proposed change. A person then reviews each proposal, checks whether the system already handles it, and decides where the accepted fix belongs, whether that is @design-agent, the product-design skill, design.md, the stylesheet, or a deterministic check. And if people start asking for a kind of page we have never tested, that request becomes a new eval scenario.

To know whether any of this is working, we count how often each kind of complaint shows up in similar work over time. Once we encode a fix, that count should start falling. When it does not, something about the fix is wrong. The rule might be unclear, it might not be loading when it is needed, the stylesheet might not have a primitive that can express it, or it might need a deterministic check instead of prose.

Build your own

You can build the same loop yourself, starting with one recurring artifact and one manual comparison.

1. Pick one repeated artifact

Use a recent task with a real reader and real inputs, like a proposal, performance report, benchmark, or microsite. Avoid broad goals such as "make it on-brand." Before generating anything, write down a short rubric. A good one checks that the supplied facts survived, that the reader's decision is clear, and that the correction you keep making by hand actually got resolved.

2. Save the baseline first

Generate the page once without any new design context, and save the prompt, inputs, configuration, and a screenshot. Keep that first output even if it looks rough, unless the harness itself failed. You cannot tell whether new context helped without a before.

3. Start from your last ten corrections

Collect the feedback you keep giving in design reviews, pull requests, or Slack, and rewrite each correction as something observable. That means writing Let evidence tables use the full available width instead of Make the table feel less cramped, since only one of those can be checked.

Put the decisions in one file with sections for scope, reader and task, observable decisions, and available primitives. That file is your first design.md.

4. Constrain repeatable mechanics

If your outputs keep inventing their own typography, spacing, or layout, publish a stylesheet and document the exact classes and tokens the agent may use. Keep your judgment in prose, and push the repeatable mechanics into CSS or deterministic checks.

5. Run one matched comparison

Generate the page one more time with the same input, model, and viewport, but now with your file loaded. Shuffle it with the baseline and score both against your rubric without knowing which is which.

You do not need a runner or a model judge to start, a single trial can reveal the large, obvious failures. To measure reliability, run multiple independent first-attempt trials (Anthropic's guide to evals for agents) and report how often the result holds.

6. Encode the correction

Review the output alongside whatever follow-up prompts you have to send, and then ask:

  • What did the user have to repeat or steer manually?

  • Is a rule missing or unclear?

  • Can the stylesheet express the correction?

  • Is the failure mechanical enough to check in code?

  • Does the correction generalize beyond this output?

Update the guidance instead of hand-tuning the generated page. Your next comparison tells you whether first attempts actually improved.

Add tooling after the manual loop starts paying off:

  • Include scenarios where the guidance should and should not apply.

  • Keep a small holdout hidden while editing.

  • Record model and guidance versions.

  • Automate mechanical checks.

  • Use multiple blind reviewers.

However far you take the automation, keep final changes human-reviewed.

Then keep the loop running. Collect feedback on a cadence, and watch whether each kind of complaint actually becomes less common after you change the guidance. A passing evaluation matters less if people keep correcting the same mistake in production.

And if you want working examples, ours are public. We load design.md into tools like v0, Codex, and Claude every day to make artifacts that feel like Vercel, and the eve design agent template will get you a Slack design agent like the one we run.

title: Why freezing completed Markdown blocks reduces streaming rendering work
description:
An AI response arrives as text deltas. A Markdown renderer normally receives a document. Connecting them with render(allTextSoFar) repeatedly asks the renderer to interpret text the reader has already seen.

I built react-stream-markdown to explore a different boundary: keep completed blocks on screen and re-parse the unfinished suffix. The repository is currently version 0.4.1 and MIT licensed. Here is how it works, where its cost still grows, and what the published benchmark actually measures.

Where repeated work comes from

Suppose a response contains N characters and arrives in chunks of c characters. A full-document parser sees c characters, then 2c, then 3c, and so on. With a linear parser, the sum of characters examined is approximately N²/(2c). This models repeated parsing work; it does not mean every part of browser rendering is quadratic.

React can reuse DOM elements after reconciliation. That does not automatically prevent an upstream Markdown parser from scanning the accumulated string. Parsing, building a tree, reconciling, layout, and painting have separate costs.

Markdown also has ambiguous intermediate states: bold delimiters and code fences may still be open. A streaming renderer needs an intermediate-display policy as well as a way to avoid revisiting stable content.

The useful boundary is a completed block

The renderer maintains a source offset, live DOM nodes, and the previous virtual representation of the live suffix. Each update parses state.text.slice(offset), converts its blocks to virtual nodes, and patches the live nodes.

After patching, it advances the offset past blocks it considers finished. The implementation freezes preceding blocks when a following block has a complete first line. Frozen DOM nodes remain in the container but leave the arrays used for subsequent patch operations.

A completed paragraph therefore stops participating in Markdown parsing and tree comparison when later paragraphs arrive. This is a finalization policy for the syntax this parser supports. It is not a universal rule that a blank line makes arbitrary Markdown immutable; document-wide dependencies would need additional invalidation rules.

Conceptually, the update is:

  1. Parse the accumulated text after the frozen offset.
  2. Compare the new suffix tree with its previous tree.
  3. Patch the live DOM nodes.
  4. Advance the offset past finalizable blocks and forget their live-state entries.

For block lengths B₁, B₂, …, repeated parsing work is closer to a sum of per-block work, roughly ΣBᵢ²/c, than repeatedly scanning the whole prefix. When blocks remain reasonably short, the parser's active working set stays small as the complete answer grows.

Flat cost has boundaries

A huge paragraph, list, or open code block can keep growing without becoming finalizable. Its active suffix still gets re-parsed. Freezing does not make that case constant-time.

The component also receives cumulative text snapshots, checks whether the new text starts with the previous text, and retains the accumulated response. String construction, prefix checks, allocation, garbage collection, and browser layout sit outside the simple per-block parser model. A larger DOM may still cost more to lay out.

The defensible claim is narrower: freezing removes repeated parser and patch work on finalized blocks. It does not prove O(1) total update cost, bounded memory, or constant latency for every document.

Patching and animation

The active suffix is compared with its previous virtual tree. DOM APIs create or change the nodes that need updating. Raw model HTML is treated as text rather than assigned through innerHTML. Links are limited to HTTP(S) and mailto, and images appear as links.

Unfinished inline syntax is rendered optimistically: a partial bold span can already appear bold. That is an intermediate-display policy, not a guarantee that malformed Markdown will match every other parser's final interpretation.

Optional fade-in applies temporary animation spans to newly arrived characters. When the animation completes, the spans collapse into text nodes. Previously visible text does not restart its animation. Creating and animating those spans still consumes CPU time.

What the benchmark measures

The published README results use production builds in headless Chromium 141, three runs, and a median. The synthetic document contains 10,201 characters with lists, code, tables, and quotes. It arrives in 24-character chunks, one chunk per animation frame: 426 updates, not a recorded provider token stream.

Each renderer uses a 720-pixel-wide host. The harness synchronously applies an update and reads offsetHeight, deliberately forcing layout into that update's timing. React-based adapters use flushSync; react-stream-markdown disables its own frame batching for this test. These choices make synchronous work measurable but do not reproduce every application's scheduling behavior.

Whole-reply work is measured using the difference in Chrome's TaskDuration counter. It is not elapsed generation time, network latency, or time to first readable text. Settling is detected when text length stays unchanged for 30 frames. This is a heuristic, not proof that every animation or formatting effect has finished. The script also subtracts a fixed 3 ms from the total; that adjustment should be disclosed when reproducing the numbers.

Renderer/configuration Published main-thread time Published slowest update
react-stream-markdown, fade off 1,100 ms 3.3 ms
react-stream-markdown, fade on 2,941 ms 7.3 ms
Vercel Streamdown 2.7.0 2,031 ms 15.3 ms
@lobehub/streamdown 1.4.0, realtime 2,609 ms 14.4 ms
react-markdown 10.1.0 + remark-gfm 4.0.1, full string each update 6,384 ms 38.7 ms

These are existing README results, not a fresh measurement of 0.4.1 on my current machine. The script takes medians of the metrics independently, so the displayed maximum update and total need not belong to the same run. Its slowest update is a synchronous measurement, not INP or a complete responsiveness score.

Within this workload, disabling fade-in reduces total main-thread work. Enabling it raises that total above both compared Streamdown configurations. A lower maximum synchronous update does not cancel a higher overall CPU cost.

Making the comparison more informative

The scripts are available in the repository. Reproduction should record the commit, lockfile, browser version, machine, viewport, and animation settings. Test ordinary short blocks and a deliberately long single block; vary chunk size and cadence too.

The harness runs renderers in a fixed order and does not explicitly warm them up. Randomized order, more repetitions, and result distributions would help distinguish repeatable differences from noise. Correctness needs separate checks: similar rendered text lengths do not establish equivalent formatting, links, tables, or accessibility.

Choosing a renderer

Vercel Streamdown offers a broader rendering ecosystem, including syntax highlighting and Mermaid integrations. react-stream-markdown takes a narrower approach with no direct runtime dependencies beyond React peer dependencies. Optional math needs a renderer such as KaTeX supplied by the application, which changes the application's bundle cost.

The repository currently reports 7.8 kB gzipped for its measured JavaScript entry, with stylesheet size listed separately. That is a bundle experiment with React externalized, not the npm tarball size. Imported plugins, styles, features, and lazy chunks matter as much as the headline number.

For a chat interface, I would choose based on required Markdown features, intermediate rendering behavior, correctness on actual responses, and profiling on target devices. This library explores how much repeated work can be removed by giving completed blocks an explicit lifetime. Its strongest result is that inspectable mechanism, rather than an unconditional claim to be the fastest renderer.

Source · Interactive demo · Benchmark scripts

title: The transactional outbox: stop losing events between your database and Kafka
description:
This is one of the most common bugs in event-driven systems, and it hides in two innocent lines:

orderRepository.save(order);                 // 1. commit to the database
kafkaTemplate.send("orders", orderCreated);  // 2. publish the event

If the process dies between line 1 and line 2 — a deploy, an OOM kill, a lost connection to the broker — the order exists, but the event never goes out. Billing never bills, the warehouse never ships, and nothing errors, because from every service's point of view nothing happened.

Swapping the lines doesn't help. Publish first, and if the database commit then fails you've announced an order that doesn't exist.

The underlying problem is a dual write: two systems, no shared transaction. You can't make a Postgres commit and a Kafka publish atomic without distributed transactions, which most teams rightly avoid. But you can make two writes to the same database atomic. That's the whole idea of the outbox.

The pattern


The business write and the event are committed together; publishing happens afterwards, as often as needed. Explore the interactive diagram

  1. In the same transaction as the business change, insert a row into an outbox table describing the event.
  2. A separate relay reads new outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka.
  3. Once Kafka acknowledges, the relay marks the row as published (or deletes it).

If the service crashes after the commit, the outbox row is still there and the relay publishes it later. If the transaction rolls back, the outbox row rolls back with it. The event exists if and only if the order does.

The table and the write 

CREATE TABLE outbox (
    id            BIGSERIAL    PRIMARY KEY,
    aggregate_id  TEXT         NOT NULL,      -- e.g. the order id; used as the Kafka key
    event_type    TEXT         NOT NULL,      -- OrderCreated, OrderCancelled, ...
    payload       JSONB        NOT NULL,
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    published_at  TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON outbox (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

@Transactional
public Order placeOrder(PlaceOrder cmd) {
    Order order = orders.save(Order.from(cmd));
    outbox.save(new OutboxEvent(order.getId(), "OrderCreated", toJson(order)));
    return order;   // both rows commit together, or neither does
}

The partial index keeps the relay's query fast no matter how many published rows you keep around.

Relay option 1: polling

The simplest relay is a scheduled loop:

@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)
@Transactional
public void relay() {
    List<OutboxEvent> batch = jdbc.query("""
        SELECT id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload
        FROM outbox
        WHERE published_at IS NULL
        ORDER BY id
        LIMIT 100
        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
        """, outboxRowMapper);

    for (OutboxEvent e : batch) {
        kafka.send("orders", e.aggregateId(), e.payload()).get();   // wait for the ack
    }
    jdbc.update("UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = ANY(?)", ids(batch));
}

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets you run several relay instances: each one locks a batch and the others skip it instead of waiting or double-publishing. Using aggregate_id as the Kafka key keeps all events for one order on one partition, so consumers see them in order.

Polling is easy to understand, needs no new infrastructure, and its latency (half a second here) is fine for most business events.

Relay option 2: change data capture

If you need lower latency or you don't want polling load on the database, use change data capture: a tool like Debezium reads the database's replication log (the Postgres WAL, the MySQL binlog) and publishes each new outbox row. Debezium even ships an "outbox event router" that maps outbox columns onto Kafka topics and keys.

The trade-off is operational: you now run Kafka Connect and Debezium, and you need to manage replication slots so they don't hold back WAL cleanup. For a team already running Kafka Connect it's the better relay. For a team that isn't, polling is usually enough to start.

The part people forget: duplicates

The outbox guarantees at-least-once, not exactly-once. If the relay publishes a batch and crashes before marking it published, the next run publishes it again. So consumers must be idempotent:

  • Give every event a unique ID (the outbox id, or a UUID in the payload).
  • In the consumer, record processed event IDs in the same transaction as the consumer's own side effect, and skip IDs it has already seen.

That's the same idea as idempotency keys for APIs, applied to messages — see Idempotency keys: making retries safe for money.

Operating it

  • Clean up. Delete published rows older than a few days with a scheduled job, or partition the table by day and drop old partitions.
  • Alert on the oldest unpublished row. now() - min(created_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL is the single best health metric: if it grows, events are stuck.
  • Keep payloads self-contained. Put the data consumers need in the event, rather than making every consumer call back to your API — otherwise you've rebuilt the coupling the events were meant to remove.

Takeaways

  • "Commit, then publish" is a dual write, and it loses events on crashes.
  • Write the event into an outbox table in the same transaction; publish it afterwards.
  • Relay by polling with SKIP LOCKED to start; move to CDC when latency or load demands it.
  • The outbox is at-least-once: consumers must de-duplicate.

title: I asked a trial registry for start dates up to 1900. It sent me January 1900.
description:
On 26 October 2026 I asked ClinicalTrials.gov for studies with a start date between 1800 and 1900. I expected no matches. The server returned 1. I opened it. The record, NCT03591926, shows a start date, a primary completion date and a completion date of January 1900. It was first posted in July 2018, and its status is withdrawn.

A date like that can mean someone had to fill a box and typed a stand-in. That is my guess. I have not confirmed why this date was entered. Think of a paper form where the date box would not stay empty, so someone wrote 01/01/1900.

I do not read this as a broken filter. The filter did its job on a record that holds a date I would not expect. This post is about telling those two cases apart.

What I wanted to know

After my earlier post about registry dates, I wanted to know if other public research APIs hide the same trap. I asked five of them two extreme questions for each date field, one about the far future and one about the far past. I also asked a normal question, about the year 2020, as a comparison.

Read this first

  • I opened only five records. Four look like placeholders or typing errors. One is a real old article. That is my reading, not the owners' word.
  • The counts are what each server reported on 26 October 2026. They change.
  • Three filters I could not judge. The Crossref index-date filter gave 0 for the normal question too. Two OpenAlex filters (created and updated) answered "too many requests" twice, so they were not measured. They are not in the script below.
  • The Europe PMC field names came from memory. Its documentation page would not load for me. The normal question returned large numbers for all three fields, but I did not check separately what each date means.
  • I told no one at these services. This is a note, not a bug report.

What I found

In this run, no extreme question returned the same count as an unfiltered search, for the filters I could judge. Where an extreme question returned a small number, I opened a few of the records.

API Far future Far past What I saw when I opened some
ClinicalTrials.gov 26 / 21 (primary completion / completion) 1 for each of three dates Two records. NCT03591926 (withdrawn): all three dates January 1900. NCT03180918 (recruiting): primary completion January 2100. Both look like placeholders; I am less sure about the second.
PubMed 0 1,299 (publication, entry and MeSH dates; creation date: 0) One record: a real article from 1800. That one is not an error.
Europe PMC 0 0 Nothing to open. The normal question returned 1,593,659 (PUB_YEAR), 1,638,722 (FIRST_PDATE) and 1,173,944 (E_PDATE).
Crossref 332 21,558 Two of the future ones: published in 2108 and 2106. Typing errors, I think. The past ones I did not open.
OpenAlex 0 2,323 (year) / 2,427 (date) I did not open any. Two other filters could not be measured.

This is not a survey

I did not measure how common these records are, and one question per field says little about a filter. I did not search the literature for earlier work on dates in these APIs.

What this does not show

  • It does not say these services are poor.
  • I cannot say the odd records are mistakes. Four of the five I opened look like placeholders or typing errors. The fifth is a real old article.
  • It does not compare the services with each other. The "far past" ranges are not the same in every API.

If you use dates from a public API

Three habits cost little. Ask a normal question too. It is a useful comparison, but it does not prove the field means what you think. Ask the impossible question, and expect a small answer sometimes. Open the odd ones before you call them wrong.

The questions

In the first run I sent 47 requests: 42 extreme-date queries and 5 unfiltered baseline queries. Then I sent 13 follow-ups: a normal question for the 11 fields where both extremes had returned 0, and two retries. That is 60 requests, three seconds apart, no account, and no API got more than twenty. On the same day I re-ran the ClinicalTrials.gov part of the script below, 18 more requests. The counts matched the first run wherever the first run had them.

The script below is a cleaned-up copy, not the code I ran. It asks the normal question for every field and leaves out the two OpenAlex filters I could not measure. I have not re-run all of it myself.

Field names came from each service's own pages: ClinicalTrials.gov from its metadata endpoint, PubMed from its help page, Crossref from its API notes, OpenAlex from its filter page.

The five records I opened

  • NCT03591926 (withdrawn): start, primary completion and completion dates all 1900-01; first submitted 2018-07-09, first posted 2018-07-19.
  • NCT03180918 (recruiting): primary completion and completion dates 2100-01; start 2015-01; first submitted 2017-05-31, first posted 2017-06-08.
  • Crossref, two works with published years 2108 and 2106.
  • PubMed, PMID 30491001: "Mr. Oliphant's Cases", published December 1800.

Script 

"""Ask public research APIs two extreme date questions per date field, plus a normal one.
Read only, no account, three seconds between requests.  Usage:
  python3 api_date_probe.py                  # all five APIs (about 60 requests)
  python3 api_date_probe.py ctgov crossref   # only some
Each line: count, API, field, which question.  The script judges nothing."""
import json, sys, time, urllib.parse as up, urllib.request

HEAD = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (research probe; read-only)"}
OUT = []

def ask(api, field, kind, url, pick):
    try:
        n = pick(json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, headers=HEAD), timeout=60).read().decode()))
    except Exception as e:
        n = f"ERROR {type(e).__name__}"
    OUT.append((api, field, kind, n))
    print(f"{str(n):>12}  {api:20} {field:24} {kind}", flush=True)
    time.sleep(3)

def ctgov():
    for f in ("StartDate", "PrimaryCompletionDate", "CompletionDate", "StudyFirstPostDate", "LastUpdatePostDate", "ResultsFirstPostDate"):
        for kind, rng in (("future", "2100-01-01,2200-01-01"), ("past", "1800-01-01,1900-01-01"), ("normal", "2020-01-01,2020-12-31")):
            url = "https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?" + up.urlencode({"filter.advanced": f"AREA[{f}]RANGE[{rng}]", "pageSize": 1, "countTotal": "true", "fields": "NCTId"})
            ask("ClinicalTrials.gov", f, kind, url, lambda d: d["totalCount"])

def pubmed():
    for tag in ("pdat", "edat", "crdt", "mhda"):
        for kind, rng in (("future", "2100/01/01:2200/12/31"), ("past", "1700/01/01:1800/12/31"), ("normal", "2020/01/01:2020/12/31")):
            url = "https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?" + up.urlencode({"db": "pubmed", "term": f"{rng}[{tag}]", "retmode": "json", "retmax": 0})
            ask("PubMed", tag, kind, url, lambda d: d["esearchresult"]["count"])

def europepmc():
    for f, form in (("PUB_YEAR", "[{a} TO {b}]"), ("FIRST_PDATE", "[{a}-01-01 TO {b}-12-31]"), ("E_PDATE", "[{a}-01-01 TO {b}-12-31]")):
        for kind, (a, b) in (("future", (2100, 2200)), ("past", (1500, 1600)), ("normal", (2020, 2020))):
            url = "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?" + up.urlencode({"query": f"{f}:" + form.format(a=a, b=b), "format": "json", "pageSize": 1, "resultType": "idlist"})
            ask("Europe PMC", f, kind, url, lambda d: d["hitCount"])

def crossref():
    for f in ("pub", "created", "deposit", "index", "update"):
        for kind, flt in (("future", f"from-{f}-date:2100-01-01"), ("past", f"until-{f}-date:1700-01-01"), ("normal", f"from-{f}-date:2020-01-01,until-{f}-date:2020-12-31")):
            ask("Crossref", f"{f}-date", kind, "https://api.crossref.org/works?" + up.urlencode({"filter": flt, "rows": 0}), lambda d: d["message"]["total-results"])

def openalex():
    for f, future, past, normal in (("publication_year", "publication_year:>2100", "publication_year:<1500", "publication_year:2020"),
                                    ("publication_date", "from_publication_date:2100-01-01", "to_publication_date:1500-01-01", "from_publication_date:2020-01-01,to_publication_date:2020-12-31")):
        for kind, flt in (("future", future), ("past", past), ("normal", normal)):
            ask("OpenAlex", f, kind, "https://api.openalex.org/works?" + up.urlencode({"filter": flt, "per-page": 1, "select": "id"}), lambda d: d["meta"]["count"])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    runners = {"ctgov": ctgov, "pubmed": pubmed, "europepmc": europepmc, "crossref": crossref, "openalex": openalex}
    for name in (sys.argv[1:] or runners):
        runners[name]()

Data: public APIs of ClinicalTrials.gov, PubMed, Europe PMC, Crossref and OpenAlex, queried on 26 October 2026.

title: A Save System Is a Promise, Not a Feature
description:
A player will never see your save code. They will feel the one time it fails.

Lost progress does not read like a technical problem to the person who lost it. It reads like a broken promise. The game said the progress counted, and then it did not.

In my game projects, Instinct does much of the implementation and testing. I stay responsible for direction and for the decision to ship. Save behavior sits exactly on that line: the assistant can build the mechanism, but the promise the mechanism keeps is a design decision. I want that promise written down before anyone writes code.

The failure is rarely the write

Most save systems write data correctly when they get the chance. The gap is timing.

A mobile game lives inside a lifecycle it does not control. The operating system can pause it, freeze it, or kill it to reclaim memory. A call arrives. The battery dies. The player swipes the app away in the middle of a reward animation because something in real life is more urgent than the next level.

If progress only reaches disk when a timer fires or when a scene closes politely, then every one of those exits is a small bet. Most days the bet wins. The day it loses, the player learns the game cannot be trusted, and that lesson is very hard to un-teach.

Write the promise in one sentence

Before choosing a mechanism, I want one sentence: what exactly must survive?

"Level progress and currency survive any exit, including a force-quit in the middle of an action." A sentence like that is short, but it rules things out. A timer that fires two seconds after a move does not satisfy it on its own. Neither does saving only when the player returns to the map.

The sentence also defines what is not promised. A half-finished animation does not need to resume. Cosmetic state can be regenerated. Being explicit here is what makes the real promise cheap enough to keep.

Save at decision points

The pattern I aim for is simple: when the game state changes in a way the player would call progress, that is a save point.

A level completed, a reward claimed, a purchase finished. If the save stays small, writing it often costs little. A few fields written at each decision point are usually a better bet than a full state dump written rarely.

Two mechanisms are worth naming. Writing to a temporary file and renaming it over the old one avoids the specific failure where a crash mid-write leaves a half-written file. It is not magic: durability still depends on the storage stack honoring the write, and the rename has to come after the write completes. Lifecycle callbacks are the second net, not the first. Android's onPause is a useful place to catch a background exit, but once the system decides to reclaim the process, no callback is guaranteed to run. A design that relies on callbacks alone is betting the promise on them.

Test the crash, not just the flow

A save you have not crash-tested is a hope.

The useful test is unglamorous: play, force-stop the app in the middle of the action, relaunch, and compare what survived with what the promise said should survive. Automate the boring version of it. Run it on the happy path and on the embarrassing paths: mid-reward, mid-purchase, mid-first-launch.

The honest limits

Even a good save design cannot guarantee that every byte reaches storage before the power is gone. What it can do is make that outcome rare, and make the promise explicit about what survives and what does not.

This is the same discipline as writing down what a test cannot prove. A persistence test that only exercises clean exits proves almost nothing about a phone in a pocket.

References:

  • Godot Engine documentation, Saving games: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/io/saving_games.html
  • Godot Engine documentation, FileAccess: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_fileaccess.html
  • Android Developers, The activity lifecycle: https://developer.android.com/guide/components/activities/activity-lifecycle

title: FedPA-LoRA: Product-Aligned Framework for Mitigating Aggregation and Initialization Errors in Heterogeneous Federated LoRA
description:
arXiv:2608.15381v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient federated fine-tuning of large language models, but its factorization creates a tension between aggregation fidelity and local optimization continuity. Factor-wise aggregation incurs aggregation mismatch but better preserves factor continuity, whereas product-space reconstruction reduces this mismatch at the cost of greater factor-level initialization mismatch. We propose FedPA-LoRA, a product-aligned framework that addresses both mismatches and establishes convergence bounds for homogeneous and heterogeneous ranks. Clients preserve local factors across rounds to eliminate initialization mismatch and align their products with rank-specific global references to reduce client drift. The server aggregates heterogeneous-rank updates in product space to mitigate aggregation mismatch and efficiently reconstructs a rank-constrained global adapter without forming the dense aggregate. By decoupling local and reference ranks, FedPA-LoRA supports client-specific computation and communication budgets. Experiments on natural language understanding and generation tasks show consistent gains under data and resource heterogeneity, including a 6.82 percentage-point improvement in average GLUE accuracy under heterogeneous ranks. The code is available at https://github.com/Juseok-Jeon/FedPA-LoRA.

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
description:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.
