title: Go Realtime Classroom Fan-Out Under Reconnects (Channels Are Not Storage)
description:
A realtime channel, explained operationally, carries classroom events to connected participants; it does not actually store chat history. That distinction becomes concrete when a page arrives during a live class: chat_duplicate_delivery_ratio has crossed 2% for ten minutes. The on-call view shows 186 reconnecting students, a healthy connection count, and no obvious server errors. Messages are moving. Some students are seeing the same answer twice, while others return from a network interruption and see a gap.

TL;DR: the least complex correct design is to use a realtime channel for low-latency fan-out to currently reachable participants, and a durable conversation log for identity, ordering, deduplication, and reconnect recovery. A channel carries an event now. It does not become a historical record merely because the connection stayed open. Give every accepted message a stable ID and room sequence, persist it before publication, let clients deduplicate by ID, and backfill from the log after reconnect.

This boundary matters more than the transport brand or protocol. I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries; the useful reflex is the same here: do not ask an ephemeral delivery path to prove durable state.

Make replay explicit.

What did the realtime channel actually promise?

A realtime channel is the live delivery relationship among a publisher, a fan-out service, and subscribers that are reachable at that moment. It may be implemented over a persistent connection, but connection lifetime and data lifetime are separate concerns. The channel can authenticate a participant, route an event to a room, apply backpressure, expose liveness, and report whether a write was accepted by the next component. None of those behaviors, by themselves, establish a durable transcript.

In an edtech room, a useful event might contain a room ID, message ID, author ID, room sequence, and payload. The stable identifiers matter because transport delivery can be retried and clients can reconnect. A timestamp is useful for display and diagnosis, but it is a poor substitute for an ordering token: clocks can disagree, and two messages can share the same display precision.

WebRTC makes this separation visible. Its data channels carry arbitrary data between peers, and the specification defines channel behavior such as ordering and retransmission controls. That describes transfer semantics. It does not define a classroom message archive that a returning student can query. An application that needs history must create that history outside the channel.

The socket is not the ledger.

The clean ownership split is:

Concern Live channel Durable message log Client
Fan-out to connected students Primary No Receives
Canonical message ID and room order Carries Owns Records
Reconnect backfill Requests or signals Serves Merges
Duplicate suppression May reduce retries Supports by stable ID Enforces for display
Presence Reports current observations Stores only if the product needs an audit record Renders as transient state

Presence is the common trap. “Student is typing” and “student is online” are short-lived observations, not transcript entries. A submitted answer, moderation decision, or teacher announcement may need durable retention because users expect it after a reconnect. Decide by product semantics, not by which events happen to share a socket.

The page starts with an ambiguous symptom

The 2% alert does not yet tell the on-call whether the server published twice, the network retried, the client merged a backfill incorrectly, or the metric counted a harmless duplicate that was suppressed before rendering. A single aggregate hides the point at which the invariant broke.

Start the trace with one message ID. The intake path should record that the command was accepted once under its idempotency key. The durable log should show one room sequence. The publisher should record attempts separately from logical publications. The client should report receipt and render decisions as different events. With those stages, the investigation can distinguish “delivered twice” from “displayed twice.” Those are different incidents.

The invariant I want in the runbook is compact: for each room sequence, the durable log contains one canonical message; a client may receive that message more than once, but it renders it at most once. Exactly-once end-to-end delivery is not assumed. The system instead combines an idempotent write, an ordered replay cursor, and deduplication at the final consumer.

A Go client-side merge can be small enough to audit. The real application would persist lastSeq locally if a process restart must resume from the same point.

package chat

import "sort"

type Message struct {
    ID     string
    RoomID string
    Seq    uint64
    Body   string
}

type Inbox struct {
    seen    map[string]struct{}
    lastSeq uint64
}

func NewInbox() *Inbox {
    return &Inbox{seen: make(map[string]struct{})}
}

func (i *Inbox) Merge(messages []Message) []Message {
    sort.Slice(messages, func(a, b int) bool {
        return messages[a].Seq < messages[b].Seq
    })

    merged := make([]Message, 0, len(messages))
    for _, message := range messages {
        if _, exists := i.seen[message.ID]; exists {
            continue
        }
        i.seen[message.ID] = struct{}{}
        if message.Seq > i.lastSeq {
            i.lastSeq = message.Seq
        }
        merged = append(merged, message)
    }
    return merged
}

func (i *Inbox) ResumeAfter() uint64 {
    return i.lastSeq
}

This example deliberately tolerates repeated receipt. It also refuses to infer missing history from connection state. When the connection returns, the client asks for messages after its durable cursor, merges that backfill with live arrivals, and suppresses IDs it has already rendered. The server must define whether the cursor is scoped to a room and what happens when retained history no longer covers it. Silence is not a recovery policy.

Instrument the boundary before tuning the alert

The earlier signal should have been a growing recovery gap, not a complaint-driven duplicate ratio. Measure the system at the boundary between accepted state and attempted delivery. At minimum, retain counts and latency distributions for accepted messages, persisted messages, publish attempts, connected recipients, reconnects, backfill results, duplicate receipts, duplicate renders, and cursor-too-old responses. Keep labels bounded; message IDs belong in traces or structured logs, not metric dimensions.

Three correlated views make the page actionable. First, track the age of the newest durable room sequence that has not yet reached the publisher. Second, track reconnect backfill latency and failures. Third, compare duplicate receipts with duplicate renders. A rise in receipts with zero duplicate renders describes extra work and capacity risk. A rise in renders is a user-visible correctness failure.

Alert on broken user invariants, then attach transport signals for diagnosis. A page for duplicate renders should identify affected rooms, client version, reconnect state, and a trace sample. A separate capacity alert can cover sustained retry amplification before correctness degrades. The runbook then has an order: confirm durable-log health, inspect the persist-to-publish lag, sample one message trace, check backfill behavior, and only then inspect connection churn.

Do not skip deployment behavior. Roll out cursor or envelope changes with readers that accept both old and new forms, then switch writers, then remove the old reader after the compatibility window. Test forced disconnects between persistence and publication, during backfill, and immediately after the live subscription resumes. Also test a duplicated event, an out-of-order arrival, a stale cursor, and two browser tabs using the same account.

Short tests catch the expensive assumptions.

Delivery guarantees are an application decision

“At most once” can lose a classroom message during a disconnect. “At least once” can repeat it. An ordered channel can preserve order for what traverses that channel while still lacking events created during an absence. These labels do not answer the product question until the boundaries are named: accepted where, acknowledged by whom, retained for how long, and ordered within which scope?

For classroom chat, I choose persist-before-publish because it gives the on-call one durable invariant to check. The sender receives success only after the message is accepted into the durable log; publication follows from that accepted record. If publication is retried, the ID stays constant. If a student reconnects between those steps, backfill and live delivery may race, which is fine because the merge is idempotent. The trade-off is visible latency from the durable write and extra storage and replay capacity. Publish-before-persist can look quicker, but a process loss between those actions can expose a message live and omit it from later history.

Retention still needs a product decision. The channel cannot decide how long a course transcript, deleted message marker, or moderation action should remain available. Define retention, deletion, and authorization on the durable store, and apply the same authorization to backfill that applies to live subscription. A reconnect must not become a way to read a room the student can no longer enter.

Capacity follows from the recovery contract. Model normal live fan-out separately from reconnect bursts: a campus network recovery can make many clients request overlapping history while live classes continue. Bound each backfill, paginate it, and keep live events mergeable with the replay. Load tests should include that overlap rather than benchmarking a steady stream on permanently healthy connections.

A useful threshold can still wake the wrong person

After adding stage-level instrumentation, tune the page around user-visible failure. Duplicate receipt rate alone is a noisy threshold because retries can increase while client deduplication continues to work. Paging on every such increase trains the on-call to ignore the signal and penalizes a recovery mechanism for doing its job.

The opposite mistake is waiting for a large duplicate-render percentage. A low global rate can hide one badly affected classroom. Use a sustained condition, a minimum event count, and a room-level view alongside the fleet aggregate. Route retry amplification to a lower-urgency capacity signal when renders remain correct; page when durable gaps grow, backfill fails, or users actually receive an inconsistent transcript. Exact thresholds must come from the service's traffic distribution and error budget, then be reviewed against real alert outcomes. There is no universal 2%.

That is the final operational boundary: a channel gives the application a path for events in motion. Storage gives it evidence of accepted state. Observability tells the on-call which side violated its contract. Confusing those jobs produces both missed messages and noisy pages.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: How to Audit Someone Else’s Backtest in 10 Minutes
description:
Four questions expose most weak backtests in minutes: trial count, costs, sample span, and what chose the parameters. Plus the baseline test every claim must pass.

You do not need a quant degree to audit a backtest. You need four questions, asked in order, and the willingness to walk away when the answers are vague. Most weak backtests fail at least two of these in the first ten minutes.

Question 1: How many trials produced this result?

If a vendor tried 500 parameter combinations and shows you the best, the headline number is partly luck. The more alternatives explored, the less a naive performance statistic means — unless it is adjusted for multiple testing. Honest answers sound like “we tried 12 configurations, here is the correction.” Evasive answers sound like “our AI found the optimal settings.” Count the trials, or discount the claim to zero.

Question 2: Were costs modelled realistically?

Commissions, spread, slippage, borrow costs, market impact. A backtest that books fills at the decision price is testing a market that does not exist. Ask for net-of-cost results specifically. If the edge disappears under realistic friction, there was no edge — there was an accounting choice. Execution friction is measurable, so an honest backtest can include it.

Question 3: Does the sample span enough market conditions?

A strategy tested only on a bull market has not been tested; it has been photographed in good light. Demand results sliced by year and by regime — uptrend, downtrend, high and low volatility. Concentration of returns in one narrow slice is a warning sign, not a track record. And remember: a strategy that looks great on six trades is a small sample wearing a big number. Six trades is a caution flag, not a victory lap.

Question 4: Did the same data choose and validate the parameters?

This is the fastest way to expose a weak backtest. If the full dataset informed the design, the features, or the tuning, then the “validation” on that same data is contaminated — even if it carries a validation label. Parameters must be chosen on training data and judged on data that played no part in choosing them. Purged, embargoed folds are the strict version of this; at minimum, demand genuine out-of-sample periods.

The baseline test (30 seconds)

Ask what the dumbest rule scored on the same data. If a directional model claims 70% accuracy but always predicting “up” scores 68%, the model added almost nothing. On a bare CSV with no price history, two honest baselines exist: always-bullish and no-change. Any claim that cannot beat those has nothing to say, however sophisticated the model sounds.

What a clean audit looks like

A credible result survives this sequence: accuracy recomputed from raw predictions (claimed columns ignored), baselines beaten, walk-forward folds stable rather than decaying, leakage gate passed, trial count disclosed and corrected for. That is the standard BuildIT Index applies mechanically — it returns a verdict and an exit code, so a failing backtest fails a pipeline instead of persuading a meeting.

Print these four questions and keep them beside every pitch deck, vendor demo, and course sales page. They will save you more money than any indicator ever will.

No trial count, no net-of-cost results, no out-of-sample period, no baseline. Any one missing answer is enough to stop the conversation.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past backtest results do not predict future returns.

title: Feature Toggle Service for Small Teams Using Node.js (2026 Pricing and Rollback Evidence)
description:
TL;DR: for small teams using Node.js, choose a feature toggle service that leaves a defensible rollback record, not merely a switch that changes quickly. Flagsmith is the better fit when on-premise hosting and privacy control lead. LaunchDarkly is stronger when hosted documentation and real-time updates shorten delivery. ConfigCat and GrowthBook suit small, straightforward targeting needs. Infrai is worth trying at the evidence boundary when one REST contract and one credential can remove integration work, but it is not a substitute for specialist flag governance.

In customer support, a feature flag can disable a broken reply composer before the next conversation is affected. The rollback is only useful later if the team can reconstruct which value the request actually saw, which release produced it, and what evidence justified the reversal. That is the operational constraint that changes the answer.

I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat a rollback record like a replay record: it must survive retries, preserve identity, and distinguish an action from an observation. I initially treated the flag console as the source of truth; the useful correction was to record the value at the application boundary. The same discipline applies to a Node.js support application. A dashboard saying composer = off is not proof that a failed reply was evaluated with that value.

What should the rollback record prove?

Start with an application-owned request ID. Store the evaluated flag key and value, build or release identifier, observation time, and a customer interaction identifier governed by your privacy policy. Keep the customer ID in structured event context rather than automatically making it a metric label; Prometheus warns that unbounded label cardinality creates an operational problem.

The flag provider should own targeting semantics. The application should own the evidence that connects a flag decision to a support interaction and an error event. That boundary matters because clients may poll, updates may arrive between two requests, and an operator needs the value used by the request rather than the value visible in a later console view.

The provider also needs to match the failure mode. A small service might accept a little manual work around deployment, but it should not accept ambiguity during a customer incident. I would write the rollback runbook before choosing the SDK:

  1. Record the request and evaluated flag value.
  2. Capture the error with the same request ID.
  3. Change the flag through a controlled operator path.
  4. Verify new requests and record the post-change observation.

That is four steps, but it is one evidence chain.

Which feature toggle service should small teams using Node.js choose?

For small Node.js teams, the meaningful comparison is setup friction plus the evidence the team must build around the product.

Service Strong fit Boundary to record
Flagsmith Open-source operation and on-premise hosting Your team carries more deployment and operational ownership
LaunchDarkly Hosted integration, strong developer documentation, and real-time flag updates Paid plans start at around $10 per user per month, and plan details can change
ConfigCat A simple hosted tool for a small use case It lacks some enterprise-grade targeting features
GrowthBook A simple hosted option with an open-source orientation It lacks some enterprise-grade targeting features for complex targeting

Flagsmith is the conservative choice for a privacy-conscious team that can operate the service. LaunchDarkly is the faster hosted path when polished documentation and real-time updates matter more than keeping the control plane in your own environment. ConfigCat and GrowthBook reduce the initial surface for a small use case, but their simpler targeting boundary becomes important as rollout rules become more involved.

The price is not the decision rule. The durable question is which evidence the service provides and which evidence your application must record. A hosted SDK can get a flag into a Node.js process quickly; it does not automatically explain a disputed customer reply.

The surrounding observability choice is separate. Sentry is a natural fit when exception grouping and error investigation are the center of the workflow. Datadog is a stronger candidate when a team wants hosted metrics, logs, and traces in one observability product. Grafana fits teams that prefer assembling dashboards around their own metrics and data sources. Those products can complement a flag service; they do not replace its targeting or rollout controls. Conversely, a dedicated flag product will not provide the full incident search and paging experience by itself.

Infrai belongs at a different layer of this comparison. Its discovery surface is public and self-describing, with a full JSON Schema, billing information, and runnable examples available without a key. The live surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules, including 23 observability routes, under one key. That breadth behind a plain REST contract is useful when the same small team needs flag operations alongside telemetry or another backend capability.

The second advantage is operationally narrower but concrete: one credential and one billing relationship can span those capabilities. A team adding evidence capture does not need to assemble another set of SDK credentials and reconcile another vendor boundary just to connect the flag decision to the incident record. That reduces setup friction; it does not create an audit log or evaluation history that the product does not provide.

How do I keep a polled flag from lying about a rollback?

A client-side polling model makes timing part of the evidence. Record the value returned to the process, the time it was observed, and the request ID that consumed it. Do not reconstruct that state from a later flag listing.

The following small Go program reads a flag value through a documented route and handles transient rate limiting. It is intentionally a read path: the write payload for a change should be generated from the live discovery schema, and a production write must use a client-supplied idempotency key. The application can use the same record shape around a Node.js flag client.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func readFlag(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    flagKey := os.Getenv("FLAG_KEY")
    if flagKey == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("FLAG_KEY is required")
    }

    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/list"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("flag read returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("evidence read remained rate limited")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    body, err := readFlag(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, key)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

There are no silent successes here: a non-2xx response is surfaced, and a 429 honors Retry-After when it is present. A write path needs the same status handling plus idempotent retry behavior. Standard queue semantics are at-least-once, and the same principle applies to evidence delivery: a duplicate event must be harmless to the incident record.

Where does the unified surface stop helping?

Infrai has useful integration properties: the API is self-describing, documented capabilities have runnable examples in 10 languages, and the broad surface is available behind one key. Those facts can reduce the time from a schema check to a first useful request, especially when a team is joining a flag decision to error or metric evidence. The service is still a component, not the complete runbook.

Its flag capability has no change audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, recycle bin, or push updates; clients poll. It also has no alerting or notification routes, so threshold checks and paging require polling a query API and building the notification path. There is no distributed-trace query or span tree, and logs can be correlated with trace_id and span_id fields only. Silent failures where a scheduled task did not run still need a Healthchecks-style tool.

The retention boundary matters for support work. There is no log-delete interface by user for a GDPR erasure request, no batch export or subscription interface, and no configuration entry for retention or cold storage even though related error codes exist. Those are governance and operations gaps, not details to hide in an integration estimate.

A specialist wins when mature alert routing, trace exploration, session replay, source-map handling, or flag governance is the primary requirement. A stack built from a dedicated flag service plus dedicated observability tools may involve more credentials and SDKs, but it can provide a deeper control plane. One platform also creates one trust boundary and one outage surface; that belongs in the review.

A decision rule for the next support incident

Choose Flagsmith when on-premise hosting and privacy control are the hard requirements. Choose LaunchDarkly when hosted documentation and real-time updates are the fastest route to a controlled release. Choose ConfigCat or GrowthBook when the targeting model is small and the missing enterprise features are acceptable.

Try Infrai for the evidence boundary when a small team needs flag state, telemetry, and other backend capabilities behind one self-describing REST surface. The recommendation is specific: it reduces credential and integration friction for connecting those records. It does not replace audit history, evaluation analytics, alerting, trace exploration, or retention controls.

That distinction is what makes the rollback safe. A switch can stop the next bad reply. Only an evidence chain can explain the last one.

The limitation is straightforward: choose a specialist when governance, alerting, or trace exploration is the product you need to operate every day. To inspect the flag kill-switch boundary, start with the feature-flag incident-response guide.

  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • ConfigCat documentation
  • GrowthBook documentation
  • Prometheus instrumentation best practices
  • web.dev Core Web Vitals
  • Infrai feature-flag kill switch guide

title: SVG to PNG in the tab when the design export is vector-only
description:
Design drops an SVG. Slack wants a PNG. The App Store listing wants a PNG. Email clients laugh at SVG. Your CI screenshot fixture wants a PNG. And you're on Linux, so "just Open in Preview → Export" is not a thing.

I hit this weekly. The vector file is correct — scale, colors, viewBox all fine — but the consumer only eats raster. Opening Illustrator (or waiting for design to re-export at 1x/2x/3x) for a one-off PNG is the slow path.

So I keep a tab workflow: SVG in → PNG out, without uploading the mark to a random converter.

When SVG alone isn't enough

SVG is great inside the product:

  • Icons that follow currentColor
  • Responsive logos that stay crisp
  • Inline chrome that never blur on retina

PNG still wins outside the product:

  • Chat / docs — Slack, Notion, Linear comments often strip or refuse SVG
  • Marketing surfaces — many email clients, some CMS uploaders, OG image pipelines
  • Stores & listings — App Store / Play / directory forms that hard-require PNG/JPG
  • Diff fixtures — visual regression baselines are almost always raster
  • Partner handoff — "send me the logo" usually means a transparent PNG, not XML

Keeping the source as SVG and deriving PNG at the moment of need beats maintaining a parallel PNG folder that drifts.

What goes wrong with the naive paths

Ask design for another export — fine for a brand refresh; painful for "I need a 512px transparent mark before standup."

Desktop converters — ImageMagick / Inkscape / Affinity work, until you're on a locked laptop, a hotel Wi‑Fi machine, or someone else's Chromebook.

Upload-to-convert sites — easiest to regret. Brand SVGs are IP. I don't want the mark sitting in someone else's temp bucket because I needed a PNG for a README.

Screenshot the SVG in the browser — you get wrong DPI, wrong background, wrong crop, and a JPEG-looking mess more often than you admit.

What I actually need from the convert step

For frontend / DX use, the checklist is boring and specific:

  1. Transparent background by default (don't bake white unless I ask)
  2. Explicit pixel size — 128 / 256 / 512 / 1024, not "whatever the viewBox felt like"
  3. No upload — file stays in the tab (DevTools Offline litmus still applies)
  4. Predictable naming — logo-512.png, not download (17).png
  5. Sanity preview before download — catch missing fonts / clipped paths early

If the tool can't do those five, I'm back to Inkscape CLI.

A tab that fits the handoff

When design already gave me the SVG and I just need raster for a non-SVG surface, I've used Uwarp's SVG → PNG tool — drop the file, pick a size, download PNG in the browser. Worth trying when the alternative is another desktop install or an upload converter you can't audit.

For a recurring pipeline (favicon set, store assets, email header), script it: rsvg-convert, inkscape --export-type=png, or a tiny Puppeteer render. The tab is for the one-offs that shouldn't block a PR.

Keep the SVG as source of truth

A few rules that stopped me from growing a junk drawer of PNGs:

  • Commit SVG in the design-system / brand repo; generate PNG at publish time
  • Name by intent + size (mark-on-dark-512.png), never final_final2.png
  • Don't "edit" the PNG — if color changes, change the SVG and re-export
  • Document the sizes you actually ship (email 600w, OG 1200×630, store 1024) so people stop inventing new ones in Slack

SVG → PNG is a packaging step, not a design decision. Treat it like that and the folder stays boring.

Tiny habit

Next time someone asks for "the logo as PNG" and you already have the SVG, don't reopen the design tool and don't upload the brand mark. Convert in a local-ish tab (or a one-liner CLI), verify transparency and size, send the file, close the loop.

Fewer blocked handoffs. Fewer mystery PNGs in Downloads. Same vector source — just the raster shape the other surface actually accepts.

title: Keeping AI Agents from Writing Wrong Data: Validation, Deterministic Checks and Fallbacks in Go
description:
An agent that answers a question wrongly is embarrassing. An agent that writes wrong data, such as moving the wrong ticket, booking the wrong slot or saving a made-up value, is a production incident. And unlike a bad answer, bad data stays around and spreads to every system that reads it.

The approach that has worked for me across Go agent projects is one rule: the model proposes, the code decides. The LLM can suggest an action. Deterministic Go code checks it, applies it, records it, or refuses it. This post covers the layers that implement that rule. The examples are simplified versions of patterns from my own projects, including a Jira-style product where a Gemini assistant changes project data only through typed backend tools, and a restaurant recommendation API where safety filters run before the LLM sees anything.

Layer 1: no free-form writes

The first decision is architectural. The agent should never produce SQL, raw API payloads or "update these fields" maps. It calls narrow, typed operations that your domain layer already supports.

// Bad: the model controls what gets written.
// update_record(table string, id string, fields map[string]any)

// Good: one intent, typed and checkable.
type AssignIssue struct {
    IssueKey string `json:"issue_key"`
    Assignee string `json:"assignee_email"`
}

type SetDueDate struct {
    IssueKey string `json:"issue_key"`
    Due      string `json:"due_date"` // YYYY-MM-DD
}

Each struct maps to one function in your service layer, the same one your REST API calls, with the same permission checks. This is how the assistant in my sprint-management product works: it acts on project data through typed backend tools, not by writing to the database directly.

Layer 2: strict decoding

Model output is untrusted input. Decode it like you'd decode a request from the public internet:

func decodeStrict[T any](raw []byte) (T, error) {
    var v T
    dec := json.NewDecoder(bytes.NewReader(raw))
    dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
    if err := dec.Decode(&v); err != nil {
        return v, fmt.Errorf("decode: %w", err)
    }
    if dec.More() {
        return v, errors.New("decode: trailing data after JSON object")
    }
    return v, nil
}

DisallowUnknownFields catches the model inventing a field like priority_level that you'd otherwise drop silently. The More() check catches responses with extra content after the JSON.

Layer 3: domain validation

Valid JSON isn't valid data. Put the business rules on the type itself, so every caller, agent or human, goes through them:

type Validator interface{ Validate() error }

var issueKeyRE = regexp.MustCompile(`^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-[0-9]+$`)

func (c SetDueDate) Validate() error {
    if !issueKeyRE.MatchString(c.IssueKey) {
        return fmt.Errorf("issue_key %q must look like ABC-123", c.IssueKey)
    }
    d, err := time.Parse(time.DateOnly, c.Due)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("due_date %q must be YYYY-MM-DD", c.Due)
    }
    today := time.Now().UTC().Truncate(24 * time.Hour)
    if d.Before(today) {
        return fmt.Errorf("due_date %s is in the past", c.Due)
    }
    if d.After(today.AddDate(2, 0, 0)) {
        return fmt.Errorf("due_date %s is more than 2 years away; confirm with the user", c.Due)
    }
    return nil
}

Write the messages for the model. When validation fails inside an agent loop, the error goes back as a tool result, and a specific message ("must be YYYY-MM-DD") lets the model fix the call instead of guessing again.

Layer 4: reference checks against real data

Hallucinated identifiers are the most common way agents write wrong data. The model "remembers" an issue key, a user email or a product ID that doesn't exist, or belongs to someone else. Format checks won't catch it. Only your database can.

func (s *Service) CheckRefs(ctx context.Context, u User, c AssignIssue) error {
    issue, err := s.issues.Get(ctx, c.IssueKey)
    if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) {
        return fmt.Errorf("issue %s does not exist; call search_issues to find the right key", c.IssueKey)
    }
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if !s.authz.Can(u, "issue:update", issue.ProjectID) {
        return fmt.Errorf("you cannot modify issues in project %s", issue.ProjectKey)
    }
    if ok, err := s.projects.IsMember(ctx, issue.ProjectID, c.Assignee); err != nil {
        return err
    } else if !ok {
        return fmt.Errorf("%s is not a member of project %s", c.Assignee, issue.ProjectKey)
    }
    return nil
}

The same idea works for read paths. In a RAG system, the IDs in the model's answer can be checked against the set of candidates that were actually retrieved and sent to it. Anything outside that set is a hallucination by definition.

Layer 5: plan, then apply

For anything with more than one write, split the work into two phases. The agent builds a plan. Code validates the whole plan, shows it to a human or policy check if needed, and only then applies it in a single transaction.

type Plan struct {
    ID      string
    Actions []Action // each Action wraps a validated, typed command
}

func (s *Service) Apply(ctx context.Context, u User, p Plan) error {
    for i, a := range p.Actions {
        if err := a.Validate(); err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("action %d: %w", i, err)
        }
        if err := a.CheckRefs(ctx, s, u); err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("action %d: %w", i, err)
        }
    }
    return s.db.InTx(ctx, func(tx Tx) error {
        for _, a := range p.Actions {
            if err := a.Apply(ctx, tx); err != nil {
                return err // rolls back everything
            }
        }
        return s.audit.Record(ctx, tx, u, p)
    })
}

Validate everything before writing anything. A plan where step 3 is invalid should leave no trace of steps 1 and 2.

Layer 6: idempotency

Agents retry. Networks retry. Sometimes the model simply repeats a tool call. Without idempotency, "create a task" twice means two tasks.

func idempotencyKey(runID string, a Action) string {
    b, _ := json.Marshal(a)
    sum := sha256.Sum256(append([]byte(runID+":"), b...))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

Store the key with a unique constraint and treat a duplicate as "already done", returning the original result. Scoping the key to the agent run means a genuine second request in a new conversation still works.

Layer 7: audit everything the agent writes

Record who asked, which run, which tool, the arguments, the before and after values, and the model used. When something looks wrong a week later, you need to answer "did the agent do this, and why?" in minutes. It also gives you the data to undo it.

Layer 8: fallbacks that are safe by construction

When the model is down, slow, or keeps failing validation, the agent needs a defined way out. The important property: the fallback must not skip the checks.

func (s *Service) Handle(ctx context.Context, u User, req Request) (Result, error) {
    plan, err := s.agent.Propose(ctx, req)
    if err != nil {
        // Model unavailable: do the safe, deterministic subset, or hand off.
        return s.deterministicPath(ctx, u, req)
    }
    if err := s.Apply(ctx, u, plan); err != nil {
        return Result{Status: "needs_review", Reason: err.Error()}, nil
    }
    return Result{Status: "applied", PlanID: plan.ID}, nil
}

In the Restaurant Suggestion System, the fallback is vector-only search when the LLM is unavailable. Run that path through the same allergen and health filters, so users still get safe, if less conversational, recommendations. In a write workflow, the fallback is often "queue it for a human" rather than "try again with a weaker check".

Testing the guardrails

The guardrails are deterministic Go, so test them like any other code. Table tests cover the cases that matter: hallucinated IDs, past dates, unknown fields, duplicate calls, a plan with one bad action, permission failures. Then add a few end-to-end runs with a scripted fake model that deliberately sends bad tool calls, and assert that nothing reaches the database.

Takeaways

  • Never let the model write free-form; give it narrow, typed operations.
  • Decode strictly, validate in the domain, and check references against real data.
  • Plan, then apply in one transaction; make writes idempotent; audit them.
  • Make the fallback at least as safe as the main path.

None of this is AI-specific. It's the same input validation and transactional discipline good backends always needed, applied to a new and very confident source of input.

Pradip Parmar is a Go backend and AI agent engineer from Surat, India, who has been writing Go since 2018. He designs LLM agents, MCP servers and RAG systems for businesses, with a focus on guardrails, typed tool calls and graceful fallbacks. Need a Go AI agent developer? Reach Pradip Parmar on LinkedIn, Upwork or Contra. Code: GitHub.

title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
description:
arXiv:2610.42001v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.

title: Connect to a MongoDB Database Using Node.js
description:
Use Node.js? Want to learn MongoDB? This is the blog series for you!

In this Quick Start series, I’ll walk you through the basics of how to get started using MongoDB with Node.js. In today’s post, we’ll work through connecting to a MongoDB database from a Node.js script, retrieving a list of databases, and printing the results to your console.

Set up

Before we begin, we need to ensure you’ve completed a few prerequisite steps.

Install Node.js

First, make sure you have a supported version of Node.js installed. The current version of MongoDB Node.js Driver requires Node 4.x or greater. For these examples, I've used Node.js 14.15.4. See the MongoDB Compatabillity docs for more information on which version of Node.js is required for each version of the Node.js driver.

Install the MongoDB Node.js Driver

The MongoDB Node.js Driver allows you to easily interact with MongoDB databases from within Node.js applications. You'll need the driver in order to connect to your database and execute the queries described in this Quick Start series.

If you don't have the MongoDB Node.js Driver installed, you can install it with the following command.

At the time of writing, this installed version 3.6.4 of the driver. Running npm list mongodb will display the currently installed driver version number. For more details on the driver and installation, see the official documentation.

Create a free MongoDB Atlas cluster and load the sample data

Next, you'll need a MongoDB database. The easiest way to get started with MongoDB is to use Atlas, MongoDB's fully-managed database-as-a-service.

Head over to Atlas and create a new cluster in the free tier. At a high level, a cluster is a set of nodes where copies of your database will be stored. Once your tier is created, load the sample data. If you're not familiar with how to create a new cluster and load the sample data, check out this video tutorial from MongoDB Developer Advocate Maxime Beugnet.

Get your cluster’s connection info

The final step is to prep your cluster for connection.

In Atlas, navigate to your cluster and click CONNECT. The Cluster Connection Wizard will appear.

The Wizard will prompt you to add your current IP address to the IP Access List and create a MongoDB user if you haven't already done so. Be sure to note the username and password you use for the new MongoDB user as you'll need them in a later step.

Next, the Wizard will prompt you to choose a connection method. Select Connect Your Application. When the Wizard prompts you to select your driver version, select Node.js and 3.6 or later. Copy the provided connection string.

For more details on how to access the Connection Wizard and complete the steps described above, see the official documentation.

Connect to your database from a Node.js application

Now that everything is set up, it’s time to code! Let’s write a Node.js script that connects to your database and lists the databases in your cluster.

Import MongoClient

The MongoDB module exports MongoClient, and that’s what we’ll use to connect to a MongoDB database. We can use an instance of MongoClient to connect to a cluster, access the database in that cluster, and close the connection to that cluster.

Create our main function

Let’s create an asynchronous function named main() where we will connect to our MongoDB cluster, call functions that query our database, and disconnect from our cluster.

The first thing we need to do inside of main() is create a constant for our connection URI. The connection URI is the connection string you copied in Atlas in the previous section. When you paste the connection string, don't forget to update <username> and <password> to be the credentials for the user you created in the previous section. The connection string includes a <dbname> placeholder. For these examples, we'll be using the sample_airbnb database, so replace <dbname> with sample_airbnb.

Note: the username and password you provide in the connection string are NOT the same as your Atlas credentials.

Now that we have our URI, we can create an instance of MongoClient.

Note: When you run this code, you may see DeprecationWarnings around the URL string parserand the Server Discover and Monitoring engine. If you see these warnings, you can remove them by passing options to the MongoClient. For example, you could instantiate MongoClient by calling new MongoClient(uri, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }). See the Node.js MongoDB Driver API documentation for more information on these options.

Now we're ready to use MongoClient to connect to our cluster. client.connect() will return a promise. We will use the await keyword when we call client.connect() to indicate that we should block further execution until that operation has completed.

Now we are ready to interact with our database. Let's build a function that prints the names of the databases in this cluster. It's often useful to contain this logic in well named functions in order to improve the readability of your codebase. Throughout this series, we'll create new functions similar to the function we're creating here as we learn how to write different types of queries. For now, let's call a function named listDatabases().

Let’s wrap our calls to functions that interact with the database in a try/catch statement so that we handle any unexpected errors.

We want to be sure we close the connection to our cluster, so we’ll end our try/catch with a finally statement.

Once we have our main() function written, we need to call it. Let’s send the errors to the console.

Putting it all together, our main() function and our call to it will look something like the following.

List the databases in our cluster

In the previous section, we referenced the listDatabases() function. Let’s implement it!

This function will retrieve a list of databases in our cluster and print the results in the console.

Save Your File

You’ve been implementing a lot of code. Save your changes, and name your file something like connection.js. To see a copy of the complete file, visit the nodejs-quickstart GitHub repo.

Execute Your Node.js Script

Now you’re ready to test your code! Execute your script by running a command like the following in your terminal: node connection.js

You will see output like the following:

What’s next?

Today, you were able to connect to a MongoDB database from a Node.js script, retrieve a list of databases in your cluster, and view the results in your console. Nice!

Now that you're connected to your database, continue on to the next post in this series where you'll learn to execute each of the CRUD (create, read, update, and delete) operations.

In the meantime, check out the following resources:

  • Official MongoDB Documentation on the MongoDB Node.js Driver

  • MongoDB University Free Course: M220JS: MongoDB for Javascript Developers

Questions? Comments? We'd love to connect with you. Join the conversation on the MongoDB Community Forums.

title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
description:
arXiv:2610.42141v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.

title: Physics-Audited Agentic Discovery in Scientific Machine Learning
description:
arXiv:2607.07379v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Agentic discovery can yield mechanics surrogates with low validation error that nonetheless violate physical requirements. We present Physics-Audited Agentic SciML (PA-SciML), a framework combining large language model agents with physics auditing. Physical requirements, encoded as contracts such as superposition, boundary conditions, and causality, are fixed before candidate search and tested on predicted fields without reference solutions, including through an adversarial search. Audit results guide later proposals and model selection but are reported separately from validation error. Single-edit tests document reusable design changes. Four solid-mechanics problems of increasing complexity, from parametric elasticity to heterogeneous stiffness fields and cyclic plasticity with combined hardening, reveal causality, zero-input, and stress-bound violations in surrogates selected by error alone. In elastodynamics, two surrogates reach nearly equal error, but only the audit-enabled one is causal by construction. Audit-enabled surrogates pass the required checks at sampled inputs while matching or exceeding audit-disabled accuracy in most comparisons.

title: Apache Airflow for Java Engineers: Orchestrating Data Pipelines Beyond Python
description:
Introduction

Most data platforms eventually reach the same problem. Jobs that once ran from a cron entry now depend on each other, run at different frequencies, fail for reasons nobody remembers, and need to be retried, backfilled, and monitored. A shell script and a crontab are no longer enough. What teams need is an orchestrator: a system that knows what should run, in which order, when, and what to do when something breaks.

Apache Airflow is one of the most widely adopted orchestrators for this job. It lets you describe workflows as code, schedule them, visualize their state, and recover from failures in a consistent way. It is written in Python, and its workflow definitions are Python files, which can make it look like a tool that lives outside the world of Java and Spring Boot. In practice, Java engineers use Airflow constantly: they trigger its workflows from services, consume its APIs, run the jobs it orchestrates, and operate the platforms it depends on.

This article explains what Airflow is, how its core concepts fit together, how to write and test a workflow, and how a Java backend can integrate with it through the REST API. The goal is not to turn you into a Python developer, but to give you a clear mental model so you can design better systems around Airflow.

The Problem Airflow Solves

Consider a typical nightly pipeline for a digital banking platform. It extracts transactions from several operational databases, validates them, aggregates them into daily balances, generates regulatory reports, and publishes the results to a data warehouse. Each step depends on the previous one. Some steps are slow, some are flaky, and some must not run if an upstream check fails.

Without an orchestrator, this usually turns into a chain of scripts with hard-coded timing. If the extraction takes longer than expected, the aggregation starts too early and produces incomplete numbers. If a step fails at 3 a.m., someone has to read logs, figure out where the process stopped, and rerun the right part without duplicating work. Backfilling a month of data becomes a manual, error-prone exercise.

An orchestrator addresses these issues by separating three concerns:

  • What needs to be done, expressed as tasks and their dependencies.
  • When it should run, expressed as schedules, triggers, or external events.
  • How failures are handled, expressed as retries, timeouts, alerts, and recovery rules.

Airflow models all three explicitly, and gives you a web interface to see what happened.

Core Concepts

Airflow is built on a small set of concepts. Understanding them makes the rest of the platform easier to reason about.

DAGs

A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) is a workflow. It is a collection of tasks with dependencies, and it has no cycles: a task cannot depend, directly or indirectly, on itself. Each DAG has a schedule, a start date, and a set of default arguments.

Tasks and Operators

A task is a unit of work inside a DAG. Tasks are created from operators, which are templates for common actions. Airflow ships with operators for running Python functions, executing shell commands, transferring files, and calling external systems. Providers add many more, covering cloud storage, databases, and messaging systems.

Dependencies

Dependencies define the execution order. In code, you express them with the >> operator or with methods such as set_downstream. Airflow uses these relationships to decide which tasks can run in parallel and which must wait.

Task Instances and DAG Runs

Each execution of a DAG is a DAG run, identified by a logical date. Each task within a run is a task instance, with its own state: queued, running, success, failed, skipped, or up for retry. This model is what allows Airflow to backfill historical data: it simply creates DAG runs for past logical dates.

Scheduler, Executor, and Metadata Database

The scheduler decides which task instances are ready to run and hands them to the executor. The executor determines where tasks run: locally, in a pool of Celery workers, or as Kubernetes pods. All state is stored in a metadata database, usually PostgreSQL in production.

Knowing this split is important operationally. The scheduler and the database are the heart of the platform, and they need the same care you would give any critical backend component.

A First Workflow

Airflow workflows are Python files placed in the dags folder. Here is a minimal example that runs three dependent tasks every day:

from datetime import datetime, timedelta

from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator


def extract_transactions(**context):
    print(f"Extracting transactions for {context['ds']}")


def validate_transactions(**context):
    print("Running validation checks")


def publish_balances(**context):
    print("Publishing daily balances")


default_args = {
    "owner": "data-platform",
    "retries": 2,
    "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5),
}

with DAG(
    dag_id="daily_balances",
    default_args=default_args,
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    schedule="0 2 * * *",
    catchup=False,
    tags=["banking", "reporting"],
) as dag:

    extract = PythonOperator(
        task_id="extract_transactions",
        python_callable=extract_transactions,
    )

    validate = PythonOperator(
        task_id="validate_transactions",
        python_callable=validate_transactions,
    )

    publish = PythonOperator(
        task_id="publish_balances",
        python_callable=publish_balances,
    )

    extract >> validate >> publish

A few details deserve attention:

  • schedule="0 2 * * *" runs the DAG every day at 02:00.
  • catchup=False prevents Airflow from creating runs for every missed interval since the start date. In production, this default is often what you want for new pipelines, but backfilling must then be an explicit decision.
  • retries and retry_delay handle transient failures, such as a database connection that times out once.
  • The >> chain defines a strict sequence. Publishing never starts unless validation succeeded.

Save this file, and Airflow's scheduler will parse it, register the DAG, and start scheduling it.

Designing Good Tasks

The example above is intentionally simple. Real workflows need more discipline. These practices make a large difference over time.

Keep tasks idempotent. If a task runs twice for the same logical date, the result should be the same as running it once. Write to partitions keyed by date and overwrite them, instead of appending rows blindly. Idempotency is what makes retries and backfills safe.

Keep tasks small but meaningful. A task should represent a recoverable step. If one task performs extraction, transformation, and publication, a failure in publication forces you to repeat everything. Splitting the work lets Airflow retry only the part that failed.

Avoid heavy computation inside the scheduler. DAG files are parsed frequently. Top-level code that queries databases or makes network calls slows the whole platform down. Put work inside tasks, not at module level.

Pass data by reference, not by value. Airflow stores small pieces of data in XCom, its mechanism for sharing values between tasks. Large datasets belong in object storage or a database, and tasks should pass only the location or identifier.

Make failures visible. Configure alerts through callbacks or notifications, and use SLAs where delays matter. A pipeline that fails silently is worse than one that fails loudly.

Testing Workflows

Because DAGs are code, they can be tested like code. At minimum, verify that every DAG imports without errors and that the dependency graph is what you expect. A simple test with DagBag catches most mistakes before deployment:

from airflow.models import DagBag


def test_dags_load_without_errors():
    dag_bag = DagBag(dag_folder="dags", include_examples=False)
    assert not dag_bag.import_errors, f"Import errors: {dag_bag.import_errors}"


def test_daily_balances_structure():
    dag_bag = DagBag(dag_folder="dags", include_examples=False)
    dag = dag_bag.get_dag("daily_balances")
    assert dag is not None
    assert dag.task_dict["validate_transactions"] in dag.task_dict["extract_transactions"].downstream_list

For tasks that call external systems, isolate the business logic in plain Python functions and test them independently with mocks. Keep the Airflow-specific code thin. This is the same separation of concerns you would apply to a Spring service: controllers stay small, and the logic lives in testable components.

Integrating Airflow with Java Services

Here is where many Java teams start to interact with Airflow. A backend service might need to trigger a pipeline after a business event, such as the end of a customer onboarding batch, or check whether the latest report has finished. Airflow exposes a stable REST API for these operations.

To trigger a DAG run, you send a POST request to the DAG runs endpoint. Authentication depends on your deployment, but a common approach is a bearer token issued for a service account. A minimal Java client using the standard HttpClient looks like this:

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.Instant;

public class AirflowDagTrigger {

    private final HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
    private final String baseUrl;
    private final String token;

    public AirflowDagTrigger(String baseUrl, String token) {
        this.baseUrl = baseUrl;
        this.token = token;
    }

    public String triggerDagRun(String dagId, String conf) throws Exception {
        String body = """
                {
                  "conf": %s,
                  "logical_date": "%s"
                }
                """.formatted(conf, Instant.now().toString());

        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                .uri(URI.create(baseUrl + "/api/v1/dags/" + dagId + "/dagRuns"))
                .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)
                .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body))
                .build();

        HttpResponse<String> response = httpClient.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());

        if (response.statusCode() >= 300) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(
                    "Airflow returned " + response.statusCode() + ": " + response.body());
        }
        return response.body();
    }
}

A few practices make this integration robust:

  • Use a dedicated service account with the minimum permissions needed to trigger specific DAGs.
  • Pass identifiers in conf, not full payloads. The DAG can fetch the details from your system.
  • Handle conflicts. Triggering a run with a logical date that already exists returns an error. Decide whether your service should reuse, skip, or fail in that case.
  • Poll or subscribe carefully. To check run status, query the DAG run endpoint with exponential backoff rather than polling in a tight loop.
  • Treat Airflow as an external dependency. Add timeouts, circuit breakers, and clear error messages, just as you would for any downstream system.

If your Spring Boot application is the caller, wrap this logic in a dedicated client component, expose it through a service interface, and cover it with integration tests against a local Airflow instance.

Operating Airflow in Production

Running Airflow well is a platform concern, and several areas need attention.

Database and scheduler health. The metadata database receives constant writes from the scheduler and workers. Monitor its connections, growth, and query latency. Plan a cleanup policy for old task instances and logs, because an unpruned database slows the entire platform.

Executor choice. Start simple. A local or Celery executor fits many teams. Kubernetes executors provide isolation and elastic capacity but add operational complexity. Choose based on workload, not on what is fashionable.

Pools and concurrency. Use pools to limit how many tasks can hit a fragile system at once, such as a legacy database. Without pools, a burst of parallel tasks can overload a dependency and cause the very failures you are trying to recover from.

Secrets and connections. Store credentials in Airflow connections or in an external secrets backend. Never hard-code passwords in DAG files, which are often visible to many engineers.

Version upgrades. Test upgrades in a staging environment with a copy of your DAGs. Check provider compatibility, deprecated operators, and changes in the scheduler behavior before applying them to production.

Observability. Export metrics to your monitoring stack, track DAG parsing time, scheduler heartbeat, and task failure rates, and define alerts for the conditions that matter to the business, such as a daily report that has not completed by its deadline.

Best Practices Checklist

  • Model workflows explicitly as DAGs with clear, documented dependencies.
  • Make every task idempotent and safe to retry.
  • Keep DAG files lightweight and free of heavy top-level code.
  • Pass references, not large payloads, between tasks.
  • Set retries, timeouts, and alerts deliberately for each pipeline.
  • Test DAG imports and structure in continuous integration.
  • Store secrets outside DAG code.
  • Limit concurrency against fragile dependencies with pools.
  • Give external callers, including Java services, a dedicated and minimally privileged account.
  • Monitor the scheduler, the database, and business-level deadlines, not only task status.

Conclusion

Apache Airflow gives data and platform teams a disciplined way to describe, schedule, and recover complex workflows. Its Python-based DAGs can look unfamiliar to Java engineers, but the underlying ideas are familiar: explicit dependencies, idempotent operations, clear configuration, testing, and operational monitoring. Those are the same principles that make backend systems reliable.

If your organization runs batch processing, reporting, or data synchronization, Airflow is worth evaluating. Start with one pipeline, make it idempotent and observable, and integrate it with your existing services through a well-designed API client. Once the first workflow runs reliably, the rest of the platform tends to follow.

Key Takeaways

  • Airflow orchestrates workflows as DAGs, separating what runs, when it runs, and how failures are handled.
  • Idempotent, small tasks make retries and backfills safe.
  • Tests for DAG imports and structure catch most errors before deployment.
  • Java services can trigger and monitor workflows through the stable REST API.
  • Production success depends on the metadata database, pools, secrets management, and observability.

title: Keep a Waiting Animation from Making a Promise About Progress
description:
Imagine a fictional web application that prepares a downloadable project bundle. Its team is considering a short animation while the bundle is being prepared. A Seedance Mini concept might help the designer explore a mood, but the animation must not imply that the application knows more about completion than it actually does.

The proposed first deliverable is one ten-second landscape motion sketch and a separate state description for the interface. This is a design exercise. The local presentation function below was tested on November 2, 2026. No application, generated clip or browser interaction was tested.

Write the state message before the motion brief

For the fictional example, the application can report that preparation is underway, but it has no meaningful percentage to show. The interface copy should describe that known state. It should not acquire a countdown merely because the visual concept contains objects moving toward a finish line.

An animation of a box steadily filling might suggest measured progress. A repeated arrangement of abstract shapes could suggest activity without the same explicit destination, although that interpretation still needs review. The motion brief should state what the team wants to communicate and which unintended promise it wants to avoid.

Do not ask the generated footage to contain status text or a real progress percentage. Keep state messages in the application design, where they can be tied to actual information and changed independently of the visual asset.

Treat the concept's end as an editing decision

Ten seconds of footage does not mean preparation takes ten seconds. Nor does the final frame establish success. A design review should include a wait shorter than the clip, a wait longer than the clip, and a transition to an error or completion message.

The team should decide how the interface leaves the waiting state based on application events. The visual sequence is supporting material. Its ending should not be used as a substitute for knowing whether the work finished.

The local view-model example below does not implement a browser component or claim a seamless loop. If the candidate needs a restart, an edit, or a static alternative, that work must be planned separately.

Review the whole waiting experience

Place the concept beside the proposed status copy and available controls. Check whether the movement competes with the information the user needs, whether the transition out of waiting is understandable, and whether the design still communicates when motion is absent.

Those are proposed review questions, not completed accessibility or usability tests. The first useful outcome is a clear relationship between visual activity and reported application state. Only after that relationship is satisfactory should the team decide whether the concept deserves implementation work.

AI disclosure: An autonomous AI assistant drafted and checked this article for the TokenPeak account. The application and concept are fictional. Five local presentation test methods were executed on November 2, 2026. No model generation, browser interface test, user outcome or settled charge was observed. No provider purchase is recommended.

Give the presentation layer only the facts it can show

This complete Python 3.10+ exercise produces a view model, not an HTML component. fraction is progress through explicitly supplied substeps; it is not a time estimate. The caller must decide whether those substeps are meaningful. A full substep counter still cannot change the application state to complete. The media player has no completion argument to this function.

from dataclasses import dataclass
import unittest

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class View:
    text: str
    fraction: float | None
    animate: bool

def present(state, done=None, total=None, *, reduced_motion=False):
    if type(reduced_motion) is not bool:
        raise ValueError("motion preference must be explicit")
    if state == "complete":
        return View("Bundle ready", None, False)
    if state == "failed":
        return View("Preparation failed; inspect the job", None, False)
    if state != "preparing":
        raise ValueError("unknown application state")
    if done is None and total is None:
        return View("Preparing your bundle", None, not reduced_motion)
    if (type(done) is not int or type(total) is not int
            or total <= 0 or not 0 <= done <= total):
        raise ValueError("a progress pair needs an explicit positive total")
    return View("Preparing your bundle", done / total, not reduced_motion)

class PresentationTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_unknown_progress_stays_unknown(self):
        self.assertEqual(present("preparing"), View("Preparing your bundle", None, True))
    def test_completed_substeps_do_not_establish_job_success(self):
        view = present("preparing", 10, 10)
        self.assertEqual(view.fraction, 1)
        self.assertEqual(view.text, "Preparing your bundle")
        self.assertTrue(view.animate)
    def test_motion_preference_does_not_change_status(self):
        normal = present("preparing", 2, 4)
        still = present("preparing", 2, 4, reduced_motion=True)
        self.assertEqual((normal.text, normal.fraction), (still.text, still.fraction))
        self.assertFalse(still.animate)
    def test_terminal_states_come_from_application(self):
        self.assertEqual(present("complete"), View("Bundle ready", None, False))
        self.assertFalse(present("failed").animate)
    def test_malformed_or_partial_progress_fails(self):
        for pair in [(None, 5), (0, None), (0, 0), (-1, 5), (6, 5), (True, 5), (1, 2.5)]:
            with self.subTest(pair=pair), self.assertRaises(ValueError):
                present("preparing", *pair)
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            present("video-ended")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

Five test methods passed locally, including partial and malformed progress pairs, reduced motion, terminal states and an unsupported media-ended state. This does not verify keyboard access, screen-reader announcements, contrast, motion comfort, looping or real task transitions. Those need a rendered component and user-facing review. The static copy still carries the application state when animation is disabled.

title: Simple Features Beat Most AI Control Monitors
description:
arXiv:2610.41713v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: AI control relies on monitors to catch a capable model that sabotages its work. These monitors are evaluated on their ability to differentiate honest from backdoored code. We show that on a standard evaluation dataset, simple features beat most monitors without ever running the code, outranking 20 of 24 open-weight models prompted as monitors. The dataset gives its labels away in two ways. People wrote the honest solutions and older language models the backdoors, so the style of the code reveals the class. Additionally, problems that LLMs can backdoor have different characteristics, so basic facts about the problem reveal it too. Swapping one class at a time for code by Claude Sonnet 5 shows that these features reward a contrast between authors, since human code against Sonnet 5's backdoors is easier to separate than the original pairs, 0.95 against 0.79. One in seven backdoors in the standard test set fails our validity checks, which distorts comparisons between attackers. A Sonnet 5 monitor appears to catch 77% of the older models' backdoors but 37% of Sonnet 5's, and 78% against 61% once both are verified. We do not show that published monitors rely on these shortcuts, but our findings suggest that a high score on such a dataset is not by itself evidence of sabotage detection. We release the rebuilt dataset and checks.

Meet Breeze v2.2.

Built on gnet. Engineered for throughput. Designed for production.

And the advantage remains across all three concurrency levels.

🧠 Performance is in the architecture.

Breeze is built around an event-driven gnet engine, with:

  • Inline execution for non-blocking handlers.
  • O(1) exact-path routing, dynamic parameters and wildcards.
  • Opt-in zero-copy request-header handling.
  • Pooled contexts, requests, responses and buffers.
  • Configurable worker pools with backpressure policies for blocking operations.

But here's where Breeze becomes more interesting.

🏗️ More than an HTTP framework.

Breeze brings an extensive set of production-ready capabilities into one ecosystem:

HTTP & Security

  • High-performance HTTP server, routing, request binding and validation.
  • 12 built-in middlewares: CORS, rate limiting, compression, ETag, logging, recovery, security headers, JWT and more.
  • OAuth2 / social login with Google, GitHub, Microsoft and Discord, including PKCE.
  • Graceful shutdown and static file serving.

Real-time & Application Development

  • Native WebSocket server and client, with connection lifecycle management and broadcasting.
  • Server-side templates, layouts, reusable components, SPA navigation, partial rendering and i18n — without a frontend framework.
  • Built-in byte-range video streaming, seeking, caching and signed URLs.

Backend Infrastructure

  • Typed, reflection-free event bus with priorities, filters, asynchronous dispatch and metrics.
  • Durable workflows with retries, timeouts, parallel DAG execution, Saga compensation and crash recovery.
  • SQL migrations and a gnet-based outbound HTTP client.
  • JSON-RPC 2.0 server, including batches and notifications.
  • gRPC server/client code generation.

Developer Experience

  • Rails-style CLI for project scaffolding and feature integration.
  • 23 modular breeze add features.
  • Code generators for resources, handlers, models, events, listeners, workflows, middleware, WebSockets, views, jobs and gRPC.
  • OpenAPI generation, interactive Scalar documentation and LLM-readable documentation.
  • Docker support and runnable examples.

Observability & Production Operations

  • Integrated live dashboard with request monitoring, RPS, latency, memory and goroutine metrics.
  • Per-request profiling, route explorer and API explorer.
  • Database browser, ORM query monitoring, cache, queue and scheduler monitoring.
  • Logs, health checks, video monitoring and Fleet views.
  • Built-in observability, diagnostics and distributed tracing across services, with W3C trace propagation, topology visualization and root-cause analysis.

AI-Native Development

  • Native MCP integration in three forms: standalone generator, read-only application runtime and in-process server.
  • Approximately 40 MCP tools for project scaffolding, code generation, feature integration, Go toolchain execution and live service inspection.
  • Auto-MCP: expose explicitly tagged, authenticated application routes as AI-callable tools.

All of this in one MIT-licensed Go ecosystem.

🚀 But performance isn't the only reason to choose Breeze.

A fast server is valuable.

But a framework that also helps you build APIs, manage workflows, handle real-time communication, monitor production, trace distributed services, generate code, document APIs and integrate AI agents is a much bigger proposition.

Less infrastructure to assemble. Fewer disconnected tools. More capabilities in one cohesive ecosystem.

That's the vision behind Breeze.

And we're still improving it.

The goal isn't just to build another fast Go framework.

It's to build a better foundation for modern Go applications.

title: Pinching Antennas for ISAC: Waveguide Architectures, Solutions, and Future Directions
description:
arXiv:2610.41380v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a core design principle for sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems, yet fixed antenna geometry limits its performance. Pinching antenna systems (PASS) guide electromagnetic waves along dielectric waveguides and radiate them through position-adaptive antennas, allowing communication links and sensing observations to benefit from spatial reconfiguration. This article reviews PASS-enabled ISAC through single-waveguide, multi-waveguide, and segmented-waveguide architectures, comparing their feed structures, spatial degrees of freedom, operating protocols, and uplink/downlink support. We organize solution pathways around physics-consistent modeling, joint spatial-signal optimization, dynamic channel acquisition, and stable real-time control. A segmented waveguide-enabled pinching-antenna array (SWAN) case study demonstrates joint segment selection, antenna po?sitioning, and transmit beamforming using segment-hysteresis reinforcement learning. The results illustrate how waveguide loss and per-segment aperture gain create communication-sensing tradeoffs. We conclude with research directions in joint transmit?receive operation, measurement-calibrated digital twins, and trustworthy control.
