title: React useEffect Dependencies — The Bug That Keeps Coming Back
description:
useEffect looks simple. Add a function, add a dependency array, done.

Then production hits you with:

  • a timer that logs the wrong count
  • a fetch that sends a stale token
  • an effect that runs forever
  • or React Strict Mode making everything run twice

These are not random React bugs. They all come from one idea:

Every render is a snapshot. Your effect remembers the values from the render that scheduled it.

Once you internalize that sentence, most useEffect pain disappears.

🧠 The Core Mental Model

When React renders your component, it creates a snapshot of props and state for that moment.

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => {
      console.log(count); // 👈 frozen at the count from THIS render
    }, 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, []); // empty deps = only first render's count

  return <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}

You click the button → UI shows 1, 2, 3…

But the interval still logs 0 forever.

Why? The callback inside setInterval is a closure. It captured count = 0 from the first render and never saw updates.

This is the famous stale closure problem — the #1 useEffect interview trap.

❌ Mistake 1: Empty [] When You Need Fresh Values 

useEffect(() => {
  fetch(`/api/user/${userId}`); // userId from first render only
}, []);

Looks clean. Breaks when userId changes via routing or props.

✅ Fix 

useEffect(() => {
  fetch(`/api/user/${userId}`);
}, [userId]); // re-run when userId changes

Rule: If your effect reads a value from the component, that value probably belongs in the dependency array.

❌ Mistake 2: Missing Dependencies (Ignoring ESLint) 

useEffect(() => {
  document.title = `Count: ${count}`;
}); // no deps → runs after EVERY render

Without deps, the effect runs on every render — often causing extra work or infinite loops if the effect also sets state.

✅ Fix 

useEffect(() => {
  document.title = `Count: ${count}`;
}, [count]);

Trust eslint-plugin-react-hooks. When it says "missing dependency", it is usually right.

❌ Mistake 3: Objects & Arrays in Deps → Infinite Loop 

useEffect(() => {
  loadData({ page, filter });
}, [{ page, filter }]); // ❌ new object every render → effect → render → ...

In JavaScript, { page, filter } !== { page, filter }. A fresh object every render means React thinks deps changed every time.

✅ Fix options

A) List primitives directly

useEffect(() => {
  loadData({ page, filter });
}, [page, filter]);

B) Memoize the object

const params = useMemo(() => ({ page, filter }), [page, filter]);

useEffect(() => {
  loadData(params);
}, [params]);

Rule: Dependencies are compared with Object.is (like ===). New references every render = infinite loop.

❌ Mistake 4: Functions in Deps Without useCallback 

function Search() {
  const [q, setQ] = useState("");

  const search = () => fetch(`/api?q=${q}`);

  useEffect(() => {
    search();
  }, [search]); // search is recreated every render → loop
}

Every render creates a new search function → deps change → effect runs → state update → render → repeat.

✅ Fix: define inside the effect 

useEffect(() => {
  const search = () => fetch(`/api?q=${q}`);
  search();
}, [q]);

Or wrap with useCallback if the function is passed to children:

const search = useCallback(() => {
  fetch(`/api?q=${q}`);
}, [q]);

Prefer moving logic inside the effect when nothing else needs that function.

❌ Mistake 5: Fetch Race Conditions 

useEffect(() => {
  fetch(`/api?q=${query}`)
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(setResults);
}, [query]);

User types fast → request for "a" finishes after "abc". UI shows wrong data.

✅ Fix: cleanup + ignore flag 

useEffect(() => {
  let cancelled = false;

  fetch(`/api?q=${query}`)
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(data => {
      if (!cancelled) setResults(data);
    });

  return () => { cancelled = true; };
}, [query]);

Or use AbortController (see AbortController guide).

Rule: If an effect starts async work, clean it up on re-run or unmount.

🔄 When You Need the Latest Value Without Re-running

Sometimes you want a stable interval/subscription but still read fresh state:

const countRef = useRef(count);
countRef.current = count; // always latest, no extra effect runs

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => {
    console.log(countRef.current); // ✅ always fresh
  }, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []); // stable setup, fresh reads

Use useRef when you need latest value but don't want the effect to re-subscribe on every change.

Related: useRef vs useState.

🧪 Why Strict Mode Runs Effects Twice (Dev Only)

In React 18+ dev mode, Strict Mode mounts → unmounts → remounts components to expose missing cleanups.

You might see:

  • double fetch in Network tab
  • double console.log on mount

This is intentional. It catches bugs like:

useEffect(() => {
  socket.connect();
  // ❌ no cleanup → duplicate connections in prod navigations too
}, []);

✅ Always return cleanup 

useEffect(() => {
  socket.connect();
  return () => socket.disconnect();
}, []);

Production does not double-invoke. Dev pain saves prod bugs.

🎯 Interview Cheat Sheet

Question Short answer
What does [] mean? Run once after mount (plus cleanup on unmount)
What if deps are omitted? Run after every render
Why stale closures? Effect callbacks capture values from their render snapshot
Why infinite loops? Unstable deps (new object/function each render)
How to fix unstable deps? Primitives in array, useMemo, useCallback, or move logic inside effect
Why double fetch in dev? Strict Mode remount test — add cleanup
useRef vs state in effects? Ref = read latest without re-running effect; state = triggers re-render

✅ The 4 Rules to Remember

  1. Every value you read inside the effect should be in deps — unless you have a deliberate reason not to.
  2. Never put freshly created objects/functions in deps — use primitives, memoization, or inline them.
  3. Always clean up — timers, listeners, fetches, subscriptions.
  4. Stale closure? Either add the value to deps, or store it in a ref if re-running is too expensive.

✨ Final Takeaway

useEffect doesn't watch live variables — it remembers the snapshot from when it was scheduled.

Write that on a sticky note. Next time a timer logs 0, a fetch sends an old token, or an effect loops forever — you'll know exactly where to look.

Suggested follow-ups

  • JavaScript Closures — the underlying mechanism
  • useRef vs useState — when refs beat state in effects
  • AbortController — cancel fetches on unmount

title: RagLeap Ansible and Terraform Resources Are Now Available for Java
description:
Two new Maven Central releases package RagLeap's existing infrastructure files for Java applications.

RagLeap has published two new Java artifacts:

  • ragleap-ansible 0.1.2
  • ragleap-terraform 0.1.1

Both are available through Maven Central.

These releases are designed for Java developers who want to read RagLeap's existing infrastructure resources from a Java application.

One important clarification:

These are resource-packaging releases, not Java ports of Ansible or Terraform.

The JARs contain the same six files distributed through the corresponding PyPI wheels. They provide small Java classes for reading those resources from the classpath.

Ansible and Terraform are not included or executed by the JARs.

Why package these resources for Java?

RagLeap is an open-source, self-hosted AI infrastructure ecosystem.

Its infrastructure packages include Ansible resources and Terraform modules. These are useful beyond the Python application itself, so I wanted to make the existing files accessible from Java projects too.

Rather than rewriting the resources in Java, the releases package the original files.

This gives Java applications a simple way to access them while keeping the Python distributions as the matching resource source.

1. RagLeap Ansible Java 0.1.2

Maven coordinates:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.antonyrag</groupId>
    <artifactId>ragleap-ansible</artifactId>
    <version>0.1.2</version>
</dependency>

Release:

https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/releases/tag/ragleap-ansible-java-v0.1.2

Maven Central:

https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/io.github.antonyrag/ragleap-ansible/0.1.2

PyPI:

https://pypi.org/project/ragleap-ansible/0.1.2/

Included resources

The JAR contains the six files from the PyPI wheel, including:

playbooks/bootstrap.yml

The Java resource reader is:

com.ragleap.ansible.RagleapAnsible

It provides:

openPlaybook(path)

and:

readPlaybookString(path)

Example:

import com.ragleap.ansible.RagleapAnsible;

public class Example {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String playbook =
            RagleapAnsible.readPlaybookString("bootstrap.yml");

        System.out.println(playbook);
    }
}

The path is resolved under the packaged playbooks/ tree.

Paths must be relative. Backslashes and parent-directory traversal are rejected.

Ansible execution is not included

This Java artifact only reads the packaged playbook resources.

It does not:

  • Include Ansible.
  • Run playbooks.
  • Start processes.
  • Connect to remote hosts.
  • Change infrastructure.

You still need Ansible separately if you want to execute the playbooks.

2. RagLeap Terraform Java 0.1.1

Maven coordinates:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.antonyrag</groupId>
    <artifactId>ragleap-terraform</artifactId>
    <version>0.1.1</version>
</dependency>

Release:

https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/releases/tag/ragleap-terraform-java-v0.1.1

Maven Central:

https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/io.github.antonyrag/ragleap-terraform/0.1.1

PyPI:

https://pypi.org/project/ragleap-terraform/0.1.1/

Included resources

The JAR contains the six Terraform files from the corresponding PyPI wheel:

modules/kind-cluster/main.tf
modules/kind-cluster/variables.tf
modules/kind-cluster/outputs.tf
modules/kind-cluster/versions.tf
examples/kind/main.tf
examples/kind/.terraform.lock.hcl

The resource reader is:

com.ragleap.terraform.RagleapTerraform

It provides:

open(...)

and:

readString(...)

Example:

import com.ragleap.terraform.RagleapTerraform;

public class Example {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String module =
            RagleapTerraform.readString(
                "modules/kind-cluster/main.tf"
            );

        System.out.println(module);
    }
}

The resource is read from the JAR's classpath.

Terraform execution is not included

The Java artifact does not include Terraform or execute Terraform commands.

The current packaged module creates a local kind cluster. Cloud modules are not included yet.

The module's actual application remains a Terraform responsibility.

3. Resource parity: the important part

Both Java releases package the same files as their corresponding Python distributions.

That was verified through file-list and file-content comparisons.

The six files in each published JAR were compared byte for byte against the matching PyPI wheel.

The result:

  • Ansible Java 0.1.2: six matching resource files.
  • Terraform Java 0.1.1: six matching resource files.

This is the main design goal.

The Java artifacts should not become a separate version of the infrastructure resources.

Keeping the packaged files identical reduces the chance of Java and Python distributions drifting apart.

4. Published artifact verification

Both releases were built from:

e5e4328837758a03cb21e1207c8aec90a88b5c87

Build environment:

OpenJDK 21.0.12
Maven 3.6.3

Build command:

mvn -Prelease clean deploy

The JAR, sources JAR, Javadoc JAR, and POM were signed.

All four signatures were verified before upload.

After publication, the JARs served by Maven Central were checked against the locally built artifacts.

Ansible 0.1.2

Published JAR SHA-256:

1e33f98f9f4bea29763686fec4de97aad6bbc14e1447d1a4a958917062319cf4

The published JAR matched the locally built JAR.

Its signature verified with the same key.

Central listed 24 files for the release.

Terraform 0.1.1

Published JAR SHA-256:

a73b1030f79c6827a7afc8689b986e2ca929cdc7097e6f2e1b4f6557f127a354

The published JAR matched the locally built JAR.

Its signature verified with the same key.

Central listed 24 files for the release.

These checks cover the published artifact, checksum, signature, and resource parity.

5. CI checks

The Ansible resource-parity workflow passed on main and on the pull request.

The Terraform resource-parity check passed on main.

The workflows compare the packaged file list and contents against the corresponding Python wheel.

The infrastructure execution tests remain in the Python package test suites:

  • Ansible: container idempotence and real-host tests on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04.
  • Terraform: live apply and destroy testing on a real kind cluster.

Those tests were not repeated by the Java JAR releases.

6. What is not tested yet?

The published JARs were not built into a separate consuming Java project.

Other JDK and Maven versions were not tested.

The JARs only package resources. They do not provide an execution environment for Ansible or Terraform.

So the current verification should not be interpreted as a claim that Java applications can execute infrastructure automation directly through these artifacts.

The releases are intentionally limited to resource access.

7. Try the releases

Ansible Java 

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.antonyrag</groupId>
    <artifactId>ragleap-ansible</artifactId>
    <version>0.1.2</version>
</dependency>
  • Maven Central
  • GitHub release
  • PyPI package

Terraform Java 

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.antonyrag</groupId>
    <artifactId>ragleap-terraform</artifactId>
    <version>0.1.1</version>
</dependency>
  • Maven Central
  • GitHub release
  • PyPI package

RagLeap Core

https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core

Final note

These releases are a small but practical step toward making RagLeap's infrastructure resources easier to use across language ecosystems.

The goal is not to replace Ansible or Terraform with Java.

The goal is to let Java applications access the same infrastructure resources that RagLeap already distributes through Python—while keeping the package boundaries clear and the verification claims honest.

More open-source infrastructure work is ongoing.

title: ProSearch: Benchmarking Multi-Constraint Protocol Retrieval in Experimental Science
description:
arXiv:2610.41396v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In AI for Science scenarios, experimental design and method reproduction require retrieving protocols that satisfy multiple interdependent constraints, yet existing benchmarks lack systematic evaluation of this capability. To address this gap, we introduce ProSearch, a benchmark for multi-constraint protocol retrieval in experimental science. ProSearch has three key features: (1) realism, with queries grounded in real experimental records and expert-defined templates; (2) complexity, with 60 experimental fields and their dependencies; and (3) diagnosticity, with 3-5 explicit constraints per query, including numerical and negation constraints. We construct ProSearch through LLM-based extraction, data-driven constraint selection, controlled query generation, and evidence-based relevance validation. The resulting benchmark contains 1,515 queries across six experimental science domains. We conduct extensive experiments on ProSearch with 19 representative retrievers and complementary analyses. The best-performing retriever achieves an average nDCG@10 of only 0.290, which improves to 0.474 with reranking. Structured diagnostic analysis shows that explicit constraint matching provides a strong ranking signal, while manual error analysis identifies joint constraint binding as a key bottleneck. ProSearch provides a testbed for systematically evaluating scientific retrieval systems.

title: Web Design Courses and College
description:
Today I came across a service I think has the potential to be pretty valuable. ScrunchUp.com plans to provide information for college students interested in the web industry. Things change on the web every day. With things happening so quickly, how can students be sure that what they are learning in the classroom is actually valuable in the workplace?

As a recent graduate I personally experienced this at college. I realize that it is not an easy task to find motivated professionals willing to take time out of their busy lives to teach. Teaching a web design or development class isn’t exactly the same as teaching history, or any other traditional subject for that matter. If your passion is history, then you will most likely aspire to be a history professor at a university with a great reputation. Some day you will find yourself at the height of your career working as a professor for that university. If you’re a web designer, things don’t quite pan out that way. You may see the height of your career as working as creative director at a high-end, cutting-edge web agency.

In order to keep current with web technologies, such as web standards, students need to find that late night drive and learn on their own. During college I knew what I was passionate about, and spent much of my free time working for that. Sure I was not the typical student, but who cares. I constantly found myself sacrificing a grade in English or Business Law in order to learn more about web design and development. This is not to say that these other courses aren’t important, but let’s face it, a low grade in some courses won’t significantly affect your life after college.

I guess what I’m really trying to get across here is that a high GPD doesn’t mean much in the field of Web Design. Skills, drive and a strong will to be a life learner do. Once ScrunchUp launches I’ll plan on frequenting their forums to provide any help I can.

title: Uptime SLAs That Mean Something
description:
An uptime SLA looks like a promise and behaves like a refund policy. Suppliers know this. Customers frequently do not, and sign a service level agreement believing they have bought availability when what they have bought is a small discount in the event they do not get it.

That is not necessarily a bad deal. It is a different deal from the one most people think they are making, and the difference matters when the system is down and somebody asks what the contract says.

Three nines sounds close to perfect and allows 43 minutes of downtime a month. Four nines allows four. If your business can absorb a 43 minute outage during a working afternoon, 99.9% is fine and you should not pay for more. If it cannot, no number of nines helps, because the agreement pays you a credit rather than preventing the outage.

What an Uptime SLA Promises in Minutes

The percentages compress a large range into a small-looking difference. Written as time, the differences are obvious.

Availability Downtime per year Downtime per month
99% 3.65 days 7.2 hours
99.9% 8.76 hours 43.2 minutes
99.95% 4.38 hours 21.6 minutes
99.99% 52.6 minutes 4.32 minutes
99.999% 5.26 minutes 26 seconds

Two things follow. The step from 99.9% to 99.99% is a tenfold reduction in permitted downtime and typically a much larger increase in cost, because it requires redundancy that removes every single point of failure including the deployment process. And anything at or beyond five nines is below the time it takes a human to notice and respond, so it can only be met by systems that fail over without anybody involved.

Decide the figure from what an outage actually costs you per hour, not from what sounds impressive. Most business systems are honestly served by 99.9%.

Service Credits Are Not Compensation

The remedy in nearly every uptime SLA is a credit against future fees, usually a percentage of the monthly charge, and often capped at that month's total. Google Cloud's compute SLA is a representative example: credits only, claimed by the customer, capped.

That means the maximum you can recover is roughly what you paid for the period, which for most services is far less than an outage costs. A platform charged at a few hundred pounds a month cannot compensate a day of lost trading, and no supplier will agree to terms where it could.

Credits are also frequently claim-based rather than automatic. You must notice the breach, calculate it, and submit a claim inside a window, sometimes as short as thirty days. Suppliers are not obliged to volunteer that they missed the target, and most do not.

The practical conclusion is to stop treating the credit as protection. It is a signal of how seriously the supplier takes their own number. What protects you is architecture, and the recovery planning covered in our disaster recovery guide.

The Clauses That Decide Everything

What counts as downtime. Total unavailability, or degraded performance too? A service responding in thirty seconds is unusable and, under most definitions, available. Get a latency threshold into the definition if response time matters.

How it is measured, and by whom. Almost always by the supplier, using their own monitoring, from their own network. That is measurement of their infrastructure rather than of your experience. Agree the measurement point, and run independent monitoring regardless, because you cannot dispute a number you did not observe.

Exclusions. Planned maintenance is usually excluded entirely, which means a supplier can be unavailable for hours a month without breaching anything. Check how much notice is required and whether there is a cap. Also excluded: anything attributed to your configuration, to a third party, or to force majeure, and those categories can absorb a lot.

The measurement window. Monthly is standard and favours you. Annual measurement lets a supplier take a long outage and still meet the target, because a full day down is inside the yearly allowance at 99.9%.

Response versus resolution. Many agreements commit to responding within a period and say nothing about fixing. A one hour response and an unbounded fix is a common shape and is much weaker than it reads.

What to Ask For Instead

Push on the things that change behaviour rather than on the headline number.

A cap on planned maintenance, with notice and a window outside your peak hours. This often affects real availability more than the percentage does.

Status transparency, meaning a public status page and a commitment to post incidents promptly. A supplier who reports their own outages is telling you something about how they operate.

A defined escalation path with names or roles and times, so an incident does not begin with finding out who to contact.

Incident reports after significant outages, describing what happened and what changed as a result. This is the single most informative document a supplier can give you, and a reluctance to provide one is itself informative.

Termination rights on repeated failure. Chronic underperformance should let you leave without penalty. That right is worth more than any credit, because it is the only remedy proportionate to the harm.

If You Are the One Offering an SLA

Offer a number you can meet on your worst month, not your average one, and measure it yourself before you commit to it. Suppliers who commit to a figure they have never verified discover the gap in public.

Define planned maintenance honestly and keep to the window. Publish a status page. Write the incident report even when nobody asks, because the customers who stay are the ones who believe you know what happened.

And price the tiers by what they actually cost you to deliver. Four nines is not a marketing decision, it is redundant infrastructure, automated failover and a deployment process that cannot take the system down, and all of that has a bill attached. The operational groundwork in our CI/CD pipeline guide is where most of it starts.

Mecanik builds and operates systems under availability commitments as part of our server security work. The commitment worth making is nearly always the one you can hold during a bad week.

Related reading

  • Software Supply Chain Security for Small Teams
  • How to Build a Web App in 2026 - The UK Developer's Guide
  • Drupal Migration in 2026: Costs, Options and Deadlines
  • AI Agents for Business: What They Cost and Where They Fail

Frequently Asked Questions

How much downtime does 99.9% uptime allow?
8.76 hours a year, or 43.2 minutes a month. The step to 99.99% cuts that to 52.6 minutes a year and 4.32 minutes a month, a tenfold reduction that typically costs far more than ten times as much to deliver because it requires removing every single point of failure including the deployment process.

Are service credits real compensation for downtime?
No. Credits are usually a percentage of the monthly fee and capped at that month's charge, so the most you can recover is roughly what you paid, which is far less than an outage typically costs. They are also often claim-based with a short window, and suppliers rarely volunteer that they missed the target.

What should I check in an uptime SLA?
What counts as downtime and whether degraded performance is included, who measures it and from where, what the exclusions cover, whether planned maintenance is capped and noticed, whether the window is monthly or annual, and whether the commitment is to respond or to resolve.

Why does the measurement window matter?
Monthly measurement favours the customer. Annual measurement lets a supplier take one long outage and still meet the target, because a full day of downtime sits inside the yearly allowance at 99.9%. The same failure would breach a monthly agreement outright.

What is worth negotiating instead of a higher number?
A cap on planned maintenance with notice outside peak hours, a public status page with prompt incident posting, a named escalation path with times, written incident reports after significant outages, and termination rights on repeated failure. The last is the only remedy proportionate to the harm.

title: A Tailwind CSS v4 Drawer That Does Not Fight the Browser
description:
A Tailwind CSS v4 Drawer That Does Not Fight the Browser

You wake up at 3:00 AM to a PagerDuty alert: users report the settings panel freezing their dashboards. DevTools shows 200ms frames during open. The culprit is a JavaScript animation loop measuring the drawer, writing its width, then triggering synchronous layout recalculations on every tick. By morning, you've also discovered keyboard users can't escape the overlay, and screen readers still navigate the page underneath.

These aren't separate bugs. They expose a missing architectural boundary: application code trying to own presentation, animation scheduling, and modal behavior simultaneously.

As an external adopter of tailwindlabs/tailwindcss, I treat Tailwind v4 as the presentation layer, not the interaction engine. Radix Dialog owns modal semantics and focus management. CSS owns motion. React supplies content and state.

The result is a reusable drawer with fewer synchronization points and no JavaScript animation loop.

Why the tutorial version breaks

A common implementation measures the drawer, then repeatedly writes its width during opening. Width changes invalidate layout; subsequent geometry reads can force synchronous layout before the browser would otherwise perform it. On a busy dashboard with live charts and data tables, that read-write cycle becomes visible as dropped frames.

The accessibility failure often arrives in the same component. A hand-written Tab handler wraps focus between two buttons, but misses conditional fields, validation messages, or nested popovers. Meanwhile, the background remains available to assistive technology, allowing users to interact with obscured content.

Moving the drawer with transform avoids changing surrounding layout during animation. It does not guarantee free rendering, but it removes width interpolation from the critical path. Delegating modal behavior to Radix avoids maintaining an incomplete focus model.

Wire Tailwind into the build

In an existing React/TypeScript Vite application, install tailwindcss@4, @tailwindcss/vite@4, and @radix-ui/react-dialog. Keep the Vite plugin and framework versions compatible with the application.

This is the complete build configuration; Tailwind v4 needs no JavaScript theme configuration for this example.

// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import tailwindcss from "@tailwindcss/vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), tailwindcss()],
});

Keep utility classes literal so Tailwind can discover them. Constructing fragments such as translate-x-${offset} is unnecessary here and makes generated styles harder to reason about.

Keep interaction semantics in the primitive

The component deliberately exposes content rather than individual form fields. Forms retain responsibility for validation and persistence; the drawer only provides a modal shell.

// SettingsDrawer.tsx
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import * as Dialog from "@radix-ui/react-dialog";
import "./app.css";

type SettingsDrawerProps = {
  title: string;
  description: string;
  children: ReactNode;
};

export function SettingsDrawer({
  title,
  description,
  children,
}: SettingsDrawerProps) {
  return (
    <Dialog.Root>
      <Dialog.Trigger asChild>
        <button
          type="button"
          className="rounded-md border px-4 py-2
            focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-4"
        >
          Open settings
        </button>
      </Dialog.Trigger>

      <Dialog.Portal>
        <Dialog.Overlay className="fixed inset-0 z-50 bg-black/40" />

        <Dialog.Content
          className="drawer fixed inset-y-0 right-0 z-50
            w-full max-w-lg overflow-y-auto bg-white
            text-slate-950 shadow-xl
            focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-blue-600"
        >
          <div className="drawer-container">
            <div className="drawer-inner space-y-6 p-4">
              <header className="space-y-2">
                <Dialog.Title className="text-xl font-semibold">
                  {title}
                </Dialog.Title>
                <Dialog.Description className="text-sm text-slate-600">
                  {description}
                </Dialog.Description>
              </header>

              {children}

              <footer className="drawer-actions flex justify-end">
                <Dialog.Close asChild>
                  <button
                    type="button"
                    aria-label="Close settings"
                    className="rounded-md bg-slate-950 px-4 py-2
                      text-white focus-visible:outline-2
                      focus-visible:outline-offset-4"
                  >
                    Close
                  </button>
                </Dialog.Close>
              </footer>
            </div>
          </div>
        </Dialog.Content>
      </Dialog.Portal>
    </Dialog.Root>
  );
}

Radix supplies the dialog role, modal ARIA state, and title/description associations. It also handles focus containment, Escape dismissal, and returning focus to the trigger. Adding competing aria-hidden logic or a second focus trap would undermine that ownership.

Animate presentation, not geometry

The container query adjusts the drawer's internal spacing according to its available width, not the viewport. The named container sits above the elements it styles: a container cannot query its own size to restyle itself.

/* app.css */
@import "tailwindcss";

.drawer-container {
  container: settings / inline-size;
}

.drawer[data-state="open"] {
  animation: drawer-enter 180ms ease-out both;
}

.drawer[data-state="closed"] {
  animation: drawer-exit 140ms ease-in both;
}

@keyframes drawer-enter {
  from { transform: translateX(100%); }
  to { transform: translateX(0); }
}

@keyframes drawer-exit {
  from { transform: translateX(0); }
  to { transform: translateX(100%); }
}

@container settings (min-width: 28rem) {
  .drawer-inner {
    padding: 2rem;
  }

  .drawer-actions {
    border-top: 1px solid var(--color-slate-200);
    padding-top: 1rem;
  }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .drawer[data-state] {
    animation: none;
  }
}

Radix can retain content during its CSS exit animation; avoid adding a competing timeout-based unmount. Reduced-motion users get an immediate transition without application-side branching.

The production boundary

This architecture adds a primitive dependency, but removes bespoke modal infrastructure. Tailwind remains responsible for visual composition; container queries handle local responsiveness; Radix owns interaction semantics.

The trade-off is intentional: closing currently discards state and saves nothing. Applications with unsaved changes need an explicit dismissal policy, usually through controlled dialog state and an onInteractOutside handler that prevents closure until the user confirms or saves.

Before shipping, test keyboard entry, reverse tabbing, Escape, focus restoration, zoom, and reduced motion. Include a screen reader pass and any portalled controls used inside the drawer. Primitive defaults are a strong foundation, not proof that the surrounding application is accessible.

The important optimization is not a shorter class string. It is eliminating the JavaScript layout loop and the home-grown focus trap from the same interaction boundary.

What's your production drawer story? Have you traced frame drops back to width measurements, or discovered focus escaping your modal at 2:00 AM? What primitives or patterns finally stabilized your overlay architecture?

title: Zoom system design interview
description:
Zoom system design interview

A Zoom system design interview looks simple until the discussion moves past "use WebRTC and an SFU." That is usually where weaker answers stall. Interviewers want to see whether you can turn a familiar product into a concrete video-conferencing system architecture with measurable constraints, failure handling, and clear trade-offs.

This matters because group video exposes several hard problems at once: low-latency real-time media, bursty traffic, unreliable networks, and room-level fan-out that can overload a design long before average traffic looks dangerous. A basic whiteboard sketch is not enough once the conversation reaches scaling and production readiness.

This newsletter covers three things:

  1. How to frame requirements with capacity and latency targets.
  2. Why an SFU is the default, and where it still breaks.
  3. How to discuss routing, shared state, failures, and metrics like an experienced engineer.

What the system must optimize for

For interview purposes, define the problem before drawing components. A Zoom-like system supports interactive group meetings in which users create rooms, join from desktop or mobile, publish audio and video, share screens, exchange chat messages, and optionally trigger recording. Those are functional requirements, but they do not tell you which architecture to choose.

The stronger signal is converting fuzzy goals into explicit targets. In a Zoom system design interview, interactive conversation usually needs sub-300 ms end-to-end latency, with audio often requiring tighter bounds to prevent people from talking over one another. You also need high availability, regional placement close to users, and adaptation when network quality changes during a call.

Capacity assumptions matter early. A set of one-to-one calls, a ten-person team meeting, and a 200-person all-hands meeting create very different traffic patterns. In practice, candidates should state room-size bands, expected concurrent rooms, and the traffic mix, such as camera video, screen sharing, and audio-only listeners.

Note: Interviewers usually care less about exact numbers than about whether the numbers are internally consistent and drive your design.

A useful split is between the control plane and the media plane. The control plane handles auth, room membership, mute state, chat, and signaling. The media plane carries real-time audio and video packets, where latency and packet loss matter most. This signaling-vs.-media-plane split is one of the clearest ways to explain the gap between the control plane and the data plane in conferencing systems.

To make that split concrete, the architecture diagram should come early.


Separate control from media from the start.

The takeaway is simple: start with SLOs, room assumptions, and traffic classes before naming technologies. That is the foundation for clarifying the functional and nonfunctional requirements that Zoom interview questions usually test. The next question is which media topology actually fits those constraints.

Why an SFU wins for most meeting workloads

A serious answer compares an SFU, an MCU, and mesh in production terms. Mesh means that every participant sends media directly to every other participant. That works for very small calls, but uplink and downlink usage grow badly as participants increase, so client bandwidth and device CPU quickly become the limiting factors.

An #key# MCU: A multipoint control unit that receives streams, decodes and mixes or composites them, and then sends back processed outputs. #key# It reduces endpoint complexity because clients receive fewer streams. The trade-off is server-side transcoding cost, higher CPU usage, and extra latency from decode, mix, and re-encode steps.

An #key# SFU: A selective forwarding unit that routes media streams between participants without decoding the media payload. #key# It is usually the default for interactive meetings. Clients still encode their own tracks, but the server forwards selected streams to subscribers with much lower compute cost than an MCU requires.

That does not mean that an SFU is cheap. Fan-out shifts the bottleneck from media processing to outbound bandwidth, packet routing, pacing, and per-subscriber congestion control. If each publisher offers simulcast layers, the server must track subscriptions and forward the right layer to each receiver efficiently.

A concrete example helps here. In a 12-person team meeting, an SFU is usually the obvious choice because each user may watch a grid of several live cameras plus a screen share, and latency matters more than perfect visual composition. In contrast, an MCU can still make sense for a recording pipeline that needs a single mixed output or for a PSTN bridge in which the endpoint cannot handle multiple live video subscriptions. This is also where meeting-recording-vs.-live-streaming trade-offs arise naturally in a system design answer.

The trade-off summary is worth stating explicitly before going deeper.

Comparison of Mesh, SFU, and MCU Topologies

Dimension Mesh SFU MCU
Latency Lowest added latency 100-200 ms added 200-400 ms added
Client Bandwidth Upload/Download (N-1) Upload 1, Download up to (N-1) Upload 1, Download 1
Server CPU Almost none Low to moderate Very high
Server Bandwidth ~0 Egress scales O(N²), Ingress O(N) Egress scales O(N)
Scalability ~4-6 participants Dozens to thousands 20-50 participants
Quality Control Full client-side control Client-side layout, encryption Server-decided layout
Best-Fit Use Case Small/secure group calls Large interactive meetings Recording, low-power clients

Practical tip: Use an SFU as the default answer, then mention an MCU as a targeted addition for recording pipelines, PSTN bridges, or very weak clients.

The main takeaway is that an SFU wins because it preserves low latency while scaling better than mesh or an MCU for meetings. After that, you need to explain how signaling and media actually move through the system and how to choose among an SFU, an MCU, and a mesh topology based on workload.

How the media and signaling planes work

Once a user joins a meeting, the path should be explained step by step. The client authenticates, fetches room metadata, opens signaling over WebSocket, and negotiates media transport using WebRTC. During setup, the client gathers network candidates through STUN and TURN, then completes ICE and DTLS-SRTP to establish secure media.

A quick sequence helps keep this answer precise:

  1. Auth and room lookup: Validate identity, authorization, and room policy.
  2. Signaling setup: Exchange offers, answers, ICE candidates, and control events.
  3. Media publish and subscribe: Send tracks to a regional SFU and receive selected remote tracks.

The signaling path carries metadata, not the media itself. It tracks membership, mute state, active-speaker hints, screen-sharing state, and subscription changes. After setup, audio and video packets bypass signaling and flow directly between the client and the SFU over SRTP, which keeps the control plane lightweight and recoverable. In practice, this is the core of real-time media routing in a Zoom-like system.

Quality adaptation depends on layered encoding. #key# Simulcast: A technique in which the sender encodes the same video at multiple resolutions or bit rates so that receivers can subscribe to different versions. #key# A related option is #key# SVC: Scalable video coding, in which a stream is encoded into dependent layers that can be selectively forwarded. #key# Both approaches let the SFU serve different receivers without server transcoding. This is the practical heart of adaptive bit rate and simulcast in video meetings.

A simple failure case makes this more concrete. If a user is on unstable Wi-Fi and the downlink drops, the SFU can switch that subscriber from a higher simulcast layer to a lower one instead of forcing a full renegotiation. If that is still not enough, the system may pause remote video tiles and preserve audio first, because degraded video is usually more acceptable than broken conversation. That is effectively how to handle packet loss and jitter in Zoom-style system discussions, even if you keep the explanation concise.

A sequence view makes this easier to discuss in an interview.


Signal first, then forward media directly.

The takeaway is that a Zoom-like design depends on a clean split: signaling manages session state, while the SFU forwards real-time media. That baseline sets up the next question: where the system actually breaks under load.

Where scaling fails under room fan-out

Many candidates say "the SFU scales horizontally" and stop there. That misses the main cost driver. In practice, load is driven less by participant count than by total active subscriptions: publishers times consumers times subscribed layers.

A 100-person room illustrates the problem. If each person publishes audio and some publish video, the system can create thousands of forwarding relationships. Even if each individual stream is modest, aggregate outbound bit rate, packet pacing, congestion feedback, and routing overhead can saturate the host.

Think in operational metrics, not just room size. Useful capacity signals include maximum outbound bit rate per server, consumers added per second, #key# jitter: Variation in packet-arrival timing that degrades smooth playback. #key# packet loss at P95 and P99, RTP router CPU, and NIC queue pressure. Autoscaling on participant count alone can hide hot rooms that dominate fan-out. This is why load estimation for video-conferencing infrastructure should focus on subscriptions and layers, not just head count.

Watch out: A room with 50 active videos can be far more expensive than several hundred mostly muted listeners. Capacity models should reflect subscription behavior, not just head count.

Mitigations are usually pragmatic rather than theoretical:

  1. Room caps per node: Limit how many large rooms or subscriptions a single host carries.
  2. Subscription pruning: Pause unseen video, prioritize active speakers, and lower layers for background tiles.
  3. Cascaded SFUs: Distribute fan-out across nodes or regions instead of concentrating all subscribers on one box.

A common failure pattern is a company all-hands meeting with one presenter and dozens of visible participants. Average regional load may still look healthy, but one SFU host can hit outbound bandwidth or packet-pacing limits because that single room dominates subscriptions. The fix is usually not "scale everything," but to shard that room more carefully, reduce unnecessary video subscriptions, or cascade forwarding across multiple routers. That is the practical answer to "how many participants can a Zoom-like system support?" It depends more on subscription behavior than on a single room-size number.

A diagram helps make the bottleneck visible.


Fan-out, not joins, usually defines the limit.

The main point is that SFU scaling fails at outbound fan-out and routing overhead, not only at raw participant totals. Once you recognize that, the next production concern is what happens when nodes or regions fail.

How to survive node and region failures

A single healthy SFU node is not enough for a production answer. Rooms need affinity so that participants in the same meeting land on the right media router, but that mapping cannot live only in process memory. Most designs keep room-to-router metadata in a fast shared store such as Redis so that signaling services can resolve where a participant should publish or subscribe.

Sticky routing helps during normal operation. A user who reconnects after a temporary disconnect should be routed back to the same room context when possible, which reduces renegotiation and state churn. However, shared state also needs versioning because stale affinity can send users to dead processes or duplicate routers after partial failures.

Failure handling is where distributed-systems depth shows up. If an SFU process crashes, signaling should detect the loss, remap the room or affected tracks, and rebuild subscriptions from preserved metadata. If a host dies entirely, clients may need an ICE restart and track republish, but user identity and room membership should survive through the control plane. This is central to building fault tolerance in live video-call systems.

Note: #key# ICE restart: A recovery step in which endpoints gather new transport candidates and renegotiate connectivity without creating a brand-new meeting identity. #key# This is common after media-path failure.

Regional failure adds another layer. You may keep control-plane identity global while placing media regionally. That allows a user to remain in the same logical room even if media must be redirected to another region with degraded quality or a temporary reconnection delay.

Consistency trade-offs should be named explicitly. A strongly consistent room mapping simplifies correctness but can slow failover. Eventual consistency can restore service faster, but without versioned updates and idempotent rebuild logic, you can expose duplicate subscriptions, dropped tracks, or split-brain routing.

One realistic failure mode is stale room affinity after a partial outage. A signaling service may still think room R belongs to process A, while health checks have already moved new publishers to process B. If rebuild logic is sloppy, some clients reconnect to the old route, others reconnect to the new one, and you get missing tracks or duplicate subscriptions until the control plane converges.

A failure matrix keeps this grounded.

Failure Modes and Management Strategies

Failure Mode Symptoms/Examples Detection Signals Recovery Mechanisms Trade-offs
Worker Crash Worker process stops, no heartbeats from worker Missing heartbeats, error logs, OS-level monitoring Restart process, job re-assignment, checkpointing Fast detection risks false positives, more frequent checkpoints add overhead
Host Failure Multiple services unreachable, host unresponsive Failing health checks, loss of OS metrics Shift workload, distributed storage, fault domain isolation Redundancy incurs cost, live migration adds overhead
Signaling Disconnect Commands not received, jobs hang Discrepancies in heartbeats vs control messages Use heartbeat channel, retry signals, fallback to defaults Complex mechanisms increase network use, timeout risks, coupling adds architectural complexity
Redis Inconsistency Replica lag, torn writes, stale cache entries Replication lag metrics, keyspace events Promote replicas, cross-shard consistency patterns Strong consistency reduces speed, eventually consistent architecture risks stale data
TURN Exhaustion Failed peer connections, high latency in relays TURN server metrics, connection failure logs Scale infrastructure, rate-limit requests, use TURN server pools Expensive bandwidth, increased cost for availability, fallbacks affect user experience
Regional Outage Unreachable services, error reports from affected region Global monitoring, provider status updates, missing heartbeats Multi-region architecture, disaster recovery plans, DNS failover Active-active complex and costly, active-passive slower with data loss risk equivalent to replication lag

Watch out: TURN exhaustion is easy to overlook. When direct connectivity drops and relay usage spikes, a healthy SFU fleet can still look broken to users.

The takeaway is that production readiness depends on shared state, routing discipline, and controlled recovery paths. After that, the final step in an interview answer is proving the design with metrics.

What to measure and how to answer

A good design answer ends with observability, because that is how you validate the architecture instead of asserting that it works. On the client side, track RTT, estimated one-way delay, packet loss, jitter, frame rate, decode failures, join time, and reconnect rate. On the server side, monitor SFU CPU, router event-loop lag, memory, packet-queue depth, NIC saturation, and subscription churn.

Room-level quality metrics matter more than host averages. A single overloaded room can hide within a healthy regional aggregate. Many teams use percentile views at P95 and P99 for join latency, audio loss, freeze rate, and reconnect success because tails determine whether meetings feel reliable.

Practical tip: Organize metrics by user session, room, router, host, and region. That makes it much easier to answer whether the issue is local congestion, bad routing, or a broader infrastructure problem.

In an interview, the closing pattern can be compact:

  1. State that the default architecture is WebRTC clients publishing to regional SFUs, with the control plane managing auth, signaling, room state, and subscriptions.
  2. Mention that MCU-style processing may still appear in side pipelines for recording, PSTN interop, or special endpoints.
  3. Call out the real scaling pressure: fan-out across consumers and layers, not simply participant count.
  4. End with the production gap: multi-node routing, shared-state consistency, and failure recovery.

If you want more practice with this style of reasoning, developers often find useful detail in resources such as Educative's system design interview courses, Educative's WebRTC-focused content, and the MDN WebRTC guides. They are most useful once you already have a rough architecture in mind and want to pressure-test the weak spots.

The takeaway is that observability closes the loop between architecture and user experience. In a Zoom system design interview, that is often what separates a component list from a convincing explanation of trade-offs in a video-conferencing system design.

Closing

A strong Zoom system design interview answer is not about naming an SFU and moving on. It is about framing the workload, identifying fan-out as the main scaling cost, and showing how routing and shared state behave during failure. In practice, these same principles also appear outside interviews: large classrooms, internal all-hands meetings, telehealth sessions, and support calls all run into the same latency, routing, and recovery trade-offs at different scales.

If you keep the control plane and the media plane separate, define measurable SLOs early, and discuss recovery paths clearly, your answer will sound like production reasoning rather than whiteboard pattern matching. That is usually what interviewers are testing for when they ask you to design a video-conferencing system architecture under interview pressure.

title: How a Student Management System Database Is Structured (Tables, IDs and Relationships)
description:
If you have ever built a CRUD app for a school project — or been asked to "just make a small system" for a local institute — you already know the trap. The first version has one big students table with everything in it. Then someone asks for guardians. Then attendance by class and date. Then fees that are somehow both per-term and per-student. Within a month the schema is held together by hope and duplicated columns.

Real school software survives because its data model matches how schools actually work. This article walks through the structure used by a production student management system database, table by table, and the design decisions that keep it sane at scale.

The core idea: entities and the IDs that connect them

A student management system is a relational database at heart. Each kind of thing gets its own table — students, guardians, courses, sections, enrollments, attendance, grades, invoices — and rows are linked by IDs rather than by copying data around.

That single decision explains almost everything else. A student's name exists in exactly one row. An attendance record does not repeat the name; it stores a student_id. A grade does not repeat the course title; it stores a course_id and a student_id. Change the name once, and every screen, report and invoice that joins through the ID shows the corrected value.

The main tables

Students — student_id, name, date of birth, contact details, status (applicant, enrolled, suspended, graduated, alumni). This is the anchor table; almost everything references it.

Guardians — guardian_id, name, relationship, contact details, linked to students through a join table, because one student can have two guardians and one guardian can have three children in the school.

Programs and courses — course_id, title, credits or hours, department. The catalogue of what is taught.

Classes and sections — section_id, course_id, teacher_id, term, room. A course becomes real when it is scheduled as a section in a term.

Enrollments — enrollment_id, student_id, section_id or program, academic year. This join table is the busiest in the system: it is what "being in a class" actually means as data.

Attendance — attendance_id, student_id, section_id, date, status (present, absent, late, excused). High volume, append-mostly, and the first place indexing really matters.

Assessments and grades — assessment_id, student_id, course_id, type (quiz, exam, assignment), score. Types and weights live in their own configuration so totals can be computed, not typed.

Fees, invoices and payments — invoice_id, student_id, term, amount, due date, status; payments as separate rows against an invoice, because part payments are normal life, not an edge case.

Users and roles — user_id, role, permissions. Teachers, finance staff, registrars and parents all read the same database through very different windows.

Decisions that separate a toy schema from a production one

Normalize first, denormalize never (almost). Duplicate student records across modules are the number one reason schools end up with several "true" versions of the same child. If a fact tempts you to store it twice, it belongs in its own table with an ID.

Model money as a ledger, not a balance. Storing a single amount_paid field destroys history. Invoices and payments as immutable rows let you answer "who changed this, and when" — a question schools ask constantly.

Audit trails are a feature, not paranoia. Grades and fees get challenged. A changed_by, changed_at and reason on sensitive tables turns a dispute into a lookup.

Soft-delete students. A student who leaves is never really deleted; their records feed transcripts and alumni reports for decades. Status flags beat DELETE.

Index for the real queries. Attendance by section and date, invoices by student and status, enrollments by year — these are the hot paths, not the primary keys alone.

Build or buy?

For a class project or a tiny single-course institute, building this schema is a great exercise and entirely feasible. The honest turning point comes with everything around the schema: role-based access, audit requirements, backups, parent portals, payment integrations and migration from whatever spreadsheet chaos came before. That is why most institutions end up adopting a platform whose data layer is already structured this way, and why asking a vendor the database questions — is it normalized, is there an API, can we export everything with relationships intact — tells you more than any feature demo.

A note on scale

None of this requires exotic infrastructure. The same schema serves a 200-student school and a 40,000-student university group; what changes is indexing discipline, partitioning of high-volume tables like attendance, and how strictly access control is enforced. Design the relationships honestly at small scale and you rarely need to redesign them at large scale — which is more than can be said for the one-big-table approach.

The takeaway

A student management system is not complicated because schools are complicated. It is complicated because one student's life touches a dozen processes, and the database has to hold all of them consistently at once. Get the entities and relationships right, keep every fact in exactly one place, and the features — attendance, grades, fees, reports — become straightforward queries instead of monthly emergencies.

title: Did your process death test actually kill the process?
description:
A screen can pass every rotation test you have and still crash the first time Android reclaims the app in the background. Here is one that does:

object Session {
    lateinit var user: String
}

class SessionActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        val user = Session.user
        // ...
    }
}

MainActivity sets Session.user before it opens this screen. Rotate the phone and nothing goes wrong, because the process and the singleton are still alive. Kill the process while the app is in the background and Android recreates SessionActivity directly. MainActivity never runs, and Session.user throws.

The quieter version of this bug doesn't crash. A ViewModel keeps a half-written form in memory, rotation keeps the ViewModel, and process death takes the form with it.

I built process-death-check to catch both. Most of the work went into a question I had underestimated: how do you know your test really tested this?

What the usual checks do

  • Rotation and ActivityScenario.recreate() recreate the Activity. The process survives, so ViewModels and singletons keep their data.
  • "Don't keep activities" destroys Activities and leaves the process running.
  • am force-stop goes too far. Android treats it as the user stopping the app and drops the back stack, so you get a cold start.
  • am kill, or a scripted kill -9, is a real kill. It only tests restoration if it happens at the right moment.

Timing is the hard part

Press Home and kill the process straight away, and the test can still pass. It just tested something else. An Activity's saved state reaches the system around the time the Activity stops, a little after Home is pressed. Kill the process before that and the system has nothing to restore, so you end up with something much closer to a cold start.

You don't have to guess or sleep. The system reports it in dumpsys activity activities:

Intent { flg=0x10000000 xflg=0x4 cmp=dev.byfedin.pdcheck.sample/.SavedFormActivity }
mHaveState=true mIcicle=Bundle[mParcelledData.dataSize=1940]
state=STOPPED delayedResume=false finishing=false

So the check polls until every Activity of the task shows STOPPED with saved state, and only then kills. The field is mHaveState on API 36 and haveState on API 26, so the parser accepts both.

Real runs added three rules I hadn't planned for:

  • Old tasks from recents appear in the same dump, and they can hold the wait forever. The wait has to look only at the task under test.
  • An Activity lower in the stack may never have been started. It sits in INITIALIZING with no state, and that's fine.
  • After an earlier process death, a record can be DESTROYED and still have saved state. That's fine too.

Coming back the way a user does

My first version started the app again with a plain launch and landed on the wrong screen. To return to the retained task, you need the task's root Intent with the flags a launcher uses, FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK | FLAG_ACTIVITY_RESET_TASK_IF_NEEDED:

adb shell am start \
  -a android.intent.action.MAIN \
  -c android.intent.category.LAUNCHER \
  -f 0x10200000 \
  -n com.example.app/.MainActivity

The action, category and component come from the same dump, so the check doesn't need to know anything about your app.

A pass has to prove something

A process death test that passes tells you very little unless it also checks that the event happened. Around the restore, the check verifies five things:

  1. The old processes are gone. It waits until ps no longer lists any process of the package, including pkg:service ones.
  2. The PID changed. If it didn't, the kill can't be proven.
  3. The same Activity came back in the same task. Landing on a different Activity is a finding, even with no crash.
  4. Nothing crashed. It reads logcat from the moment of the kill, then waits a little longer, because a crash in onResume or in the first frame arrives late.
  5. Typed text and toggles match. It compares two uiautomator dumps and skips password fields.

There is one more decision I'd copy into any device test: "the check could not run" and "the check found a bug" are different results. pdcheck exits with 1 for a bug and 2 when it couldn't get a reliable answer, for example when the window is unreadable after the restore. A broken emulator shouldn't look like a bug in the app, and it definitely shouldn't look like a pass.

Running it

Open a screen, type something and run:

pdcheck kill -p com.example.app

On the sample app's form that keeps its input in remember, the result looks like this:

  Saved state acknowledged for 2 Activity(s)
  Killed dev.byfedin.pdcheck.sample (5244) with RUN_AS
FAIL dev.byfedin.pdcheck.sample/dev.byfedin.pdcheck.sample.ForgetfulFormActivity
  - UI state lost after process death (2)
      field#1: "hello" -> ""
      toggle:Urgent: "checked" -> "unchecked"

Checking screens one by one gets old quickly, so there is also a sweep. It taps through whatever it can reach and runs the check on each screen, with no test script. In a Gradle project:

plugins {
    id("com.android.application")
    id("dev.byfedin.pdcheck") version "0.1.0"
}

./gradlew :app:pdcheckSweepDebug

It writes JUnit XML, so a failed check shows up in CI like a failed test. The project's own CI runs it against the sample on API 26 and API 36 emulators.

What it won't do

  • run-as needs a debuggable build. Release builds fall back to am kill, which only kills a process the system already considers safe to kill.
  • The sweep presses whatever buttons it finds, so point it at a test account. It never types, which means it stops at sign-in screens.
  • In a single-Activity app it compares the Activity, not the Compose destination. Falling back to the start destination is only caught if a field or toggle on the lost screen had a value.
  • Reloading a list after process death is legitimate, so loaded data and scroll position are out of scope. Assert those in your own tests.

A good first target is any screen that reads a singleton, or one that's normally reached through several others. Run pdcheck kill there once. The code is on GitHub under MIT, and if it gets your app wrong, an issue with the dumpsys output from the report folder is the most useful thing you can send.

title: cPGuard Update Channel Hijacked to Backdoor Linux Servers and Collect Password Hashes
description:
An attacker broke into the update system of the cPGuard security tool on November 2 and used it to send a malicious script to customers' Linux servers.

The script installed a backdoor and collected password hashes and other sensitive files from servers that ran it, cPGuard maker OPSSHIELD said in an advisory. The attacker has since taken some of that data.

cPGuard 5.88.25 and later versions
