title: The Node.js Brotli flaw: your server decompresses whatever APIs send back
description:
On October 21, Node.js fixed a flaw in its Brotli decoder, CVE-2026-111497. I went through the Node images in my projects. Two Next.js frontends are built on a tag that still ships Node 22.21.1. That tag will never get the fix.

TL;DR: a crafted Brotli stream can make Node write outside the memory it reserved. The process can crash, leak memory, or run an attacker's code. You are exposed if your server decompresses Brotli that comes from outside. Node's fetch, axios and Express 5 all do it by default. Move to Node 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1. Node 18, Node 20 and some Docker tags will never be fixed.

Versions and source status: snapshot as of October 31, 2026. Check the latest fixes before deploying.

This article is for Node.js developers and for teams that ship Node in containers. You do not need to know Brotli to follow it.

Who decompresses Brotli without knowing it

The flaw has one condition. Your application must decompress Brotli data supplied by someone else. So the real question is simple. Which code on your server decompresses Brotli?

I read the source code of Node, undici, axios and body-parser. The table sums up what each one does.

The fetch case is the quietest one. Node built it on undici, the HTTP library of the Node.js project. Over HTTPS, fetch asks the server for Brotli on its own, with an accept-encoding header that includes br. Then it decompresses the response without asking you.

Changing that header does not protect you. In undici's code, the decoder depends on the response's Content-Encoding header. A hostile server can send you Brotli even if you did not ask for it.

The risk comes from URLs you do not control. Think of a webhook entered by a customer, a link preview, an RSS feed or an image to download. A compromised third-party API is enough too.

For incoming requests, Express 5 relies on body-parser 2. That version decompresses bodies sent with Content-Encoding: br. So any client can push a Brotli stream at you. Express 4 uses body-parser 1, which does not know Brotli.

An image that only builds a frontend receives no traffic. It still needs the update, but it is not the priority.

What Node.js fixed on October 21

On October 21, Node.js shipped three security releases: 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1. The advisory lists ten flaws. Four are rated "high". Only one can lead to code execution, the one in the Brotli decoder.

A server that compresses with Brotli says so with the Content-Encoding: br header. The client must then decompress the response before reading it. That is the decoder's job.

The decoder reads the stream piece by piece. When it hit an invalid section, it thought it was just missing a few bytes. It waited for more instead of rejecting the stream.

Meanwhile, it kept storing the next bytes in a small eight-byte buffer. It did not stop at the edge. So it wrote into the memory next to it. This is called an out-of-bounds write.

Node lists three possible effects. The process can crash. It can leak part of its memory. Or the attacker can run their own code inside your Node process.

Node rates the flaw "high". The CVE record, written by Google, scores it 9.2 out of 10. The NVD, the US vulnerability database, scores it 9.8.

The bug comes from Google's Brotli library. Google shipped the fixed versions the same day: 1.0.10, 1.1.1 and 1.2.1. But Node ships its own copy of Brotli.

I checked with ldd in two official images. The node binary loads no Brotli library from the system. So updating the packages in your image changes nothing for Node. It is the same trap as Go's eMudhra fix, which I covered yesterday.

Confirmed exploitation since October 27

On October 22, the CVE record still said "Exploitation: none". CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on October 27. That catalog records confirmed exploitation. The assessment changed to "active" the next day.

On October 30, Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency also reported a public proof of concept. These sources describe successive states. They do not give an account of a specific attack here. This snapshot ends on October 31, 2026.

My lab: 14 FROM node lines, three versions that will never be fixed

I listed the FROM node: lines in every Dockerfile of my projects. I count 14 of them, in 11 files. For each tag, I read Docker Hub, then ran node --version in today's image.

The tag that surprised me is node:22-alpine3.21. It looks like it follows Node 22. In fact, it ships Node 22.21.1, and it has not moved in a year.

Alpine is a very small Linux distribution. The alpine3.21 suffix pins its version. The team behind the Node images dropped Alpine 3.21 on December 4, 2025. Today it only builds the Alpine 3.23 and 3.24 variants.

Since then, that tag gets no new Node version at all. Nothing warns you. The build passes and the image starts.

One of the two repositories does have a Dependabot that watches Docker images. In May, it proposed moving to node:25-alpine3.21. It kept the suffix, so it stayed inside the frozen family. Node 25 reached end of life three weeks later, on June 1.

node:18-alpine and node:20-alpine are frozen for another reason. Node 18 has been end of life since April 30, 2025, Node 20 since April 30, 2026. Their copy of Brotli is version 1.1.0, inside the affected range. Node's advisory says it plainly. These official releases remain vulnerable because their release lines received no fix.

One last detail, on my laptop. The cached node:24-alpine image dates from August 3. It holds Node 24.19.0, without the fix. A build that reuses that copy makes a vulnerable image, even with an up-to-date tag on Docker Hub.

Then I searched my code for anything that decompresses Brotli. No service calls the Brotli functions of zlib. None uses Express. The two Next.js frontends make no server-side fetch in production. Their API calls leave from the browser.

A single route makes a server-side fetch. It only turns on in local development, toward a storage service I control. So my real exposure is low.

But a grep does not see what my dependencies do. And the next server-side fetch will arrive without anyone rereading the FROM line.

The Brotli version number proves nothing

Node shows the version of its libraries in process.versions. I compared two Node 22 images, one vulnerable and one fixed:

docker run --rm node:22-alpine3.21 node -p "process.version + ' brotli ' + process.versions.brotli"
# v22.21.1 brotli 1.1.0
docker run --rm node:22-alpine node -p "process.version + ' brotli ' + process.versions.brotli"
# v22.23.4 brotli 1.1.0

Both show Brotli 1.1.0. Node applied Google's fix to its copy without changing that number. Node 24 is the same, with 1.2.0 before and after. Compare the Node version with 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 instead.

The fix also adds a constant to zlib.constants. In my tests, it only exists in the fixed versions. It makes a quick check in a running container:

docker exec my-container node -p "process.version + ' ' + ('BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH' in require('zlib').constants)"
# v22.23.4 true   (fixed)
# v22.21.1 false  (vulnerable)

What to change

If you cannot deploy today, two settings reduce the risk. With Express 5, the inflate: false option rejects compressed bodies with a 415 error:

app.use(express.json({ inflate: false }))
// a body sent with Content-Encoding: br gets a 415 error

With axios, the decompress: false option turns decompression off. Your code then gets the compressed bytes, and handling them is up to you. For fetch, I found no matching setting. Only a Node update protects it.

The checklist

A Node fix only protects the container where it actually runs.

  • [ ] List every FROM node: line in your Dockerfiles
  • [ ] Spot end-of-life versions: Node 18, Node 20 and older
  • [ ] Spot tags tied to an Alpine version that is no longer built, such as alpine3.21
  • [ ] Run node -p process.version in every production container
  • [ ] Do not trust process.versions.brotli
  • [ ] Look for server-side fetch and axios calls to URLs you do not control
  • [ ] Look for Express 5 and direct calls to the Brotli functions of zlib
  • [ ] Rebuild with --pull, then redeploy

The takeaway

The Brotli flaw does not need you to call Brotli yourself. fetch, axios and Express 5 do it for you, on data that comes from outside. And a Docker tag can look current while it ships a version that is a year old.

Open your Dockerfiles today. Look for Node 18 and 20, and for tags that pin an Alpine version. Nobody will update them for you.

Want a review of your images and your build pipeline? See my DevSecOps pipeline offer, or let's talk.

Sources: Node.js, October 21, 2026 security releases · Node.js 22.23.4 release notes · CVE-2026-111497 record · NVD, CVE-2026-111497 · CISA KEV catalog · Singapore CSA, alert AL-2026-154 · Brotli 1.2.1 release notes · undici 6.29.1, fetch source · body-parser 2.4.0, body reading · axios HTTP adapter · Node.js zlib documentation · Node.js release schedule · docker-node, Alpine 3.21 removal · Docker Hub, node image · docker build documentation

title: 8 .gitattributes Lines That Shrink Agent Diffs and Calm Parallel-Branch Merges
description:
• Book: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Three coding agents, three branches, one Go service. Each agent fixed its bug and then did the polite thing: it added a bullet under ## [Unreleased] in CHANGELOG.md. The first branch merges clean. The second stops on conflict markers in a file where both sides are right. The third one bumped a dependency, so its pull request opens with a screen of go.sum checksums before you reach the code you need to read.

Git merges and diffs every file the same way unless you tell it otherwise. The place you tell it is .gitattributes, and eight lines cover the files parallel agents tend to collide on: the changelog, lockfiles, generated code and snapshot fixtures.

The whole file, then line by line

Here it is. Commit it on main before you start the agents, so every branch cut from main carries the same rules.

# 1. LF in the repo and in every worktree
* text=auto eol=lf
# 2-3. Function names in hunk headers
*.go  diff=golang
*.php diff=php
# 4. Keep both sides' changelog bullets
CHANGELOG.md merge=union
# 5-6. Lockfiles: no local diff hunks
go.sum            -diff linguist-generated
package-lock.json -diff
# 7. Codegen GitHub can't spot on its own
api/gen/** linguist-generated
# 8. Snapshot images: never convert, never merge
testdata/**/*.png binary

Two rules from the gitattributes docs explain the layout. When several patterns match a path, "a later line overrides an earlier line", and that happens per attribute. So line 8 can switch off the text that line 1 switched on, for PNGs only. And a pattern that names a directory does not match the files inside it: write api/gen/**, not api/gen/.

Line 1: * text=auto eol=lf. Git decides per file whether it is text, and for text files it stores LF. With eol=lf, the working tree gets LF on checkout too, on every OS. That matters when one agent runs on Windows or one tool saves with CRLF: without the rule, a file whose endings flip shows every line as changed.

Files already committed with CRLF are not converted on their own; the docs give the fix, run once from a clean tree: git add --renormalize ., then commit. To check, git ls-files --eol prints each file's endings in the index (i/), in the working tree (w/) and the attribute in force (attr/). If a Windows script needs CRLF, add *.bat text eol=crlf below line 1.

Lines 2 and 3: diff=golang and diff=php. Every hunk starts with @@ -a,b +c,d @@ and then a line of context git picked as the "function name". By default that is the nearest line that "begins with an alphabet, an underscore or a dollar sign", the same rule GNU diff -p uses. Go puts func at column zero, so the default often finds it anyway. diff=golang makes the choice deliberate with a Go pattern. The docs also say each built-in language ships a word regex, so git diff --word-diff splits Go tokens properly.

PHP is the case that needs it: methods sit indented inside a class, the default rule skips indented lines, and the hunk header usually names the class instead of the method. Both golang and php are in git's built-in list, so there is nothing to configure beyond the attribute.

Line 4: merge=union for the changelog

This is the line that ends the fake conflict in the opening. The docs describe the built-in union driver like this: "Run 3-way file level merge for text files, but take lines from both versions, instead of leaving conflict markers."


Three branches, one changelog: union keeps every new line instead of stopping on markers.

Two agents each add a bullet under ### Added. A normal merge sees both sides inserting at the same spot and stops. Union keeps both bullets. That is what an append-only file wants.

Read the warning that comes with it, though, because it is in the same paragraph of the docs: union "tends to leave the added lines in the resulting file in random order and the user should verify the result. Do not use this if you do not understand the implications." In practice that means two things for a changelog:

  • Union is right for added lines and wrong for edited ones. If two branches both change the same existing line, say a version number in a heading, you get both versions and no warning.
  • It never applies to code. Keep it on files where every line stands alone.

You can try it before you commit the rule. git merge-file takes three files in the order current, base, other, and --union resolves conflicts by keeping both sides:

git merge-file -p --union \
  changelog-ours.md changelog-base.md changelog-theirs.md

-p prints the result instead of overwriting the first file, so it is safe to run on copies.

One more thing to check: whether your host's merge button honours the attribute. A GitLab issue notes that GitLab reads built-in drivers like union from .gitattributes, while custom drivers defined in git config don't run in merge requests. If branches land through a web button on your host, test it on a throwaway pull request first.

Lines 5 to 7: keep lockfiles and codegen out of the way

Lockfiles and generated code change for real, and you do want them committed. You don't want to read them line by line in a review, and you don't want an agent spending context on them when it runs git diff to check its own work. Two different attributes cover the two places you read diffs.

-diff is for your terminal. The docs: a path with diff unset will "generate Binary files differ". So git diff and git log -p print a one-line notice for go.sum instead of hunks of hashes. The file still merges as text, because -diff says nothing about merging. When you want the content, git diff --text go.sum shows it anyway (--text means "treat all files as text").

go.sum is a good target. The Go modules reference describes it as "cryptographic hashes of the module's direct and indirect dependencies". The change a human reviews is in go.mod, which stays diffable. package-lock.json gets the same treatment if the repo has a web front end.

linguist-generated is for GitHub. GitHub's docs say files marked with it are hidden by default in diffs and left out of the repository's language statistics. GitHub already spots some files without help. Linguist's generated.rb catches package-lock.json and composer.lock by name, and Go files with a // Code generated line in their first 40 lines. That is the Go convention (^// Code generated .* DO NOT EDIT\.$), so most .pb.go and other codegen output is covered already.

go.sum is not on that list, which is why line 5 sets both attributes. Line 7 is for generated output that carries no such header, like a bundled OpenAPI spec or a generated TypeScript client under api/gen/.

Don't reach for binary on lockfiles. It is a macro for -diff -merge -text, and with merge unset git takes the current branch's version and declares a conflict every time both branches change the file. For a lockfile, a text merge followed by go mod tidy or npm install is the better path.

Line 8: binary for snapshot fixtures

Image snapshots are the opposite case. A line merge of two PNGs is never useful, and a converted byte breaks the test. Under line 1 alone, text=auto leaves git to decide by itself whether each PNG is text; line 8 takes that decision out of git's hands. The docs define the macro as [attr]binary -diff -merge -text: no text diff, no line merge, no end-of-line conversion. Because it sits after line 1, it wins for these paths.

testdata/ is the right home for them in Go. The go command docs say the tool "will ignore a directory named 'testdata', making it available to hold ancillary data needed by the tests."

When two agents both re-record a snapshot, the merge now stops on that file, keeping your branch's copy, and you regenerate it from the merged code. For text golden files that get regenerated whole, use -merge on its own instead. You keep a readable diff in review and still get the stop-and-regenerate behaviour on merge.

Prove each line applies with git check-attr

A typo in a pattern fails silently. git check-attr tells you what git will actually use for a path. With -a it lists every attribute that is set, unset or given a value for each path you name:

git check-attr -a -- CHANGELOG.md go.sum \
  api/gen/client.ts testdata/golden/home.png

The output format is <path>: <attribute>: <info>, one line per attribute. You are looking for merge: union on the changelog, diff: unset and linguist-generated: set on go.sum, and diff, merge and text all unset on the PNG. Line 1 matches every path, so each one prints at least eol: lf and a text line. If that is all a path shows, none of the specific lines matched it, so check that pattern for a typo. Add --cached to read .gitattributes from the index only, which tells you what is committed rather than what sits in your working tree. Run it once before you cut the agents' branches.

Reviewing several agents' branches by file

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. In Hermes, ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) starts each task on its own hermes/<name> branch in its own worktree, with the task as the agent's first prompt. Those branches and worktrees are plain git, so a .gitattributes committed on the branch you start from is in every worktree.


Two agent sessions side by side: Codex on orders-types and Claude Code on orders-api, each in its own hermes/ worktree, with the sessions sidebar (status, context use, cost, branch) on the left.

The Review Desk (⌘G, or Ctrl+Shift+G) shows a task's changes by turn or by file, with risk flags, and a line comment goes back to the agent that wrote that line. In either view, line 1 keeps a commit from showing every line changed over line endings, and the changed-files list lets you pass over go.sum and the changelog to spend your attention on the code.


The Review Desk (⌘G) in By turn view: two turns, turn 1's diff of src/db.ts, the changed-files list, and a commit message drafted from the turns.

When a task is ready, Land commits, opens a pull request or merges locally into the branch the task started from, and it can be undone. If the remote is on GitHub, a pull request opened that way gets GitHub's collapsed view for go.sum and api/gen/. Hermes is free to download, source-available under BSL 1.1, and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. It is not affiliated with Nous Research, Anthropic, OpenAI or any agent vendor. Download it here, and the source is on GitHub.

If this was useful

A .gitattributes file only calms the merges. Whether three agents can work on one Go service without stepping on each other comes down to how the code is split: clear packages, clear boundaries, small files that change for one reason. Thinking in Go is my two-book series on that, first the language itself, then hexagonal architecture in Go, where the domain sits behind ports and the adapters change on their own.

title: AI SDK 7.0.160 Started Enforcing dataPartSchemas. Your Loading States Might Now Throw
description:
If you pass dataPartSchemas to useChat and bump ai to 7.0.160 or later, a chat that worked yesterday can end up in status: 'error' with a TypeValidationError. You didn't change anything. Your schemas just started running.

What changed

useChat and Chat accept dataPartSchemas, keyed by the bare part name (weather for a data-weather part). The stream processor looked the schema up by the full chunk type (data-weather), so the lookup always missed and streamed data parts were never validated. That's issue #24241, fixed in PR #24298 and shipped in ai 7.0.160: "Invalid data parts now raise a TypeValidationError."

So a patch release turned on a check that was configured but never ran.

What I ran

I didn't want to guess at the edge cases, so I drove the Chat class from @ai-sdk/react with a fake transport that replays fixed UI message chunks. No model, no network. useChat runs on that same class (its chat option even takes an existing Chat instance), so the stream handling is the same code path. I ran the same script against ai 7.0.159 with @ai-sdk/react 4.0.163, ai 7.0.162 with @ai-sdk/react 4.0.166, and ai 6.0.322 with @ai-sdk/react 3.0.325, all with zod 4.6.7 on Node 20.19.2.

Stream 7.0.159 7.0.162
Valid data-weather part ready ready
city: 42, then some text ready, bad data kept in parts, text arrives error, no assistant message at all
Loading update without weather, then the final value ready error, earlier text kept, final value lost
Transient part that fails the schema ready, onData called error, onData not called
data-notice part with no schema ready ready

On 6.0.322 every row matched the 7.0.159 column: bad data went through without an error.

The one that'll bite: progressive updates

The streaming data docs use a progressive pattern: write { city, status: 'loading' } first, then write to the same id again with the real value. The docs type weather as optional (weather?: string), which fits that pattern. But if your zod schema was written for the finished shape, the loading chunk fails now. Here's the excerpt from my test script (start and end are the start/finish chunks, text() writes one text part, and run() sends a message through Chat with these chunks):

const strictSchemas = {
  weather: z.object({
    city: z.string(),
    weather: z.string(),
    status: z.enum(['loading', 'success']),
  }),
};

// Case 3: a loading update, then the final value under the same id
await run('3 loading update without weather, then final', [...start,
  ...text('t0', 'Checking...'),
  { type: 'data-weather', id: 'w1', data: { city: 'Berlin', status: 'loading' } },
  { type: 'data-weather', id: 'w1', data: { city: 'Berlin', weather: 'sunny', status: 'success' } }, ...end]);

On 7.0.162 this ended with Type validation failed for message.parts[2].data (data-weather, id: "w1"). The "Checking..." text that streamed before it stayed in the message, the final value never arrived, and chat.status was error.

Every chunk is checked, not just the last one per id. Transient parts too, even though they never land in message.parts.

The fix

Make the schema describe every state the server actually sends. A discriminated union keeps the final shape strict:

const unionSchemas = {
  weather: z.discriminatedUnion('status', [
    z.object({ status: z.literal('loading'), city: z.string() }),
    z.object({ status: z.literal('success'), city: z.string(), weather: z.string() }),
  ]),
};

With this schema the same stream finished with status: ready on both versions, and the part ended up as { city: 'Berlin', weather: 'sunny', status: 'success' }.

Before you upgrade, I'd do three things:

  1. Search the client for dataPartSchemas.
  2. For each data-* type in there, check every writer.write() on the server against its schema, including loading, progress and transient writes.
  3. Make sure the UI shows error from useChat. In my runs a failed part stopped the whole response, so a silent failure here looks like a chat that just stops.

Data parts with no schema aren't checked at all, so a schema-less type won't start failing.

I'd rather have the error than let city: 42 slip into message.parts without a word, which is what 7.0.159 did. Have you hit this one after updating, or were your schemas already matching what the server sends?

References

  • ai 7.0.160 release notes
  • Issue #24241: useChat/Chat never validates streamed data parts against dataPartSchemas
  • PR #24298: validate streamed data parts against dataPartSchemas
  • AI SDK docs: Streaming custom data
  • AI SDK docs: useChat reference

title: Everything we changed when we rebuilt the token console — and the small annoyances we removed
description:
This is for people who launch tokens, add liquidity, run a presale or lock LP tokens — and who don't want to
read a smart-contract audit in order to do it. We just finished rebuilding the platform underneath, so here's
what actually changed for you, in plain terms, plus the small things we fixed that you'd otherwise notice only
as "huh, that used to be annoying."

Fifteen chains, one top bar

BNB Chain, Ethereum, Arbitrum, Polygon, Base, opBNB, Core, X Layer, Conflux eSpace, ApeChain, Morph, ECO,
Robinhood, ARC, plus the BNB testnet. Switching chains in the top bar carries the rest of the page with it:
which exchange and pool you're looking at, which fee steps that exchange offers, what a batch operation costs
in that chain's own coin. You don't re-enter anything, and nothing silently keeps the previous chain's
settings.

One honest boundary: Solana, TON, Sui and Tron are separate sites. This one is EVM chains only.

"I created the pool but I can't find it" used to be normal

Usually nothing had failed. Different exchanges have different fee steps — PancakeSwap's third tier is 0.25%,
Uniswap's is 0.3%. Ask one venue for the other's step and the pool you just made doesn't show up where you look
for it.

Now the fee options follow the exchange you picked, and the default is always a step that venue actually
offers.

For pools that are already live and out of balance there's repair liquidity (/tool/liquidity): it reads
the current reserves, works out how much each side is short, and deposits only the gap — you don't have to do
the ratio math or risk over-depositing.

Fewer confirmation popups, and failures you can act on

Multi-step flows used to make you confirm approvals one at a time, with a pause between each. They're bundled
now, so there's less clicking — and because the whole bundle is checked before it's broadcast, when something
goes wrong the message tells you which step failed instead of just "the transaction reverted."

Batch jobs also wait for each transaction to land before starting the next. That sounds obvious, but the
previous version started the next one while the earlier was still pending, and nodes rejected it. The kind of
"random" failure where retrying a minute later made it work was usually this.

Batch tools that point at the actual line

If you do airdrops, distributions or sweeps, you paste lists of addresses and amounts hundreds of rows long.
The rule we set for ourselves: one error per field, shown while you type, with a line number.

  • Fill a field and it checks immediately — you don't find out after pressing Confirm.
  • Bad address? It names the row. Nobody scans a 600-row box for row 481.
  • Duplicate addresses merge when you click away, so you don't pay the same wallet twice.
  • A limit that means "unlimited" displays as unlimited, not as a 77-digit number.

Neighbouring tools: migrate assets (/wallet/migrate) sweeps tokens and gas out of a batch of wallets with
a gas budget per wallet, and a paying wallet that checks its own balance before sending anything; spread
startup capital (/wallet/distribute) fans one funding wallet out to many, so your launch doesn't look like
one blob in the explorer. Change a scanning setting halfway through and the tool tells you the list you already
have is out of date.

Your private keys stay in your browser

The wallet vault encrypts locally before anything is saved, and a Passkey (face or fingerprint) can unlock it
instead of a password. Nothing is uploaded and no server holds your keys.

Two details that matter day to day:

  • Reloading the page doesn't lock you out again. The unlock lives in the current tab and expires after 15 minutes of inactivity, so you're not typing a password every refresh — and closing the tab really does end it.
  • There's a manual exit. A lock indicator in the top bar and a "lock now" button share that same 15-minute rule, so the interface can't show "locked" while a refresh quietly unlocks it.

Backups export as a CSV you can store somewhere else, not just to the clipboard — because "I copied 50 keys and
then closed the tab" has happened to everyone.

Also new, and worth five minutes

  • Vanity wallets (/wallet/vanity): want an address ending in 8888? Your browser searches for one locally. No transaction, no gas, and the result is an ordinary wallet — nothing special about it, just easy to recognise.
  • Bot workspace (/bot/robot): it picks the pool that's actually worth refreshing rather than the first one it finds; the wallet cap per round comes from one rule shared by the input box and the engine, so switching speed tiers adjusts your number instead of failing mid-run; and the run log survives a crash, so you can see what had already gone out.
  • Project website builder (/site): generate a landing page for your token and point your own domain at it with a CNAME record.
  • Contract calls (/tool/call) for changing parameters directly, token snapshot for holder lists, batch image upload for NFT artwork (returns ordinary https links plus IPFS addresses).
  • Read-only browsing: you can walk through the whole platform, including what your parameters would produce, without connecting a wallet.

The small things we spent real time on

These are the ones you'll notice without naming:

  • Changing language doesn't erase your form. Same page, Chinese to English, everything you typed stays. Move to a different page and it clears — on purpose, so half a form for one tool can't leak into the next.
  • Dates refuse the past and stop at the minute, so you can't schedule a lock for a time that already happened.
  • Long addresses are shortened with a copy icon, and hovering shows the whole thing — including names the chain gives back to us.
  • On a phone, dialogs slide up from the bottom with full-width stacked buttons, and fields are big enough that iOS doesn't zoom the page when you tap one.
  • Every fee is quoted in that chain's own coin, not in one fixed network's symbol.

What isn't finished

The AI-launch section is still labelled "in development" in the menu — we built part of it and pulled a piece
back out. Presale and IDO pages work today, but I'm not going to promise you a roadmap for them. And we verify
on the BNB testnet before mainnet, so if a flow behaves differently on a chain we test less often, tell us:
with fifteen chains live, your real transaction is a better test than ours.

Guides for each feature are under /en/guide, the FAQ is
/en/guide/faq, and the console is at gtokentool.com.

title: Building a Real-Time Restaurant Price Index & Menu Guide: The St-Hubert Barbecue Case Study
description:
When developing data aggregation platforms for the food and hospitality sector, tracking menu inflation, regional pricing disparities, and meal combo structuring across Canadian dining franchises presents several unique technical hurdles.

In this case study, we share insights from engineering the independent consumer directory for St-Hubert across Eastern Canada (Quebec, Ontario, and New Brunswick), available live at St-Hubert Menu & Prices Canada.

The Problem: Pricing Discrepancies in Canadian Casual Dining

Founded in Montreal in 1951, St-Hubert is one of Canada's most celebrated restaurant chains. However, consumer price transparency can be complicated due to three distinct dining formats:

  1. Traditional Dining Rooms: Full sit-down service with complete beverage programs, dessert carts, and seasonal promotions.
  2. Express Rotisserie Counters: Fast-casual ordering tailored for quick lunch pickups and suburban drive-throughs.
  3. Catering & Family Feasts: Bulk bundles optimized for family gatherings, workplace catering, and sports events.

To solve this for diners, we established a structured database tracking the complete st hubert menu with real-time price comparisons across rotisserie chicken dinners, barbecue ribs, and traditional Quebec poutines.

Architecture & Data Modeling

1. Hierarchical Menu Schema

Each restaurant item is modeled with relational attributes capturing meal modifiers:

  • Base Item: Quarter chicken dinner (Cuisses vs. Poitrine).
  • Format Options: Sit-down rotisserie dining at st hubert vs. Express takeout counters.
  • Side Pairings: Traditional Canadian fries, coleslaw (creamy vs. traditional), and signature rotisserie dipping sauce.
  • Catering Bundles: Pricing breakdown for large group packages at st-hubert barbecue.

2. Mobile-First Presentation

Over 82% of Canadian diners browse restaurant pricing on mobile devices right before visiting or ordering. We prioritized responsive data tables, low Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), and sub-second Largest Contentful Paint (LCP).

Community Discussion

How do you approach real-time menu data synchronization when aggregating multi-unit restaurant chains without official public GraphQL or REST APIs? Do you rely on headless browser scrapers, webhook triggers, or crowd-sourced receipt validation?

Check out the live directory at https://st-hubertmenu.ca/ and share your architectural thoughts below!

title: Your JSON is valid and your invoice is wrong
description:
Imagine a perfectly reasonable backend refactor.

client.name becomes customer.legalName. The new shape is clearer. The JSON parses. The application tests are green.

Then someone opens an invoice.

Beautiful margins. Correct logo. No customer.

The document has successfully generated an invoice addressed to absolutely nobody.

This is an illustrative failure in a loosely checked integration, but the underlying problem is useful to think about: valid JSON tells you surprisingly little about whether a document is correct.

I'm building Bitavu, a visual template editor with a JSON-to-PDF API. The boundary between incoming data and a saved document template is one of the places where a visible error can be much more useful than a successful download.

The customer did not disappear

Here is the data the template originally expected:

{
  "client": {
    "name": "Harbor Studio"
  }
}

And here is the new upstream shape:

{
  "customer": {
    "legalName": "Harbor Studio"
  }
}

Both are valid JSON. Both contain the same company name.

But a template bound to client.name does not automatically understand that customer.legalName is its replacement.

If the integration quietly converts a missing value into an empty string, the PDF may still render. The mistake has simply moved from an error response into a document someone will send.

The refactor is reasonable. The unchanged binding is the problem.

Three different checks are involved here:

  • Syntax: can the input be parsed as JSON?

  • Structure: does it contain the paths and types the template requires?

  • Meaning: are those values the right ones for this document?

Passing one does not prove the others.

A blank string is not always a fallback

Some fields really are optional. An absent delivery note might reasonably leave no visible text.

A missing billing recipient deserves a different decision.

If the document requires a customer name, make that requirement explicit before rendering. Even a small guard is better than quietly substituting a blank:

function requireClientName(data) {
  const name = data?.client?.name;

  if (typeof name !== "string" || name.trim() === "") {
    throw new TypeError("Expected a non-empty client.name");
  }

  return name;
}

This checks one field. A real document contract needs to cover its other required fields, types, arrays, and allowed values too.

Notice what happens with the refactored payload: the guard fails.

That is useful. You now have a specific integration change to review before an invoice leaves the system.

An empty string would have been quieter. The customer would have discovered the problem for you.

The more convincing bug passes the type check

Now suppose the input contains both of these:

{
  "billing": {
    "name": "Harbor Studio"
  },
  "shipping": {
    "name": "Harbor Warehouse"
  }
}

Both names are present. Both are strings. Both look like sensible things to put on a business document.

Only one belongs in this invoice's Bill to field.

This is why a mapping can be technically valid and still be wrong.

A structural validator can check that a string exists at a declared path. It cannot infer which business entity you intended to bill just because two field names look related.

When you review a mapping, ask a more useful question than "does the preview have text now?"

Ask: "Is this the person or company the document is supposed to name?"

The wrong name often looks more finished than a blank one. That does not make it a better result.

Treat a proposed mapping like a code change

For the first example, a deliberate mapping might be:

customer.legalName → client.name

That is a small transformation with a specific meaning: this upstream legal name supplies this template's client name.

Review it against the document's purpose. If an AI tool proposes the mapping, the same review still applies. A plausible field match is a proposal, not evidence that the two fields mean the same thing.

Before adopting it, use a few synthetic examples:

Input case Expected result
A normal customer legal name The intended name appears in Bill to
Billing and shipping names that differ The billing recipient is used
A missing or blank required name An explicit failure rather than a blank recipient
A number where the name should be A type error rather than silent coercion

The second case is especially helpful. If every name in your fixture is "Test Company," the wrong mapping can look perfectly correct.

Give the warehouse a different name. Let your test data disagree with itself in the ways real data does.

Make the mismatch visible

In Bitavu, a detected schema mismatch is reported as 422 SCHEMA_DRIFT. After reviewing a transformation, you can save a mapping and reference its mappingId in render requests.

Saved mappings target a particular template revision. That gives the reviewed transformation a defined destination instead of treating it as a universal fix for every document.

Conceptual workflow illustration, not a Studio screenshot.

That mechanism helps make the mismatch explicit. It still needs a well-defined template contract and a person who understands what the fields mean.

The useful outcome is a document whose data and presentation have both been checked.

A green check beside "valid JSON" cannot do all of that work.

What is harder to catch in your documents: a missing value, or a completely believable wrong one?

Disclosure: I'm building Bitavu. All four illustrations are AI-generated conceptual scenes using synthetic examples.

title: CRM'de veri maskeleme tasarlamak: Rol bazlı görünüm, sunucu tarafı maskeleme, açma kaydı ve test ortamı için tokenizasyon
description:
Bir gayrimenkul satış ekibinde CRM ekranını açan herkes aynı şeyi görmemeli. Çağrı merkezindeki yeni başlayan bir temsilci, lead'i aramak için telefon numarasına ihtiyaç duyar ama o numarayı listede toplu halde görmesine gerek yoktur. Pazarlama analisti kampanya performansına bakarken kimin telefonu olduğunu hiç bilmemelidir. Bir entegrasyon ortağının destek ekibi hata ayıklarken gerçek e-posta adreslerini görmemelidir. Ben Koray Yalçın olarak lead yönetimi ve CRM kurulumlarında bu ayrımı en sık atlanan güvenlik katmanı olarak görüyorum: herkes "yetki" konuşur, ama yetkili olan kişinin bile neyi, ne kadarını ve ne zaman göreceği konuşulmaz.

Veri maskeleme, kişisel verinin yetkisiz ya da gereğinden fazla göz önüne çıkmasını engellemek için değerin bir kısmının gizlenerek gösterilmesidir. En bilinen örneği 0532***1234 biçiminde gösterilen telefon numarasıdır. Bu yazıda kavramı sözlük tanımından çıkarıp bir geliştiricinin gözünden ele alıyorum: maskelemeyi nerede yapacağız, kurallarını nasıl veri olarak tutacağız, "numarayı göster" düğmesinin arkasında ne olmalı, dışa aktarma ve loglar nasıl korunacak, test ortamına gerçek veri nasıl sızmayacak.

Maskeleme, şifreleme ve yetkilendirme aynı şey değil

Bu üç kavram sık karıştırılır, oysa farklı soruları yanıtlarlar.

  • Yetkilendirme "bu kullanıcı bu kayda erişebilir mi?" sorusunu yanıtlar. Erişemiyorsa kayıt hiç gelmez.
  • Şifreleme "veri diskte ya da ağda çalınırsa okunabilir mi?" sorusunu yanıtlar. Uygulama içinde yetkili kullanıcıya çözülmüş haliyle gelir.
  • Maskeleme "erişimi olan kullanıcı alanın tamamını görmeli mi?" sorusunu yanıtlar. Kayda erişim vardır, ama belirli alanlar kısmen gizlenir.

Yani maskeleme, yetkilendirmenin alan düzeyindeki ince ayarıdır. Bir temsilci kendisine atanmış lead'e erişebilir (yetkilendirme), telefon sütunu veritabanında şifreli durabilir (şifreleme), ama liste ekranında numara maskeli görünür ve yalnız arama anında tam haliyle açılır (maskeleme). Üçü birbirinin yerine geçmez; birlikte çalışır.

Kural 1: Maskeleme sunucuda yapılır, arayüzde değil

En yaygın hata, tam veriyi API'den gönderip arayüzde CSS ya da JavaScript ile gizlemektir. Tarayıcının geliştirici araçlarını açan herkes ağ sekmesinde tam numarayı görür. Mobil uygulamada da aynı şey geçerlidir: yanıt gövdesi cihazda önbelleğe alınır.

Doğru yer, verinin sunucudan çıktığı son katmandır: serileştirme (serializer) ya da yanıt dönüştürücü. Böylece hangi uç noktadan gelirse gelsin aynı kural uygulanır. Kuralı her endpoint'e tek tek yazmak yerine tek bir fonksiyona bağlamak, yeni bir endpoint eklendiğinde maskelemenin unutulmasını engeller.

# Tek giriş noktası: her yanıt bu fonksiyondan geçer
def serialize_lead(lead: dict, viewer: Viewer, context: str) -> dict:
    out = {}
    for field, value in lead.items():
        rule = FIELD_RULES.get(field)
        if rule is None:
            out[field] = value          # kişisel veri olmayan alan
            continue
        level = resolve_level(rule, viewer, context, lead)
        out[field] = apply_mask(value, rule.kind, level)
    return out

Burada context parametresi önemlidir: aynı kullanıcı liste ekranında, kayıt detayında, dışa aktarmada ve raporda farklı görünürlük seviyesine sahip olabilir.

Kural 2: Kuralları kodda değil veride tut

Hangi alanın kimde nasıl görüneceği zamanla değişir. Yeni bir rol eklenir, bir alan kişisel veri olarak işaretlenir, hukuk ekibi e-postanın da maskelenmesini ister. Bunu her seferinde kod değişikliğiyle yapmak hem yavaştır hem de denetlenmesi zordur. Kuralları bir tabloda tutmak, kimin neyi ne zaman değiştirdiğini de kayıt altına almayı kolaylaştırır.

CREATE TABLE field_mask_rule (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  entity       text NOT NULL,          -- 'lead', 'contact', 'deal'
  field        text NOT NULL,          -- 'phone', 'email', 'national_id'
  mask_kind    text NOT NULL,          -- 'phone', 'email', 'full', 'none'
  role         text NOT NULL,          -- 'agent', 'analyst', 'manager', 'partner'
  context      text NOT NULL,          -- 'list', 'detail', 'export', 'report', 'log'
  level        text NOT NULL CHECK (level IN ('hidden','masked','revealable','clear')),
  updated_by   bigint NOT NULL,
  updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (entity, field, role, context)
);

Dört seviye pratikte yeterli oluyor:

  • hidden: Alan yanıtta hiç yer almaz.
  • masked: Alan maskeli gelir, açılamaz.
  • revealable: Alan maskeli gelir, kullanıcı gerekçeyle açabilir; açma kaydedilir.
  • clear: Alan tam gelir.

Varsayılan değer her zaman en kısıtlayıcı olandır. Tabloda kuralı olmayan ama kişisel veri olarak işaretlenmiş bir alan hidden sayılmalıdır. Böylece yeni eklenen bir alan için kural yazmayı unutmak veri sızıntısına değil, eksik görünüme yol açar. Eksik görünüm şikayet getirir ve düzeltilir; sızıntı ise çoğu zaman fark edilmez.

Maskeleme biçimleri: ne kadarını göstermeli?

Maskelemenin amacı veriyi tamamen yok etmek değil, işi yapmaya yetecek kadarını bırakmaktır. Temsilci "bu, dün aradığım numara mı?" diye ayırt edebilmeli; analist aynı kişinin iki kez form doldurup doldurmadığını anlayabilmelidir.

import re

def mask_phone(v: str) -> str:
    digits = re.sub(r"\D", "", v or "")
    if len(digits) < 7:
        return "***"
    return f"{digits[:4]}***{digits[-4:]}" if len(digits) >= 10 else f"***{digits[-3:]}"

def mask_email(v: str) -> str:
    if not v or "@" not in v:
        return "***"
    local, domain = v.split("@", 1)
    head = local[:1]
    return f"{head}***@{domain}"

def apply_mask(value, kind, level):
    if level == "clear":
        return value
    if level == "hidden":
        return None
    if kind == "phone":
        return mask_phone(value)
    if kind == "email":
        return mask_email(value)
    return "***"

Birkaç pratik not:

  • Telefonda ülke kodu ve operatör önekini bırakmak çoğu zaman yeterli bağlam verir; son dört hane ayırt etmeyi sağlar. Kısa numaralarda daha az hane gösterin, aksi halde maskeleme anlamsızlaşır.
  • E-postada alan adını açık bırakmak, kurumsal lead'leri ayırt etmeye yarar. Ama küçük bir şirketin alan adı tek başına kişiyi belli edebilir; hassas projelerde alan adını da maskeleyin.
  • Kimlik numarası, pasaport numarası gibi alanlar için kısmi gösterim yerine full maskeyi ve revealable seviyesini tercih edin.

"Numarayı göster" düğmesi: açma kaydı ve gerekçe

revealable seviyesindeki bir alanın açılması, ayrı bir uç noktaya yapılan bilinçli bir istektir. Liste yanıtı hiçbir zaman tam değeri taşımaz; kullanıcı düğmeye bastığında tek bir kaydın tek bir alanı için istek gider, sunucu yetkiyi yeniden kontrol eder, açma olayını kaydeder ve değeri döner.

CREATE TABLE pii_reveal_log (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  viewer_id   bigint NOT NULL,
  entity      text NOT NULL,
  entity_id   bigint NOT NULL,
  field       text NOT NULL,
  reason      text NOT NULL,      -- 'call', 'whatsapp', 'appointment', 'other'
  note        text,
  ip          inet,
  revealed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX ON pii_reveal_log (viewer_id, revealed_at DESC);

Gerekçe alanı ilk başta bürokrasi gibi görünür, ama iki işe yarar. Birincisi, kullanıcıyı bir an durdurur; "neden bu numaraya ihtiyacım var?" sorusunu sordurur. İkincisi, denetimde anlamlı bir iz bırakır. Arama gerekçesiyle açılan bir numaranın ardından gerçekten bir arama kaydı (call log) oluşmuş mu, bunu karşılaştırmak mümkün hale gelir.

Daha da iyisi, birçok durumda numarayı hiç açmadan işi yaptırmaktır. Temsilci "Ara" düğmesine bastığında santral ya da tıkla-ara entegrasyonu numarayı sunucu tarafında çevirir; temsilci numarayı hiç görmez. WhatsApp mesajı da aynı şekilde şablon üzerinden sunucudan gönderilebilir. Benim kurduğum lead yönetimi akışlarında hedef, temsilcinin günlük işinin büyük kısmını tam numarayı görmeden tamamlayabilmesidir. Açma düğmesi istisna için kalmalıdır.

Anormal açma davranışını yakalamak

Açma kaydı tutulduktan sonra basit kurallarla ciddi riskleri yakalamak mümkündür:

-- Son bir saatte olağan dışı sayıda açma yapan kullanıcılar
SELECT viewer_id, count(*) AS reveals
FROM pii_reveal_log
WHERE revealed_at > now() - interval '1 hour'
GROUP BY viewer_id
HAVING count(*) > 40;

Eşik değer ekibin gerçek iş yüküne göre belirlenmelidir; buradaki 40 yalnızca örnek bir değerdir. Eşiği aşan kullanıcı için açma uç noktası geçici olarak yavaşlatılabilir, yöneticiye bildirim gidebilir. İşten ayrılmadan önceki günlerde toplu numara açma, bu tablonun en sık ortaya çıkardığı örüntülerden biridir.

Dışa aktarma: en büyük sızıntı kapısı

Ekranda maskeleme ne kadar iyi olursa olsun, "Excel'e aktar" düğmesi tüm emeği boşa çıkarabilir. Dışa aktarma ayrı bir context olarak ele alınmalı ve kuralları ayrıca tanımlanmalıdır. Benim önerim:

  • Dışa aktarmada revealable seviyesi yoktur; ya masked ya clear. Toplu açma, tek tek açmanın kaydını anlamsız kılar.
  • clear dışa aktarma yalnız belirli rollere açıktır ve her dışa aktarma işi kimin, hangi filtreyle, kaç satır aldığıyla birlikte kaydedilir.
  • Dosya kalıcı bir bağlantıyla değil, kısa süreli imzalı bir bağlantıyla indirilir.
  • Analiz amaçlı dışa aktarmalarda telefon ve e-posta yerine sabit bir takma kimlik (pseudonym) verilir. Analist aynı kişiyi tekrar eden satırlarda tanıyabilir ama kim olduğunu bilmez. 
import hmac, hashlib

def pseudonym(value: str, secret: bytes, scope: str) -> str:
    norm = re.sub(r"\D", "", value) if scope == "phone" else value.strip().lower()
    mac = hmac.new(secret, f"{scope}:{norm}".encode(), hashlib.sha256)
    return mac.hexdigest()[:16]

Sırrı (secret) dışa aktarma işine özel ya da döneme özel tutmak, iki farklı dosyanın birleştirilerek kişilerin eşleştirilmesini zorlaştırır.

Loglar ve hata izleme araçları

Uygulama logları, hata izleme servisleri ve kuyruk mesajları kişisel verinin en sessiz biriktiği yerlerdir. Bir hata yığını (stack trace) tüm istek gövdesini içerebilir; bir webhook hatası gelen lead'in telefonunu loglara yazabilir. Burada context = 'log' için kural genellikle masked ya da hidden olmalıdır ve log kütüphanesine bir filtre eklenmelidir:

import logging

SENSITIVE_KEYS = {"phone", "email", "national_id", "passport_no"}

class PiiFilter(logging.Filter):
    def filter(self, record):
        if isinstance(record.args, dict):
            record.args = {k: ("***" if k in SENSITIVE_KEYS else v)
                           for k, v in record.args.items()}
        return True

Anahtar adına göre filtrelemek tek başına yetmez; serbest metin içinde geçen telefon ve e-posta kalıplarını düzenli ifadeyle temizleyen ikinci bir katman da eklemek gerekir. Hata izleme servislerinin çoğu gönderim öncesi veri temizleme kancası sunar; bu kancayı aynı kural kümesine bağlamak tutarlılığı korur.

Test ve geliştirme ortamı: gerçek veri olmadan gerçekçi veri

Üretim veritabanının bir kopyasını test ortamına almak hızlıdır ama riskli. Test ortamları genellikle daha zayıf korunur, daha çok kişi erişir ve üçüncü taraf araçlara bağlanır. Burada ekranda maskeleme yeterli değildir; verinin kendisi dönüştürülmelidir. Buna statik maskeleme ya da tokenizasyon denir.

İyi bir test verisi dönüşümünün üç özelliği olmalı:

  1. Tutarlılık: Aynı gerçek telefon her tabloda aynı sahte telefona dönüşmeli; böylece tekilleştirme ve eşleştirme mantığı testte de çalışır.
  2. Biçim koruma: Sahte telefon geçerli bir telefon biçiminde olmalı, sahte e-posta geçerli bir e-posta olmalı; doğrulama kuralları kırılmamalı.
  3. Geri döndürülemezlik: Test ortamına erişen biri sahte değerden gerçeğine ulaşamamalı. 
def fake_phone(real: str, secret: bytes) -> str:
    h = int(pseudonym(real, secret, "phone"), 16)
    return "0599" + str(h % 10_000_000).zfill(7)   # kullanılmayan bir önek seçin

def fake_email(real: str, secret: bytes) -> str:
    return f"user{pseudonym(real, secret, 'email')[:10]}@example.test"

Sahte numaralar için gerçek bir operatöre ait olmayan bir önek seçmek, testten yanlışlıkla gerçek bir kişiye SMS ya da arama gitmesini engeller. Aynı şekilde sahte e-postalar için example.test gibi teslim edilemeyen bir alan adı kullanılmalıdır. Dönüşüm sırrı test ortamında hiç bulunmamalıdır.

KVKK ve GDPR açısından nereye oturur?

Maskeleme, kişisel verinin işlenme amacıyla sınırlı ve ölçülü tutulması ilkesinin teknik karşılıklarından biridir. KVKK ve GDPR, kişisel verilere erişimin işin gerektirdiği ölçüyle sınırlanmasını ve uygun teknik tedbirlerin alınmasını bekler. Maskeleme tek başına uyumluluk sağlamaz; açık rıza, aydınlatma metni, saklama süresi ve silme süreçleri ayrıca kurulmalıdır. Ama bir veri sızıntısı soruşturmasında "liste ekranında numaralar maskeliydi, açmalar gerekçeyle kaydediliyordu, dışa aktarma rol bazlıydı" diyebilmek, alınan tedbirin somut kanıtıdır. Hukuki yorum için her zaman bir uzmana danışılmalıdır; burada anlattıklarım mühendislik pratiğidir.

Uygulamaya alırken kontrol listesi

  • Kişisel veri alanlarını bir kayıt defterinde işaretleyin; işaretli ama kuralı olmayan alan varsayılan olarak gizli olsun.
  • Maskelemeyi tek bir serileştirme katmanına bağlayın; arayüze tam veri göndermeyin.
  • Liste, detay, dışa aktarma, rapor ve log için ayrı bağlam kuralları tanımlayın.
  • Açma işlemini ayrı uç noktaya taşıyın; gerekçe ve kayıt zorunlu olsun.
  • Tıkla-ara ve şablon mesaj ile numarayı göstermeden iletişim kurulmasını sağlayın.
  • Açma kayıtlarında anormal hacmi izleyin.
  • Test ortamına yalnız dönüştürülmüş veri aktarın.
  • Kuralları her çeyrek rol değişiklikleriyle birlikte gözden geçirin.

SSS

Veri maskeleme ile anonimleştirme arasındaki fark nedir?
Maskeleme, yetkili bir kullanıcı için veriyi kısmen gizler; gerçek değer sistemde durur ve gerektiğinde açılabilir. Anonimleştirmede ise veri kişiyle bir daha ilişkilendirilemeyecek şekilde dönüştürülür. Test ortamı için yapılan geri döndürülemez dönüşüm anonimleştirmeye yakındır; ekran maskelemesi değildir.

Maskelemeyi veritabanı düzeyinde yapmak daha güvenli değil mi?
Bazı veritabanları dinamik maskeleme özelliği sunar ve ek bir savunma hattı olarak işe yarar. Ama bağlam (liste mi, dışa aktarma mı, log mu) bilgisi genellikle uygulama katmanındadır. Pratikte en sağlam yapı, uygulama katmanında bağlam duyarlı maskeleme ve veritabanında rol bazlı erişim kısıtlamasının birlikte kullanılmasıdır.

Temsilci numarayı görmeden nasıl arama yapar?
Tıkla-ara entegrasyonu ile CRM, numarayı sunucu tarafında santrale iletir; temsilcinin telefonu çalar ve görüşme bağlanır. Temsilci ekranda yalnız maskeli numarayı görür. WhatsApp ve SMS için de şablonlu gönderim aynı mantıkla çalışır.

Maskeli telefonla tekrar eden lead'ler nasıl tespit edilir?
Tekilleştirme mantığı sunucuda tam değer üzerinde çalışır; kullanıcıya yalnız sonuç gösterilir. Analiz tarafında ise sabit takma kimlik kullanılır; aynı kişi farklı satırlarda aynı kimlikle görünür.

Yönetici rolü her şeyi açık görmeli mi?
Hayır. Yönetici rolü genellikle rapor ve performans ekranlarında çalışır; orada tam numaraya ihtiyaç yoktur. Yöneticinin de revealable seviyesinde olması ve açmalarının kaydedilmesi, hem kötüye kullanımı önler hem de ekibe doğru örnek olur.

Küçük bir ekip için bu yapı fazla değil mi?
Dört kişilik bir ekipte bile liste ekranında maskeleme ve dışa aktarmanın kısıtlanması birkaç saatlik iştir ve en büyük riski kapatır. Açma kaydı, anormallik izleme ve test verisi dönüşümü ekip büyüdükçe eklenebilir. Önemli olan, varsayılanın en baştan kısıtlayıcı olmasıdır.

Koray Yalçın — lead yönetimi, CRM mimarisi, dijital pazarlama ve PropTech üzerine çalışıyor.

title: Your SMTP connection pool is probably leaking
description:
A worker opens a connection, sends, and forgets to close it. Nothing breaks for a week, then the provider starts refusing new connections and every send fails at once.

Connections are the scarce resource

Providers cap concurrent connections per account and per IP, often at a low number. A pool that grows because closed connections are not returned will hit that cap, and the failure mode is total rather than gradual: once the cap is reached, every new send blocks.

Where the leak comes from

An exception between MAIL FROM and QUIT skips the close. A timeout on DATA leaves the socket open until the OS reaps it. A retry path that creates a fresh connection without releasing the failed one doubles the count. None of these show up in a happy-path test.

The fix

Wrap the whole conversation in a context manager that guarantees QUIT, and on any exception close the socket rather than returning it to the pool — a connection in an unknown protocol state is worse than no connection. Then export the pool size as a metric and alert when it approaches the provider's cap.

One detail worth copying

Reuse connections for multiple messages to the same domain, but reset state with RSET between recipients. Reconnecting for every message is slow and looks like abuse to the receiver; not resetting leaks the previous envelope into the next send.

Volanea manages the SMTP session per domain and exposes connection and deferral counters next to the send log.

title: Building a Matter Gateway in Rust: Bridging Devices to Apple Home
description:
In the previous post, we paired a prototype gateway with Apple Home using a computer and a phone. This time, let's look at the Rust code behind the Matter side. The project uses rs-matter. Real Bluetooth Mesh interoperability, the Linux board and large deployments remain untested.

A gateway is not one big light

The gateway appears as a Matter node. Endpoint 0 provides its root functions, endpoint 1 is the aggregator, and each bridged light gets its own endpoint. The device types and clusters tell the controller what each device is and can do: Descriptor, On/Off, Bridged Device Basic Information and Groups are included in this prototype.

Mapping endpoints to devices

A small device table holds the endpoint ID, device address, name, on/off state and reachability. When Apple Home asks to turn on endpoint 2, the gateway finds the matching device address and sends a command downstream. Real products need additional provisioning, security and recovery data.

Commands and state reports

The prototype updates its local state optimistically when a command arrives, sends the command, and uses a subsequent status report to correct the state. If the device never responds, the display may temporarily be wrong. Timeouts, retries, polling and offline detection still need work.

The reverse path matters too: a physical switch can change the light. The gateway matches the incoming device address, updates the endpoint state and notifies Matter subscribers. In the phone demonstration, repeated identical broadcasts are deduplicated to avoid restoring stale state. Those plaintext broadcasts are only a demo, not a real Mesh test.

Adding devices and surviving restarts

Devices can be added or removed while the prototype runs. It assigns increasing endpoint IDs instead of immediately reusing a deleted ID, reducing the risk of confusing controller state. Long-term allocation and recovery still need design and testing.

The device mapping is saved locally, while rs-matter has its own persistent store. The mapping is written to a temporary file before replacement; this reduces the chance of corrupting the old file but is not a complete power-failure guarantee. Actual device state must be confirmed again, and real Mesh keys need a secure backup and recovery plan.

What has been tested?

The demonstration verified pairing with Apple Home, displaying and controlling simulated bridged devices, simulated status reports, and basic addition, removal and restart behavior. It has not verified the real Mesh network, operation on the target Linux board, failure recovery or hundreds of devices. Test credentials are not production certification.

The Rust release profile enables size optimization, LTO and symbol stripping. One previous desktop build was about 2.3 MB; other targets and configurations need their own measurements. Next we will replace the simulation with real hardware and test the control and reporting paths.

title: React Fiber Explained: How React’s Engine Actually Works
description:
React Fiber is the internal engine that powers React’s rendering and reconciliation.

It’s what makes React’s updates smooth, interruptible, and concurrent.

🧩 What is React Fiber?

React Fiber is React’s reconciliation engine — the system that decides what needs to be rendered and when.

Before React 16, React updates were synchronous and blocking. Once rendering started, React couldn’t pause or reprioritize work — large trees could freeze the UI.

Fiber was a complete rewrite that made React’s rendering:

  • ⏸ Interruptible
  • ⏱ Prioritized
  • 🔁 Incremental (chunked)
  • 💾 Recoverable (resumable)

In short: Fiber = React’s virtual call stack for async rendering.

🕰️ The Old Model (Before Fiber)

Before Fiber, React used a recursive rendering approach — like this:

function renderTree(node) {
  node.render();
  node.children.forEach(renderTree);
}
  • Large trees blocked the main thread.
  • The browser couldn’t respond to user input until React finished.
  • No way to pause, abort, or prioritize rendering.

⚡ Fiber: The New Architecture

React Fiber breaks the rendering work into small units of work, called fiber nodes.

This lets React:

  • Pause between chunks of work.
  • Resume later if the browser is busy.
  • Assign different priorities to updates.
  • Reuse previous work if nothing changed.

So React no longer blocks the main thread — it cooperatively yields to the browser.

🧱 The Fiber Node Structure

Each React component is represented by a Fiber node — a JavaScript object with pointers and metadata.

Field Description
type The component or DOM type
key Used for list diffing
child, sibling, return Pointers to other fiber nodes (linked list tree)
pendingProps, memoizedProps, memoizedState Stores component state & props
flags Marks what changed (update, placement, deletion)
alternate Link to the previous fiber (for diffing old vs new trees)

📘 Think of it as two trees:

  • Current tree → what’s on screen.
  • Work-in-progress tree → what React is preparing.

When ready, React commits the new tree and swaps references.

🔁 The Two Phases of Rendering

1️⃣ Render Phase (Reconciliation)

  • React builds a new Fiber tree (work-in-progress).
  • Diffs elements vs previous render.
  • Calculates what to change.
  • Can be paused, aborted, or restarted.

2️⃣ Commit Phase

  • React applies all DOM mutations.
  • Runs effects (useEffect, componentDidMount, etc.).
  • This phase is synchronous — React cannot pause it.

🧠 Render phase = “thinking”

⚡ Commit phase = “doing”

🧠 Scheduling and Priority

Fiber works with React’s scheduler, which assigns priority to updates:

Priority Example
Immediate User input (typing, clicking)
High Animations
Normal State updates
Low Background tasks
Idle Prefetch, pre-render

React checks between chunks:

“Browser, do you have time? If not, I’ll yield and resume later.”

This is what enables Concurrent Rendering.

⚙️ Concurrent React (Fiber + Scheduler)

With Concurrent Mode (React 18+), Fiber can prepare multiple UI versions in parallel.

React can:

  • Prepare new UI while showing the old one.
  • Cancel or pause updates mid-render.
  • Prioritize urgent updates (like typing).

Example:

const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

function handleInput(e) {
  const value = e.target.value;
  startTransition(() => setFilter(value)); // low priority render
}

React keeps input responsive because it renders background updates at a lower priority.

🧬 Visualization 

      [Root Fiber]
          │
    ┌─────┴─────┐
 [App]        [Modal]
   │              │
 [Header]       [Button]

Each node is a Fiber linked by child, sibling, and return.

React walks this structure instead of the JS call stack — so it can pause or resume at any point.

💡 Key Benefits of Fiber

✅ Interruptible, non-blocking rendering

✅ Priority scheduling for updates

✅ Recoverable rendering (pause/resume)

✅ Enables Suspense, useTransition, and concurrent features

✅ Better error isolation and performance profiling

🧠 Why It Matters (Even if You Don’t Use It Directly)

You don’t write Fiber code yourself, but understanding it helps you reason about:

  • Why React sometimes delays updates.
  • Why “render” can happen multiple times before commit.
  • How useTransition and Suspense work.
  • Why strict mode double-invokes renders (simulates concurrency).

✅ Summary

Concept Description
Fiber React’s internal unit of work for rendering
Fiber Node Represents one component or element
Render Phase Diff & prepare work (async, interruptible)
Commit Phase Apply updates (sync)
Scheduler Manages priorities of updates
Concurrent Rendering Lets React multitask smoothly

✨ React Fiber turned React from a recursive renderer into an asynchronous virtual machine for UI.

It’s the reason React 18 feels fast, smooth, and intelligent.

title: Set per-user budgets on AI Gateway
description:
You can now use AI Gateway budgets to set a dollar spending limit for each user on your team.

The limit covers spend from every API key attributed to the user, along with their app tokens. After it's reached, AI Gateway rejects new requests until the budget resets or is increased.

This is useful for controlling spend from coding agents and other workloads that run without supervision, and prevents one user from consuming all of the team's shared budget.

Set user budgets

Open the Users view on the Budgets page to set two kinds of user budgets:

  • Default budget: If set, applies separately to every person without a custom budget, including users added later. Each user gets their own allowance rather than sharing one limit across the team.

  • Custom budget: Applies to one person and overrides the default. Removing it returns that user to the default budget.

Both default and custom budgets reset monthly by default, but you can change them to reset daily, weekly, or not at all. Budgets also support usage alerting via email to notify when you are at 50%, 75%, and/or 100% of your allocation.

User budgets don't replace API key, project, or team budgets. A request must remain within every budget that applies to it. Reaching any applicable limit blocks new requests.

API keys are attributed to the user who created them by default. If a key belongs to a production application or another shared workload, attribute it to the team from the API Keys page to keep its spend out of the key creator's budget. Keys created prior to the user budget feature release were attributed to the team for backwards-compatibility, so rotate to new keys if you wish to have current usage fall under the user scope.

Set budgets from the CLI

Upgrade to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade. You need Vercel CLI 59.6.2 or newer for user budgets, then set a default or custom user budget:

Identify a member by their email address, username, or user ID.

Team owners can manage user budgets, and can also grant other members AI Gateway Budget Manager permissions from team member settings. Spend using Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) credentials doesn't count toward user budgets.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade to get started, and learn more in the AI Gateway budgets documentation.

title: 接手一个陌生项目，先别从第一行读起：/onboard 的 5 条硬规则
description:
（整理自完整版 commands/onboard.md 实测文本与 /onboard 公开 Gist，非本次新实测；/onboard 不在 Lite 免费版、只在完整版。）

刚 clone 一个仓库，README 只有两行；接手别人的项目，不知道先看哪个文件——最容易踩的坑是从第一行开始硬读，读了半天还不知道这个项目是干什么的。/onboard 只做一件事：当导游，不当卫星地图——讲路线，不讲每块砖，10 分钟讲清它是干什么的、代码怎么组织、从哪开始改。

调用方式：/onboard <项目路径，可附你的角色：开发/运维/只想用>。

5 条：

  1. 先给一句话定位，再画地图。先看 README、package.json/pyproject 等，回答“这个项目是干什么的、给谁用的”，一句话说清。然后列出核心目录/模块，每个一句话说明职责，并标出入口文件（main/cli/app 入口在哪）。没有入口标注的地图，等于没画。
  2. 关键路径 5 步以内讲清。挑一条最核心的调用链（如“请求进来→处理→返回”），用 5 步以内讲清数据怎么流的。示例（实测文本里的小模块）：load_orders → batch_settle → summarize。超过 5 步还没讲清，说明挑错了链——换一条更核心的。
  3. 上手三步必须是可复制的命令。“跑起来”的最小步骤：安装→配置→跑一个例子，每步是可复制的命令，不是“大概装一下”“配置一下”这种描述。示例：python -c "from orders import ..."——能直接粘贴跑通，才算一步。
  4. 第一刀砍在哪，要精确到文件和函数。回答“如果我要加一个小功能，第一刀砍在哪”：指出最可能要改的 1–2 个文件和函数，并说明为什么是这里。示例：batch_settle 的 level 取值处（已知健壮性问题）。只说“改核心模块”等于没说。
  5. 没看懂就标 [没看懂]，不编。没看懂的部分明确标 [没看懂]，不编造业务逻辑。超过 200 个文件的项目，先说“这是局部导游，建议按模块再问”。

输出长什么样（取自 onboard.md 的格式）：一句话、地图（每个目录一句话职责＋入口标注）、关键路径（1. xxx → 2. xxx → …）、上手三步（可复制的命令）、第一刀砍在哪（文件＋函数＋原因）、没看懂的（[没看懂] 项）。

什么时候不要用：项目就一个文件——自己读，比导游快；想让它讲“每一行代码”——导游讲路线，不讲每块砖；仓库有 10 万行——先指定一个子目录；完全没文档也没注释的祖传代码——先接受“导游只能带你看结构”，读不懂的业务逻辑得问人。

免费先试：Lite 免费版含 /review、/commit、/test 三条命令，双兼容 Claude Code 与 Codex CLI，见 Lite 仓。
完整版含 /onboard 在内的 10 条命令，早鸟 ¥9.90（限前 100 份）／正式 ¥19.90，付款后 12 小时内私信交付，7 天无理由退款。国内账号风控提示：优先用 Codex。

title: Shopify script tags deprecation: what breaks on March 1, 2027
description:
On March 1, 2027, Shopify stops injecting script tags into storefronts. Since October 1, 2026, apps can no longer create or update them. Anything an old app added to your store through that mechanism, such as a review widget, a popup, a sticky bar or an upsell, will vanish without an error message.

This article is for store owners and e-commerce leads, not app developers. It explains why the quiet failure is the real risk, how to find out in an afternoon which parts of your storefront depend on script tags, and what to do before the deadline.

A deadline that comes with no warning banner

The dates are simple. According to Shopify's developer documentation, from October 1, 2026 the create and update calls for script tags return a permission error on every API version. Existing tags keep running. On March 1, 2027 Shopify stops loading them, and "any dependent features stop for that store."

Here is what makes this different from a normal deprecation. Shopify planned a warning banner for app users and then dropped it. In a September post on the Shopify developer community, a Shopify staff member said the install warning would not ship on October 1, that an earlier email had been overstated, and that the dates had not changed. Shopify said it would watch script tag usage through the fourth quarter and revisit the question in January.

Read that as a merchant. The platform will not tell you which of your apps still depend on the old mechanism. The developers who wrote those apps are complaining in public that they cannot reach their own customers. One developer in the thread said 70 to 75 percent of their users still rely on script tags. I can't verify that number, but even if it is half right, a lot of stores will hit March with live features that quietly stop.

Your analytics will not flag it either. A missing review widget is not a 500 error. It is a page that looks slightly emptier, and the conversion rate drifts down over a few weeks.

Which storefront features usually depend on script tags

Script tags were the easy way for an app to put JavaScript on every page of a store without touching the theme. That makes them common in the parts of a storefront that sit on top of the design rather than inside it. Think review stars on product cards, exit-intent popups, free-shipping progress bars, countdown timers, currency or language switchers, cookie banners, size guides, chat bubbles and cross-sell drawers.

These are also the features that carry conversion weight. Reviews are the clearest case. Northwestern's Spiegel Research Center report found that a product with five reviews is 270 percent more likely to be purchased than one with none. Treat that number carefully. It comes largely from one retailer's data and is higher for expensive products. The same report says nearly all of the lift arrives within the first 10 reviews. So the loss from a vanished review widget depends on how many reviews you have, how pricey the product is, and whether shoppers can still find the reviews anywhere else on the page.

Few stores will lose anything like 270 percent. The risk is that these features are ones a design review never checks, because they live in the browser, injected after load, not in the theme code.

A related shutdown has already happened at checkout. A vendor write-up from Aimerce reports that Additional Scripts on the Thank You and Order Status pages stopped for non-Plus stores after August 26, 2026, and that conversion pixels for Meta, Google or TikTok stop firing with no error in the admin. It is a vendor blog selling its own fix, so weigh its advice accordingly. Its audit trick is still good. Compare conversions reported in each ad platform against orders in Shopify, and a growing gap means lost tracking.

The replacement is not automatic

Shopify's documented replacement is an app embed block, shipped inside a theme app extension. For tracking only, the replacement is a web pixel. The two behave very differently for you.

A web pixel needs no action from the merchant. You approve permissions when you install or update the app, and it runs. An app embed block is the opposite. In Shopify's words, "app embed blocks are inactive until an app user turns them on." The developer is supposed to send you to the theme editor with the embed switched on, and confirm it is active on the published theme before deleting the old script tag. Otherwise, as the docs put it, "you leave a gap where neither works."

That creates three failure modes you can plan for.

First, the app updated, but nobody told you to flip the toggle. The developer thread says there is currently no programmatic way to enable an embed for existing merchants, so some developers are relying on emails that merchants don't read. Second, embeds are per theme. If you duplicate your theme for a holiday redesign and publish the copy, the embed has to be turned on again. Third, both versions can run at once. Shopify warns that doing so loads the script twice, which can double-count analytics or show a popup twice.

Stores on legacy themes have a further problem. App blocks need JSON templates, though Shopify says embed blocks work on vintage and Online Store 2.0 themes. Developers in the thread asked what happens to merchants who cannot move, and the thread shows no Shopify commitment to an exception. If your theme is more than a few years old and heavily edited, this is the most likely place for surprises.

A one-afternoon audit before the deadline

You do not need a developer to find out how exposed you are. You need a list of apps, a browser and a few hours.

Start in Shopify admin and list every installed app. For each one, write down what it shows shoppers and where. If an app has no visible storefront element, such as a pure back-office tool, cross it out. What remains is your risk list.

Next, open your live store in a private window with the browser's developer tools on the Network tab, and load the home page, a collection page, a product page and the cart. Filter requests to JavaScript. Files served from cdn.shopify.com with an app's name in the path, or from the app vendor's own domain, tell you which apps inject code. Write down the app, the page and the visible feature it controls. This gives you a map from feature to app, which is the document most stores don't have.

Then contact each vendor on the risk list with one precise question. Ask whether the app still uses script tags on your store, and if so, what you need to do and by when. Ask them to confirm in writing that the app has moved to an app embed block or a web pixel. If the answer is vague, treat it as a no.

Finally, work out your fallback. For any feature that drives revenue, such as reviews, upsells or shipping thresholds, decide now what you will do if it disappears in March. That might be a different app that already uses theme extensions, or a native theme section. Shopify also describes a route for admin-created custom apps. Move the script into the theme itself, ideally as a custom Liquid block. The catch is that the script stays after the app is removed, and Shopify notes that editing theme code takes the theme out of automatic upgrades.

What I would do this month

Treat the deadline as a release date for your own store. Work backward from March 1 and leave a buffer, because app vendors will be answering the same question from thousands of merchants at the same time in February.

In November, build the feature-to-app map and email vendors. In December, avoid redesigns and new theme publishes if you can, since each one resets the embed activation question. In January, check the Shopify developer changelog, because Shopify has said it will revisit the situation then and may announce targeted notices. Between mid-January and mid-February, have each vendor activate its embed on a staging copy of the theme, then do the same on the published theme, with a before-and-after screenshot of every template that carries an app feature.

After each change, compare the page with your screenshots. Watch for a doubled popup, a missing badge, a layout shift where a widget used to load, and a conversion pixel that fires twice. Compare ad platform conversions against Shopify orders for a week afterward.

One habit for later. At every app demo, ask whether it runs through a theme app extension and web pixel, or still injects a script tag.
