title: 1,740 board runs, one human, a crew of AI agents: making Python up to 2,000 faster for Speed Demon 2026
description:
My write-up for Speed Demon 2026 by Hackathon Raptors. The code is public: github.com/SaudSatopay/speed-demon-2026. Every number below comes from the board's run log or a track's PERF.md, where you can check it.

Speed Demon hands you four slow, correct Python programs and one rule: make them fast without changing a single byte of output. You never submit a timing. The organisers build your Docker image and run it on their own machine, an i5-13500 with turbo off, 12 threads and 8 GB, and they hash every output. One wrong byte and the track scores zero. It's a very fair system, in the way a guillotine is fair.

I entered solo, in Rust with only the standard library, and I'll be upfront: I wrote very little of the code myself. AI agents did most of the typing, mainly Claude Code, with Codex for a stretch. My job was to write the rules they worked under, decide what to keep, read the board at unreasonable hours, and stop the whole operation from quietly setting itself on fire. So this post is about two things: what made the code fast, and what I learned running a crew of AI agents against a stopwatch for 72 hours.

The short version: our final builds ran about 500× to 2,050× faster than the references, every output byte-identical. On the live final run, on a dataset nobody had seen, we came 3rd on the machine score with 84.68, a whole 0.11 points behind 2nd. I've made my peace with that 0.11. Mostly. The judges' 35% isn't in yet.

The scoring, in one paragraph

Each track gets an efficiency number:

K = (T_ref/T)^0.50 × min(M_ref/M, 50)^0.20 × min(S_ref/S, 1)^0.15 × (D_ref/D)^0.15
speed points = 50 × log10(K)

T is wall time, M is peak memory, S is lines of code after a formatter, D is dependencies. Time is half the weight and has no cap, so every 2× speedup is worth the same 7.5 points, whether you go from 10× to 20× or from 1,000× to 2,000×. Memory stops paying at 50× better than the reference. Lines and dependencies can only cost you, which is the formula's way of saying "we know about npm". That shaped the whole plan: get all four tracks correct on the board first, then always take the cheapest 2× on offer, on whichever track it is.

The overall title is the geometric mean of your best three tracks, and the judges score 35% of each track on code quality, technique and the optimisation log.

The four tracks

Track What it does Reference on the box Our best board run Speedup
A · Ingest Hourly latency percentiles from a 72-hour access log 32.05 s, 228 MB 0.0156 s, 16.1 MB ~2,050×
B · Index 50,000 boolean and phrase queries over a 254 MB corpus 56.35 s, 2,200 MB 0.0643 s, 29.2 MB ~880×
C · Join A deliberately hostile CSV joined to a region table 14.44 s, 367 MB 0.0189 s, 10.0 MB ~760×
D · Traverse Shortest paths on a 5-million-edge road graph 72.69 s, 893 MB 0.1444 s, 42.2 MB ~500×

"Deliberately hostile" is the spec's own spirit, not my editorialising: quoted fields, doubled quotes, commas and line feeds inside quotes, byte-order marks. Someone enjoyed writing that generator.

Before the first line of code

The rules disqualify any solution code committed before kickoff, so the two days before it went into everything else. Three things paid off.

Reading the referee's code

I read all four specs and the scoring harness source, which is not how most people spend a Wednesday. Two places disagreed with the website: which dataset the board used for Track B (the spec said the 10% sample; the board's code ran the full set), and the final-scoring timeout (3× in the script, 10× on the site). I asked on Discord, and the organisers fixed both in the repo the same day. If a contest publishes its harness, read it like a contract. It's the only document that can't be wrong about what the harness does.

A local scorer that measures like their box

I rebuilt the measurement from the organisers' own harness: their timer, their runner, their line counter, and Docker's cgroup memory peak. The source-size baselines matched the published ones exactly (56, 91, 108 and 43 lines), and Track C's memory came within 0.4% of the box.

One finding mattered more than the rest. The box's kernel sets transparent huge pages to always, while my WSL2 kernel uses madvise. On the box, touching one byte of a sparse table can be billed as a whole 2 MB page. My scorer switches the setting while it measures, because finding that out from the live board would have cost a day.

Then, on day two, the untouched reference got 16% slower. I ruled out the harness update, the CPU clocks, the power plan, Windows updates and the RAM. The culprit was the Realtek audio driver, burning a full CPU thread all day with nothing playing. WSL2's virtual CPUs are ordinary Windows threads, so the driver's hobby landed on my cores. After a reboot, the reference ran 8.084 s against an 8.083 s baseline. A local benchmark is only as good as the machine's quietest moment, and apparently my machine's quietest moment requires turning it off and on again.

191 answer sets

A wrong answer on the hidden final seed zeroes a track, so correctness came before speed. Before kickoff there were:

  • 15 generator seeds, with the expected outputs computed by the official reference.
  • 32 answer-preserving rewrites of those datasets: line endings flipped (one variant has exactly two CRs in a 20 MB file), a BOM before every record or none at all, empty fields swapped between quoted and unquoted, lines and edges shuffled or reversed.
  • 19 synthetic limit files, checked against each spec's grammar: an empty log, every endpoint length from 1 to 125 bytes, sums past 2^32, every kind of unreachable query.

A thread sweep re-runs everything at 1, 2, 3, 7, 12 and 64 threads, which moves every chunk boundary; I tested it with a bug that only appears at 3 threads, and it caught it by name. A pre-push hook built the exact commit offline in the official image and ran the grid before anything reached the board.

The rules shaped the AI side too. Every agent worked under the same written rules: Rust standard library only, no precomputed answers, nothing tuned to the public seed, one idea per push, and every key compared in full. That last rule cost us speed, and I'd keep it. More on that below.

The first push landed 4 minutes 50 seconds after kickoff. An agent wrote Track A's first version from the design notes, which is the most satisfying 4 minutes 50 seconds of preparation I've ever cashed in.

What made it fast

The first versions were already 19× to 160× faster than the references, because the references are naive on purpose: Track A's spends about 77% of its time in strptime, and Track D's is 89% Dijkstra. Turning on twelve threads was the next big jump: Track A went from 0.443 s to 0.062 s, and Track C from 0.770 s to 0.086 s. After that, every gain had to be earned.

Track A: one integer per line

The log is mapped, not read, and parsed in place at fixed offsets. The hour comes from one multiply on an 8-byte load, and each line becomes one 32-bit integer whose plain integer order is the sort order, so percentiles fall out of a radix sort with no comparisons. Hours are finished and written while the parse is still running, because the log arrives nearly in order: that took memory from 18.8 to 16.4 MB and time from 0.0245 to 0.0221 s.

"Nearly in order" is doing a lot of work there, and the spec promises no bound on lateness. So the early finishing is checked, not assumed: a line that arrives more than 1/48 of the log late restarts the run with early finishing switched off, which about doubles the time. It never fires on generated data, and it's the kind of insurance you buy precisely so you never get to use it.

Track B: never store a posting

The reference builds a set for each of 609,833 distinct terms, which is thorough and exactly what you'd do if time were free. We index only the roughly 75,000 terms the queries actually use, and answer every query in one scan of the corpus. A rare term is an "anchor": documents are checked only around its occurrences. Boolean queries become small truth tables, so checking a document is a table lookup, not a formula. That chain took T from 0.308 s to 0.211, then 0.100, then 0.078, and later choosing anchors over the whole query got it to about 0.068.

Track C: break the record-to-record chain

A normal CSV parser finds each field from the end of the last one, so every record waits on the previous one. That's about 75 cycles of waiting per record, multiplied by a lot of records. We first list every separator in each 64-byte block, with quote parity from a carry-less multiply (so doubled quotes and commas inside quotes cost no branches), and only then read records from the list. Counting distinct names uses one shared lock-free table with one cache line per name.

Track D: put neighbours next to each other

The input's node IDs are random, so every edge is a cache miss with a long commute. Renumbering the graph so neighbours sit together took the queries from about 190 ms to about 105 ms. Removing low-degree nodes with shortcuts took T from 0.166 s to 0.152 s and memory from 67.9 to 46.0 MB. The search is a two-ended Dijkstra that alternates sides by work done, not by which side looks closer, because a query towards an unreachable island otherwise wastes millions of settles proving a negative.

The biggest single Track D win was embarrassing in hindsight: 1.74 million locked increments on one shared counter. Removing them took T from 0.389 s to 0.272 s. Contention on a single cache line is the kind of bug that doesn't show up in a profile so much as in a sigh.

The two smallest changes with the best return per line

Some of the cheapest wins weren't in the algorithms at all, but in the few milliseconds around them. The clock starts at exec, so everything before your first instruction counts.

Static linking: one line of config, zero lines of code. A normal Rust binary loads glibc through the dynamic loader at startup, and on the box that loading happens through the container's overlay filesystem, inside the timed run. Adding +crt-static to the target features in .cargo/config.toml removes it. An empty main measured 1.25 ms dynamic against 0.58 ms static under the harness's Docker flags. On Track A that was a paired 315 µs locally, about 0.5 ms of the box's 25 ms at the time; on Track C, 235 µs. Two percent for one line is a deal you don't get often.

Skipping Rust's own startup. Before your main runs, Rust's standard runtime reads /proc/self/maps, installs signal handlers and gives each thread a signal stack: about 15 system calls the timer counts, plus about 5 more per thread, some of them taking the address space's lock for writing. System calls cost far more on the box than on my PC. So three of our tracks declare main as the C entry point and skip all of it. It's a few lines, it's documented in the code, and the reason it works is the reason it's slightly rude.

The measurements that lied

This is the part I'd most want to read in someone else's write-up.

My PC and the box disagreed, and only one of them counts

My machine is a Zen 4. The box is a Golden Cove with a smaller shared L1 and about half the clock (2.5 GHz with turbo off). So:

  • On Track C, cutting branch mispredicts from 1.42 to 0.56 per record changed nothing on the board. Very satisfying locally. Completely ignored by the scoreboard.
  • Aligning Track C's input mapping cut local page faults from 3,094 to 651. The box didn't move either.
  • On Track B, three block-size settings ranked one way by local cycles (2.10G, 2.13G, 2.16G) and a different way on the board (0.0996, 0.0909, 0.0942 s).
  • On Track A, a "shorter dependency chain" cut single-thread cycles from 225.7M to 199.5M locally, and the board read 0.0220 s against 0.0193. Slower.
  • On Track D, our own scorer predicted 0.253 s for one change; the board read 0.389.

We ended up trusting local numbers only to rank instruction-count cuts, and settling everything else on the box. The box, it turns out, has opinions, and it doesn't share them in advance.

Exit is part of the timed run

The clock runs until the process exits, and exit tears down the mapped input page by page, on one thread, while the clock watches. On Track A, mapping the log lost on the board three times, until the threads shared releasing its pages before exit. On Track C the same teardown cost about 3.6 ms, roughly 15% of the run; without the shared release, K fell from 46.91 to 42.74. The fastest code in the world still has to clean up after itself, and it does so on company time.

Some savings were worth exactly nothing

On Track B, memory stops paying at 50× better than the reference, which works out to about 44 MB, because the board measured the reference at 2,199,961,600 bytes. Once under that, cutting memory from 42 MB to 27 MB earned zero points. A genuinely impressive optimisation with a genuinely impressive return of nothing. We stopped there and spent the spare memory buying time instead.

The memory peak counts more than your data

The cgroup's peak includes each CPU's unused charge batch, up to 252 KB per CPU, and threads racing to touch the same huge page each get billed for clearing their own copy. On Track C the main thread now faults in, up front, the pages a worker would otherwise be charged for. Being charged for memory you didn't use is a very modern experience.

Noise was bigger than most of our ideas

Fifteen runs of one Track B build spanned T 0.0681 to 0.0726 s, so a 1% gain was invisible in a single run. 234 runs of the final Track D source spread from 0.143 to 0.190 s. One afternoon, a bit-identical Track A build read 0.0290 s against 0.0255 s earlier: the box had moved, and the code had not. Track A also has a slow mode we never fully explained: identical code sometimes reads 0.018 s instead of 0.0158.

So the rule became: never decide between two builds on one timing, and report medians. Our best board numbers are the best of many runs. The full spread is in the numbers section below. Anyone quoting only their best run is quoting their luckiest one.

The changes that should have helped

  • Track C: batching lock writes, to do fewer locked operations, made T worse: 0.0244 against 0.0199, because the batch cost a second cache-line fill per record, about 22%.
  • Track D: capping the search at six threads, one per physical core, made it slower too, 0.196 s. Hyper-threads hide memory latency, and a graph search is almost all memory latency.
  • Track D again: looking nodes up by hash instead of renumbering them was about 5× slower. Hashing is wonderful until it's the bottleneck.
  • Track B: a filter to skip tokens that appear in no query added 13% more instructions and was reverted. The cheapest work is the work you don't add.

Correctness: the bugs the grid didn't catch

The multi-seed grid caught plenty, usually within seconds. A backwards digit-parsing trick on Track A failed 43 of 44 cells at once. A radix-queue experiment on Track D gave wrong answers immediately, and a too-large candidate silently dropped by a compare-before-check was caught by the answer bank the same way. Those are the friendly bugs. The scary ones were the bugs it couldn't see.

  • Track A: a race every check passed. The lock-free name table had a window where two threads inserting the same new key at the same instant could clash. Nothing caught it: it needs two threads, a new key, and the same nanosecond. After the fix, 300 repeated runs became a standing check, and the final build passed 130,233 runs with no bad output.
  • Track B: a hang at one thread. An adversarial review found a helper that could park twice, while a thread keeps only one wake-up. Pinned to one thread, it hung 10 runs out of 10. The thread sweep would have caught it. Normal runs never would.
  • Track C: 2 crashes in 1,900 runs. A review agent found a pointer and length read before the atomic that makes them valid. It only showed up on a spec-legal stress input, which is the worst kind: legal, rare, and fatal.
  • Track B: a late start. Threads sometimes started late because the threads pre-faulting the corpus held the kernel's memory-map lock. Not a wrong answer, just a mystery that looked like noise until someone read the kernel side.

We also tested the tests: 56 bugs were planted one at a time on Track B, and the fuzzing caught 49. Of the seven it missed, three couldn't change the output, two were races that need a particular input, one was caught by AddressSanitizer, and one was a coincidence the tests never produced.

Check it yourself, with one command

All of that testing ships with the repo, outside the scored track folders. python3 tools/verify.py needs only Docker, git and Python. It builds every track offline, the way the board does, runs it in the board's sandbox (no network, read-only root, 8 GB, an unprivileged user), and checks it against 171 datasets: 15 seeds at two scales, the answer-preserving rewrites, the limit files, and five repeated runs for determinism. Every expected answer comes from the organisers' own reference, run on their own generators' data. A cold start took 16 minutes on my PC. If you'd like to check a claim in this post, that's the fastest way to catch me out.

Exact keys, on purpose

Several of the fastest entries match names or tokens by hash alone and accept a small chance of a wrong answer; one README puts it at about 1 dataset in 3,000 for its search track. That's a reasonable engineering bet, right up until it isn't. Our rule was the opposite: every key compared in full, plus a test build where every key gets the same hash, which must still produce the right output. It cost some speed. On the final run, on a seed nobody had seen, all four of our tracks passed, and I slept better for it, which at that point in the week was saying something.

Running a crew of AI agents

Most of what I learned that isn't in a PERF.md is about orchestration.

Context is the real cost

By Sunday, the two main sessions (one owning tracks A and B, one C and D) were carrying 833K and 685K tokens of history, and every turn paid for all of it. Imagine re-reading a 600-page diary before every sentence you write. We switched to fresh sessions that start from a short written handover in a shared PROGRESS.md. In the next 1 hour 45 minutes, the overall score rose from 82.21 to 82.97 and took 1st on the live board, while usage fell from about 3.1% to 1.3% of the weekly limit per hour. A fresh session with a good handover beats a long one that remembers everything, which is also true of meetings.

More agents is not more progress

Early on, a 13-agent prototyping workflow at maximum effort burned the whole 5-hour usage window in about 50 minutes, and every agent was cut off before reporting. Zero results. A dozen brilliant colleagues who all leave before saying anything is, it turns out, the same as no colleagues. After that: two or three agents at a time, each with a narrow brief, and the deterministic test rig as the judge instead of more agents.

The handover file is the team

Any agent could be cut off at any moment, by a usage limit, a crash or me closing the wrong window. So PROGRESS.md had a "now" block, a table per track, and the reason for every decision. A new session could pick up a half-finished experiment from the file alone. Without it, every handover would have restarted the work from scratch.

Agents need guard rails, not trust

A few that earned their keep:

  • A pre-push gate no agent could skip, so nothing broken reached the board. Skipping it with --no-verify was in the rules as something you confess to the human first.
  • No experiment as the last commit at freeze, and a scheduled check 45 minutes before the freeze that compared each track against its chosen final source.
  • An audit for line-count tricks, after the organisers warned that judges check for them. Comments that game the line counter had already got one team caught.
  • One shared checkout, carefully. At one point I found it detached on an old commit, probably by another agent: the software equivalent of a colleague leaving the office printer on "envelope". After that, risky jobs ran in their own git worktrees.
  • Interrupted is not stopped. A command into WSL can keep running inside Linux after the tool reports it as rejected. One push landed that way. After that, the first thing after any interruption was to check the processes and git log.
  • Check the boring parts. The scheduled task that made the repo public at the deadline used a command-line flag our version of gh didn't have. It would have failed, quietly, ten minutes before the cutoff. A last-hour check caught it with about 25 minutes to spare.

Decide on the box, not on the story

Agents are very good at explaining why a change should be faster. Fluently, confidently, with diagrams if you let them. The board was the only thing that settled it, and it overruled the explanation often enough that "one idea per push, median of several runs" became the whole method. Our repo has 583 commits, 344 of them marked exp:: experiments sent to the box to answer one question each. The agents wrote most of the code. The box decided what stayed.

What I'd do differently

  • I'd stop neglecting Track D sooner. Its code hasn't changed since Oct 31, because it was outside our best three tracks, and the overall title counts only those. That was correct for points, but D had the most headroom: the leader on that track ran in 0.085 s against our 0.144.
  • I'd treat lines of code as a real budget from day one. Track B ended at 1,077 lines against the reference's 91, and against a rival with about 800 lines, the line factor alone cost us about 4.5% of K. Another team moved two tracks from Rust to C++ for 22–28% fewer scored lines at about the same speed. Rust-only was our own rule, not the contest's. I chose it; I'd probably choose it again; I'd just stop pretending it was free.
  • I'd take back the late memory redesigns on Track C. On the last day, one session spent hours on designs that cut memory to about 8 MB but lost time, and every one was rejected on the board. A smaller budget of experiments, decided earlier, would have bought more.
  • I'd write the "a human understood this" part as I went. The rules say PERF.md must show a human understood the work. With agents doing the typing, that means reading every decision as it lands, not speed-reading 300 log rows the night before judging.

The numbers

Every board run of the exact source we froze, not just the lucky ones:

Track Runs of the final source K: worst / median / best T in s: best / median / worst Best run overall Rank by K on the board
A 65 47.70 / 56.72 / 58.58 0.0156 / 0.0164 / 0.0228 run-a3d80d9d43be, K 58.58 3
B 26 42.47 / 44.03 / 44.60 0.0645 / 0.0662 / 0.0712 run-4d59d4dfba18, K 44.70 2
C 26 43.84 / 46.75 / 47.26 0.0193 / 0.0195 / 0.0222 run-d8ffdb6e4d14, K 47.28 6
D 234 24.02 / 27.10 / 27.68 0.1432 / 0.1488 / 0.1896 run-ba733dba1abf, K 27.68 15

The best runs on B and C came from earlier, slightly different sources, which is why they sit just above the final source's own best. Track A's worst run, K 47.70, is the slow mode in its natural habitat.

Over the 72 hours the board ran our code 1,740 times, from 435 pushes. The PERF.md files log 342 steps across the four tracks, failed experiments included, each with its board run ID.

On the final run, on the hidden dataset, our tracks scored 88.3, 82.3, 83.5 and 72.2 speed points, for a machine score of 84.68: 3rd, behind LippInc (86.49) and another ello (84.79). Track A's 88.3 tied the best on that row. The judges' scores land by Nov 13, and I'll be refreshing the page with the composure of someone who definitely isn't refreshing the page.

One more run, after the freeze

Curiosity being what it is, I ran the top four teams' frozen code (LippInc, another ello, SALAAR and ours) through the organisers' harness on my own PC, on a freshly generated seed, 576548, that no one had ever seen. Five runs per track, sixteen tracks in all. Every single one produced the right answer, including the hash-only entries, which is a reminder that a 1-in-3,000 risk usually doesn't fire.

My PC put us first on speed. I'd love to report that as a prediction, but this whole post is about why I can't: on Track C my PC ranked one rival's design below ours, while the real box has it about 20% ahead. Same code, opposite verdict. The box is the referee, and the referee was in Falkenstein.

Links

  • The repo, with every step and failed experiment in each track's PERF.md: github.com/SaudSatopay/speed-demon-2026
  • The event, by Hackathon Raptors: speeddemon.dev

Thanks to the Hackathon Raptors organisers for publishing the harness, answering questions within hours, and running a contest where the only thing you can't argue with is a SHA-256.

title: Your Dev Environment Doesn’t Need to Work Nights
description:
It's 2 AM. Your dev environment is up and running. Nobody is using it.

For a lot of teams, that's just the default. Spin it up, leave it on, move on to the next thing. It's convenient. But your dev and test environments don't need production-style, around-the-clock availability.

Off-hours scheduling asks one simple question: when does this environment actually need to be running? For most dev environments, the answer is easy: tuck them in at 6, wake them up at 9.

Development infrastructure shouldn't need an overnight shift.

Start with the working schedule

Say your dev environment is used from 9 AM to 6 PM, Monday through Friday. That's 45 hours out of a 168-hour week. In this example, it sits outside its schedule for 123 hours, about 73% of the week.

Illustrative schedule: running 9 AM–6 PM on weekdays and stopped otherwise. Stopping compute doesn't stop every charge.

To be clear, that is not 73% off your AWS bill. It's the share of runtime you could remove from the resources you schedule. What you actually save depends on how each service bills while it's stopped, whether Reserved Instances or Savings Plans already cover that usage, how long things take to start, and everything else in the account that keeps running.

The best place to start is anything with predictable hours: dev databases, internal test systems, and staging environments that are only used during the workday.

Find out what can safely stop

Before you schedule anything, talk to the people who own and use the environment. Ask about:

  • overnight CI pipelines and scheduled data jobs
  • backups and maintenance windows
  • teammates in other time zones
  • on-call engineers who might need to debug at night
  • integrations that assume a service is always reachable

Then check what each resource can actually do. Not every AWS service has a stop button, and the ones that do behave differently:

  • EC2 instances stop compute billing while stopped, but attached EBS volumes keep billing, and so do Elastic IP addresses. An instance without an Elastic IP gets a new public IPv4 address when it starts again.
  • RDS DB instances and Aurora clusters can be stopped for up to seven days at a time. After that, AWS starts them automatically. Some setups, like read replicas, can't be stopped at all. Storage and backups keep billing.
  • Redshift clusters can be paused and resumed, and storage keeps billing while they're paused.
  • Auto Scaling groups can be scaled to zero. That terminates the instances, so anything stored on them is gone when new ones launch.

An off-hours schedule should be a deliberate decision, not a blind timer.

Caution: A database that AWS restarts after seven days will run, and bill, until your next scheduled stop. Make sure your scheduler stops it again. Don't assume something you stopped once stays stopped.

Know what keeps costing money

Stopping compute cuts compute charges for the hours it's off. It doesn't touch the cost of storage, snapshots, backups, Elastic IP addresses, load balancers, NAT gateways, or monitoring that stays in place.

So treat any runtime estimate as an estimate for the resources you schedule, not a promise about your whole bill. Track the scheduled resources' compute charges separately from everything else, and you'll see exactly what the schedule changed.

Time zones and exceptions are part of the plan

A simple schedule can trip up when your team spans time zones, or when daylight saving time shifts everyone's working hours.

Pick one clearly defined time zone for each schedule. Plan for holidays, release nights, and the occasional late evening. Decide up front how someone starts an environment outside its window, and who can change the schedule.

People also need to see what's going on. Owners should be able to tell why an environment is stopped, when it'll start again, and whether the last stop or start failed.

Before enabling off-hours

  • [ ] Every scheduled resource has an owner who agreed to the schedule
  • [ ] Overnight jobs, backups, and CI pipelines have been moved or accounted for
  • [ ] The schedule uses one defined time zone and handles daylight saving time
  • [ ] There is a known way to start an environment outside its window
  • [ ] Stopping and restarting has been tested, including start-up time

Start small and measure

  1. Pick one low-risk environment, and write down its current cost and how it's actually used.
  2. Confirm who owns it and what depends on it.
  3. Set a conservative schedule, tell the team, and test both stopping and starting.
  4. Watch for anything that breaks, and track the scheduled resources' charges against everything else.
  5. Adjust as usage changes, then roll it out to other nonproduction environments.

The safest cost optimization is the one your team can explain, schedule, and reverse.

Ways to do it

You don't need a product to get started. AWS gives you a few building blocks:

  • Instance Scheduler on AWS, an AWS solution that starts and stops EC2 and RDS resources on schedules you define.
  • Amazon EventBridge Scheduler, which can call AWS APIs like StopInstances and StartInstances on a cron schedule.
  • Scheduled actions for Auto Scaling groups and Redshift clusters, built right into those services.

Whichever you pick, keep the schedule in one place, ideally next to the rest of your infrastructure code, so it gets reviewed and versioned like any other change.

Where CloudBudgie fits

CloudBudgie's Off-Hours Mode stops or pauses supported resources outside working hours and starts them again automatically. Today that covers RDS DB instances, Aurora clusters, Redshift clusters, DocumentDB and Neptune clusters, and Auto Scaling groups, which scale to zero. You choose the resources and the hours. You see the estimated monthly savings before you confirm. If a scheduled stop or start fails, you see the error on the resource, and you can edit or remove a schedule any time.

I'll be honest about what it doesn't do. Not every cloud service can be switched off. NAT gateways and many cache services have no stop operation, so saving money on them means deleting and recreating them. That's a different kind of change, and Off-Hours Mode doesn't do it.

The idea is simple: match your infrastructure to when it's actually used, keep the schedule easy to understand, and keep your team in control.

References

  • Stop and start Amazon EC2 instances
  • Stopping an Amazon RDS DB instance temporarily
  • Stopping and starting an Amazon Aurora DB cluster
  • Pausing and resuming Amazon Redshift clusters
  • Scheduled scaling for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
  • Instance Scheduler on AWS
  • Amazon EventBridge Scheduler
  • AWS public IPv4 address charge

title: Cross Browser Favicons
description:
Once you have a 16px by 16px PNG, GIF, JPG or ICO file adding a favicon, or favorite icon, to your website is easy. On the other hand it will take a few extra steps to comply with all browser’s.

If you need to convert an icon to .ico I’d suggest the Project Fondue Favicon Generator, it’s a no-bullshit tool that’s simple.

All Major Browsers

Depending on the type of file you’re using one of the following is the standard way to add a favicon in well-built web browsers.

<link rel="icon" type="image/png" href="https://www.example.com/image.png">
<link rel="icon" type="image/gif" href="https://www.example.com/image.gif">
<link rel="icon" type="image/jpeg" href="https://www.example.com/image.jpg">
<link rel="icon" type="image/vnd.microsoft.icon" href="https://www.example.com/image.ico">`</pre>

Internet Explorer 7 & Below

MSIE does NOT support PNG, GIF and JPEG type icons, only ICO files. After you have the ICO file you can use the following code to add a favicon in IE5, IE6 or IE7.

<link rel="shortcut icon" href="https://www.example.com/image.ico" />
<link rel="address bar icon" href="https://www.example.com/image.ico">

Cross Browser Approach

The best cross browser approach I’ve found assumes that you have a PNG, GIF or JPEG for major browsers, and a fallback ICO file to use for IE7 and below.

<link rel="icon" type="image/png" href="https://www.example.com/image.png">
<!--[if IE]><link rel="shortcut icon" href="https://www.example.com/alternateimage.ico"/><![endif]-->

title: Why We Migrated a Python Service to Go: Lessons from the MakeMyTrip Flights Backend
description:
At MakeMyTrip, I led the migration of the Flights backend from Python to Go. The result: resource usage dropped by 60%, and our AWS costs went down with it.

Let me be upfront about what this post is and isn't. The internal details of that system aren't mine to publish, so you won't find architecture diagrams or traffic numbers here. What I can share is why Go is a good fit for that kind of service, the Go patterns that typically produce savings like this, and the migration practices I recommend. I've done this kind of move more than once: earlier, at THB, I moved a medical-data sync service from Node.js to Go and its ETL time went from 3 hours to 10 minutes. At Talentica, working on PlanetScale's Vitess, I migrated Python test cases to Go.

Why a flights backend suits Go

A flight search or booking backend is mostly I/O: calling upstream services, waiting, combining responses, caching (we used Redis), and serving REST APIs. That workload pays off in Go for a few reasons.

Cheap concurrency. A goroutine starts with a few kilobytes of stack, and the Go runtime schedules many of them across all CPU cores in one process. In a typical Python web deployment, each worker process handles a limited number of concurrent requests, so you scale by adding processes, and each process carries its own copy of the interpreter and your application's memory. Go serves the same concurrency from one process per instance.

Predictable memory. Go structs are compact and laid out contiguously. Python objects carry more per-object overhead. For services that hold lots of small records in memory, such as fares, segments or cached responses, that difference adds up.

Real parallelism for CPU work. Parsing, merging and sorting large JSON responses is CPU-bound. Go uses every core without multiprocessing workarounds.

Simple deployment. A static binary in a small container image. No virtualenvs, no dependency drift between machines.

Less CPU and memory per request means fewer or smaller instances for the same load. That is where a resource cut like 60% turns into a lower AWS bill.

A core Go pattern for aggregation services: bounded fan-out

The typical hot path in an aggregation service calls several upstreams at once and merges the results. In Go, errgroup makes this concise and safe. (The code samples in this post are simplified illustrations, not MakeMyTrip's code.)

import "golang.org/x/sync/errgroup"

type Quote struct {
    Supplier string
    Fares    []Fare
}

func (s *Service) Search(ctx context.Context, q SearchQuery) ([]Fare, error) {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    results := make([]Quote, len(s.suppliers))
    g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)
    g.SetLimit(8) // bound concurrency per request

    for i, sup := range s.suppliers {
        g.Go(func() error {
            fares, err := sup.Search(ctx, q)
            if err != nil {
                s.log.Warn("supplier failed", "supplier", sup.Name(), "err", err)
                return nil // a partial result beats no result
            }
            results[i] = Quote{Supplier: sup.Name(), Fares: fares}
            return nil
        })
    }
    if err := g.Wait(); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return merge(results), nil
}

The details matter:

  • One deadline for the whole request, passed via context, so slow upstreams are cut off and their goroutines exit.
  • SetLimit bounds concurrency, so a traffic spike doesn't become thousands of outbound connections.
  • Writing to results[i] avoids a mutex: each goroutine owns its own index.
  • Partial failure is a decision, not an accident. Here one supplier failing is logged and skipped.

(Since Go 1.22, each loop iteration has its own i and sup, so capturing them in the closure is safe.)

Small things that cut memory and CPU

Moving to Go gives you a better baseline. These habits keep it lean:

// Reuse HTTP connections: one shared client with a tuned transport.
var upstream = &http.Client{
    Timeout: 3 * time.Second,
    Transport: &http.Transport{
        MaxIdleConns:        200,
        MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 50,
        IdleConnTimeout:     90 * time.Second,
    },
}

// Stream-decode large responses instead of reading them into memory first.
func decodeFares(r io.Reader) ([]Fare, error) {
    var payload struct {
        Fares []Fare `json:"fares"`
    }
    err := json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(&payload)
    return payload.Fares, err
}

The default MaxIdleConnsPerHost is 2, which causes constant reconnects to a busy upstream. That one setting is easy to miss after a migration. Then measure, don't guess: net/http/pprof on an internal port shows where CPU and allocations go.

How to migrate without breaking production

A rewrite is risky. A migration of a service people depend on is riskier. The practices I recommend:

1. Freeze the contract first. Write down the existing API's request and response formats, including the odd parts. Then write contract tests against the Python service and run the same tests against the Go one.

2. Watch for JSON differences. Most migration bugs are serialization differences, not logic errors:

type FareResponse struct {
    // Python returned null when missing; a Go string would return "".
    PromoCode *string `json:"promo_code"`
    // Python may omit a key entirely; match that with omitempty only if clients expect it.
    Baggage   []Bag   `json:"baggage,omitempty"`
    // Keep money as integer minor units; don't let float formatting change.
    TotalPaise int64  `json:"total_paise"`
}

Go's zero values ("", 0, false, [] vs null) differ from Python's None. Decide field by field, and test it.

3. Compare responses before switching. Send the same requests to both implementations and diff the outputs, ignoring fields that legitimately differ, such as timestamps:

func diffJSON(a, b []byte, ignore map[string]bool) (bool, error) {
    var x, y map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(a, &x); err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    if err := json.Unmarshal(b, &y); err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    for k := range ignore {
        delete(x, k)
        delete(y, k)
    }
    return reflect.DeepEqual(x, y), nil
}

4. Migrate endpoint by endpoint. Put a router in front and move routes one at a time, starting with read-only, high-volume endpoints where the resource savings are largest and the risk is smallest.

5. Keep a rollback switch. Routing back to the old service should be a config change, not a deploy.

Lessons beyond performance

The same period at MakeMyTrip taught me that code structure matters as much as runtime efficiency. I also worked on the Unification Project, building shared libraries used by both MakeMyTrip and Goibibo. That cut development costs by 40%, and over the same period we cut average feature delivery time from 1.5 months to 20 days across both brands. A migration is a good moment to pull repeated logic (clients, retries, caching, logging) into shared Go packages, so the next service starts from a better place.

When not to migrate

Go isn't automatically the answer. If a service is small, cheap to run and rarely changes, a rewrite's risk outweighs its savings. If the work is mostly data science or depends on Python-only ML libraries, keep it in Python and put a Go service in front of it if you need one. Migrate when the service is I/O- or concurrency-heavy, costs real money to run and will be maintained for years.

Takeaways

  • I/O-heavy, high-concurrency services are where Go saves the most.
  • Bounded fan-out with errgroup and context deadlines is the core pattern.
  • Most migration bugs are contract and serialization bugs. Test the contract.
  • Move endpoint by endpoint, with a rollback switch.

Pradip Parmar is a Go backend and AI agent engineer from Surat, India, who has written Go since 2018. At MakeMyTrip he led the Python-to-Go migration of the Flights backend, and today he builds Go backends, RAG systems, MCP servers and LLM agents for businesses as an independent engineer. Contact him on LinkedIn, Upwork or Contra, or browse GitHub.

title: How to check an ML benchmark for train/test copies
description:
PowerCons is a small time series dataset: 180 training rows, 180 test rows, two classes. It is one of the 128 datasets in the UCR archive, which researchers use to compare classifiers. 67 of its 180 test rows are also in its training set, value for value. A 1-nearest-neighbour classifier gets all 67 right, because each one has its own answer sitting in the training data.

I found this while auditing the UCR and UEA archives row by row, and the audit became a preprint. This post leaves the statistics to the paper and covers the check itself. It takes about 20 lines of Python and a fraction of a second, and you can point it at your own benchmark today. I ran every code block below against the real archive files, and every output is pasted from those runs.

Why nothing warns you

A random split assumes the rows are independent. Copies break that assumption silently. Nothing throws, the shapes are right, the class counts look fine, and the score goes up. A higher score looks like a better model, so nobody goes looking for the cause.

Comparing every test row with every training row would find them, but that is n * m comparisons of long vectors. A hash set does it in one pass over each split. Give each row a fingerprint, put the training fingerprints in a set, and look up each test row.

Two passes, one lookup per test row.

Two details decide whether this is useful. Leave the label out of the hash, because a copy with a different label is still a copy, and it is one of the more interesting things you can find. And keep the row indices rather than a count, because every later step needs them.

Run it on a .ts file

UCR and UEA ship in the .ts format. audit_ts.py reads it with only the standard library. A row's identity is its text with the label cut off, so this is the whole idea:

audit_ts.py

def read_ts(path):
    keys, labels = [], []
    in_data = False
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for raw in f:
            line = raw.strip()
            if not line or line.startswith(b"#"):
                continue
            if in_data:
                body, _, label = line.rpartition(b":")
                keys.append(hashlib.md5(body).digest())
                labels.append(label.decode())
            elif line.lower().startswith(b"@data"):
                in_data = True
    if not keys:
        sys.exit(f"{path}: no @data rows found")
    return keys, labels

MD5 is fine here. Nobody is attacking this hash, and all it has to do is tell rows apart. Download the archive zip, then run it on a train and test pair:

git clone https://github.com/mahmadmanzoor/archive-audit
python archive-audit/audit_ts.py PowerCons_TRAIN.ts PowerCons_TEST.ts

n_train: 180
n_test: 180
duplicate_rows: 130
test_rows_with_train_twin: 67
test_twin_pct: 37.22
twin_rows_with_conflicting_label: 0
groups_with_conflicting_labels: 0

test_rows_with_train_twin is the number that matters. duplicate_rows counts across both splits: 360 rows in total, 230 distinct, so 130 are repeats. The two conflict lines count copies whose labels disagree, and here there are none.

It stays fast on bigger data. Crop has 24,000 rows, and the same command finished in 0.06 seconds and reported 2,753 of 16,800 test rows, or 16.39%. Add --json to get the row numbers.

17 of 128 UCR datasets and 3 of 30 UEA datasets leak on their default split. Eight of the UCR ones leak at least 1%.

The same check for arrays and dataframes

Your benchmark probably is not in .ts files. Once the data is numeric you can hash the values instead of the text, which also means 1.0 and 1.00 finally match.

fingerprint.py

import hashlib
import numpy as np

def fingerprints(X, decimals=6):
    """One hash per row, after rounding away float noise."""
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float64)
    X = np.round(X, decimals) + 0.0  # + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
    return [hashlib.blake2b(row.tobytes(), digest_size=16).hexdigest()
            for row in X]

def leak_report(X_train, X_test, decimals=6):
    train = set(fingerprints(X_train, decimals))
    test = fingerprints(X_test, decimals)
    twins = [i for i, h in enumerate(test) if h in train]
    pct = round(100 * len(twins) / len(test), 2)
    return {"test_rows": len(test), "twins": len(twins),
            "pct": pct, "indices": twins}

row.tobytes() does not care about shape, so this works on a batch of images as well as on a table. If you want to follow along with the archive files, this loader turns them into arrays:

load.py

import numpy as np

def load_ts(path):
    X, y = [], []
    in_data = False
    for line in open(path):
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        if in_data:
            body, label = line.rsplit(":", 1)
            X.append([float(v) for v in body.split(",") if v != "?"])
            y.append(label)
        elif line.lower().startswith("@data"):
            in_data = True
    return np.array(X), np.array(y)

The decimals argument needs checking, because rounding is a trade-off. Too strict and float noise hides real copies. Too loose and different rows collapse into one. So run it at several values and see if the count holds:

X_train, y_train = load_ts("PowerCons_TRAIN.ts")
X_test, y_test = load_ts("PowerCons_TEST.ts")
for d in (2, 3, 4, 6, 10):
    print(d, leak_report(X_train, X_test, decimals=d)["twins"])

noisy = X_test + 1e-9
strict = leak_report(X_train, noisy, decimals=12)["twins"]
rounded = leak_report(X_train, noisy, decimals=6)["twins"]
narrow = leak_report(X_train, X_test.astype(np.float32))["twins"]
print("noise, decimals=12:", strict)
print("noise, decimals=6: ", rounded)
print("float32:           ", narrow)

2 67
3 67
4 67
6 67
10 67
noise, decimals=12: 0
noise, decimals=6:  67
float32:            67

The count is flat from 2 to 10 decimals, so these are real copies and not an artefact of rounding. The noise lines show why exact bytes are not enough: add 1e-9 to every value and a strict match finds nothing at all, while decimals=6 still finds all 67. If your own count climbs as you lower decimals, you are starting to merge rows that are merely similar.

Exact matching also misses a copy that has been rescaled. If your pipeline normalises each row, hash after normalising:

def znorm(X):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float64)
    std = X.std(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    std[std == 0] = 1
    return (X - X.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)) / std

scaled = X_test * 2
raw = leak_report(X_train, scaled)
normed = leak_report(znorm(X_train), znorm(scaled), decimals=3)
print("raw:         ", raw["twins"])
print("z-normalised:", normed["twins"])

raw:          0
z-normalised: 67

With a dataframe, pandas has the hash built in. Drop the label column first:

import pandas as pd
from pandas.util import hash_pandas_object

columns = [f"x{i}" for i in range(X_train.shape[1])]
train_df = pd.DataFrame(X_train, columns=columns).assign(label=y_train)
test_df = pd.DataFrame(X_test, columns=columns).assign(label=y_test)

features = [c for c in train_df.columns if c != "label"]
def row_hashes(df):
    return hash_pandas_object(df[features].round(6), index=False)

is_copy = row_hashes(test_df).isin(set(row_hashes(train_df)))
print(is_copy.sum(), f"{is_copy.mean():.2%}")

67 37.22%

Those are the same 67 rows the array version found.

Measure what the copies do to your score

A leak rate tells you copies exist. It does not tell you what they cost. For that, split your accuracy into twin rows and the rest:

from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

X_train, y_train = load_ts("PowerCons_TRAIN.ts")
X_test, y_test = load_ts("PowerCons_TEST.ts")

report = leak_report(X_train, X_test)
is_twin = np.zeros(len(X_test), dtype=bool)
is_twin[report["indices"]] = True

model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=1).fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = model.predict(X_test)
correct = pred == y_test
print(f"all rows:  {correct.mean():.2%} ({len(correct)})")
print(f"twin rows: {correct[is_twin].mean():.2%} ({is_twin.sum()})")
print(f"the rest:  {correct[~is_twin].mean():.2%} ({(~is_twin).sum()})")

all rows:  97.78% (180)
twin rows: 100.00% (67)
the rest:  96.46% (113)

This is raw values on the one default split, so treat it as a demonstration. The twin rows are a free 100%, and removing them takes the score down by over a point. Worms on the same setup goes from 45.45% to 37.31%.

For a fairer estimate the paper averages 30 resamples with and without twins:

  • 1-NN on z-normalised values: PowerCons 91.67% to 86.63%, Worms 47.75% to 35.52%, Crop 71.06% to 65.47%.
  • MiniRocket (2,000 kernels): PowerCons 95.52% to 92.83%, Worms 70.48% to 66.48%, Crop 69.99% to 65.44%.

So this is not only a nearest-neighbour effect. A model that trains on a row and is tested on that same row benefits whatever its design. On the published fold-0 predictions, the mean over 17 classifiers on Crop goes from 74.7% to 69.8%.

Warning: Do not try to find twins with kneighbors and distance == 0. On PowerCons, sklearn reported a non-zero nearest distance for 24 of the 67 rows I had confirmed identical, as high as 1.58e-06. Compare fingerprints instead.

Check both directions

Everything above asks how much of the test set is in train. InsectEPGSmallTrain shows why that is not enough:

X_a, _ = load_ts("InsectEPGSmallTrain_TRAIN.ts")
X_b, _ = load_ts("InsectEPGSmallTrain_TEST.ts")

in_train = leak_report(X_a, X_b)["twins"]
in_test = leak_report(X_b, X_a)["twins"]
print(in_train, "of", len(X_b), "test rows are in train")
print(in_test, "of", len(X_a), "train rows are in test")

15 of 249 test rows are in train
15 of 17 train rows are in test

Reported the usual way, this dataset leaks 6% and you move on. Flip the arguments and 15 of its 17 training rows are in the test set. Freezer's SmallTrain variant has 26 of 28, while MixedShapes' is clean. A dataset that exists to test learning from a few examples should not test on nearly all of those examples.

Same copies, very different headline.

Read the copies before you call it a bug

Not every copy is a mistake. ElectricDevices has 208 test rows with a training twin, 2.7% of its test set. But 54 of its twin groups carry conflicting labels, and 101 test rows have no training twin with their own label. Over 30 resamples, removing the twins there raises 1-NN accuracy slightly, from 69.39% to 69.65%, because twin rows only score 61.5%. So copies do not always help.

The reason shows up when you count distinct values in each twin row:

def median_distinct(X_tr, X_te):
    rows = X_te[leak_report(X_tr, X_te)["indices"]]
    counts = [len(set(row)) for row in rows]
    return int(np.median(counts)), rows.shape[1]

X_e, _ = load_ts("ElectricDevices_TRAIN.ts")
X_f, _ = load_ts("ElectricDevices_TEST.ts")
print("ElectricDevices:", median_distinct(X_e, X_f))
print("PowerCons:      ", median_distinct(X_train, X_test))

ElectricDevices: (2, 96)
PowerCons:       (77, 144)

Each result is the median number of distinct values and the row length. ElectricDevices twins are mostly on/off patterns, so two different appliances can produce the same row by coincidence. PowerCons twins are far richer, which makes a chance match much less believable. A copy can also be legitimate in the sense that real deployments see it too. So I would report the score both ways, and I would not quietly delete rows.

Do not loosen the match

The tempting upgrade is near-duplicate detection, because exact matching obviously misses some copies. Here is what a strict-looking correlation threshold does on OliveOil:

X_o, _ = load_ts("OliveOil_TRAIN.ts")
X_q, _ = load_ts("OliveOil_TEST.ts")

best_r = (znorm(X_q) @ znorm(X_o).T / X_o.shape[1]).max(axis=1)
share = (best_r >= 0.9999).mean()
print("best r >= 0.9999:", f"{share:.0%}", "of test rows")
print("lowest best r:   ", round(float(best_r.min()), 6))
print("exact twins:     ", leak_report(X_o, X_q)["twins"])

best r >= 0.9999: 100% of test rows
lowest best r:    0.999963
exact twins:      0

Every test row correlates above 0.9999 with something in train, and none of them is a copy. These are smooth spectra, and smooth spectra correlate. The paper sees the same thing on Wine (92.6%) and Meat (83.3%). A near-match is fine as a lead to go and look at, but I only count exact matches as leakage, and I accept that the result is a lower bound.

Fix the split

If you control the split, make the fingerprint the group, so all copies of a row land on the same side:

from sklearn.model_selection import (GroupShuffleSplit,
                                     StratifiedGroupKFold)

X = np.vstack([X_train, X_test])
y = np.concatenate([y_train, y_test])
groups = np.array(fingerprints(X))

def show(tr, te):
    twins = leak_report(X[tr], X[te])["twins"]
    print(len(tr), "train,", len(te), "test,", twins, "twins")

splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.5, random_state=0)
show(*next(splitter.split(X, y, groups=groups)))

folds = StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=2, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
show(*next(folds.split(X, y, groups=groups)))

180 train, 180 test, 0 twins
181 train, 179 test, 0 twins

GroupShuffleSplit does not balance classes, so use StratifiedGroupKFold when that matters. Both keep repeated rows together instead of deleting them.

Random resampling does not wash this out. It makes copies on both sides the normal case.

If the split is fixed, because it is the official one, keep it and report a second number without the twins. You do not need to retrain anything. Drop the rows from your existing predictions. For UCR and UEA the indices are already in the release folder:

import json

path = "release/clean_default_test_ucr.json"
entry = json.load(open(path))["PowerCons"]
drop = entry["test_rows_to_drop"]
keep = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(entry["n_test"]), drop)

before = (pred == y_test).mean()
after = (pred[keep] == y_test[keep]).mean()
print(f"{before:.2%} -> {after:.2%}")

97.78% -> 96.46%

Make it fail in CI

A check you ran once protects one version of the data. Put it next to the code that builds the split, so a new data drop cannot bring copies back unnoticed:

check_split.py

def assert_no_copies(X_train, X_test, max_pct=0.0, decimals=6):
    report = leak_report(X_train, X_test, decimals)
    if report["pct"] > max_pct:
        raise AssertionError(
            f"{report['twins']} of {report['test_rows']} test rows "
            f"are in train ({report['pct']}%): {report['indices'][:5]}"
        )

assert_no_copies(X_train, X_test, max_pct=40.0)  # passes
assert_no_copies(X_train, X_test)                # fails

AssertionError: 67 of 180 test rows are in train (37.22%): [6, 8, 9, 14, 15]

max_pct is there for data like ElectricDevices, where you have read the copies, decided they are fine and want to catch only an increase.

What this does not catch

  • Anything inexact. Shifted windows, augmented rows and resampled versions all hash differently. Every count here is a lower bound.
  • Shared sources. Two recordings of one patient are not copies but they still leak. For that you need a subject or source column to group on, and a hash cannot replace it.
  • Whether a ranking is wrong. More copies do not automatically mean a broken leaderboard, and in the archives the ranking barely moved.

On that last point, among the 15 classifiers I could rescore, 0 of 105 pairwise outcomes changed on twin-free fold 0. That is a weak test, since only 16 datasets have twin test rows, and the newest classifiers publish no per-row predictions, so I could not rescore them. I would still trust the broad order of the field. I would trust one score on one of these datasets a lot less. The paper is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. I could not find an earlier report of these copies, though that does not prove there is none, and the claim is about what the scores measure, not about the people who built the archives.

If you only take one thing from this, take fingerprint.py and run it on whatever you are benchmarking next. The row indices for both archives and the audit script are in the repo.

Originally published on my site. More posts and projects at mahmadmanzoor.com.

title: Introducing Three-Live: turning AI-generated Three.js into interactive 3D, AR, and WebXR across web and mobile
description:
by Jonathan Bingham, AI Foundations

Want to add AI-generated 3D or XR to your web or mobile app? Unsure how to get started? That’s why we created the open source cross-platform project Three-Live—written entirely by Google Antigravity, in partnership with one former software engineer turned product manager. (Three-Live is not an officially supported Google product.)

You can think of Three-Live as a simple, unofficial companion to the more capable and feature-rich XR Blocks, Android XR’s web-based cross-platform framework for XR. The goal of Three-Live is to make it easy to get started with 3D and XR that’s AI-authored in Three.js. Three-Live combines the familiar developer experience of <model-viewer> and native mobile libraries with a sandboxed compiler for on-device or server-side compilation of untrusted LLM-generated JavaScript. Large language models (LLMs) have gotten remarkably good at writing software, and that includes generating 3D code in procedural Three.js JavaScript that describes objects, materials, lighting, and animations. But runtime AI-generated code is not trusted, and requires security sandboxing for safe execution. Also, mobile devices provide native support for 3D and XR rendering, and forcing them to run a webview limits the performance.

Today, we are excited to release Three-Live (v1.0.0, Developer Preview) under the Apache 2.0 license. It’s a lightweight, cross-platform open source library and on-device compiler that bridges the gap between AI-generated Three.js code and high-performance 3D, AR, and WebXR rendering across web, Android, and iOS.

How Three-Live works

Rather than use Three.js as a browser-only rendering loop, Three-Live treats a declarative subset of the Three.js API as a universal, portable scene description language:

Sandboxed execution with strict resource quotas: On the web, untrusted scripts execute inside an isolated Web Worker (with an optional opaque-origin sandboxed <iframe> tier) where network primitives (fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket, dynamic import()) are stripped before a single line of user code runs. On Android, iOS, macOS, and the command line, scripts execute inside an embedded Rust compiler powered by the Boa ECMAScript engine. Both runtimes enforce hard execution timeouts and geometry quotas (capping vertices, triangles, meshes, and procedural textures) so runaway scripts cannot freeze the host application.

Fast on-device compilation to GLB and USDZ: As the script constructs geometries, physically based rendering (PBR) materials, procedural canvas textures, hierarchy groups, and keyframe animations, Three-Live serializes the resulting scene graph directly into standard binary glTF 2.0 (.glb) and uncompressed Apple USDZ (.usdz) byte buffers in memory—typically in two to five milliseconds.

Platform-optimized rendering: Because the output is a standard binary 3D asset coupled with declarative animation bindings, each platform renders it using its built-in graphics pipeline:

  • Web (three-live and xr-live): A custom zero-dependency WebGL2 PBR renderer and <three-live> web component—inspired by <model-viewer>—complete with procedural Studio HDRI reflections, screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO), bloom, shadow mapping, and a single-click AR handoff to Android Scene Viewer, Apple AR Quick Look, or immersive WebXR. At launch, the standard bundle with sandboxed scripting and AR is about 45 KB gzipped, and the xr-live spatial computing suite is about 55 KB.
  • Android (com.google.threelive:compiler): A Kotlin SDK and multi-architecture JNI library (arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, x86_64) that compiles Three.js strings on a background coroutine straight into ByteBuffer assets for Google Filament ModelViewer and Scene Viewer AR.
  • iOS and macOS (ThreeLiveCompiler): A Swift Package and five-slice XCFramework that compiles Three.js scripts on-device for RealityKit ModelEntity and ARQuickLookPreviewController.

Declarative 3D and spatial WebXR in HTML

On the web, adding an interactive, AI-generated 3D model with built-in orbit controls and mobile AR support requires just a single HTML custom element:

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three-live@1.0.0/dist/three-live.min.js"></script>
<three-live allow-client-scripts camera-controls ar shadow-intensity="1" environment-image="studio">
  <script type="text/three-live">
    const knot = new THREE.Mesh(
      new THREE.TorusKnotGeometry(0.6, 0.2, 128, 32),
      new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({
        color: 0x4285f4,
        metalness: 0.85,
        roughness: 0.15
      })
    );
    scene.add(knot);
    // Baked into a looping glTF animation (4 seconds by default).
    scene.userData.animate = (t) => {
      knot.rotation.y = t * (Math.PI / 2);
    };
  </script>
</three-live>

The script runs in the sandbox described above. Because inline scripts are client-modifiable, they require the explicit allow-client-scripts opt-in; server-generated scripts can be loaded with script-src instead.

Only need to display existing models? The viewer-only build drops the script compiler and AR handoff and weighs about 23 KB gzipped at launch—tiny compared to the full Three.js library. The Three-Live viewer focuses on fast-loading PBR display, orbit controls, and glTF animation:

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three-live@1.0.0/dist/three-live-viewer.min.js"></script>
<three-live src="chair.glb" camera-controls auto-rotate></three-live>

For spatial computing headsets and mobile AR browsers, the companion xr-live package adds <xr-live> and <xr-scene>, enabling six-degrees-of-freedom (6DoF) hand-tracking gestures (pinch, grab, two-hand scale), spatial DOM projection, and real-time voice- or text-to-3D object synthesis inside an active WebXR session.

Try it today

We built Three-Live to make 3D and spatial computing accessible to web, mobile, and AI developer communities without requiring complex 3D modeling pipelines. You can explore the project and try it right in your browser:

  • Interactive browser playgrounds: Launch the live Three-Live Studio and XR-Live Playgrounds to edit procedural Three.js code and inspect real-time GLB compilation in your browser.
  • Source code and prebuilt binaries: Visit the google/three-live GitHub repository and the v1.0.0 GitHub Release for prebuilt Linux, macOS, and Windows CLI binaries (three-live-cli), Android .aar archives, and Apple .xcframework bundles.
  • Package managers: Install three-live and xr-live from npm, three-live-compiler from Crates.io, or add https://github.com/google/three-live.git in Xcode via Swift Package Manager.

Three-Live is currently in Developer Preview, and we welcome feedback, bug reports, and pull requests from open source developer communities on GitHub.

title: An open socket is not a connected device
description:
An operator sends a command to immobilize a vehicle. The server looks up the device's connection, writes the command to the socket, and the write succeeds. That does not show the device received it, much less that it carried it out.

In vehicle tracking, the TCP connection is only a means of communication. It is not a guarantee of availability. That is what this note is about.

The figures in the examples are illustrative: they come from a simulator with an assumed fleet, not from measurements of our gateways or of any carrier.

Connections that die without notice

We have worked with receiving gateways for GPS devices, telemetry and vehicle cameras. With JT808 and other tracking protocols, the device opens a persistent TCP connection and keeps it to send positions, alarms and other messages. How it behaves depends on the protocol and the manufacturer.

With mobile devices, that connection can stop working without the server receiving a close: the vehicle loses coverage, switches networks, or the carrier's NAT forgets the connection for being idle. The server keeps a socket that looks open, even though the device no longer has connectivity.

Three ways to find out

There are three mechanisms to learn that a connection died, and they are not equivalent:

  • Application activity: how long it has been since the device's last valid message.
  • The protocol's heartbeat: whether the device keeps sending its periodic presence messages.
  • TCP keepalive: the operating system's mechanism to detect connections that stopped responding.

In the simulator, a fleet of 2,000 devices sends a position every 30 seconds while moving and a heartbeat every five minutes while parked, and each device loses coverage about four times a day. In one day, 7,762 connections die without notice. This is how long the server takes to find out, at the median:

  • With three missing heartbeats, 12.8 minutes.
  • With TCP keepalive at Linux's defaults (two hours idle and nine probes), 2.2 hours.
  • If, on top of that, the same device's new session closes the old one, 10.3 minutes.

The system's keepalive, at its factory values, is no use for this, and on top of that it is off by default on each socket. And none of them is instant: during those minutes, the socket looks open.

I do not have a single heartbeat interval documented for our whole fleet: it depends on the protocol, the manufacturer and the configuration. Nor would I attribute a NAT expiry time to a carrier without having measured it. In the simulator they are assumptions, and you can change them.

What a heartbeat costs

A small heartbeat does not cost only its bytes. A 20-byte heartbeat, with the TCP/IP headers, its response and the ACK, is about 160. In the simulator, the fleet spends 1.22 MB a month per device just staying connected; counting only the heartbeat and its response it would look like 0.30. In a large fleet, that difference adds up.

Stretching the heartbeat to save data has a limit: the NAT. If the heartbeat is 15 minutes and the NAT forgets after 10, every heartbeat from a parked device hits a connection that no longer exists and forces a reconnection. In the simulator, the data drops by a quarter, from 1.22 to 0.91 MB, and the connections that die without notice go from 7,762 to more than 170,000.

Sent is not received

The command case is the most delicate. That is why I would distinguish four states:

  1. Command generated.
  2. Command sent to the connection.
  3. Command confirmed by the device.
  4. Action executed and verified.

Going from the second to the third takes a confirmation from the protocol; from the third to the fourth, where it applies, an independent check of the final state.

On the simulator's day, 988 commands are sent. Of them, 24 are written to a socket that was already dead: the server "sent" them and they never arrived. If "sent" counted as done, those would be 24 false successes. With a lifecycle that waits for the confirmation, eight are resent over the new session and 16 expire unconfirmed, in plain view of whoever sent them. And if the heartbeat goes past the NAT, the commands written to dead sockets rise to 322.

Two sessions from the same device

A device loses communication, reconnects and opens a new session before the server detects that the previous one no longer works. If the system manages connections only by socket, it can end up with two sessions from the same device.

My approach is a session registry per device, with a session identifier or generation. When a new, authenticated, valid session arrives, it replaces the previous one under an explicit policy, and the old one is invalidated and closed in a controlled way. You also have to keep a late close of the old session from accidentally wiping out the reference to the new one. I do not present this as a failure we suffered, but as a condition the design has to resolve.

The simulator compares the two registries. In its day, devices reconnect 4,579 times with the old session still open. With a registry by socket, which registers the device with every message and deletes the entry when any of its sessions closes, 4,566 of those late closes wipe out the new session. The device is still connected and the system takes it as disconnected until its next message: 335 device-hours in the day. If the registry were only updated at authentication, the device would stay "disconnected" until it reconnected again: 20,801 device-hours, and 429 commands would expire without finding a session. With a registry by generation, none.

Several instances

With several gateways, each device may be connected to a different instance. Knowing its IMEI is not enough: you have to know which instance holds its connection. I would design a distributed session registry with the device's identifier, the instance, the session's identifier and generation, the last valid activity, and its state and validity.

The command is routed to that instance, and the instance checks that it still holds the session before transmitting it. I would not send it to every gateway. And you have to account for the device moving to another instance while the command is in transit. The registry finds the connection, but it does not replace the protocol's confirmation or guarantee that the command was executed.

The restart that becomes a second failure

When a gateway restarts, the sessions in that process are cut. What happens next depends on the devices: some reconnect at fixed intervals, others with other strategies, and it cannot always be controlled from the platform. I have no documented incident of a mass reconnection, or a figure for devices that reconnected at once. What I do consider essential is that recovery must not turn into a second failure.

And three things have to be told apart: an accepted TCP connection, an authenticated device and a session ready to receive commands. In the simulator, the gateway is down for 15 seconds; it accepts 1,000 connections a second with a queue of 511 (the one Node.js uses unless told otherwise), authenticates 100 devices a second and initializes 200 sessions. With 2,000 devices retrying together every 30 seconds, 2,000 attempts arrive in one second. The queue fills up: Linux drops 3,323 SYNs, which the devices resend; 900 attempts are abandoned after waiting too long, and every session is ready for commands after 79 seconds. With a random wait of up to a minute, the peak is 74 attempts a second, nothing is dropped and all are ready after 60 seconds, a time that cannot go below that wait: the last device does not try before it. With 5,000 devices the gap grows: 195 seconds against 64, and with a fixed interval 27,363 SYNs are dropped.

What matters is not how many attempts arrive per second, but how long the system takes to recover every session. In a new design I would use staggered restarts where the architecture allows it, load distribution, and random waits on reconnection where the firmware supports them.

The limits you do not see

I have no documented incident from running out of file descriptors, memory or ports in our tracking gateways. But they are part of what has to be sized: the available descriptors, memory per connection, event loop usage, TCP accept queues and socket states. I would not assume a server can handle thousands of connections just because it has memory and CPU to spare.

What I would do today

In our current architectures we mainly use Node.js and NestJS for TCP reception, with specialized services per protocol, and RabbitMQ to decouple reception from processing. If I designed a gateway for thousands of devices from scratch today:

I would separate four responsibilities. Transport: sockets, connections, disconnections, timeouts and bytes. Protocol: identifying devices, parsing frames, validating messages and handling confirmations. Sessions: the device's identity, its current connection and the instance holding it. Messaging and processing: handing telemetry to the rest of the platform without blocking reception.

I would give commands a lifecycle of their own, with unique identifiers, execution states, expirations and confirmations.

I would measure from the start how many connections there are, how many are really active, how many reconnections happen per minute, how long it takes to detect a dead session and how many commands are left unconfirmed.

I would run load tests that go beyond sending positions: thousands of persistent connections, silent disconnections, duplicate sessions and gateway restarts.

To try it with another fleet, another heartbeat, another NAT or another gateway, there is the connection simulator: it runs in the browser, and everything it says is a model, not a measurement.

An open socket does not show that the device is effectively connected. A command sent does not show that it arrived. And an acknowledgment of receipt does not necessarily show that the action was carried out. When we manage many devices, reliability depends less on how many connections we can open and more on our ability to know the real state of each session and to recover correctly when communications fail.

The real challenge is not keeping thousands of sockets open, but managing thousands of devices whose connectivity can change at any moment.

Your turn

How does your platform know a device is really connected: the last message, a protocol heartbeat, or TCP keepalive? And when you send a command, what does your system show between "sent" and "confirmed"? If you want to try your own heartbeat, NAT and gateway numbers, the simulator is at crtdrops.mx/conexiones.

Israel Negrete Lepe is an electronics engineer. Twenty-five years making different systems work together under real conditions: from the sensor, the vehicle or the transaction to the backend, the data, security and operations. Today, increasingly, edge AI. I take on projects by the hour or by deliverable: israel0negrete@gmail.com.

I send a short email when a new note or lab result comes out: subscribe here.
