title: Testing callback ref cleanup on the same DOM node and in TypeScript
description:
A React callback ref can return a cleanup function as well as receive a DOM node. This capability, added in React 19, was tested through ResizeObserver registration and disconnection.

Unmounting is only part of the behavior. Even when the same DOM node remained, changing the callback reference ran the previous cleanup and the next registration.

Return disconnection from the callback that creates the observer

This function creates a callback ref and records its activity. With legacy: false, it returns cleanup. With true, it disconnects when called with null.

function makeTrackedRef(legacy) {
  let observer;
  function disconnect() {
    observer.disconnect();
    trace.active.delete(observer);
    trace.events.push('cleanup');
  }
  return node => {
    if (node === null) {
      trace.events.push('null');
      if (observer) disconnect();
      return;
    }
    observer = new ResizeObserver(() => {});
    observer.observe(node);
    trace.active.add(observer);
    trace.events.push('attach');
    if (!legacy) return disconnect;
  };
}

The fixture creates a real browser ResizeObserver and observes the node. trace.active tracks observers whose disconnection has not been recorded. Resize notification counts are not part of this comparison.

The test compares preserving a callback with creating a new one on every render:

export function RefExperiment({ stable, legacy }) {
  const [tick, setTick] = useState(0);
  const stableRef = useMemo(() => makeTrackedRef(legacy), [legacy]);
  const ref = stable ? stableRef : makeTrackedRef(legacy);
  return <section>
    <button id="rerender" onClick={() => setTick(previous => previous + 1)}>Render {tick}</button>
    <div id="observed" ref={ref}>Observed node</div>
  </section>;
}

Clicking the button rerenders the parent while the target div remains the same node. The root is then unmounted to verify cleanup.

A different callback triggers cleanup on the same node

Build and callback construction Initial log Log added by rerender Log added by unmount
Production, same callback, returns cleanup attach None cleanup
Production, new callback, returns cleanup attach cleanup → attach cleanup
Production, same callback, cleans up on null attach None null → cleanup
Development root Strict Mode, same callback, returns cleanup attach → cleanup → attach None cleanup
Development root Strict Mode, new callback, returns cleanup attach → cleanup → attach cleanup → attach cleanup
Development root Strict Mode, same callback, cleans up on null attach → null → cleanup → attach None null → cleanup

All 6 conditions had one tracked observer after initial processing and after rerender, then 0 after unmount. Even the version creating new callbacks paired setup with cleanup, so observers did not accumulate in this implementation.

The callback ref reference distinguishes returned cleanup, cleanup and reattachment when callbacks change, and the extra development cycle. No null call appeared in the returned-cleanup version's logs. Do not expect a second copy of the same cleanup through a null callback.

Direct comparison of node references before and after rerender confirmed that the DOM node stayed the same. Callback activity and DOM replacement are separate observations.

An implicit value return can fail type checking

Type behavior was also checked with TypeScript 7.0.2, @types/react 19.3.0, strict checking, and react-jsx.

import React from 'react';
const nodes = new Map<string, HTMLDivElement | null>();
export const view = <div ref={node => nodes.set('preview', node)} />;

Map.set returns the Map, so this callback did not satisfy the required void-or-cleanup return type and produced TS2322. A cleanup written as () => nodes.delete('preview') also produced TS2322 because it returns a boolean.

The version using a block and returning no value from cleanup passed:

import React from 'react';
const nodes = new Map<string, HTMLDivElement>();
export const view = <div ref={node => {
  if (!node) return;
  nodes.set('preview', node);
  return () => { nodes.delete('preview'); };
}} />;

This type comparison corresponds to the change described in the React 19 upgrade guide. When the operation is storing a node in a Map, avoid forwarding the Map operation's return value as the ref callback result.

Separate cleanup behavior from state-update loops

An existing article examined a ref callback that repeatedly updated state in an image preview. This experiment leaves state updates out of the observer callback and compares callback identity with cleanup timing. It does not establish that returning cleanup fixes arbitrary state-update loops.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with React and React DOM 19.3.0, Node.js 24.15.0, esbuild 0.28.2, macOS arm64, and Headless Chrome 152 and no React Compiler. The production cases also had a Strict Mode wrapper, but did not run the extra development cycle. Observer counts come from fixture registration and disconnection records, not measurements of the browser's internal resource usage.

The fixture code, logs for the 6 conditions, and 3 type-checking cases separate changes to the DOM node from changes to the callback reference.

title: Customize the Design of Your AddThis Widget
description:
I love the ease of use and rich feature set of the AddThis social media service. However, due to it’s popularity the design has become overused and mundane. I decided to see if I could customize it to match the overall experience of kevinleary.net.

The results came out pretty nice in my opinion. I may eventually swap out the [ + ] icon in the future, but for now I think it works. I’m always a bit hesitant to re-design consistencies.

Widget Code (trimmed)

<!-- AddThis Button BEGIN -->
<a href="https://apitracker.io/a/addthis" class="addthis_button_compact"></a>

Note that kevinlearynet is my AddThis username, so you’ll need to change this if you plan on using this for your website.

body #at15s_head,
body #at16pf
{
    display:none;
}

That’s it!

title: AWS PrivateLink is now available on Pro and Enterprise
description:
AWS PrivateLink is now available for Pro and Enterprise teams as part of Advanced Networking. It allows Vercel Functions and builds to connect to AWS-hosted services without sending traffic over the public internet.

Use it to reach AWS-hosted databases such as RDS, Aurora, and Neon; SaaS services such as Snowflake and MongoDB Atlas; internal services behind an AWS Network Load Balancer; and S3 or DynamoDB through gateway endpoints.

To configure PrivateLink, open your project's Networking settings and enable Advanced Networking. Select New Connection, then enter the service name and region.

The service must accept connections from all AWS principals or allowlist the IAM role Vercel provides for your team.

Vercel creates the connection and provides a stable hostname. Use this hostname from your Functions and builds to reach the service privately.

Pricing:

  • The first AWS PrivateLink connection is included with Advanced Networking. Each additional connection costs $30 per month.

  • PrivateLink data transfer costs $0.04 per GB.

Learn more in the AWS PrivateLink documentation.

title: Vercel Drives is now generally available
description:
Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. Its files remain available after the sandbox stops, so later runs and other sandboxes can access them by mounting the same Drive.

Use Drives to preserve an agent’s workspace or file-based memory across runs, or to make datasets, models, dependencies, and build artifacts available across sandboxes.

You can also fork a Drive into independent writable Drives. Forks inherit the source Drive's data, region, and maximum size, then store their own changes. Parallel workers can start with the same files and make changes without affecting the original or one another.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: React Context Explained: How It Works Under the Hood
description:
React’s Context API lets you share data between components without passing props manually through every level.

It’s designed for global values like theme, language, or authentication — where many components need access to the same data.

🧩 What is React Context?

Context provides a way to share values like theme, user, or locale deeply in the component tree without prop drilling.

It helps solve this problem:

// Before: prop drilling
<Layout theme="dark">
  <Header theme="dark">
    <Logo theme="dark" />
  </Header>
</Layout>

With Context:

<ThemeProvider value="dark">
  <Layout />
</ThemeProvider>

⚙️ How Context Works (Under the Hood)

Step 1 — Create 

const ThemeContext = React.createContext("light");
  • Creates a Context object with two parts:
    • A Provider component.
    • A reference for the current value inside React’s internal Fiber tree.

Step 2 — Provide 

<ThemeContext.Provider value="dark">
  <App />
</ThemeContext.Provider>
  • React stores the value on the Provider’s Fiber node.
  • Keeps track of all child consumers that read from this context.

Step 3 — Consume 

const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);
  • React looks upward in the component tree to find the nearest Provider.
  • Returns its value.
  • If the Provider’s value changes, React re-renders all consumers that depend on it.

🧠 What Happens Internally

  • Every Context keeps a _currentValue reference on its Provider.
  • useContext subscribes the component to that Provider.
  • When the Provider’s value changes, React marks all consumers for re-render.
  • React compares by reference, not by deep value.

So:

// ❌ Causes re-renders each time
<ThemeContext.Provider value={{ mode: "dark" }}>...</ThemeContext.Provider>

// ✅ Stable reference
const theme = useMemo(() => ({ mode }), [mode]);
<ThemeContext.Provider value={theme}>...</ThemeContext.Provider>

🧱 How to Use Context

Create a Context + Provider 

import { createContext, useContext, useState, useMemo } from "react";

const ThemeContext = createContext();

export function ThemeProvider({ children }) {
  const [mode, setMode] = useState("light");
  const value = useMemo(
    () => ({
      mode,
      toggle: () => setMode(m => (m === "light" ? "dark" : "light"))
    }),
    [mode]
  );

  return <ThemeContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</ThemeContext.Provider>;
}

export const useTheme = () => useContext(ThemeContext);

Use it in Components 

function Header() {
  const { mode, toggle } = useTheme();
  return (
    <header className={mode}>
      <button onClick={toggle}>Switch to {mode === "light" ? "dark" : "light"}</button>
    </header>
  );
}

Multiple Contexts 

<AuthProvider>
  <ThemeProvider>
    <App />
  </ThemeProvider>
</AuthProvider>

🔍 When (and When Not) to Use Context

✅ Use Context for:

  • Theme, locale, user, config
  • Shared but stable global data
  • App-wide settings

⚠️ Avoid for:

  • Rapidly changing values (inputs, lists, timers)
  • High-frequency updates — causes re-renders in all consumers

Use state libraries (Zustand, Redux, Jotai, etc.) or split contexts.

🧠 How React Handles Context Internally (Fiber)

  • Each Provider is a node in the Fiber tree.
  • Context changes propagate downward through fibers.
  • Each consumer using useContext subscribes to that Provider.
  • On update, React traverses the subtree to re-render affected components.
  • React guarantees consistency: all consumers see the same value in one render pass.

🚀 Optimization Tips

  1. Memoize values 
   const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, logout }), [user]);
  1. Split context 
   const UserContext = createContext();
   const ThemeContext = createContext();

→ Changing theme won’t re-render user consumers.

  1. Selector pattern Use libraries like use-context-selector for fine-grained subscriptions.
  2. Avoid passing new objects/functions each render.

✅ Summary

Concept Description
Context Share data deeply without prop drilling
Provider Sets value for all descendants
useContext Reads nearest Provider’s value
Triggers re-render When value prop changes by reference
Avoid Rapid updates or non-memoized objects

✨ React Context = global data flow with React’s rendering guarantees.

Used right, it’s powerful and efficient — used wrong, it becomes a hidden re-render trap.

Originally published on Bitlyst.

title: Debug and Test Laravel FCM Push Notifications with Pushbox
description:
You create a push notification in Laravel, send it through Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM), and... nothing appears on your phone.

What went wrong?

  • Is the notification payload correct?
  • Is Firebase configured properly?
  • Is the device token valid?
  • Did FCM accept the message?
  • Is the problem with the notification content or delivery?

Debugging these issues can take time, especially when you need to change code, trigger the notification again, and check the result.

I built Pushbox, an open-source Laravel package that helps you test FCM sending and preview push notifications from a visual interface.

What is Pushbox?

Pushbox is a notification testing and debugging tool for Laravel.

Its two main features are:

  1. Test sending — send a notification directly to a real device through FCM and check the sending result.
  2. Notification preview — inspect the generated notification content and FCM data payload without sending anything.

It also supports notification variants, translations, and different recipients.

The screenshots use an order-shipped notification from a demo store. The setup below uses WelcomePush to keep the code example small.

1. Install Pushbox

Pushbox supports Laravel 12/13 and PHP 8.4/8.5.

Install the package:

composer require andriichuk/pushbox
php artisan pushbox:install

For FCM support, install the Laravel notification channel:

composer require laravel-notification-channels/fcm:^6.2

Open /pushbox in your browser.

2. Register a notification

Let's create a simple FCM notification.

php artisan make:notification WelcomePush

use Illuminate\Notifications\Notification;
use NotificationChannels\Fcm\FcmChannel;
use NotificationChannels\Fcm\FcmMessage;
use NotificationChannels\Fcm\Resources\Notification as FcmNotification;

class WelcomePush extends Notification
{
    public function via(object $notifiable): array
    {
        return [FcmChannel::class];
    }

    public function toFcm(object $notifiable): FcmMessage
    {
        return new FcmMessage(
            notification: new FcmNotification(
                title: 'Welcome!',
                body: 'Hello '.($notifiable->name ?? 'developer').'!',
            ),
            data: [
                'screen' => 'welcome',
            ],
        );
    }
}

Now register it in routes/pushbox.php:

use App\Notifications\WelcomePush;
use Andriichuk\Pushbox\Facades\Pushbox;

Pushbox::add(WelcomePush::class);

Your notification is now available in Pushbox.

You can select it from the interface, inspect its content, and test sending it.

3. Send a test push notification to your device

This is especially useful when your notification is not arriving and you want to check whether the FCM sending request works.

First, configure Firebase credentials using the Laravel FCM notification channel.

Enable test sending in your .env:

PUSHBOX_ALLOW_SEND=true

You can optionally configure a default device token:

PUSHBOX_FCM_TOKEN=your-device-token

Or enter your FCM token directly in the Pushbox interface under Device settings.

Make sure the token belongs to the same Firebase project as your credentials.

For the failure example below, I’m deliberately using an invalid demo token. Use your own device’s FCM token when testing delivery.

Now:

  1. Open /pushbox.
  2. Select your notification.
  3. Check the generated payload.
  4. Click Send notification.
  5. Check the sending result and your device.

Pushbox sends the notification immediately through FCM.

The result can be:

Status Meaning
Accepted FCM accepted the sending request
Failed The sending request failed
Skipped The notification wasn't sent

Important: An accepted result does not guarantee that the notification was delivered or displayed on the device.

But it helps narrow down the problem.

If sending fails, you can investigate your Firebase configuration, credentials, device token, or message. If FCM accepts the request but nothing appears on the phone, you'll need to investigate device-side delivery and handling.

Inspect a failed send

Here’s Firebase rejecting the invalid demo token. Pushbox displays the failure in the workspace and provides a shortcut back to Device settings.

Expand Technical details to inspect the status, masked target, notification class, FCM channel, and the provider’s error response. Here, Firebase reports that the registration token is invalid.

You can test the notification without triggering the normal application flow every time.

4. Preview the notification payload before sending

Sometimes the problem isn't Firebase.

The notification itself may contain an incorrect title, body, translation, or data payload.

For example:

public function toFcm(object $notifiable): FcmMessage
{
    return new FcmMessage(
        notification: new FcmNotification(
            title: 'Your order is ready',
            body: 'Order #1234 is ready for pickup.',
        ),
        data: [
            'screen' => 'orders',
            'order_id' => '1234',
        ],
    );
}

Pushbox lets you inspect the generated notification and its data fields before sending it.

You can check:

  • Notification title and body
  • FCM data payload
  • Values generated for a specific recipient
  • Different notification variants

Expand Raw payload to inspect the serialized FCM message. Platform settings shows values such as Android’s time to live.

This is useful when debugging notifications that open the wrong screen, display incorrect text, or contain missing data.

You don't need a physical device just to inspect the payload.

5. Test notifications with different recipients

Notification content often depends on the user.

For example:

body: 'Hello '.($notifiable->name ?? 'developer').'!',

To preview a notification with a specific recipient:

use App\Models\User;
use App\Notifications\WelcomePush;
use Andriichuk\Pushbox\Facades\Pushbox;

Pushbox::to(
    User::factory()->make([
        'name' => 'Ada',
    ])
)->add(WelcomePush::class);

Now you can inspect the notification generated for Ada.

Using factory()->make() avoids creating an actual user record.

This makes it easier to reproduce different notification scenarios during development.

6. Compare notification variants

Sometimes you need to test multiple versions of a notification.

Pushbox lets you organize notifications into categories and register named variants.

Pushbox::to(
    User::factory()->make(['name' => 'Ada'])
)
    ->category('Onboarding')
    ->group(function () {
        Pushbox::add(WelcomePush::class)
            ->variant(
                'Another greeting',
                fn (): WelcomePush => new WelcomePush()
            );
    });

This example registers a named variant. You can return a differently configured notification instance to compare actual content changes.

It's useful when working with different notification messages or testing alternative payloads.

In the demo, the Long order reference variant provides a longer title and body to check text wrapping.

Check collapsed and expanded previews

Switch between Collapsed and Expanded to check how much text fits. Long titles and bodies can be truncated in the collapsed preview. The Android preview is an approximation; actual rendering depends on the device and client app.

7. Preview notifications in different languages

If your application supports multiple languages, you probably need to check how push notifications look for each locale.

For example:

new FcmNotification(
    title: __('notifications.welcome_title'),
    body: __('notifications.welcome_body'),
);

Pushbox supports a locale selector.

Publish the configuration:

php artisan vendor:publish --tag=pushbox-config

Configure available languages:

// config/pushbox.php

'locales' => [
    'en' => 'English',
    'uk' => 'Ukrainian',
],

Now you can switch between languages in the interface and inspect the generated notification.

This helps catch missing or incorrect translations before sending them to users.

8. Restrict access

Pushbox is a developer tool, so don't leave it publicly accessible.

You can disable it:

PUSHBOX_ENABLED=false

Or protect it using a Laravel Gate:

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Gate;

Gate::define('viewPushbox', function (?User $user): bool {
    return $user !== null
        && $user->can('use-developer-tools');
});

Pushbox also supports middleware and IP allowlists.

Configure access restrictions before using it in a publicly accessible environment.

Final thoughts

Debugging push notifications shouldn't require repeatedly triggering your application's normal notification flow just to check a payload or test FCM sending.

With Pushbox, you can:

  • Send test notifications directly to a real device.
  • Check whether FCM accepted or rejected a sending request.
  • Preview notification content and payloads before sending.
  • Test different recipients, variants, and translations.

It's not a replacement for Firebase delivery diagnostics, but it makes the Laravel side of push notification debugging easier.

GitHub: https://github.com/andriichuk/pushbox

Pushbox is open-source and MIT-licensed.

I'd love to hear how other Laravel developers debug push notification issues.

How do you currently test FCM sending and inspect notification payloads in your projects?

title: The Anti-Awkward First Date Playbook: Why Center-Table Physics Breaks the Ice
description:
A first date can start out feeling like a job interview in nice clothes.

"What do you do for work?"

"Where did you grow up?"

"Do you come to this cafe often?"

Those questions aren’t inherently bad. The trouble is that they put all the pressure on two people to continuously produce the next line of dialogue. When a pause arrives, both people notice it, get self-conscious, and suddenly the awkward pause becomes the entire focus of the table.

A shared activity gives your mutual attention somewhere else to go.

1. Put Something in the Middle of the Table

Table Mode in Wobbly Bottle was designed for a single phone placed flat in the middle of the table between both drinks.

The bottle spins on that screen; two people take turns and use the prompt as a natural springboard for conversation.

The phone becomes a small shared focal point. Instead of staring across the table and trying to invent the next clever question, both people react to the same visual moment: the spin, the suspense as the physics slows down, and the comic relief of a squeaky rubber chicken squawking on screen.

2. Why a Shared Object Changes the Chemistry

When every pause seems to demand an immediate conversational recovery, tension builds up. A small game changes the psychological rhythm:

  1. There is a simple next action: Swipe to spin.
  2. There is a shared result to react to: Both eyes are locked on the same outcome.
  3. A prompt opens a door: It leads naturally into travel stories, funny childhood phases, or playful debates.
  4. Either person controls the depth: You can keep the answer light and sarcastic, or take it in a deeper direction.

The point isn’t to outsource the date to a mobile app. It’s to have a gentle fallback when the conversation needs a nudge.

3. Comfort Comes Before Competition

The best icebreaker is one both people actually want to play. In Wobbly Bottle:

  • Zero account creation or sign-up walls: Start playing in 2 seconds.
  • Easy pass option: If a question feels too personal for date one, skip it with a tap.
  • Works 100% offline: No cellular data or Wi-Fi needed in noisy bars or cozy cafes.

When the conversation finds its own rhythm and the ice is broken, put the phone back in your pocket and enjoy the evening.

title: Choosing Matter Gateway Development Boards: A Hardware and Validation Checklist
description:
Gateway shopping lists grow quickly: a Linux board, a Bluetooth kit, a debugger, a serial adapter, a packet sniffer, power supplies, cables and breakout boards. Each item seems useful.

Then you start connecting them. One board is missing a pin. A firmware image targets a different chip. Another tool turns out to be unnecessary for the experiment in front of you. You have bought the hardware, but still cannot assemble the connection you wanted to test.

Our project bridges Bluetooth Mesh devices into Matter. A Linux host handles Matter and device mapping; a Silicon Labs module runs the Bluetooth Mesh stack; Telink-based lights and switches sit downstream. The PC prototype already connects to Apple Home, and we have built a Linux system image. Flashing the target board, testing real Silicon Labs–Telink Mesh interoperability and verifying the complete system are still ahead.

That makes my purchasing rule straightforward: each purchase should help answer a specific unresolved question.

Draw the connection before buying hardware

An operation in Apple Home should follow this path:

Apple Home
    ↓ Matter over the local network
Linux host: device mapping, commands, state synchronization
    ↓ UART / BGAPI
Silicon Labs module: Bluetooth Mesh NCP firmware
    ↓ Bluetooth Mesh
Telink device: light or switch

When someone presses the device's physical button, its new state must travel back and update Apple Home.

This diagram prevents a few common purchasing mistakes. The Matter connection in this design uses Ethernet or Wi-Fi. The downstream radio network is Bluetooth Mesh. Bluetooth Mesh and Thread are different protocols, despite both being mesh networks.

Using Matter here does not automatically require a Thread development kit or a Thread border router. Those become relevant if we later develop or connect Matter-over-Thread devices. Apple Home controllers, home hubs and software versions should follow Apple's current compatibility requirements.

Built-in Bluetooth on a Linux board also does not automatically replace our NCP. It normally comes with a different driver and host software arrangement. Our architecture places the Mesh stack on a separate module and accesses it through BGAPI; replacing that layer means evaluating the software interface and stack as well.

Start with the Bluetooth experiment

The PC-and-phone prototype let us work on Matter before the hardware arrived. The next useful purchase should establish whether the Silicon Labs module can control the Telink devices as required.

An existing PC can remain the host. Connect the Silicon Labs kit through its supported serial interface or a suitable USB-to-UART adapter. Get provisioning, control and status reporting working before moving the host to a Linux board. That gives each failure fewer possible causes.

Item What to check Question it answers
Silicon Labs development kit Exact chip and board IDs, Mesh NCP example support, programming and serial interfaces Can the intended SDK and firmware run on this hardware?
Telink board or controllable light sample Reflashable firmware, known Mesh models, factory-reset procedure Do provisioning, model control and status reporting interoperate?
Programmer/debugger Whether the kit includes it and whether it connects to this target Can we flash, recover and inspect the firmware?
USB data cable, power supply and wiring Data capability, power specifications, connectors and signal levels Are power and connections reliable?
USB-to-UART adapter, if needed Exposed flow-control pins and logic levels Can the host communicate with the NCP?

One device board running a standard on/off model is enough to start. Observing its LED is easier than immediately connecting a mains-powered light.

After the smallest setup works, add a second node, dimming and multi-channel devices to exercise group control, multiple elements and different models. One working node proves the basic procedure; it says little about network capacity or long-term reliability.

Match the Silicon Labs board to the firmware

A search for an “xG24 development board” produces kits with different chips, connectors and accessories. “BG24 module” in a design document is not a precise enough order specification.

Our planned module is in the BGM240 family. Before ordering, match the production module, the evaluation board's chip, the SDK version and the example project. Sharing “24” in their names does not mean two boards can run the same firmware binary.

I would confirm five things:

  1. Can the chosen Bluetooth Mesh SDK create the required NCP project for this exact board?
  2. Are the provisioner and required client models covered by examples or documented configuration?
  3. Does the target meet the project's Flash, RAM and component requirements?
  4. Does the kit include a debugger or development mainboard? What else is needed if buying a radio board separately?
  5. Where are UART, flow-control, reset and debug signals, and can an external host reach them?

A working Bluetooth example establishes support for that example. We need Bluetooth Mesh NCP specifically, so I would ask the supplier to identify the corresponding board and project.

The NCP application and its bootloader are also separate components. Flashing through a debugger proves that programming path. If the Linux host will later update the module over UART, we must also check the bootloader, pins, update-entry procedure and compatible firmware combination.

A complete kit may cost more than a bare board, but included debugging, serial access and documentation can save a lot of piecemeal setup.

A USB-to-UART chip name is not enough

Small FT232- or CP2102-based adapters are easy to buy without much thought. Some expose only TX, RX, ground and power. Even if the chip supports other signals, inaccessible pins on the finished adapter are no help.

For this design, I would choose an adapter exposing TX, RX, RTS, CTS and GND, then confirm driver support at the required baud rate. Check the finished board's pinout and schematic.

RTS/CTS coordinates the two ends of the connection. Wire signals according to their direction and both board manuals. The NCP configuration, host settings and physical wiring must agree: an endpoint waiting for flow control that is not connected may never communicate normally.

Hardware flow control reduces loss caused by an overwhelmed receiver. It does not provide error checking or retransmission. Electrical interference, wiring faults and parser errors still need their own diagnosis. Whether flow control is enabled depends on both ends; our hardware plan reserves the necessary connections.

Check voltage levels too. A board's UART might use 1.8V or 3.3V. A “3.3V/5V” jumper may select only the adapter's power output, without changing TX/RX logic levels.

Before ordering, establish the signal voltage, exposed flow-control pins and supported baud rates. TTL UART and RS-232 are not directly interchangeable. If the target already has its own supply, decide whether to connect the adapter's power pin according to the board's power design.

Choose the Linux board for its SDK and usable interfaces

We already compared processors in the RK3506, RK3562, RK3576 and RDK X5 article. Purchasing is now about development conditions.

Route Useful for Check before buying
RK3562 board The planned standard gateway platform Vendor BSP, UART pin muxing, flow control, Wi-Fi drivers and module availability
RK3506 board Evaluating a smaller configuration once functionality works 32-bit toolchain, measured memory use, storage layout and security support
RDK X5 Continuing our existing SDK and system-image work Board revision, image compatibility, flashing and interface configuration
Existing Linux computer or board Host-program and serial-protocol development Program compatibility and suitable serial or USB connections

We do not need all four. RK3562 is the planned standard product platform, while system-image work began with the X5 SDK. An existing platform can answer useful questions before the final hardware is selected.

I want four things from a Linux board supplier.

A rebuildable SDK: download access, version, build environment, toolchain and board configuration. A preinstalled image alone leaves us dependent on the supplier when trimming the system or changing drivers.

A usable application UART: a processor having many UARTs does not guarantee that a full TX/RX/RTS/CTS set reaches an accessible header. Check pin sharing and device-tree configuration. Keep the debug console separate so boot logs do not enter the NCP protocol stream.

A recovery path: flashing interface, recovery mode, debug console and partition documentation. When a custom image fails to boot, these become more valuable than extra compute performance.

Networking and persistent storage suited to the system: check IPv6, local discovery, Wi-Fi drivers and where configuration and device data survive reboots. Routers, VLANs, client isolation and firewalls can interfere with discovery. This is separate from purchasing public IPv6 service from an ISP.

Our earlier Buildroot work found IPv6 disabled in the default configuration. Booting successfully and reaching the internet are only the beginning of checking a Matter gateway.

Buy sniffers and logic analyzers when needed

The original topic notes included an nRF52840 Dongle. I would not make it mandatory in the first order.

Tools such as nRF Sniffer for Bluetooth LE can help observe radio traffic. Supported hardware, firmware and capture methods must match the tool version. Mesh analysis also depends on the bearer, encryption, keys and decoding software.

Buying a Bluetooth dongle does not automatically make all Mesh application traffic readable. Buy it once a problem really requires radio-level observation and the tool supports the traffic of interest. It also does not automatically serve as a Thread sniffer or the gateway's NCP.

A logic analyzer is useful for UART activity: bytes on the line, flow-control transitions and the stream around a fault. Choose input levels, channel count and sampling capability appropriate for the actual signals.

For the first experiments, capture serial logs, command responses, Mesh status events and timestamps. Add electrical or radio observation when those logs leave a specific question unanswered.

Test each layer after the boards arrive

Stage Work Evidence that this layer works
Development kit Flash supported firmware; connect serial, reset and debugger Stable communication and expected startup events or version information
Minimal Mesh network Provision and configure through a supported host example or tool Device operates and returns status
State in both directions Operate the device's physical button The host receives the change
Our host program Implement commands, responses and events Add, control, query and remove the same device
Matter bridge Map the device to Matter endpoints Apple Home controls it and receives device-side changes
Linux integration Move to the target board; configure startup, networking and UART Correct startup and restoration of device identity and persistent data
Recovery Restart host, module and device separately; disconnect network and power Explain the displayed state during failure and recover control and synchronization

Sending a command and completing a physical operation are different milestones. A successful serial write means bytes reached the serial subsystem. An NCP response must be interpreted according to the operation it acknowledges. Device state needs the relevant Mesh Status, observation of the device and agreement with the Matter display.

If Apple Home immediately shows a light as on while the real light remains off, the test has not passed. With optimistic state updates, also unplug the device and test response timeouts: the interface should not retain an incorrect state indefinitely.

Split recovery tests as well. Recovering from a host reboot does not prove module replacement works. A retained device list does not prove keys, sequence numbers and network state are handled correctly. Module replacement and network restoration need dedicated reliability work.

How I would place the orders

First, buy a Silicon Labs kit that supports the intended NCP firmware and one controllable Telink device board. Fill gaps in power, cables and programming access. Use the PC to establish provisioning, model control and status reporting.

Second, add the target Linux board and migrate the working host program. Confirm the SDK, complete UART interface and recovery procedure, preferably within a vendor ecosystem that can also support the future production module.

Then increase device variety and count. Test multi-channel switches, dimming, disconnections and recovery. Buy specialist capture and measurement tools as problems justify them.

Here is a supplier request you can reuse:

We are building a Linux-hosted gateway with a Bluetooth Mesh NCP. Please provide the exact board model and hardware revision, matching SDK and example project, required programming/debugging accessories, and the pinouts and logic levels for UART, RTS/CTS, reset and debug. For the Linux board, please also confirm UART device-tree configuration, system rebuild instructions and recovery flashing.

Clear answers make a board worth considering. A useful development setup helps resolve firmware compatibility, interoperability, return status and recovery one question at a time. Once those are understood, cost reduction and a custom carrier board become much better-informed decisions.

Working on Silicon Labs NCP, Telink interoperability or Linux UART integration? Get in touch.

References: Silicon Labs Bluetooth Mesh API, RDK documentation, Luckfox Lyra RK3506, nRF Sniffer for Bluetooth LE.

title: DPU Offload vs Host Cores: When the 100G NIC Stops Being Free
description:
A serving node that pushes 100 Gbps of model traffic does not do it for free. Depending on kernel, MTU and how many small requests you handle, the host burns somewhere between two and six cores on network stack work: interrupts, softirq, socket copies, TLS record processing. On a 64-core machine that is 3% to 9% of the machine, which sounds acceptable until you remember that inference is often memory-bandwidth-bound and those cores are also competing for the same uncore resources.

The obvious answer is to offload the network to a DPU. The obvious answer is also where most teams waste $200,000. Here is the arithmetic that decides it.

Part One: What the host actually does per request

Take a realistic serving configuration: HTTPS, 4 KB average request body, 40 KB response, 300 requests per second per node. Per request the host performs a TLS handshake amortised across connections, parses HTTP headers, copies the body into user space, runs tokenisation, and copies the response back out. The network-attributable portion is roughly 45 to 70 microseconds of CPU time per request on a modern core with kernel bypass disabled.

At 300 requests per second, that is 13 to 21 milliseconds of core time per second, or 1.3% to 2.1% of a single core. Multiply by 40 nodes and you have spent less than one core across the fleet. Offloading that to a $2,000 DPU per node is obviously wrong.

Now change one variable: request size. Agent workloads send 20 KB to 200 KB of context per call. At 80 KB average, per-request network CPU rises to roughly 180 to 260 microseconds, and at 300 requests per second you are at 5% to 8% of a core per node, plus softirq contention that shows up as p99 jitter rather than throughput loss.

Change a second variable: connection churn. If clients reconnect per request instead of pooling, TLS handshakes dominate and you can lose a full core per node. This is common in multi-tenant gateways and almost never measured.

The offload decision is not about bandwidth, it is about CPU-seconds per byte and how much of them land on the critical path of your p99.

Part Two: What a DPU actually takes off the host

A DPU is an Arm-based SoC with a NIC attached. It can host a full network stack: OVS, IPsec, TLS termination, load balancing, telemetry collection. When configured well, the host sees a virtio or SR-IOV device and the entire packet path disappears from its CPU accounting.

Three things are worth offloading, in order of payoff. First, IPsec or WireGuard for inter-node traffic: this is pure per-packet cost with no application value, and it typically costs 0.8 to 1.5 cores per node at 100 Gbps. Second, TLS record processing at the edge: it removes both CPU and the associated cache pollution. Third, telemetry and flow logging, which is the classic death-by-a-thousand-cuts workload.

Three things are usually not worth offloading. Application-layer load balancing, because you need model-aware routing that a DPU cannot do. Request-level authentication, because it needs the same state as the model server. And anything with a fast-changing policy, because every change becomes a DPU firmware deployment.

Part Three: The break-even arithmetic

A current-generation 200G DPU with dual 100G ports and reasonable Arm cores lists around $1,800 to $2,600, and consumes 25 to 45 watts. Amortised over three years that is roughly $55 to $80 per month per node, plus the switch port and the operational cost of a second operating system to patch.

A cloud vCPU costs $18 to $35 per month at committed rates. On-prem, the fully loaded cost of a core is $12 to $20 per month. So a DPU pays for itself when it frees roughly four to six cores per node.

Four to six cores is a lot. That threshold is only crossed when you are doing IPsec at line rate, terminating a high-churn TLS workload, or running a service mesh sidecar per pod. For a plain HTTP inference server with connection pooling, the DPU is a $2,000 device that saves one core.

This is why the adoption pattern looks odd from the outside. Hyperscalers with custom silicon deploy DPUs everywhere, because they are also running overlay networks, encryption at line rate and per-tenant telemetry. Mid-size clusters buy DPUs, enable SR-IOV, and never turn on the offload features, which is the worst of both worlds: you paid for the device and still burn the cores.

Part Four: What changes by 2030

Two trends move the break-even point.

Confidential computing moves it toward the DPU. Encrypting all inter-node traffic in memory is now a compliance requirement in several regulated industries, and doing that in software costs 10% to 25% of throughput. A DPU does it in hardware for close to nothing. As confidential inference becomes standard for healthcare and financial workloads, the DPU stops being optional.

Smaller models move it away. A 3B-parameter model serving short requests has very little per-request network cost, and the fleet that serves it does not need a $2,000 NIC. If the industry's inference volume shifts toward many small models rather than a few large ones, the DPU market grows more slowly than the optimists expect.

My estimate: DPU attach rate in AI serving clusters goes from roughly 15% today to 45% to 55% by 2030, with the growth concentrated in regulated and multi-tenant environments. The device market grows to $8 to $12 billion, but the more interesting number is the software market around it, which is where the operational pain actually lives.

The daily-life angle

Every time you use a voice assistant and it responds before you finish your sentence, some part of that latency budget was spent moving audio frames through a network stack. Offload decisions made by an infrastructure team you will never meet determine whether that feels instant or slightly laggy. The same is true of a translation feature in a browser, or a photo feature that runs server-side. Users experience the sum of a hundred such decisions as a single quality judgement: "this app feels fast."

For engineers, the actionable version is unglamorous. Instrument CPU time attributable to the network before you buy anything. On Linux, perf on softirq plus ss -ti for retransmit and queue stats gives you most of the answer in an afternoon.

If you cannot attribute at least four cores per node to network work, a DPU is a purchase you will regret in the second year, when the firmware is three versions behind.

The transferable lesson

Offload hardware follows a predictable lifecycle. It arrives expensive and specialised, gets adopted by the few operators whose workload genuinely justifies it, then drifts into general procurement as a default because nobody wants to be the team that skipped it.

The teams that get value are the ones who keep measuring. The teams that do not are the ones who bought the device for the brochure and left the features off. In infrastructure, the difference between a 20% efficiency gain and a 20% cost increase is usually one afternoon of measurement, taken before the purchase order rather than after.

title: Cursor Cloud Agents can now run in Vercel Sandbox
description:
Cursor Cloud Agents can now run in Vercel Sandbox instead of Cursor's hosted machines.

Cursor manages the agent harness and inference loop. Its Self-Hosted Machines APIs let you supply the execution environment where agents clone repositories, edit files, and run commands and tests. Self-Hosted Machines requires a Cursor Enterprise plan.

Vercel Sandbox provides that execution environment as an isolated Firecracker microVM for each agent request. Vercel Functions and Vercel Workflows form a durable control plane that claims queued agent requests, provisions workers, monitors sessions, and cleans up automatically.

With this architecture, you get:

  • A scale-to-zero worker pool without long-lived virtual machines

  • A dedicated, isolated Sandbox for every agent request

  • Durable retries when a worker or session fails

  • Short-lived, user-scoped credentials inside each Sandbox

title: Beyond 1,000 Rows: Building a TypeScript Data Grid That Actually Scales Across React, Vue, and Angular
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Most data grids start dying the moment you cross a thousand rows. The DOM chokes, the scroll janks, and your framework's reactivity system turns into a bottleneck. The fix isn't a library—it's an architecture. In this deep-dive, we'll build a framework-agnostic TypeScript data grid core that handles 100,000+ rows smoothly, then show how to plug it into React, Vue, and Angular without rewriting the logic.

  • 1. Why Data Grids Break Past 1,000 Rows
  • 2. Architecture: Framework-Agnostic Core
  • 3. Virtualization: The Key to Scale
  • 4. State Management and Change Detection
  • 5. Rendering Strategies for React, Vue, and Angular
  • 6. Implementing the Grid: A Complete Example
  • 7. Performance Tuning and Best Practices
  • 8. Conclusion
  • Frequently Asked Questions

1. Why Data Grids Break Past 1,000 Rows

A typical grid renders one <tr> per row. At 1,000 rows, that's 1,000 DOM nodes plus cells—already heavy but manageable. At 10,000 rows, you're pushing 100,000+ nodes, and the browser's layout engine spends more time recalculating styles than painting content. The problem compounds with reactive frameworks: every state change triggers a diff across the entire tree.

Three bottlenecks dominate:

  1. DOM size — The browser must create, style, and layout every node. Even if you render once, a 10,000-row table costs hundreds of milliseconds to paint.
  2. Framework reconciliation — React's virtual DOM, Vue's reactivity, and Angular's change detection all iterate over the full data set on updates.
  3. Scroll performance — Native scroll events fire at 60+ Hz. Without virtualization, every scroll event forces a full re-render.

The solution isn't to optimize the framework—it's to sidestep it. We'll build a core that manages data, selection, sorting, and virtualization in plain TypeScript. The framework layer becomes a thin adapter that only renders what's visible.

2. Architecture: Framework-Agnostic Core

Our design uses a core-plus-adapter pattern. The core is pure TypeScript, framework-agnostic, and testable. The adapter handles DOM mounting and framework-specific reactivity.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Framework Adapter              │
│  (React / Vue / Angular)                    │
│  - Subscribes to core events                │
│  - Renders visible rows only                │
│  - Handles user interactions                │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                       │
                       │  events / commands
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Grid Core                   │
│  - Data store (rows, columns)               │
│  - Selection & sorting state                │
│  - Virtualization math                      │
│  - Event emitter                            │
│  - Pure functions, no DOM                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The core exposes a simple API:

// core/types.ts
export interface GridColumn<T> {
  key: keyof T & string;
  header: string;
  width: number;
  sortable?: boolean;
  renderer?: (value: T[keyof T], row: T) => string;
}

export interface GridState<T> {
  rows: T[];
  columns: GridColumn<T>[];
  sortKey: keyof T | null;
  sortDirection: 'asc' | 'desc' | null;
  selectedRowIds: Set<string>;
  scrollTop: number;
  viewportHeight: number;
  rowHeight: number;
}

export interface GridEvent<T> {
  type: 'row-click' | 'sort' | 'selection-change' | 'scroll';
  payload?: T | keyof T | number;
}

The core is a class that maintains state and emits change events:

// core/GridCore.ts
import { GridColumn, GridEvent, GridState } from './types';

export class GridCore<T extends { id: string }> {
  private state: GridState<T>;
  private listeners: Array<(event: GridEvent<T>) => void> = [];

  constructor(rows: T[], columns: GridColumn<T>[], rowHeight = 40) {
    this.state = {
      rows,
      columns,
      sortKey: null,
      sortDirection: null,
      selectedRowIds: new Set(),
      scrollTop: 0,
      viewportHeight: 600,
      rowHeight,
    };
  }

  subscribe(listener: (event: GridEvent<T>) => void) {
    this.listeners.push(listener);
    return () => {
      this.listeners = this.listeners.filter((l) => l !== listener);
    };
  }

  private emit(event: GridEvent<T>) {
    this.listeners.forEach((l) => l(event));
  }

  setRows(rows: T[]) {
    this.state.rows = rows;
    this.emit({ type: 'selection-change' }); // generic refresh
  }

  sortBy(key: keyof T) {
    if (this.state.sortKey === key) {
      this.state.sortDirection = this.state.sortDirection === 'asc' ? 'desc' : 'asc';
    } else {
      this.state.sortKey = key;
      this.state.sortDirection = 'asc';
    }
    const dir = this.state.sortDirection === 'asc' ? 1 : -1;
    this.state.rows = [...this.state.rows].sort((a, b) => {
      if (a[key] < b[key]) return -1 * dir;
      if (a[key] > b[key]) return 1 * dir;
      return 0;
    });
    this.emit({ type: 'sort', payload: key });
  }

  selectRow(id: string) {
    if (this.state.selectedRowIds.has(id)) {
      this.state.selectedRowIds.delete(id);
    } else {
      this.state.selectedRowIds.add(id);
    }
    this.emit({ type: 'selection-change', payload: id });
  }

  getVisibleRows(scrollTop: number, viewportHeight: number): T[] {
    const { rows, rowHeight } = this.state;
    const startIndex = Math.floor(scrollTop / rowHeight);
    const endIndex = Math.min(
      rows.length,
      Math.ceil((scrollTop + viewportHeight) / rowHeight) + 1
    );
    return rows.slice(startIndex, endIndex);
  }

  getState() {
    return this.state;
  }
}

The core never touches the DOM. It only computes which rows are visible based on scrollTop and viewportHeight. That's the foundation for virtualization.

3. Virtualization: The Key to Scale

Virtualization means rendering only the rows that fit in the viewport, plus a small buffer. For a 100,000-row grid with a 40px row height and a 600px viewport, you render about 16 rows instead of 100,000.

3.1 The Math

Given scrollTop, viewportHeight, and rowHeight:

  • startIndex = floor(scrollTop / rowHeight)
  • endIndex = ceil((scrollTop + viewportHeight) / rowHeight)
  • Add a buffer of 2–5 rows above and below to avoid blank flashes during fast scrolling.

3.2 Overscan Buffer

A buffer of 3 rows is usually enough. For smooth scrolling, we render startIndex - 3 to endIndex + 3. This hides the moment when a row enters the viewport but hasn't been rendered yet.

3.3 Fixed vs. Variable Row Heights

Fixed heights are easy—the math above works. Variable heights require measuring each row after render and storing offsets. For simplicity, we'll assume fixed heights. If you need variable heights, maintain a Map<rowId, height> and compute cumulative offsets with a Fenwick tree or binary search.

4. State Management and Change Detection

The core emits events, but it doesn't know about frameworks. Each adapter subscribes and maps events to its own reactivity system. This keeps the core pure and makes it testable with plain Node.

4.1 Event-Driven Updates

Instead of frameworks polling the core, the core pushes changes. This is critical—if the framework has to check every row on every scroll, you're back to O(n) work.

4.2 Avoiding Full Re-renders

When the user scrolls, only the visible window changes. The adapter should:

  1. Compute the new visible rows via core.getVisibleRows().
  2. Update only the DOM nodes that changed, not the entire table.

In React, this means using useMemo and React.memo on row components. In Vue, use computed and v-memo. In Angular, use ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush and track by index.

5. Rendering Strategies for React, Vue, and Angular

Each framework has its own idiom for rendering a list of visible rows. The key is to never iterate over all rows in the template.

5.1 React 

// ReactAdapter.tsx
import React, { useMemo, useState, useEffect } from 'react';
import { GridCore } from './core/GridCore';

interface Props<T> {
  core: GridCore<T>;
  viewportHeight: number;
}

export function DataGrid<T extends { id: string }>({ core, viewportHeight }: Props<T>) {
  const [scrollTop, setScrollTop] = useState(0);

  const visibleRows = useMemo(
    () => core.getVisibleRows(scrollTop, viewportHeight),
    [core, scrollTop, viewportHeight]
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    const unsubscribe = core.subscribe((event) => {
      if (event.type === 'sort' || event.type === 'selection-change') {
        // Force re-render by updating a dummy state
        setScrollTop((prev) => prev);
      }
    });
    return unsubscribe;
  }, [core]);

  const handleScroll = (e: React.UIEvent<HTMLDivElement>) => {
    setScrollTop(e.currentTarget.scrollTop);
  };

  return (
    <div
      style={{ height: viewportHeight, overflowY: 'auto' }}
      onScroll={handleScroll}
    >
      <table>
        <thead>
          <tr>
            {core.getState().columns.map((col) => (
              <th key={col.key} style={{ width: col.width }}>
                {col.header}
              </th>
            ))}
          </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          {visibleRows.map((row) => (
            <Row
              key={row.id}
              row={row}
              columns={core.getState().columns}
              isSelected={core.getState().selectedRowIds.has(row.id)}
              onSelect={() => core.selectRow(row.id)}
            />
          ))}
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>
  );
}

const Row = React.memo(function Row<T extends { id: string }>({
  row,
  columns,
  isSelected,
  onSelect,
}: {
  row: T;
  columns: GridColumn<T>[];
  isSelected: boolean;
  onSelect: () => void;
}) {
  return (
    <tr
      onClick={onSelect}
      style={{ backgroundColor: isSelected ? '#e0f7fa' : 'transparent' }}
    >
      {columns.map((col) => (
        <td key={col.key}>{col.renderer ? col.renderer(row[col.key], row) : String(row[col.key])}</td>
      ))}
    </tr>
  );
});

5.2 Vue 

<!-- VueAdapter.vue -->
<template>
  <div ref="scrollContainer" class="grid" :style="{ height: viewportHeight + 'px' }">
    <table>
      <thead>
        <tr>
          <th v-for="col in columns" :key="col.key" :style="{ width: col.width + 'px' }">
            {{ col.header }}
          </th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr
          v-for="row in visibleRows"
          :key="row.id"
          :class="{ selected: isSelected(row.id) }"
          @click="core.selectRow(row.id)"
        >
          <td v-for="col in columns" :key="col.key">
            {{ col.renderer ? col.renderer(row[col.key], row) : row[col.key] }}
          </td>
        </tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref, computed, onMounted, onUnmounted } from 'vue';
import { GridCore } from './core/GridCore';

const props = defineProps<{
  core: GridCore<any>;
  viewportHeight: number;
}>();

const scrollTop = ref(0);
const scrollContainer = ref<HTMLElement | null>(null);

const columns = computed(() => props.core.getState().columns);
const visibleRows = computed(() =>
  props.core.getVisibleRows(scrollTop.value, props.viewportHeight)
);

const isSelected = (id: string) => props.core.getState().selectedRowIds.has(id);

const handleScroll = () => {
  if (scrollContainer.value) {
    scrollTop.value = scrollContainer.value.scrollTop;
  }
};

let unsubscribe: () => void;
onMounted(() => {
  unsubscribe = props.core.subscribe(() => {
    scrollTop.value = scrollTop.value; // trigger reactivity
  });
  scrollContainer.value?.addEventListener('scroll', handleScroll);
});

onUnmounted(() => {
  unsubscribe();
  scrollContainer.value?.removeEventListener('scroll', handleScroll);
});
</script>

5.3 Angular 

// angular-grid.component.ts
import { Component, Input, OnDestroy, OnInit, ChangeDetectionStrategy, ElementRef, ViewChild } from '@angular/core';
import { GridCore } from './core/GridCore';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-data-grid',
  template: `
    <div #scrollContainer class="grid" [style.height.px]="viewportHeight" (scroll)="onScroll()">
      <table>
        <thead>
          <tr>
            <th *ngFor="let col of columns" [style.width.px]="col.width">{{ col.header }}</th>
          </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr
            *ngFor="let row of visibleRows"
            [class.selected]="isSelected(row.id)"
            (click)="core.selectRow(row.id)"
          >
            <td *ngFor="let col of columns">
              {{ col.renderer ? col.renderer(row[col.key], row) : row[col.key] }}
            </td>
          </tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>
  `,
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
})
export class DataGridComponent<T extends { id: string }> implements OnInit, OnDestroy {
  @Input() core!: GridCore<T>;
  @Input() viewportHeight = 600;
  @ViewChild('scrollContainer') scrollContainer!: ElementRef<HTMLElement>;

  columns: GridColumn<T>[] = [];
  visibleRows: T[] = [];
  private unsubscribe: () => void = () => {};

  ngOnInit() {
    this.columns = this.core.getState().columns;
    this.updateVisibleRows();
    this.unsubscribe = this.core.subscribe(() => {
      this.updateVisibleRows();
    });
  }

  ngOnDestroy() {
    this.unsubscribe();
  }

  onScroll() {
    this.updateVisibleRows();
  }

  private updateVisibleRows() {
    const scrollTop = this.scrollContainer?.nativeElement.scrollTop ?? 0;
    this.visibleRows = this.core.getVisibleRows(scrollTop, this.viewportHeight);
  }

  isSelected(id: string) {
    return this.core.getState().selectedRowIds.has(id);
  }
}

6. Implementing the Grid: A Complete Example

Let's wire it all together with a concrete dataset. We'll generate 100,000 rows and render them in React (the same core works for Vue and Angular).

// main.tsx
import React from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { GridCore } from './core/GridCore';
import { DataGrid } from './ReactAdapter';

interface User {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  age: number;
}

const rows: User[] = Array.from({ length: 100_000 }, (_, i) => ({
  id: String(i),
  name: `User ${i}`,
  email: `user${i}@example.com`,
  age: Math.floor(Math.random() * 60) + 18,
}));

const columns = [
  { key: 'id', header: 'ID', width: 80, sortable: true },
  { key: 'name', header: 'Name', width: 200, sortable: true },
  { key: 'email', header: 'Email', width: 300 },
  { key: 'age', header: 'Age', width: 80, sortable: true },
] as const;

const core = new GridCore<User>(rows, columns, 40);

const App = () => (
  <div style={{ padding: '20px' }}>
    <h1>Scalable TypeScript Data Grid</h1>
    <button onClick={() => core.sortBy('age')}>Sort by Age</button>
    <DataGrid core={core} viewportHeight={600} />
  </div>
);

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(<App />);

This renders 100,000 rows in memory but only ~20 in the DOM. Sorting by age triggers a single core event, which re-renders only the visible window.

7. Performance Tuning and Best Practices

7.1 Use content-visibility: auto

CSS content-visibility: auto tells the browser to skip rendering off-screen content. Combined with virtualization, it reduces layout cost further.

.grid-row {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: 40px; /* matches row height */
}

7.2 Debounce Scroll Events

Scroll events fire too fast for React's setState to handle at 60fps. Use requestAnimationFrame to throttle:

let ticking = false;
const onScroll = (e: Event) => {
  if (!ticking) {
    requestAnimationFrame(() => {
      setScrollTop((e.target as HTMLElement).scrollTop);
      ticking = false;
    });
    ticking = true;
  }
};

7.3 Memoize Cell Renderers

Expensive cell renderers (e.g., formatting dates, computing badges) should be cached. Use a WeakMap keyed by row object to avoid recomputing on every scroll.

7.4 Avoid Recreating Column Arrays

Pass columns as a stable reference. If you define columns inline in the template, React will treat them as new on every render, breaking React.memo.

7.5 Use trackBy / key Correctly

Always provide a stable key (row.id) to help the framework identify which rows changed. Without it, frameworks will re-render all visible rows on every scroll.

7.6 Profile with DevTools

Use the Performance panel to check for layout thrash. If you see purple bars, you're reading layout properties (like offsetHeight) inside a scroll handler. Cache measurements instead.

8. Conclusion

A scalable data grid isn't about choosing the right framework—it's about separating concerns. Keep the data logic in a framework-agnostic TypeScript core, use virtualization to limit DOM nodes, and let each framework's adapter handle only the visible slice. With this architecture, 100,000 rows feel as smooth as 100.

If you want to see this pattern applied to real-world projects, check out Tamiz's Insights for more engineering deep-dives.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Why not just use a library like AG Grid or TanStack Table?

Libraries are great for generic needs, but they often bring their own rendering model and can be hard to customize. Building a core gives you full control over performance-critical paths and lets you integrate with any framework without fighting a library's abstractions. For very large datasets with complex interactions, a custom core is often worth the effort.

Q: How do I handle variable row heights?

Maintain a Map<rowId, height> and a prefix-sum array. On scroll, binary search for the start index using the cumulative offsets. After each row renders, measure its height and update the map. This is more complex but essential for grids with text wrapping or dynamic content.

Q: Does this work with server-side data?

Yes. The core only needs a slice of data. Replace getVisibleRows with an async fetch: when the scroll position crosses a threshold, request the next chunk from the server. The core's setRows method can append the new rows, and the adapter re-renders only the visible window.

title: PDFBox 3 in Java: Line Breaks, Page Breaks and Unicode
description:
A 60-row statement drawn with Apache PDFBox needs Java code to decide where page 1 ends, and a cover letter needs Java code to decide where each line breaks. Apache PDFBox is the Apache Software Foundation's PDF library for Java, and its 3.0.8 release has been on Maven Central since 11 July 2026. We wrote this for teams producing documents with it, and it covers the issues that show up once the first real templates go through it, each one with run output or the project's own documentation behind it.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

Who Decides Where a Line Breaks?

The calling code does. PDFBox accepts neither HTML nor CSS. The project FAQ calls it low-level, offering text and image drawing but no API above that for laying out pages or flowing paragraphs. A paragraph is therefore a list of lines the program builds itself by measuring words with getStringWidth, which returns widths in 1/1000 units of text space.

import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDDocument;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDPage;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDPageContentStream;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.common.PDRectangle;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.font.PDType0Font;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class DrawWrappedLetter {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        String body = "Thank you for your order. The parcel left our warehouse in Gdańsk this morning "
                + "and should reach you within three working days. Reply to this letter if any item is missing.";

        try (PDDocument document = new PDDocument()) {
            PDPage page = new PDPage(PDRectangle.LETTER);
            document.addPage(page);
            PDType0Font font = PDType0Font.load(document, new File("fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf"));
            float fontSize = 12;
            float margin = 72;
            float maxWidth = page.getMediaBox().getWidth() - 2 * margin;

            // Each showText call draws one line, so the program measures words and decides the breaks itself.
            List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
            String line = "";
            for (String word : body.split(" ")) {
                String candidate = line.isEmpty() ? word : line + " " + word;
                if (font.getStringWidth(candidate) / 1000 * fontSize > maxWidth) {
                    lines.add(line);
                    line = word;
                } else {
                    line = candidate;
                }
            }
            lines.add(line);

            try (PDPageContentStream content = new PDPageContentStream(document, page)) {
                content.beginText();
                content.setFont(font, fontSize);
                content.setLeading(fontSize * 1.4f);

                // PDF coordinates start at the bottom left, so the first baseline sits one margin below the top edge.
                content.newLineAtOffset(margin, page.getMediaBox().getHeight() - margin);
                for (String text : lines) {
                    content.showText(text);
                    content.newLine();
                }
                content.endText();
            }
            document.save("letter.pdf");
            System.out.println("Lines: " + lines.size());
        }
    }
}

It printed Lines: 3 and saved a 7,336-byte letter.pdf on a 612 by 792 point US Letter page, the paragraph broken into three lines inside one-inch margins. A dozen lines of Java do the job a browser does for a <p> element, and they handle only plain words, with no hyphenation, justification, bold runs or links. For richer layouts the FAQ sends readers elsewhere, to Apache FOP when the source is XML, or to add-on layout projects like Boxable and easytable that sit on top of PDFBox.

Page Breaks Are Tracked by Hand

The same applies one level up. newLine moves the baseline down by the leading and nothing more, so a table longer than the page keeps drawing below the bottom edge unless the program opens a new page itself.

import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDDocument;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDPage;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDPageContentStream;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.common.PDRectangle;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.font.PDType1Font;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.font.Standard14Fonts;

import java.io.IOException;

public class ManualPagination {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        float margin = 50;
        float leading = 16;
        PDType1Font font = new PDType1Font(Standard14Fonts.FontName.HELVETICA);

        try (PDDocument document = new PDDocument()) {
            PDPageContentStream content = null;
            float y = 0;

            for (int row = 1; row <= 60; row++) {
                // The program tracks the baseline itself and opens a new page once it has dropped below the bottom margin.
                if (content == null || y < margin) {
                    if (content != null) {
                        content.endText();
                        content.close();
                    }
                    PDPage page = new PDPage(PDRectangle.A4);
                    document.addPage(page);
                    content = new PDPageContentStream(document, page);
                    content.beginText();
                    content.setFont(font, 11);
                    content.setLeading(leading);
                    y = page.getMediaBox().getHeight() - margin;
                    content.newLineAtOffset(margin, y);
                } else {
                    content.newLine();
                    y -= leading;
                }
                content.showText("Line " + row + "    " + String.format("%.2f", row * 1.25));
            }

            // Each page's content stream has to be closed before the document is saved.
            content.endText();
            content.close();
            document.save("paginated-statement.pdf");
            System.out.println("Pages: " + document.getNumberOfPages());
        }
    }
}

The run printed Pages: 2, with rows 1 to 48 on the first A4 page and rows 49 to 60 on the second, all inside the page bounds. Repeating a header row, keeping a row's cells together or adding a page number would each be more code of the same kind. Without the y < margin check, rows keep going below the bottom edge of the first page, still present in the content stream and invisible in a viewer.

Names Like Łódź and Gdańsk Need PDType0Font

The letter above loads Noto Sans through PDType0Font.load for a reason. With the Standard 14 Helvetica, which needs no font file and is created in 3.x through new PDType1Font(Standard14Fonts.FontName.HELVETICA), showText on the word Gdańsk threw an IllegalArgumentException reporting that U+0144 ('nacute') is not available in Helvetica's WinAnsiEncoding, and Łódź failed the same way on U+0141. The FAQ's fix for that message is the Type 0 font, which PDType0Font.load(PDDocument, File) embeds as a subset of the TrueType file. Any service printing customer names or addresses with letters like these has to ship and load font files for each script it needs.

What Moving From 2.x to 3.x Changes

The 3.0 migration guide lists the API changes that stop 2.x code compiling. PDDocument lost its load methods to the new Loader class, the Standard 14 fonts lost their static fields, and a StreamCacheCreateFunction took the place of the MemoryUsageSetting parameter. Merging shows the new signature.

import org.apache.pdfbox.io.IOUtils;
import org.apache.pdfbox.multipdf.PDFMergerUtility;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;

public class MergeInvoicePack {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        PDFMergerUtility merger = new PDFMergerUtility();
        merger.addSource(new File("invoice.pdf"));
        merger.addSource(new File("statement.pdf"));
        merger.setDestinationFileName("invoice-pack.pdf");

        // The stream cache argument arrived in 3.x, and a memory-only cache suits small inputs.
        merger.mergeDocuments(IOUtils.createMemoryOnlyStreamCache());
    }
}

With a one-page invoice and a three-page statement as sources, it wrote a four-page, 10,381-byte invoice-pack.pdf. IOUtils lives in the separate pdfbox-io module that 3.0 introduced, which Maven pulls in with pdfbox alongside fontbox and commons-logging 1.4.0. A 2.x codebase has to rewrite every PDDocument.load call, font field and memory setting before it compiles against 3.0.8, or stay on the 2.0 line, which published 2.0.37 to Maven Central on 15 July 2026.

Security Advisories by Version

Ten CVE records appear on the PDFBox security page, and a fixed release exists for each. Scores are the ones NVD displays, from NIST for the older records and from CISA's ADP program for the 2026 pair.

  • CVE-2026-33929, CVSS 4.3 from CISA ADP: A path traversal in the ExtractEmbeddedFiles example and an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-23907, affects 2.0.24 to 2.0.36 and 3.0.0 to 3.0.7 and is fixed in 2.0.37 and 3.0.8.
  • CVE-2026-23907, CVSS 5.3 from CISA ADP: The original path traversal in that example, affects 2.0.24 to 2.0.35 and 3.0.0 to 3.0.6 and is fixed in 2.0.36 and 3.0.7.
  • CVE-2019-0228, CVSS 9.8 from NIST: XML external entity processing through a crafted XFDF file in 2.0.14, fixed in 2.0.15.
  • CVE-2016-2175, CVSS 7.8 from NIST: XML external entity processing through a crafted PDF in 1.8.0 to 1.8.11 and 2.0.0, fixed in 1.8.12 and 2.0.1.
  • CVE-2018-8036 and CVE-2018-11797, CVSS 6.5 and 5.5 from NIST: A parser loop and a long page-tree computation on crafted files, fixed in 2.0.11 and 2.0.12.
  • CVE-2021-27807, CVE-2021-27906, CVE-2021-31811 and CVE-2021-31812, CVSS 5.5 each from NIST: Infinite loops and out-of-memory errors on crafted files, fixed in 2.0.23 for the first two and 2.0.24 for the last two.

The project footnotes the 2026 pair as affecting only the examples module, but the NVD record for the later one lists the main apache:pdfbox CPE as vulnerable below 2.0.37 and 3.0.8, which is why NVD-based scanners raise it on the core artifact. Upgrading pdfbox to 3.0.8 or 2.0.37 clears all ten, and code copied from ExtractEmbeddedFiles needs the change from pull request 427. Maven Central has no fixed build of pdfbox-examples, though, since that artifact ends at 3.0.7 and 2.0.36. One more point from the same page affects upload services. Under the project's policy, crafted files that throw unchecked exceptions, loop without end or use memory out of proportion fall outside its security scope, and applications reading untrusted PDFs in volume are expected to set their own timeouts and memory caps.

Rendering the Statement From HTML Instead

Teams whose letters and statements already live as HTML can hand them to IronPDF for Java, Iron Software's commercial PDF library, which takes the layout and font work above off the Java side. It renders HTML with a full Chromium engine, so line breaks, table widths and page breaks follow the markup and its CSS, a TrueType file named in an @font-face rule of an HTML file embedded in our 2026.10.1 run with Łódź and Gdańsk intact, and page JavaScript runs when setEnableJavaScript is on, with setWaitFor delaying the render for a set time or a network-idle signal. The calls are PdfDocument.renderHtmlFileAsPdf for an HTML file or renderHtmlAsPdf for a string, then PdfDocument.merge, extractAllText or getSecurity() on the result before saveAs.

The Maven coordinate is com.ironsoftware:ironpdf, and Maven Central lists ten 2026 releases of it up to 2026.10.1 from 1 October 2026. A free trial key covers a test against your own templates, and the generation settings example walks through the render options.

The PDFBox Checklist in Short

PDFBox 3.0.8 leaves line wrapping, page breaks and Unicode font loading to the calling code, takes no HTML or CSS, asks 2.x code to be rewritten for its 3.x API and carries ten CVE records that 3.0.8 and 2.0.37 fix. For teams with HTML templates, we point to IronPDF for Java as the solution, with guides to merging PDFs and filling PDF forms on the same document object.

What reached your team first with PDFBox, the layout code, the fonts or the scanner report?

Apache PDFBox, PDFBox and Apache FOP are trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation, we have no affiliation with the foundation, and the details here rest on the project's own pages and on NVD and Maven Central records.
