title: Ax-Prover: A Deep Reasoning Agentic Framework for Theorem Proving in Mathematics and Quantum Physics
description:
arXiv:2510.12787v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We present Ax-Prover, a multi-agent system for automated theorem proving in Lean that can solve problems across diverse scientific domains and operate either autonomously or collaboratively with human experts. To achieve this, Ax-Prover approaches scientific problem solving through formal proof generation, a process that demands both creative reasoning and strict syntactic rigor. Ax-Prover meets this challenge by equipping Large Language Models (LLMs), which provide knowledge and reasoning, with Lean tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which ensure formal correctness. To evaluate its performance as an autonomous prover, we benchmark our approach against frontier LLMs and specialized prover models on two public math benchmarks and on two Lean benchmarks we introduce in the fields of abstract algebra and quantum theory. On public datasets, Ax-Prover is competitive with state-of-the-art provers, while it largely outperforms them on the new benchmarks. This shows that, unlike specialized systems that struggle to generalize, our tool-based agentic theorem prover approach offers a generalizable methodology for formal verification across diverse scientific domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate Ax-Prover's assistant capabilities in a practical use case, showing how it enabled an expert mathematician to formalize the proof of a complex cryptography theorem.

title: The quote gap: why the cheapest moving quote is rarely the cheapest move
description:
We run a moving cost calculator that has priced 27,854 routes, and the most common complaint we hear is not that moving is expensive. It is that the quote a customer accepted was not the price they paid. The gap between quote and final bill is where most moving misery lives, and it is usually explainable before anyone signs anything.

The first cause is scope. A quote that covers loading, transport and unloading sounds complete, but the expensive parts of a move often sit outside those words: stairs, long carries from truck to door, packing materials, disassembly and reassembly, storage between homes. A quote that omits them is not cheaper, it is incomplete, and the missing items reappear on moving day at the worst possible moment, when you cannot shop around.

The second cause is weight versus volume. Long-distance moves are usually priced on weight or on cubic feet, and the two methods give different answers for the same household. A home full of books is heavy but compact; a home full of light furniture is bulky but light. A quote that does not say which method it uses cannot be compared with one that does, and comparing two quotes priced on different bases is how the cheapest-looking option wins and then loses.

The third cause is the estimate type. A non-binding estimate can move, legally, and it usually moves up. A binding estimate cannot, provided the inventory does not change. Customers who choose on price alone usually choose a non-binding estimate, because it looks lower, and then discover the difference when the truck is weighed. The binding quote that looked expensive was often the honest one.

None of this means movers are dishonest. It means quotes are documents with fine print, and the fine print is where the price lives. The questions that close the gap are simple: is this binding or non-binding, priced on weight or volume, and does it include stairs, long carries, packing and storage? A mover who answers all four clearly is usually a mover you can trust, whatever the number.

We built our calculator to answer the price question before the fine print matters: a free long-distance estimate at My Fast Movers, with no address form required: https://myfastmovers.com

title: SoK: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Taxonomy, Architectures, Evaluation, and Research Directions
description:
arXiv:2603.07379v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly evolving into agentic architectures where large language models autonomously coordinate multi-step reasoning, dynamic memory management, and iterative retrieval strategies. Despite rapid industrial adoption, current research lacks a systematic understanding of Agentic RAG as a sequential decision-making system, leading to highly fragmented architectures, inconsistent evaluation methodologies, and unresolved reliability risks. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) paper provides the first unified framework for understanding these autonomous systems. We formalize agentic retrieval-generation loops as finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes, explicitly modeling their control policies and state transitions. Building upon this formalization, we develop a comprehensive taxonomy and modular architectural decomposition that categorizes systems by their planning mechanisms, retrieval orchestration, memory paradigms, and tool-invocation behaviors. We further analyze the critical limitations of traditional static evaluation practices and identify severe systemic risks inherent to autonomous loops, including compounding hallucination propagation, memory poisoning, retrieval misalignment, and cascading tool-execution vulnerabilities. Finally, we outline key doctoral-scale research directions spanning stable adaptive retrieval, cost-aware orchestration, formal trajectory evaluation, and oversight mechanisms, providing a definitive roadmap for building reliable, controllable, and scalable agentic retrieval systems.

title: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX terminated because a duplicate key was found
description:
You make a column unique on a table that has been in use for a while:

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX UX_Account_Email ON dbo.Account (Email);

Msg 1505, Level 16, State 1, Line 1
The CREATE UNIQUE INDEX statement terminated because a duplicate key was found for the object name
'dbo.Account' and the index name 'UX_Account_Email'. The duplicate key value is (a@x.com).

The message names exactly one value. It is the first collision found, not a report — there may be one more or four hundred, and fixing the named one just gets you the next message.

A unique constraint fails the same way, with an extra line, because a constraint is an index underneath:

ALTER TABLE dbo.Account ADD CONSTRAINT UQ_Account_Email UNIQUE (Email);

Msg 1505, Level 16, State 1, Line 1
The CREATE UNIQUE INDEX statement terminated because a duplicate key was found ...
Msg 1750, Level 16, State 1, Line 1
Could not create constraint or index. See previous errors.

Two nulls are a duplicate

This is the part that surprises people, and it is why the message so often reads The duplicate key value is (<NULL>):

INSERT dbo.Account VALUES (4, NULL), (5, NULL);

Two rows with no email at all will defeat a unique index. In comparisons, NULL = NULL is unknown; for a unique index, SQL Server treats nulls as equal to each other, so exactly one row may have no value. That is the opposite of what most people expect from "the email must be unique", where the intention is nearly always unique when there is one.

The fix for that case is a filtered index:

SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX UX_Account_Email ON dbo.Account (Email) WHERE Email IS NOT NULL;

Now any number of rows may have no email, and the ones that do have one must differ.

SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON matters. It is on by default in SQL Server Management Studio and in most application connections, which is why this is rarely seen interactively — but it is off by default in sqlcmd, so a migration script run that way fails on the filtered index and only on the filtered index:

Msg 1934, Level 16, State 1, Line 1
CREATE INDEX failed because the following SET options have incorrect settings: 'QUOTED_IDENTIFIER'.

Put the SET at the top of the script and it applies to the whole batch.

List every duplicate, not just the first 

SELECT Email, COUNT(*) AS Rows_, MIN(AccountId) AS KeepThisOne
FROM   dbo.Account
WHERE  Email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC;

Email      Rows_  KeepThisOne
---------  -----  -----------
a@x.com    2      1

Leave the WHERE Email IS NOT NULL out if you are building an unfiltered index and need the nulls counted too.

To see the whole rows rather than the values — usually what you need, because the decision is which row survives:

WITH Duplicated AS
(
    SELECT *, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY Email) AS CopiesOfThisEmail
    FROM   dbo.Account
    WHERE  Email IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT *
FROM   Duplicated
WHERE  CopiesOfThisEmail > 1
ORDER BY Email, AccountId;

Choosing what to keep

"Keep the lowest id" is the usual reflex and it is often wrong. The oldest row may be an abandoned signup while the newest is the account in daily use. Before deleting anything, ask what points at these rows:

SELECT OBJECT_NAME(parent_object_id) AS ReferencingTable, name AS ForeignKey
FROM   sys.foreign_keys
WHERE  referenced_object_id = OBJECT_ID('dbo.Account');

Every table in that list has rows pointing at an account id you are about to remove, and they need repointing at whichever row you keep — before the delete, or the delete fails on the foreign key.

When the duplicates are genuinely the same thing and nothing references them, this deletes all but one of each:

WITH Ranked AS
(
    SELECT AccountId, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Email ORDER BY AccountId) AS Copy
    FROM   dbo.Account
    WHERE  Email IS NOT NULL
)
DELETE FROM Ranked WHERE Copy > 1;

Run it as a SELECT first. ORDER BY AccountId is the decision about which copy survives, and it is the only line in there worth arguing about.

A gentler order of work

Adding the index last is the reflex, and it means the cleanup and the constraint are the same deployment. The alternative is to add the filtered unique index first against the rows that are already clean, which stops the duplicates growing while you decide what to do with the ones you have.

Seeing it before you run it

What makes this change expensive is never the index; it is the rows pointing at the ones you are about to merge, in tables you did not know were involved.

WoodFireERD draws that for you — pick the table, follow what points at it, and take the change out as an ordered script with the index, the constraint and the clean-up steps in the order they have to run.

Originally published at woodfireerd.com. Every statement in it was run against a real SQL Server before publishing — the error messages are copied from the output, not from memory.

title: How We Eliminated Cache Stampedes in Node.js & Bun with Single-Flight Coalescing
description:
Every engineer who has scaled a high-traffic backend has lived through this nightmare:

You have an expensive endpoint (e.g., aggregating leaderboard data or rendering a personalized dashboard). To protect your database, you cache the result with a 60-second TTL.

Everything runs smoothly until the key expires while receiving 1,500 requests per second.

Within a 50-millisecond window, hundreds of concurrent requests see a cache miss. All of them immediately hammer the primary database simultaneously to recompute the same data. Your connection pool saturates, CPU spikes to 100%, latency explodes, and your server crashes.

This is the thundering herd / cache stampede problem.

The Traditional (Fragile) Workarounds

  1. Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch algorithm): Recomputes the value before it expires based on an exponential probability. While effective, it wastes backend CPU cycles recomputing keys that may never be accessed again.
  2. Distributed Mutex Locks (Redlock): Acquiring a distributed lock before computing. This introduces noticeable network roundtrip latency and runs the risk of deadlocks if a worker dies mid-flight.

The Zero-Overhead Alternative: Single-Flight Promise Coalescing

Instead of locking distributed infrastructure, we can coalesce concurrent requests in-process at the execution runtime layer.

When Key A is requested and misses the cache:

  1. Check if an execution promise for Key A is currently in-flight.
  2. If YES: Do not touch the database. Return the existing promise and await it.
  3. If NO: Register a new in-flight promise, execute the database fetcher, cache the result, resolve all awaiting callers, and deregister the promise in a finally block. 
// How KVDock implements zero-overhead single-flight coalescing:
const running = this.inFlight.get(key);
if (running) {
  this.metrics.stampedeCoalesced++;
  return (await running) as T;
}

const run = (async () => {
  try {
    const cached = await this.get<T>(key);
    if (cached !== null) return cached;
    const fresh = await fetcher();
    await this.set(key, fresh, options);
    return fresh;
  } finally {
    this.inFlight.delete(key);
  }
})();

this.inFlight.set(key, run);
return (await run) as T;

⚡ Real-World Benchmark: 1,000 Concurrent Requests

We ran a controlled benchmark under 1,000 concurrent requests to an uncached endpoint with 25ms simulated database query latency:

Metric Traditional Caching KVDock (getOrSet) Net Improvement
Incoming Requests 1,000 1,000 Same Load
Database Queries Executed 1,000 queries (Herd) 1 query (Single-Flight) 99.90% DB load reduction
Coalesced Waiting Callers 0 999 Zero lock contention
Connection Pool Exhaustion 💥 Saturated 🟢 Baseline Stable Zero connection contention

Open Source & Polyglot

We built this into KVDock — an open-source, zero-dependency caching engine with multi-tier storage (L1 RAM + L2 Persistent):

  • Zero runtime dependencies in core
  • Multi-tier caching with automatic backfill
  • Cross-runtime support across Node.js, Bun, Deno, and Cloudflare Workers
  • Native polyglot implementations in Rust (kvdock-rs), Go (kvdock-go), Swift (kvdock-swift), and Kotlin (kvdock-kt)

⭐ Explore the code & star on GitHub: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock

👤 Follow the maintainer: @zisam-glitch for low-latency systems engineering deep dives!

title: Anthropic's $895 Billion Compute Commitments Change How Teams Should Buy AI
description:
A software team can compare AI APIs by model quality, latency, and price per token. Anthropic's November 2, 2026 IPO amendment adds another question: what happens to your product if the provider's ability to serve you depends on infrastructure deals measured in hundreds of billions of dollars?

The filing reports about $895.4 billion in aggregate committed spend under purchase commitments and lease agreements, substantially all related to compute and infrastructure. It does not say Anthropic must pay that whole amount now. About $447.5 billion is expected before the end of 2030, and nearly $70 billion is due in the 12 months after September 30, 2026. The distinction between a headline total and the timing of cash obligations matters. Anthropic's SEC filing lays out the detail; Associated Press reporting independently confirms the quarterly results and near-term commitment figure.

This does not mean Anthropic is about to fail, or that companies should stop using Claude. It is a reminder that AI vendor risk now includes the physical supply chain behind a model. Engineering teams cannot predict a provider's future, but they can design systems that handle a change in price or product terms.

What the $895 billion figure actually means

The figure combines several types of agreements. Anthropic describes purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments and leases that have not yet started. The total is an aggregate committed-spend figure, not a bill due today, not annual spending, and not a forecast of compute that has already been delivered. The filing says roughly half is expected before 2031, with most of the rest expected from 2031 through 2045. The SEC filing's risk discussion gives those time ranges.

That time horizon says something about the business model. A frontier AI provider cannot treat compute like a small, flexible cloud add-on if it needs to reserve data-center capacity years ahead. It may sign long agreements to secure access before customers arrive. If demand grows, those reservations can support service expansion. If demand, model efficiency, or the business changes, fixed commitments can become a constraint.

The filing itself describes both sides. Anthropic says access to large-scale compute is important to train and serve models, and that its results may fluctuate with substantial compute-related spending. It also reports that in the third quarter, $5 billion of short-term compute cost significantly more than comparable capacity under multi-year commitments. The extra compute reduced revenue per dollar of compute compared with the previous quarter. That is the operating tradeoff: short-term capacity can cost more, while long-term commitments create obligations that may last well beyond current product cycles. This is the company's disclosure, not a prediction that its contracts will go wrong.

Revenue is growing fast, but that is not the same as an easy business

The amendment shows third-quarter revenue of about $17 billion, while Anthropic still reported a quarterly net loss of $23.3 billion. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue was $33.2 billion and the reported net loss was $104 billion, including a $94 billion accounting charge related to financing agreements, according to the Associated Press's breakdown of the filing.

Those numbers need context. A large reported net loss does not mean the company paid that same amount in cash during the period. The filing identifies a major non-cash accounting charge. Fast revenue growth also does not erase the need to pay for infrastructure and customer acquisition. AP reports that revenue for the first nine months rose to $33.2 billion from $2.6 billion a year earlier. That growth is striking, but it does not prove that each product or customer segment has durable margins.

The engineering lesson is narrower than an investor verdict: model access can be commercially valuable and still depend on a costly, capacity-constrained supply chain. A software team buying an API is buying a service layered on top of that chain.

Why application teams should care

Capacity is part of reliability. An API can be reachable while a provider still changes rate limits, queues, available model options, or regional capacity. Contracted infrastructure can help a provider meet demand, but it does not guarantee every customer a fixed service level. Your product needs a plan for timeouts and temporary model unavailability.

Price is connected to utilization and efficiency. Providers can change prices as hardware supply, model efficiency, and usage patterns shift. A workload that is affordable at today's rates may become expensive when users send longer prompts or agents make more calls. Measure cost per completed user task, rather than per API request.

A model name is not a stable interface. Model versions can be retired, behavior can change, and product features may be tied to one provider. If important business logic depends on a particular model's response style or tool behavior, a migration may take more than changing a URL. The system needs tests that capture what the application actually expects.

Cloud relationships can affect distribution and supply. Anthropic's filing discusses its reliance on outside compute providers and the risk that those relationships may not always fit its long-term interests. This is not unique to Anthropic. AI services depend on links between model developers and infrastructure suppliers. Teams should understand which parts of their application rely on a single supplier.

A practical AI-provider review for engineering teams

You do not need to build a universal multi-model platform on day one. You do need to know what would break if a provider became unavailable or changed its terms. Use this checklist before putting a model at the center of a product:

  • Name the critical path. List which user journeys require the model, which can degrade gracefully, and which must stop safely. A support-summary feature and an account-access decision should not share the same fallback policy.
  • Measure by completed task. Track task outcomes and cost for representative user requests. A cheaper response that creates more retries or human correction may cost more overall.
  • Keep a versioned evaluation set. Save representative inputs and expected output properties. Re-run it when the model or prompt changes. Measure task success and harmful errors, not whether output merely looks fluent.
  • Separate business rules from model choice. Keep authorization and irreversible actions in ordinary application code. Let a model suggest or classify; use deterministic checks to decide what the system is allowed to do.
  • Build a tested degraded mode. Decide whether the product should queue work or ask the user to retry. Test the behavior rather than assuming a fallback will work under load.
  • Read the commercial terms. Check rate limits, notice periods, model retirement policies, data handling, support commitments, and any minimum-spend terms that apply to your account. A public pricing page is not a substitute for the contract you signed.
  • Estimate the cost of leaving. Identify provider-specific prompts, tool calls, embeddings, stored data, and evaluation work. Put a rough migration estimate in the architecture record, even if you decide the current integration is worth it.

A second provider can help, but only when it has been tested against real tasks. Different models may return different formats, refuse different requests, or need different context. A routing layer without shared evaluations can make it harder to notice regressions. For a small application, a clear primary provider plus a documented manual fallback may be safer and cheaper than a complex abstraction that nobody exercises.

The larger shift: AI is an infrastructure buying decision

For years, teams could treat many software APIs as replaceable services. AI makes that assumption less reliable because quality, inference cost, data-center capacity, and model behavior are tied together. The provider is not simply returning a static lookup. It is allocating scarce compute to produce each result while also investing in future models and infrastructure.

Anthropic's filing makes the scale visible, but it does not tell us which provider will win or whether its commitments will produce a return. The company has disclosed its view of the opportunity and its risks in a preliminary securities filing. It is not an independent forecast. What teams can take from it is a more practical point: the vendor's capacity plan is part of the environment your application runs in, even when your code only calls an API.

That means procurement and architecture should meet earlier. Before adopting an AI feature, product owners should say what user value justifies its ongoing cost. Engineers should define what happens when the model is slow or unavailable. Finance and procurement should understand the service terms and exposure to usage growth. Those are normal software reliability questions, now applied to model services.

A decision rule worth saving

Before making a model provider a critical dependency, ask three things:

  1. Can the product remain safe and useful during an outage or rate-limit event?
  2. Can the team detect a quality or cost change before users bear the impact?
  3. Can the team move the workflow, or narrow its use, without rebuilding the whole application?

If the answer to all three is no, the immediate problem is not that the provider has large infrastructure commitments. It is that the application has no plan for dependence on an external service. Fix that while the integration is still small.

title: Converting Excel Worksheets to Images in Java: A Practical Look
description:
Excel workbooks are designed for data manipulation and analysis, but there are scenarios where a static image is more appropriate. Whether you are generating report snapshots for a web dashboard, embedding table data into an email, or archiving records in a format that prevents accidental edits, converting worksheets to images is a practical requirement. In Java, this task is not natively supported by the standard library. While Apache POI is the de facto standard for reading and writing Excel files, it does not include a rendering engine to produce visual output. This is where third-party libraries come into play.

This article examines the practical aspects of converting Excel content to images in a Java environment using Spire.XLS for Java as an example tool. It covers the library's approach to rendering, the code required for common conversion scenarios, and the trade-offs developers should consider.

Why Convert Excel to an Image?

Before diving into implementation, it is worth understanding the contexts where this conversion is beneficial. Excel files, while rich in data, are not always the most portable format for presentation. An image file (PNG or JPEG) can be viewed on any device without spreadsheet software, embedded directly into HTML without complex browser rendering, and shared without exposing the underlying formulas or raw data structure.

Common use cases include generating visual snapshots for automated reporting systems, creating thumbnails for document management systems, or preparing data for platforms that only accept image uploads. The key constraint is that the conversion must preserve the visual fidelity of the original sheet—cell formatting, merged regions, and layout must remain intact.

How the Library Handles Rendering

Spire.XLS for Java operates as a standalone library that does not require Microsoft Office or Excel to be installed on the host machine. It includes its own rendering engine that interprets Excel formatting and outputs it to standard Java BufferedImage objects or directly to files. This is a relevant architectural characteristic for server-side applications where installing Office is impractical or prohibited by licensing.

The library supports two primary conversion modes: saving an entire worksheet as an image, or extracting a specific range of cells. For scenarios requiring higher output quality, the library exposes DPI (dots per inch) settings through its ConverterSetting class, allowing developers to adjust resolution for print-oriented outputs. Chart objects within worksheets can also be converted independently, which is useful when the visual element of interest is a graph rather than the raw data table.

Converting a Worksheet to an Image

The most straightforward operation is converting an entire worksheet. The workflow involves loading the workbook, selecting the desired sheet by index, and invoking the save method.

import com.spire.xls.*;

public class ExcelToImage {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();
        workbook.loadFromFile("input/sample.xlsx");

        Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);
        sheet.saveToImage("output/sheet_image.png");

        workbook.dispose();
    }
}

This method produces a PNG file representing the used range of the worksheet. The library determines the output dimensions based on the content and default rendering settings. For many internal reporting needs, this level of simplicity is sufficient. However, developers should be aware that very large worksheets may result in correspondingly large image files, which could impact performance in memory-constrained environments.

Extracting Specific Cell Ranges

In many reporting workflows, only a subset of the sheet is relevant. Exporting the entire sheet introduces unnecessary whitespace and can make the output image difficult to read when embedded in documents or web pages. The library provides an overload that accepts row and column indices to define a rectangular region.

import com.spire.xls.Workbook;
import com.spire.xls.Worksheet;
import javax.imageio.ImageIO;
import java.awt.image.BufferedImage;
import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;

public class RangeToImage {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();
        workbook.loadFromFile("input/sample.xlsx");

        Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

        // Convert from row 1, column 1 to row 7, column 4
        BufferedImage image = sheet.toImage(1, 1, 7, 4);
        ImageIO.write(image, "PNG", new File("output/range_image.png"));

        workbook.dispose();
    }
}

The toImage method returns a BufferedImage, giving the developer full control over the output format and any subsequent processing. This approach is particularly useful for generating summary tables or extracting a single report section from a larger financial model.

Controlling Output Resolution

The default rendering DPI may be adequate for screen display but insufficient for printing or high-density displays. The library allows explicit configuration of horizontal and vertical DPI before conversion. This setting affects the pixel dimensions of the output while maintaining the same physical layout proportions.

Workbook workbook = new Workbook();
workbook.loadFromFile("input/sample.xlsx");

workbook.getConverterSetting().setXDpi(300);
workbook.getConverterSetting().setYDpi(300);

Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);
sheet.saveToImage("output/high_res.png");

Setting the DPI to 300 or higher is a standard practice for print-oriented outputs. It is important to note that higher DPI values increase memory consumption during rendering and produce larger file sizes, so the choice should be driven by the target medium rather than arbitrary quality preferences.

Practical Considerations and Limitations

While the library simplifies the conversion process, developers should evaluate several factors before integrating it into a production system.

Formatting Fidelity: The library renders cell styles, fonts, and borders with reasonable accuracy, but complex Excel features such as conditional formatting, data bars, or sophisticated custom number formats may not translate perfectly. Testing with representative files from the actual business domain is essential.

Font Availability: Since the rendering happens in the Java Virtual Machine, the fonts used in the Excel file must be available on the host system. If a specified font is missing, the library will substitute another, potentially altering text layout and causing content to overflow cell boundaries. On Linux servers, this often requires explicit installation of common fonts.

Licensing and Cost: Spire.XLS is a commercial product. While a free version exists, it imposes restrictions such as watermarks or limits on the number of rows processed per file. For projects with strict budget constraints or high-volume processing requirements, the licensing terms must be carefully reviewed. Open-source alternatives using Apache POI combined with manual Graphics2D rendering exist, but they require substantially more development effort to handle formatting and layout correctly.

Memory Management: Loading large Excel files and rendering them to high-resolution images can consume significant heap memory. The Workbook object should be disposed of explicitly after use to release resources, especially in long-running server processes.

Conclusion

Converting Excel worksheets to images in Java is a solvable problem with the right library. Spire.XLS for Java offers a direct API that handles the rendering complexity, supporting full-sheet conversion, range extraction, and DPI configuration without requiring Office dependencies. The approach is suitable for server-side automated reporting and archival workflows where visual fidelity is important, but the Excel application itself is not available.

Developers should approach this capability with an understanding of its boundaries. Font dependencies, the commercial nature of the library, and the inherent differences between spreadsheet rendering and browser/print rendering mean that output quality should be validated against specific use-case requirements. For simple tables and standard formatting, the library performs reliably. For highly complex or highly customized spreadsheets, a proof-of-concept phase with actual production files is recommended before committing to a particular solution.

title: Crediting crypto deposits safely: confirmation thresholds per network (with code)
description:
Any app that accepts on-chain deposits — exchanges, wallets, games — has to answer one question: when is a deposit real enough to credit? Credit too early and a reorg or double-spend costs you money. Credit too late and users file support tickets.

I worked through this for casino wallets, where the other half of the problem is operational: support and payments staff need to see each deposit's state without becoming blockchain specialists (that side is covered in Spinlab Studio's admin panel guide). This post is the engineering side, and it applies to any custodial wallet.

Model deposits as a state machine 

SEEN (in mempool / first block) → CONFIRMING (n of N) → CREDITED → (rare) REVERSED

Store each deposit with tx_hash, network, asset, amount, block_number, confirmations, status. Never credit from the mempool state.

Thresholds are per network, not per asset

USDT on Ethereum and USDT on TRON are different risks. Make the threshold a config keyed by (network, asset) and optionally by amount band:

type Rule = { network: string; asset: string; maxAmountUsd: number; confirmations: number };

const rules: Rule[] = [
  { network: "bitcoin",  asset: "BTC",  maxAmountUsd: 1_000,    confirmations: 1 },
  { network: "bitcoin",  asset: "BTC",  maxAmountUsd: Infinity, confirmations: 3 },
  { network: "ethereum", asset: "*",    maxAmountUsd: Infinity, confirmations: 12 }, // or wait for finalized
  { network: "tron",     asset: "USDT", maxAmountUsd: Infinity, confirmations: 19 }, // ~solidified
  { network: "solana",   asset: "*",    maxAmountUsd: Infinity, confirmations: 0 },  // use 'finalized' commitment instead
];

export function required(network: string, asset: string, usd: number): number {
  const r = rules.find(r => r.network === network && (r.asset === asset || r.asset === "*") && usd <= r.maxAmountUsd);
  if (!r) throw new Error(`no confirmation rule for ${network}/${asset}`); // fail closed
  return r.confirmations;
}

The numbers above are common starting points, not gospel — tune them to your risk appetite, and prefer the chain's own finality signal (Ethereum finalized block tag, Solana finalized commitment) where one exists.

Three bugs I see constantly

  1. Crediting twice. Make the credit operation idempotent on (network, tx_hash, output_index). Webhooks from node providers will be delivered more than once.
  2. Ignoring reorgs. After crediting, keep watching until finality. If the block disappears, move the deposit to REVERSED and lock the balance delta instead of silently subtracting.
  3. Failing open on unknown networks. If a user sends a token on a network you don't support, don't guess. Park it in a manual-review queue.

Show the state to the user

A progress indicator ("2 of 3 confirmations") removes most support tickets. Expose the same state machine to your internal tools so an agent can answer "where's my deposit?" from one screen. Users tolerate waiting; they don't tolerate not knowing.

Questions about edge cases — RBF transactions, token contracts with transfer fees, chain halts — are welcome in the comments.

title: Best ERD Database Design Tools: SQLDBM, dbdiagram, DrawSQL, Lucidchart & Eraser Features Compared
description:
Database design is one of those things that quietly decides whether your project ships smoothly or turns into a six-month cleanup project. I've been building and reviewing data systems long enough to know that the right ERD tool saves hours of back-and-forth, prevents nasty migrations, and keeps engineers and analysts actually talking to each other. The wrong one gets abandoned in a Google Doc somewhere.

So I spent time with the most popular ERD and database modeling tools on the market right now. Some are lightweight sketch tools built for a quick diagram. Others are full modeling platforms that handle warehouse-scale schemas with governance baked in. A few sit somewhere in the middle, trying to serve both crowds.

In this roundup I'll walk through what each tool is good at, where it falls short, and which one I'd actually recommend depending on your team's size and workflow. SqlDBM takes the top spot, but I'll be fair about the trade-offs across the board.

How I Evaluated These Tools

I looked at each tool through five lenses: the quality of the visual ERD workflow, how well it handles reverse and forward engineering against real databases, collaboration features for teams, support for modern cloud warehouses like Snowflake and BigQuery, and how pricing scales as your team grows. I also paid attention to niceties that matter in practice, things like version history, AI assistance, Git integration, and whether the tool treats governance as a first-class concern or an afterthought.

1. SqlDBM - Best Overall

The ERD tool that grows from your first diagram to your five-thousandth table, without ever leaving the browser.

I've tested a lot of ERD tools, and SqlDBM is the one I keep coming back to. It's a fully cloud-native, browser-based platform that lets you design entity-relationship diagrams without writing a single line of code, yet it scales all the way to enterprise complexity without breaking a sweat.

What immediately stood out is how complete the ERD workflow feels. You can reverse-engineer a live Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, or Azure Synapse database into a visual diagram in seconds, refine the schema visually, and then forward-engineer the changes back as production-ready DDL or alter scripts. That round-trip between diagram and database is something lightweight ERD tools like dbdiagram and DrawSQL simply can't match. Comparitech put it well when they noted SqlDBM is "pretty hard to beat because it can model existing databases, support new database design, and also generate out object creation scripts."

Collaboration is baked into every corner. Multiple team members can edit the same ERD in real time, think Google Docs for database design, with version history that tracks changes down to individual column nullability and data types. For larger organizations, subject areas let distributed teams keep diagrams organized while maintaining global visibility.

The feature that genuinely sets SqlDBM apart is its semantic modeling layer. You can define governed semantic views on top of your physical ERD, giving BI tools, dbt models, and AI systems one accurate definition of what your data actually means. Standalone semantic tools like dbt and Cube skip visual modeling. Visual modeling tools skip the semantic layer. SqlDBM is the only platform I've seen that bridges both.

The proof is in the adoption. Over 400,000 users trust it globally. Mercadona governs nearly 5,000 tables in the platform. Les Mills manages 1,000+ Snowflake tables after choosing SqlDBM over erwin. It won Database Modeling Solution of the Year in 2023 and 2024, and PwC reports it cuts modeling time by 25 percent. With an AI Copilot and Git/CI/CD integration for DDL and dbt YAML, it's the most complete ERD tool I've tested.

Pros

  • Full round-trip ERD workflow: reverse-engineer live databases, design visually, and forward-engineer DDL or alter scripts across Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Azure Synapse, and more
  • Real-time multi-user collaboration with granular version history that tracks column-level data types and nullability, trusted by 400,000+ users globally
  • The only visual ERD tool in this roundup with a governed semantic modeling layer, bridging physical schema design with business-context definitions for BI and AI
  • Enterprise-proven at scale: Mercadona governs nearly 5,000 tables, Les Mills runs 1,000+ Snowflake tables, PwC reports 25% faster modeling
  • Built-in AI Copilot plus Git and CI/CD integration keeps diagram-to-production workflows seamless

Cons

  • The depth of enterprise features can mean a steeper learning curve for users who just need a quick ERD sketch
  • Primarily focused on relational and warehouse platforms, so teams working exclusively with NoSQL databases won't find native support

Pricing: SqlDBM has a free tier so you can start modeling without any commitment. Paid plans are quote-based and scale with your team size, with enterprise packaging that includes premium support, SSO, RBAC, and advanced security options. Contact sales for a tailored quote.

2. dbdiagram.io

dbdiagram.io, built by Holistics, is a diagram-as-code tool. You write schema definitions in DBML (Database Markup Language) and the ER diagram updates beside the editor as you type. You can import existing SQL and export to SQL DDL, PDF, or PNG. It's paired with dbdocs for publishing schemas as browsable documentation, and a CLI for CI/CD workflows.

It's aimed at developers, analysts, and small teams who want to sketch or document a schema quickly without installing a heavy desktop modeler. The free tier is generous for solo use. Paid plans add private diagrams, version history, and team workspaces, and a Custom plan adds SSO and priority support.

Honestly, this is a lightweight schema visualizer rather than a governed modeling platform. There's no live database sync and no built-in governance layer, so it suits early design and documentation more than regulated, warehouse-scale modeling.

Pros

  • Fast, keyboard-driven DBML workflow that's easy to version-control and diff
  • Free plan to start, with no-install, shareable diagrams
  • Imports from SQL and exports to SQL, PDF, and PNG
  • dbdocs publishing and a CLI for CI/CD included in the same plan

Cons

  • You need to learn DBML, a barrier for non-technical users
  • Free plan limits diagram count and published docs (10 published docs)
  • No live database sync, limited governance, standards enforcement, or lineage

Pricing: Free plan with limits on diagrams and published docs. Older third-party sources cite Personal Pro at about $8 to $9/month, while dbdocs's April 2025 announcement lists Personal Pro at $20/month ($16 annual) and Team at $60/month ($50 annual) for the combined plans. Custom plan for enterprises is quote-based. Check the pricing page for current figures.

3. DrawSQL

DrawSQL is a web-based ERD tool for designing relational schemas. You can paste CREATE TABLE statements, import DBML, use AI to generate a schema, or draw from scratch. It auto-detects MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQL Server and uses each engine's native column types and constraints. Exports include SQL DDL, Laravel and AdonisJS migrations, and PNG.

Paid team plans add real-time multiplayer editing with live cursors and sticky notes on tables. It's popular with application developers, especially in the Laravel ecosystem, who want clean, presentable diagrams. There's also a public template library of well-known schemas to start from.

The caveats are worth noting. It supports only three database engines, so there's no native cloud-warehouse support. It also doesn't have governance, lineage, or data-architecture features. Users I've spoken to say the free plan's limits feel restrictive once a project gets real.

Pros

  • Clean, intuitive visual editor with strong SQL and DBML import
  • Real-time multiplayer collaboration on paid plans
  • Exports to SQL DDL and framework migrations (Laravel, AdonisJS)
  • Free tier plus a public template library

Cons

  • Supports only MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server, no native cloud-warehouse support
  • Table-per-diagram and private-diagram caps push growing teams to costlier plans
  • Limited governance, standards enforcement, and enterprise data-architecture features

Pricing: Free plan (public diagrams, 15 tables per diagram, 1 user). Third-party listings show Starter at $19/month (10 private diagrams, 50 tables), Growth at $59/month (unlimited private diagrams, up to 5 users), and Large at $179/month (up to 25 users), with annual discounts. Enterprise is quote-based.

4. Lucidchart

Lucidchart, from Lucid Software, is a browser-based diagramming tool that covers flowcharts, org charts, architecture diagrams, and ERDs. For ERDs you can build a diagram manually with the ERD shape library using crow's foot or UML notation. You can also import a schema from MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, or SQL Server, or generate an editable diagram with Lucid AI. Database import is a paid-plan feature.

Real-time co-editing, comments, and integrations with Confluence, Google Workspace, and Microsoft products make it a fit for cross-functional teams. Business analysts, product managers, and architects who need ER diagrams alongside other documentation tend to use it. Enterprise plans add SSO and admin controls.

Lucidchart is a drawing tool rather than a dedicated data-modeling platform. It doesn't manage database versions, generate schema-migration code, or enforce naming standards. For teams that need an ERD alongside twenty other diagram types, that's fine. For data teams, it's going to feel thin.

Pros

  • Flexible: ERDs, flowcharts, UML, and architecture diagrams in one tool
  • Imports schemas from MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server (paid plans)
  • Mature real-time collaboration, commenting, and a wide integration ecosystem
  • Large template library and AI-assisted diagram generation

Cons

  • Not purpose-built for data modeling, no forward-engineering or governance workflows
  • Free plan is tight on documents and objects per document, database import requires a paid plan
  • Per-user pricing becomes costly across big teams

Pricing: Free plan with limited editable documents and objects per document. Published prices vary by source and billing, with Individual at about $9/month, Team at about $10/user/month billed annually (with a free trial), and Enterprise on custom pricing. Check lucid.co for current rates.

5. Eraser

Eraser is a documentation and diagramming workspace for technical teams. It produces diagrams as editable code, so the same diagram can be adjusted in text, refined with AI prompts, or changed on a visual canvas. ER diagrams are one of its supported diagram types, alongside cloud architecture, flowcharts, and sequence diagrams.

AI diagram generation can work from prompts, images, code files, schemas, and Git repositories. Eraser also offers collaborative Markdown documents for design docs, plus integrations with GitHub, Notion, Confluence, and a VS Code extension. Pricing is per member, and every plan allows unlimited free guests. It suits software and platform engineers who want ER diagrams and architecture docs kept close to their code.

The limitations are clear. It's a general technical-diagramming tool, so it lacks reverse and forward engineering, DDL generation, schema lineage, and data governance. AI features are credit-capped and SAML SSO is reserved for higher tiers.

Pros

  • Diagram-as-code output that's easy to edit, version, and keep in sync with repos
  • AI generation from prompts, images, code, and Git repositories
  • Unlimited free guests and real-time collaboration
  • Integrations with GitHub, Notion, Confluence, and VS Code, plus 3,000+ tech icons

Cons

  • Not a dedicated database modeler, no reverse or forward engineering or schema lineage
  • Free plan is very limited (about 3 files and 3 AI credits)
  • AI usage is credit-capped and SSO is limited to higher tiers

Pricing: Free plan ($0, about 3 files, 3 AI credits, 7-day version history, unlimited guests). The current pricing page lists Business at $45/member/month billed annually ($60 monthly) and Business Plus at about $42/member/month, with a custom Enterprise tier. Some older third-party sites list a Professional tier at $15/month. Confirm on eraser.io/pricing.

6. Vertabelo

Vertabelo is a browser-based data modeling tool aimed at teams who want more structure than a simple diagramming app. It supports both logical and physical models, with reverse engineering of existing databases, SQL script generation, live model validation, versioning, and sharing. Because it runs in the browser, models are accessible from any device.

It's closer in scope to a dedicated modeler than dbdiagram, DrawSQL, Lucidchart, or Eraser, which makes it a useful comparison point for readers weighing diagram-focused tools against full modeling platforms. Typical users are database developers, architects, and analysts working on relational systems.

That said, its enterprise-style features are lighter than heavyweight tools like ER/Studio. It depends on an internet connection, and reviewers note that performance can vary with very large models. Its modern cloud-warehouse and governance coverage is also narrower than what enterprise platforms offer.

Pros

  • Supports both logical and physical modeling
  • Reverse engineering, SQL generation, and live model validation
  • Browser-based with real-time collaboration and versioning
  • Team plans designed for shared model management

Cons

  • Paid-only after a trial, with a higher entry price than lightweight diagram tools
  • Requires an internet connection, performance can vary on large models
  • Narrower cloud-warehouse and governance coverage than enterprise modeling platforms

Pricing: 7-day free trial. Third-party sources list Individual at about $24/month, Team (5 members) at about $83/month, and custom Enterprise pricing for 25+ users. Verify current rates on vertabelo.com.

Final Verdict

If you want a quick DBML sketch for a side project, dbdiagram.io is fine. If your whole stack is Laravel and MySQL, DrawSQL will do the job. Lucidchart is great if ERDs are just one of many diagram types your team draws. Eraser fits engineering teams who care more about docs-as-code than database governance. Vertabelo sits in a thoughtful middle ground for pure relational modeling.

But if you want one tool that actually scales from your first table to your five-thousandth, with reverse and forward engineering, real-time collaboration, Git integration, an AI Copilot, and a semantic layer that no other visual tool offers, SqlDBM is the clear winner. It's the only one in this roundup I'd trust to run a serious data platform on Snowflake, Databricks, or BigQuery without hitting a wall six months in. Start on the free tier, try it against a real database, and I think you'll see why 400,000+ users have made the same choice.

FAQ

What's the difference between an ERD tool and a data modeling platform?
An ERD tool draws entity-relationship diagrams. A data modeling platform does that plus reverse engineering, forward engineering to DDL, version control, governance, and often semantic or lineage layers. dbdiagram and DrawSQL sit in the first camp. SqlDBM sits in the second.

Which ERD tool is best for Snowflake, Databricks, or BigQuery?
SqlDBM is the strongest fit. It natively supports all three warehouses with full round-trip modeling and forward-engineers DDL that works with each engine's specifics. Most other tools in this roundup only support traditional relational databases.

Can I use a free tool for a real production project?
For a small schema, sure. But free tiers almost always cap diagram count, table count, or collaborators. Once you have real teammates and a real schema, you'll outgrow the free limits fast, especially on dbdiagram, DrawSQL, and Eraser.

Does SqlDBM really have a free tier?
Yes. You can sign up and start modeling without committing. Paid plans are quote-based and scale with your team, so you only move up when you actually need enterprise features like SSO, RBAC, or premium support.

title: Pourquoi la Physique Déterministe a Sauvé la Synchro de 15 Téléphones en Flutter
description:
Nous sommes l'équipe de développement indépendante derrière Wobbly Bottle.

Lors des soirées étudiantes ou des apéros, 10 personnes se bousculent presque toujours autour d'un seul smartphone de 6 pouces. Wobbly Bottle élimine ce problème : jusqu'à 15 participants rejoignent le salon avec un code PIN à 6 lettres, et la bouteille tourne en temps réel, synchronisée à 60 FPS sur l'écran de chaque joueur.

1. Pourquoi streamer chaque image a échoué

Notre première idée : diffuser l'angle de la bouteille 60 fois par seconde via WebSockets aux 14 autres téléphones.

Le résultat a été catastrophique :

  • Consommation de données excessive : 60 paquets par seconde multipliés par 14 clients saturent la bande passante.
  • Saccades et décalages : Dès qu'un réseau 4G subit une micro-coupure, l'animation devient hachée.
  • Surchauffe thermique : Sur les anciens appareils Android, décoder des flux JSON intensifs entraînait des chutes de framerate.

2. La solution : Synchroniser l'événement, calculer en local

Au lieu de diffuser des coordonnées, l'hôte transmet un seul message initial :

{
  "type": "spin_started",
  "roundId": "round-42",
  "initialAngle": 1.2,
  "impulse": { "angularVelocity": 18.7 },
  "startAt": 1730000000000
}

Chaque téléphone exécute ensuite localement la même formule de décélération dans un CustomPainter Flutter à 60 FPS :

const fixedStep = 1 / 60;
const damping = 0.985;

void onTick() {
  angularVelocity *= damping;
  angle += angularVelocity * fixedStep;
}

Grâce à cette physique déterministe, la bouteille ralentit et s'arrête au même angle exact sur tous les écrans du salon.

3. Reconnexion instantanée : Snapshot au lieu de Replay

Si un joueur perd momentanément la connexion, nous ne rejouons pas l'historique des animations passées. Le client demande un instantané d'état (qui doit jouer, quelle carte est tirée) et reprend la partie immédiatement sans latence.

title: CSS Units Explained: A Beginner’s Guide to px, %, em, rem, vh and vw
description:
If you're learning CSS, you've probably encountered code like this:

font-size: 16px;
width: 50%;
padding: 1rem;
height: 100vh;

And perhaps you've wondered:

Why are there so many different units?

Why can't we simply use px for everything?

What's the difference between em and rem?

What exactly are vh and vw?

And perhaps the biggest question:

Which CSS unit should I actually use?

The good news is that you don't need to memorize every CSS unit before you can become comfortable with CSS.

Instead, focus on understanding what each unit is relative to and what problem it helps you solve.

Once you understand that idea, choosing CSS units becomes much easier.

In this beginner-friendly guide, we'll explore six commonly used CSS units:

  • px
  • %
  • em
  • rem
  • vh
  • vw

We'll look at what they mean, how they work, where they can be useful, and some common beginner mistakes.

Why Do CSS Units Matter?

Before looking at individual units, let's understand why CSS needs them in the first place.

When you're writing CSS, you're constantly telling the browser how large or how far apart something should be.

For example:

p {
font-size: 18px;
}

You're telling the browser:

"Make this text 18 CSS pixels in size."

Or:

.container {
width: 80%;
}

You're telling the browser:

"Make this element 80% of the relevant containing block's width."

CSS units provide the reference the browser needs to calculate these values.

And different units use different references.

That's the key idea.

  1. Understanding px

Let's start with one of the easiest units to understand:

px

px stands for pixel.

For example:

h1 {
font-size: 32px;
}

Here, 32px specifies a CSS length of 32 pixels.

You can also use pixels for things such as:

.card {
padding: 20px;
border-radius: 8px;
border: 1px solid black;
}

Pixels are useful when you want a specific, predictable length.

For example, a developer might use pixels for:

  • Border thickness
  • Small gaps
  • Border radius
  • Icon dimensions
  • Specific spacing
  • Certain fixed-size elements

However, that doesn't mean you should use px for absolutely everything.

One reason CSS has relative units is that websites often need to adapt to different screens, layouts, and user preferences.

  1. Understanding %

The % unit is a relative unit.

It expresses a value as a percentage relative to another value.

For example:

.container {
width: 50%;
}

The exact reference depends on the property, but for an ordinary width, the percentage is generally calculated relative to the containing block's width.

Imagine a container that's 1000px wide.

If a child has:

width: 50%;

its width would be 500px in that simplified example.

That's useful because the child doesn't have to remain a fixed 500px wide.

Its size can change as the available space changes.

This is one reason percentages are useful for flexible layouts.

A Practical Example of %

Imagine you're building a webpage with a content area.

You could write:

.content {
width: 80%;
}

Instead of saying:

.content {
width: 800px;
}

The percentage-based version can adapt as the containing block changes.

This can be useful when building responsive layouts.

However, percentages aren't automatically the solution to every responsive-design problem.

The important thing is understanding what the percentage is relative to.

  1. Understanding em

Now things become slightly more interesting.

The em unit is a relative unit associated with font size.

For example:

.parent {
font-size: 20px;
}

.child {
font-size: 2em;
}

The child's font-size is 40px in this example because 2em is calculated from the parent's computed font size.

So:

20px × 2 = 40px

This makes em useful when you want something to scale relative to typography.

But there's an important detail beginners should understand:

The reference for em depends on the property.

For font-size, em is based on the parent's computed font size.

For many other properties, such as padding and margin, em is based on the element's own computed font size.

That distinction matters.

Why Can em Sometimes Become Confusing?

Because em is relative, its value can depend on context.

Imagine several nested elements:

.parent {
font-size: 20px;
}

.child {
font-size: 1.5em;
}

.grandchild {
font-size: 1.5em;
}

The values can compound as you move deeper into the hierarchy.

That's not necessarily bad.

In fact, this behavior can be useful when designing components that should scale based on their typography.

But if you're a beginner and you're trying to create a consistent sizing system across an entire website, rem can often be easier to reason about.

Which brings us to our next unit.

  1. Understanding rem

rem stands for root em.

Unlike em, which can depend on context, rem is based on the computed font size of the root element.

The root element in an HTML document is normally:

For example:

html {
font-size: 16px;
}

h1 {
font-size: 2rem;
}

Here:

2rem = 32px

because:

2 × 16px = 32px

This gives you a more predictable reference point.

Why Do Developers Like rem?

Imagine you want consistent typography throughout a website.

You could define:

h1 {
font-size: 2rem;
}

h2 {
font-size: 1.5rem;
}

p {
font-size: 1rem;
}

If the root font size is 16px, these correspond to:

  • 2rem → 32px
  • 1.5rem → 24px
  • 1rem → 16px

The advantage is that all of these values share the same reference point.

This makes rem particularly useful for creating consistent sizing systems.

You may see rem used for:

  • Font sizes
  • Padding
  • Margins
  • Component spacing
  • Buttons
  • Layout dimensions

em vs rem: What's the Difference?

This is one of the most common beginner questions.

Here's a simple way to think about it:

em → relative to font-size context

rem → relative to the root element's font size

For example:

html {
font-size: 16px;
}

.parent {
font-size: 20px;
}

.child {
font-size: 2em;
}

The child becomes:

40px

because its 2em is based on the parent's 20px font size.

But:

.child {
font-size: 2rem;
}

would be:

32px

because rem refers to the root's 16px font size.

So when you're choosing between em and rem, ask:

"Do I want this value to respond to local typography, or do I want it tied to the root sizing system?"

That's much more useful than simply memorizing their definitions.

  1. Understanding vh

Now let's move away from font-relative units.

vh stands for viewport height.

One vh unit represents 1% of the viewport's height.

Therefore:

100vh = 100% of the viewport height

For example:

.hero {
height: 100vh;
}

This tells the browser to make the element's height equal to the viewport height.

This can be useful for certain hero sections or full-screen layouts.

What Is the Viewport?

The viewport is essentially the visible area of the browser window available for the webpage.

Its dimensions can change depending on:

  • Screen size
  • Browser window size
  • Device
  • Orientation

So a desktop browser and a smartphone can have very different viewport dimensions.

That's why viewport units can be useful when you want an element to respond directly to the available viewport.

  1. Understanding vw

vw stands for viewport width.

One vw represents 1% of the viewport's width.

So:

100vw = 100% of the viewport width

For example:

.hero {
width: 50vw;
}

This means the element's width is 50% of the viewport width.

Unlike %, which is often relative to a containing block, vw is tied directly to the viewport.

That difference is important.

% vs vw

These two units can sometimes look similar but solve different problems.

Consider:

.container {
width: 50%;
}

The percentage width is generally calculated relative to the containing block.

Now compare:

.container {
width: 50vw;
}

This is based on half of the viewport width.

So ask yourself:

"Should this size respond to its parent, or directly to the browser viewport?"

That question helps you choose between % and vw.

A Simple CSS Units Cheat Sheet

Let's put everything together.

Unit

px

Basic idea

Specific CSS length

Common use

Borders, precise spacing

Unit
%

Basic idea

Relative to another value

Common use

Flexible widths and sizes

Unit
em

Basic idea

Relative to font-size context

Common use

Scalable component typography/spacing

Unit
rem

Basic idea

Relative to root font size

Common use

Consistent typography and spacing

Unit
vh

Basic idea
Relative to viewport height

Common use

Viewport-based vertical sizing

Unit
vw

Basic idea
Relative to viewport width

Common use

Viewport-based horizontal sizing

Remember:

The goal isn't to memorize the table.

The goal is to understand the reference point behind each unit.

Which CSS Unit Should You Use?

This is where many beginners get stuck.

They ask:

"Should I always use px?"

Or:

"Are rem units better than pixels?"

There isn't one unit that is always the correct choice.

Your choice depends on the problem you're solving.

For example:

Need a specific small border?

px may make sense.

border: 1px solid;

Need a flexible width?

% may be appropriate.

width: 80%;

Need sizing that follows local typography?

em may be useful.

Need a consistent root-based scale?

rem is often a good choice.

Need sizing based on the viewport height?

Consider vh.

Need sizing based on the viewport width?

Consider vw.

The important thing is to choose intentionally.

Don't Use Units Just Because You See Other Developers Using Them

When you're learning to code, it's easy to copy code from tutorials.

You might see:

padding: 1rem;

and simply assume:

"1rem must be better than 16px."

That's not necessarily the right way to think about it.

The better question is:

"Why did the developer choose rem here?"

Perhaps they want spacing to follow the site's root sizing system.

Likewise, if you see:

width: 50vw;

don't simply conclude that vw is better than %.

Ask:

"Why should this element be relative to the viewport rather than its parent?"

Understanding the reasoning behind the code is what makes you a better developer.

Common Beginner Mistakes With CSS Units

  1. Using px for Everything

Pixels are useful, but using them for every single dimension can make it harder to build flexible layouts.

Learn how relative units work so you can choose appropriately.

  1. Thinking em and rem Are the Same

They're both relative, but they don't use the same reference.

Remember:

em → local font-size context

rem → root font size

  1. Assuming % Always Means Percentage of the Screen

It doesn't.

For many properties, the percentage is calculated relative to a relevant containing block or another property-specific reference.

If you want a value directly tied to the viewport, viewport units may be more appropriate.

  1. Using vh Without Considering Real-World Viewport Behavior

100vh can be useful, but mobile browsers have dynamic browser UI that can affect the usable viewport.

Modern CSS provides newer viewport units such as svh, lvh, and dvh for more specific viewport behavior.

You don't need to master these immediately, but it's useful to know that 100vh isn't always the complete story on mobile devices.

  1. Choosing Units Without Understanding the Layout

CSS isn't about randomly choosing units until something looks right.

First understand the relationship between the elements.

Then choose a unit that expresses that relationship.

A Better Way to Learn CSS Units

Instead of memorizing:

"px means this."

"rem means that."

Try asking these questions:

What should this value be relative to?

Is it relative to:

  • A specific length?
  • The parent?
  • The element's font size?
  • The root font size?
  • The viewport width?
  • The viewport height?

Once you know the reference point, the appropriate unit becomes much easier to identify.

Practice With a Small Project

One of the best ways to understand CSS units is to experiment.

Create a simple card:

Learn CSS


Understanding CSS units makes layouts easier to control.

Then try different units:

.card {
width: 80%;
padding: 1rem;
border: 1px solid;
border-radius: 8px;
}

.card h2 {
font-size: 2rem;
}

.card p {
font-size: 1em;
}

Then experiment.

Change the width.

Change the root font size.

Change the padding.

Try em instead of rem.

Resize the browser.

Watch what changes.

This type of experimentation will teach you more than simply memorizing definitions.

The Bigger Lesson

Learning CSS isn't really about collecting hundreds of properties and values in your memory.

It's about understanding relationships.

When you understand that:

  • px gives you a specific CSS length
  • % relates a value to another relevant size
  • em works relative to font-size context
  • rem uses the root font size
  • vh responds to viewport height
  • vw responds to viewport width

you have already built a strong foundation.

And that's the important part.

You don't need to use every CSS unit in every project.

You need to understand why you would choose one unit over another.

Final Thoughts

CSS units might seem like a small topic, but they have a major impact on how you build layouts.

The difference between:

width: 50%;

and:

width: 50vw;

isn't simply different syntax.

They communicate different relationships.

Likewise, choosing:

font-size: 2em;

instead of:

font-size: 2rem;

changes what the value is relative to.

That's why learning CSS units is less about memorization and more about developing the ability to ask:

"What should this value be relative to?"

Once you start thinking that way, CSS becomes less about guessing and more about making deliberate decisions.

And that's an important step toward becoming a better frontend developer.

You don't need to memorize every CSS unit.

Understand the problem each unit solves—and choosing the right one becomes much easier. 💻

Which CSS unit did you find most confusing when you first started learning CSS: %, em, rem, vh, or vw?

title: Invoice and Payment: How to Build a Billing Flow Users Can Trust
description:
A customer clicks “Pay” and sees a success message. They close the page assuming everything is complete. A few minutes later, the dashboard still shows an unpaid balance.

Now they have a question: should they try again?

This is where billing becomes a product problem. The connection between invoice and payment affects user confidence, support requests and the accuracy of business records.

For developers, building this flow means thinking beyond a payment button. The system needs to explain what is owed, record what happened and recover when something goes wrong.

Understanding Invoice and Payment

An invoice

is a request for payment. It describes what a customer owes for products or services and usually includes a reference number, item details and a due date.

A payment is the transfer of money toward that amount.

These records are related, but their relationship is not always one to one. A customer might pay an invoice in two instalments. A single bank transfer might also cover several outstanding bills.

Keeping the records separate makes those situations easier to represent. The application can track the original charge while recording each contribution toward the balance.

Start With Clear Business Rules

Before designing screens or database tables, agree on how billing should work.

Ask questions such as:

When should an invoice be created?

Can customers make partial payments?

Which payment methods are accepted?

Who can approve an adjustment?

What happens when a transaction fails?

How are refunds recorded?

These answers shape the implementation.

For example, a subscription service may create invoices on a schedule. A consulting platform might generate them after a project milestone is approved.

Writing down these rules early prevents developers and finance teams from making different assumptions.

  1. Give Every Invoice a Reliable Identity

Each invoice needs a stable internal identifier. A customer-facing reference helps people discuss it with support or their finance department.

Keep these references consistent across the billing page, email notification and downloadable document.

Useful information includes:

Customer account

Issue date

Due date

Currency

Line items

Discounts and applicable charges

Total amount

Remaining balance

An issued invoice should also preserve the details used when it was created. Changing a product’s current price should not silently rewrite an earlier bill.

Historical records need to remain understandable.

  1. Design Statuses Around Real Events

A single “paid” checkbox cannot explain every situation.

An invoice may be a draft, issued, partly paid or settled. It may also be cancelled under the business’s approved process.

A payment can be pending, successful or failed. Refunds may require their own records and states.

Define what triggers each change. For instance, opening a checkout page does not mean money has been received.

Be careful with overdue labels too. An invoice becomes overdue because its deadline passes while an amount remains outstanding. That is different from a failed payment attempt.

Clear definitions make reports and customer messages more consistent.

  1. Keep Amounts Precise

Small calculation differences can create confusing balances.

Choose a representation that supports exact monetary calculations. Avoid ordinary binary floating-point arithmetic for amounts that must match precisely.

Record the currency alongside each amount. Establish clear rules for rounding and apply them consistently across line items, discounts and totals.

Do not assume every currency uses the same number of decimal places.

The value displayed on the invoice should agree with the amount requested at checkout. When those numbers differ, even slightly, users have a reason to question the transaction.

  1. Treat Payment Confirmation Carefully

A browser redirect is useful for navigation. It should not be the sole evidence that a transaction succeeded.

The customer may close the tab before returning. Their connection might fail after the payment provider accepts the transaction.

Use the provider’s supported server-side confirmation process to establish the result. Verify incoming notifications according to that provider’s documentation.

Then update the payment record and apply the confirmed amount to the appropriate invoice.

The interface can show a pending message while confirmation is incomplete. Honest status information is more helpful than a premature success screen.

  1. Make Repeated Requests Safe

Users double-click buttons. Networks retry requests. External services may deliver the same notification more than once.

The application should handle repetition without creating duplicate charges or applying the same receipt twice.

Use a stable reference for each payment attempt. Where supported, use the payment provider’s mechanism for preventing duplicate requests.

Record processed transaction and event identifiers so repeated notifications can be recognised.

Also consider simultaneous processing. Two workers receiving related updates should not both apply the same amount.

This behaviour deserves attention before launch because duplicate billing can quickly damage customer trust.

  1. Plan for Partial Payments and Refunds

Real billing rarely follows a perfect straight line.

Imagine an invoice for 1,000 units of a currency. The customer pays 600 today and the remaining 400 next week.

The system should preserve both transactions while showing the correct outstanding amount after each one.

A refund introduces another question: does the customer still owe the original amount, or has the underlying charge also been reduced?

That answer depends on the business event. Record refunds and approved invoice adjustments separately so the history explains both the movement of money and the amount owed.

  1. Give Users a Helpful Billing Screen

A good invoice and payment experience answers common questions immediately.

Customers should be able to find the amount due, deadline and current status without searching through several menus.

Show a clear description of the purchase. Provide access to the invoice document and relevant payment history.

After a failed attempt, explain the next useful action. Avoid displaying only an internal error code.

If confirmation is pending, say so. Give users a way to check the latest result before attempting another payment.

Clear wording can prevent unnecessary retries and support tickets.

  1. Build Reconciliation Into the Process

Reconciliation means checking that internal records agree with external payment information.

Even a well-designed integration can encounter delayed notifications or interrupted processing. A regular comparison helps find transactions that need investigation.

Look for cases such as:

Successful payments missing from the application

Receipts assigned to the wrong invoice

Refunds without matching internal records

Amounts or currencies that do not agree

Keep an exception queue with enough detail for someone to investigate.

A dashboard that shows no errors is only useful if the underlying records have actually been checked.

  1. Test the Awkward Scenarios

A successful checkout proves only one path works.

Test repeated clicks, delayed confirmation and duplicate notifications. Check what happens when the customer leaves midway through payment.

Include partial settlements, expired invoices and failed attempts followed by successful retries.

Confirm that rounding remains consistent. Verify that users cannot view or pay another account’s invoice by changing a reference in the address bar.

These checks focus on the places where billing mistakes become visible to customers.

Final Thoughts

A dependable invoice and payment flow connects clear charges with accurate transaction records.

Start with agreed business rules. Keep monetary calculations precise. Confirm results through trusted server-side processes and make repeated events safe to handle.

When the interface and records tell the same story, customers can understand what they owe and what they have paid. That clarity makes the product easier to use and the billing process easier to support.

title: Your POA&M Is a Plan, Not a Parking Lot: CMMC's POA&M Rules
description:
A Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) lists the security requirements you have not met yet and how you will close them. Under CMMC, it is not a place to leave gaps open. 32 CFR 170.21 limits what can go on it and how long it can stay.

Level 1: no POA&M

A POA&M is not permitted at any time for a CMMC Level 1 self-assessment. Every one of the 15 requirements must be met.

Level 2: three conditions

You can reach a Conditional Level 2 status with a POA&M only if all of these are true:

  • Your assessment score divided by 110 is at least 0.8. That means a score of at least 88.- No requirement on the POA&M is worth more than 1 point under the CMMC scoring method. The one exception is SC.L2-3.13.11, CUI encryption, when encryption is in place but not FIPS-validated.- None of these requirements are on it: AC.L2-3.1.20 External Connections, AC.L2-3.1.22 Control Public Information, CA.L2-3.12.4 System Security Plan, PE.L2-3.10.3 Escort Visitors, PE.L2-3.10.4 Physical Access Logs and PE.L2-3.10.5 Manage Physical Access.## The 180-day closeout A POA&M closeout assessment checks only the NOT MET requirements on the POA&M. It must confirm they are closed within 180 days of your Conditional status date. For Level 2 (Self), you run the closeout the same way as the initial self-assessment and post the results in SPRS. If you miss the 180 days, your Conditional status expires. Under 32 CFR 170.16, you are then ineligible for new awards that require Level 2 (Self) or higher for that system until you achieve a new status. ## What to do now
  • Score all 110 requirements honestly.- Close the requirements that can never go on a POA&M first, starting with your SSP.- Put a date and an owner on every remaining item, and plan to finish well inside 180 days.CMMC Phase 2 is suspended, but contracts can still require Level 2 (Self), and these POA&M rules apply to it. ## Start here Cyberneza is a veteran-owned, 100% US-based cybersecurity and compliance firm in Orlando, Florida. Our free SPRS score worksheet shows your score and your gaps: https://cyberneza.com/sprs-score-worksheet Sources: 32 CFR 170.21, 32 CFR 170.16, 32 CFR 170.15
