title: Adding JSON‑LD Structured Data to a Small Business Site: Organization, WebSite, BlogPosting, and BreadcrumbList
description:
Why JSON‑LD Matters for a Small Business

When I rebuilt my own site for Dream Futures Tech, the first thing I wanted was a clean way to tell search engines who I am, what I offer, and how my content is organized. Google recommends JSON‑LD because it lives in a <script type="application/ld+json"> tag, keeps the markup out of the HTML flow, and is easy to validate with the Rich Results Test.

In this article I walk through the four most useful schema types for a typical small‑business site:

  • Organization – the business identity.
  • WebSite – the site as a searchable entity.
  • BlogPosting – each blog article.
  • BreadcrumbList – the navigation trail.

I’ll show the exact JSON I use, where I drop it in the page, and a few gotchas I ran into while keeping the syntax valid.

1. The Organization Block

The Organization object is the anchor for everything else. It tells Google the name, logo, address, and contact details.

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Organization",
  "name": "Dream Futures Tech",
  "url": "https://dreamfuturestech.com",
  "logo": "https://dreamfuturestech.com/assets/logo.png",
  "contactPoint": [{
    "@type": "ContactPoint",
    "telephone": "+1-954-555-0123",
    "contactType": "Customer Service",
    "areaServed": "US",
    "availableLanguage": ["English"]
  }],
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "123 Ocean Drive",
    "addressLocality": "Pompano Beach",
    "addressRegion": "FL",
    "postalCode": "33062",
    "addressCountry": "US"
  }
}
</script>

I keep this block in a partial file (_org-ld.html) and include it in the <head> of every page via my templating engine (I use PHP with Blade‑like syntax, but the idea works in any stack).

<?php include 'partials/_org-ld.html'; ?>

2. Declaring the WebSite

The WebSite schema lets Google know the primary search URL for the site and optionally provides a potentialAction for site search.

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "WebSite",
  "url": "https://dreamfuturestech.com/",
  "name": "Dream Futures Tech",
  "potentialAction": {
    "@type": "SearchAction",
    "target": "https://dreamfuturestech.com/search?q={search_term_string}",
    "query-input": "required name=search_term_string"
  }
}
</script>

I only add this once, right after the Organization block. Because both blocks share the same @context, I could combine them into a single JSON array, but keeping them separate makes debugging easier.

3. Structured Data for Blog Posts

Every article on my blog now carries a BlogPosting object. The key fields are headline, author, datePublished, image, and articleBody (or a short description). I generate the JSON dynamically from the post metadata, so the markup always matches the content.

<?php
$ld = [
  "@context" => "https://schema.org",
  "@type" => "BlogPosting",
  "headline" => $post->title,
  "image" => $post->featured_image,
  "author" => [
    "@type" => "Person",
    "name" => "Kaleb Martinez"
  ],
  "publisher" => [
    "@type" => "Organization",
    "name" => "Dream Futures Tech",
    "logo" => [
      "@type" => "ImageObject",
      "url" => "https://dreamfuturestech.com/assets/logo.png"
    ]
  ],
  "datePublished" => $post->date->format('Y-m-d'),
  "dateModified" => $post->updated_at->format('Y-m-d'),
  "description" => $post->excerpt,
  "mainEntityOfPage" => [
    "@type" => "WebPage",
    "@id" => $post->url
  ]
];
?>
<script type="application/ld+json"><?php echo json_encode($ld, JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES|JSON_PRETTY_PRINT); ?></script>

A few practical notes:

  • Images must be absolute URLs – relative paths break the validator.
  • mainEntityOfPage ties the markup back to the canonical URL, which helps Google avoid duplicate‑content warnings.
  • I omit articleBody because the full HTML body can be huge; a concise description is enough for most rich‑result types.

4. BreadcrumbList for Navigation

Breadcrumbs improve internal linking and appear as a navigation trail in SERPs. The schema is a simple ordered list of ListItem objects.

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
  "itemListElement": [
    {
      "@type": "ListItem",
      "position": 1,
      "name": "Home",
      "item": "https://dreamfuturestech.com/"
    },
    {
      "@type": "ListItem",
      "position": 2,
      "name": "Blog",
      "item": "https://dreamfuturestech.com/blog/"
    },
    {
      "@type": "ListItem",
      "position": 3,
      "name": "<?= htmlspecialchars($post->title) ?>",
      "item": "<?= $post->url ?>"
    }
  ]
}
</script>

I generate the breadcrumb array in PHP based on the current route. If a page isn’t part of the blog hierarchy (e.g., a service page), I adjust the list accordingly.

5. Keeping the JSON Valid

The biggest practical hurdle for me was keeping the JSON syntax correct while mixing server‑side variables. A missing comma or an unescaped quote will cause the entire block to be ignored. Here are the safeguards I use:

  1. Always generate JSON with json_encode – never hand‑type the final string.
  2. Enable JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES so URLs stay readable.
  3. Run the output through the Rich Results Test after each deployment. The tool points out exact line numbers for syntax errors.
  4. Version‑control the partial files (_org-ld.html, _website-ld.html, etc.) so any accidental change shows up in a diff.

6. Deploying and Verifying

After I push the changes, I clear the Cloudflare cache (I use Cloudflare for CDN) and then run two checks:

  • Google’s Rich Results Test – paste the live URL, verify that each schema type appears without errors.
  • Schema.org’s validator – useful for catching warnings like missing @id fields.

If a warning shows up, I usually add an @id that points to the canonical URL of the entity. It isn’t required, but it helps Google treat the object as a stable identifier.

7. What I Learned

  • JSON‑LD is lightweight, but the devil is in the details: absolute URLs, proper dates (YYYY‑MM‑DD), and matching @type names.
  • Keeping the markup in reusable partials makes updates painless – a single logo change propagates to all schema blocks.
  • Validation tools are your friends; they catch the tiny syntax slip that would otherwise silently break the rich results.

With these four schema types in place, my site now shows a logo in the knowledge panel, breadcrumb trails in search results, and enhanced blog snippets when Google deems the content relevant. The implementation is straightforward, and the SEO payoff is visible without any exotic hardware or third‑party services.

I build sites and automations for small businesses at dreamfuturestech.com.

title: Fleet Maintenance Alerts Fire Twice: Deduplicating OBD-II Fault Codes in a Telematics Backend
description:
A fleet maintenance alert should help a technician decide what needs attention. It should not force the maintenance team to investigate the same engine fault three times because a telematics device retransmitted a message, a vehicle reported the same diagnostic code through two channels, or a backend retry created a duplicate notification.

This problem often appears when a fleet management platform begins connecting vehicles from different manufacturers, aftermarket OBD-II devices, and telematics providers. The initial implementation may work well with a small number of vehicles. As the number of connected assets grows, duplicate fault events can overwhelm dashboards, inflate notification counts, and weaken trust in automated maintenance workflows.

The solution is not simply to ignore repeated diagnostic trouble codes. A reliable backend needs to distinguish duplicate messages from recurring faults, continuing faults, and truly new incidents.

Why OBD-II Fault Codes Generate Duplicate Alerts

OBD-II systems expose diagnostic information that can help fleet operators identify engine and emissions-related problems. Depending on the vehicle, diagnostic interface, and telematics provider, the backend may receive fault information at different intervals or through different event formats.

Several conditions can produce repeated messages.

Device retransmission: A tracker temporarily loses network connectivity and sends buffered messages after reconnecting.

Webhook retries: A telematics provider retries a delivery because the receiving API did not acknowledge the original request within the expected time.

Polling overlap: A backend polls the same vehicle repeatedly and receives an unchanged diagnostic code.

Multiple data sources: A vehicle's OEM telematics feed and an aftermarket device report the same underlying fault.

Repeated fault observations: The vehicle continues reporting an active code over multiple trips. These observations may represent one ongoing incident rather than multiple new maintenance cases.

The challenge is that these situations can look similar at the message level while requiring different treatment in the maintenance system.

Start With Event Identity, Not Notification Logic

A common implementation checks whether a diagnostic code already exists for a vehicle. If it does, the backend discards the incoming event.

That approach can suppress useful information.

Consider a vehicle that reports a diagnostic code on Monday. The technician investigates and closes the maintenance case on Tuesday. The same code appears again on Friday.

If the system permanently deduplicates that vehicle-code combination, it may suppress the Friday incident even though the fault has returned.

A better design separates the raw event, the fault state, the maintenance incident, and the notification.

  • Raw event: The original diagnostic observation received from a device or provider.
  • Fault state: The backend's current understanding of the code for a specific vehicle.
  • Maintenance incident: The actionable case assigned to a technician or maintenance team.
  • Notification: The message delivered to the people responsible for responding.

This separation allows the system to retain every useful observation without creating a new maintenance case or sending another notification for every repeated message.

Build a Layered Deduplication Strategy

1. Normalize incoming diagnostic events

Before deduplication, convert incoming messages into a consistent internal structure.

A normalized event may include:

  • Fleet and vehicle identifiers
  • VIN, when available and verified
  • Telematics device identifier
  • Source provider and reporting module
  • Diagnostic trouble code
  • Code status, where supported
  • Source event timestamp
  • Backend receipt timestamp
  • Device sequence number, when available
  • Relevant diagnostic data and source payload

Normalization matters because different providers may represent the same diagnostic code differently. The backend should preserve the original payload while mapping the event into a common format.

Do not assume the device identifier, vehicle identifier, and VIN are interchangeable. Devices can be replaced, vehicles can change ownership, and hardware can be reassigned.

2. Use idempotency keys for message retries

When a provider supplies a stable event ID or sequence number, use it to identify repeat deliveries of the same message.

An idempotency key can be constructed from trusted source fields, such as the provider event ID and source account. If the provider does not supply a stable ID, a carefully designed fingerprint may combine the vehicle, source, diagnostic code, event time, and relevant status fields.

The fingerprint must reflect the source's actual behavior. A timestamp alone is rarely sufficient because devices may have clock drift, and several distinct events can occur close together.

Store processed event identifiers with a uniqueness constraint. When the same event arrives again, the backend should acknowledge it without repeating the business operation.

3. Track active fault episodes

Message deduplication cannot determine whether a fault is still active or has returned after resolution. That requires a state model.

For each vehicle and normalized fault identity, maintain a record containing fields such as:

  • Current status
  • First observed time
  • Last observed time
  • Last notification time
  • Associated maintenance case
  • Resolution or clear time, where known
  • Source observations and event history

Repeated observations can update the last-seen timestamp and diagnostic history. They do not automatically need to create a new incident.

When a fault is confirmed as cleared and later reappears, the system can open a new episode according to the relevant code's rules.

A missing observation should not automatically mean a fault has cleared. A disconnected device may simply have stopped sending data.

4. Separate fault severity from duplicate suppression

Not all diagnostic codes deserve the same notification policy. A recurring, low-priority warning and a potentially safety-critical fault should not be handled identically.

Use code-specific rules to determine whether the system should:

  • Update an existing incident silently
  • Notify the assigned technician
  • Escalate an unresolved incident
  • Reopen a resolved case
  • Create a new maintenance incident

Deduplication should reduce repetitive noise, not hide important changes in severity or status.

Make Event Processing Safe Under Retries

A telematics backend often has several asynchronous stages: event ingestion, normalization, persistence, rule evaluation, notification dispatch, and maintenance-system integration.

If the same message is processed by two workers simultaneously, both may decide that no incident exists and create one.

Use database transactions, unique constraints, or another concurrency-safe mechanism to enforce the incident-creation rule. A distributed lock can be useful in specific architectures, but it should not replace durable data-level safeguards.

Notification delivery needs its own idempotency mechanism. Creating one maintenance incident does not guarantee that an email, push notification, or webhook will be delivered only once.

For reliable processing, store notification intent in a transactional outbox or equivalent durable queue. A worker can dispatch the notification and record its delivery state. Since external delivery systems may still retry, use a stable notification key wherever the destination supports it.

Example: One Fault, Multiple Messages

Suppose a delivery truck reports diagnostic code P0420 through an aftermarket telematics device. The device sends the same buffered message twice, and the provider retries the webhook once.

The backend receives three messages.

A robust implementation would:

  1. Persist or identify the original event.
  2. Recognize repeated deliveries using the event ID or fingerprint.
  3. Maintain one active fault episode.
  4. Create one maintenance incident if the configured rules require it.
  5. Dispatch the initial notification once.
  6. Preserve later observations and retry details for audit purposes.

If the fault is cleared and subsequently returns, the backend evaluates the new evidence and may create another incident.

The important distinction is that three deliveries do not necessarily mean three faults, while three observations do not always mean one fault forever.

Test the Cases That Break Naive Deduplication

Before deploying the logic across a fleet, test more than a simple repeated-message scenario.

Include:

  • The same event delivered several times
  • The same code reported with different timestamps
  • Two providers reporting the same fault
  • Two distinct faults arriving almost simultaneously
  • A delayed message arriving after a newer event
  • A fault disappearing from the feed without an explicit clear event
  • A cleared fault returning days later
  • Concurrent workers processing the same vehicle
  • A notification provider timing out after accepting a message
  • A vehicle being reassigned to a different telematics device

Track duplicate-event rates, incidents created per fault episode, notification retries, processing delays, and faults reopened after resolution. These metrics help determine whether deduplication is reducing noise without hiding real maintenance needs.

What Fleet Management App Development Should Include

Fleet management app development is not limited to a map, a vehicle list, and a maintenance reminder screen. When the product consumes telematics data, its backend needs reliable event processing, fault history, configurable escalation rules, and connections to work orders and technician assignments.

A development team should understand the difference between raw telemetry and actionable operational events. It should also plan for mixed hardware, inconsistent provider payloads, intermittent connectivity, and data ownership across fleet accounts.

Recommended Fleet Software Development Companies

Dev Technosys is a fleet management software development company that builds custom fleet and logistics software, including applications that can connect operational workflows with telematics integrations, vehicle maintenance records, and management dashboards. Its 250+ professionals support software delivery across different business requirements. The project scope should explicitly define diagnostic event handling, integration responsibilities, and fault lifecycle rules.

IBM provides enterprise technology and integration capabilities that can support complex data and operational systems. Its enterprise engineering ecosystem can be relevant when telematics needs to connect with existing business platforms and analytics infrastructure.

Accenture works across enterprise software, cloud, data, and systems integration. Its delivery capabilities can be relevant to organizations modernizing fleet operations across several departments or existing technology platforms.

Final Thoughts

Duplicate OBD-II alerts are not merely a notification problem. They expose how a telematics backend identifies events, maintains fault state, and coordinates work across distributed systems.

The most reliable approach combines source-level idempotency, normalized diagnostic data, fault episode tracking, concurrency-safe incident creation, and independently controlled notification delivery.

The goal is not to suppress every repeated code. It is to make sure every message contributes to a trustworthy maintenance record while each actionable incident receives the appropriate response.

title: VLA Policies Do Not Know When Not to Act: Unintended Task Execution and Start Suppression
description:
arXiv:2610.41609v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A robot should act only on an instruction from a person or on an intent that the robot explicitly represents and generates. Unintended actions taken without such an instruction can cause risk or inconvenience to people and the environment. We examine how recent vision-language-action (VLA) policies respond when the instruction is missing or meaningless. We apply a paired protocol with empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible, and wrong-task instructions to six model checkpoints in LIBERO-Goal simulation. Holding the initial state fixed and varying only the instruction, we ask three questions: whether the robot starts to move, which task it completes, and what the instruction determines. Even when the instruction was empty, the robot started moving in every episode with all six checkpoints, and with five of them it often completed a task that the instruction had not specified. On two GR00T checkpoints, the instruction determined which task was executed but not whether the robot started moving; the robot moved even on infeasible instructions. We then tested three methods for suppressing the start: prepending "if no task is given do not move" to the instruction; a gate that holds the robot when the first action chunk for the given instruction nearly equals that for an empty instruction; and fine-tuning the policy to hold still on non-task inputs. The prefix stopped the robot in none of the six checkpoints, and the gate held it on non-task inputs in five of the six checkpoints. The fine-tuned policy never completed a task on non-task inputs, but it did not reliably keep the robot still, and it failed to suppress the start on infeasible instructions.

title: AI evaluators favor job applications written by certain AI models, independent of candidate quality
description:
arXiv:2610.41866v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Job applicants increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to write cover letters, while employers deploy LLMs to screen them. In this all-AI setting, we ask whether the \emph{choice of model} affects hiring outcomes independently of candidate qualifications. We introduce a multi-model auditing framework pairing eleven LLM writer agents with nine API-hosted evaluator agents across ten job descriptions and fifty candidates per job. Four findings emerge. First, we identify a generative preference hierarchy: a consistent global ranking of writer models by evaluator acceptance, in which locally hosted models are systematically disadvantaged regardless of their license, compounded by self-preference bias where evaluators favour their own outputs. Second, evaluator models differ substantially in how much bias they introduce based on applicants' tool choice, offering actionable guidance for fairer screening design. Third, this hierarchy has measurable competitive consequences: in the most adverse pairing, approximately two (1.8) out of twenty-five qualified candidates are filtered out purely due to model mismatch. Fourth, a common mechanism explains the patterns above: writer preference and self-preference trace to a combination of how much each writer leans on specific stylistic cues and how strongly evaluators, often unanimously, reward or penalise those same cues. A further check finds little evidence that an unmeasured "writer fingerprint" remains once these same features are accounted for. We discuss implications for algorithmic fairness in employment, regulation of AI-assisted screening, and the design of auditing frameworks that can be reapplied as the model landscape evolves.

title: Your payment webhook is wrong, and you'll find out when a paying user loses their plan
description:
Your payment webhook is wrong, and you will only find out when someone who just subscribed loses access to the Pro plan.

Webhooks do not arrive in order. A "subscription canceled" event can show up after "subscription renewed", and a handler that applies each event in the order it arrives will take the plan away from someone who just paid. Providers say so in their docs, but it is easy to read that sentence and keep writing if (event.type === "canceled") downgrade(user).

This is how I handled it in a side project: a time-tracking app with a Free and a Pro plan, where the payment provider is the source of truth for who is Pro and my database keeps a local copy. The stack is TypeScript, Drizzle and Postgres, but the idea fits any of them.

The three ways it goes wrong

Three different problems hide behind "out of order":

  • Stale events. An old event is delivered after a newer one, or the same event is delivered twice. Applying it rolls the user back to a state they already left.
  • Events from a different subscription. A user cancels their old subscription and buys a new one. The provider then sends the late "ended" notice for the old one. If you only look at the user, that notice removes the plan the user just paid for.
  • Final states that are not final. An order is refunded, then a delayed "paid" event arrives. Without a guard, a refunded order becomes paid again.

Ordering with a timestamp from the provider

Every subscription event carries the time the provider last modified the subscription. I store that time next to the plan, in an event_at column, and only apply an event that is not older than the one I already saved.

The check and the write have to be one statement. If you read the row, compare in application code and then write, two events arriving together can both pass the check. Postgres can do it in a single conditional upsert:

await db
  .insert(userPlans)
  .values({ ...values, userId })
  .onConflictDoUpdate({
    target: userPlans.userId,
    set: values,
    setWhere: sql`
      (excluded.event_at is null
        or user_plans.event_at is null
        or excluded.event_at >= user_plans.event_at)
      and
      (excluded.plan <> 'free'
        or user_plans.subscription_id is null
        or user_plans.subscription_id = excluded.subscription_id)`,
  })
  .returning({ userId: userPlans.userId });

When the setWhere condition is false, Postgres leaves the row alone and returning comes back empty. That tells me the event was ignored, which I use to decide whether to run side effects such as pausing paid features.

When two events for the same user run at the same time, Postgres locks the conflicting row for the ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE and checks the condition against the latest version of it. So they are applied one after the other, not on top of each other.

Only the right subscription can take the plan away

The second half of the condition is about subscriptions. A change to free is accepted only if it names the subscription stored for that user, or if none is stored yet.

That covers the case from earlier. The user cancels sub_old, buys sub_new, and then a late "ended" notice for sub_old arrives. Its subscription id does not match the stored one, so nothing happens and the user keeps the plan. A change that grants a plan is always allowed, because a purchase is how a new subscription id gets in.

A refund stays a refund

Payments use the same idea at the column level. The order id is unique, so recording the same payment twice is one row. The status update refuses to leave refunded:

.onConflictDoUpdate({
  target: payments.providerOrderId,
  set: {
    status: sql`case when payments.status = 'refunded'
                     then 'refunded'
                     else excluded.status end`,
    updatedAt: now,
  },
});

Test it with the ugly order

The tests that matter replay events in the wrong order against a real database. This is the shape of the one for subscriptions:

await active("sub_old", "2026-01-01");   // Pro
await revoked("sub_old", "2026-02-01");  // Free
await active("sub_old", "2026-01-01");   // stale re-delivery: ignored

await active("sub_new", "2026-03-01");   // bought again: Pro
await revoked("sub_old", "2026-04-01");  // late notice for the old one: ignored
// the user is still Pro on sub_new

await revoked("sub_new", "2026-02-15");  // older than what we have: ignored
await revoked("sub_new", "2026-05-01");  // the current subscription ends: Free

Each line asserts both the resulting plan and whether the event was applied. These tests run against Postgres, not a mock, because the behaviour I care about lives in the database.

What this costs

Be clear about the trade-offs:

  • Old events are dropped, not queued. I rely on the provider's timestamp being trustworthy. If a provider reuses or rounds timestamps, two different changes can look identical and the later one can be ignored.
  • It protects the plan, not your whole system. Side effects that already ran, such as an e-mail, are not undone. The applied flag exists so they only run when the write took effect.
  • You still need monitoring. An ignored event is the correct outcome, but a stream of ignored events is worth a look. Log them.

Takeaway

If your billing code has a handler per event type that writes straight to the user, try this: replay your events backwards and twice, and see who ends up with which plan. It is a cheap test, and the failure is the kind that shows up as a support ticket from someone who paid.

Have you been bitten by out-of-order webhooks? I would like to hear how you handled it.

title: The eval set is the spec: how to build the gate that every model change has to pass
description:
§ 01 · Why this note, this week

Three frontier models shipped in seven days. One of them is cheap enough that someone on your team has already opened a pull request to switch. Meanwhile a provider can roll a floating alias underneath a running agent with no deploy and no notice, as one team discovered when their triage agent quietly got worse over a weekend.

Both of those are the same event: the most important dependency in your system changed. The only thing that stands between that change and your production behavior is an eval set. Not a benchmark. A benchmark tells you how a model performs on someone else's tasks. An eval set tells you whether it still does yours.

This is why we say the eval set is the spec. Your prompt is an instruction. Your architecture is a set of boundaries. But the answer to "what does correct behavior mean for this agent" exists nowhere in your codebase except in the cases you decided to test. If those cases are thin, your definition of correct is thin, and every model change is a coin flip you are calling heads.

§ 02 · What an eval set is not

Three things get mistaken for an eval set, and none of them gate anything.

Not the public benchmark. A frontier model that scores at the top of the index can still be worse than a weaker one for your specific instruction. The triage agent's replacement model was better on every public measure and read urgency differently on the one instruction that mattered. The leaderboard is the provider's evidence. You need yours.

Not the demo set. The dozen inputs the team pasted in while building are all cases that already worked. An eval set built from them tests that the model can do the thing you already saw it do. It contains no information about the boundary of failure, which is the only place a regression shows up.

Not the vibe check. Someone runs a few prompts against the new model, likes what they see, and approves. This is not a control. It is a mood, and it will be a different mood on a different afternoon.

── The four case classes ──

§ 03 · The four case classes

An eval set that gates a production agent needs four kinds of cases. Most teams build the first, sometimes the second, and skip the two that catch the failures that actually happen.

◆ Class I, the golden path. Ordinary, representative tasks with a known correct outcome. These prove the model still does the job. They are the easiest to build, they are necessary, and they are the only class most teams have. Weight them by frequency in your real traffic, so the eval mirrors the mix production actually sees.

◆ Class II, the known failures. Every case that ever broke in production goes in here, permanently, with the correct outcome recorded. The lost confirmation on a payment. The invoice with the ambiguous identifier. The outage report written in calm language. This class is the accumulated memory of your system, and it is the reason the same bug does not ship twice. Every failure report on this site is a case in someone's Class II.

◆ Class III, the adversarial cases. Inputs that carry hidden instructions, malformed tool outputs, content designed to hijack the agent. Given the rates at which models follow embedded instructions in documents they read, this class is not paranoia, it is a measurement. A model change is exactly the moment your injection resistance can silently regress, and nothing in Class I will notice.

◆ Class IV, the drift sentinels. Cases at the edge of the agent's judgment, where the correct answer is defensible but not obvious. Their purpose is not pass or fail. Their purpose is to be sensitive. When a model changes character, subtly weighting tone over impact, being more or less willing to escalate, these are the cases whose answers move first. They are the canary, and they are what a golden path set can never give you, because on the golden path both models are right.

── Scoring the path ──

§ 04 · Score the path, not just the destination

A pass or fail on the final answer is not enough, and the invoice matching agent is the proof. A candidate model reached the right answer often enough to clear the threshold, and cost more in production because of how it got there: more turns, more retries, more escalations.

So every eval case records four things beyond correctness. Turns to completion, because turn count multiplies token cost rather than adding to it. Retries triggered, because a retry pays for the whole run again. Whether the run would have escalated, because an escalation is denominated in human minutes and is the most expensive term in the equation. And cost per successful task, the composite that finance actually pays.

A model that matches your current accuracy in twice the turns is a regression. On a correctness only eval it is a pass. This single change to how you score is the difference between an eval set that protects you and one that waves through the thing that doubles your bill.

── The gate ──

§ 05 · The gate: how the eval set is actually used

The eval set is worth nothing as an artifact. It is worth something as a gate, wired into three places.

On every model change, before production. A pinned version is replaced only after the candidate runs the full set and is compared against the incumbent, case by case, not against an abstract threshold. The question is never "did it pass." The question is "which cases did it lose that the current model wins." A model with a higher aggregate score that regresses on Class II is not an upgrade. It is a promise to repeat a bug you already paid for.

On a schedule, against the live model. Run the set against production daily. If a provider rolls a version underneath you, the score moves, and the score moving is an alarm. This is the canary that turns a four day silent regression into a Saturday morning alert.

On every prompt and architecture change. The eval set is the spec, so it gates changes to the spec's implementation too, not only to the model. A prompt edit that improves one case and quietly breaks three is exactly the change an eval set exists to catch.

── How eval sets decay ──

§ 06 · Eval sets decay, and the decay is invisible

An eval set is not a fixed asset. It rots, in three ways, and each is silent.

Distribution drift. The mix of real traffic moves. A case set built in March mirrors March's inputs, and by July the agent is seeing a class of task that is well represented in production and absent from the eval. The set still passes. It is measuring the wrong thing. Re-weight Class I against real traffic quarterly.

Overfitting to the set. The team tunes prompts until the eval is green. The eval is now a test the agent has memorized rather than a measurement of whether it can do the job. Keep a held out slice of cases that no prompt work is ever tuned against, and treat the gap between the tuned score and the held out score as a measure of how much you are fooling yourself.

Staleness of the correct answer. Business rules change. The escalation threshold moves, a category is renamed, a policy is updated, and the eval set is still grading against last quarter's definition of correct. Now the eval is actively defending the wrong behavior. Review the expected outcomes when the business rules change, not when the eval breaks.

── The file ──

§ 07 · The EVALS.md

Create an EVALS.md alongside the case set. It records the four classes and the count of cases in each, how Class I is weighted against real traffic, the scoring definition including the path metrics and the cost per successful task calculation, the gates the set is wired into, the held out slice and its most recent gap, the last re-weighting date, and the owner.

It also records the incumbent model's current scores, case by case. That table is the thing you compare a candidate against, and without it "the new model is better" is a claim, not a finding.

── The economics ──

§ 08 · Why this file shapes every agent decision

The orchestration layer is commoditizing. The model is a dependency you rent and can be swapped underneath you. The framework you chose this year is likely replaceable next year. Very little of the stack you are building is durable.

The eval set is. It is a written, executable definition of what your agent is supposed to do in a specific business, accumulated from real failures, and no platform vendor can ship it to you. When the model changes, it is what tells you whether to move. When a client asks how you know the agent works, it is the answer. It is the closest thing an agent engineering practice has to an asset that appreciates, and it is built the same way every time: one production failure at a time, written down and never removed.

── End of note ──

◆ A benchmark is the provider's evidence about someone else's tasks. An eval set is your evidence about yours. Only one of them can gate a model change.

◆ Four classes: the golden path, the known failures, the adversarial cases, and the drift sentinels. Most teams build only the first, and the first is the one that never catches a regression.

◆ Score the path, not just the answer. A model that is right in twice the turns is a regression on the invoice, whatever the accuracy column says.

◆ Eval sets decay silently through distribution drift, overfitting, and stale expected answers. Re-weight against real traffic, hold a slice out, and update the answers when the business rules change.

ORBIRESEARCH

Originally published on the OrbiResearch Lab. We build production AI agents at orbiresearch.com.

title: How to Export Signed Files with Download Links from Storage Buckets in Node.js (Retention)
description:
The decision rule is straightforward: generate an export into private object storage, issue a short-lived signed GET URL only after authorization, and make the deletion deadline part of the export record rather than a promise hidden in a worker. For a B2B SaaS product retaining signed documents, this keeps large-file throughput away from the application process while preserving a clear audit trail.

The link is not the export.

The examples below use a small Go reference implementation for the storage boundary. The same boundary is what a Node.js service should call: CreateExport, SignDownload, and DeleteExpired. Keeping those operations narrow matters more than choosing a particular bucket API. The tradeoff is real: direct-to-storage transfer reduces pressure on the application tier, but it adds lifecycle state, reconciliation work, and another policy boundary to operate. For a small file with no retention requirement, a normal application response can be easier to reason about.

How can Node.js export files with signed download links?

Start with an export record. It needs a tenant identifier, object key, byte count when known, creation time, expiration time, deletion deadline, and state. The object key should be generated by the service, not accepted verbatim from a browser. A useful key has no customer-controlled path segments that can become confusing during incident response.

Authorization happens before signing. A signed URL is a bearer credential, so anyone who obtains it can use it until its signature expires or the object is removed. The endpoint should check the requesting principal against the export record, then return a URL with a lifetime shorter than the business retention window. Those are different clocks.

A deletion deadline is also not the same as URL expiry. A link can stop working in ten minutes while the document remains retained until the contractual deadline. I keep both timestamps because conflating them produces either accidental early deletion or an archive that outlives its policy.

Step 1: Define a storage-neutral export contract

The application owns policy; the storage adapter owns bytes and signatures. That split makes the throughput decision measurable. If a 2 GB export is streamed through the Node.js process, memory may remain bounded, but application connections, egress, retries, and deployment interruptions still become part of the transfer path. A direct upload or multipart writer to the bucket moves the large-file path out of the request handler.

Here is a runnable contract sketch. It deliberately leaves signing primitives behind an interface because signature formats and canonical-request rules belong to the selected storage protocol.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Export struct {
    TenantID     string
    ObjectKey    string
    CreatedAt    time.Time
    URLExpiresAt time.Time
    DeleteAfter  time.Time
}

type Storage interface {
    SignGet(ctx context.Context, key string, expiresAt time.Time) (string, error)
    Delete(ctx context.Context, key string) error
}

func issueDownload(ctx context.Context, store Storage, export Export, tenantID string, now time.Time) (string, error) {
    if export.TenantID != tenantID {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("export is outside tenant scope")
    }
    if now.After(export.URLExpiresAt) {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("download link expired")
    }
    return store.SignGet(ctx, export.ObjectKey, export.URLExpiresAt)
}

func main() {
    fmt.Println("storage boundary ready")
}

The decision check is intentionally boring. Tenant scope, export state, and URL expiry are policy checks; the adapter should not silently invent them. In production, persist the export before returning a link and record the signing event without recording the bearer token itself.

Step 2: Stream the large file without making Node.js the bottleneck

The producer should write to a multipart-capable upload stream, finalize it, and only then mark the export available. For a Node.js implementation, use backpressure and do not collect chunks in an array. The Go example below shows the state transition and a bounded copy; it is also a useful executable model for tests around the adapter.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
)

type Uploader interface {
    Open(ctx context.Context, key string) (io.WriteCloser, error)
}

func writeExport(ctx context.Context, up Uploader, key string, src io.Reader) error {
    dst, err := up.Open(ctx, key)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("open upload: %w", err)
    }
    defer dst.Close()

    if _, err := io.Copy(dst, src); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("stream export: %w", err)
    }
    if err := dst.Close(); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("finalize upload: %w", err)
    }
    return nil
}

There is a small trap here: a successful copy is not necessarily a durable, readable export. The adapter must treat finalization as a separate operation, and the record should move from writing to ready only after that operation succeeds. If a worker dies between those events, a reconciler can inspect old writing records and either resume or remove them according to policy.

For capacity planning, measure bytes per minute, concurrent uploads, average and p99 completion time, retry volume, and the temporary storage consumed by unfinished multipart uploads. A 2 GB export that takes 90 seconds in a quiet test says little about a queue carrying 40 concurrent exports, so capacity review should exercise the queue, the worker pool, the network path, and cleanup together. Set an SLO for link issuance separately from the export-completion SLO. A user waiting for a URL and a user waiting for a 2 GB report are observing different services.

Keep it measurable.

Which failure signals change the design?

A rising p99 upload duration with flat application CPU points toward the storage path or network, not a need to add web workers. A growing count of writing exports points toward worker interruption, finalization, or reconciliation. Repeated authorization failures for otherwise valid records deserve a tenant-scope investigation; they should not be “fixed” by making links longer-lived.

The operational table I use during review is deliberately plain:

Concern Application responsibility Storage boundary responsibility
Tenant isolation Authorize export ownership Enforce object-key access policy
Large-file throughput Schedule and retry work Stream, multipart, finalize
Link exposure Set short URL lifetime Validate signature and method
Retention Persist deletion deadline Remove the object when instructed
Recovery Reconcile state transitions Report object and multipart status

Test the ugly paths. Expire the URL before fetching it. Kill the worker after the last byte but before finalization. Retry deletion after a timeout. Send a request from an untrusted tenant. Verify that a browser download from a separate origin has the intended CORS response headers, because CORS controls browser access and does not replace authorization.

Step 3: Verify deletion and keep rollback possible

Deletion is a workflow, not a cron expression. A periodic job can select records whose delete_after is in the past, claim them, delete the object, and mark the record deleted. Make the operation idempotent: an already absent object should not make the record permanently stuck. Keep a small reconciliation report with counts for ready, writing, expired-link, deletion-pending, and deletion-failed records.

Before rollout, run a canary tenant through a complete export, download, expiry, and deletion cycle. Compare the stored byte count with the source count, verify that the returned content disposition is suitable for the filename, and inspect audit events for tenant, export ID, actor, and timestamps. Never put the signed URL in normal request logs.

Rollback should disable new export creation or route it to the previous adapter while leaving already-ready objects governed by their existing deadlines. Do not bulk-delete during rollback. That separation gives the platform team room to correct signing or scheduling logic without changing retention outcomes.

The important boundary is therefore not the URL helper. It is the record that ties authorization, throughput, expiry, and deletion together. Once that record is durable, Node.js can remain the control plane while the storage service carries the large file.

References

  • MDN, “Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)”: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • RFC 9110, “HTTP Semantics,” status and method semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • RFC 7234, “HTTP/1.1 Caching,” cache control considerations: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7234
  • OWASP, “Logging Cheat Sheet”: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: Unlocking AI Search: Introducing Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search
description:
We are excited to announce the public preview of Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search (available in Public Preview in MongoDB Community Edition), a groundbreaking feature designed to make building sophisticated, AI-powered applications easier than ever. Since 2023, MongoDB has offered integrated vector search alongside our operational database, and last year we announced the acquisition of Voyage AI, bringing state-of-the-art embedding and reranking models to our customers. 

Now, with Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search and the integration of Voyage AI’s state-of-the-art models, we’re giving developers a feature which solves a major point of friction: one-click automatic embedding directly inside MongoDB, which eliminates the need to sync data and manage external models.

Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search

At its core, Automated Embedding in Vector Search offers seamless, secure, and scalable AI-powered search natively in MongoDB. By automatically generating vector embeddings (numerical representations of your data to capture semantic meaning), we eliminate the significant complexity typically required when building semantic search, recommendation engines, RAG apps, and AI agents.

The complexity we’re eliminating

Before this release, building vector search into applications presented significant challenges:

  • Manual embedding generation: Choosing an embedding model from over 100 available options and figuring out how to integrate external API services (authentication, input payload, output parameters) is challenging. Developers had to generate embeddings using external providers as part of their application code before inserting data or querying vector search.

  • Synchronization overhead: Every insert, update, or delete required keeping source data and vector embeddings in sync. Developers had to set up custom pipelines, monitor change streams, and write logic to trigger re-embedding and synchronize vectors every time source data changed. 

  • Additional API complexity: Each vector search query necessitated an extra API call to generate query embeddings. 

  • Managing large data ingestion: While simple embedding creation can be straightforward, embedding millions of documents becomes a production nightmare that developers need to monitor at scale. Teams must build complex MLOps pipelines with queuing systems, specialized workers, and retry logic to handle failures, integrate monitoring and alert systems, and ensure that primary database operations aren't blocked by slow or failing embedding endpoints.

The Solution: Streamlined AI-powered search

Automating the embedding process reduces complexity and makes getting started with semantic search as simple as creating a vector search index.

For the first time, you can simply choose an embedding model while setting up a vector search index, and the entire embeddings generation process is automated—no longer needing to rely on different vendors for embedding models and vector databases, which adds complexity and integration risks.  Now, you can simply select the embedding model that best matches your needs, including best-in-class embedding models from Voyage AI. This simplified approach significantly reduces the effort required to get started with key AI use cases, while Voyage AI's industry-leading embedding models ensure high-accuracy retrieval.

Offers architectural simplicity

Our streamlined architecture eliminates the need to manage separate embedding generation workflows, especially when handling complex, high-volume ingestions. 

Developers no longer need to maintain external embedding models, freeing up valuable engineering time that was previously spent on custom pipelines, complex error handling, and performance tuning. This simplification allows you to focus on improving application functionality rather than building embeddings from scratch or having to bring in external third parties. With MongoDB, you now get the benefits of OLTP database, vector search, and Voyage AI embedding models in one unified system, eliminating the need for multiple systems and messy data syncs.

Eliminates embedding mismatches with automation

The system automatically generates vector embeddings for text data during initial data sync when creating indexes, during document insertions and updates, and during query processing. Vector embeddings stay synchronized as underlying data changes, eliminating the risk of stale or mismatched embeddings.

Powered by state-of-the-art Voyage AI embedding models

Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search features state-of-the-art embedding models from Voyage AI, including voyage-4-large, voyage-4, voyage-4-lite and voyage-code-3. These models deliver industry-leading performance on retrieval benchmarks (such as RTEB) with multilingual support.

Optimized for performance and reliability

Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search eliminates the context window and rate-limiting headaches that plague direct API integrations. 

Through asynchronous dynamic batch processing that optimizes for maximum tokens per request allowed for a model, the system achieves optimal throughput during index creation - automatically adjusting batch sizes based on document shape and size. With built-in automatic retries and error handling, your embedding operations run reliably without blocking primary database operations. This production-ready infrastructure means you can ingest millions of documents without building complex MLOps pipelines or monitoring systems.

Future-proofs your AI applications 

With Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search, you can create indexes across multiple models and compare them side-by-side, making it simple to find the optimal price-performance for your use case. Model lifecycle management becomes effortless with automatic re-embedding capabilities when upgrading to newer, better-performing models. 

We know many users have delayed migrating from older embedding models precisely because of the complexity involved in re-embedding entire datasets across multiple services. Now transitioning to next-generation models requires no custom code or complex coordination across your data services, and you can compare the performance of different models on your own dataset.

Simplification for everyone

Automated Embedding in MongoDB simplifies vector search adoption, allowing Software Engineers, ML Engineers, and Data Scientists from large enterprises to startups to focus on building applications rather than managing embedding integrations. It provides a low-friction path to unlocking powerful AI-driven capabilities for a wide range of use cases, including:

  • Generative AI: Building RAG (retrieval augmented generation) systems.

  • E-commerce: Delivering personalized product recommendations.

  • Content management: Implementing robust semantic search capabilities.

  • Customer service: Creating sophisticated question-answering functionalities.

  • Data science: Professionals who need efficient ways to process large datasets and streamline the transition from prototyping with state-of-the-art models to production.

  • Migration path: Providing an easy migration path for existing text search users looking to upgrade to vector and hybrid search capabilities for improved relevance.

Reducing development overhead and speeding results

We invited a select number of customers across industries, including healthcare, financial services, transportation, and media, to test automated embedding and provide feedback during our private preview. These customers saw the massive benefits, including immediate performance enhancements and reduced overhead. Two preview customers had the following to say: 

"We deployed MongoDB’s automated embedding in vector search across our 40‑million‑document corpus, converting weeks of engineering into a low‑maintenance, production‑grade workflow that materially improved retrieval speed and relevance while reducing development overhead.”

—Ohad Levinkron-Fisch Vice President of R&D and AI MedINT Medical Intelligence

"Being able to drop MongoDB’s automated embedding into an in-flight, production-scale system and see immediate performance and simplicity gains is huge - and we’re thrilled to deepen our partnership with MongoDB, given how much of our stack already runs on MongoDB."

—Joe Marta Senior Director, Applied AI Coalfire

How to get started with the Public Preview

By automatically generating and synchronizing vector embeddings using Voyage AI models, Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search eliminates traditional vector search complexities. This secure and scalable solution is native to MongoDB, accelerating the creation of powerful AI-enabled applications and significantly improving the developer experience. 

Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search in Community Edition is available now, with MongoDB Atlas and MongoDB Vector Search in Enterprise Edition access coming soon. Use your favorite MongoDB language drivers (Python, JavaScript, Java, C#, and GoLang), AI frameworks like LangChain and LangGraph, and the MongoDB MCP server. 

Jump in with our quick start guide.

title: Implicit Assumptions About Tasks in Continual Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.41792v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Continual learning is the study of how a model accumulates knowledge from data received over time, rather than all at once. In practice, this is typically achieved by dividing a dataset into tasks and presenting them sequentially. Explanations of the resulting measurements take into account factors such as the similarity between segments, the rate at which the data changes and the order of presentation. Each of these factors can be defined in terms of the underlying data, the partition imposed on it, or the learner that encounters it. These levels do not necessarily coincide, and it is usually left implicit which level a reported quantity refers to. We separate these and identify which properties acquire a value at each level. In controlled teacher--student experiments, we demonstrate that partitioning the same underlying trajectory at different levels of granularity, changing the order of presentation, and varying the similarity structure of the underlying data all result in different measured outcomes. We review representative benchmarks to determine which of these properties are stated. Where the underlying data cannot be inspected, as in foundation models built on undisclosed pre-training corpora, its properties are inherited by the model's initial state, and the training applied on top of it can be described.

title: Kubernetes Controller Manager Explained | K8s With Pravesh - Episode 6
description:
Hola Amigos 👋

Welcome back to K8s-With-Pravesh!

After covering the Datastore of Kubernetes: etcd, we're going deep into what is popularly known as the "Autopilot" of the Kubernetes Control Plane: the Controller Manager.

We'll understand how it plays a crucial role in continuously reconciling the state of our cluster.

For those of you who are new here, I'm Pravesh, an AWS Community Builder and IBM Champion. In this series, we're dissecting all the important components of a Kubernetes cluster.

So, get your terminals ready, and let's dive right in!

What is Kubernetes Controller Manager?

The Kubernetes Controller Manager (kube-controller-manager) is a core component of the Control Plane that runs multiple built-in controllers within a single process.

Each controller has a specific responsibility, but they all follow a similar mechanism: they continuously watch the state of the cluster, and whenever the actual state differs from the desired state, they take action to bring things back in sync.

This process is popularly known as the Reconciliation Loop.

The reconciliation loop operates through three major steps:

  • Watch: Watches the API Server to get updates about the current state of the cluster.
  • Compare: Compares the actual state against the desired state defined in the YAML configuration (which is stored in etcd).
  • Act: If there is a mismatch (a "drift"), it takes action to correct it.

Let's take a simple example.

Imagine you have deployed an application with 3 replicas. Due to some reason, one of the Pods gets deleted.

Now the Controller Manager notices that the current state has only 2 Pods, whereas the desired state specifies 3.

What happens next?

The ReplicaSet Controller notices this mismatch and takes action to create another Pod.

And just like that, Kubernetes brings the cluster back to its desired state.

Pretty cool, right?

Different Types of Controllers

The Kube Controller Manager is not a single controller. It is actually a combination of multiple built-in controllers compiled together into a single binary to avoid the overhead of managing multiple independent processes.

Here are some of the most critical controllers:

  • Node Controller: Monitors node health and handles situations where a node stops responding.
  • ReplicaSet Controller: Ensures that the desired number of Pods keeps running at any given time.
  • Deployment Controller: Manages declarative updates for Deployments and ReplicaSets, including rolling out new versions and rolling back to previous ones.
  • EndpointSlice Controller: Maintains EndpointSlice objects that keep track of the Pods associated with a Service.
  • Service Account Controller: Automatically creates a default ServiceAccount for newly created namespaces.
  • Job Controller: Watches Job objects and manages the lifecycle of batch tasks, ensuring that they run to completion.

There are several other controllers as well, but these are some of the most commonly encountered ones.

What about Cloud Controller Manager?

If you're using Kubernetes on a cloud platform like AWS, GCP, or Azure, there's another interesting component called the Cloud Controller Manager.

It allows the core Kubernetes project to remain independent of cloud-provider-specific implementations while allowing cloud vendors to manage their own infrastructure integrations.

For example:

  • Cloud Load Balancers
  • Node routing
  • Underlying storage volumes

Unlike the built-in controllers running inside kube-controller-manager, the Cloud Controller Manager runs as a separate component.

Controller Manager vs Scheduler

It's very common to confuse these two components, but both have completely different responsibilities.

  • Controller Manager: Ensures that the required objects exist and that the actual state matches the desired state. For example, maintaining 3 replicas of a Deployment.
  • Scheduler: Decides where those unscheduled Pods should run. For example, assigning Pod A to Node 3 and Pod B to Node 2.

The Scheduler considers several factors during node selection, including available CPU, memory, resource requests, scheduling constraints, taints, and tolerations.

So, remember:

Controller Manager decides WHAT needs to happen, while Scheduler decides WHERE a Pod should run.

High Availability Architecture: Active-Passive

If you've watched the previous episode of this series, where we discussed the RAFT consensus algorithm for Active-Active quorum, things are going to be a little different here.

The Controller Manager uses an Active-Passive (or Leader-Standby) architecture for High Availability.

Here's how it works:

  • We can run 3 or more instances of kube-controller-manager on different Control Plane nodes for redundancy.
  • Only one instance will be designated as the Leader (Active) and will actively run the reconciliation loops.
  • The other instances remain in Standby (Passive) mode, waiting for the leader to fail so they can take over.

But how does Kubernetes decide who becomes the leader?

Well, here's where things get interesting.

Leader Election Using Kubernetes Leases

The Controller Manager uses a built-in Kubernetes resource called Lease to coordinate leader election.

Here's the process:

  • When the Control Plane starts, all instances of Controller Manager compete to acquire or update a specific Lease object in the kube-system namespace.
  • Out of all the instances, the one that successfully acquires the Lease becomes the leader.

(The winner takes it all! 😄)

  • The leader must continuously renew this Lease (by default, every 2 seconds) to prove that it is still alive.
  • If the leader node crashes or loses network connectivity, it fails to renew the Lease.
  • Once the Lease expires (the default lease duration is 15 seconds), another standby instance notices the vacancy and competes to acquire the Lease.

And just like that, a new leader is elected, and the process continues.

This is how Kubernetes maintains High Availability for the Controller Manager without allowing multiple instances to actively perform the same controller work under normal circumstances.

Performance Tuning: Handling Large Clusters

By default, the Controller Manager is configured with reasonable settings to balance CPU and memory consumption.

However, in a large cluster (probably hundreds of nodes and thousands of Pods), the default settings can sometimes cause reconciliation delays.

For example, imagine scaling a Deployment from 3 to 100 replicas, but it takes several seconds before the controllers start processing all the changes.

This is where performance tuning comes into the picture.

Kubernetes provides several flags to control the concurrency of different controllers.

Here are two examples:

  • --concurrent-deployment-syncs: Controls how many Deployment objects can be synchronized concurrently. By default, it is 5. Increasing this value can help speed up Deployment reconciliation in large clusters.

  • --concurrent-endpoint-syncs: Controls how many Service endpoint synchronization operations can run concurrently. This can be useful when dealing with frequent scaling operations in large clusters.

Of course, increasing concurrency isn't always the answer. More concurrent operations also mean more CPU, memory, and API Server load.

So, always monitor your cluster before changing these values.

Split-Brain Scenario

While Leader Election (which we discussed earlier) is excellent, network partitions can cause a scary scenario called Split-Brain.

Let's understand it with an example.

Imagine Controller Manager A is currently the leader.

Suddenly, the network splits, and Controller Manager A can no longer communicate with the API Server. As a result, it cannot renew its Lease.

Controller Manager B notices that the Lease has expired and takes over as the new leader.

However, Controller Manager A might still be alive and could potentially continue executing some operations based on its local state.

Now we have a problem: two instances potentially behaving like leaders.

How does Kubernetes protect against this?

One important mechanism is Optimistic Concurrency Control at the API Server level (something we touched upon in our previous episode).

Kubernetes resources have a resourceVersion, which helps detect conflicting updates.

If Controller Manager A tries to update an object using an outdated version, the API Server rejects that update with a conflict.

This helps prevent stale updates from overwriting newer cluster state.

It's important to understand that resource version checks are not a universal solution to every possible split-brain side effect. Leader election is the primary coordination mechanism, while optimistic concurrency provides an additional layer of protection for resource updates.

Enough Theory, Let's Get Our Hands Dirty!

Now let's open our terminals and see the Controller Manager doing its work in action.

The code and commands for today's practical demonstration are available in the GitHub repository of the K8s-with-Pravesh series.

Navigate to the part-06-CM directory, and you'll find everything you need.

1. Setting Up the Kubernetes Cluster

Before we dive in, we need a Kubernetes cluster.

For the sake of simplicity, let's use Minikube.

Make sure your Docker daemon is up and running, and spin up a Minikube cluster using the following command:

minikube start

If you don't have Minikube or Docker installed, head over to their official websites and install them according to your operating system and architecture.

2. Testing the Self-Healing Mechanism

Now let's see the self-healing feature of Kubernetes in action.

We'll create an Nginx Deployment with 3 replicas using the following command:

kubectl create deployment nginx-demo --image=nginx --replicas=3

Open a new terminal and run the following command to continuously watch the Pod lifecycle:

kubectl get pods -l app=nginx-demo -w

In another terminal, list the created Pods:

kubectl get pods

Now, copy the name of one of the Pods and delete it:

kubectl delete pod <Pod-name>

Switch back to the terminal where we're watching the Pod lifecycle.

You'll notice something interesting.

The moment the Pod gets terminated, Kubernetes notices that the desired number of replicas is no longer being maintained.

Within a few seconds, another Pod is created!

That's the Reconciliation Loop in action.

The ReplicaSet Controller noticed the mismatch and took action to bring the cluster back to its desired state.

Once the practical demo is done, make sure to delete the Deployment:

kubectl delete deployment nginx-demo

3. Inspecting Controller Manager Leader Election

Now let's explore something more interesting: Leader Election using Kubernetes Leases.

We can inspect the Lease objects using the following command:

kubectl get leases -n kube-system

For a more detailed YAML output:

kubectl get leases -n kube-system -o yaml

If you're using a multi-Control-Plane architecture, you can specifically inspect the Controller Manager Lease:

kubectl get lease kube-controller-manager -n kube-system -o yaml

Look for the holderIdentity field.

This field tells us which instance currently holds the Lease.

We can also continuously watch the Lease:

kubectl get lease kube-controller-manager -n kube-system -w

In a multi-Control-Plane setup, you can observe the Lease changing when leadership transfers to another instance.

A small catch with Minikube:

Since we're using a single-node Minikube cluster, it generally runs only one Controller Manager instance. So, we can inspect the Lease mechanism, but we cannot properly demonstrate an actual leader takeover using this setup.

For that, you'll need a multi-Control-Plane Kubernetes cluster with multiple Controller Manager instances.

Once you're done with the experiments, make sure to delete your cluster:

minikube delete

What About Custom Controllers and Operators?

After going through all of this, you might have another question:

"If the Controller Manager already has so many built-in controllers, how do custom operators like Prometheus Operator or cert-manager work?"

Great question!

The built-in controllers are compiled into the Kubernetes Controller Manager binary. We cannot simply add our own controller code to that existing process without modifying and rebuilding it.

But Kubernetes provides a way to extend its functionality using Custom Operators.

These operators run as separate workloads (usually Pods) inside the cluster.

They follow the exact same Reconciliation Loop pattern that we discussed earlier, but instead of only watching core Kubernetes resources, they can watch Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) and manage the resources associated with them.

This is one of the most powerful features of Kubernetes because it allows developers to extend Kubernetes with their own custom automation.

Conclusion

And that's the end of our deep dive into the Kubernetes Controller Manager!

Today, we explored its functionalities, different built-in controllers, how Lease-based Leader Election works, how Kubernetes handles conflicting updates, and finally, we got our hands dirty with a small practical demonstration.

But the journey is not over yet!

We've covered etcd, the Controller Manager, and the API Server. Now it's time to explore another important component of the Control Plane.

In the next episode, we'll dive into the Kubernetes Scheduler and see what actually happens behind the scenes when Kubernetes decides where to run our Pods.

If you enjoyed this blog, make sure to follow me on my socials. I regularly share my DevOps experiments, Kubernetes learnings, and cloud projects there.

Until then, keep learning, keep experimenting!

title: Muse Spark 1.3 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Muse Spark 1.3 from Meta is now available on AI Gateway, in both the standard and contributor pricing tiers.

This model improves on prior Muse Spark models at agent work and coding, with a 1M token context window and text, image, and PDF input. On coding it takes fewer turns and writes less filler than the previous release.

To use Muse Spark 1.3, set model to meta/muse-spark-1.3:

Contributor tier

Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor is a pricing tier on the same model rather than a separate one, with the same weights, capabilities, and context window. The difference is that Meta uses the inputs and outputs sent to this tier to train and improve its models, and pricing is lower in exchange.
